## [Upcoming ROS 1 End of Life](https://www.ros.org/blog/noetic-eol/)

### 12/16/2024, Kat Scott

## ROS 1 Noetic Ninjemys goes End-of-Life 2025-05-31

If you have been directed to this page it was probably because you saw one of the notifications we slipped into the source code for ROS Noetic or RViz. We’ve heard from a number of users that they were unaware that ROS 1 Noetic, and consequently all of 1, [will go end-of-life on **May 31st, 2025**](https://wiki.ros.org/Distributions). We’re sorry that we interrupted your work, but it is crucial that you know what happens once ROS 1 goes end-of-life.

ROS Noetic Ninjemys, the [last ROS 1 release](https://www.openrobotics.org/blog/2020/5/23/noetic-ninjemys-the-last-official-ros-1-release), will reach End of Life in May 2025. Over the past five years we focused our efforts on making ROS 2 a world class framework for professional robot development, and our user community seems to agree. author: Raspberry Pi

Our friends over at  iroh  have developed some really clever software that enables your devices, apps, and cloud instances to form a secure and reliable mesh network via IP-based network links, such as cellular and Wi-Fi, as well as non-IP based networks like Bluetooth-LE and LoRa.

article_content:
Setting up reliable mesh networks can be tricky. Our friends over at  iroh  have developed some really clever software that enables your devices, apps, and cloud instances to form a secure and reliable mesh network via IP-based network links, such as cellular and Wi-Fi, as well as non-IP based networks like Bluetooth-LE and LoRa.

What is iroh?

iroh  is a modular networking stack written in Rust. It provides the building blocks to create applications that can communicate using fast, cheap, and reliable connections. It’s a lightweight native library meant to be embedded directly into your application.

The team at iroh has ported their Rust-based stack to our nifty  RP2350 microcontroller  and are  showing it off  on Pimoroni’s  Presto  product using Wi-Fi as the networking interface.

Rear view of the Raspberry Pi–powered Pimoroni Presto

We think this is a fantastic development, and we’re excited to see what mesh systems customers will build with Raspberry Pi and iroh.

Raspberry Pi Radio Module 2

Last year, we launched our first standalone Wi-Fi and Bluetooth radio module.  Raspberry Pi Radio Module 2  was designed for use with Raspberry Pi microcontrollers and packages the same Infineon CYW43439 radio used on  Raspberry Pi Pico W  and  Pico 2 W , making it an ideal choice for  RP2040 – and  RP2350 -based products that require turnkey wireless connectivity.

Our teeny-tiny Radio Module 2

RP2350, our secure, high-performance microcontroller, pairs very well with Raspberry Pi Radio Module 2 — using them together allows you to add affordable yet performant real-time compute and connectivity to your products, which  Raspberry Pi Approved Reseller  Pimoroni figured out when they created the Presto desktop companion used in iroh’s own demo!

Rüdiger Klaehn’s  excellent blog post  explains the engineering process and clever workarounds used to make the iroh networking library run natively on a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 without Wi-Fi, as well as on the aforementioned Pimoroni Presto with Wi-Fi and a touchscreen display. You can dig deeper into the codebase or try the implementation yourself by checking out the  iroh-pico-examples repository on GitHub .

The post  iroh comes to our RP2350 microcontroller  appeared first on  Raspberry Pi .

article_content:
Done right, product compliance opens up new markets and sets your product apart. Done wrong, it can mean lost sales, destroyed stock, and fines. In the latest episode of the  Raspberry Pi Podcast , Alex Branton, Global Market Access Lead at Raspberry Pi, talks to Tom Westcott, who leads product compliance, about how Raspberry Pi helps industrial customers bring fully compliant products to market faster.

Listen now wherever you get your podcasts, or watch as the words emerge from real humans on YouTube

Together, they cover what product compliance actually means and how testing works, from Raspberry Pi’s in-house 3-metre RF anechoic chamber to formal testing at UKAS-accredited labs. Tom explains the extra testing Raspberry Pi carries out, including shock and vibration tests, thermal modelling, reliability studies, UV-accelerated weathering, and XRF material analysis. They also explain how to find declarations of conformity, FCC approvals, and test reports on the Raspberry Pi Product Information Portal (PIP), and how to subscribe to receive product change notifications (PCNs).

The discussion also covers Raspberry Pi’s Global Market Access (GMA) service — which handles country-specific approvals on your behalf — and the support available at each stage of the design cycle.

Find everything you need on our Product Information Portal

All our certificates, declarations of conformity, and test reports are on our  Product Information Portal , where you can browse and download documents and notices for all Raspberry Pi products. You can also subscribe to receive product change notifications. If you need approvals in a new country, our  Global Market Access service  can get them for you.

Connecting you with the right designers

Our network of approved  Design Partners  can help take your idea from concept to market. Countless businesses use Raspberry Pi to jump-start the design process of their products, and to build in proven, powerful computing. If you have an idea or a product and need a design partner to help you integrate Raspberry Pi technology, we can connect you with designers who can help.

From the cutting-room floor

One of our hosts tells the story of the only other time he’s been on camera: a health and safety video about hard hats, in which he held his newborn daughter next to the actor who played Harry Potter’s dad. Spoiler alert: just like James Potter, his character doesn’t meet a pleasant end…

In another outtake, the hosts accidentally mess with the visual continuity of the episode.

Request a podcast topic and subscribe

What would you like to listen to next? Leave us a comment requesting a topic and we’ll try to lure the appropriate Pi Towers-dweller behind the microphone for you.

Subscribe to the Raspberry Pi Podcast on  Spotify ,  Amazon , or  Apple  podcasts. We’ll also be releasing each episode on our  YouTube channel , where you can watch for free. (Here’s  a handy RSS feed  for those asking!)

The post  Product compliance, demystified: how Raspberry Pi helps you get to market  appeared first on  Raspberry Pi .

title: Price rises for some 16GB Raspberry Pi products
author: Raspberry Pi
description: Frequent readers of the blog will know that we have had to make selective price increases on the products most affected by the  steep rises in the cost of memory  over the past two years. Other businesses in the sector have had to do likewise, and we continue to do everything we can to minimise the costs passed on to our customers, including qualifying alternative parts to give us more flexibility in sourcing. Unfortunately, a lack of alternative  supply for 16GB DRAM, compounded by other ongoin...
article_content:
Frequent readers of the blog will know that we have had to make selective price increases on the products most affected by the  steep rises in the cost of memory  over the past two years. Other businesses in the sector have had to do likewise, and we continue to do everything we can to minimise the costs passed on to our customers, including qualifying alternative parts to give us more flexibility in sourcing. Unfortunately, a lack of alternative  supply for 16GB DRAM, compounded by other ongoing component shortages, means we now need to make further price increases on some of our highest-density products.

From today, we are raising the price of the  16GB variant of Raspberry Pi 5  by $80, to $385. The 16GB Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5 variants are increasing in price by $40, and updated prices for these can be found in the product brief on the  Compute Module 5 product page . As with previous price rises, we have avoided making blanket increases across the entire product line, and we are holding the price of  Raspberry Pi 500+ , our premium all-in-one desktop computer built into a mechanical keyboard, which also features 16GB of RAM.

Though these increases are unavoidable, we know they are unwelcome news for our customers. We encourage you to make sure you’re not paying for more memory than you need; integrating lower-density variants or earlier Raspberry Pi models into your projects, or making memory optimisations in your applications, are among ways you can ensure you have the memory your use case needs at the lowest possible cost. Individual customers can check out  Raspberry Pi Official Magazine ’s  guidance on how to make the most of your memory , or ask other users for advice over on the  Raspberry Pi forums . (You can often find our engineers responding to enquiries on the forums, too.) Business customers can get in touch to discuss memory optimisation at industry@raspberrypi.com.

We are holding the price of Raspberry Pi 500+, our premium desktop computer

We’re aware that a few bad actors have been taking advantage of the current memory supply circumstances to sell Raspberry Pi products at inflated prices or shift products that aren’t what they seem. All of our products are available to buy at our official prices through our trusted global network of Raspberry Pi Approved Resellers. If in doubt, find your nearest vetted supplier on our  Approved Reseller page .

As we’ve said from the beginning, the current memory landscape is difficult but ultimately temporary, and we look forward to rolling back our price increases when memory costs fall once again.

The post  Price rises for some 16GB Raspberry Pi products  appeared first on  Raspberry Pi .

article_content:
Spooky season is upon us, so it seems only fitting to share with you a Halloween-themed project that I’ve been working on at home. Inspired by videos of self-playing chessboards driven by magnets beneath the board, I decided to apply the same approach to creating a Ouija board that spells out messages without the touch of human hands.

The build

The first step in the project was to create a lightweight core XY CNC machine. For this I drafted in my husband, and he was able to put something together within a couple of days using 3D-printed parts, fishing line, some motors, and an ESP32 that he had lying around.

(The core XY he built for this project turned out so well that he used what he learnt to make a slightly beefier version as the basis for a CNC plasma cutter.)

He also put together a wooden enclosure made of plywood and moulding, which he then turned over to me for decoration. A bit of wood stain and gold spray paint brought it a little closer in style to the golden age of Spiritualism.

After determining how much of the box’s surface the planchette could cover, I made a stencil to apply the letters to that area. That left a lot of blank space on the surface where, inside the box underneath, space was taken up by the axes and electronics. A few painted flower and skull motifs filled those gaps.

A big challenge was making sure that the magnets got enough grip on the planchette to move it over the board’s surface. It was a fairly heavy piece of wood with a large surface area, and hence caused a fair amount of friction. So, we added more magnets to both the planchette and the CNC head. We also added springs to the mechanism holding the magnets beneath the board to ensure the magnets were always pressed against the underside of the board with no gaps. Eventually, we embedded some free-spinning ball bearings in the bottom of the planchette for it to run on. That did the trick.

The software

We recently freed up a  Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+  that had faithfully served as a print server for many years. What better new life — or rather, afterlife — for it than to become the ghost in the machine controlling my Ouija board?

I used Raspberry Pi Imager to install Raspberry Pi OS Trixie and configure Raspberry Pi Connect on the device. I knew Connect would be very useful, as I would be moving the Ouija board from network to network, which changes its IP address each time; to access the web UI I planned on using to control it, I needed to know its current IP address. Raspberry Pi Connect enabled me to easily log in to the Raspberry Pi whenever it was online and find out its IP address.

The Ouija-specific software is a Python Flask project. It takes words typed into a web UI and converts those to G-code instructions that match the letter locations. Then it sends the G-code directly through the USB serial port to the ESP32, which drives the motors. I tasked my husband with this and he delegated it to ChatGPT Codex.

Then came the most time-consuming part: mapping out the G-code coordinates of all the letters and words on the board and adding them to a JSON file to be read by the app.

Last but not least, I played around with the CSS of the web UI to match the design of the box.

What’s next?

The current iteration of the Ouija board relies on a human listening to the questions being asked and typing a response into the web UI. The next improvement might be to incorporate a microphone and an AI model that parses the question and puts together a short response (perhaps based on some ghost character information provided for it to work from).

If I decide to go all out on my pseudo-séance, I could even build a crystal ball that creates a Pepper’s ghost illusion, or tap into my smart home automation to flicker the lights!

The post  OuijaCNC  appeared first on  Raspberry Pi .

article_content:
Who knew that the humble launderette is having a moment as a social space to hang out with friends? According to  Korea Laundry , the washateria is an increasingly desirable destination, with lifestyle branding alongside turn-up-and-wash convenience. Another company mixing things up its own way is Sweden’s  Elk Audio , which lets audiophiles have free rein over almost every aspect of their mixes, including almost every hardware element – Raspberry Pi 4 and Compute Modules among them. Yet more choice comes from  Handlet , which gives you the option to run one of its Raspberry Pi-based tablets off a built-in battery and also offers customisations galore.

Beebot OS is an intelligent management and payment system for unattended kiosks such as self-service laundries

These three examples illustrate the flexibility of Raspberry Pi hardware and how readily Raspberry Pi has been adopted by both industrial and consumer clients, as well as how the market for high-quality Raspberry Pi products has gone global. 

“From Stockholm to Sydney, South Korea to Slovakia.”

This showcase of  Powered by Raspberry Pi  products features innovations from Stockholm to Sydney, South Korea to Slovakia. Although prototyping and iterating can be relatively cost-effective, once you have a marketable product, there are compliance testing hoops to jump through. Raspberry Pi introduced  Powered by Raspberry Pi  accreditation to help manufacturers with this process, standardising compliance regulations and testing procedures for every Raspberry Pi. This info can be found at the  Production Information Portal . Accreditation is also a visual and visible mark of quality and rigour that helps manufacturers stand out from other brands and helps give customers confidence.

Horace 2 photo booth

France  | rpimag.co/horace-photobooth

The Horace photo booth is an excellent addition to any party or social occasion. Featuring two Raspberry Pi High Quality Cameras, the booth comes in 1.5m- and 85cm-tall versions, meaning there are options for adults and smaller photo fans, as well as wheelchair-using partygoers. Raspberry Pi 5 and Node-RED control everything inside the booth and provide a live 2K video stream of what the cameras can see. The photo booth’s dye-sublimation printer produces Instagramable prints in less than 30 seconds. The whole setup weighs 35kg and can be folded flat for easy transportation. It has been incredibly well received in France, where Horace is based and where customers can hire him for special events along with a fun selection of photo backdrops. 

Elk Audio

Sweden  | rpimag.co/elk-audio

Stockholm-based Elk Audio describes Raspberry Pi as “the go-to platform for prototyping and experimentation”. Thanks! We are also rather taken with the firm’s 8GB Raspberry Pi 4-based audio endeavours. Raspberry Pi 4 was chosen for its quad-core processing power, efficiency, and scalability. Elk’s low-latency DSP (digital signal processing) platform offers multichannel audio inputs and outputs, synthesis engines, samples, and effects. Audio nerds have the option of accessing the source code and playing around with absolutely everything, or choosing a reference design such as Nina, a twelve-voice motorised analogue polysynth. Elk offers a Raspberry Pi development board, Compute Module system on module, and the Stomp dev kit, giving audiophiles complete freedom over how to explore sound. 

YUMA-X-FCC

Germany  | rpimag.co/yuma-products

YUMA Engineering specialises in embedded technology, particularly aerospace computing. The company’s precise engineering and creative thinking result in mission-ready hardware and software that can be used despite real-world uncertainties. Its YUMA-X-FCC airborne Linux-based computing platform features highly embedded, scalable AI and machine learning that’s controlled, of course, by Raspberry Pi. The non-TSO (technical standard order) avionics platform is ideal for rapid prototyping. It features dual u-blox GPS with dead reckoning, 3D accelerometer, magnetometer, and gyroscope, and a barometer, along with a 5G/LTE modem, wireless LAN and two Gigabit Ethernet ports. This can be used alongside other smart components as an autopilot, for real-time moving digital maps, as a flight data recorder, jet engine recorder, or visual navigation and landing aid. 

Handlet

Finland  | rpimag.co/handlet

Handlet is a 5-inch battery-powered Raspberry Pi computer. As you may guess, the Assembled model works straight out of the box, but there is another option, the build-it-yourself Hobbyist version

( rpimag.co/handlet-5 ) Equipped with Raspberry Pi 4 with 2GB RAM, the base version is priced competitively enough to attract schools and hobbyists keen to use it for mobile projects. Handlet includes a ruggedised VESA-mountable case with easy access to the microSD card slot, speaker, and 40-pin GPIO port. Customisation options include a choice of touchscreen covers and cases to provide protection, as well as speaker and buttons that boost the Handlet’s entertainment credentials. 

Korea Laundry

South Korea  | rpimag.co/beebot

Beebot OS is an intelligent management and payment system for unattended kiosks such as self-service laundries. It has become synonymous with its origins in the Korea Laundry Co. and its hundreds of WashEnjoy lounges. The complete management system – based on Raspberry Pi and IoT capabilities – toggles each washing machine on and off, recognises and updates members’ cards, takes one-off payments, and manages account top-ups. Raspberry Pi tracks each laundry site’s performance figures, providing details to Korea Laundry’s centralised network about each commercial washer’s and dryer’s operational status. Screens embedded in each kiosk can display offers and marketing information, providing added value via the Beebot 360 Manager software. This aspect is becoming increasingly important as there is built-in downtime at launderettes and Korea Laundry boasts a revisit rate of at least 80% at what it terms “a unique lifestyle space” with leisure and marketing potential. 

System-IS STL.one

Slovakia  | rpimag.co/stl-one

Showing up is half the battle for some of us! If it’s your role to keep tabs on everyone’s comings and goings,

STL.one makes things much simpler. The check-in terminal is a 240 × 165mm, 8-inch touchscreen with a built-in card reader, running your favourite embedded computer and Fenix remote management software. Colleagues log themselves as present at meetings, events, and in specific rooms or zones using attendance cards or tags. A webcam checks that individuals are registering themselves as present, ensuring accurate attendance figures. The system not only monitors and summarises attendance; it also prepares a monthly report for managers.

title: Emulate Apple II on Raspberry Pi
author: Raspberry Pi
description:
It’s the last  Maker Monday  before Halloween and we still don’t have a costume sorted, so instead, we’re going to follow this treat of a tutorial from   The Raspberry Pi Guide to Retro Gaming   to disguise our Raspberry Pi as the classic 8-bit Apple II   computer  .

article_content:
It’s the last  Maker Monday  before Halloween and we still don’t have a costume sorted, so instead, we’re going to follow this treat of a tutorial from   The Raspberry Pi Guide to Retro Gaming   to disguise our Raspberry Pi as the classic 8-bit Apple II   computer  .

The  Apple II  was not the first personal or home computer, but it was part of the iconic ‘trinity’ of computers that came out in 1977: Apple II,  Commodore PET , and  TRS-80 . The Apple II wasn’t as capable a gaming computer as some of the other 8-bit systems of the era, but it was designed with games in mind. In designing the Apple II, Steve Wozniak took inspiration from his work on the Breakout arcade game during his time at Atari. It’s why the Apple II has colour graphics, support for paddle controllers, and even audio.

Playing a piece of computing history!

(10 points to anyone who can tell us what this is in the comments)

Apple II audio was quite limited: anything more complex than a beep was quite CPU-intensive. Add-on audio boards, such as the Mockingboard, became popular and enjoyed support from a number of game developers.

The Apple II included a version of the BASIC language that only supported integer numeric data types: by eschewing floating-point numbers, Wozniak’s Integer BASIC, as it was called, processed numbers extremely fast. This made it less than ideal for certain programming tasks, but it was fantastic for video games. Integer BASIC was supplied in the system ROM image of the Apple II, while a more full-featured BASIC, Applesoft BASIC, was originally supplied on cassette tape (it would be baked into the system ROM beginning with the Apple II Plus, though).

Install an Apple II emulator

For Apple II emulation on Raspberry Pi, we are using the  LinApple emulator . It’s a fork of the AppleWin emulator which was originally created by Mike O’Brien. David Baucum (maxolasersquad) and several other contributors got it running on Linux. You may also want to have a look at audetto’s fork of the  AppleWin emulator . Because audetto’s fork is regularly synchronised with the original AppleWin GitHub repository, it tracks AppleWin features more closely.

LinApple can emulate Apple II sound cards such as the Mockingboard (enabled by default in the configuration file). LinApple is not available through the Raspberry Pi OS apt repository, so you’ll need to compile it yourself. Fortunately, it’s quite easy to do this. First, open a Terminal window. This is where you’ll install dependencies, download the source code, and compile, then install it.

In the Terminal window, run these commands to update your operating system packages and to install the dependencies needed to compile LinApple. You may be prompted for your password when you run the commands that use sudo. 

$ sudo apt update

$ sudo apt -y full-upgrade

$ sudo apt -y install git g++ cmake

libzip-dev libsdl3-dev libsdl3-image-dev libcurl4-openssl-dev zlib1g-dev imagemagick

Now you’re ready to clone the emulator repository. If you’d prefer not to check the source code out into the root of your home directory, create a directory and change into it before you clone it. For example,  mkdir ~/src  would create a  src  directory under your home directory, and  cd ~/src  would change into it. You can clone the repository with this command:

$ git clone

https://github.com/linappleii/linapple.git

After you’ve cloned it,  cd  into the  linapple  folder and build the project:

$ cd linapple

$ cmake -B build -DBUILD_TESTING=OFF

$ cmake --build build -j4

The first  cmake  command prepares the source code, and the second compiles it. The  -j4  argument tells cmake to use as many as four CPU cores. Once it’s compiled successfully, install it under the  /usr/local  folder with:

$ sudo cmake --install build

Now you can run the emulator from any Terminal window with the command  linapple . But before you do that, let’s customise some options. First, copy the default configuration file and sample disk image to your home directory. You’ll need to create a couple of directories before you copy files into them:

$ mkdir -p ~/.config/linapple/

$ cp /usr/local/etc/linapple/linapple.conf ~/.config/linapple/

$ mkdir -p ~/.linapple/disks/

$ cp /usr/local/share/linapple/Master.dsk ~/.linapple/disks/

Next, edit your configuration file with your favourite editor, for example using  nano ~/.config/linapple/linapple.conf , and make these changes:

Find the entry that reads  Joystick 0 = 2  and change  2  to  4 . This lets you use your mouse as a joystick, which you’ll either love or hate (give it a try in Brickout later in the article!). The configuration file describes the other options you can choose.

Locate the  Screen factor = 1.0  entry and change  1.0  to  2.5 . This will make the emulator window a bit bigger.

Save the config file and exit your editor. If you’re using the nano editor, press  CTRL+X , answer  Y  for yes, then press  ENTER  to confirm the file name. Let’s test LinApple and make sure everything is working. In the Terminal window, run the following command:

$ linapple --autoboot --d1

~/.linapple/disks/Master.dsk

LinApple should open and display the screen shown in  Figure 1 . If you find that the emulator has taken over control of your mouse, press  F1  to release it (this will display the help screen, but you can press  F1  again to turn it off). You can toggle full-screen mode with the  F6  key.

Figure 1:  LinApple is up and running

Here’s a little BASIC program you can try running. You can either type it into the emulator, or you can find the program in the  ch03/AppleIIBasicPrograms.dsk  file in the  GitHub repository . To use the disk image, launch the emulator with  linapple --autoboot --d1 AppleIIBasicPrograms.dsk , type  LOAD BLOCKMOVE  at the  ]  prompt and press  ENTER , then type  RUN  (and press  ENTER ).

10 HGR

20 X = 140: Y = 80: D = 3: REM INITIALISE

30 HCOLOR = 3: GOSUB 1000: REM DRAW CUBE

40 REM WAIT FOR AND READ KEYPRESS

50 K = PEEK (- 16384): IF K < 128 THEN 40

60 REM CLEAR STROBE

70 POKE - 16368, 0: K$ = CHR$ (K - 128)

80 HCOLOR = 0: GOSUB 1000: REM ERASE CUBE

90 IF K$ = "W" THEN Y = Y - D

100 IF K$ = "S" THEN Y = Y + D

110 IF K$ = "A" THEN X = X - D

120 IF K$ = "D" THEN X = X + D

130 IF X < 0 THEN X = 0

140 IF X > 272 THEN X = 272

150 IF Y < 0 THEN Y = 0

160 IF Y > 184 THEN Y = 184

170 GOTO 30 : REM BACK TO TOP OF LOOP

1000 REM DRAW CUBE IN CURRENT HCOLOR

1010 HPLOT X, Y TO X + 8, Y TO X + 8, Y + 8 TO X, Y + 8 TO X, Y

1020 RETURN

This will draw a small square on screen. Use the  W ,  A ,  S , and  D  keys to move it around the screen. The program is quite simple. It first defines the starting X and Y position, as well as the number of pixels the square should move each time (the variable D). After that, it sets the drawing colour to 3 and calls the subroutine to draw the cube. The program then waits for a key press, and when it has a key press, it clears the  keyboard strobe , which is a bit of hardware that indicates when a key press has been read.

After that, the program converts the integer key press value ( K ) into a string ( K$ ) that contains the character typed. From there, it updates the X and Y position, makes sure the square hasn’t run off-screen, and returns to the top of the loop (line 30).

Figure 2:  Moving a simple object around your screen

After you type in the program, type  RUN  followed by  ENTER . Try moving the square with the  WASD  keys, and press  CTRL+C  when you’re done to exit the program.  Figure 2  shows the program in action. Notice that the vertical and horizontal lines are different colours, and that the vertical lines change colour as you move. This is due to the way Apple II graphics work: the Apple II only generates a monochrome display signal, but it uses some signalling tricks to generate colour artefacts. Game programmers could manipulate these artefacts to create colour combinations they wanted.

After you run a graphical program, you’ll only have a small text area below the graphics mode portion of the emulator screen. You can type the  TEXT  command and press  ENTER  to return to text-only mode. You’ll also find these commands helpful:

LIST  — lists all the lines of the current BASIC program.

RUN  — runs the current program.

NEW  — erases the current program and lets you start afresh.

CATALOG  — lists all files on the disk image.

SAVE NAME  — saves the current BASIC program under whatever file name you specify.

LOAD NAME  — loads the program with the specified file name.

CTRL+C  — use this key combination to stop a running BASIC program.

Apart from  CATALOG , these commands only apply to BASIC programs. Many games are binary executable files that don’t include BASIC source.

You can find some fun type-in programs in  Lee Fastenau’s collection of short programs . Lee’s programs are intentionally dense, as most are designed to be entered on one or two lines of code. So, take your time typing them in!

Read more like this in  The Raspberry Pi Guide to Retro Gaming

This tutorial is part of a series of emulation guides in   The Raspberry Pi Guide to Retro Gaming   — a definitive guide on how to play your favourite games of yesteryear on a Raspberry Pi. You can also find it in the latest issue of   Raspberry Pi Official Magazine  .

You can buy a print edition of  The Raspberry Pi Guide to Retro Gaming  for an introductory price of £9.99 from  Raspberry Pi Press , or wherever else books are sold. Contributors can access a  free e-book version .

title: Recreate the Apollo Guidance Computer
author: Raspberry Pi
description:
While the latest issue of   Raspberry Pi Official Magazine   is a weather-monitoring projects special, we couldn’t resist sharing this build, as we are powerless in the face of anything space-themed. The maker, Michael Newton, is a commercial aircraft avionics engineer based in Calgary, Alberta  .   When he’s not on the flight line, he’s learning about and recreating historical aircraft and spacecraft hardware using modern technology and techniques.

In 1966, three years before Neil Armstro...
article_content:
While the latest issue of   Raspberry Pi Official Magazine   is a weather-monitoring projects special, we couldn’t resist sharing this build, as we are powerless in the face of anything space-themed. The maker, Michael Newton, is a commercial aircraft avionics engineer based in Calgary, Alberta  .   When he’s not on the flight line, he’s learning about and recreating historical aircraft and spacecraft hardware using modern technology and techniques.

In 1966, three years before Neil Armstrong became the first human to set foot on the Moon, the Charles Stark Draper Laboratory at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology introduced the Apollo Guidance Computer (AGC). Installed on board each Apollo Command Module and Lunar Module, its power was on a par with the Apple II computer with less than 100kB of memory and a clock speed of 1.024MHz. Yet, as Michael Newton points out, it allowed astronauts to execute navigation routines, autopilot manoeuvres, burns, orbital rendezvous, and Earth entry from their spacecraft. It was also the first computer to be based on silicon integrated circuits.

The case is designed to be as faithful as possible to the original and looks like it came straight from the spaceship

Michael is an engineer who is passionate about building historical spacecraft hardware using modern technology and techniques and he’s been leading an open source project called Recreate Apollo. It uses a Raspberry Pi computer running the Virtual AGC emulator to power a 1:1 scale 3D-printed DSKY – the Display and Keyboard used by Apollo astronauts. Specifically running the Apollo 13 Command Module software, it grants anyone the chance to get hands-on with a piece of computing and space history.

“My interest in the project began many years ago when, during the COVID-19 pandemic, a group of Apollo enthusiasts began translating the original MIT Instrumentation Lab engineering documents into modern-day CAD files with the eventual goal of 3D printing,” Michael says. The documents had been made available following a public records request and they were archived by the Virtual AGC group.

Michael has built his DSKY as a prototype for an improved version, but all the printed parts are modelled on archived NASA drawings

“I lost touch with most of their progress as life carried on, but about a year ago I came across another maker named Eric who runs a blog called   mkme.org   and I saw that he had created a DSKY based off of the now nearly-completed drawings uploaded on GitHub. Unsure where he sourced his files, I went on the hunt for them myself. I found many in different GitHub repos or other open-source projects, but other parts needed some work to refine and some others still I had to model on my own. After a few weeks of work, I had a full set of .stp files ready to print that I was satisfied with. I purchased a 3D printer and began learning that world.”

Lift off

Michael began learning as he went along, identifying three main tasks. First, he would print, finish, and paint the case. Then he would organise and wire the hardware. He also needed to write the code and software. “I tackled each part of the project over a few months, in that order, taking my time and learning as I went along,” he says. “But one of my biggest goals for this project was documentation. I wanted anyone who is interested to be able to build one of these, even those with no prior knowledge. My guide, available on GitHub, is the fruit of those labours.”

Driven by his love for the Apollo mission and the AGC, he wanted to be as faithful to the original as possible. “Physically, the DSKY is about 90% authentic,” he says. “From the outside, I strived for a perfect visual representation and I’m satisfied where it’s at.” Michael had to make adjustments internally, changing the mounting points for the microcontrollers and the Raspberry Pi computer.

All of the CAD models, schematics, and a 100-page build guide are free to use and view on GitHub

“I also needed to get a bit creative with the screen mounting, since the PCB that the screen mounts on is physically larger than the part designed to hold the original,” he says. “I modelled a clip-style holder for the screen and made a few minuscule adjustments to get the fit down perfect. The keycaps were also made a bit differently than the originals, since the lettering was too small for me to print with great definition. Even though the font matches the historical one (yes, someone recreated the font!), the words are just a bit larger.”

Rocket science

A Raspberry Pi computer felt like a perfect fit. “It is nearly purpose-built for this project,” Michael says. “It integrates through microcontrollers via USB, it doesn’t need a lot of power, it has wireless LAN built in for SSH and remote applications, and it also runs cool. Raspberry Pi OS is very easy to install, too, and you can create a custom distribution to send an entire OS instance to other users, which makes that section of the build easy to copy.”

More than that, however, Raspberry Pi easily runs yaAGC, VirtualAGC’s computer program that replicates every characteristic of the real AGC. “This includes the unique asynchronous timing (interrupt) that saved Apollo 11 (1201/1202 alarm codes), the 15-bit-plus-one-parity word length, and the archaically slow 1.024MHz clock speed,” Michael says.

This is the original Apollo Guidance Computer with the DSKY as used on Apollo spacecraft.

Source:  Wikipedia

The data used by the AGC is fundamentally different from how all modern computers are engineered. The individual 1s and 0s are arranged as a 15-bit data block with a single parity bit used for error checking. Michael says the emulation proved extremely difficult to achieve. But the programmers managed to emulate the AGC with the exact same logic, using the same timing, as the original.

“Fundamentally, the exact same constraints are preserved in this emulation because the timing of the AGC is kept intact and the memory that the computer reads is virtualisation of the real code that was woven into core rope ROM and magnetised in the RAM,” Michael explains. “In fact, it emulates the real computer so well that, to me, VirtualAGC is not an emulator. It’s a real Apollo Guidance Computer that borrows your processor.”

Great minds

The result is an amazing, fully usable device, one that allows users to interact using a keypad. For this, Michael used off-the-shelf mechanical keys with the highest actuation force and most solid ‘click’ he could find. “I settled on Kailh Box Navy,” Michael says. “They feel and sound OK, and they are easy to get, but they are far from the real keypad.” He’s currently looking to create a much more premium DSKY with a full aluminium body, better annunciators, and maybe a real electroluminescent display. This, he says, would incorporate a better keypad.

There is also an option to switch to a ‘peripheral’ mode by long-pressing one of the keys. This allows the DSKY to be used over a local network with Project Apollo – NASSP, an add-on for the Orbiter space flight simulator released on the PC, which simulates all of the Apollo missions

As it is, however, the Recreate Apollo project has allowed Michael and others to learn much more about the AGC. He says the ingenuity of those behind the original computer is clear. “The memory alone was an ingenious design of magnetism and did you know that the Apollo Guidance Computer used only ONE type of logic gate: the 3-input NOR? All the mathematics, data movement, navigation, autopiloting, burns – everything, was just voltage levels going through 3-input-NORs, and the occasional diode arrangement. Truly incredible minds were necessary to design that kind of thing.” 

Issue 171 of  Raspberry Pi Official Magazine  is out NOW!

This article appeared in  issue 171  of  Raspberry Pi Official Magazine , which you can  access online . You can also  subscribe  to the print version of our magazine. Not only do we deliver worldwide, but those who sign up to the six- or twelve-month print subscription will receive a FREE  Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W !

You can find  Raspberry Pi Official Magazine  on  Facebook ,  X ,  Threads ,  LinkedIn , and  Mastodon . You can also contact the team via email: magazine@raspberrypi.com

title: Introducing the Raspberry Pi Guide to Retro Gaming
author: Raspberry Pi
description:
Hey there, folks, Rob again! When I said I’d “see you next year” in the  Raspberry Pi Official Annual 2027  blog post, I was lying. Fortunately, it was for a good reason, because I’m back to announce our brand-new   Raspberry Pi Guide to Retro Gaming  , out now.

Raspberry Pi and retro games go hand in hand, with people emulating classic consoles and computers on Raspberry Pi devices since shortly after the release of the original Raspberry Pi. Today, emulation on a Raspberry Pi is extremely pow...
article_content:
Hey there, folks, Rob again! When I said I’d “see you next year” in the  Raspberry Pi Official Annual 2027  blog post, I was lying. Fortunately, it was for a good reason, because I’m back to announce our brand-new   Raspberry Pi Guide to Retro Gaming  , out now.

Raspberry Pi and retro games go hand in hand, with people emulating classic consoles and computers on Raspberry Pi devices since shortly after the release of the original Raspberry Pi. Today, emulation on a Raspberry Pi is extremely powerful, with loads of individual emulators and packaged operating systems to choose from, allowing you to play games on hundreds of platforms. You can even make handhelds and arcade machines, and run them all on CRT TVs with your own tweaks and optimisations.

We show you how to build your own portable retro gaming machine

The definitive guide

With so many ways to play retro games on a Raspberry Pi, getting started might seem daunting, so we decided to make this book to demystify it all. It begins with an easy quick-start guide I wrote to get you gaming as fast as possible. Sorted.

If you’d like to take your time and learn about what’s on offer, I also wrote about the various emulation operating systems available for Raspberry Pi and what each individual Raspberry Pi computer can handle.

While I’m very confident in my knowledge of retro console emulation, when it comes to classic computers I defer to Brian Jepson’s expertise. As well as being my boss and Publishing Director here at Raspberry Pi Press, he’s also a volunteer at the Rhode Island Computer Museum and has a vast wealth of knowledge around 1980s and early 1990s computers — and how to emulate them. He’s written several tutorials on how to emulate about a dozen computers from the 8- and 16-bit era, along with a few early 32-bit systems. Each is a little different on Raspberry Pi, but you’re in safe hands with Brian’s tutorials.

We also look at DOSBox Staging, the fantastic fork of the original DOSBox

Advanced emulation

As I wanted this book to be pretty definitive, we go quite in-depth with emulation. Our resident retro gaming expert K.G. Orphanides did a deep dive on tweaking your emulation settings to get the most out of your setup, and also showed us how to build a full arcade machine and use old CDs, floppy disks, and DB9 joysticks on a modern Raspberry Pi.

Not sure where to find games for your new retro powerhouse? I put together a guide with K.G. on where to find legal ROMs sold on modern digital stores like Steam and GOG — it turns out there are a lot if you know where to look! Don’t forget the homebrew scene either, with folks still making new games for 40-year-old consoles.

Brian and I also took a look at running a Raspberry Pi on CRT displays and old tellies thanks to some nifty Raspberry Pi add-ons. A lot of retro games were designed to use scanlines and other peculiarities of old screens, and they look much better if you have space for one in your house. You can even use a classic PS2 light gun with them.

Get an old telly from a car boot sale so you can truly retro game

DIY retro

Finally, Sean McManus shows us how to program games on a Speccy via an emulator, complete with listings you can type out! But never fear — unlike the mags of the 1980s, the code is all available online and can be downloaded straight to your machine if need be.

We’ve all been working very hard on this book over the last year, and I’m very excited to see it in people’s hands. I hope it can help inspire — or level up (sorry) — your retro gaming journey.

You can grab the book online  from our store  for just  £19.99  £9.99 (introductory price), on  Amazon UK  and  Amazon US , or at the official Raspberry Pi Store in Cambridge. Now if you’ll excuse me, Hydrocity Zone won’t play itself…

The post  Introducing the Raspberry Pi Guide to Retro Gaming  appeared first on  Raspberry Pi .

title: A Raspberry Pi Pico Halloween
author: Raspberry Pi
description:

This year we’re focusing on the tiny  Raspberry Pi Pico  as the dark driver of your foul festivities – don’t be fooled by its small stature, though; it too can produce supernatural spooks to scare your gruesome guests. So start practising your programming sorcery – the witching hour ...
article_content:
Welcome, foolish mortals, to another year of haunted hacks from   Raspberry Pi Official Magazine  . These brutal builds are sure to send a chill down your spine and ‘liven up’ even the putrid parties of the undead.

This year we’re focusing on the tiny  Raspberry Pi Pico  as the dark driver of your foul festivities – don’t be fooled by its small stature, though; it too can produce supernatural spooks to scare your gruesome guests. So start practising your programming sorcery – the witching hour awaits…

Simple spooky Pico hacks

At this time of year, you’re sure to find a lot of Halloween tat – excuse us – icky items of terror in your local supermarket or hardware store. Some of them may even be very cool (and very reasonably priced), but could use something… a little extra.

While there are plenty of projects with servos and sensors and HaaS (Halloween-as-a-Service, natch), the quickest way to spruce up these fiendish finds is simply with some lighting upgrades from our friends at  Pimoroni .

Pico Unicorn Pack

An LED strip with buttons that is barely bigger than a Raspberry Pi Pico,  these programmable lights  can be easily slipped inside decorations and programmed with greens, oranges, and purples to give off a Halloween vibe. You need to provide a Pico yourself, but programming is very easy.

Wireless Plasma Kit

This  lighting kit  includes at the very least a strip of programmable LEDs and a  Plasma 2350 W  (basically a custom Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W designed to control LEDs), perfect for creating a custom lighting scheme for any Halloween prop. Pimoroni also sells a version that comes with a skull bottle to put the lights in – Dan Aykroyd not included – as a quick Halloween decoration in itself.

Dastardly DIY decorations

Pico pumpkins

Not dissimilar to what we mentioned on the previous page about upgrading some decorations with simple lighting, although the lights in  these jack-o’-lanterns  are much more advanced with LED matrices used to create eyes. You’ll also need to carve the pumpkin yourself, which means you don’t have to do a traditional spooky face or even normal eyes to go in them.

Spooky Scary Skeleton

Kevin McAleer makes a lot of great robots over at   kevsrobots.com   and he created this  ‘bare bones’ robot  (get it?) for Halloween one year. It’s made up of 3D printed parts and has ultrasonic sensors, eye-shaped sensors usually used to detect distance, to sense when someone is in front of it. When it detects movement, it starts moving its mouth and eyebrows.

Bag o’ Bones

The  bag o’ bones  is a decoration that maker 314Reactor found in a Sainsbury’s supermarket. He upgraded it with a PIR motion sensor, various motors, and even a speaker so that any unsuspecting passers-by would be scared sockless by the suddenly writhing bones that begins to play Toccata and Fugue in D minor – which most folks will know as the cliché spooky organ music.

Possessed Portrait

We cannot tell a lie;  this portrait of George Washington  following you around the room with his eyes is very creepy. Usually for a project like this, folks would make use of computer vision to track faces; however, this one uses ultrasonic sensors, much like the skull robot. The servos actually just move a bit of card around behind the picture – very low-tech but very effective.

Issue 170 of  Raspberry Pi Official Magazine  is out NOW!

This article appeared in  issue 170  of  Raspberry Pi Official Magazine , which you can  access online . You can also  subscribe  to the print version of our magazine. Not only do we deliver worldwide, but those who sign up to the six- or twelve-month print subscription will receive a FREE  Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W !

You can find  Raspberry Pi Official Magazine  on  Facebook ,  X ,  Threads ,  LinkedIn , and  Mastodon . You can also contact the team via email: magazine@raspberrypi.com

title: Building the next generation of hardware founders
author: Raspberry Pi
description:

We asked  Furqan Rydhan , Founder and CEO, and  Mike Shin , COO, to explain what  Founders, Inc.  is doing in the hardware space and why Raspberry Pi fits so well.

The next generation of iconic companies won’t be making software alone; they’ll combin...
article_content:
Our summer tour of various maker events took us to San Fransisco, where we were invited to visit a unique campus incubating what hope to be future-defining companies ,  many of which are using Rasberry Pi hardware to get their ideas off the ground. We asked  Furqan Rydhan , Founder and CEO, and  Mike Shin , COO, to explain what  Founders, Inc.  is doing in the hardware space and why Raspberry Pi fits so well.

The next generation of iconic companies won’t be making software alone; they’ll combine AI, robotics, autonomous systems, advanced manufacturing, and frontier hardware. Founders, Inc.’s mission supports this: give wildly ambitious technical founders the space, community, and first cheque they need to build from day one.

The 42,000 sq. ft. campus at Fort Mason, San Francisco is buzzing with founders working on everything from robotic manipulation and drones to AI infrastructure, developer tools, defence technology, and consumer hardware. Founders, Inc. doesn’t see themselves as a traditional accelerator; instead, they’ve built a place where founders learn from one another, share prototypes, break things, and iterate fast alongside some of the best technical builders in the world.

One of the reasons Raspberry Pi has become such a common sight around the Founders, Inc. campus is that it was found to lower the barrier between an idea and a working prototype. Whether someone is building a robot, an industrial sensor, or an edge AI device, or is validating an idea over a weekend, Raspberry Pi hardware makes it possible to get something into the real world quickly. For founders, speed matters more than perfection in the early stages of turning an idea into a real  thing .

Tell us a little about Founders, Inc.

We’re often the first believers in the bold ideas founders bring to us. We write the first check, but the check is the smallest part. What matters is surrounding founders with the people, tools, and environment they need to build something that lasts.

Every day, our campus is filled with engineers building robots, testing drones, training AI models, assembling hardware prototypes, and helping each other through hard technical problems.

“This is the space I dreamed of having when I was 18 — just tinkering, exploring, and building things with friends, fuelled by curiosity and passion. A place where we could experiment freely, supported by a community of people who deeply believed in us.”

– Furqan Rydhan, Founder and CEO of Founders, Inc.

Why is hardware becoming exciting again?

We’re at a rare moment where AI has dramatically expanded what physical systems can do. Robots are becoming genuinely useful because of foundation models. Drones are becoming more autonomous. Manufacturing is getting smarter. Edge AI is enabling products that simply weren’t possible a few years ago.

Hardware is still hard — but it’s never been more accessible. Better development boards, open source software, affordable sensors, and modern manufacturing mean a small team can hit meaningful milestones in weeks, not years.

“Now with a 3D printer and a Raspberry Pi, anyone can build a scalable AI hardware product.”

– Mike Shin, COO of Founders, Inc.

How does Raspberry Pi fit into that journey?

Raspberry Pi is one of those rare platforms that works just as well for a student building their first robot as for an experienced founder validating a commercial product.

Around our campus, we’ve seen Raspberry Pi at the heart of:

Robotics control systems

Computer vision prototypes

Edge AI applications

Drone control and telemetry

Environmental sensing

Industrial automation

IoT infrastructure

Smart manufacturing tools

Most importantly, it helps founders answer the question that matters most at the start:

Can this actually work?  

Instead of spending months designing custom hardware, they can prove the concept in days.

What are some of your favourite things founders have built?

The most exciting trend we’ve seen is founders using Raspberry Pi as the foundation for increasingly sophisticated robotics.

We’ve watched teams build autonomous robots that navigate complex environments, edge AI systems that run computer vision locally without touching the cloud, intelligent manufacturing equipment that monitors factory operations in real time, and drone platforms for inspection, mapping, and logistics.

Beyond robotics, founders here have built smart agriculture systems, environmental monitoring platforms, connected medical devices, and educational tools that make advanced engineering more accessible.

What excites us isn’t any single project. It’s watching a rough weekend prototype become a venture-backed company solving a real problem.

“Many of the companies we back started exactly this way: build something quickly, put it in front of users, learn, iterate, and keep improving.”

– Furqan Rydhan, Founder and CEO of Founders, Inc.

Why do you think community matters for hardware founders?

Building hardware can be lonely. Unlike software founders, hardware founders have to think about manufacturing, supply chains, mechanical engineering, firmware, electrical systems, compliance, testing, and AI — often all at once.

Having dozens of other founders working through the same problems changes everything. Someone has already solved the issue you’re stuck on. Someone knows the supplier you’re hunting for. Someone has already broken the component you’re about to order. That shared knowledge compounds fast.

Droids get tired too

What advice would you give founders interested in hardware startups?

Start building. Don’t wait for the perfect design. Use off-the-shelf components. Use Raspberry Pi. Use open source software. Buy sensors. Print parts. Build something people can actually touch.

The founders who win are rarely the ones with the perfect idea — they’re the ones who build, test, and improve faster than everyone else. Hardware has never been more accessible, and AI is opening up entire categories of products waiting to be built. There has never been a better time to become a hardware founder.

No idea what this is, but it looked cool and important so I included it

Looking ahead

We’re incredibly optimistic about the future of physical AI. Over the next decade, intelligent robots, autonomous vehicles, drones, factories, and edge computing will become everyday infrastructure. The companies building that future won’t come from isolated garages — they’ll come from communities where ambitious founders can collaborate, prototype quickly, and learn from one another.

“We’re excited to see Raspberry Pi continue lowering the barrier to entry for hardware innovation and helping the next generation of founders turn ambitious ideas into real companies. If you’re a hardware founder, come build with us.”

– Mike Shin, COO of Founders, Inc.

title: Fireworks says you’re wasting money on AI unless you’re using all the models
author: The Register
description:
Fireworks AI is fine with helping companies run AI models in their own datacenters, though VP Rob Ferguson argues against doing so.

article_content:
Fireworks AI is fine with helping companies run AI models in their own datacenters, though VP Rob Ferguson argues against doing so.

Ferguson told  The Register  in an interview that while Fireworks AI, a managed inference provider, supports on-prem AI, "we're trying to push people more and more away from it because frankly, it's just the economics."

The GPU hardware is just so expensive that if you can't keep it fully utilized, it's a waste of money, he contends. Ten thousand GPUs, he said, represent a billion dollars of capital.

"You don't want those things to be sitting idle," he said.

For companies with particularly sensitive workloads, Ferguson said, Fireworks is happy to work something out – it offers a service called Sovereign for just that purpose and it has partners like Microsoft that can help. But most inference work probably doesn't need that level of protection, he said.

"The state of the art for everyone is to have a portfolio of models," he explained. "In fact, I think most people don't know that the best model in the world's not Astra. The best model in the world's not Fable. The best model is literally a portfolio and we can prove it. You are always better routing between a few models than to do one singular model."

That's what Fireworks does through Nexus and its API, alongside competitors like Together AI, Baseten, and DeepInfra. As a managed inference platform, Fireworks AI routes inference tasks to whichever model, frontier model subscription, or API is best suited to handle them.

But the company is not just doing naive routing like an AI gateway. It's evaluating tasks as they come in and directing them to the optimal model.

"We build custom routers," Ferguson explained. "Our auto model is continuously updating so that we actually go through and we grade the difficulty of the task and we see if there're affinities that the models have, like Kimi is slightly better at JavaScript than Python, things like this."

The company's competitive edge, he contends, is its crack engineering team, which follows from its founders' work on PyTorch, a widely used open source machine learning library.

"We're performance experts both on the training and inference side," he explained. "People I think don't understand how important, for example, numerics is. So when you use a model, it's always called a mixture of experts – an expert is a different machine.

"And so you have all these different machines. It actually matters when you're training that you go back to precisely the right machine, because if you don't, the other machine will still answer the question, but it'll answer in a slightly different way. So we have to know how to build the topology to write back the data to the right space. We have to understand floating point precision [to handle very small values]. We have to be able to do all this where we're routing through a complex fabric through potentially more than one provider depending on what everything is. And so we're really systems experts."

Hyperscalers, he argues, will give you a GPU but then it's your responsibility to put it to use. Fireworks' advantage involves being able to maximize utilization at scale while maintaining model precision and speed.

Ferguson said AI keeps coming back to economics.

"People are just trying to figure out more and more things to use AI for and [to answer questions like] just how much more can I send to cached models, how much more can I send to open models, when do I need this specialization?" he said. "So we're constantly working with customers to help them come up with their own evaluation criteria."

One reason for this, Ferguson explained, is that frontier model companies are not transparent about their caching rates. He said Fireworks was working with a data science company and was caching about 90 percent of the tasks.

"We looked at [Anthropic's] Opus and it was caching 30 percent of the time," he said. "It was doing AI rework constantly. And with AI, rework is by far your biggest cost. If it's not hitting a cache, then your costs are absolutely insane. And so the token cost is not the real cost. It's the cost per task. And they're hiding that from you. And so we always tell our customers to be tracking cost per task, because that's the real number."

Another factor that companies should consider in their cost calculations, Ferguson suggested, is the value of their data and whether they're giving that data away for training.

"I think people grossly underestimate the value of their data," he said.

Fireworks AI has a zero data-retention policy, "but a lot of times," Ferguson said, "these other companies [do] not, and you should be getting paid for your data. Nobody really knew at the beginning of this current era that these models are memorizers. But now there's plenty of evidence that these models are. So if they're going to be using your data, then you should be getting value for it."

But it's not just about cost. Speed, said Ferguson, is underappreciated.

"Speed is the thing that people often don't know they can ask for," he said. "It's such a game changer for me and how I work with AI is so different when the responses come back as fast as I ask them."

What's the advantage of model ensembling, as the company refers to its model routing activities? A bill that's at least 50 percent smaller, Ferguson claims.

"So we say six to eight times cheaper," he said. "The reality is that because a lot of folks have a preference in their tooling, we kinda guarantee that in the case where you're still using a combo of closed and open models, we can always guarantee that your bill will drop by half right away. Like we're sure about that. And then the question is can we just get you to use more stuff?" ®

title: NHS breach helpline left staff carrying a 'significant emotional burden'
author: The Register
description:
NHS staff drafted into a helpline after colleagues' health data was exposed online faced distressed callers, safeguarding concerns, and a "serious emotional impact," a review has found.

The  report  [PDF] comes almost exactly a year after the Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust disclosed a data breach affecting 8,003 people, including current and former trust staff and non-trust workers.

A member of the public discovered the exposure in November 2025. An Excel workbook published in response to ...
article_content:
NHS staff drafted into a helpline after colleagues' health data was exposed online faced distressed callers, safeguarding concerns, and a "serious emotional impact," a review has found.

The  report  [PDF] comes almost exactly a year after the Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust disclosed a data breach affecting 8,003 people, including current and former trust staff and non-trust workers.

A member of the public discovered the exposure in November 2025. An Excel workbook published in response to a Freedom of Information request in February 2023 retained underlying sickness absence records that users could reveal through its pivot tables.

Staff assigned to the helpline described difficult calls involving shouting, anger, and distress.

Particularly difficult calls involved people distressed by the sensitivity of the disclosures or potentially in danger from domestic abuse. Call handlers said they had to make safeguarding assessments without training or an established process.

"Such occurrences of anger or distress were not infrequent, and this reflected the heightened emotions and distress experienced by callers to varying degrees due to the breach," the review noted.

"This placed significant emotional burden on individuals working in the contact center, who were not prepared or provided support on how to deal with those."

Members of the trust's clinical governance team were told just a day beforehand that they would staff the helpline. Despite their experience dealing with patient trauma, they received little preparation for the calls that followed.

"The staff working in the call centers had a short training session and then the calls started coming in within minutes of the team being set up," the review noted. "Some staff had not finished reading the pre-prepared script which had arrived only 30 minutes before the center went live."

Most call handlers only learned that their own data had been exposed while already working on the helpline, sometimes minutes before supporting others affected.

Call handlers also said they had little choice about taking on the work and were expected to maintain their usual duties alongside it.

The review stated that some staff members gave up weekends and worked long past their scheduled hours to meet the demands of both roles.

"It's typical NHS, it runs on goodwill," one staffer told the team that compiled the report.

The call center was only supposed to run for two weeks in December 2025, but due to the volume of calls, it was eventually stood down after 11 weeks, in February 2026.

According to officials speaking at a trust board meeting on Thursday, the review and its findings have since been circulated among staff, and published online.

How the spreadsheet slipped through  Responding to a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request thought to be from a journalist researching a story about stress in the NHS, the Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust uploaded a spreadsheet to its public FOI Disclosure log in February 2023.

This contained personal data and inadvertently exposed sickness absence information and sensitive health data related to 7,715 staff, 288 non-trust workers, as well as a small number of unidentified records.

Crucially, this spreadsheet was uploaded in a format that allowed users to access the pivot table from which some data was derived. The data in these pivot tables would normally have been too sensitive to be included in FOIA responses.

The first failure was that the request was handled by the trust's e-Rostering team instead of the People Information Unit, which had the expertise in responding to FOIA requests with complex datasets.

The e-Rostering team compiled the response using the team's own data, but incorrectly believed they had stripped the spreadsheet of the sensitive data that would later be exposed.

Standard procedures instructed request handlers to follow several steps to ensure sensitive data was stripped before documents are published, some of which were skipped.

For starters, one FOI officer assigned to the response either failed to run the spreadsheet through Excel's Document Inspector, which formed part of the usual procedures, or failed to act upon its recommendations.

This feature can flag pivot tables and potentially hidden cached data, but cannot determine whether that data is sensitive or automatically remove the cache.

Staff also failed to follow instructions to convert the spreadsheet to PDF. Investigators found that doing so prevented users clicking through to the underlying records, although they could not guarantee that no hidden data remained technically accessible.

At the time, internal guidance did not require conversion to CSV, which would have removed the workbook's pivot-table functionality and embedded cache.

The trust's sign-off process also focused on answering the request's questions and meeting their public relations duties, and falsely assumed that the data had been adequately sanitized before the final review.

The spreadsheet was made available for 33 months, although the trust is not sure how many times it was viewed during that time.

Its logs only covered the 12 months before a member of the public alerted it to the pivot table issue. These indicated that it had been accessed 340 times, although the review noted there was no way of knowing how many of these, if any, led to pivot tables being accessed, or even if it was viewed by a human, with web crawlers adding to the total view count.

The trust has since implemented a number of changes to prevent a recurrence of the breach, including the mandatory password-protecting of any  Excel  workbook as part of FOIA responses.

A senior information governance officer must now approve spreadsheet responses before executive sign-off. Revised guidance circulated in November 2025 also called for conversion to CSV, although investigators found that this requirement had not been incorporated into the formal operating procedure and recommended updating it.

The review says the Information Commissioner's Office closed its case after the trust implemented its recommendations.

A spokesperson for the Royal Cornwall Hospitals said: "We are deeply sorry for the accidental sharing of sickness absence data which we reported in November 2025, and for the distress and concern it caused those colleagues whose data was involved.

"An independent investigation has now been completed, and the report has been published in full on our website in the interests of transparency and accountability.

"The investigation has helped us understand what happened and identify areas where improvements were needed. We have already implemented a number of measures to strengthen our processes, particularly around the management of Freedom of Information requests and responses.

"The protection of personal information is of the utmost importance to us, and we remain committed to learning from this incident and preventing a similar event from happening again.

"We continue to provide support to colleagues who have been affected." ®
ai_summary: NHS staff drafted into a helpline after colleagues' health data was exposed online faced distressed callers, safeguarding concerns, and a "serious emotional impact," a review has found. The report [PDF] comes almost exactly a year after the Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust disclosed a data breach affecting 8,003 people, including current and former trust staff and non-trust workers.
main_event: NHS breach helpline left staff carrying a 'significant emotional burden'

article_content:
A roadside display at Cherwell Valley services has stopped dispensing information and started asking for help.

The eagle-eyed  Register  reader who spotted the stricken screen told us: "UK motorway signs often tell us that tiredness can kill, urging us to take a break. This poor thing at Cherwell Valley services took the advice to heart."

The display at the Moto services appears to have run into trouble during a restart. Windows offers another attempt or access to repair tools, although the latter options are hidden – perhaps somewhere on the top floor of the neighboring Travelodge. Getting things moving again will probably require access to the computer behind the screen.

The Automatic Repair screen is all too familiar to Windows users. Not to be confused with the classic blue screen of death, it might indicate a misbehaving driver during a reboot, an update that did something unexpected, or some sort of hardware failure. Hopefully it isn't the latter – with memory and storage prices the way they are at the moment, a motorway services sandwich or gallon of fuel will seem a positive bargain by comparison.

Our reader is right: taking a break is sensible advice. Getting Windows to end one can be another matter. ®
