title: How we halved DNS build delay and cut memory use by 85%
author: Alex Fattouche
description: When I   last wrote about our DNS propagation pipeline in 2022  , the Zone Builder received about 250 DNS record changes per second. Today it receives about 700, nearly three times as many, plus about 100 other events, such as   zone   setting changes. However, the number of events was never the real problem. The problem was the kind of work some of those events needed, and how that work grows with the size of a zone. Some zones now hold more than 20 million records, and we expect them to keep g...
article_content:
When I   last wrote about our DNS propagation pipeline in 2022  , the Zone Builder received about 250 DNS record changes per second. Today it receives about 700, nearly three times as many, plus about 100 other events, such as   zone   setting changes. However, the number of events was never the real problem. The problem was the kind of work some of those events needed, and how that work grows with the size of a zone. Some zones now hold more than 20 million records, and we expect them to keep growing toward hundreds of millions.

Each event starts a clock that measures how long it takes us to turn that change into data our authoritative DNS servers can use. We call that work a build. A build reads the current database state, converts it into the format used at the edge, and writes any changes to   Quicksilver  .

In 2022, per-record builds were 150 times faster than full builds on average. On a test zone with one million records, per-record builds were 4,250 times faster. We ended that post with the obvious next step: do the same thing for zone settings.

Why doesn't the Zone Builder just rebuild the setting that changed?

It should, and that is where we ended up. However, proving when it was safe took most of the work. A record event identifies what changed. A zone event can come from many Cloudflare products, may not say why the zone changed, and can alter data shared by several zones with the same name. Choosing too much work wastes capacity. Choosing too little can leave stale or incorrect DNS data at the edge.

We built a targeted build planner that chooses the smallest build we can prove is safe, and a new scheduler that combines work for the same zone. Zone setting changes no longer rebuild zones with tens of millions of records. Together, they cut peak memory by 85%, and the extra headroom let us safely shorten waits the pipeline has always needed for resilience, halving the time from a DNS change to its data being written to Quicksilver.

How DNS changes reach the edge  A DNS zone is the collection of records and settings for a domain. Cloudflare uses a multi-stage pipeline to turn a change to that zone into data available across our   global network  .

A customer changes a DNS record through the   DNS Records API   or dashboard, or another Cloudflare service changes a zone setting.

The change is stored in a database.

The database change or another system produces a   Kafka   event.

The DNS Kafka Aggregator combines events from several Kafka topics and sends them to the Zone Builder.

The Zone Builder reads the required zone data and converts it into keys understood by our authoritative DNS servers.

The Zone Builder compares those keys with   Quicksilver  , our distributed key-value store. It writes only what changed, and Quicksilver propagates those changes across Cloudflare's network.

This is a simplified view. The Zone Builder does not copy database rows directly to the edge. It combines records with zone settings, applies DNS serving rules, and organizes the result so our authoritative DNS servers can read it quickly.

Why full builds stopped scaling  The original Zone Builder had one useful property: it did not need to know why a zone changed. It rebuilt the desired state from the current database state.

Read the current zone and its settings.

Read every DNS record in the zone.

Convert those records into Quicksilver keys.

Compare the new keys with those already stored.

Remove stale keys, write changed keys, and update zone metadata.

The final write contains only changed keys. However, a full build still reads, encodes, and compares every record, and holds the whole zone in memory while it does so. That is cheap for a small zone. For our largest zones, with tens of millions of records, the zone does not fit in memory at all. I explain how we handle that below.

Zone settings made targeting harder.   Universal SSL   is one example. Enabling or disabling it updates metadata and can change Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) records at the zone apex, the bare domain, such as  example.com .   CAA records   tell certificate authorities whether they may issue a certificate for the domain.

A full build only needed to know that the zone changed. A targeted build must answer three questions:

Which DNS names can change?

Can shared metadata or the list of published zones change?

What previous state must be removed from Quicksilver?

Answering those questions safely meant solving five problems, which the rest of this post covers in order:

Events had to say what changed.

Each change had to map to the smallest build that is still correct.

Builds had to account for data shared by every zone with the same name.

The database could change between the event and the build.

Combining work could not lose a Kafka message.

Making events say what changed  We changed the event producer to include changed zone fields and settings, with previous and new values when available. We then traced each setting through the code that generates DNS output and classified what it could affect.

Not every event was that specific. Some database functions only update a timestamp to say, in effect, "something about this zone changed." Sometimes that is harmless bookkeeping. Sometimes it means data changed elsewhere and must be read again.

Those cases look identical in the event. Until we can identify the caller and its purpose, a timestamp-only update still causes a full build. The same rule applies to missing details, unknown events, or any change that may affect records anywhere in the zone. The planner never turns uncertainty into less work.

Choosing the smallest safe build  Quicksilver output has two parts that matter here. Record keys contain the DNS answers for one zone and name. A smaller shared metadata key tells our authoritative DNS servers how to use that zone, including where to find special records such as nameservers and wildcards. Some events change only record keys; others must update both.

With that distinction, the planner can choose one of five build types:

Resources only:  Rebuild the records at specific DNS names, which we call resources, without changing zone metadata. Ordinary A, AAAA, TXT, and CNAME changes usually take this path.

Resources and metadata:  Rebuild specific names and shared metadata. Nameserver and wildcard changes use this path.

Apex and metadata:  Rebuild the zone apex and metadata. Settings such as Universal SSL can use this path.

Purge:  Remove a zone that should no longer be published.

Full zone:  Rebuild every record when smaller work cannot be proven safe.

The rule is simple: every key a targeted build writes must be byte-for-byte identical to what a full build would write. If we cannot prove that, we do a full build.

Removing old state works as it did for per-record builds in 2022. Record events include deleted records and the previous version of updated ones. The Zone Builder then scans Quicksilver for the existing keys under each name it rebuilds, removing any that the new build did not write.

Full builds remain necessary when a change can affect records anywhere in the zone or when a zone may need to be published for the first time.

There is one deliberate exception. A full build holds every record from the database and every existing Quicksilver key for the zone in memory at once, and our largest zones do not fit. Above a fixed record-count threshold, the Zone Builder never escalates to a full build. It rebuilds the apex, the metadata, and every name identified by the queued events instead. We accept this tradeoff because a full build of those zones cannot finish, and, while it retries, it holds back every other change on its Kafka partition. Many of the cases that would otherwise need a full build involve several zones sharing one name, and   zone holds   reduce that risk by stopping the same name from being added to another account. For the rare cases that remain, such as enabling a zone on another network, we can manually rebuild individual names in the zone.

When one name means more than one zone  Quicksilver stores each zone's record keys separately. It also stores one metadata key shared by every Cloudflare zone with that domain name. This shared key acts like a directory: it tells our authoritative DNS servers which internal zone IDs they may use when answering a query.

Why can one name have several zone IDs? During customer onboarding, offboarding, and other   lifecycle   changes, multiple Cloudflare zone objects can briefly exist for the same public domain. We use a priority policy to choose a small, bounded set to publish.

Consider four internal zones for  example.com : Zone 101, Zone 202, Zone 303, and Zone 404. The metadata key currently lists Zones 101, 202, and 303. Zone 404 exists, but it is not selected. The numbers identify separate Cloudflare zone objects; customers still see one domain name.

A TXT record change at  www.example.com  in Zone 202 affects only Zone 202's record keys, so the metadata key does not change. Nameserver and wildcard changes are different because the metadata key records information about them. Those builds must update both the zone's records and the metadata key.

At execution time, the Zone Builder reads the current list again. If it writes the metadata key, it rebuilds the whole key from that fresh view rather than patching an older copy. It writes the triggering zone's records before the metadata that refers to them.

Planning from the event, verifying before writing  An event describes what happened in the past. A build may wait while more events arrive and the database changes, so planning happens twice. The event first creates a conservative work list. Immediately before execution, the Zone Builder reads a fresh publication snapshot: the current zone settings, whether this Zone Builder should publish the zone to its network, and which same-name zone IDs belong in the metadata key. Here, a network is a separate, isolated copy of Quicksilver for one environment. Each Zone Builder deployment writes to one network, and a zone can be enabled on some networks but not others. For example, a zone can be served from Cloudflare's global network and also from the   China Network  .

Fresh state can change the result in four ways:

A targeted build can become a full build if the zone now has a feature that requires complete-zone work.

A build can become a purge if the zone should no longer be published to this network.

A build can be skipped if the triggering zone no longer belongs in the metadata key.

A metadata build can reconstruct the shared key from the current candidate set.

The fresh read comes from read-only copies of the database, called replicas, so builds do not compete with customer writes. Kafka delivery and database replication move independently: an event can arrive before its database change is visible on a replica. The DNS Kafka Aggregator delays events long enough to cover normal lag, and a final database check rejects the read if that replica is still behind.

Combining changes in one scheduler  Record work and full-zone work previously used different schedulers. Each could combine its own work, but not work from the other scheduler. We replaced them with one unified scheduler. The planner decides what must be built, and the scheduler decides when it can run.

When several events for one zone arrive before a build starts, the scheduler combines their work:

An A record changes at  www.example.com , requiring that name.

A wildcard changes at  *.example.com , requiring that name and shared metadata.

The scheduler combines both names and the metadata update into one build.

Merging only adds work. If any event requires the complete zone, the combined build becomes a full build. A purge overrides every rebuild because its desired result is that the zone is no longer published.

The scheduler tracks two things separately: the DNS work that must be performed and the Kafka messages waiting to be acknowledged. A retry preserves both. Even when a full build or purge no longer needs the individual record names, the messages stay attached until the result is safely written.

Keeping Kafka moving  One slow build can delay unrelated customers even when workers are available. Kafka divides messages into ordered partitions. For each partition, it stores one committed offset: the point before which every message is known to be complete. Moving that offset past unfinished work could lose a customer change after a restart.

We use soft committing, which I previously described in my   Secondary DNS deep dive  . A build can finish out of order and be marked complete in memory, but Kafka's committed position advances only after every earlier message has also finished.

In the diagram, message 2 is still running, so messages 3 through n cannot be committed. If the Zone Builder restarts, those in-memory completions disappear and Kafka replays messages 2 through n. We deliberately choose repeated work over losing a change.

Targeted plans reduce how long the oldest message stays unfinished. The scheduler also prevents one busy zone from taking every worker. After a zone builds, its next build waits for a per-zone rebuild interval, which differs by Cloudflare plan. Changes that arrive in the meantime are merged into that next build. The scheduler normally enforces this interval, but lets old queued work run before it blocks a Kafka partition for too long. Zone locks and retry delays still apply, so a failing build cannot run in a tight loop.

Releasing safely  A smaller build is useful only if it produces the same DNS data. We added equivalence tests for nameserver, wildcard, and apex paths. Each test runs a full build and a targeted build from the same database state, pins time-dependent values, and compares every Quicksilver key owned by the targeted plan byte for byte. Planner and scheduler tests cover classification, same-name zones, merging, purges, and escalation.

During rollout, we also ran a full build next to every targeted build and compared the output. It was expensive by design, reading the complete zone every time, so we used it only until the mirror comparison below gave us the same confidence.

Tests cannot reproduce every customer combination, so every release also runs through a mirror Zone Builder. It consumes the production Kafka stream and reads production database state, but writes to a separate Quicksilver environment that serves no customer traffic.

A comparer checks a 20% sample of zones for missing keys, extra keys, and different values. The two environments do not always build a zone at the same instant, so a temporary mismatch is not automatically a regression. We look for new types of differences that remain after both pipelines catch up. That gives us confidence that targeted builds produce the same output as production.

We built the DNS Mirror Dashboard to group those differences and keep examples for investigation. Naturally, it runs on the   Cloudflare Developer Platform  : a   Worker   receives results,   Durable Objects   maintain state, and   Cloudflare Access   protects it. The critical groups in the screenshot below were each checked and confirmed safe before release. The diff rate is the share of compared zones where production and mirror disagreed on at least one key at the moment of comparison. Most of those are timing differences that disappear once both pipelines catch up, so we watch two things: that the rate stays low, and that no new kind of difference appears.

After the mirror results remained healthy, we rolled the scheduler out by a hash of the zone name. Hashing the name rather than the zone ID kept every zone sharing a name on the same scheduler, so two schedulers never wrote the same metadata key. We increased the percentage for free zones, then repeated the process for paid zones.

Results  Over 24 hours, we measured 86.81% of builds as resources only, 2.54% as resources and metadata, 2.30% as apex and metadata, and 1.30% as purges. Together, 92.95% of builds avoided rebuilding the complete zone. Full builds were the remaining 7.04%.

The two metadata build types were full builds before, even for large zones. Together, they account for 4.84% of builds. Combined with the 7.04% that are still full builds, that is 11.88%, so full builds fell by about 40%. Their share of the count also understates the work avoided, because they include the largest zones. The full builds that remain average 0.35 seconds, because the events that still trigger them, such as a zone being published for the first time, mostly affect new zones with few records.

In 2022, we also planned a batching system. The unified scheduler makes it unnecessary: it does not wait to form batches, and it merges events only when work is already queued for the same zone. Before, long full builds held back the committed offset for their partition. With fewer of them, we now consume Kafka at the rate events arrive, instead of falling behind and catching up in bursts of up to 1,550 messages per second.

We also measured build completion delay: the time from a DNS record or zone setting change until the Zone Builder finished writing to Quicksilver. It does not include Quicksilver's distribution across our network, which varies by location and is unaffected by this work. Production ran the old schedulers, and the mirror ran the unified scheduler on the same events over the same 24 hours. The two environments are identical apart from the code: they consume the same Kafka events, read from the same database, and write equivalent data to Quicksilver. That makes this a controlled, side-by-side comparison. The figures combine every build type and customer plan, so they are not a latency guarantee for an individual zone. A large share of this time is the rebuild interval described earlier, not build work. At each measurement point, p99 is the time within which 99% of events finished. Typical delays barely changed here, because most builds were already small. The difference is in the tail: the largest p99 spike fell from 14.6 minutes to 1.21 minutes, a 12-fold reduction. The chart uses a logarithmic scale.

Targeted builds also load complete large zones far less often. Aggregate working-set memory, the memory actively used by the deployment, fell from an average of 49 GiB to 7 GiB, an 86% reduction. Peaks fell from 79 GiB to 12 GiB, an 85% reduction.

Those were the immediate results of the new scheduler. They also let us revisit two safeguards. The first is the rebuild interval, which stops one busy zone from rebuilding constantly and taking capacity from everyone else. With builds now cheaper, and far fewer of them reading complete zones, we could safely shorten that interval on most plans. The second is how long the DNS Kafka Aggregator holds each event, to make sure database replicas have caught up before we read from them. Once our databases began rejecting reads from replicas that had fallen behind, that buffer could safely be smaller. Together, these halved the median build completion delay, from about 7.7 seconds to about 3.3 seconds. In the chart below, the first step down is the DNS Kafka Aggregator change. The red band marks the Zone Builder release with shorter rebuild intervals. That release rolled out gradually across our servers, so the delay falls in two further steps rather than all at once.

The p90 and p99 lines in that chart are less precise than they look. The histogram had buckets at 1, 5, 10, and 30 seconds, and a percentile that falls between two edges is estimated as if delays were spread evenly across that range. Most delays sit near the bottom of their range, so those estimates come out high: p99 reads close to 30 seconds, and p90 above 7 seconds. The exact average, which does not depend on buckets, confirms the halving. We have since switched to a   native histogram  , which chooses fine-grained buckets automatically. It puts p90 at about 5.5 seconds and p99 at about 12 seconds.

Why full builds still exist  In 2022, we said we planned to eliminate full builds entirely. We now know that is neither realistic nor useful. A zone being published for the first time needs every record written. A change that can affect records anywhere in the zone needs every record checked. An event that does not say what changed still gets a full build, because the planner never turns uncertainty into less work. For a small zone, a full build is also cheap.

As we learn what more events change, we will keep moving them to targeted builds. However, the biggest gain has already landed: the events that used to rebuild our largest zones no longer do, and the full builds that remain are mostly triggered by events, such as first publication, that affect new, small zones.

Want to know what happens after the Zone Builder writes a change? Read how   Quicksilver distributes configuration   to every Cloudflare data center in seconds.

title: 4 real? Tracking exploitation and patching of eMudhra’s weak keys
author: Maxime Guerreiro
description:

Not even four digits, just the number 4. The other seven keys were similarly weak: 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230 and 237.

article_content:
On October 19, 2026, we learned about eMudhra’s eight shockingly weak keys: where eMudhra was trusted to pick a 115-digit number for their virtual combination lock protecting the Internet, they picked the number 4. Not even four digits, just the number 4. The other seven keys were similarly weak: 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230 and 237.

The next day, we wrote a   blog post   on the immediate action we took to mitigate this leak, and what customers   needed to do   on their end to stay secure. Now, we are sharing a more in-depth follow up on the evidence we’ve seen of exploitation, and the progress seen on visitors patching their systems.

Let's start with the scale of the problem. A certificate authority (CA) with weak keys this serious is unprecedented, and the potential consequences are significant. While there have been plenty of compromised certification authorities in the past (such as   DigiNotar  ,   TÜRKTRUST  , and   TrustWave  ), access to their keys has always been contained to a degree; these incidents gave a limited set of attackers or organizations the ability to issue fraudulent certificates. The eMudhra incident is fundamentally different; the affected intermediate private keys could be recovered almost instantly by  anyone  from the public certificates themselves. Anyone can independently recover these same signing keys and create certificates for any domain that an unpatched client not enforcing Certificate Transparency would accept.

eMudhra   announced   they’re exiting the public CA business and have claimed a   mistake   in a key generation script, but have not yet shared the script. They   signed   a certificate revocation list (CRL) with what might’ve been a correctly generated key, and subsequently corrected it to be signed with the weak key.

How did that come to be and why didn’t that set off alarms? Much has to be cleared up, including the role of the auditors and cross signers. This blog proposes the fixes and next steps for organizations to ensure they are secure.

Patching Cloudflare  Our primary concern remains the security impact on Cloudflare, our customers, and the Internet as a whole. At the time of writing, all high priority Cloudflare systems have been patched. A small number of confirmed low impact tickets are being worked on.

We started patching high-impact systems immediately on October 19. These included customer origin-facing proxies using   Pingora  , responsible for most of our outbound connections. These were patched in hours to reject the vulnerable eMudhra keys. At the same time, we started an AI-assisted analysis of our source code to find all other systems that trust these weak keys. Within four hours we had a full analysis. We assigned a ticket with preliminary analysis for each system, and asked the team to confirm and/or adjust the analysis before the end of the day. Where high impact was identified, we asked to patch immediately, and for the lower impact, remediation was due at the end of last week.

Has Cloudflare seen exploitation across its network?  To track whenever a customer’s server (or attacker) presents a certificate signed by eMudhra’s weak keys, we added logging to Pingora. As this outbound service accounts for the vast majority of outgoing TLS connections from a Cloudflare machine, any attacker attempting to snoop using the eMudhra keys would trigger this logging. The logging finished rolling out October 21.

At the time of writing, a week later, we’ve seen about 22,000 attempted handshakes with the weak eMudhra keys. Two-thirds of the attempts were fetches of test sites such as   emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com   (which   we mentioned   in the developer guidance in our earlier post). Almost all of the remaining third went to origins who appeared to set up a certificate for themselves using the weak intermediate. Every handshake configured to verify the certificate was refused, as we already patched.

About 160 of these handshakes stood out: the certificates’ Subject Alternative Names (SANs) were naming other organizations’ domains, unrelated to the Server Name Indication (SNI) requested in the handshake. Some of those names were domains related to consumer IoT devices. We noticed as well that those forged certificates were made after the keys leaked and some were valid for over two years, longer than any public CA may issue. However, these certificates looked like the servers' own default certificates rather than part of an attempt to intercept our connections. They named domains other than the ones being connected to, so they would have failed hostname verification anyway. And in several cases, a server presented the same certificate to connections from many of our locations, which means it came from the server itself rather than from something on a single network path.

Thus while there is no evidence of the weak keys being used to intercept Cloudflare's connections so far, these keys appear to have been used to forge certificates within hours of the weakness becoming public: one of the forged certificates we saw was dated October 20 at 18:19 UTC, less than an hour after Mozilla's bug report was made public. This does not exclude carefully targeted interception. For that we have to rely on the usual indirect signals of system compromise — and so far, we have not seen any such signals.

How many visitors are still vulnerable?  So much about patching Cloudflare, but what about our visitors? We cannot directly test whether a visitor still trusts the weak keys without breaking connections, so we have to do something more indirect. For that we used our   challenge pages  :

We rolled out an update to send out two probe connections on a fraction of challenge pages: one probe to   ca1.cloudflarecaptcha.com   and one to   ca2.cloudflarecaptcha.com  . Initially we installed an eMudhra signed certificate on ca1.cloudflarecaptcha.com and a regularly signed certificate on ca2.cloudflarecaptcha.com as control. Then we record whether these probes succeeded. This allows us to see if visitors that are served a challenge page still trust the weak eMudhra keys.

What did we find? With 50 million probes over the last week, we see this:

Big caveat upfront: by design the traffic to these challenge pages is highly skewed. There are many (unconfirmed) bots in there. Also, only clients that execute JavaScript (like browsers) will send probes.

The jump in the data is due to the following changes—all times are UTC:

October 23 15:30, we changed our control endpoint to also serve an eMudhra certificate, but this time without   signed certificate timestamps   (SCTs). There were some differences in acceptance, but not large. We could’ve added a new endpoint, but that would’ve required a slow release of our challenge platform. Changing the endpoint was easier.

October 23 16:30, our challenge platform rolled back to a previous version because of an unrelated issue. The probes returned October 27 at 10:00.

October 27 16:37, we noticed we did not send the   G3 cross-sign  , which not all clients knew about, and added it to both endpoints. We removed SCTs from both.

October 27 16:49, we switched ca2 to chain up to the AAA Certificate Services root.

October 27 18:18, we ramped up probes to be included from 1% to 10% of all challenge pages served on non-paying customer zones.

With those caveats out of the way: what do we notice? Up-to-date modern browsers are mostly patched, but bots and old browsers are not. Also embedded browsers, like Android WebView, lag behind patching with 30–40% still accepting. Over the first weekend (with the monitoring gap), we see clear evidence of patching, but afterwards we see little movement.

On October 29 around 18:00 UTC, we released a detection that caught a large influx of bot traffic identifying as Chrome 150-154 on macOS. This can look like patching in the top graph, but it is actually a change in traffic classification: the same user agents show a corresponding increase in acceptance among traffic with bot signals detected in the bottom graph.

Chrome 150-154 on Linux is the notable exception: its acceptance continues to decline, consistent with further patching in that cohort. Given the bot-heavy and changing traffic mix, that evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive. Otherwise, we still see little movement.

Breaking down by network (ASN) we see:

Across the large networks, more than half of probes still accept the compromised chain, both among traffic with no bot signals detected (top graph) and traffic with bot signals detected (bottom graph). Over the weekend we saw some patching, but afterwards the trend has been flat.

The big caveat still holds: traffic is skewed by (unconfirmed) bots. But bots are also just software that need security updates. And if they’re in any way representative of overall software updates, then the picture is quite dire indeed.

What can you do?  Patch! Dennis Jackson has a great   crowdsourced website   with instructions. Especially if you’re a developer on macOS, you want to follow   these instructions  . If you’re a Cloudflare customer, check out last week’s blog post on   what needs to be done on your end   when using certain products like WARP or Tunnel.

Looking ahead  At Cloudflare, we have a quick-revocation mechanism in place in some products. To bring it to more systems at Cloudflare and industry, we’re excited about projects like   upki   that understand a trust store can’t be a static list of root certificate authorities, but needs the ability to be quickly updated with information like revocation and certificate transparency keys. As vulnerabilities are discovered at a faster pace than ever, it is vital that they can be addressed quickly and effectively.
ai_summary: On October 19, 2026, we learned about eMudhra’s eight shockingly weak keys: where eMudhra was trusted to pick a 115-digit number for their virtual combination lock protecting the Internet, they picked the number 4. Not even four digits, just the number 4.
main_event: 4 real? Tracking exploitation and patching of eMudhra’s weak keys
potential_concerns: Based on unconfirmed reports or anonymous insider sources. Awaiting official confirmation.

author: Enrique Somoza

article_content:
Today, Cloudflare services for private origins is generally available. Point a proxied DNS record at a private IP, and Cloudflare reaches the origin over your existing   Cloudflare One connection  . Your origin stays private, while web application firewall (  WAF  ),   caching  ,   bot management  , and   Workers   work just as they do for public origins.

In June,   we launched this capability in closed beta   to address a problem we kept hearing from customers: Their internal APIs, AI agent backends, MCP servers, and operational tools weren’t built to face the Internet, but those services still need to accept requests from partners, customers, or agents over the Internet. Before the beta, putting Cloudflare in front of these services meant exposing a public IP, opening a firewall port, or running  cloudflared  alongside the origin.

Those requirements often left private applications without the same protections and controls they used for public applications, including WAF, bot management, rate limiting, caching, traffic acceleration, rewrites, and Workers.

What is generally available today  During the closed beta, eligible customers requested access through their account team. Today, we’re opening access beyond that beta group.

Point a proxied A or AAAA record at a private IP, and Cloudflare’s application services work as they do for public origins:

WAF and managed rules

Bot management

Rate limiting

Caching

Transform and rewrite rules

Workers

Some limitations remain.   Argo Smart Routing   and   Dedicated CDN Egress IPs   aren’t supported, and origin health checks require   Load Balancing  . See the   developer documentation   for the full list of current limitations.

Your origin keeps its private IP, with no inbound firewall exception required. With   Cloudflare WAN  ,  no connector software on the origin is required. With   Cloudflare Mesh  , a connector runs within your private network and can serve multiple origins.

How it works  Create a proxied A or AAAA record pointing to your origin. For supported private IP ranges,  use   private network routing  is enabled automatically. If your origin uses a public IP that’s reachable only through your private network, you can enable the setting manually.

The rest of the request flow stays the same: TLS termination, WAF, rules, and caching continue to run on Cloudflare’s network.

The setting turns on automatically for RFC 1918 private IPv4 addresses, RFC 6598 CGNAT addresses (100.64.0.0/10), and RFC 4193 unique local IPv6 addresses (fc00::/7). It can’t be turned off for these ranges; attempts to disable it through the API return an error.

What the API looks like  For customers automating deployments through the API, private routing is simply an additional attribute on a standard DNS record.

POST /zones/{zone_id}/dns_records

{

"type": "A",

"name": "app.example.com",

"content": "10.0.0.50",

"ttl": 300,

"proxied": true,

"private_routing": true

}

Behind the scenes, Cloudflare's proxy platform determines where to send traffic for  app.example.com  by querying Cloudflare's Origin API. The response includes metadata indicating that the destination should be reached through a private network path:

{

"zone_name": "example.com",

"ipv4_addresses": ["10.0.0.50"],

"private_routing": true

}   The  private_routing  flag is the key signal. When our proxy sees it, instead of attempting to connect directly to the private IP address over the public Internet, it hands the request to our private networking layer, which then routes the connection across the customer's existing private network connectivity, whether that's   IPsec  ,   GRE  ,   Cloudflare Tunnel  ,   CNI  , or Cloudflare Mesh.

The   beta post   covers the routing layer in more detail.

Get started  Before you begin, you’ll need:

The Private Origins entitlement on your account. Ask your account team to turn it on.

Cloudflare One connectivity   using IPsec, GRE, CNI, Cloudflare Tunnel, or   Cloudflare Mesh  .

Unified Routing enabled on your account, unless you connect over Cloudflare Tunnel (Tunnel doesn't need it). New and existing accounts can upgrade through their account team.

If you connect over Cloudflare WAN or Cloudflare Mesh, configure a return route for Cloudflare’s source ranges: 100.64.0.0/12 for IPv4 and 2606:4700:cf1:5000::/64 for IPv6. Then, create a proxied A or AAAA record for the private IP and confirm that  Use private network routing  is enabled. Your existing WAF, cache, and bot management configuration applies to that hostname without further changes.

Then, create a proxied A or AAAA record for the private IP and confirm that  Use private network routing  is enabled. Your existing WAF, cache, and bot management configuration applies to that hostname without further changes.

One note from the beta: if requests time out and nothing arrives at the origin, check the return route first. A missing route for Cloudflare’s source range was the most common setup failure we saw.

Once enabled, follow our   developer documentation  , which walks through the full setup.

What comes next  Today’s release covers public traffic reaching private origins. Next, we’re working on private-to-private traffic: users, services, and AI agents on private networks reaching applications on other private networks through Cloudflare’s application services.

Engineering work is underway, and we’re targeting a closed beta in early 2027. If you’d like to participate, talk to your account team.

The goal is to give private applications the same protections and controls as public applications. An employee opening  wiki.company.internal , for example, could benefit from WAF, rate limiting, and bot management. Service-to-service traffic between clouds and data centers could use those controls too, even when neither side touches the public Internet.

For now, today’s release brings the WAF, caching, bot management, and Workers you use for public applications to private origins over connectivity you already operate.

Questions or feedback? Join the conversation in our   community forums   or reach out to your account team.

title: Cloudflare DDoS Threat Report 2026 Q3: More swarms, fewer giants
author: Cloudforce One
description:
Welcome to the 26th edition of Cloudflare's DDoS Threat Report. This edition covers the third quarter of 2026 — July, August, and September — and returns the series to its quarterly cadence following the combined H1 2026 volume. The analysis is produced by   Cloudforce One  , Cloudflare's Threat Intelligence organization, providing a comprehensive analysis of the evolving threat landscape of   Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks   based on data from the   Cloudflare network  .

Key insi...
article_content:
Welcome to the 26th edition of Cloudflare's DDoS Threat Report. This edition covers the third quarter of 2026 — July, August, and September — and returns the series to its quarterly cadence following the combined H1 2026 volume. The analysis is produced by   Cloudforce One  , Cloudflare's Threat Intelligence organization, providing a comprehensive analysis of the evolving threat landscape of   Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks   based on data from the   Cloudflare network  .

Key insights   Short-burst, low-bandwidth attacks lasting under 10 minutes and 1 Gbps surged by 208%. Conversely, hyper-volumetric attacks exceeding 1 Tbps plummeted by nearly 69% from Q2, possibly a reflection of law enforcement actions against four major Internet of Things (IoT) botnets earlier in the year. However, variants continue to emerge, proving that IoT botnets remain a durable, high-volume threat to network infrastructure.

Threat actors dramatically shifted their reflection and amplification tactics, abruptly abandoning CLDAP floods, which collapsed by 99.5% quarter-over-quarter. Instead, attackers pivoted heavily toward other connectionless protocols, driving a 215% surge in DNS amplification and a 122% increase in general UDP floods.

Attack targets broadened significantly across both industries and geographies, with the United States reclaiming the most-attacked position from China. Canada and Israel experienced sharp spikes in targeted attacks — jumping 10 and 7 spots respectively — while juggling geopolitical tensions, trade disputes, and contentious domestic events. At the same time, the operational focus shifted away from media organizations toward a wider array of industry targets, including consumer services, Internet infrastructure, and adult entertainment.

Q3 by the numbers: 8,200 DDoS attacks every hour  Across its network in the third quarter of 2026, Cloudflare autonomously mitigated 18.2 million network-layer DDoS attacks and 14.4 trillion HTTP DDoS requests. That works out to approximately 8,226 network-layer DDoS attacks per hour, or about 197,400 per day — one attack every 0.44 seconds. The quarter's mitigated traffic totaled 272.6 PB at the network layer and 95.1 PB at the HTTP layer.

More swarms, fewer giants  Short-burst, mid-range, high-count attacks — the operational signature of DDoS-for-hire "booter" services — accelerated this quarter. These attacks primarily targeted computer software, gambling and casinos, and information technology industries. Cloudflare autonomously mitigated 18.2 million network-layer DDoS attacks in Q3 2026, a +208% increase from   the same quarter in 2025  :

96% ended in under 10 minutes

98% stayed under 1 Gbps, more than enough to overwhelm a server or website

On the other hand, network-level hyper-volumetric attacks (those exceeding 1 Tbps) reversed course, dropping to 251 attacks in Q3 from   805 in Q2   — coinciding with   law enforcement action   in early 2026 that dismantled four of the largest IoT DDoS botnets: Aisuru, KimWolf, JackSkid, and Mossad.

Still, IoT-based botnets remain a durable high-volume threat as the ecosystem churns through new variants such as   Dysphoria   and   Evooo1Bot  .   Mirai  -classified mitigation peaked in August at 57.23 PB, representing 46.5% of all mitigated network-layer bytes in Q3, including four days — August 16, 19, 23, and 25 — that each cleared three petabytes. The quarter's longest sustained Mirai attack ran 49.7 hours between August 19 and August 21.

Vector shifts: the collapse of CLDAP and rise of UDP  The most dramatic vector shift of the quarter was downward.   CLDAP   (Connectionless Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) attacks — where small queries with a forged victim IP address trick public domain controllers (UDP 389) into reflecting massive, amplified responses back at the target — experienced a dramatic +580% quarter-over-quarter surge in the first half of the year before collapsing to just 0.05% of attacks in Q3.

Meanwhile,   DNS amplification   surged 215% to account for 3.43% of all network-layer attacks, exploiting open   DNS resolvers   in a similar reflection-and-amplification pattern to CLDAP: small spoofed queries, large replies directed at the victim. Other   UDP floods   climbed from 14.06% to 31.31% of network-layer attacks. UDP is a connectionless transport protocol, which makes it a convenient vehicle for raw volumetric attacks: attackers send large numbers of UDP packets to random or specific ports on the target, forcing the target to check for a listening application and respond, consuming its network and compute resources.

Most-attacked industry  While Media, Production & Publishing remained the most-attacked industry in Q3 2026, its overall share is roughly a quarter of its Q2 level, and the focus has moved across a wider set of industries. Internet rose from outside the top 10 to #6; Consumer Services and Adult Entertainment also climbed in, reaching #8 and #9 respectively.

Most-attacked locations  Geographic surges: Canada and Israel climb the ranks  Adding to an already turbulent period of bilateral trade disputes, Canada jumped from #16 to #6, driven by attacks against its Retail, Telecommunications, Service providers & carriers, and Marketing & advertising industries.

Israel moved 7 spots to take #10 as a result of sustained DDoS activity in mid-September. While this period was marked by   contentious decisions   ahead of parliamentary elections and the Rosh Hashanah holiday, there was also a massive, documented   surge in hostile cyber warfare   targeting Israel this year.

Top 10  The United States was the most-attacked location in Q3 2026, while China was number #2 and Indonesia rose into the top three at 2.93% of total attacks. The U.S.-China pairing at the top is consistent with the first half of 2026, when China finished #1 and the U.S. #2; the countries have traded positions as attention and attacker preferences shift.

Strengthening global defenses and helping to defend the Internet

Cloudflare's network is designed to absorb this kind of growth in DDoS threats. Every service on our network is protected by   free, unmetered DDoS protection   that runs   at every one of our 330+ cities globally  , backed by   500 Tbps of network capacity  . Autonomy is the point: our systems detect and mitigate attacks   without human intervention  . And they need to, because as this quarter's distributions make clear, most attacks end long before a human analyst could see the alert, and the largest attacks still regularly exceed 1 Tbps at a cadence measured in hundreds per quarter.

To help hosting providers, cloud computing platforms, and Internet service providers identify and take down the abusive IP addresses and accounts that launch these attacks, we leverage Cloudflare's unique vantage point on DDoS attacks to provide   a free DDoS Botnet Threat Feed for Service Providers  .

Over 800 networks worldwide have signed up for this feed, and we've already seen great collaboration across the community to take down botnet nodes. For a continuously-updated view of attack trends across the Internet, visit   Cloudflare Radar  .    

About Cloudforce One  Driven by a mission to help defend the Internet,   Cloudforce One   draws on telemetry from Cloudflare's global network — which protects more than 20% of the web — to drive threat research and operational response, protecting critical systems for millions of organizations worldwide.

title: Introducing the Cloudflare PHP Capture the Flag challenge
author: Celso Martinho
description:
Update — October 30, 2026:  Thank you to everyone who has participated in the PHP Capture the Flag challenge. We have received a strong response from the security research community, and the submissions have helped us harden our existing php2shell WAF protections and create new detections.

Details of managed-rule changes are available in the   Cloudflare WAF changelog  .

The CTF remains open. We encourage researchers to continue submitting materially distinct, reproducible bypasses through the...
article_content:
Update — October 30, 2026:  Thank you to everyone who has participated in the PHP Capture the Flag challenge. We have received a strong response from the security research community, and the submissions have helped us harden our existing php2shell WAF protections and create new detections.

Details of managed-rule changes are available in the   Cloudflare WAF changelog  .

The CTF remains open. We encourage researchers to continue submitting materially distinct, reproducible bypasses through the Cloudflare HackerOne program. We will share further information and feedback as the challenge progresses. Thank you again for your contributions.

Last week was one for the Internet security history books. First,   eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised  , creating the possibility of forged certificates that could be used to impersonate servers. Then came   php2shell  : serious vulnerabilities in PHP, the runtime behind a large portion of the Web.

Cloudflare worked around the clock as these events unfolded to protect our customers and help protect the Internet. We shipped client updates and   multiple mitigations  , updated our web application firewall (WAF) with new rules to block attackers from exploiting the PHP vulnerabilities, and introduced a new feature called   full transaction detection  .

As always in situations like this, these new capabilities were made available on all plans, including Free.

Put our WAF to the test  Protecting systems from vulnerabilities like these is always an ongoing process, not a one-time event. The widespread adoption of AI allows attackers to discover new vectors with unprecedented speed and efficiency, so collecting real-world data to test our assumptions and strengthen defenses is essential.

That’s why today we're launching the   Cloudflare PHP Capture the Flag challenge  , run through our   Bug Bounty program  . We've put a deliberately vulnerable PHP installation behind our WAF, and we're inviting security researchers on HackerOne to try to bypass the protections and capture a flag.

How this Capture the Flag (CTF) works  We are keeping this simple. The challenge focuses on   CVE-2026-109618   and   CVE-2026-109619  , the two PHP vulnerabilities behind   php2shell  . The target runs stock   PHP 8.5.11   (with standard PHP extensions), Apache 2 (via mod_php), and an empty index.php inside a   Cloudflare Container  , with our default WAF protection rules for these vulnerabilities enabled in front of it. Inside the sandbox is a file called  /flag .

The sandbox is reset every few minutes, including the flag file.

Your mission, should you choose to accept it:  bypass the WAF protections, exploit the PHP sandbox, and recover the contents of /flag . You can use your own research tools. The   challenge page   has the environment details, scope, and flag verification form.

Challenge requirements  This limited-time challenge is run via   Cloudflare's Bug Bounty program on HackerOne  . All aspects of this challenge are subject to HackerOne   terms   and the Cloudflare HackerOne   program rules   the (“Bounty Terms”). If you find an eligible bypass, you must follow these requirements in order to claim the bounty:

All participants must sign up for a HackerOne account and review and agree to the Bounty Terms   before   participating in the CTF.

Demonstrate attacker-controlled PHP code or command execution inside the sandbox through an authorized POST request.

Use that remote code execution (RCE) to recover the current contents of /flag, then successfully verify the flag through   the CTF user interface   (UI). Verify promptly before a reset; retain the successful result for later review.

Submit a private report to Cloudflare on HackerOne. Include PHP CTF in the title and provide:  The endpoint, complete payload, and request sequence, preserving relevant headers, encoding, and body bytes.

Raw request/response captures or a readable proof of concept sufficient to reproduce the full chain.

An explanation of the WAF bypass, executed code or command, and how that execution recovered /flag.

The attempt ID, successful UI verification result, and exploit/verification UTC timestamps. Include the flag privately if needed for verification.

What makes the method or payload materially distinct, and related submissions you know about.

UI verification does not submit a   HackerOne   report or establish reporting priority. File disclosure without RCE, RCE without successful flag recovery and UI verification, local-only exploits, rediscovery of the known PHP vulnerabilities, and WAF detection differences or partial chains without the full objective are not eligible.

Awards require a  materially distinct Firewall (WAF) bypass method , even for the same PHP CVE. Reports using the  same Firewall-bypass mechanism are duplicates , regardless of differences in the PHP exploit, payload, RCE technique, or flag-recovery method. New flags, resets, attempt IDs, or cosmetic changes—including equivalent encodings—do not qualify as unique. Equivalent submissions are duplicates even if unfixed; only the first complete, reproducible HackerOne report is considered. Cloudflare makes final duplicate and reward decisions.

We record attempted metadata and request payloads to help analyze reports, so please use test data only. Do not send credentials, personal information, or anything else you would not want included in a research record. Read Cloudflare’s   privacy notice   before testing.

Testing is authorized only against the challenge hostname's WAF-protected  /php/*  endpoints (POST method only). Other Cloudflare services, direct access to the underlying infrastructure, the upstream PHP project, and third-party systems are out of scope. No denial of service, high-volume scanning, persistence, social engineering, or attacks on other participants. If you get a 429 or 503, back off.

In the event of any conflict between this blog post and the Bounty Terms, the Bounty Terms shall prevail.

Cloudflare reserves the right to suspend or terminate this challenge at any time. Once the competition is removed from HackerOne, it is officially terminated, so please refer to the Cloudflare HackerOne page for the most up-to-date information on whether this challenge remains open.

Not a substitute for patching  Our WAF protects you, but it is not a replacement for fixing vulnerable software. Response blocking can prevent exposed data from reaching an attacker, but it cannot undo actions already performed at the origin. If you run PHP, follow the   latest PHP security advisories   and apply the relevant updates.

Last week was a reminder that helping build a better Internet often takes many people—researchers, maintainers, and teams across the industry—doing difficult, urgent work together.

We hope this challenge gives everyone a useful way to join in. Head over to   php-rce.cloudflare.app   if you want to participate: the flag is there, and we'd like to know if you can get it.

We have received a strong response from the security research community, and the submissions have helped us harden our existing php2shell WAF protections and create new detections.

title: What took the Internet offline in Q3 2026
author: Lai Yi Ohlsen
description: The Internet can feel invisible when everything is working normally. But when connectivity breaks, the many systems it depends upon become evident in an instant. Because Cloudflare’s global network handles more than 20% of the web’s traffic, it offers a unique perspective of how Internet traffic is behaving. When failures in infrastructure, power, policy, or security disrupt access to the Internet,   Cloudflare Radar   can observe the impact by monitoring traffic to our customers. Each quarter, ...
article_content:
The Internet can feel invisible when everything is working normally. But when connectivity breaks, the many systems it depends upon become evident in an instant. Because Cloudflare’s global network handles more than 20% of the web’s traffic, it offers a unique perspective of how Internet traffic is behaving. When failures in infrastructure, power, policy, or security disrupt access to the Internet,   Cloudflare Radar   can observe the impact by monitoring traffic to our customers. Each quarter, we review the disruptions detected and annotated on Radar, highlighting what happened, where it happened, and the broader conditions that shaped each event.

In this post, we examine the major categories of Internet disruptions observed during the third quarter of 2026, including government-directed shutdowns, power outages and natural disasters.

Disruptions at a glance  Between July and September, Internet disruptions were largely driven by failures in the systems the Internet depends on. Power grids failed in Cuba, Honduras, Guam, Ukraine, and several other countries. Natural disasters damaged electricity and telecommunications infrastructure from Nepal to Colombia. Government-directed shutdowns remained the most frequent source of disruption, driven largely by exam-related shutdowns in Iraq, while renewed conflict in Ethiopia’s Tigray region showed how quickly connectivity can become part of a broader political and humanitarian crisis. Outages within the United States, Japan, and Portugal — countries with a relatively strong history of Internet resilience — remind us that no country is immune to disruption.

In total, Cloudflare Radar recorded 49 disruptions during the quarter. Government-directed shutdowns accounted for 19 incidents, including 18 exam shutdowns in Iraq. Power outages followed with 14 incidents, while natural disasters accounted for five.

Power failure was a leading cause of disruptions  The Internet is designed to be distributed and resilient, but that resilience still depends on electricity. When power fails, routers, mobile base stations, data centers, interconnection facilities, and the networks that connect them can fail with it. Over the past three months, that dependency was one of the clearest patterns in Radar’s disruption data.  Power outages were the second-most common cause of disruptions by incident count this quarter, behind government-directed exam shutdowns.

In Cuba, Internet disruptions followed the erratic patterns of an unstable power grid. Radar observed four power-related outages across the quarter, meaning connectivity was affected by grid failures at least once a month. The outages took place July 6, July 14, August 3, and a three-day blackout from September 18 to 20. The traffic volume decreases ranged from 18% on July 14 to 59% on August 3.

Honduras illustrated how a localized infrastructure failure can produce national-level effects. A power failure on September 10 at an interconnection facility affected at least 11 major providers, showing how concentrated traffic exchange points can become single points of failure. The outage lasted approximately three hours, during which HTTP traffic across the country fell by 63%.

Two notable exceptions were the cross-border provider Telecomunicaciones de Guatemala (AS14754) and mobile carrier Celtel (AS52262), which were unaffected. This suggests that their Honduran connectivity may rely more heavily on infrastructure outside the country.

Cloudflare Radar - Traffic volume by autonomous system

On July 5, a power outage in Sevastopol, Ukraine, caused an eight-hour blackout, with HTTP traffic dropping by 98%. A little over a month later, on August 12, drone strikes targeting energy infrastructure caused another power outage, resulting in a ten-hour Internet disruption and up to a 95% decline in traffic volume. As discussed in more detail below, geopolitical conflict remains a major driver of Internet disruptions. These incidents also show how conflict, energy infrastructure, and Internet connectivity are fundamentally intertwined.

Cloudflare Radar - HTTP traffic

Cloudflare Radar - HTTP traffic

Also of note: on August 13, a cooling system failure at a data center in the U.S. city of Phoenix caused a near-total drop in Internet traffic from  Namecheap (AS22612) . Outages such as these will be important to watch as the role of cooling systems becomes increasingly critical.

Beyond the larger outages in Cuba, Honduras, and Ukraine, power-related disruptions also appeared across a wide range of countries, including Eswatini, Botswana, Tajikistan, Kenya, Saint Lucia, Georgia, and Gabon. Some of these events were caused by sudden failures, while others, such as planned load-shedding in Eswatini, reflected deliberate efforts to manage constrained power supply. Their scale and duration varied, but together they point to the same underlying dependency: when power systems become unstable, Internet connectivity often becomes unstable with them.  In total, Radar observed 14 power-related disruptions across 10 countries during the quarter.

The physical world takes the virtual world offline  Last quarter,   Radar reported   on the impact of Super Typhoon Sinlaku, as it moved through the Mariana Islands, knocking out power and, in turn, Internet connectivity in Guam, where   HTTP traffic took four days to return to typical levels  .

Super Typhoon Bavi followed Sinlaku by less than three months, giving Guam two major storm-related connectivity disruptions in a single year. Officials appeared to take earlier preparedness steps ahead of Bavi, including declaring a state of emergency before peak storm conditions. Even so, the storm caused widespread power outages. The   Guam Power Authority   reported that strong winds brought down key transmission lines, leaving only about 25% of distribution feeders online at one point. From a connectivity perspective, the outcome was familiar: widespread power outages, downed transmission lines, and a multi-day recovery period for Internet traffic.

Cloudflare Radar - HTTP traffic

In Japan, an earthquake of similar magnitude, 7.1, prompted evacuation orders affecting roughly   150,000 people in Kumamoto  . The impact on Internet connectivity primarily appeared in desktop traffic, while mobile traffic remained largely unaffected.

Cloudflare Radar - HTTP requests time series for Kumamoto, Japan

In Colombia, a magnitude 7.4 earthquake in August caused building collapses, injuries, mass evacuations, and a four-and-a-half-day Internet disruption. Damage to fiber-optic infrastructure, compounded by the wider earthquake aftermath, drove a   significant drop in traffic from Colombia Telecomunicaciones (AS3816)  .

Cloudflare Radar - HTTP traffic

Finally, in Nepal, sudden flash floods swept through the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river systems on August 26, affecting communities across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading districts. The flooding damaged homes, infrastructure, and essential services, including power, which in turn disrupted regional Internet connectivity. The outage recorded on Radar lasted two hours, during which HTTP traffic dropped by up to 18%.

Cloudflare Radar - HTTP traffic

Exam shutdowns continue in Iraq  Government-directed shutdowns were the largest cause of disruptions in Q3, the majority of which occurred in Iraq with separate scheduled shutdowns occurring throughout the quarter. The shutdowns took place on a strict schedule 03:30–04:00 UTC, lasting about 15-90 min each. The majority occurred between August 26 and September 28, with three occurring between July 1 and 8.

Cloudflare Radar - HTTP traffic

Per   Internet Society Pulse  , “In a   video message  , Minister Mustafa Sanad, Iraq's Minister of Communication, confirmed the shutdown and vowed to develop a digital system that would eliminate the need for centralized exam distribution and, by extension, the need to shut down Internet access on exam days.” Cloudflare Radar will continue to monitor the country’s networks as the development of the new system progresses.

Notably, Syria and Sudan, two countries that have also frequently used exam-related Internet shutdowns in recent years, did not record similar disruptions this quarter. However, this likely reflects differences in exam calendars rather than a clear shift in policy. Radar will continue to monitor whether future national exam periods bring renewed shutdowns in either country.

Disruptions coincide with political events    In Ethiopia, renewed conflict in the Tigray region was accompanied by a government-directed Internet shutdown that lasted 10 days. Traffic dropped by 100%, signaling a full-scale shutdown.

Cloudflare Radar - HTTP traffic

The disruption revived memories of the extensive blockade imposed during Ethiopia’s civil war from 2020 to 2022, when Tigray was largely cut off from telecommunications, electricity, banking services, fuel, and humanitarian aid (  France24  ), which the World Health Organization   described   as a “de facto blockade.” Although this latest outage appears to have remained localized to Tigray, its impact was still visible in country-level traffic, with HTTP traffic falling by up to 30%.

Cloudflare Radar - HTTP traffic

On September 19, during nationwide elections, fiber-optic cable damage in Russia’s Far East caused regional connectivity disruptions affecting Chukotka, Magadan Oblast, Kamchatka Krai, and Sakhalin Oblast. Rostelecom   described   the incidents as deliberate damage to backbone fiber lines and said connectivity was restored using backup channels. Radar data alone cannot determine whether the cable damage was related to the elections, but the timing is notable.

Cloudflare Radar - HTTP traffic

Cloudflare Radar - HTTP traffic

Cloudflare Radar - HTTP traffic

A quarter shaped by shutdowns and power outages, but also resilience  Across Q3 2026, government-directed shutdowns were the most frequent source of disruption, driven largely by Iraq’s exam-related shutdowns. Power outages were close behind, affecting networks across Cuba, Honduras, Ukraine, Eswatini, Botswana, Tajikistan, Kenya, Saint Lucia, Georgia, and Gabon. Natural disasters and conflict added another layer of disruption, reminding us that Internet resilience depends on far more than routers and cables. It depends on electricity, physical infrastructure, policy decisions, and the ability of networks to route around failure.

Radar also observed outages inside individual networks, including   One Communications (AS19863)   in Guyana following a   cable cut  ,   MEO (AS3243) in Portugal   following a reported “  mass attack  ”,   Digicel Haiti (AS27653)  ,   TurkNet (AS12735)   in Turkey, and   Fanap Telecom (AS206065)   in Iran.

Each of these events demonstrates the Internet’s fragility, but also its resilience. Many disruptions were brief: 14 saw traffic return to typical levels in under an hour, and 16 recovered in less than three hours. But short outages can still have real consequences for the people affected, especially during storms, earthquakes, conflict, or political unrest. Access to the Internet is often access to information, coordination, safety, and help.

Cloudflare Radar will continue to monitor Internet disruptions around the world and share what we see from Cloudflare’s global network. Follow Cloudflare Radar on X   @CloudflareRadar   and Bluesky   @radar.cloudflare.com   for updates.

title: Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model, and our remediation with SGLang
author: Kevin Flansburg
description:

article_content:
On September 8, 2026, we were alerted by a security researcher, Gadi Evron from  Knostic , to a tenant isolation issue affecting the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model ( @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 ) starting on August 27, 2026. We have remediated the issue, and we restored the model on September 9. We have confirmed that no other model hosted on Workers AI was affected.

Between August 27 and September 9, a small number of customers using the GLM 5.3 Workers AI model received responses that contained data from other customers' requests made to the same model shortly before theirs. In total, 155 responses were affected, all to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens.

After excluding our own testing and the researcher's, the requests we identified are consistent in timing and volume with ordinary long-context use, not with someone repeatedly exploiting the bug. We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation.

Today we are publishing this report alongside a post from SGLang, the open-source inference engine that we use, as a coordinated disclosure. This post describes the bug that caused this issue, our response timeline, and the subsequent hardening we have conducted on our production SGLang deployments. We also detail our continued efforts with the upstream maintainers of SGLang to address this and similar bugs.

What happened  GLM is a text generation model from  Z.ai  that is built for agentic coding workflows; it is one of the many   models   available through Workers AI. Gadi Evron submitted a report on September 8 through our HackerOne program stating that very long prompts sent to  @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3  on Workers AI sometimes returned text that belonged to other users' sessions. Cloudflare reproduced the issue the next morning and took the model offline within 40 minutes of declaring an incident. We then deployed a corrected configuration and a patched inference engine, and restored service the same day.

This specific report of cross-request KV cache exposure was the result of two overlapping issues. The first was a misconfiguration of the open-source inference engine, SGLang, used by Cloudflare. We deployed GLM 5.3 with a 1,048,576-token context window, but the KV cache pool on our prefill GPUs only had room for 681,280 tokens. We were aware of this mismatch before launch. We expected the engine to return an error for any prompt it could not process, and our long-context tests returned successful responses, so we did not believe this to be an issue.

The second was a bug in how SGLang handled the resulting over-length requests in disaggregated prefill/decode mode. A prompt that did not fit the pool was internally marked as rejected and replaced with a one-token placeholder, but instead of aborting the request and returning a client error, prefill generated the KV cache for the placeholder prompt and transferred it to the decode node. The decode node received a "transfer complete" message and assumed that prefill overwrote the KV cache from previous requests with the full prompt for this request, when in fact it left the majority of the previous state intact. The decode node subsequently generated a response while attending over stale cache pages that still held data from earlier requests. As a result, responses to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens could contain data from other users' GLM 5.3 sessions.

Immediate remediation  After   disabling the model  , we took the following actions to correct this vulnerability before restoring public access to it:

To fix our configuration, we made the pool hold the full context.  We adjusted our GLM 5.3 configuration to match our GLM 5.2 configuration, which freed enough GPU memory that the prefill KV pool now holds about 2.04 million tokens, roughly twice the 1,048,576-token context length. A prompt that fits the context window now always fits the pool, so the rejection path is never reached for a valid request. This alone prevents the bug from being exercised.

To fix the engine, we also made the rejection path safe.  Relying on pool size alone is fragile: any change to quantization, tensor parallelism, CUDA graph sizes, or a future model version changes the pool size in a way that's easy to miss. Furthermore, there may be other situations in which the prefill scheduler can reject a request and trigger the same bug. To prevent this, we also patched the engine so that a request carrying a pending rejection is retired at the disaggregation admission queue, with its original error, before any bootstrap, allocation, or KV transfer happens. We proposed this upstream as   #38704  , which also had the decode node verify that the number of tokens transferred matches the number it reserved. The fix was already on SGLang  main  in   #36988  , merged September 6 for a related failure path but not yet released. The maintainers also merged   #38935  , which rejects these requests earlier, following our approach.

We validated both changes against the researcher's reproduction script and our own canary-marker tests before restoring the model.

Background: how we serve GLM 5.3  Workers AI runs GLM 5.3 with SGLang in a disaggregated configuration: a pool of prefill GPUs processes the prompt and produces the model's KV cache for it, then hands that cache over remote direct memory access (RDMA), via  Mooncake , to a pool of decode GPUs that generate the response. We have written about this architecture before in our posts on   high-performance LLMs   and   smaller, faster, safer models  .

The KV cache in GPU memory is a shared pool of fixed-size pages. Each request is assigned pages when it is admitted and releases them when it finishes. Pages are not currently zeroed between requests; the next request that gets a page simply overwrites it. This approach is common among inference engines and is necessary to achieve the best performance, but it means that the inference engine is responsible for tracking ownership of these memory pages. KV cache page ownership and lifetime tracking has to deal with not just shared ownership within a node (KV cache offload and token generation both access the memory with different lifetimes), but also ownership that is technically shared with the remote prefill node (which holds a simultaneous mutable reference to the page).

Furthermore, the size of this pool is not a configuration value. SGLang sizes it at startup from whatever GPU memory remains after loading the model weights. The model's advertised context length is a separate configuration value. Nothing forces the two to agree, and it is our job to check that they do.

Issue one: misconfiguration  On our GLM 5.3 prefill nodes with our configuration, the pool came to 681,280 tokens while the model's context length is 1,048,576 tokens. The selected KV pool size is printed by SGLang in logs during startup and exposed as a metric. We were aware of this size mismatch; however, during pre-launch testing we observed successful HTTP status codes and a streaming body with no error frames during benchmarking. We assumed that the engine was capable of gracefully handling the difference between the KV cache pool and requested context window via streaming or some other mechanism.

This was one critical gap in our testing: we only validated HTTP response codes and engine performance at long contexts, without validating model output and coherence. We now check KV pool size against context length directly, from the running engine, before any disaggregated deployment change ships, rather than inferring it from response codes.

Issue two: SGLang bug  In v0.5.21, the SGLang team has now addressed this bug in how it was handling prompts longer than the KV pool size. Here’s what was happening before.

When a prompt arrived that was longer than the KV pool could hold, SGLang's scheduler rejected it. The rejection path ( Req.set_finish_with_abort ) recorded the error to be returned to the client and swapped the prompt for a one-token placeholder so that the request could drain through the normal batch machinery without allocating real memory. On a single-node deployment this worked: the placeholder ran, the batch finished, and the client received an error.

In disaggregated mode such as we operate, the admission queues on both prefill and decode checked whether a request was  finished , not whether it was  rejected . A rejected request reported itself as live. So:

Bootstrap.  The router told the decode node the prompt length (8 pages in the diagram). Decode reserved 8 KV pages for the request.

Prefill admission.  The prefill admission queue admitted any request where  req.finished()  was False. A rejected request stored its rejection in  to_finish , not  finished_reason , so  finished()  still returned False. The rejected request was admitted.

Prefill forward pass.  Rejection had already replaced the prompt with a one-token placeholder. Prefill ran a trivial forward pass on that one token.

KV transfer.  Prefill sent one page of KV to decode and signaled that the transfer was complete.

Decode admission.  Decode's admission queue had the same  finished()  check, so it accepted the handoff.

Decode attention.  Decode started generating and attention read all 8 reserved pages. Only page P0 had been written by this request. Pages P1 to P7 still held what earlier requests left in them: other users' prompts and partial generations.

Response.  The client got HTTP 200 instead of HTTP 400.  prompt_tokens  matched the long prompt and the reply was coherent. It arrived faster than an 8-page prefill should take, and it contained content from other users' KV pages.

Every request over the threshold behaved this way. This bug had been reported to SGLang by another user as issue   #30233   on July 6, 2026, which Cloudflare noticed while investigating this incident. We had been flagging these types of issues with SGLang since v0.5.10 and this security incident sped up work that Cloudflare had already started in collaboration with the SGLang team. The patch for this issue was released in SGLang v0.5.20, with follow-ups in v0.5.21 and v0.5.22, and is available for all other operators dependent on SGLang to use. We highly recommend all operators update SGLang dependencies to v0.5.22 or later. For more details on specific PRs, read on below.

GLM 5.3 was the only model affected by this bug. Every other disaggregated deployment on Workers AI has KV pools larger than its context length on both prefill and decode, so no request could reach the rejection path. We have applied the engine fix and the hardening described below to every model we serve with SGLang, and our deployment checks require them for every new deployment.

Timeline  All times UTC.

When

What

Aug 27, 2026

Sep 8, 2026 - 23:11

Sep 9, 2026 - 13:22

Security incident declared. Product Security reproduced the leak using two independent accounts within 25 minutes.

Sep 9, 2026 - 14:00

After confirming the scope of the issue, GLM 5.3 was set to private. Requests return HTTP 400. Status page updated.

Sep 9, 2026 - 14:35

Root cause identified as the prefill pool being smaller than the context length. Canary prefill node with a larger pool confirmed not susceptible.

Sep 9, 2026 - 14:52

All prefill nodes rolled to the corrected configuration.

Sep 9, 2026 - 19:04

Full deployment rebuilt with the corrected configuration plus a Cloudflare-authored engine patch that correctly returns errors for requests rejected by the prefill scheduler. Validated against the researcher's reproduction script.

Sep 9, 2026 - 19:40

Upstream SGLang merges the admission fix, per-transfer checksums, abort-ACK preservation, and turns deferred KV release on by default.
