Ongoing hardening effort  This bug belongs to a class of KV cache memory-safety bugs that Cloudflare has been working to address for several months. In each case, a page is freed, reused, or read while something else still has a claim on it. We see two common causes.

The first is page lifetime within a single node. Several tasks on a decode node can hold the same page at once: token generation, offload to host memory, the KV transfer receiver, and the abort and error paths. If one of them frees the page while another is still using it, a new request can be given that page while it is still being read or written. Our earlier fixes for decode offload (  #24226  ,   #30899  ) and double release on grammar errors (  #30937  ) were of this kind.

The second is a race across nodes. When a request is aborted while prefill is still writing its KV cache to decode over RDMA, the writes already sent cannot be recalled. If decode frees those pages right away, those pages can be given to another request, and the late writes land in that request's KV cache. Cloudflare has contributed to the effort to fix this race through proposed fixes (  #31357  ,   #38961  ) and a reproduction script (  #32564  ). In both cases the result is corrupted output, or one user's data in another user's response, with no error raised. The bug in this incident was different: a rejected request went through the handoff every time, rather than by a timing accident. But it had the same result: decode reading pages this request never wrote. None of these covered the failure in this incident in which prefill rejected the request, and decode never learned of it.

Since the incident, we have:

Extended deferred release to hold prefill's source pages as well, and to cover every failure type, not just aborts. We proposed it upstream as   #38961  , which was superseded by   #40645  ,   #41402  , and   #41404  .

Deployed bounded Mooncake transfer batches (  #32758  , from the SGLang community), so no single transfer call can outlast the release timeout.

Changed our load balancer so a client disconnect no longer aborts a request mid-transfer. It holds the prefill connection until prefill finishes and the decode connection until the first token, then closes both.

Added a check to every disaggregated deployment change: KV pool size measured against context length, deferred release on both roles, transfer batch bounds inside the release timeout, and all required patches applied.

All of these changes were released to our disaggregated production deployments.

Working with the SGLang team  We met with the SGLang maintainers at RadixArk on September 10, the day after the incident. We agreed that RadixArk would investigate the race conditions we had reported, upstream the integrity-checking idea, and build reproduction tests for this class of bug.

The following have landed on SGLang  main  to address this incident and related KV cache race conditions, and all but one are included in v0.5.22. Operators running disaggregated SGLang should update to v0.5.22 or backport these patches as needed.

Broader KV Canary and KV Checksum model and feature support

What we recommend to other operators  If you run SGLang in disaggregated prefill/decode mode, we recommend the following:

Measure your KV pool and compare it to your context length , on every prefill and decode node, from the engine's startup log, after every change to weights, quantization, parallelism, or memory fraction. If the pool is smaller, lower the context length to fit. Do not rely on a proxy to enforce the limit, and do not assume the engine will reject what does not fit. This is the check we did not enforce.

Upgrade to a build that includes   #36988   and   #38935   (v0.5.22 or later) , so an over-length request is rejected before handoff regardless of pool size. This is the engine-side fix, and it is the backstop for the day your check in step one is wrong.

Run with deferred KV release on both roles  (default after   #41023  ), and bound your Mooncake transfer batches so a single timed-out call cannot leave an unbounded tail of writes.

Turn on corruption detection where your model supports it.   --disaggregation-enable-kv-checksum  and  --kv-canary  do not yet cover every model architecture. Check your logs to confirm requests are being verified. We are working with the SGLang team to extend both checks to more architectures, including GLM 5.3, GLM 5.3 Flash, and DeepSeek V4.

Ensure your proxy is not generating unnecessary aborts.  Configure your load balancer to allow requests to proceed up to the first token, so that you do not trigger an abort that requires cross-node coordination.

Longer term  Integrity by construction  Configuration checks and lifecycle fixes reduce the number of ways a page can be misused. They do not make misuse impossible, and this incident is a reminder that the next bug will have a shape we have not seen. The durable answer is for the engine to detect, at read time, that a request is about to attend over a page it does not own, and fail that one request rather than return someone else's data.

We built a prototype of this over the summer and   described it in August  . Every physical KV page carries a tag that changes when the page is reallocated, each request records the tags it expects, and the mapping is checked before decode reads the cache. In our tests it cost under 1% in throughput and tail latency. We tested it on GLM 5.2 in mid-August, but disabled it shortly afterwards due to reliability issues.

The prototype was also tied to specific attention backends and model architectures, so it could not be a general fix. We are working with the SGLang team to build a production version into the engine that works across every model, rather than maintaining Cloudflare-specific patches. The per-transfer checksum in   #39500   is a first step: it validates the handoff from prefill to decode. Page-level tags go further, because they check every read, including reads long after the transfer.

Integrity by mathematical impossibility  RDMA copies data directly from one node’s memory to another’s. It’s vital for the two machines to agree on where the data goes, how large it is, and when it’s finished; any mismatch can cause the receiver to read the wrong data. This bug is an example of a consistency failure in a distributed system, in which the two machines had inconsistent views of the state of that system.

Elsewhere in Cloudflare, we have put effort into proving the safety of distributed systems using formal verification methods.   Topaz   enables conflict-free IP selection for our authoritative DNS servers. Models of   Meerkat’s   QuePaxa implementation have demonstrated consistency bugs that were subsequently fixed.

We are now directing our experience in formal methods to KV cache transfer engines. This will start with modeling and proving the safety of an RDMA-based KV cache transfer protocol. The goal is to model our production SGLang’s distributed KV cache system using Mooncake, then track and fix any divergence from the safety properties we want to guarantee. The aim is to prove — as far as possible — that a bug like this cannot occur again. Realistically, we expect gaps in what the provers can tell us, but proving the rest of the system allows us to more closely review and monitor those gaps.

Coordinated disclosure  We are publishing this report as part of a coordinated disclosure. We want to thank the researcher, Gadi Evron, who reported this through our HackerOne program with a clear, reproducible script and gave us time to fix it and to coordinate with the SGLang maintainers before publishing. We also want to thank the SGLang team at RadixArk, who treated this as their problem as well as ours and landed the upstream fixes with urgency.

Read more at   the post from the SGLang team  .

If you find a security issue in Workers AI, please report it at   hackerone.com/cloudflare  .

title: Origin Range Requests: Serving large files without range-request tuning
author: Matthew Gumport
description:
A video player seeking to the middle of a movie asks for a few megabytes. Under our old range caching, that one request could make Cloudflare pull 128 MiB from the origin and move it between data centers, sometimes after the viewer had already left. Range requests are how large files get delivered, and caching them naively easily leads to wasted network bandwidth and wasted disk operations when running a CDN at scale.

So we rebuilt how our cache handles them. For R2, Cloudflare's object storage...
article_content:
A video player seeking to the middle of a movie asks for a few megabytes. Under our old range caching, that one request could make Cloudflare pull 128 MiB from the origin and move it between data centers, sometimes after the viewer had already left. Range requests are how large files get delivered, and caching them naively easily leads to wasted network bandwidth and wasted disk operations when running a CDN at scale.

So we rebuilt how our cache handles them. For R2, Cloudflare's object storage, p99 time to first byte dropped by about half, and a follow-up improvement cut   tiered cache   traffic for R2 and similar workloads by about 6%.

Today, we're making that new implementation available as   Origin Range Requests  , a self-service feature on all plans. There's no range size to tune and no need to contact support. Turn it on with a  Cache Rule , and Cloudflare handles the rest.

A request for part of a file  An HTTP range request asks for part of a resource instead of the whole resource. The client sends a normal  GET  with a  Range  header:

GET /movie.mp4 HTTP/1.1

Host: example.com

Range: bytes=1048576-2097151   If the server supports the request, it returns  206 Partial Content  and identifies the returned bytes with  Content-Range :

HTTP/1.1 206 Partial Content

Content-Range: bytes 1048576-2097151/524288000

Content-Length: 1048576   Range requests are common for large objects. A video player can request bytes around a seek position instead of the whole file. A download manager can resume after an interruption. A package manager can fetch part of an artifact. A client can inspect the end of a file without downloading everything before it.

The client decides whether to request a range, and Cloudflare does not change that request. Instead, Origin Range Requests changes how Cloudflare satisfies it.

The range-size problem  Cloudflare has supported range-request caching for years via static zone configuration.

The previous implementation resembled the cache-slicing described in   an nginx blog post  : each client request was mapped to fixed-size ranges of the file, with the range size and file extensions configured per zone.

The size of each range created a tradeoff: small ranges led to many small origin requests and memory pressure on Cloudflare from coalescing all of the requests in-memory, while large ranges caused Cloudflare to download much more data than the client requested. Updates to the range size itself would invalidate cache entries, since the size was part of the cache key.

This design also meant people requesting content through our network could have unpleasant experiences accessing these files. Concurrent requests that fell inside the same range, no matter how far apart each client’s requested range was, could block each other. Our nginx-based cache also couldn’t combine range caching with   concurrent streaming  , a feature we built to let multiple clients read a file from cache while it's still being written. Turning both on together cut responses short, so each range had to be fully downloaded before anyone could read it, and popular files needed a separate origin fetch for every range.

The extra bytes could also cross several parts of our distributed cache: from the origin to one data center, between cache tiers, and then toward the client. Every hop multiplied the waste. No value works equally well for a small seek, a sequential download, a large media file, and every origin and cache topology.

Our internal cache limitations were directly exposed to customers, who should not need to understand our capabilities in-depth to have files served efficiently.

Fortunately, our transition from nginx to a   Pingora  -based caching server created an opportunity to address the implementation problems that had forced a hard-to-use setting onto customers.

Fixed-size cache chunks  The fix came from something Pingora was already doing. To make it easy to resume interrupted downloads, it stores every cached file on disk in fixed-size chunks. If the cache already thinks in chunks, the range size doesn't need to be a setting at all, it can just be the chunk!

For a range request, Cloudflare checks which requested bytes are already cached. It serves those bytes directly. For missing bytes, it fetches origin ranges aligned to the cache's fixed-sized-chunk boundaries, stores the result in the same chunks used for ordinary cache storage, and returns only the bytes requested by the client.

For example, a request for bytes  150-250  can cause Cloudflare to fetch the aligned chunk containing those bytes. The downstream response still contains only  150-250 .

This does not eliminate extra work for requests smaller than our chunk size — such a request can still require fetching the whole chunk containing it. We also are taking on the cost of more work for non-aligned ranges. The difference is that the extra work is bounded and predictable, and no longer determined by a customer-selected range size that can cause unpredictable effects on us and origins.

Coordinating cached and in-flight data  Parsing the  Range  header is straightforward. The harder problem is producing one correct response when the requested bytes are split across cached data, an origin response, and downloads already in progress.

At a high level, the edge:

Looks up the asset headers and range-coverage metadata.

Reads whatever part of the asset it can from disk or streaming in memory.

Fetches missing coverage from the origin using aligned ranges.

Writes the new bytes and records the completed range in metadata.

Combines the pieces and sets  Content-Range  and  Content-Length  for the client response.

This is a coordinator, not a single cache lookup. One request can use a cached prefix, an in-flight download, and a newly fetched suffix. The internal origin response can be larger than the downstream response, but the downstream status and headers describe only the requested range.

If an existing download covers another request's bytes, the second request can attach to that download instead of starting another origin fetch. This shares work during bursts for popular large files.

The design uses the existing cache data model. Headers identify the asset version, the body is stored in bounded chunks, and metadata records which ranges were written successfully.

Validate before composing  Composed range responses are valid only when all bytes belong to the same representation. The coordinator checks that each origin response matches the requested range, that the total asset size is stable, and that the entity tag remains consistent across subrequests.

The  If-Range  header lets a client request a range only if the representation still matches a known validator. If it does not match, Cloudflare returns the full representation instead of combining bytes from different versions.

Cloudflare also avoids composing ranges for a representation it is about to decompress because the range over a set of compressed bytes would be different from those selected by the range in a decompressed response. In these cases, Cloudflare serves the transformed full response rather than advertising a range it cannot honor correctly.

The resulting behavior is standard HTTP:

A satisfiable range receives  206 Partial Content  with an accurate  Content-Range .

An unsatisfiable range receives  416 Range Not Satisfiable .

A response that cannot safely be ranged is served as the complete representation.

What changed in production  Before opening Origin Range Requests to everyone, we moved existing users of the old range-caching feature onto the new implementation, starting with the workloads that hurt us most.

Those workloads had a lot of concurrent range requests against very large files, often on very spiky traffic. Configured range sizes on the old system ran from tens of kilobytes to tens of gigabytes. With a large range size, a request that wouldn't fill a floppy disk could make us download a few DVDs' worth of data from the origin and move it across several data centers, sometimes after the client had already given up and gone elsewhere. With a small range size, one request turned into a long line of tiny origin requests, each holding memory while it waited. Both patterns caused real operational incidents for us.

R2 was the largest internal user. Its configured range size was 64 MiB, so a small read that crossed a range boundary could cost us 128 MiB of transfer between data centers. After moving R2 to the new implementation, we saw:

Faster responses.  Across R2's storage regions, p99 time to first byte dropped by roughly half on both cache hits and misses.

Fewer bytes on our network.  Our most recent change taught the coordinator to combine bytes already on disk with bytes fetched from upstream in a single response. Before, a request was served either entirely from cache or entirely from upstream. After we turned this on for R2, tiered cache traffic for R2 and similar workloads dropped about 6% week over week, which is petabytes less data moving between our data centers every day.

Getting started  Once the cache no longer depended on a customer-selected range size, the product configuration could not be simpler. Customers select matching traffic through   Cache Rules  . Cloudflare handles the chunking and cache coordination.

Origin Range Requests is intended for traffic where clients naturally request parts of a large cacheable object:

Progressive and seekable video such as MP4

Resumable large downloads

Software distributions and package repositories

Disk images, archives, and other multi-gigabyte objects

AI training and inference workloads that transfer large model files or fetch selected regions of model artifacts

Clients that fetch metadata or a small region of a larger file

We intend to make this the default way certain file types are served on our network, modifiable by cache rules.

This feature does not change normal cache eligibility. Enabling it does not make an otherwise uncacheable response cacheable. The origin also needs to support byte ranges for partial origin fetches to be useful.

To turn it on, create a   Cache Rule   that matches your large-file traffic and set Origin Range Requests to On. You can do this in the dashboard under Caching > Cache Rules, or through the API with  origin_range_requests: { "mode": "on" } . Customers choose the traffic; the edge handles the cache coordination and correctness requirements.
ai_summary: A video player seeking to the middle of a movie asks for a few megabytes. Under our old range caching, that one request could make Cloudflare pull 128 MiB from the origin and move it between data centers, sometimes after the viewer had already left.
main_event: Origin Range Requests: Serving large files without range-request tuning

title: Bringing post-quantum cryptography to geographically fenced key management
author: Chetan Agrawal
description:
Today, Cloudflare is launching a post-quantum geographically restricted key manager in support of our Data Localization Suite (DLS) in closed beta. This new PQ GeoKey Manager is a cornerstone of Cloudflare’s data sovereignty solutions, making sure that a customer's decryption keys are only accessible in their chosen geography. GeoKey Manager implements this by wrapping each decryption key such that it can only be decrypted by Cloudflare servers that are located in the allowed geography.

While g...
article_content:
Today, Cloudflare is launching a post-quantum geographically restricted key manager in support of our Data Localization Suite (DLS) in closed beta. This new PQ GeoKey Manager is a cornerstone of Cloudflare’s data sovereignty solutions, making sure that a customer's decryption keys are only accessible in their chosen geography. GeoKey Manager implements this by wrapping each decryption key such that it can only be decrypted by Cloudflare servers that are located in the allowed geography.

While general availability (GA) is planned for Q1 2027, today’s launch is an important milestone on our journey to support our customers’ data sovereignty goals while also migrating all Cloudflare products to   post-quantum (PQ) cryptography  .

Governments, financial institutions, healthcare providers, and defense organizations process highly sensitive data that can remain sensitive for years or decades after it is produced. Encryption is often required to protect this data. When classical, public-key encryption is used, adversaries do not immediately need a quantum computer today to put that data at risk: they can store the ciphertext and retain them until quantum computers can break the public key cryptography protecting it — an attack strategy known as harvest now, decrypt later.

For organizations with geographic requirements, resisting that threat is only half the challenge. At Cloudflare's scale, high availability requires replicating customer data across many servers across our global network. However, many data sovereignty regulations require that certain types of data be processed only within a given geographical region. We must therefore ensure the data is end-to-end encrypted such that only servers within the region have access to the plaintext. In this post, we describe the system that makes this work.

The evolution of GeoKey Manager  Cloudflare pioneered the concept of geo-restricted transport layer security (  TLS  ) keys back in 2017 with   GeoKey Manager  . This gave customers control over the locations where their private TLS keys could be unwrapped on Cloudflare’s anycast network to provide stronger technical guarantees of which region their requests are decrypted into. For instance, a customer could choose to only unwrap their private keys in India. So instead of allowing decryption across Cloudflare’s entire global network, GeoKey Manager makes sure TLS signing for each customer request happens in our India network.

GeoKey Manager evolved again in 2022 with   ciphertext policy attribute based encryption   (ABE). Instead of tying encrypted keys to a fixed set of data centers, ABE expressed geographic requirements using attributes such as country or region, like “region = European Union” or “region = Canada + United States + Mexico”. Newly authorized servers could receive matching decryption capabilities without rewrapping every customer key.

That flexibility created a challenge and opportunity for the post-quantum transition. No production-ready post-quantum ABE scheme is available today, and customers do not need a large number of regions. A simpler design meets the requirement and is easier to maintain and operate. Cloudflare therefore uses hybrid   ML-KEM-768   and   X25519   protection with two kinds of keys, out of which ML-KEM-768 is a   NIST   standard that also opens doors to highly sensitive customers. A regional root key is a symmetric secret tied to one region, and an application-specific key pair is derived from it for a single service, such as   Gateway   or   Tunnel  . This protects private-key material against harvest now, decrypt later while preserving regional key-use boundaries.

Global ciphertext, regional key unwrapping  In its new form, GeoKey Manager is the key foundation for Cloudflare’s data sovereignty solutions. It controls which region protected decryption keys can be used from and when. Separate workstreams determine where tunnels terminate, where traffic is inspected, how it is routed, and where plaintext processing occurs. But all of them depend on the region where a customer’s private key can be unwrapped, because TLS traffic can only be decrypted where that key is available.

During initialization, the edge key service (the component on each Cloudflare edge server that unwraps customer private keys and uses them to serve requests) verifies that it has loaded every regional root key required by its configuration. If a configured key is missing or malformed, the service does not start. After initialization, an individual request also fails closed (Cloudflare rejects it rather than risk unwrapping a key out of region) if its metadata identifies a regional root key that is not locally available. If a request for Germany was somehow trying to decrypt in Spain or France it would fail, since neither Spain nor France have the regional root key for Germany. This guarantees that a regional root key never leaves its region, no matter what.

Cloudflare needs to maintain high performance while keeping our customers’ regionalized data secure at scale. This is where the next version of GeoKey Manager comes in. We are enabling fast performance while logically separating our network by using post-quantum cryptography to restrict where customers’ private keys are unwrapped. Most of our regions will be available for customers to regionalize their workflow, and there may be product specific caveats. Customers select a region and Cloudflare manages everything else needed to unwrap their private keys within the region’s boundary.

How GeoKey Manager ensures that keys are only available in a region  GeoKey Manager controls where wrapped private keys can be unwrapped and used on the data plane. It does not control where requests are forwarded or routed (that’s   Regional Services  ), where tunnels terminate, or where traffic inspection happens (also Regional Services).

GeoKey Manager separates globally distributed wrapped private keys from the regional root key required to unwrap it.   Quicksilver  , our global configuration distribution system, distributes wrapped private keys and its metadata across our network. It does not distribute regional root keys; that happens through a separate provisioning service that stores regional root keys and delivers them only to edge servers authorized for each region. Regional root keys follow a separate, controlled path. On the data plane, a node’s regional configuration, which region a node belongs to, determines which nodes can receive which regional root keys.

Defining key hierarchy and application-specific keys  Every wrapped customer private key carries metadata identifying its service context, regional boundary, and epoch.

The service context is the Cloudflare service that uses the key, such as Tunnel or Gateway. The regional boundary is the approved set of Cloudflare data centers where the key may be unwrapped and used, such as data centers in Germany or the European Union. The epoch identifies which generation of the regional root key the key belongs to; each rotation creates a new epoch.

For example, Acme Co. might have one key for Tunnel in Germany (acme0001) and another for Gateway in Germany (acme0002). Road Runner Inc. might have one key for Tunnel in Germany (runner0001) and another for Gateway in the European Union (runner0002).

Keys with the same service context, regional boundary, and epoch use the same application-specific key pair. Therefore, compromising the Tunnel-Germany application-specific private key could expose both acme0001 and runner0001, but not the Gateway keys. Compromising the Germany regional root key could affect every application-specific key derived from that root for the same epoch, including acme0001, acme0002, and runner0001.

In the current architecture, the application-specific key pair is asymmetric. The public component wraps the customer's private key material, while the private component is required to unwrap it. The resulting wrapped private key is distributed with its service context (  Access  , Gateway, Tunnel,   Cloudflare One client  ), region, and epoch.

Provisioning regional root keys   When Cloudflare/Admin configures a region for a CF1 use case, key management service (which also derives application-specific key pairs and wraps customer private keys) creates a regional root key and associates it with a regional boundary and epoch and sends it to provisioning service for storage and distribution which under the hood uses Vault, which is managed by us on-premises.

Authorizing edge servers for a region   Before an edge server can receive a regional root key, provisioning service evaluates three inputs:

Trusted Platform Module   (TPM) proves that the server possesses a registered hardware identity

Zinc  , Cloudflare's server inventory system, maps that identity to a data center and location

Provisioning service determines which regional root keys the server may access

Zinc updates its membership records for each edge server. This asynchronous process adds new servers as the network grows and removes servers when they are decommissioned. As Cloudflare performs maintenance on data centers in Germany, the definition of which data centers belong in Germany changes in Zinc. That definition is swiftly propagated through our network with Quicksilver so that our edge is up to date. The reverse also works. As we add capacity to our network, the definition of Germany, or any other region, is updated in Zinc and that is also swiftly propagated through our network with Quicksilver.

Zinc also associates a registered hardware identity with a server and physical location, which supports   FIPS 140-3   compliance. TPM-backed identity, server inventory data, and regional configurations determine which region an edge server belongs to and what regional root keys it can access.

Each edge server calls the control plane’s provisioning service, and provides its registered hardware identity. After verifying the server’s hardware identity and regional membership, the provisioning service issues a token that permits the server to retrieve only the regional root keys authorized for its location. Each edge server receives its token and uses it to fetch the regional root keys.

Authorized edge servers load regional root keys into the   kernel keyring   rather than persisting them on disk. Process level access controls limit which services can use them. Because this memory is volatile, a machine restart removes the keys and the server must authenticate and provision them again. This adds operational complexity in exchange for reducing persistent key material which could be an attack vector for adversaries.

Wrapping private keys for global distribution  When the key-management service receives a customer's private key material with a service context and regional boundary, it will use the request’s regional boundary to get the regional root key and its latest configured epoch. It will then derive the corresponding asymmetric application key pair and use its public component to wrap the private key. The result is a wrapped private key and its metadata.

Quicksilver will then distribute the wrapped private key and metadata across our network. Since the wrapped key requires the specified region to decrypt, global wrapped key distribution does not grant edge servers global access to the private key because unwrapping still requires the corresponding regional root key and service context.

Unwrapping using application-specific keys on the data plane   Why we chose this cryptographic design  Symmetric roots with asymmetric key wrapping  Regional root keys are 256-bit symmetric secrets. GeoKey Manager derives application-specific keys from each regional root key. For the current Cloudflare One path, the control plane’s key management service derives an application-specific   Hybrid Public Key Encryption   (HPKE) key pair.

HPKE with hybrid post-quantum KEM  The Cloudflare One path uses HPKE, as defined in   RFC 9180  . Its key-encapsulation mechanism (KEM) combines   ML-KEM-768   with   X25519  , while   HKDF  -SHA-256 provides key derivation and AES-256-GCM provides authenticated encryption. Combining post-quantum and classical components preserves confidentiality as long as at least one component remains secure.

Designing for rotation   The validated design supports two types of key rotation: soft rotation and hard rotation.

A soft rotation creates a new epoch for the regional root key while retaining controlled access to a limited number of previous regional root-key epochs — let’s say one previous generation, as an example. The customer’s new private-key material is wrapped using the latest epoch, while older wrapped private keys are still usable during the transition. This is a similar concept to when a credit card company allows you to use a previous version of your credit card for recurring payments from an authorized retailer. In this case, the number of epochs we support determine how many generations of previously wrapped private keys — credit cards — are usable. This allows customers to preserve their service uptime while they transition.

A hard rotation instead rewraps affected customers’ wrapped private keys under a replacement epoch so access to the previous epoch can be removed. In this case, it would be like the credit card company not allowing you to use the previous credit card for a transaction under any circumstances.

Security and availability tradeoffs  Failing closed is a very intentional design choice. Failing open would mean unwrapping a customer’s private key outside its allowed region rather than rejecting the request. We never do that: if any required check fails (service context, region, epoch, etc.), the request is rejected. At startup, each edge’s key service loads every configured regional root key from its Linux kernel keyring. Missing or malformed root keys prevent the edge key service from initializing. Once running, the edge key service uses in-memory copies so that it can’t be tampered with, preventing out of region or cross-region unwrapping. In practice, an edge server serves requests for a region only once its configuration and key provisioning are complete.

The trust boundary (all services that can access the regional root key) includes the key-management service, the provisioning service, and authorized edge key services because each can access regional root keys. The key-management service uses them to derive application-specific keys, the provisioning service stores and distributes them, and edge key services use locally authorized copies of them. Quicksilver remains outside this boundary because it receives only wrapped private keys and associated metadata.

Operating GeoKey Manager  Cloudflare’s network is constantly changing. As servers enter or leave service, Cloudflare’s fleet inventory updates regional membership. This means the list of data centers that make up a region like Spain is not static. GeoKey Manager’s provisioning layer refreshes that membership several times each day, granting or removing access to regional root keys as the network changes. This process is separate from key rotation and requires no customer action.

When regional membership changes, the provisioning service immediately synchronizes the server’s Linux kernel keyring with the latest authorized regional root keys. The edge key service caches these keys in process memory until it restarts or the cache expires. It then reloads the current authorized set from the kernel keyring.

What’s next: Cloudflare One integration and CDN  GeoKey Manager is the basis for an improved Regional Services offering for Cloudflare One; these new capabilities will be announced in a few months.

Older versions of GeoKey Manager already provide geographic controls for private keys associated with CDN certificates. We are developing a separate integration that will bring this new post-quantum GeoKey Manager described here to that existing CDN capability. We will share testing and transition details when that work is ready.

Getting started  If you are a current DLS customer who is regionalizing CDN traffic, you can register intent to test this feature before it’s generally available for CDN traffic   here  .

Thank you to everyone who made this product a reality. It was a huge effort across the Data Localization Suite, Cloudflare One, and Cloudflare Research teams.

This new PQ GeoKey Manager is a cornerstone of Cloudflare’s data sovereignty solutions, making sure that a customer's decryption keys are only accessible in their chosen geography.

title: Introducing full transaction detection for Cloudflare WAF
author: Daniele Molteni
description:
Today, we are expanding our web application firewall (WAF) by adding two new capabilities: full transaction detections and response rules. Full transaction detections evaluate each HTTP request alongside its response to identify evidence of exploitation. article_content:
Today, we are expanding our web application firewall (WAF) by adding two new capabilities: full transaction detections and response rules. Full transaction detections evaluate each HTTP request alongside its response to identify evidence of exploitation. It helps answer both "Does this request look malicious?" and "What happened when the application handled it?" Response rules can then block the origin’s response before it reaches the requester.

These are valuable protections because the latest frontier models are uncovering vulnerabilities buried deep in widely used software, giving defenders clarity on what to fix — and attackers new paths to exploit. The recent   php2shell   vulnerability shows the stakes: a flaw in a common software component can put applications across the Internet at risk. AI agents scanning for vulnerabilities can be extremely persistent, adapting payloads using feedback, and chaining vulnerabilities, credentials, and permissions. An application's response can reveal whether an attempt worked and give an attacker information that helps them go deeper.

Inspecting incoming requests remains essential for stopping recognizable attacks before they reach an application. But some threats become clear only when the request is considered alongside what the origin returns. A suspicious input followed by a response exposing sensitive information tells a different story from the same input followed by a rejection or an error.

With these new capabilities, customers can use Cloudflare-managed protections or build their own policies combining request and response properties. This extends our always-on application security framework, with detection results available in Security Analytics to support investigation. Our first managed protections using this capability address the recently disclosed php2shell vulnerability.

And the best part? We are making these new capabilities generally available to all Cloudflare customers, including Free plans.

Request inspection is not enough    Cloudflare WAF   protects websites and APIs with managed rules, custom rules, and rate limiting. Managed rules provide protection for known attack techniques and vulnerabilities while custom rules let teams create their own policies using parameters such as an IP address, URL path, headers, and request body. These controls operate at the request level to stop exploits or unwanted traffic from reaching the origin.

For many threats, this is the right place to act. However, treating every suspicious request as a confirmed exploit creates a difficult choice. Broad request signatures can catch more potential attacks, but they can also show “false positives”, such as matching legitimate traffic — which then breaks the applications. Deploying only rules that do not trigger false positives reduces that risk, but can leave more room for more ambiguous traffic to reach the server.

The response provides the missing evidence. Cloudflare can now correlate it with the request that produced it, so detections can account for the outcome of the entire HTTP transaction.

As an illustrative example, consider an application that lets users download files. An attacker manipulates the file parameter to request a private configuration file outside the permitted directory:

GET /download?file=../../config/database.ini   Request inspection can recognize this path traversal attempt and block it before it reaches the application. The request alone, however, cannot establish whether the application would expose the file. It might reject the request, ignore the traversal, or return an error. If the request reaches the origin, a response like this provides additional evidence:

200 OK

Content-Type: text/plain

[database]

username=app_service

password=EXAMPLE_SECRET    Full transaction detection  provides a missing piece: it can correlate the attempted file access with response content characteristic of a private configuration file. Configuration-like text can legitimately appear in documentation or example downloads; combining it with a traversal attempt provides stronger evidence of sensitive data exposure than either signal alone.  A response rule  can then replace the origin response with a Cloudflare WAF block page and HTTP 403 before it reaches the requester, effectively blocking the exploit by preventing sensitive information from reaching the attacker.

Detection and mitigation are separate by design  Full transaction detection extends the   always-on detection framework   we introduced earlier this year. Detections analyze traffic and attach metadata to the request and response, rules then decide what to do with those results.

Separating those jobs gives customers visibility before they design a policy. Security teams can inspect detections in their own traffic, understand which endpoints and signatures are involved, and choose the response that fits their application. Similar to the approach for the request-based   Attack Signature Detection  , the outcome of the detections are stored in fields that can be accessed in the response custom rules or used in managed detections to block traffic.

Mirroring the request detection fields, the following new fields are added to our platform:

Field

Description

cf.waf.signature.response.confidence

Confidence values associated with matching signatures

cf.waf.signature.response.categories

Categories associated with matching signatures

cf.waf.signature.response.ref

Signature reference IDs, up to 10

The first full transaction detections focus on exploit confirmation for high profile vulnerability. It correlates suspicious input with response signals that indicate an exploit may have succeeded.

We will expand coverage over time by supporting other use cases, including detecting data exposure and exfiltration signals. This is important for the Internet beyond any one application: defenses can distinguish probing from evidence of impact, while detection of exposed data and services can reach customers that do not have a dedicated security team tuning every WAF rule.

Create rules on the response  Detecting evidence of exploitation is most useful if you can act on it in real time. Response custom rules turn full transaction detections into inline protection by blocking a matching origin response before it reaches the requester, although it cannot undo actions already performed at the origin.

Security teams can now combine request and response properties with detection results to decide which responses to block. When a blocking rule matches, Cloudflare replaces the origin response with a WAF block page or a custom response.

Response phase controls are available in the Cloudflare dashboard at the bottom of the  Security > Security Rules  page, with both managed protections and custom rules.

We have released both managed and custom rules to all plans, including Free plans. Over time, we will follow the same approach we use for request detections, where managed detections for free plans   focus on high-profile vulnerabilities  , while paying customers get a richer catalog of detections.

Managed detections  All customers get the protection of the full array of transaction detections through the  Cloudflare Managed Response Firewall Default  ruleset, which is designed for a simple one-click deploy and simplified configurability. When a signature matches, the managed detection will block the response and return a standard WAF block page.

You can edit the  Cloudflare Managed Response Firewall Default  scope to run detections only on a portion of their applications, for example by excluding or restricting the detection to a specific path. Paying customers can use detection fields in custom response rules to create more tailored policies.

Custom rules  Custom response rules are designed to give customers full control of the rule logic. A useful rule can stop an administration interface from being exposed when an authentication gateway has not marked the request as internal. For example:

http.request.uri.path starts_with "/admin" and not http.request.headers["x-internal-user"][0] eq "true" and http.response.code eq 200 and http.response.headers["content-type"][0] contains "text/html"

This blocks only when an unauthenticated request targets `/admin` and the origin actually returns a successful HTML administration page. It does not block ordinary authentication failures, redirects, or non-administration traffic.

All customers can create up to three custom response rules supporting  Log  and  Block  actions. The fields and functions available in response to custom rules mirrors what your plan gives you access to in   request custom rules   already. Creating rules on the response body is not yet available.

Following the   Attack Signature Detection   approach, paying customers also have access to the outcome of attack detections through the  cf.waf.signature.response.*   fields listed above. These fields can be combined with other parameters (such as a hostname, URL path, source IP, request header) to enable protection on a single path, or limit the policy to application-specific context. We are currently rolling out the response fields to all our accounts. If you don’t have access to them yet, please contact your account team.

Investigating matching requests  When a managed or custom response rule logs or blocks a transaction, the event is available in Security Events. This means responders can trace any detection back to the full context of the request and the specific rule that took action.

At the moment, both request-only rules and full-transaction rules are shown together in the same analytics page. In Security Events, the events generated by response rules are part of the Managed Rules or Custom Rules service. You can filter events belonging to a specific rule ID in the relative rule list section.

Get started today  Full transaction detection is generally available for all zones proxying traffic through Cloudflare. To verify that you’re protected, go to  Security > Security Rules  in the Cloudflare dashboard. If you want to customize your policy, start by reviewing full transaction detections in Security Analytics, then create the response phase policy that fits your application.
ai_summary: Today, we are expanding our web application firewall (WAF) by adding two new capabilities: full transaction detections and response rules. Full transaction detections evaluate each HTTP request alongside its response to identify evidence of exploitation.
main_event: Introducing full transaction detection for Cloudflare WAF

article_content:
Update - On October 23, the PHP project published an  informational advisory  for a related vulnerability, CVE-2026-115560, in PHP's session upload progress feature. It affects fully patched PHP releases, including 8.5.12, and will be fixed in PHP's next regular release.

All Cloudflare WAF customers are protected against known exploit attempts if their site uses PHP's default upload progress field name. Customers who have changed  session.upload_progress.name  are not covered by the WAF rule.

The existing rules "PHP Remote Code Execution Attack (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) #6" protects against this vulnerability.

More information to follow.

October 21, Calif.io, Wiz, OpenAI and Quarkslab disclosed two   vulnerabilities in PHP, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and known as   php2shell  . The vulnerabilities affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later and they may allow an attacker to cause denial of service, remote code execution, and data exposure when an application processes specially crafted HTTP traffic.

Cloudflare has been part of a coordinated effort to deploy mitigations to protect the Internet, working with   PHP foundation  ,   OpenAI   and   Wiz   among others. Cloudflare has developed and deployed web application firewall (WAF) protections since early October 2026, which were deployed about 9 hours ahead of public disclosure.  Starting on October 21 3:02 am UTC, Cloudflare customers using our free or paid WAF were protected by default against php2shell.

Cloudflare successfully deployed multiple mitigations for all its customers while the vulnerability was leaked before the official release date and we observed attack traffic targeting our customers. We observed how attackers were mutating the attack payload to try to bypass our protections by tracking the volume of matches and cross-referencing with the rule logic.

Protecting against php2shell required more than standard request-based rules. Request data alone does not always provide enough evidence to distinguish an exploit from legitimate traffic. The origin’s response adds context, helping identify whether an exploit succeeded while reducing the risk of false positives.

To deliver this protection, we developed full transaction detection, a new Cloudflare WAF capability that combines signals from the request and response within the same HTTP transaction. Response rules can then block a matching origin response before it reaches the requester. The php2shell protections are the first managed detections we have released using this capability.

Customers should patch their PHP repos even with WAF protections providing an additional layer of defense-in-depth mitigation. Our security analysts continue monitoring attack activity and update the rules when and if new techniques and variations emerge in the hours and days ahead. You can track new rules in the   changelog  .

The protections are available and deployed automatically on all plans with WAF deployed, including Free users.

What we know about the vulnerabilities  PHP is used by almost   70% of websites  . The php2shell vulnerabilities affect the PHP runtime itself and can allow attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers, expose customer data, or disrupt services. Because PHP underpins widely used platforms such as WordPress and Magento, these flaws could potentially affect a large number of applications across the Internet.

The two vulnerabilities involve how PHP handles memory when something goes wrong while processing a HTTP request. Normally, PHP allocates memory to store the data it needs to process a request, then releases it when that work finishes. If processing stops unexpectedly, for example because it runs out of memory, PHP fails to clean up the memory safely. These vulnerabilities arise when PHP handles an error and then tries to use data that was not fully set up or memory that has already been released.

An attacker can send specially crafted HTTP requests to trigger these conditions. Large requests are one way to put memory under pressure, but the problem goes beyond consuming server resources. By manipulating the data PHP encounters in this invalid memory, an attacker may be able to crash a PHP process, expose sensitive information, or execute code provided by the attacker.

The two vulnerabilities differ in when the unsafe memory access happens:

Vulnerability

What goes wrong

CVE-2026-109618

PHP runs out of memory and interrupts its work before some internal data has been properly initialized. During cleanup of that request, PHP may use this unfinished data as though it were valid.

CVE-2026-109619

A fatal error interrupts a request, leaving PHP holding references to memory that is released when the request ends. When the same PHP process handles a later request, it may follow those outdated references and access memory that is no longer valid and expose sensitive data.

These flaws are in the PHP runtime, so updating website code or a plugin(s) alone does not fix these vulnerabilities. Administrators need to update the PHP software running their applications. If a hosting provider manages PHP, ask the provider to apply the security update.

Administrators can follow the PHP advisory for affected versions and remediation instructions. Keep Cloudflare WAF protections enabled while patching. Restricting unnecessary uploads and limiting upload sizes can also reduce exposure, but these measures do not replace the PHP fix.

New rules  For Free customers, new rules have been released under the Cloudflare Managed Free Ruleset (Ruleset ID 77454fe2d30c4220b5701f6fdfb893ba). Free customers don’t have to take any actions to enable the protection. To override the ruleset behavior, you can refer to our   documentation  .

Rule Description

Rule ID

PHP Remote Code Execution Attack (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)

4e315666e8e344cdb64119a3b5ccf32f

PHP Remote Code Execution Attack (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) #2

Copy prompt to fix!   # Security task: check and fix "php2shell" (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)

Two critical PHP runtime vulnerabilities were disclosed on 2026-10-21 (CVSS v4.0 9.2).

They allow unauthenticated remote code execution, data exposure and DoS through crafted

HTTP requests. Exploitation is already happening. The bug is in the PHP runtime itself,

so updating app code, frameworks, WordPress or plugins does NOT fix it.

Official advisory (treat as source of truth, re-fetch it in case it was updated):

https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php#2026-10-21-5

- GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w (CVE-2026-109618, RCE via OOM corruption)

- GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp (CVE-2026-109619, RCE via stale global state)

**Fixed upstream versions:** 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, 8.2.35

**Affected:** every PHP install that serves web requests (PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php,

php-cgi, FrankenPHP, LiteSpeed). mod_php has the highest risk: a demonstrated exploit

triggers before any application code runs.

## Rules

- Do NOT guess. If you can't confirm a version or setting, say so.

- Ask me before changing anything on production or shared infrastructure,

restarting production services, or editing deploy config. Read-only discovery is fine.

- Don't stop at the first finding. Inventory everything, then report.

## Step 1: Inventory every place PHP runs

Search the current repo/workspace AND any machines/containers I have access to:

- Repo: `*.php`, `composer.json`/`composer.lock` (check `require.php` and

`config.platform.php`), `Dockerfile*`, `docker-compose*`, `.php-version`,

`.tool-versions`, `.devcontainer/`, CI files (GitHub Actions `setup-php`, GitLab CI

`image:`), IaC (Terraform, Ansible, Helm, k8s manifests), PaaS config

(`app.yaml`, `Procfile`, Platform.sh, Laravel Forge/Vapor, etc.).

- Base images: list every `FROM php:*`, `FROM wordpress:*`, `FROM bitnami/*`,

`FROM serversideup/*`, `FROM dunglas/frankenphp*` and similar, with tags.

- Running hosts/containers (if accessible): `php -v`, `php-fpm -v`, `php -i | grep -i "server api"`,

`apachectl -M | grep -i php`, `docker ps` + `docker exec <c> php -v`.

- Note the SAPI for each (FPM / mod_php / CGI / FrankenPHP / LiteSpeed / CLI-only).

- Note long-running workers (Laravel Octane, RoadRunner, Swoole, FrankenPHP worker

mode). These are relevant to the stale-state bug.

If no PHP is found anywhere, tell me clearly and stop. Nothing else is needed.

## Step 2: Decide if each instance is vulnerable

For each instance, classify it as PATCHED / VULNERABLE / UNKNOWN:

- Upstream builds: vulnerable if below 8.5.12 / 8.4.27 / 8.3.36 / 8.2.35 on that branch.

- **PHP 8.1 and older are EOL upstream:** vulnerable unless a vendor backport is confirmed.

- **Distro packages (Debian/Ubuntu/RHEL/Alpine/etc.)** often backport fixes WITHOUT

bumping the upstream version, so `php -v` alone isn't enough. Check the package

changelog for the CVE IDs, e.g.

`apt changelog <php-pkg> | grep -E "CVE-2026-10961[89]"` or

`rpm -q --changelog <php-pkg> | grep -E "CVE-2026-10961[89]"`.

- If PHP comes from `rpms.remirepo.net`: the advisory says it will not have same-day

updates. Flag this and recommend distro packages or building from source.

- Managed hosting / shared hosting / PaaS: mark UNKNOWN and tell me to ask the provider.

## Step 3: Fix (only after I approve the plan for prod)

1. Upgrade PHP to a fixed version (or the vendor-patched package):

- Bump Docker base image tags to a fixed patch release, rebuild, redeploy.

- Update CI `php-version` pins.

- `apt`/`dnf`/`apk` upgrade of the distro PHP packages.

- 7.4 / 8.0 / 8.1 built from source: the PHP security team published minimal

backport branches linked from the advisory. Otherwise upgrade to a supported version.

2. **Restart EVERY PHP worker** (FPM pools, Apache, FrankenPHP, LiteSpeed, Octane/

RoadRunner/Swoole). Old processes keep running vulnerable code until restarted.

3. Verify each instance afterwards (version + changelog check) and report the evidence.

## Step 4: Temporary mitigations (ONLY if patching isn't possible right away)

These reduce exposure but do NOT make the server safe. Apply them in php.ini / the FPM

pool / server config (not `ini_set()` or `.user.ini`) and restart every worker:

- CVE-2026-109618:

- `memory_limit=-1`, set non-overridably (e.g. `php_admin_value`), and confirm nothing

re-applies a finite limit.

- Low `post_max_size` (8M with no uploads, 32M with uploads), with

`upload_max_filesize` below it.

- Enforce request size / field count / multipart part count / header limits at the

web server or proxy, including requests without `Content-Length`.

- Use container/cgroup memory limits. Do NOT use `RLIMIT_AS`/`RLIMIT_DATA`.

- CVE-2026-109619:

- `session.upload_progress.enabled=0`.

- On PHP 8.5: `fatal_error_backtraces=0`.

- Remove invalid/deprecated per-request settings that emit diagnostics early (hiding

them via `error_reporting`/`display_errors`/`@` does not help).

- Fix attacker-reachable fatal errors and timeouts.

- If the site sits behind Cloudflare: confirm the WAF Managed Ruleset is deployed in

**block** mode (Free plans get the Managed Free Ruleset automatically). This is

defense in depth, not a replacement for patching.

## Step 5: Look for signs of compromise (read-only)

Since exploitation started before disclosure, check what you can access:

- PHP-FPM/Apache error logs for segfaults, "Allowed memory size exhausted", or

worker crashes, especially clustered around unusually large POST/multipart requests.

- Recently modified or unexpected files in web roots (webshells), new cron jobs,

unexpected processes or outbound connections from PHP users.

Report anything suspicious. Do not delete evidence.

## Final report

Give me a table: location | how PHP is provided | SAPI | version | status

(PATCHED/VULNERABLE/UNKNOWN) | action taken or needed. Then list:

- What you changed (files, commands), what still needs my approval, and anything that

needs a hosting provider.

- Mitigations applied as stopgaps and when they should be removed.

- Any compromise indicators found.
ai_summary: Update - On October 23, the PHP project published an informational advisory for a related vulnerability, CVE-2026-115560, in PHP's session upload progress feature. It affects fully patched PHP releases, including 8.5.12, and will be fixed in PHP's next regular release.
main_event: Cloudflare deploys protections against php2shell vulnerability

title: How Commerce.com and Cloudflare are getting storefronts ready for AI agents
author: Jenny Lea
description:

That’s because websites were built for humans, not agents. Most agents that shop for someone today work from a site’s HTML — they look at the page, guess which button does what, click, and try again when they get it wrong. Enter WebMCP: a browser standard from Google that gives AI agents s...
article_content:
AI can write code and pass the bar exam, but it still struggles to buy a pair of shoes online.

That’s because websites were built for humans, not agents. Most agents that shop for someone today work from a site’s HTML — they look at the page, guess which button does what, click, and try again when they get it wrong. This process is slow, uses a lot of tokens, and something as seemingly innocuous as a theme change can break it.

Enter WebMCP: a browser standard from Google that gives AI agents structured tools on a page, like  search_products . Instead of hunting for buttons, the agent calls the exact tool it needs directly, making shopping faster, cheaper, and far more reliable. Because WebMCP is still an experimental proposed browser standard in early preview, it’s currently available behind experimental Chrome flags ( chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ), in Chrome Origin Trials, in some agentic browsers, and across developer environments like   Cloudflare Kitesurf  .

In August, we launched   edge implementation of WebMCP   in beta. Turn it on, and Cloudflare injects a tiny script at the edge to make those tools available automatically, without site owners writing a single line of code.

Commerce.com  , a flexible commerce platform built for the age of AI, already uses Cloudflare to run their almost 100,000 domains. So when the preview came out, they asked:  Can we turn this on for all of our stores at once?

Here’s why Commerce.com wanted WebMCP, how we built edge-level opt-outs to give every merchant control, and what we learned along the way.

Why Commerce.com wanted WebMCP  Kristina Pototska, Product Management Director at Commerce.com, explains why this matters for storefronts:

“Merchants keep asking us how they can keep up with agentic shopping. When a shopper asks an agent to find something, merchants want their store to be in the answer. They want to keep the customer, keep control of the checkout, and do it without rebuilding their site. WebMCP helps with all three. The agent gets real tools to search products, check details, build a cart, and get a checkout link, so it doesn’t have to guess its way around the page. The human shopper stays on the merchant’s site, and the merchant keeps the relationship.    We wanted to turn this on in a secure way, and without asking merchants to edit their theme or do anything by hand. That’s where the Cloudflare partnership worked perfectly.    WebMCP also works side by side with our server-side   MCP  , and together they cover the different ways people shop with agents. Server-side MCP supports agents that connect to a store directly, like an assistant helping someone shop across several sites. WebMCP supports agents that work in the shopper’s browser. It’s the same set of shopping tools in both cases, so merchants don’t have to choose between the two or manage them separately.”  Under the hood, this integration relies on two key principles. First, the WebMCP tools execute directly inside the shopper's active browser session on the storefront's domain, ensuring the agent sees the same prices and cart. No credentials go to a third party, and the visit still happens on the merchant's site. Second, Cloudflare serves as the edge delivery layer for Commerce.com’s backend MCP server, proxying tool definitions and actions unchanged so merchants maintain full control over their tool logic.

What a shopper's agent sees  When visiting an enabled Commerce.com storefront, an AI assistant no longer has to guess how to navigate the site. Instead, it can instantly discover tools via WebMCP.

Suppose you tell your agent:  "Find me a waterproof trail running shoe under $140 in size 10 and add it to my cart."

Without WebMCP:  The agent attempts to simulate human clicks, only to get blocked by cookie banners, misinterpret variant drop-downs, or get tripped up by bot challenges that try to distinguish automated traffic from real customers.

With WebMCP:  The agent detects the store's tools on  document.modelContext  and makes two clean calls:

search_products({ query: "trail running shoe", max_price: 140, size: 10 })

add_to_cart({ product_id: "shoe_123" })

Because the agent runs inside your active browser session on the store's domain, your cart updates in real time. Commerce.com’s backend MCP server determines the commerce flow: when you’re ready to complete the purchase, you click checkout yourself — keeping your payment details secure and leaving you in complete control of the final buy.

What we built together  When Commerce.com asked to turn on WebMCP across almost 100000 storefronts, we ran into a practical challenge: WebMCP was originally designed as a single on-or-off switch for an entire domain zone.

Commerce wanted to enable our mcp-server-client toolpack, which acts as an edge bridge — proxying tool definitions and requests directly from Commerce.com’s backend MCP server to the visitor's browser. Because Commerce.com uses Cloudflare for SaaS to host thousands of merchant vanity domains on shared zones, we needed a way to deliver this platform-wide while giving individual store owners an easy way to opt out.

1. On for all stores on Commerce.com, with an opt-out for each merchant  Instead of building a complex custom allowlist, we hooked WebMCP into the existing Cloudflare concepts of   Configuration Rules   and   custom hostname metadata  .

Commerce.com turns WebMCP on for their main zone, then adds a rule at the edge that checks merchant metadata. If a merchant flips the "opt-out" switch in their Commerce.com dashboard, Cloudflare bypasses WebMCP for that specific storefront automatically:

{

"action": "set_config",

"expression": "cf.hostname.metadata.webmcp_opt_out eq \"true\"",

"action_parameters": {

"webmcp_enabled": false

}

}   Because Cloudflare evaluates these rules at the edge before serving the page, an opted-out store gets zero extra latency, no remote lookups, and no injected scripts.

2. Tailored endpoints and safe fallbacks  As with any preview release, working with a partner in the real world revealed a few practical details we hadn't accounted for:

Custom MCP paths:  When the mcp-server-client toolpack was enabled, our bridge originally expected to find every site's MCP server at /mcp. Commerce.com’s server lives at /api/mcp. To handle this, we added a configurable MCP URL setting at the zone level. When this is set, we pass the custom path into the injected script tag:

<script type="module"

src="/.webmcp/bridge.js"

data-packs="c2pa,mcp-server-client"

data-mcp-url="/api/mcp"></script>    Seamless fallbacks:  If a store's MCP server is offline or a customer's browser doesn't support WebMCP, the script exits. The storefront loads normally and human shoppers aren't affected.

What's next  We'll keep investing in WebMCP as the standard evolves, starting with helping agents find a site's tools more easily. Cloudflare and   Commerce.com   will continue to work together to make shopping with agents fast, reliable and safe for both merchants and shoppers.

If you're at   Cloudflare Connect   in San Francisco on October 21, 2026, come see us at   Getting your storefront agent ready for peak season  , a panel discussion featuring Kristina Pototska (Product Management Director, Commerce), Justis Blasco (CTO and Co-Founder, Popmenu), Ross Harvey (Head of Infrastructure, Fruugo), and Josh Mills (VP of Engineering, Gopuff).
ai_summary: AI can write code and pass the bar exam, but it still struggles to buy a pair of shoes online. That’s because websites were built for humans, not agents.

title: 8 eMudhra certificates are compromised. Here's what you need to know
author: Christopher Patton
description: On October 19, 2026, at approximately 17:00 UTC, Cloudflare became aware that private keys associated with eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised. These certificates were widely trusted by browsers, operating systems, and also within Cloudflare. Because the keys themselves are weak, an attacker can create a forged certificate for any domain and use it to impersonate servers to intercept or modify traffic. This is a serious security incident with implications across the Internet...
article_content:
On October 19, 2026, at approximately 17:00 UTC, Cloudflare became aware that private keys associated with eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised. These certificates were widely trusted by browsers, operating systems, and also within Cloudflare. Because the keys themselves are weak, an attacker can create a forged certificate for any domain and use it to impersonate servers to intercept or modify traffic. This is a serious security incident with implications across the Internet. For reference,   here is a link   to more information about how SSL certificates work and why they are so critical to the operation of the Internet.

We immediately prioritized patching critical services across Cloudflare to protect our customers ahead of the public disclosure of the vulnerability. Our security review has not identified active exploitation of this issue on Cloudflare services.

We have released updates for the Cloudflare One Clients, also known as WARP or the 1.1.1.1 app, and Cloudflare Tunnel, also known as cloudflared. We have also deployed mitigations across our CDN, Developer, and Zero Trust products. If you are using Cloudflare Zero Trust with Gateway and an up-to-date client (see below), you are automatically protected.

Our response  We prioritized updating services that use public certificates to authenticate remote endpoints, including proxies connecting to origins and applications calling external APIs. In parallel, we updated shared trust stores, base images, and other shared foundations, providing a common mitigation path for services that inherit their certificate trust from those sources. We paired these updates with reloads, restarts, and image deployments needed to activate them. Applications with bundled or custom trust stores received separate assessment and updates. This work addresses certificate-based authentication, not a weakness in TLS’s encryption algorithms.

Teams across Cloudflare are presently working on further remediation. We are making progress, but there's much work still to be done.  Some customers will need to take action on software or trust configurations that they operate, especially on their origin servers.  The recommended actions are summarized below.

What customers should do   Developer guidance  For developers, look beneath the SDK.

An API client may delegate certificate verification to an HTTP library, a language runtime, the operating system, or a custom trust configuration. Updating the SDK alone may not change the underlying policy.

Once you patch, you may notice certificate errors in your dashboards.  It's important to not resolve these errors by disabling verification.  That would remove the authentication protection these updates are intended to restore.

This incident affects many software stacks that rely on the WebPKI for authentication. Mozilla’s Dennis Jackson has crowdsourced   a list of commonly used packages   that have been patched. We advise readers to upgrade as soon as possible. (Note that some of these may be indirect dependencies of your software stack, so look at the dependency tree.) Apply the relevant dependency updates, rebuild affected images, and confirm whether applications require a reload, restart, or redeployment.

Dennis Jackson’s   test site   provides browser checks, non-browser testing instructions, and package update information. Results apply to the verification path being tested, not every application on the device. Validate through the application’s actual TLS path. A successful browser test does not prove that a background service is protected. Neither does a curl test if the application uses a different verifier.

Timeline  The timeline of events so far is below.

Date and Time

Event

October 19, approximately 17:00 UTC

Cloudflare becomes aware of the compromise and begins assessment.

October 20, 02:00 UTC

Cloudflare One Client and WARP app security updates published across platforms.

October 20 09:15 UTC

Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) security update published.

October 20 19:20 UTC

CDN and server-side Zero Trust mitigations fully deployed.

Looking forward  The impact of this incident is not felt equally. Browser maintainers were able to remediate the issue with a flip of a switch. They of course have just  one  application to update, instead of hundreds, but they do have a neat trick up their sleeves: most browsers use quick-revocation mechanisms (like Chrome CRLSets). At Cloudflare we also use such a mechanism for some of our products. To bring it to more systems at Cloudflare and industry, we’re excited about projects like   upki   that understand a trust store can’t be a static list of root certificate authorities, but needs the ability to be quickly updated with information like revocation and certificate transparency keys.
ai_summary: On October 19, 2026, at approximately 17:00 UTC, Cloudflare became aware that private keys associated with eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised. These certificates were widely trusted by browsers, operating systems, and also within Cloudflare.
