Here's the actual implementation: function syncPanel() { var o = state.opts; ['layout', 'cols', 'rows', 'paper', 'orient', 'label', 'lines', 'tsize', 'font', 'colors'].forEach(function (f) { q('[data-field="' + f + '"]').value = String(o[f]); }); q('[data-field="captions"]').checked = o.captions; q('[data-field="frame"]').checked = o.frame; q('[data-field="numbers"]').checked = o.numbers; q('[data-field="gap"]').value = String(o.gap); q('[data-out="gap-val"]').textContent = o.gap + ' mm'; q('[data-field="pages"]').value = state.pages; if (document.activeElement !== q('[data-field="title"]')) { q('[data-field="title"]').value = state.title; } var strip = o.layout === 'strip'; q('[data-out="cols-label"]').textContent = strip ? 'Frames per strip' : 'Columns'; q('[data-out="rows-label"]').textContent = strip ? 'Strips per sheet' : 'Rows'; q('[data-field="lines"]').disabled = !o.captions || o.layout === 'notes'; q('[data-field="frame"]').disabled = strip; ui.listWrap.hidden = state.pages !== 'list'; } The function reads the current options from state.opts and updates the corresponding controls. For example, it sets the selected font, text size, caption line count, and paper settings. It also handles layout-specific controls. In Film strip mode, the columns and rows labels change to Frames per strip and Strips per sheet. The caption-line control is disabled when captions are turned off or when the Panels with notes layout is selected. Fitting Captions Inside Panels Long captions need to fit inside the available panel space. The application uses a wrap() helper to divide text into lines based on the available canvas width. Here's how the actual drawing code uses that helper: if (o.captions && captionFor(n)) { ctx.font = '400 ' + fs + 'px ' + FONTS[o.font]; ctx.fillStyle = C.ink; var maxL = cell.notes ? Math.max(1, Math.floor( (t.y * k + t.h * k - y + lh - fs) / lh )) : o.lines; lines = wrap( ctx, captionFor(n), t.w * k, Math.min(maxL, cell.notes ? 40 : o.lines) ); lines.forEach(function (ln, j) { ctx.fillText(ln, t.x * k, y + j * lh); }); } The application selects the font using FONTS[o.font] and calculates the available number of caption lines based on the panel layout. For regular layouts, the selected o.lines setting controls the maximum number of lines. For Panels with notes, the available space determines how many lines can be displayed. The wrap() function breaks the caption into lines that fit the available width. The fillText() method then draws each line onto the canvas. When there isn't enough space for the selected caption settings, the preview displays a warning suggesting fewer caption lines, fewer rows, or a smaller text size. The application also supports panel frames and sheet numbers. These options are stored in the application state and applied when the storyboard is drawn. This gives users control over the appearance and readability of their storyboard captions without changing the original PDF. Navigating Between Storyboard Sheets A large PDF may require several storyboard sheets. The application provides Previous and Next controls so users can review each sheet individually. It also displays the current sheet number and the total number of sheets. The selected sheet is stored in state.sheet . The application uses this value to determine which storyboard sheet should be displayed. Handling the Previous and Next Buttons The application handles sheet navigation inside its main click event listener. Here's the actual implementation: case 'sheet-prev': if (state.sheet > 0) { state.sheet--; drawPreview(); } break; case 'sheet-next': state.sheet++; drawPreview(); break; When the user clicks Previous, the application checks whether the current sheet number is greater than zero. If it is, state.sheet is decreased by one and drawPreview() refreshes the displayed sheet. When the user clicks Next, the sheet number is increased and the preview is refreshed. The application also prevents users from moving beyond the available sheets. Inside drawPreview() , it checks the current sheet position and disables the navigation buttons when necessary: state.sheet = clamp(state.sheet, 0, L.sheets - 1); ui.sheetPos.textContent = 'Sheet ' + (state.sheet + 1) + ' of ' + L.sheets; q('[data-act="sheet-prev"]').disabled = state.sheet <= 0; q('[data-act="sheet-next"]').disabled = state.sheet >= L.sheets - 1; The clamp() function keeps the selected sheet within the valid range. The sheet counter displays the current position, starting from 1, and the total number of sheets. The Previous button is disabled on the first sheet, while the Next button is disabled on the last sheet. This makes it easier to review large documents without displaying every storyboard sheet at once. Reading Scanned Pages with OCR Some PDF documents contain selectable text, while others contain scanned images of printed pages. PDF.js can extract text from pages containing actual text data. But it can't directly extract words from a scanned page that contains only an image. To handle these pages, the application provides an optional OCR feature using Tesseract.js. When users select Read scanned pages with OCR, the application identifies scanned pages that don't already have captions and processes them using the OCR engine. Loading Tesseract.js When Needed The application loads Tesseract.js only when the user requests OCR. It first checks whether the library is already available and reuses an existing loading promise if the script is still being loaded. Here's the actual loadTesseract() implementation: var tessPromise = null; function loadTesseract() { if (window.Tesseract) { return Promise.resolve(window.Tesseract); } if (tessPromise) { return tessPromise; } tessPromise = new Promise(function (resolve, reject) { var s = document.createElement('script'); s.src = TESS + 'tesseract.min.js'; s.async = true; s.onload = function () { if (window.Tesseract) { resolve(window.Tesseract); } else { tessPromise = null; reject(new Error('engine')); } }; s.onerror = function () { tessPromise = null; reject(new Error('engine')); }; document.head.appendChild(s); setTimeout(function () { reject(new Error('engine')); }, 45000); }); return tessPromise; } The function checks window.Tesseract to see whether the OCR library is already available. If it is, the function returns it immediately. If the library is still loading, the existing tessPromise is returned instead of creating another script request. Otherwise, the application creates a script element, sets its source to the Tesseract.js library, and adds it to the document. The onload and onerror handlers detect whether loading succeeds or fails. Creating the OCR Worker After the library loads, the application creates a Tesseract worker configured for English text recognition. The following excerpt comes from the actual runOcr() function: var T = await loadTesseract(); checkCancel(); var w = await T.createWorker('eng', 1, { workerPath: TESS + 'worker.min.js', corePath: TESS_CORE, logger: function (m) { if (!m || token !== state.loadToken || !state.busy) { return; } if (/loading language/i.test(m.status)) { setProgress( m.progress || 0, 'Getting the English language data (first time only)…' ); } else if (/recogniz/i.test(m.status)) { setProgress( (done + (m.progress || 0)) / list.length, 'Reading page ' + list[done] + ' (' + (done + 1) + ' of ' + list.length + ')…' ); } } }); state.worker = w; checkCancel(); await w.setParameters({ debug_file: '/dev/null' }); The createWorker() method initializes the OCR engine with the English language data. The worker and core paths tell Tesseract.js where to load its supporting files. The logger reports language-loading and text-recognition progress. The application uses this information to update its progress indicator while OCR is running. Recognizing Text from Scanned Pages The application processes each eligible scanned page individually. It renders the page at a higher resolution before sending it to Tesseract.js. Here's the actual page-processing excerpt from runOcr() : for (; done < list.length; done++) { checkCancel(); var n = list[done], page = await state.doc.getPage(n), b = page.getViewport({ scale: 1 }); var c = await renderPage( n, Math.min(b.width * 300 / 72, 2600), Math.min(b.height * 300 / 72, 2600) ); checkCancel(); var png = await pngBytes(c); c.width = 1; var res = await w.recognize(png); checkCancel(); if (token !== state.loadToken) { return; } var cap = captionFromText(res.data && res.data.text); if (cap && !captionFor(n)) { state.captions[n] = cap; var ta = ui.grid.querySelector('[data-cap="' + n + '"]'); if (ta) { ta.value = cap; } } } The function retrieves each scanned PDF page and calculates its original dimensions. It then renders the page at approximately 300 DPI, with a maximum dimension of 2,600 pixels. The pngBytes() helper converts the rendered canvas into PNG image data. Tesseract.js receives this data through w.recognize(png) and returns the recognized text. The application passes the recognized text to captionFromText() to clean and shorten it. If the result is useful and the page still has no caption, the application saves it in state.captions and updates the corresponding caption field. The application also checks for cancellation and verifies that the PDF-loading operation is still current before updating the results. After processing, the application displays a message asking users to review the generated captions. OCR isn't guaranteed to recognize every word correctly. Image quality, handwriting, unusual fonts, and page orientation can affect the result. Users should review generated captions before downloading the storyboard. Generating the Final Storyboard PDF Once the user is satisfied with the layout and captions, the application can generate the final PDF. This process uses PDF-lib to create a new PDF document. The application creates one output page for each storyboard sheet. It then places the original PDF pages inside their calculated panel positions and adds the storyboard's titles, labels, and captions. Creating the PDF Document The actual application uses the exportPdf() function to generate the storyboard. It first creates a new PDF document and checks whether the original PDF pages can be embedded as vector content. Here's the first part of the actual implementation: async function exportPdf(snap, token) { await engine(); var PL = window.PDFLib, L = snap.L, o = snap.o, list = snap.list; var out = await PL.PDFDocument.create(), src = null, embedded = {}; if (state.vector) { try { src = await PL.PDFDocument.load( state.bytes.slice(0), { updateMetadata: false } ); } catch (e) { src = null; } } var k = exportScale(L, 300, 14e6); for (var s = 0; s < L.sheets; s++) { checkCancel(); if (token !== state.loadToken) { return; } setProgress( s / L.sheets, 'Making sheet ' + (s + 1) + ' of ' + L.sheets + '…' ); var page = out.addPage([L.W, L.H]); var c = document.createElement('canvas'); c.width = Math.round(L.W * k); c.height = Math.round(L.H * k); var drawn = await drawSheet( c.getContext('2d'), o, list, L, s, k, 'overlay', null ); if (!drawn) { return; } The function first waits for the required PDF libraries using engine() . It then creates a new PDF document with PDFDocument.create() . The snap parameter contains a snapshot of the selected layout, options, and page list. The application uses these values so the export follows the settings selected by the user. The state.vector check determines whether the original PDF can be loaded through PDF-lib for vector embedding. The application also calculates a rendering scale targeting 300 DPI, subject to a maximum pixel limit. The loop creates one output PDF page for every storyboard sheet. It also calls drawSheet() in overlay mode to prepare the titles, panel labels, and captions that will be placed over the original PDF pages. Preserving Original PDF Pages When vector embedding is available, the application embeds the original PDF pages rather than converting them into ordinary images. The following excerpt shows how it handles each selected panel: for (var i = 0; i < drawn.length; i++) { checkCancel(); var d = drawn[i], r = d.rect, yb = L.H - r.y - r.h; page.drawRectangle({ x: r.x, y: yb, width: r.w, height: r.h, color: PL.rgb(1, 1, 1) }); if (src) { var sp = src.getPage(d.n - 1); if (!embedded[d.n]) { var cb = sp.getCropBox(); embedded[d.n] = await out.embedPage(sp, { left: cb.x, bottom: cb.y, right: cb.x + cb.width, top: cb.y + cb.height }); } var em = embedded[d.n], rot = ((sp.getRotation().angle % 360) + 360) % 360; var turned = rot === 90 || rot === 270, sx = r.w / (turned ? em.height : em.width); var ew = em.width * sx, eh = em.height * sx, at = { x: r.x, y: yb }; if (rot === 90) { at = { x: r.x, y: yb + ew }; } else if (rot === 180) { at = { x: r.x + ew, y: yb + eh }; } else if (rot === 270) { at = { x: r.x + eh, y: yb }; } page.drawPage(em, { x: at.x, y: at.y, width: ew, height: eh, rotate: PL.degrees(-rot) }); } The application retrieves the original PDF page using its page number. It then uses embedPage() to embed that page into the new PDF document. The embedded object caches embedded pages so the same original page doesn't need to be embedded repeatedly. The code also checks the original page rotation and adjusts its position and dimensions before drawing it. This helps preserve the correct orientation when placing pages inside storyboard panels. Handling Protected PDFs If the original PDF can't be embedded as vector content, the application uses a raster fallback. Here's the actual fallback code: else { var pic = await renderPage( d.n, r.w * k, r.h * k ); var jpg = await new Promise(function (res) { pic.toBlob(function (b) { b.arrayBuffer().then(function (a) { res(new Uint8Array(a)); }); }, 'image/jpeg', 0.92); }); pic.width = 1; page.drawImage( await out.embedJpg(jpg), { x: r.x, y: yb, width: r.w, height: r.h } ); } In this case, the application renders the original PDF page onto a canvas and converts it into JPEG image data. PDF-lib then embeds the image inside the corresponding storyboard panel. This fallback is used when vector embedding is unavailable, including protected PDFs that can't follow the normal vector workflow. Adding Captions and Saving the PDF After the original page images or vector content have been placed, the application adds the storyboard's titles, labels, captions, and other drawing elements as an overlay. The following excerpt shows how the overlay is added and the final PDF is saved: var over = await out.embedPng(await pngBytes(c)); c.width = 1; page.drawImage(over, { x: 0, y: 0, width: L.W, height: L.H }); await nextFrame(); After all sheets have been processed, the application checks for cancellation and prepares the final PDF: checkCancel(); setProgress(1, 'Saving the PDF…'); out.setTitle(state.title || state.base + ' storyboard'); out.setCreator('AllInOneTools PDF Storyboard'); out.setProducer('AllInOneTools (pdf-lib)'); var bytes = await out.save(); if (token !== state.loadToken) { return; } save( new Blob([bytes], { type: 'application/pdf' }), state.base + '-storyboard.pdf' ); toast( 'Saved ' + plural(L.sheets, 'sheet', 'sheets') + ' as ' + state.base + '-storyboard.pdf.' ); The embedPng() method adds the storyboard overlay to the PDF page. This overlay contains the titles, panel labels, captions, and other visual elements. The application then sets the PDF metadata, saves the document as bytes, and creates a downloadable PDF file. Progress updates and cancellation checks are used throughout the export process, which is particularly helpful when generating storyboards with multiple sheets. The final PDF combines the original PDF pages with the storyboard layout and captions, ready to download, share, or print. Downloading PNG Storyboard Sheets Users who don't need a PDF can choose PNG sheets. The application renders each complete storyboard sheet as a PNG image at 200 DPI. If the storyboard contains only one sheet, the browser downloads a single PNG file. If it contains multiple sheets, the application packages them into a ZIP archive. Exporting the Storyboard as PNG The application handles PNG exports inside the exportJob() function. It first calculates the rendering scale and then processes each storyboard sheet. The following excerpt shows the actual PNG export implementation: var k = exportScale(L, 200, 16e6), files = []; for (var s = 0; s < L.sheets; s++) { checkCancel(); setProgress( s / L.sheets, 'Drawing sheet ' + (s + 1) + ' of ' + L.sheets + '…' ); var c = document.createElement('canvas'); c.width = Math.round(L.W * k); c.height = Math.round(L.H * k); var ok = await drawSheet( c.getContext('2d'), o, list, L, s, k, 'full', function (n, w, h) { checkCancel(); return renderPage(n, w, h); } ); if (!ok) { return; } files.push({ name: state.base + '-storyboard-sheet-' + pad2(s + 1) + '.png', data: await pngBytes(c) }); c.width = 1; } if (files.length === 1) { save( new Blob([files[0].data], { type: 'image/png' }), state.base + '-storyboard.png' ); } else { save(makeZip(files), state.base + '-storyboard-sheets.zip'); } toast( files.length === 1 ? 'Saved the storyboard as a PNG.' : 'Saved ' + files.length + ' sheets as PNG files in a ZIP.' ); The application uses exportScale() to calculate a suitable rendering scale for 200 DPI while keeping the canvas within a maximum pixel limit of 16 million pixels. For every sheet, it creates a canvas and calls drawSheet() in full mode. This draws the PDF page previews together with the storyboard titles, labels, captions, and other selected settings. The pngBytes() helper converts the completed canvas into PNG data. Each image is added to the files array with a filename containing its sheet number. After processing all sheets, the application checks how many PNG files were generated. A single sheet is downloaded directly as a PNG. Multiple sheets are packaged into a ZIP archive using makeZip() . This format is useful for sharing storyboard previews in presentations, messages, and other applications. Downloading Individual Page Pictures The third export option is Page pictures (ZIP). Unlike the PNG sheets option, this export contains individual pictures of the PDF pages selected for the storyboard. The application renders each selected page separately and places the resulting PNG files into a ZIP archive. Exporting Individual PDF Pages The actual application handles this option inside the exportJob() function. It first creates a unique list of selected pages and then renders each page individually. Here's the actual implementation: var pages = unique(list), out = []; for (var i = 0; i < pages.length; i++) { checkCancel(); setProgress( i / pages.length, 'Saving page ' + pages[i] + ' (' + (i + 1) + ' of ' + pages.length + ')…' ); var pg = await state.doc.getPage(pages[i]), vb = pg.getViewport({ scale: 1 }), sc = Math.min( 2, Math.sqrt(12e6 / (vb.width * vb.height)) ); var pc = await renderPage( pages[i], vb.width * sc, vb.height * sc ); out.push({ name: 'panel-' + pad2(list.indexOf(pages[i]) + 1) + '-page-' + pad2(pages[i]) + '.png', data: await pngBytes(pc) }); pc.width = 1; } save(makeZip(out), state.base + '-panels.zip'); toast( 'Saved ' + plural(out.length, 'page picture', 'page pictures') + ' in a ZIP.' ); The function first calls unique() to remove duplicate page numbers from the selected list. It then processes each page individually. The getPage() method retrieves the original PDF page, and getViewport() obtains its dimensions. The scale calculation limits the rendering scale to 2 while keeping the rendered page within approximately 12 million pixels. This helps control memory usage when processing large pages. The renderPage() function creates the page image, while pngBytes() converts the canvas into PNG data. Each image is added to the out array with a filename containing both its panel position and original PDF page number. This makes it easier to identify the pictures and maintain their storyboard order. Finally, makeZip() packages all the generated PNG images into a ZIP archive, which the browser downloads. This option is useful when users want to work with individual PDF page pictures rather than complete storyboard sheets. Performance and Important Considerations Rendering large PDFs and generating high-resolution images can consume significant browser memory. The application uses page-preview caching, temporary canvases, progress reporting, and cancellation controls to manage this work. For better results, use fewer panels per sheet when working with large documents. A3 paper can also provide more room when a storyboard contains many panels. Remember that layout preferences are remembered on the device, but the PDF and captions remain in the current browser tab. Download your work before closing the tab. Demo: PDF Storyboard Generator You can try the finished application here: PDF Storyboard Generator – AllInOneTools Upload a PDF, arrange its pages, add captions, customize the storyboard, and download the finished result. Conclusion Building a PDF Storyboard Generator combines several useful browser technologies into one application. PDF.js handles PDF loading and page rendering. Tesseract.js provides optional text recognition for scanned pages. PDF-lib creates the final storyboard PDF, while HTML canvas handles previews and image exports. By connecting these components with JavaScript, we can create a practical tool for organizing presentation slides, comic pages, scripts, and other PDF documents. The project also demonstrates how browser-based applications can process documents locally without requiring users to upload their files to a server. With the complete workflow in place, users can turn ordinary PDF pages into organized storyboard sheets that are easier to review, print, and share.
ai_summary: PDF files are commonly used to share presentations, scripts, reports, lesson materials, comic pages, and other visual documents. But reviewing a long PDF page by page can take time, especially when someone needs to understand the overall sequence of scenes, slides, or visual content.
main_event: How to Build a PDF Storyboard Generator Using JavaScript

article_content:
A top-down action roguelite only works when combat feels sharp, rooms feel connected, and every run asks you to trade power for risk. Godot 4 has the tools for that, but most tutorials stop before those systems fit together into a game someone else can open and play.

We just published a comprehensive 10-hour course on the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel that will teach you how to build a complete top-down action roguelite in Godot 4.7.2, from an empty project to an exported game. This course is taught by Omar Zaki, creator of Coding Quests, and most lessons include a Your Turn section where you build the next piece yourself before you see the solution.

Here is what the course covers:

Dash Combat & I-Frames

Build weighty movement, aiming, and a dodge with invincibility frames so combat feels fair instead of cheap.

Enemies, Telegraphs & a Boss Tell

Create five enemy types from a shared base, then add a boss with a clear warning before the hard hit lands.

Procedural Connected Rooms

Generate random floors of linked rooms in code, track where you are, and lock a fight until the room is clear.

Items, Corruption & Shops

Stack items into builds, take corruption that trades power for fragility, and risk gold at shops and a gambling altar.

Run Loop, Unlocks & Export

Wire death, permanent unlocks, a title screen, sound, and an export so a stranger can download and play your game.

Watch the full course on  the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel  (10-hour watch).

article_content:
If you've built a couple of React Native apps, the following probably feels familiar. You start with a  colors.ts  file and a simple  Button  component. Everything looks fine at first. Then the design changes a few times, and that small color file starts growing. Your Button also picks up another prop every time someone asks for a slightly different style.

The setup works at first, but after a few design changes, even a small update can mean checking several files across the project.

Here's what a typical color file looks like after a while:

export const colors = {

primary: '#6e4836',

primaryPressed: '#5a3a2b',

textPrimary: '#261d16',

textSecondary: '#72665e',

// and forty more

};

And here's what a typical  Button  looks like after a few redesigns:

<Button

variant="primary"

size="md"

fullWidth

loading={busy}

containerStyle={styles.checkoutButton}

labelStyle={styles.checkoutLabel}

/>

These are simplified examples, but you get the idea. The color object keeps growing, and the Button collects more props to handle every new design request.

Each change seems reasonable when you make it. But the annoying part comes later, when changing one design decision means checking several files to see that nothing else has changed unexpectedly.

Part of the problem is how many component libraries are distributed. Their code lives in  node_modules , so you usually customize them through the props and options they expose. When the library doesn't cover your exact use case, you add another prop or override. Keep doing that and the component can become harder to maintain than the original problem you were trying to solve.

This is one reason I like shadcn/ui's approach. You don't install a traditional component package and treat its components as fixed. The CLI copies the source code into your project, where you can change it whenever you need to. For React Native, there's a project built around the same idea called  React Native Reusables .

To make this practical, I'll use React Native Reusables, Expo, and Uniwind to build a  cart and checkout screen for a coffee shop's pickup orders . It includes order items with quantity controls, a pickup-time dropdown, a name field, an "own cup" toggle, a bill summary, a checkout bar that stays at the bottom, and an order-confirmation dialog. If you want to see how reusable sections come together in complete interfaces, you can also browse  shadcn templates .

I'll also point out a few things that are easy to miss when working with these components, including:

How shadcn/ui and its CLI work, and why you own the component code

How design tokens (named colors) replace a  colors.ts  file

How to use components such as Card, Select, Switch, and AlertDialog in React Native

How to handle mobile-specific issues, such as safe areas, keyboards, and tap targets

How to switch between light and dark mode, and how to change the whole theme from one file

Resources

Prerequisites

To follow along, you should have:

Node.js 20 or newer.  You can use pnpm, npm, yarn, or bun. The commands in this tutorial use pnpm, so swap the prefix if you use something else.

Basic knowledge of React and TypeScript , especially hooks such as  useState .

Some familiarity with React Native , such as  View ,  Text , and  ScrollView . You don't need to know Tailwind, but it helps.

Optional:  Xcode or Android Studio if you want to run the app in a simulator. Everything also runs in a web browser through React Native Web, and that's how the screenshots in this tutorial were taken.

You don't need any accounts or API keys, and nothing here costs money.

Tools You Will Use

Before creating the app, let's look at the tools in this project. Each one has a specific job, and knowing that will make the setup easier to follow.

shadcn/ui  is a collection of UI components for the web. It's not installed as a package. Instead, a command-line tool (CLI) copies the source code of each component into your project, and from then on the code is yours to edit.

React Native Reusables  is the React Native version of shadcn/ui. It gives you components such as Button, Card, Select, and Dialog that are written for React Native and styled with Tailwind-style class names. It uses the same CLI idea as shadcn/ui.

RN Primitives  is a React Native port of Radix UI, which is the library that shadcn/ui uses for behavior on the web. A "primitive" is a component that handles the behavior but has no styling. For example, the  select  primitive knows how a dropdown opens and closes and how it's announced to screen readers, but it has no colors or borders. React Native Reusables adds the looks on top.

Uniwind  is a tool that lets you style React Native components with Tailwind CSS class names, such as  className="bg-primary p-4" . It converts those classes into regular React Native styles while the app is being bundled, so there's no extra work at runtime.  Nativewind  does a similar job, and React Native Reusables supports both. This tutorial uses Uniwind.

Expo and Expo Router  provide the project setup, the development server, and file-based navigation. If you have used Next.js, Expo Router works in a similar way.

How shadcn/ui Works

The React Native Reusables documentation opens with a quote from shadcn:

This is not a component library. It is how you build your component library.

You won't add shadcn/ui as a regular dependency in  package.json . It uses a  registry  instead. A registry is a collection of JSON files hosted on a server. Each file describes a component and includes the information the CLI needs to add it to your project. When you run the CLI, it reads the relevant file and copies the component's source code into your project.

To see what this looks like, here's the registry entry for the  Badge  component. A Badge is a small label, such as the "Medium" tag next to a coffee in the cart you will build later. This is a shortened version of the real file:

{

"$schema": "https://ui.shadcn.com/schema/registry-item.json",

"name": "badge",

"type": "registry:ui",

"title": "Badge",

"author": "@mrzachnugent",

"description": "Displays a badge or a component that looks like a badge.",

"dependencies": ["@rn-primitives/slot"],

"registryDependencies": ["https://reactnativereusables.com/r/uniwind/text.json"],

"files": [

{

"path": "./node_modules/@rnr/registry/src/uniwind/components/ui/badge.tsx",

"content": "import { TextClassContext } from '@/components/ui/text';\nimport ...",

"type": "registry:ui"

}

]

}

The file is public, so you can look at it yourself:

curl https://reactnativereusables.com/r/uniwind/badge.json

Here's what the important fields mean:

content  holds the full source code of the component, stored as a string.

dependencies  lists npm packages that the component needs. The CLI installs these first.

registryDependencies  lists other registry entries that the component needs. In this case, Badge needs the  Text  component, which is a small wrapper around React Native's  Text  that you will read about in Step 3. When you run the CLI to add Badge, it also adds Text for you because of this field.

That's how a component gets from the registry into your app. The registry stores the component information, and the CLI uses it to create the files in your repository. React Native Reusables uses the shadcn CLI behind the scenes, so you can follow the same workflow when adding React Native components.

There are a few reasons this approach is useful when you're building an app:

You own the file:  A component such as  components/ui/button.tsx  sits in your repository and shows up in your Git diffs. If you want a darker pressed state, you edit that line. You don't need to invent a new prop, maintain a fork, or open an issue.

Design lives in named colors instead of props:  Colors are declared once as named roles, such as  primary ,  muted ,  border , and  destructive . You then use them in class names, like  className="bg-primary" . This replaces the  colors.ts  file from the introduction, because there's one place that defines your colors, and every component reads from it. You'll set this up in Step 2.

Behavior comes from a separate package:  Things such as focus handling, open and close state, and screen reader support live in RN Primitives. You only write the styling.

There's one trade-off to keep in mind. Since the component code is copied into your project, updates from the registry aren't applied automatically. If a bug is fixed upstream, you'll need to run the CLI again with  --overwrite . If you have customized that component, you may also need to reapply your changes. This is worth considering before you make large changes to several components.

What React Native Reusables Gives You

At the time of writing, React Native Reusables includes thirty components: accordion, alert, alert-dialog, aspect-ratio, avatar, badge, button, card, checkbox, collapsible, context-menu, dialog, dropdown-menu, hover-card, input, label, menubar, popover, progress, radio-group, select, separator, skeleton, switch, tabs, text, textarea, toggle, toggle-group, and tooltip. The available components cover many of the building blocks you need for a typical app interface.

React Native is different from the web in several ways, so the components can't be an exact copy of the web version. The documentation lists the main differences, and you'll run into each of them in this tutorial. If you're also building web interfaces with shadcn/ui,  shadcn components  can be useful when you need more ready-made examples to work from.

Step 1: Create the App

We can let the React Native Reusables CLI create the initial project for us. It sets up Expo Router, the styling configuration, the theme file, and a few starter components. Run the following command to get started:

pnpm dlx @react-native-reusables/cli@latest init

Answer the CLI's Questions

The CLI asks four questions.

What is the name of your project?  The name you type becomes the folder name. It suggests  my-app .

Select a template.  There are three options, and the one you need isn't the one selected by default:

❯ Minimal (Nativewind)

Minimal (Uniwind)

Clerk auth (Nativewind)

Press the down arrow once and choose  Minimal (Uniwind) . This is the one choice that's tricky to change later. Nativewind and Uniwind are two different ways to use Tailwind in React Native, and the CLI keeps a separate registry for each one. The components it writes for Uniwind are different from the ones it writes for Nativewind, so the code in this tutorial won't match if you pick Nativewind.

Would you like to install dependencies?  Choose yes, and select the package manager you use.

Would you like to initialize a Git repository?  Choose yes. You're about to replace the starter screen, and having a commit to compare against is helpful.

Look at the Project Structure

The CLI creates the following files:

shadcn-react-native-app/

├── app/

│   ├── _layout.tsx        # ThemeProvider, Stack, and the PortalHost

│   ├── +html.tsx          # web only, the root HTML shell

│   ├── +not-found.tsx

│   └── index.tsx          # the starter screen

├── components/ui/

│   ├── button.tsx

│   ├── icon.tsx

│   └── text.tsx

├── lib/

│   ├── theme.ts           # the same palette again, in JavaScript

│   └── utils.ts           # cn()

├── global.css             # the theme tokens

├── components.json        # the shadcn config, same as on the web

├── metro.config.js        # withUniwindConfig

└── uniwind-types.d.ts     # generated, do not edit

Before moving on, let's take a look at a few files in this structure. You'll use them throughout the tutorial:

components.json  is the same shadcn configuration file used on the web. It tells the CLI where to put components ( @/components/ui ) and where the  cn()  helper lives ( @/lib/utils ).

global.css  holds your theme tokens, which you'll learn about in Step 2.

lib/utils.ts  exports  cn() , a helper that combines class names and resolves conflicts between them.

app/_layout.tsx  contains a  PortalHost  component. It looks like leftover scaffolding, but you must not delete it. Step 7 explains why.

Uniwind reads  global.css  while Metro bundles the app and turns your class strings into React Native style objects. This happens at build time, so a long  className  string doesn't slow down your app.

Run the App

Press  w  to open it in the browser,  i  for the iOS simulator, or  a  for Android. The starter screen has a theme toggle in the header, which shows that the theme setup is working.

You can also run a diagnostic command at any point if something seems wrong:

Step 2: Understand the Theme File

Now that the app is running, let's look at its theme setup. The  global.css  file is where we'll define the colors used by the components. If you've previously kept these values in a  colors.ts  or  theme.ts  file, this is the setup that replaces it.

@import "tailwindcss";

@import "uniwind";

@import "tw-animate-css";

@theme {

--radius: 10px;

--radius-sm: calc(var(--radius) - 4px);

--radius-md: calc(var(--radius) - 2px);

--radius-lg: var(--radius);

--radius-xl: calc(var(--radius) + 4px);

--spacing-hairline: hairlineWidth();

}

@layer theme {

:root {

@variant light {

--color-background: oklch(1 0 0);

--color-foreground: oklch(0.145 0 0);

--color-card: oklch(1 0 0);

--color-primary: oklch(0.205 0 0);

--color-muted-foreground: oklch(0.556 0 0);

--color-border: oklch(0.922 0 0);

/* the rest of the list */

}

@variant dark {

--color-background: oklch(0.145 0 0);

--color-foreground: oklch(0.985 0 0);

--color-card: oklch(0.205 0 0);

--color-primary: oklch(0.922 0 0);

--color-muted-foreground: oklch(0.708 0 0);

--color-border: oklch(1 0 0 / 10%);

/* the rest of the list */

}

}

}

There are two conventions in this file that you need to know.

First, the  --color-  prefix creates the class names. When you declare  --color-primary , Tailwind automatically creates  bg-primary ,  text-primary , and  border-primary . If you declare  --primary  instead, you only get a CSS variable that nothing uses.

This is important because most shadcn theme generators produce the web format, where the variables are named  --primary . If you paste that output without renaming the variables, nothing breaks, but nothing changes either. Step 12 shows you how to convert them.

Second,  @variant light  and  @variant dark  replace  :root  and  .dark . On the web, dark mode works by adding a  .dark  class to the page. A phone has no page to add a class to, so Uniwind manages the switch. When you call  Uniwind.setTheme , it swaps the active values. You'll use this in Step 11.

You may also notice that the file uses  oklch()  colors. Phones don't have a browser to read that format, but Uniwind converts the colors to a format React Native understands while bundling, so you can use modern color syntax anyway.

The Palette Also Exists in  lib/theme.ts

If you open  lib/theme.ts , you'll find the same colors again as a JavaScript object. This duplication is needed because React Navigation, which draws the header and screen background, reads colors from a plain JavaScript object and can't read CSS variables. As a result, you have to keep two copies of your palette in sync. Step 12 shows what happens when they differ.

Try It: Change One Color

Let's change one of the tokens to see how the theme works. Update the primary color in the light theme to a value that's easy to notice:

--color-primary: oklch(0.6 0.24 25);

Save the file and look at the starter screen. The  Browse the Docs  button is now red, even though you didn't edit  button.tsx :

Notice that every component using  bg-primary  picks up the new color. You only changed one token, but the button updated without touching its component file. Change the value back before continuing.

Step 3: Read Three Core Components

The starter project already gives us three components:  Text ,  Button , and  Icon . I'd take a few minutes to look through them before building the screen. They introduce patterns you'll see again in the other registry components.

The Text Component

In React Native, styles don't cascade the way they do in CSS. If you set a text color on a  View , the text inside it doesn't inherit that color. This is a problem for a component such as  <Button variant="destructive"> , which needs its label to be white. The label is a  Text  component that the Button doesn't control, because it comes in through  children . On the web, the Button would simply set a color and let it flow down to the label.

React Native Reusables solves this with React context. This is the code in  components/ui/text.tsx :

const TextClassContext = React.createContext<string | undefined>(undefined);

function Text({ className, asChild = false, variant = 'default', ...props }) {

const textClass = React.useContext(TextClassContext);

const Component = asChild ? Slot : RNText;

return (

<Component

className={cn(textVariants({ variant }), textClass, className)}

role={variant ? ROLE[variant] : undefined}

aria-level={variant ? ARIA_LEVEL[variant] : undefined}

{...props}

/>

);

}

A parent component, such as Button, puts a class string into the context. Every  Text  inside it reads that string and applies it. Your own  className  still wins because it comes last in the  cn()  call.

The  Text  component also has a  variant  prop with options like  h1  to  h4 ,  p ,  code ,  lead ,  large ,  small , and  muted . For example,  <Text variant="muted">  gives you the mobile version of  text-muted-foreground text-sm . The variants also set the  role  and  aria-level  props, so screen readers announce headings correctly without any extra work.

The Button Component

The Button in  components/ui/button.tsx  uses  cva  (class-variance-authority) the same way the web version does. Here's a shortened version:

const buttonVariants = cva(

cn(

'group shrink-0 flex-row items-center justify-center gap-2 rounded-md shadow-none',

Platform.select({

web: "focus-visible:border-ring focus-visible:ring-ring/50 ... transition-all",

})

),

{

variants: {

variant: {

default: cn(

'bg-primary active:bg-primary/90 shadow-sm shadow-black/5',

Platform.select({ web: 'hover:bg-primary/90' })

),

/* ... */

},

},

}

);

There are four differences from the web version:

flex-row   is written out:  React Native lays out children in a column by default, which is the opposite of CSS. Every horizontal layout in this tutorial includes  flex-row  for that reason.

active:   replaces   hover:  :  A finger can't really hover, so  active:  is the pressed state on a phone.

Web-only classes are wrapped in   Platform.select  :  Classes such as  focus-visible:ring-[3px]  mean nothing in React Native, so they're only included in the web build.

A   TextClassContext.Provider   wraps the   Pressable  :  This uses the context from the previous section, and it's why  <Button variant="destructive"><Text>Delete</Text></Button>  has white text automatically.

The Icon Component

Icons from  lucide-react-native  take  color  and  size  as props, not as class names. The  Icon  component in  components/ui/icon.tsx  teaches Uniwind how to convert one into the other:

const StyledIcon = withUniwind(IconImpl, {

size: { fromClassName: 'className', styleProperty: 'width' },

color: { fromClassName: 'className', styleProperty: 'color' },

});

This code reads the  width  from the class string and passes it as  size , and it reads the  color  and passes it as  color . That's why  <Icon as={PlusIcon} className="size-4 text-muted-foreground" />  works the way you would expect.  withUniwind  is useful any time you use a third-party component that takes props where you want to use classes.

You don't need to run anything for this step. The important part is understanding what  TextClassContext  is doing. Once that clicks, the other components in the registry are much easier to follow.

Step 5: Set Up the Data and the Screen

Before we start building the UI, let's add the sample menu data and decide where the screen state will live. I'm going to store prices in cents rather than floating-point numbers. This avoids calculation results such as  $4.7499999 .

We'll also keep the state in the main screen component and pass the relevant values down as props. That way, changing an item quantity or selecting the own-cup option automatically updates the bill.

Create  lib/menu.ts :

export type CartItem = {

id: string;

name: string;

detail: string;

size?: 'Small' | 'Medium' | 'Large';

emoji: string;

/** Cents. Money in floats is how you end up charging someone $4.7499999. */

unitPrice: number;

qty: number;

};

export const INITIAL_CART: CartItem[] = [

{

id: 'flat-white',

name: 'Flat white',

detail: 'Oat milk, extra shot',

size: 'Medium',

emoji: '☕️',

unitPrice: 475,

qty: 2,

},

{

id: 'cold-brew',

name: 'Cold brew',

detail: 'Hold the ice',

size: 'Large',

emoji: '🧋',

unitPrice: 525,

qty: 1,

},

{

id: 'croissant',

name: 'Almond croissant',

detail: 'Warmed',

emoji: '🥐',

unitPrice: 390,

qty: 1,

},

];

export const PICKUP_TIMES = [

{ value: 'asap', label: 'As soon as it is ready' },

{ value: '15', label: 'In 15 minutes' },

{ value: '30', label: 'In 30 minutes' },

{ value: '60', label: 'In an hour' },

];

export const CUP_DISCOUNT = 25;

export const TAX_RATE = 0.0825;

export function money(cents: number) {

const sign = cents < 0 ? '-' : '';

return `${sign}$${(Math.abs(cents) / 100).toFixed(2)}`;

}

export function billFor(items: CartItem[], ownCup: boolean) {

const subtotal = items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.unitPrice * item.qty, 0);

const discount = ownCup && subtotal > 0 ? CUP_DISCOUNT : 0;

const tax = Math.round((subtotal - discount) * TAX_RATE);

return { subtotal, discount, tax, total: subtotal - discount + tax };

}

The  PICKUP_TIMES  list is in this file instead of inside a component because two different components need it. You'll see why in Step 7.

The Screen Layout

This is basically how  app/index.tsx  looks. The parts that don't exist yet are left as comments, and you'll write the full file later in Step 10.

<View className="bg-background flex-1">

<ScrollView

className="flex-1"

contentContainerClassName="gap-4 p-4 pb-8"

keyboardShouldPersistTaps="handled"

automaticallyAdjustKeyboardInsets>

There are three details in this layout that you should examine more closely:

First,  className  on a  ScrollView  styles the scroll container, not its content. This is the class name version of the  style  and  contentContainerStyle  split in React Native. If you put padding in  className , it gets clipped, and  gap  has no effect. Use  contentContainerClassName  for anything that should apply to the content. Uniwind adds this prop to  ScrollView .

There's no  space-y-4 . In CSS,  space-y-*  works by selecting siblings, and React Native has no selectors. Use  gap-4  on the parent instead, which React Native supports on iOS, Android, and the web.

keyboardShouldPersistTaps="handled"  keeps taps working while the keyboard is open. Without it, the first tap after the keyboard appears only closes the keyboard, so the user has to tap twice.  automaticallyAdjustKeyboardInsets  is an iOS feature that scrolls the content so the focused input isn't hidden behind the keyboard.

The order row has quite a bit going on in a small space: an avatar, product name, size badge, price, and quantity controls. Long names make this especially tricky on a phone, so we'll handle the layout carefully.

Create  components/cart/order-row.tsx :

</AvatarFallback>

</Avatar>

<View className="flex-row items-start gap-3">

<View className="flex-1 gap-1">

<View className="flex-row items-center gap-2">

{item.name}

</Text>

{item.size ? (

<Badge variant="secondary">

<Text>{item.size}</Text>

</Badge>

) : null}

</View>

<Text numberOfLines={1} variant="muted">

{item.detail}

</Text>

</View>

<Text className="text-sm font-medium tabular-nums">

{money(item.unitPrice * item.qty)}

</Text>

className="size-7 rounded-full"

onPress={() => onChangeQty(item.id, item.qty - 1)}>

<Icon as={lastOne ? Trash2Icon : MinusIcon} className="size-4" />

</Button>

size="icon"

A few details in this component deserve a closer look.

First,  Avatar  requires the  alt  prop. TypeScript won't compile without it. The value becomes the accessibility label, so a screen reader says "Flat white" instead of just "image".

The radius is repeated on the avatar fallback.  Avatar  and  AvatarFallback  are each  rounded-full  by default. If you only set  rounded-2xl  on  Avatar , the emoji background stays a circle and pokes out of the rounded square.

You should also use  numberOfLines={1}  instead of  truncate . Tailwind's  truncate  relies on  text-overflow: ellipsis , which React Native doesn't support, and Uniwind doesn't convert it. The class compiles to nothing, so a long product name pushes the price off the screen. The  numberOfLines  prop is the React Native way to do this, and it also works in the web build.

The name has  shrink  and its column has  flex-1 . Without  shrink , a long name won't get smaller and will push the badge out of the row. This is regular Flexbox behavior, but it shows up more on a phone because there's less width to work with.

hitSlop={8}  makes small buttons easier to tap. Apple recommends touch targets of at least 44 points and Android recommends 48dp, but a  size-7  button is only 28 points wide. The  hitSlop  prop makes the touchable area larger without changing how the button looks. There's no CSS equivalent.

Finally,  tabular-nums  keeps digits the same width. In most fonts, the digit  1  is narrower than  8 , so prices would shift sideways every time the quantity changes. Uniwind converts  tabular-nums  to React Native's  fontVariant , so it works on iOS, Android, and the web.

After adding this component and rendering it inside a Card (which you'll do in Step 10), you should see three rows:

Tapping plus on the flat white should change its price from  $9.50  to  $14.25 . Tapping the trash icon on an item with a quantity of one should remove the row. The minus button turns into a trash icon whenever the quantity is one.

// Look the label up from our own data. The Option handed back by onValueChange

// does not carry a usable label on web. See the note below.

const selected = PICKUP_TIMES.find((time) => time.value === pickupValue);

const contentInsets = {

top: insets.top,

bottom: insets.bottom,

left: 16,

right: 16,

};

return (

<View className="gap-2">

<Label nativeID="pickup-time">Pickup time</Label>

<Select

value={selected}

onValueChange={(option) => {

if (option) {

onPickupValueChange(option.value);

}

}}>

<SelectTrigger className="w-full" aria-labelledby="pickup-time">

<SelectValue placeholder="Pick a time" />

</SelectTrigger>

<SelectContent insets={contentInsets} className="w-full">

{PICKUP_TIMES.map((time) => (

<SelectItem key={time.value} value={time.value} label={time.label} />

))}

</SelectContent>

</Select>

</View>

<View className="gap-2">

<Label nativeID="order-name">Name for the order</Label>

<Input

aria-labelledby="order-name"

value={name}

onChangeText={onNameChange}

placeholder="Who is picking it up?"

autoCapitalize="words"

autoComplete="name"

returnKeyType="done"

/>

</View>

<View className="flex-row items-center justify-between gap-4">

<View className="flex-1 gap-1">

<Label nativeID="own-cup" onPress={() => onOwnCupChange(!ownCup)}>

Bringing my own cup

</Label>

Problem 1: Portals and the PortalHost

When a dropdown opens, it needs to appear above the other content on the screen. For that reason,  SelectContent  isn't rendered in the same place where you declare it in the component tree. It uses  @rn-primitives/portal  to render the content in another part of the app. This technique is called a portal.

On the web, a portal renders into  document.body , and every page has one. React Native has nothing like that. So the portal package keeps a list of portal contents in memory, and a component called  PortalHost  reads that list and displays it. This is a simplified version of that code from  node_modules/@rn-primitives/portal/dist/index.js :

var DEFAULT_PORTAL_HOST = "INTERNAL_PRIMITIVE_DEFAULT_HOST_NAME";

var updatePortal = (hostName, name, children) => { /* writes into the map */ };

function PortalHost({ name = DEFAULT_PORTAL_HOST }) { /* reads the map */ }

If no  PortalHost  is mounted, the content is saved but never displayed. The dropdown opens into nothing, and you get no error or warning.

The template already includes a  PortalHost  at the bottom of the root layout:

<ThemeProvider value={NAV_THEME[theme ?? 'light']}>

<StatusBar style={theme === 'dark' ? 'light' : 'dark'} />

<Stack />

<PortalHost />

</ThemeProvider>

It looks like unnecessary code, but you need to keep it. The AlertDialog in Step 10 uses it too.

Problem 2: Safe Area Insets

There's another issue to consider when showing a dropdown on a phone. Parts of the screen are reserved for the operating system, such as the area around the notch and the home indicator. If a dropdown opens near the bottom of the screen, one of its options could appear underneath the home indicator. In that area, a tap may be handled by the operating system instead of your app.

To avoid this, pass the safe area insets to the content:

const insets = useSafeAreaInsets();

const contentInsets = { top: insets.top, bottom: insets.bottom, left: 16, right: 16 };

<SelectContent insets={contentInsets} className="w-full">

The  insets  prop is part of  PositionedContentProps  in  @rn-primitives/types , so every positioned component in the registry accepts it, including Popover, DropdownMenu, HoverCard, Tooltip, and Select. It's a good habit to pass it every time.

Problem 3: The Select Value Is an Object

One more thing to watch out for is the value returned by  onValueChange . It may look like you're selecting a string, but the callback returns an  Option  object:

type Option = { value: string; label: string } | undefined;

This causes a bug that only appears on one platform. If you store the whole  Option  in state and show  option.label  later, such as in a confirmation dialog, it displays correctly on a phone ("In 30 minutes") but incorrectly in the browser ("30").

The reason is in the primitive's source code. This is the native version, from  select.js :

onValueChange({ value: itemValue, label });

And this is the web version, from  select.web.js . It uses Radix, which only returns a value:

onValueChange({ value: val, label: val });

So the label is correct on native, but on the web it's a copy of the value. If you only test in a simulator, you won't notice this problem.

The fix is to keep only the value in state and look up the label from your own list:

const selected = PICKUP_TIMES.find((time) => time.value === pickupValue);

This is why  PICKUP_TIMES  is in  lib/menu.ts . The pickup card needs it to build the options, and the main screen needs it to write the confirmation message.

Making the Label Tappable

The switch itself is quite small, so users may tap the label next to it instead. It makes sense to let that label toggle the switch as well. You can do that by adding an  onPress  handler to the  Label :

<Label nativeID="own-cup" onPress={() => onOwnCupChange(!ownCup)}>

Bringing my own cup

</Label>

<Switch nativeID="own-cup" checked={ownCup} onCheckedChange={onOwnCupChange} />

Giving both elements the same  nativeID  connects them for screen readers. The  onPress  on the  Label  is what makes the text toggle the switch, because React Native has no automatic  <label for>  behavior.

While you're here, open  components/ui/switch.tsx . On the web, shadcn colors a switch with  data-[state=checked]:bg-primary , which reads an attribute set in the DOM. React Native has no  data-*  attributes, so the component checks the prop in JavaScript:

props.checked ? 'bg-primary' : 'bg-input dark:bg-input/80',

The result is the same. Keep this in mind if you copy a  data-[state=...]  selector from a web example and it has no effect.

Keyboard Props for the Name Field

Input  is a  TextInput  with your border and radius applied. You should set these four props on every text input:

autoCapitalize="words"  capitalizes each word, which suits a name.

autoComplete="name"  lets the operating system offer to fill in the name.

returnKeyType="done"  changes the return key label to "Done".

keyboardType="number-pad"  shows a numeric keyboard when you need digits.

Together with  automaticallyAdjustKeyboardInsets  on the ScrollView from Step 5, this keeps the field visible while the keyboard is open. If you need more control,  react-native-keyboard-controller  is already a dependency of the template, and it provides  KeyboardAwareScrollView  and  KeyboardProvider .

When you open the dropdown, it should appear right under the trigger at the same width, with a check mark next to the current value:

Try picking a time and check that the trigger updates. Tap the words "Bringing my own cup" and confirm the switch flips. Type in the name field and confirm the keyboard doesn't cover it. If the dropdown opens and shows nothing, check your  PortalHost .

Step 8: Build the Bill Component

The bill component is pretty small, but there are two details you should pay particular attention to here, especially when the values change while someone is editing their order.

Create  components/cart/bill.tsx :

import { Separator } from '@/components/ui/separator';

import { Text } from '@/components/ui/text';

import { cn } from '@/lib/utils';

import { money } from '@/lib/menu';

import { View } from 'react-native';

type BillProps = {

subtotal: number;

discount: number;

tax: number;

total: number;

};

function Line({ label, value, tone }: { label: string; value: number; tone?: 'muted' | 'credit' }) {

return (

<View className="flex-row items-center justify-between">

<Text className={cn('text-sm', tone === 'muted' && 'text-muted-foreground')}>{label}</Text>

<Text

className={cn(

'text-sm tabular-nums',

tone === 'muted' && 'text-muted-foreground',

tone === 'credit' && 'text-foreground'

)}>

{money(value)}

</Text>

</View>

);

}

export function Bill({ subtotal, discount, tax, total }: BillProps) {

return (

<View className="gap-2">

<Line label="Subtotal" value={subtotal} tone="muted" />

{discount > 0 ? <Line label="Own cup" value={-discount} tone="credit" /> : null}

<Line label="Tax" value={tax} tone="muted" />

<Separator className="my-1" />

<View className="flex-row items-center justify-between">

<Text className="font-medium">Total</Text>

<Text className="text-lg font-semibold tabular-nums">{money(total)}</Text>

</View>

</View>

);

}

First, use  tabular-nums  on every number. Right-aligned prices in a proportional font don't line up at the decimal point, and using  tabular-nums  fixes that, as in the order rows.

Second, only show the discount row when it applies. The code uses  {discount > 0 ? <Line /> : null}  instead of  {discount && <Line />} . In JSX, if the left side of  &&  is the number  0 , React renders the  0 . In React Native, a bare number outside a  Text  component throws the error  Text strings must be rendered within a <Text> component . Using a boolean check and returning  null  avoids this whole category of bugs.

To test it, turn on the own cup switch and scroll down. An  Own cup  line should appear with  -$0.25 , and the tax should change from  $1.54  to  $1.52 , because tax is calculated on the discounted subtotal:

The total changes from  $20.19  to  $19.92 , which is 27 cents lower instead of 25. The extra two cents come from the lower tax.

Step 9: Build the Fixed Checkout Bar

I want the total and checkout button to remain visible while the user scrolls through the cart. On the web, you might reach for  position: sticky  and  bottom: 0 . React Native doesn't work that way, but we can get the same result with a simple flex layout.

You can get the same result with Flexbox. This is the layout from Step 5 again:

<View className="bg-background flex-1">

<ScrollView className="flex-1" ...>{/* content */}</ScrollView>

<CheckoutBar ... />

</View>

The outer  View  is a column. The  ScrollView  has  flex-1 , so it takes all the leftover height. The checkout bar is a sibling placed after it, so it sits at the bottom and doesn't scroll. You don't need any positioning or z-index.

Handling the Home Indicator

On phones without a home button, the bottom 34 points or so belong to the system. A button drawn there is hard or impossible to press. To avoid this, add the bottom safe area inset as padding.

const insets = useSafeAreaInsets();

<View

className="border-border bg-background flex-row items-center gap-4 border-t px-4 pt-3"

style={{ paddingBottom: insets.bottom + 12 }}>

The bottom padding is an inline  style  instead of a class because its value depends on the device and is only known when the app runs. Using  className  and  style  on the same element is fine, and this is the case it's meant for.

On devices with no gesture bar, and in a browser tab,  insets.bottom  is 0, so the extra  12  keeps the bar from looking cramped.

Create the full component in  components/cart/checkout-bar.tsx . It includes the confirmation dialog, which Step 10 explains.

A Note on Thin Borders

border-t  draws a line that's one logical point thick, which is two or three physical pixels on most modern screens. Next to a true one-pixel line, it looks heavy. React Native's  StyleSheet.hairlineWidth  gives you the thinnest line the screen can draw, and the template connects it to Tailwind with this line in  global.css :

--spacing-hairline: hairlineWidth();

This adds  hairline  to Tailwind's spacing scale, so  h-hairline  gives you a divider that's one physical pixel tall. The Common Mistakes section later explains one catch when you try to use it as an override.

Step 10: Add the Confirmation and Put the Screen Together

The checkout bar already contains the confirmation dialog. Before putting the full screen together, there are two differences between the React Native implementation and the web version that are worth looking at.

1. It Also Needs the  PortalHost

On iOS, it also wraps itself in  FullWindowOverlay  from  react-native-screens , so it draws above the native navigation header instead of under it. This is handled inside  alert-dialog.tsx , which is why that file imports something that looks unrelated.

2. The Footer Reverses its Order on Phones

AlertDialogFooter  uses  flex-col-reverse  and only becomes a row at the  sm:  breakpoint. On a phone, the button you write last is shown on top. Writing Cancel first and Action second puts the confirm button where the thumb is and the cancel button below it.

Haptics

When the customer confirms the order, the  confirm  function calls  Haptics.notificationAsync(Haptics.NotificationFeedbackType.Success) . This gives a short success vibration on supported devices.

You might expect to wrap this call in a platform check because browsers don't have the same haptics support as native apps. In this case,  expo-haptics  already includes a web implementation that uses  navigator.vibrate , with a fallback for iOS Safari. If the browser can't provide haptics, the call simply does nothing, so we don't need an extra platform check.

notificationAsync  is meant for outcomes such as success or failure.  impactAsync  is for physical collisions, and  selectionAsync  is for moving through a list of options. Using the wrong one won't cause an error, but it feels slightly off.

The Full Screen

Now we can bring everything together in the main screen. This is where we'll keep the state, calculate the bill using  billFor , and pass the required values and callbacks to each component.

When an order is placed, it sets  orderNumber , and the screen shows a confirmation instead. Inside that confirmation,  <Stack.Screen options>  changes the header title to "Order sent" without navigating anywhere, so the whole flow stays in one file and one route.

Step 11: Add Dark Mode

We already added the theme toggle in Step 10. Here's the component again so we can look at how it switches between light and dark mode:

import { Uniwind, useUniwind } from 'uniwind';

function ThemeToggle() {

const { theme } = useUniwind();

return (

<Button

onPressIn={() => Uniwind.setTheme(theme === 'dark' ? 'light' : 'dark')}

size="icon"

variant="ghost"

className="ios:size-9 web:mx-4 rounded-full"

accessibilityLabel="Switch theme">

<Icon as={THEME_ICONS[theme ?? 'light']} className="size-5" />

</Button>

);

}

Uniwind.setTheme  changes the values behind every token, so everything that uses  bg-card ,  text-muted-foreground , and similar classes updates at once.  useUniwind  subscribes the component to the current theme, so the icon changes too.

This code also uses the  ios:  and  web:  prefixes. Uniwind supports platform variants, so  web:mx-4  only adds margin in the browser, and  ios:size-9  only applies on iOS. It's similar to  Platform.select , but it stays inside the class string.

Three things aren't handled by  setTheme , and if you forget them, you end up with a screen that's only partly dark. The template already sets up the first two.

1. The Navigation Header

React Navigation takes its colors from a plain object, so the root layout needs to pass it the right one:

const { theme } = useUniwind();

<ThemeProvider value={NAV_THEME[theme ?? 'light']}>

2. The Status Bar

The clock and battery icons are drawn by the operating system, so you need to tell it which style to use. Without this, you can get dark text on a dark bar.

<StatusBar style={theme === 'dark' ? 'light' : 'dark'} />

3. Saving the Choice

Uniwind.setTheme  only applies to the current session. The next time the app starts, it follows the system setting again. To keep the user's choice, save it with  expo-secure-store  or  AsyncStorage  and call  setTheme  when the app starts. You can call  setTheme('system')  to go back to following the operating system.

When you tap the header icon, the cards, borders, inputs, switch, header, and status bar should all change together. You can explore more ready-made  shadcn blocks  if you want examples of how these components are used in larger interfaces:

Look for anything that stays light while the rest goes dark. A light header usually means the  ThemeProvider  is not receiving the new  NAV_THEME .

--color-input: oklch(1 0 0 / 15%);

--color-ring: oklch(0.85 0.09 75);

}

}

}

If you don't want to choose thirty colors by hand, you can generate a theme with the  shadcn theme generator  or  tweakcn . Both export CSS variables, but you need to make two changes before the output works in this project:

Rename each variable to include the  --color-  prefix. For example,  --primary  becomes  --color-primary .

Move the  :root  block inside  @variant light , and the  .dark  block inside  @variant dark .

Also remove  --radius  from what you paste, because the template already defines it along with the derived sizes. Remove any  --shadow-*  variables too, since nothing in the registry reads them.

Update lib/theme.ts

After you save and reload, the result looks like this:

The page is cream, the button is brown, and the badges have the right color, but the header is still white with a visible line under it. The reason is that React Navigation draws the header using  lib/theme.ts , and that file still has the old palette. Nothing is broken and nothing warns you, so this mistake is easy to miss. If you're designing the same interface in Figma, the  shadcn Figma resources  can also help you keep the design and implementation aligned.

Update  lib/theme.ts  to match:

import { DarkTheme, DefaultTheme, type Theme } from 'expo-router/react-navigation';

export const THEME = {

light: {

background: '#fcf8f3',

foreground: '#261d16',

card: '#fffffd',

primary: '#6e4836',

border: '#e3d9cd',

destructive: '#e7000b',

/* the rest of the list */

},

dark: {

background: '#130e0a',

foreground: '#f4f1ec',

card: '#201913',

primary: '#f1c68b',

border: '#3a3129',

destructive: '#ff6467',

/* the rest of the list */

},

};

export const NAV_THEME: Record<'light' | 'dark', Theme> = {

light: {

...DefaultTheme,

colors: {

background: THEME.light.background,

border: THEME.light.border,

card: THEME.light.background,

notification: THEME.light.destructive,

primary: THEME.light.primary,

text: THEME.light.foreground,

},

},

dark: {

...DarkTheme,

colors: {

background: THEME.dark.background,

border: THEME.dark.border,

card: THEME.dark.background,

notification: THEME.dark.destructive,

primary: THEME.dark.primary,

text: THEME.dark.foreground,

},

},

};

This isn't a direct copy of  global.css , so three points need explanation:

Use hex colors instead of   oklch()  :  Uniwind converts  oklch()  for your classes, but React Navigation does not, so give it a format that React Native can read directly. You can convert a color with any online converter, or paste the  oklch()  value into your browser's developer tools color picker and read the hex value.

Map React Navigation's   card   to your   background  , not your   card  .  The two names look the same but mean different things. In shadcn,  card  is a raised surface on top of the page. In React Navigation,  card  is the background of the screen and header. If you map them by name, the header ends up a shade lighter than the page. You won't notice this with the stock template because it uses the same value for  card  and  background . It only shows up once you create a theme where cards stand out from the page, like this one.

Use a solid color in place of a transparent border.  In dark mode,  --color-border  is  oklch(1 0 0 / 12%) , which is white at 12% opacity. A navigation theme needs a solid color, so work out what that border looks like on your background and use that value.

After this change, the header and page match in both light and dark mode, and you didn't edit any component files:

Switch between light and dark a few times and watch the header. If it's a shade lighter or darker than the page, one of the values in  lib/theme.ts  is still from the old palette.

Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them

If you're coming from web development, some of these differences may catch you off guard. I've collected the issues covered in the tutorial in the table below, along with the fix for each one. You can refer back to it when something doesn't behave as expected.

What you do

What happens

The fix

<Badge>Medium</Badge>

Red screen: "Text strings must be rendered within a  <Text> ."

Wrap the text:  <Badge><Text>Medium</Text></Badge> . The same applies to  Button .

{count && <Line/>}  when  count  is  0

The same error, caused by a stray  0

{count > 0 ? <Line/> : null}

space-y-3  on a column

Nothing happens and there is no warning

Use  gap-3  on the parent

className="p-4"  on a  ScrollView

Padding is clipped and gaps are ignored

Use  contentContainerClassName

truncate  on a long name

The text isn't truncated and the price is pushed off screen

Use  numberOfLines={1}

Using  flex  and expecting a row

Items stack vertically

React Native defaults to a column, so add  flex-row

hover:bg-accent

Nothing happens on a device

Use  active:  for the pressed state

Deleting  PortalHost  from the layout

Dropdowns open into nothing, with no error

Put it back

A Select near the bottom of the screen

The last option is under the home indicator

Pass  insets  to  SelectContent

Showing  option.label  from  onValueChange

Correct on native, but the raw value on the web

Look up the label from your own data

A bottom bar with only  p-4

The button is under the gesture bar

Use  paddingBottom: insets.bottom + 12  in  style

28-point stepper buttons

Hard to tap with a thumb

Add  hitSlop={8}

Changing only  global.css  for a new theme

The header keeps the old colors

Update  lib/theme.ts  too

<Avatar>  without  alt

TypeScript won't compile

alt  is required, and it becomes the accessibility label

rounded-2xl  on  Avatar  only

A circular fallback inside rounded corners

Repeat it on  AvatarFallback

Guarding haptics with  Platform.OS !== 'web'

A working web fallback is removed

expo-haptics  already handles the web

Right-aligned prices in a normal font

Digits shift whenever the number changes

Use  tabular-nums , which also works on native

<Separator className="h-hairline" />

Both height classes are kept

See below

The last row needs more explanation, because it looks like a bug in  cn() , but it's not.

cn()  uses  tailwind-merge , which resolves conflicts between classes. It knows the default Tailwind scale, but it doesn't know about custom values you declare in  global.css . The value  hairline  comes from  --spacing-hairline: hairlineWidth() , so  tailwind-merge  can't tell that  h-hairline  and  h-[1px]  set the same property, and it keeps both:

cn('h-[1px] w-full', 'h-hairline my-1')  // 'h-[1px] w-full h-hairline my-1'

cn('h-[1px] w-full', 'h-2 my-1')         // 'w-full h-2 my-1'

The second result is correct. In the first, which height wins depends on the order of the CSS. The other overrides in this tutorial, such as  size-14  over  size-8 , work correctly because those are names  tailwind-merge  recognizes. If you want it to understand your custom scale, you can teach it with  extendTailwindMerge  in  lib/utils.ts . Otherwise, use an arbitrary value, or edit the component file directly, since you own it.

There's a related case in the stepper buttons. They pass  size-7  to a  Button  whose icon size is  h-10 w-10 sm:h-9 sm:w-9 :

cn('h-10 w-10 sm:h-9 sm:w-9', 'size-7 rounded-full')

// 'sm:h-9 sm:w-9 size-7 rounded-full'

size-7  replaces the base  h-10 w-10 , but the two  sm:  classes stay, because  tailwind-merge  treats a responsive variant as a different class. On a phone this makes no difference, since  sm:  starts at 640px and phones are narrower than that. In a desktop browser, though, those buttons grow to 36 points.

Conclusion

In this tutorial, we built a coffee shop cart and checkout screen with React Native Reusables, Expo, and Uniwind. We added the order rows, pickup options, bill summary, fixed checkout bar, and confirmation dialog. We also looked at how the registry and CLI add component source code to the project and how the theme tokens control the app's colors.

One thing worth getting into the habit of is checking the component source when something doesn't behave the way you expect. Since the components live in your project, you can open them and see how they work. That's how we understood the difference in the Select label between web and native. It also makes customization easier because you can see which part of the component needs to change instead of adding more workarounds around it.

You can find the complete project in the  GitHub repository . If you run into an issue or want to compare your code with the finished screen, clone the repository and check the implementation. If you're looking for more complete starting points for your next project, take a look at  shadcn templates .

I captured the screenshots using the React Native Web build at a phone-sized viewport. The same project also runs on iOS and Android. I've called out the platform differences in the relevant sections, including the Select label and portal host in Step 7, safe area handling in Step 9, and haptics in Step 10.

The repository : MIT licensed

Any registry entry is a public URL:  reactnativereusables.com/r/uniwind/<name>.json  or  .../r/nativewind/<name>.json

title: What a CAPTCHA Farm Attack Actually Looks Like
author: freeCodeCamp
description:
CAPTCHAs are something most of us have come across while browsing the internet. Sometimes we're asked to identify traffic lights in pictures, solve a small puzzle, or simply tick a box to confirm we're human. Websites use these challenges to help distinguish real users from automated bots.
