title: Coding Agent Horror Stories: The CVE That Did Not Exist
author: Docker Blog
description:
This is Part 6 of our    AI Coding Agent Horror Stories series   , where we look at real security incidents involving AI coding agents and at how Docker Sandboxes contain agent execution at the boundary rather than at the command line.

Every story in this series so far has been about an agent reaching for something it should not have touched. We have seen agents wander into home directories, drop production databases, leak credentials, and run shell commands that did something very different fr...
article_content:
This is Part 6 of our    AI Coding Agent Horror Stories series   , where we look at real security incidents involving AI coding agents and at how Docker Sandboxes contain agent execution at the boundary rather than at the command line.

Every story in this series so far has been about an agent reaching for something it should not have touched. We have seen agents wander into home directories, drop production databases, leak credentials, and run shell commands that did something very different from what the developer expected. In each case, the damage came from the agent having more reach than it needed.

This story is the opposite. The agent in this one reached nothing at all, because it was deliberately built so that it could not. And yet, on the night in question, it was still the most dangerous thing in the pipeline.

This story was shared by Pratik Kumar Singh as part of our Agent Hall of Shame contest on social media.

Today’s Horror Story: The Review That Made Everything Up

A platform engineer built a code review bot for his team. The idea was simple and useful. Every time someone pushes code, the bot reads what changed and writes a review into the pipeline, the same kind of first pass a human teammate would give before a person looks at the change.

He named the bot  BuaJi . In India, your bua is your father’s sister, and in many families she is the relative who inspects everything you do and always manages to find something wrong with it. For a code reviewer, it is a fitting name.

What made BuaJi interesting was how carefully it was set up. The bot runs on local models through Ollama, which means the model weights sit on the engineer’s own hardware and no request ever goes out to an AI vendor. It also runs as a job in his CI pipeline, triggered whenever someone pushes code. Taken together, this makes the whole setup self-hosted. The code it reads is company source code, and with this design none of it ever leaves the building. That was a deliberate choice, because his company takes that seriously.

He also gave BuaJi one firm rule: it can read, and it can comment, and that is all. It cannot run  terraform apply , which is the command that creates or changes real cloud infrastructure. It cannot run  kubectl apply , which changes what is actually running in the Kubernetes cluster. And it cannot push a commit, so it has no way to change the code itself. Those are the commands that change the real world, and BuaJi was given none of them. On paper, this is exactly how you would want an AI reviewer to be built.

The version of BuaJi in the companion  repo  is a deliberately minimal reviewer. It checks Go files against a handful of style rules. The report below is the kind of free-form finding any reviewer produces once you let it comment in prose rather than pass/fail, which is exactly the direction these bots get pushed in practice.

The change he pushed that night

His product ships with a bundled copy of PostgreSQL. Older PostgreSQL releases have published vulnerabilities with CVE numbers attached, and upgrading to a newer patch release is how you make those known issues go away. So he bumped the version.

- POSTGRES_VERSION=16.11

+ POSTGRES_VERSION=16.13

This is about as boring and as responsible as a code change gets. It touches a few lines, it changes a version number, and its only purpose is to close security holes that are already public. Any reviewer, human or machine, should look at it and approve it in a few seconds. There is nothing in that diff to be suspicious about, and that is precisely why what happened next matters.

What came back

BuaJi responded with roughly fifteen hundred words rejecting the change. For context, a normal review comment is a sentence or two.

The report described the version bump as an “architectural takeover,” a structural change smuggled into the codebase under the cover of routine maintenance. It claimed that the new PostgreSQL build was a vehicle for sending internal data to a third-party company, and it named that company outright. The company does not exist.

It went further. It referred to specific Kubernetes resources by name, as though it had inspected the cluster and found them. Those resources had never existed, and BuaJi had no access to the cluster that would have let it look. It then wrote Go scripts to “isolate the infected PostgreSQL nodes,” even though nothing was infected. Finally, it told the engineer to revoke all IAM access immediately, an action that would lock out every person in the organization, including the people who would be needed to fix any real problem.

Holding the whole argument together was a CVE number that has never been issued by anyone. Of everything in the report, this is the detail worth pausing on. A CVE identifier is one of the easiest things in security to verify, since you can look it up in a public registry in a few seconds. The bot invented a fact in the one place where invented facts are easiest to catch.

And yet the report looked completely convincing. The Markdown was clean and well structured. The YAML it proposed would have parsed without errors. The tone was urgent and confident, the way a senior security engineer writes when they have found something serious and need you to act before it gets worse. The engineer spent about two minutes reading the CI logs, realized that none of it was real, and went back to what he was doing.

In this issue, you’ll learn:

Why a read-only agent that only writes comments can still get your cluster taken down

What makes a fabricated security finding harder to dismiss than an obviously broken one

Why agent output belongs in the untrusted column, the same as agent input

How to move a real AI code reviewer into a Docker Sandbox, step by step, and what that does and does not protect you from

Caption: Comic illustrating how a confident, well-formatted security report from an AI reviewer can be entirely fabricated, and what happens when somebody acts on it.

The Problem

It is important to say clearly that the read-only rule did its job. BuaJi could not carry out any of its own recommendations, and it never had any access to the cluster. Because of that, the entire episode cost the engineer two minutes of his evening and nothing more.

The trouble is that the rule only controlled what BuaJi could do. Nobody had thought about what BuaJi could say. A read-only agent is still allowed to tell people what to do, and the person reading its output usually has exactly the access that the agent was denied. BuaJi could not run the scripts it wrote, but it could write them down and hand them to someone who could.

This engineer caught the problem because he knows his own cluster well. He knew those Kubernetes resources were not real and that nothing had been compromised. Now imagine a newer engineer on call at two in the morning, half awake, looking at a long and alarming security report in the pipeline. Revoking all IAM access in production in the middle of the night is an outage all by itself. Running an unreviewed Go script against your database nodes could be considerably worse. In both scenarios, BuaJi would not have done anything. A person would have done all of it, in good faith, because the report told them to.

What makes this so hard to defend against is that no permission model would have flagged it, because no permission was ever violated. The agent stayed within its boundary. The engineer had every right to run those commands on his own systems. The only thing in the entire chain that was false was the content of the report.

How Docker Sandboxes Contain This

Here’s the honest part: a sandbox is not a fact-checker. No microVM boundary will ever make a review comment accurate. What a boundary changes is what that fabricated output can do once it exists.

Remember where BuaJi’s read-only rule actually lived, in a convention. One engineer configured it in his own pipeline and has to keep remembering to leave it in place. Rules like that hold until someone is in a hurry, or a new teammate copies the config and drops a section they did not understand, or a small exception made for a good reason quietly becomes permanent. None of this needs bad intent; it is just how real teams work.

Docker Sandboxes run agents inside isolated microVMs each with its own kernel, its own filesystem, and a network that denies everything by default. An agent inside one can invent anything it likes, but the invention has nowhere to go: no credentials to use, no cluster to reach, no commit to push, unless someone allowed that access ahead of time. The read-only rule stops being something a person remembers and becomes a property of the environment. And when a report claims it inspected your cluster, the policy log is your proof it never could have.

That protects you from the agent. It does nothing for the human who reads the output, and no sandbox ever will. For that half, treat agent review output the way you already treat agent input, untrusted until something checks it: label it so it doesn’t carry a colleague’s weight, verify any CVE numbers, and never run agent-written remediation until a person has read and understood it.

This is the same pattern as the  sandbox escapes  Pillar published in July. The boundary itself was never broken; a file was written inside the sandbox, and a tool outside later trusted it. An agent’s output is always an input to whatever reads it next and somewhere downstream, something trusts what it receives. Very often, that something is a person.

Let’s move BuaJi into a Docker Sandbox, one step at a time. By the end, the read-only rule is enforced by the environment, not by memory.

How BuaJi runs today

BuaJi is a small Python script,  buaji.py . Its GitLab job installs Ollama on a GPU runner, starts  ollama serve , loads the model named in  LLM , and runs the script.

The script reads review rules from  rules.md  and finds the changed files with  git diff HEAD^ HEAD --name-only . It sends each file and rule to Ollama at  http://localhost:11434  and prints the answers to the CI log.

The catch is that everything shares one container: the model, the script, the checkout and every CI variable, including  CI_JOB_TOKEN . BuaJi is read-only only because the script happens not to write anything.

What we want instead

We split the job in two. The model stays on the runner next to the GPU. BuaJi moves into a microVM that can read the code, talk to the model, and nothing else.

One open path to the model, everything else blocked, and a CVE check on the way out.

Step 1: Let BuaJi find Ollama somewhere other than localhost

Inside a sandbox,  localhost  is the sandbox itself. So we read the Ollama address from an environment variable and keep the old value as the default:

-    url = "http://localhost:11434/api/generate"

+    base = os.environ.get("OLLAMA_URL", "http://localhost:11434")

+    url = f"{base}/api/generate"

Outside a sandbox, nothing changes. Inside one, we point  OLLAMA_URL  at the runner.

Step 2: Bake BuaJi’s dependencies into a sandbox image, once

Today the job runs  apt-get  and  pip3 install  on every run, which needs internet access each time.

Instead, build a small image once with everything BuaJi needs, so the sandbox never downloads anything:

FROM docker/sandbox-templates:shell

USER root

RUN apt-get update \

&& apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends python3 python3-requests git \

&& rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

USER agent

Push it to your registry and store its name in a CI variable called  BUAJI_TEMPLATE .

Step 3: Keep the model on the runner

Ollama stays on the runner with the GPU. Install it once on the runner instead of running  curl | sh  in every pipeline.

ollama serve > /tmp/ollama.log 2>&1 &

sleep 2

ollama pull "$LLM"

The model never enters the sandbox. BuaJi reaches it through one port, opened in Step 5.

Step 4: Create the sandbox with the code mounted read-only

This step decides what BuaJi can see and change.

mkdir -p "$CI_BUILDS_DIR/buaji-scratch"

sbx run -d --name "$SBX_NAME" -t "$BUAJI_TEMPLATE" \

shell "$CI_BUILDS_DIR/buaji-scratch" "$CI_PROJECT_DIR:ro"

Here is what each part does:

--name  gives each pipeline its own sandbox.

-t  uses the image from Step 2.

shell  is the agent type. BuaJi is a plain script, so a shell sandbox is enough.

buaji-scratch  is an empty folder, the only place BuaJi can write.

:ro  mounts the repository read-only. BuaJi can read files and run  git diff , but cannot change anything.

Notice what is missing: no GitLab token, no kubeconfig, no cloud credentials. Even if BuaJi tried  kubectl  or  terraform , it would have nothing to connect with.

Step 5: Open one network path, to the model

Sandboxes block all outgoing traffic by default. We open one path, for this sandbox only. (This assumes the runner’s default policy is deny-all; on a balanced or open default, set the default to deny-all first.)

sbx policy allow network --sandbox "$SBX_NAME" localhost:11434

The allow target (localhost:11434) and the address BuaJi dials (host.docker.internal:11434) are two names for the same runner port,  the first from the runner’s point of view, the second from inside the microVM. Kubernetes, your cloud APIs, and GitLab all stay blocked. If a report claims BuaJi “inspected the cluster,” this rule proves it could not have.

Kubernetes, your cloud APIs and GitLab all stay blocked. If a report claims BuaJi “inspected the cluster,” this rule proves it could not have.

Step 6: Run the review

BuaJi runs as before, just in a new place with only two variables:

sbx exec -w "$CI_PROJECT_DIR" \

-e LLM="$LLM" \

-e OLLAMA_URL=http://host.docker.internal:11434 \

"buaji-$CI_PIPELINE_ID" python3 buaji.py | tee buaji-review.log

-w  starts in the checkout, where  buaji.py  expects  rules.md .

The two  -e  flags are the only variables BuaJi can see.

tee  saves the review to a file on the runner, outside the sandbox.

The review is now just text. BuaJi cannot post it, act on it, or change what happens to it next.

Step 7: Check every CVE number before anyone acts on the report

This check would have caught the fake report in seconds. It runs on the runner, so BuaJi cannot skip it.

It looks up every CVE ID in the NVD database and fails the job if any of them do not exist:

unverified=""

for id in $(grep -oE 'CVE-[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{4,}' buaji-review.log | sort -u); do

count=$(curl -s "https://services.nvd.nist.gov/rest/json/cves/2.0?cveId=$id" \

| jq -r '.totalResults // 0')

[ "$count" = "0" ] && unverified="$unverified $id"

done

if [ -n "$unverified" ]; then

echo "⚠️ BuaJi output mentions CVE IDs that do not exist:$unverified"

echo "⚠️ Treat this review as unverified. Do not run any commands it suggests."

exit 1

fi

Because the job is  allow_failure: true , GitLab marks it “passed with warnings.” The pipeline keeps moving, but nobody mistakes the report for a trusted one. This degrades the signal, it does not block the human. The warning is a nudge, not a guardrail ~ a tired on-call engineer can still scroll past it..

It won’t catch every made-up detail, like a fake Kubernetes resource name. But it catches the one that holds most fake reports together.

Step 8: Check what BuaJi tried to reach, then clean up

Finally, review the policy log and remove the sandbox:

sbx policy log "$SBX_NAME"

sbx stop "buaji-$CI_PIPELINE_ID"

sbx rm -f "buaji-$CI_PIPELINE_ID"

The log shows every host BuaJi tried to reach. On a deny-all runner, a healthy run shows only the model on port 11434. Anything else is a signal worth looking at.

Removing the sandbox means every pipeline starts clean.

The complete pipeline job

Put together, the  buaji  job in  .gitlab-ci.yml  looks like this:

# BuaJi, moved into a Docker Sandbox. The read-only rule is now a property of

# the environment, not a convention in the script: the code is mounted :ro, no

# credentials are passed in, and only one network path (to the model) is open.

buaji:

stage: buaji

tags:

- self-hosted-gpu-kvm   # GPU for Ollama, KVM for sbx microVMs

variables:

LLM: gemma

GIT_DEPTH: "2"          # buaji.py diffs HEAD^ against HEAD

SBX_NAME: buaji-$CI_PIPELINE_ID

before_script:

- ollama serve > /tmp/ollama.log 2>&1 &

- sleep 2

- ollama pull "$LLM"

- mkdir -p "$CI_BUILDS_DIR/buaji-scratch"

- sbx run -d --name "$SBX_NAME" -t "$BUAJI_TEMPLATE"

shell "$CI_BUILDS_DIR/buaji-scratch" "$CI_PROJECT_DIR:ro"

- sbx policy allow network --sandbox "$SBX_NAME" localhost:11434

script:

- sbx exec -w "$CI_PROJECT_DIR"

-e LLM="$LLM" -e OLLAMA_URL=http://host.docker.internal:11434

"$SBX_NAME" python3 buaji.py | tee buaji-review.log

- ./scripts/verify-cves.sh buaji-review.log

after_script:

- sbx policy log "$SBX_NAME"

- sbx stop "$SBX_NAME" && sbx rm -f "$SBX_NAME"

allow_failure: true

only:

changes:

- "**/*.go"

The runner needs a GPU and KVM, which usually means self-hosted.  GIT_DEPTH: "2"  gives  buaji.py  the two commits it compares. The cleanup sits in  after_script , so it runs even when the job fails.

What changed

Before, the read-only rule lived in the script. Now it lives in the environment: a read-only checkout, one network path, no credentials, and only checked text coming out.

What hasn’t changed is the human reading the output. The sandbox stops BuaJi from running its scripts. Only the CVE check and a careful reader stop someone else from running them.

Best Practices

Treat an agent’s security finding as a hypothesis, not a conclusion.  A report from an AI reviewer is a claim with good formatting. When a human reviewer flags a security issue, there is an implied step where they checked their reasoning. With an agent, that step has not happened, so you have to do it yourself.

Verify every CVE number before acting on it.  This is the cheapest check in the whole process and it catches the single most convincing part of a fabricated report. Automate it, as in Step 7, so it runs on every review without anyone having to remember.

Never run agent-written remediation without reviewing it first.  Scripts and commands supplied by an agent are the point where a false finding turns into a real incident. Read them with the same care you would give an unknown script from the internet.

Make read-only a property of the environment, not a habit.  A restriction you enforce by hand in a pipeline config is always one rushed change away from disappearing. Mount the code read-only, pass in no credentials, and open only the network paths the agent needs, as in Steps 4 to 6.

Clearly label agent review output as agent output.  When a bot’s review looks identical to one from a senior engineer, it borrows authority it has not earned. A clear label helps readers apply the right level of skepticism.

Keep an eye on your signal-to-noise ratio.  The curl story is the warning here. A review channel that fills up with noise eventually stops being read, and a review channel nobody reads is worse than having none, because people still assume it is protecting them.

Conclusion

The engineer who built BuaJi was right that the read-only rule protected him, and it genuinely did. BuaJi could not touch the cluster, could not revoke anyone’s access, and could not run a single line of the code it had so carefully written. What the rule could not do was stop BuaJi from asking somebody else to run it.

Every other story in this series has been about an agent reaching too far. This one never reached at all. It stayed inside its boundary, did exactly what it was permitted to do, and still produced a document that would have caused a real outage if the person reading it had been a little more tired, or a little less familiar with their own cluster.

As we give agents more responsibility in our pipelines, containing what they can do is only half the job. A sandbox handles that half. The other half is deciding how much we trust what they tell us, and that part is still up to us.

Every story in this series so far has been about an agent reaching for something it should not have touched.

description:
Over the past year, almost every conversation I’ve had with a partner has ended in the same place. Their customers are moving AI agents out of the lab and into production, and the moment they do, the question changes. article_content:
Over the past year, almost every conversation I’ve had with a partner has ended in the same place. Their customers are moving AI agents out of the lab and into production, and the moment they do, the question changes. It stops being “Can we build this?” and becomes “Can we trust it, secure it, and govern it?” The partners who can answer that second set of questions are the partners customers keep.

Today, we are launching the  Docker Navigator Partner Program  to help you become that partner. This post explains what we’ve built, why we built it around AI governance, and how you can get the most from it.

Why “Navigator”

AI adoption is not following a normal technology curve. Every team, every vendor, every model provider, and every hyperscaler is racing to ship agentic capability, and no single company sees the whole stack. Identity, observability, supply chain security, MCP gateways, models, and clouds are each building their piece. What enterprises are missing is a trusted, common layer that lets those pieces work together safely.

That’s Docker’s role. Docker is where agents, models, and tools actually run: vertically integrated where it matters, and horizontally open to everything our customers already use. We describe it as being the Trusted Navigator for the agentic era; the constant that helps customers make sense of a landscape moving faster than any one team can track.

Partners are how that promise reaches customers. Whether you build technology, run a cloud, deliver services, or sell through the channel, you extend our reach and turn the Docker platform into a complete, governable stack. So the program carries the same name, and its tiers describe the journey a partner takes with us.

Three tiers, one partner journey

Every partner in the Docker Navigator Partner Program is navigating the agentic era with Docker. The tiers mark how far along that journey you are, and the top tier carries the program’s name on purpose: it’s the title you earn when you have shown you can navigate it for customers.

Crew  is where every partnership starts: signed, onboarded, portal profile complete, first opportunities registered.

Explorer  partners are enabled and certified, actively selling and co-marketing AI governance solutions with us.

Navigator  partners are our most strategic: co-selling with Docker, embedded in joint account plans, co-authoring reference architectures, and leading customers through the agentic era alongside us. A Navigator is a partner Docker would put in front of its own customers.

article_content:
Two security events landed side by side this week, PHP2Shell and the eMudhra certificate compromise. Both reached the same place, the foundation their applications are built on.

PHP2Shell is a pair of critical flaws in the PHP engine itself, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. They let an unauthenticated request become code execution on the server, on any PHP application, however careful its own code is, and PHP runs about 69% of the websites whose server-side language is known.

The eMudhra compromise is a different kind of problem. Eight intermediate certificates from the certificate authority eMudhra turned out to have private keys that can be computed from the public certificates, which let anyone issue a certificate for any website and have it accepted. Browsers revoke certificates like these on their own, but a container image carries its own trust store and keeps trusting them until it is rebuilt.

Docker Hardened Images published a fixed PHP image within 24 hours

The dhi.io/php image was rebuilt on the patched PHP and published early on October 22, within 24 hours of the upstream release and after the DHI testing and verification steps. Pulling the current tag puts you on the fixed version. The few DHI images that bundle their own PHP application, such as composer and nextcloud, follow as their upstream projects release.

Rebuilt across the catalog, verifiable tag by tag

The certificate compromise touched the whole catalog, because every image carries a trust store. In the 48 hours after the PHP release, the DHI build system ran 16,567 package and image builds across the catalog.  By 10pm UTC on October 22, almost all catalog tags were on the fixed CA store, with most of the rest in the build queue.  That percentage comes from the SBOM that ships with every image, read for every published tag to check which CA store and which PHP version it carries, and you can run the same check on anything you pull.

How to make sure your environments are covered

If you run PHP on Docker Hardened Images, pull the current tag for your branch and redeploy, and rebuild anything you built on top of a DHI image so it picks up the new base docker pull  dhi.io/php:8.4

Customizations built through the DHI Enterprise workflow are rebuilt automatically when the base layer is patched. For the certificate fix the same applies to every image you build from a DHI base, PHP or not. The  Docker Security update from October 22  lists the affected PHP versions and the support path.

If you run PHP in any other container, check the PHP version running inside it rather than the tag on the outside, and rebuild it on a patched base.

Build from a trusted foundation

Weeks like this one will keep coming, but a trusted foundation will make all the difference.

If you are not building on hardened images yet, this week is the wake-up call and the week to start. Both events landed on the foundation, and that is where the fix has to happen, in the image itself, rebuilt from fixed sources before anyone pulls it.

This is exactly what Docker Hardened Images were built for. Docker builds, patches and maintains the system packages inside each image from source, and the build system is event-driven, so an upstream release or a changed package triggers rebuilds of everything that depends on it. Each image ships signed, with its SBOM, SLSA Build Level 3 provenance and VEX data attached, which is why a rebuild of this size can be measured as well as done.

The catalog is free and open source under Apache 2.0, with near-zero CVEs on every image. It stays compatible with the Alpine and Debian your teams already run, so adoption is a one-line change to the FROM line in your Dockerfile, with no migration project attached. DHI Select and DHI Enterprise add SLA-backed remediation with critical CVE fixes within 7 days, FIPS and STIG variants, image customization with the guarantees kept, and Extended Lifecycle Support for the versions upstream has stopped patching. All of it is in the  Docker Hardened Images catalog , free to pull today.

article_content:
Summary

On Tuesday, October 20, 2026, Docker began tracking two critical vulnerabilities in PHP,  CVE-2026-109618  and  CVE-2026-109619 , commonly known as PHP2Shell. The vulnerabilities allow attackers to execute code remotely in PHP core, and they affect PHP packages going back to version 5.4: the supported versions 8.2 through 8.5, and the end-of-life versions 5.x, 7.x, 8.0, and 8.1.

To address these vulnerabilities, PHP released 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35, and advised anyone running PHP to  update to the latest version immediately .

Although this is a vulnerability in PHP itself, not in Docker’s systems, it nonetheless affects Docker users who build on PHP images and packages. In response, we have updated the Docker Hardened Images and Docker Official Images on Docker Hub, and advise customers to immediately update.

What Happened

Along with other package repositories and secure package providers, Docker has been made aware of and is tracking two recently discovered critical vulnerabilities in PHP packages distributed since version 5.4. The two critical vulnerabilities, now commonly referred to as “PHP2Shell,” are identified and tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. (The PHP Foundation has published a  detailed report on the discovery  that we recommend reading for full context.)

In short: these vulnerabilities could allow remote code execution in PHP core by malicious actors. Both are flaws in how PHP manages request memory. In CVE-2026-109618, when PHP runs out of memory mid-request and aborts, some code paths leave memory uninitialized, and PHP’s cleanup step then reads it. In CVE-2026-109619, PHP’s internal state can keep pointing at memory that has already been freed, and a later request then uses that stale state. Attackers have multiple ways to trigger either condition and turn it into remote code execution.

Affected versions include the currently supported versions (8.2 through 8.5), as well as the EOL and unsupported versions 5.x, 7.x, 8.0, and 8.1.

Impact to Anyone Using PHP

Whether you are a Docker user or not, if you are using any of the above affected versions of PHP,  you should immediately upgrade to the latest version.  That includes PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, or 8.5.12, or a later release in the corresponding branch.

There is no other comprehensive remediation for the affected versions.  Updating is the only complete mitigation path.

If for any reason you are unable to complete an immediate update, we strongly recommend taking your system offline until such time that you can initiate mitigation. This the guidance of not only Docker,  but of the FBI , and numerous experts throughout the cybersecurity community.

Impact to and Actions for Docker Users

While this vulnerability exists in PHP itself and not directly in Docker’s systems, there is nonetheless potential risk and exposure to Docker customers who run PHP in their applications, including anyone using PHP images or packages from Docker Hub, Docker Official Images, or Docker Hardened Images.

For users of Docker Official Images:

Docker Official Images have already been updated and released to Docker Hub and mirrored to Amazon ECR. Customers using either of these sources should update immediately.

For users of Docker Hardened Images (DHI):

Docker Hardened Images have already been updated and released to Docker Hub. The currently supported versions of PHP were updated as follows:

8.2.34 → 8.2.35

8.3.35 → 8.3.36

8.4.26 → 8.4.27

8.5.11 → 8.5.12

The updates to our images were completed and released within 24-hours of the upstream patches being made available. These images were made available after successfully executing the DHI testing and verification processes.

What’s next

If you have any issues accessing the updated images or migrating to the new versions, please contact Docker Support at    app.docker.com/support/contact . As always when it comes to matters of security, we appreciate your diligence.

article_content:
Even security teams that have invested in a hardened base image often can’t say what’s running on top of it. In a recent survey of 250 North American DevSecOps leaders, 91% named visibility into container components as their single biggest blind spot. Not the base image, but everything layered onto it. And 90% said their teams still run lightly modified public images with little to no hardening.

That gap is getting harder to ignore. AI coding assistants are adding dependencies faster than teams can review them. Vulnerability databases can no longer keep pace with the volume of submissions. New regulatory requirements, including the EU Cyber Resilience Act, are also increasing expectations around vulnerability handling, remediation, and software supply chain transparency.

Docker Hardened Images meet ActiveState’s Curated Catalog

Docker, Inc. and ActiveState today announced a reselling partnership that brings Docker Hardened Images (DHI) together with ActiveState’s curated open source packages, giving enterprises a more consistent way to secure both the container base and the software dependencies layered on top.

DHI provides secure-by-default, minimal container images, with 4,000+ images built from source, near-zero CVEs, signed SBOMs, and SLSA Build Level 3 provenance. The catalog is free and open source under Apache 2.0, with production tiers backed by a 7-day SLA for critical and high-severity CVEs.

ActiveState extends that trusted foundation to the open source dependencies developers add on top. Its curated components span more than a dozen language ecosystems, including Python, JavaScript, Java, Perl, Tcl, and Ruby. Components are built from source, continuously maintained and remediated against contractual SLAs, and delivered through the package managers, pipelines, IDEs, and AI coding tools development teams already use.

Trust across the software stack

A more consistent approach to trusted open source : Pair a hardened container base with curated open source dependencies, reducing the need to source and manage each layer separately

Verifiable provenance across the stack : With both Docker and ActiveState building from source to SLSA Build Level 3 standards, teams get a more consistent evidence trail across the software supply chain

Fewer vulnerabilities, without slowing teams down  : DHI delivers near-zero CVEs, 95% smaller attack surface, 7-day SLA on critical/high CVEs. ActiveState provides 95% fewer CVEs and 90% faster remediation than community open source, backed by a 5-day SLA on critical vulnerabilities.

Available Now

The Docker and ActiveState reselling partnership is available now.  Explore the partnership .

title: How we review 4x more AI code without reading every line
author: The New Stack
article_content:
Do you need to read every line of AI-generated code to trust it?  

Not necessarily. Instead, check five things: the intent behind a change, its acceptance criteria, the invariants it can’t break, the decisions made along the way, and evidence that it works.

At  Aviator , that shift let the same nine engineers merge 4× more pull requests, cut  median time to merge  from 2.1 days to 3.4 hours, and drop reverts by 40%. A human still signs off on every PR. What changed is what that human reads.

“Decisions need a person, and a diff is the worst place to make them.”

We got the insight by sorting our own review comments. Most of what a reviewer writes on a PR is either a rule they’ve written before or a decision. Machines should check rules every time. Decisions need a person, and a diff is the worst place to make them.

The problem: Code review doesn’t scale with AI

Our code flipped from human-written with AI help to AI-generated with human help. Weekly merged PRs went from about 100 to more than 400. Our median AI-generated PR reached 640 lines, well past 400 lines, widely considered the limit where bug detection falls off.

Catching bugs was never the main point of code review anyway. In Microsoft’s 2013 study (Bacchelli & Bird), only 14% of review comments were about defects. Review is how  engineers share knowledge  and keep their mental model of the system current, and that’s the part worth protecting. When agents write most of the code, it’s also the part most at risk.

“Catching bugs was never the main point of code review anyway. Review is how engineers share knowledge and keep their mental model of the system current, and that’s the part worth protecting.”

Since I argued that  code reviews are dead , the most common pushback I hear is, “So you just stopped reviewing?” No. We stopped reviewing the diff.

So, what didn’t work?

An AI reviewer.  On one of my own PRs, it opened 16 of 18 threads: magic numbers, array-index React keys, a component that ran too long. One thread caught a real race condition. The two comments that mattered, both design decisions from teammates, got buried under nits.

A four-hour review SLA.  We couldn’t add reviewers, so we added a rule. First reviews got faster, and approvals got emptier, as reviewers skimmed to hit the clock and their own work stalled.

A self-review skill tuned to our conventions.  Its findings were far better than the generic bot’s. But it still read the diff after the code was written, and the most useful part of the exchange, what it argued about and what we decided, died in a chat window.

All three tried to read the diff better. But the diff is the  least important part of code review  anyway. It shows what changed, never why.

To see what review actually contained, I went back to a PR I’d reviewed in 2025. It had 14 threads. Eight came from a bot and caught one real bug. Three of my six comments were rules I’d already written on other PRs, like “Use GraphQLRetryableException so Celery retries on it.” Only two were real decisions, like “No comments extracted: should we tell the user on the PR?”

What did work: Verify intent, not lines

Code review used to do several jobs at once: catch bugs, enforce team conventions, settle design decisions, and keep everyone’s understanding of the system current. We split those jobs up and gave each one a better home.

Argue before the PR exists.  Our review agent cross-examines the author’s agent, running on a different model, and writes down every disagreement. On one recent PR, the agents raised four disagreements and settled three with a stated reason. The only one left for a human was a naming call.

Capture intent and acceptance criteria.  Not as an up-front spec, but captured from the coding session with the agent. Every time an engineer corrects the agent or answers its question, we create a criterion. We used to throw those away when the session ended. Intent answers why we’re making the change; acceptance criteria answer how it should behave. Intent without criteria can’t be checked, and criteria without intent can’t be judged.

“Intent answers why we’re making the change; acceptance criteria answer how it should behave. Intent without criteria can’t be checked, and criteria without intent can’t be judged.”

Codify repeated comments as invariants.  We mined a year of review history in three passes: drop the noise (bot summaries, bare “LGTMs”), classify every comment as a rule, proposal, one-off fix, or question, then merge the repeats. 11,400 comments became 212 candidate rules and 64 approved  invariants . Each has a scope, a verification method, provenance, and an owner.

Take “Every config change writes an audit-log entry, only when something changed.” It covers GraphQL mutations and API handlers that write config, is verified by a preview run that saves twice and reads the audit log, was mined from 23 review threads across 17 PRs, and belongs to the platform team.

A model checking every invariant on every PR is slow and not perfectly repeatable, so where possible an agent compiles invariants into ast-grep rules that run in shadow beside the model until they agree. A comment we’d left on nine PRs, “Add a timeout, this hung a worker,” is now an eight-line rule. Nineteen invariants run deterministically, in 0.3 seconds.

Prove every criterion with evidence.  Each criterion becomes a scenario. An agent spins up a preview environment, drives it like a user, and records screenshots, requests, and logs. For the audit-log invariant, it saves a setting, confirms one new log entry, saves again with nothing changed, and confirms there’s still one.

That second half is exactly what a reviewer reading the diff would never check. Not every criterion needs a browser: an API contract is proven by a recorded request and response, a code rule by an ast-grep match or a file-and-line citation. Pick the cheapest proof that settles the question. A  green CI check  only says the tests you thought of passed.

Debate the decisions.  Decisions come from three places: the coding session, the agents’ argument, and failed verification runs. The PR lists every one, where it came from, and who settled it. On a PR that added retries for failed webhook deliveries, four of five decisions were settled; the agents disagreed on whether to deduplicate retried deliveries, so a person settled that one. 

Reviewers skim what’s settled, settle what the agents couldn’t, reopen anything they’d call differently, and talk it through with the author. That conversation builds understanding of the system.

Own the rules.  Engineers stop  reading every line . They own the rules that check every line, and keep their understanding of the system by reading intent, evidence, and decisions.

The results

PRs merged per week: 4×, with the same nine engineers

Median time to merge: 2.1 days → 3.4 hours

Human threads per PR: 6.2 → 1.3

Reverts per 100 PRs: down 40%

Review work didn’t disappear. It moved to refining invariants, debating decisions, and improving verification. Expect the transition to hurt: month one is double work, by month two invariants catch up enough that reviews shrink, and by month three you read intent and evidence, not code.

The post  How we review 4x more AI code without reading every line  appeared first on  The New Stack .

title: In the software factory, engineers become process engineers
author: The New Stack
description:
For most of software’s history, the scarce resource was people who could write code. Every process the industry built assumed it. Sprints, code review, staging, and release trains were all designed around humans doing the work by hand.

That assumption is gone. By September,  more than 40% of pull requests on GitHub started with an agent’s first draft , up from 17% in March. Work is moving to machines, but the process around it hasn’t caught up.

Agents made  generating code cheap  and fast. For...
article_content:
For most of software’s history, the scarce resource was people who could write code. Every process the industry built assumed it. Sprints, code review, staging, and release trains were all designed around humans doing the work by hand.

That assumption is gone. By September,  more than 40% of pull requests on GitHub started with an agent’s first draft , up from 17% in March. Work is moving to machines, but the process around it hasn’t caught up.

Agents made  generating code cheap  and fast. For the most part, they have not yet had the same impact on shipping it. CircleCI’s 2026 delivery data showed  average daily workflow runs grew 59% year over year , with the top 5% of teams up 97% and the bottom quartile showing no measurable increase. A study of one company that mandated doubling pull request output found that  load per reviewer doubled  and automated review overtook human review in coverage within months.

“When work gets automated in any industry, the people don’t disappear. They stop doing the work and start designing the system the work runs through.”

When work gets automated in any industry, the people don’t disappear. Their job changes. They stop doing the work and start designing the system the work runs through. Software engineers are becoming process engineers, and what they build is a software factory.

Three manufacturing lessons carry over to agents

Software is not a car plant. A factory builds the same product thousands of times, and software never ships the same change twice. But three ideas carry over, because they are about running a system where machines do the work.

The first is that people design the system, not the output. Ford’s Model T went from  12.5 hours per car to one every 93 minutes by 1914 , and the workers did not get eight times faster. Engineers redesigned the line.

Second, quality gets built in at every step. Sakichi Toyoda invented  a loom that stopped automatically when any thread broke , so one operator could run many machines instead of watching one. Toyota built its production system around that idea, and W. Edwards Deming spent decades telling manufacturers to stop relying on end-of-line inspection.

The third is that the slowest step sets the pace. That was Eliyahu Goldratt’s point in “The Goal.” Speed up any step other than the bottleneck, and you pile up work in front of it. Agents sped up coding, and the pile is now in review and verification.

A software factory is a network of agents

A software factory runs on many specialized agents, each good at one job, passing work to others across the lifecycle. A research agent turns usage data and customer calls into a brief, and a spec agent writes requirements with acceptance criteria. A coding agent writes the change, and a review agent reviews the change. A test agent runs the change and sends failures back, and a release agent rolls it out behind feature flags. A site reliability engineering (SRE) agent triages what breaks in production and opens the next piece of work.

Most handoffs in that loop are agent-to-agent, and that changes what a handoff is. Between humans, a handoff can be a Slack thread and some shared context. Between agents, it has to be a contract that states what gets passed, in what shape, and with what proof. A spec without acceptance criteria gives the coding agent nothing to aim at, and a change without test evidence gives the release agent nothing to trust.

“A spec without acceptance criteria gives the coding agent nothing to aim at, and a change without test evidence gives the release agent nothing to trust.”

Agent-to-agent work also fails in new ways. Errors compound, because each agent builds on the last one’s output. Agents can agree too easily, or loop forever trading the same fix back and forth. A factory of agents needs what a factory of machines needs: checks between the stations, and someone who decides where those checks go.

Software engineers become process engineers

That someone is the software engineer. The job moves from writing code to designing the system that writes, tests, and ships it. That is more technical, not less, because you are now responsible for how all the code gets made. The work comes down to four jobs, and the first is designing the flow: which agents exist, what each one owns, what runs in parallel, and what each handoff must contain.

The second is defining good. An agent can’t hit a target nobody wrote down. Specs, acceptance criteria, performance budgets, and API contracts used to live in people’s heads. Now they have to be explicit enough for a machine to check.

The third is improving the line. When an agent ships a bug, the useful question is not why the agent did that but why the line let it through. Every escaped defect is a process bug.

The fourth is placing the human gates. Humans belong where a mistake is expensive, and the call takes judgment. Line-by-line human review of every agent pull request is a craft-era habit, the factory equivalent of hand-inspecting every bolt.

“When an agent ships a bug, the useful question is not why the agent did that but why the line let it through. Every escaped defect is a process bug.”

Agents write code and fix tests. A schema migration is costly to get wrong but cheap for a machine to check, so agents run it behind hard checks. User interface (UI) copy tastes but is cheap to change, so a human reviews it after it ships. What to build and where a security boundary sits gets a human gate.

Quality gets built into every change, not inspected at the end

Most teams still run the old model of quality assurance. Changes pile up, then go through one inspection at the end: a shared staging environment and a human reviewer. That is a single test bench for the whole plant, and once agents multiply the number of changes, it becomes the  bottleneck Goldratt described .

Toyoda’s loom freed the operator because it checked every thread as it ran and stopped the moment one broke. Agent-written code needs the same mechanism. In a working software factory, the test agent checks every change as it is made, the coding agent fixes what fails, and nothing moves until it passes.

That check only means something if it runs where the failure would show up. Mocks don’t count, because they tell you a change works in a world that doesn’t exist. They were a stopgap that made sense when the pace of change was slow and standing up a production-like environment for every change was hard.

So, each change gets its own environment that behaves like production, with the services, databases, and APIs it will meet after release. A human only sees the change if it hits a gate, and by then it already works, with the evidence attached.

That model needs a test station for every change, cheap enough to use on every attempt. In practice, that means an environment that comes up in seconds, deploys only what the change touched and shares everything else so that you can verify the change end to end before merge.

Guardrails belong in the line, not in the prompt

Verification catches mistakes. Guardrails stop the ones that would cost too much to catch late. Assume agents will do anything the line allows, and design the line so that everything it allows is safe.

Manufacturing calls this error-proofing. You don’t put up a sign telling workers to insert the part the right way. You build a fixture that fits only one way. For agents, an instruction in a prompt is a sign on the wall, and a permission boundary is a fixture.

So each agent holds only the access its station needs, and the coding agent never holds production credentials. Every run is isolated, so one agent’s test can’t corrupt another’s. Required checks are enforced, every release can roll back on its own, and when a check can’t run, the change stops.

A line that quietly skips a broken inspection is worse than no inspection, because everyone believes it’s working. Agent-to-agent work adds one more rule: trust doesn’t pass down the chain. A review agent approving a change shouldn’t widen what the release agent can do.

Judgment stays human, and it becomes most of the job

Factories didn’t get rid of engineers. They created industrial engineering. You can’t design a line for work you don’t understand, so the best factory builders will be engineers who know what good code, good tests, and a safe rollout look like from doing it by hand.

Some work stays off the line. The first version of something new, a strange production bug, and a design nobody has tried are bench work. They stay hands-on until they are understood well enough to standardize.

Some decisions never move to a machine: what’s worth building, what a customer means rather than what they said, when to trade speed for risk and who answers for what ships. Those were always the hard part of the job. Now they’re most of it.

The best process wins, not the best model

Agents made code cheap, and every team can reach for the same models. What separates the teams pulling ahead is the line they build around those agents, with contracts between stations, human gates where judgment matters, and  verification on every change . Designing that line is now the software engineer’s job. We built  Signadot  to give every change its own test station, and it is a practical place to start building yours.

The post  In the software factory, engineers become process engineers  appeared first on  The New Stack .
ai_summary: For most of software’s history, the scarce resource was people who could write code. Every process the industry built assumed it.
main_event: In the software factory, engineers become process engineers

title: Cognition turned an open model into a coding beast. But it won’t release the weights.
author: The New Stack
description:

Released Wednesday,  SWE-2 Flash  costs one-fifth as much as Cognition’s larger SWE-2 model and generates tokens roughly three times faster, according to the company. Built on Thinking Machines Lab’s open weight Inkling-Small, the new model comes with a catch: Cognition is keeping its weights private, citing cybersecurity concerns.

Inkling-Small is ...
article_content:
Cognition built its newest coding model on a foundation that anyone can download, yet the company is keeping its own finished version locked away.

Released Wednesday,  SWE-2 Flash  costs one-fifth as much as Cognition’s larger SWE-2 model and generates tokens roughly three times faster, according to the company. Built on Thinking Machines Lab’s open weight Inkling-Small, the new model comes with a catch: Cognition is keeping its weights private, citing cybersecurity concerns.

Inkling-Small is a 276-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 12 billion active parameters that Thinking Machines Lab, the startup led by co-founder and CEO  Mira Murati , released on July 30 under an Apache 2.0 license, which means anyone can pull the weights from Hugging Face and build on them.

“a practical way to turn a weak open base into a usable agent model,”

Cognition says the bulk of its performance gains came from adding a mid-training stage before reinforcement learning, and the numbers it published are striking — on Terminal-Bench 4.0, Flash scored 20% against Inkling-Small’s 0.9%, and its FrontierCode 2.0 score climbed from the base model’s 3.2% to 24%, narrowly edging out SWE-2’s 23.8%.

CultOfAI, an AI commentary  account on X , calls mid-training “a practical way to turn a weak open base into a usable agent model,” though the same account cautions that the figures are Cognition’s own rather than independently verified.

Cheaper, faster, still trailing

Flash doesn’t keep pace with the larger model on every test, coming within a hair on SWE-Bench Pro v2 Hard at 89.9% to SWE-2’s 90.6% but trailing on DeepSWE 1.1 and Terminal-Bench 4.0, while competitors including Claude Haiku 5.5 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash outscore it on several benchmarks.

Open base, private weights

Building on a model released under Apache 2.0, one of the more permissive  open source licenses , doesn’t obligate Cognition to open its own work, since the license lets developers modify and commercialize derivatives without sharing their changes — so keeping SWE-2 Flash’s weights private sits well within the company’s rights even as it cuts against the spirit of the base it borrowed.

The decision caught the attention of  David Hendrickson , CEO of GenerAIte Solutions, who praised Cognition for turning Inkling-Small into a “coding beast” but  pointed out on X  that “the improved weights aren’t public.”

His observation comes as open-weight models close the performance gap with proprietary alternatives and become  serious contenders for coding platforms . Cognition’s decision to keep its improved model private contrasts with that trend.

Cognition says it’s building a program to share the weights with select industry partners and research labs that could inspect, fine-tune, and run the model on their own infrastructure, an arrangement likely to appeal to enterprises and governments wary of sensitive code leaving their systems.

More details are coming in the next few weeks, the company says, and for now it remains unclear who will qualify, what restrictions they’ll face, or whether they’ll be allowed to share models built on SWE-2 Flash.

Cybersecurity drives the lockdown

Cybersecurity is central to Cognition’s decision to restrict the weights. The company included cybersecurity tasks in Flash’s training, raising its ExploitBench score from Inkling-Small’s 11.3% to 34.8%. That’s a significant improvement, although the benchmark doesn’t establish how the model would perform in real-world attacks or whether releasing its weights would increase the risk of misuse.

Cognition points to a rise in AI-enabled cyberattacks as justification for limiting access.

The concern is that capabilities used to find and investigate vulnerabilities could just as easily help attackers. Cognition points to a rise in AI-enabled cyberattacks as justification for limiting access. Similar challenges are trending across the industry; AI tools can now  identify tens of thousands of potential vulnerabilities in open-source projects  faster than maintainers can investigate and fix them.

American model, limited access

Cognition describes SWE-2 Flash as a fully American coding model and claims it beats every American open-weight model on leading evaluations, including models three times its size, a qualification that carries weight because the company’s own benchmark table shows models built outside the United States, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash among them, outscoring Flash on several tests.

Developers can try SWE-2 Flash through Devin Desktop and CLI, and the model is free through November 30.

title: Meta’s best AI model now trains the one most of its users get
author: The New Stack
description:
Starting on Friday, everyone using Meta’s Muse agent and Meta AI gets new models the company trained using Muse Wonder, its frontier model. Subscribers still get Wonder itself for harder tasks.

Meta hasn’t named the new models, though we can assume  their codenames don’t involve fruits . The company calls them “specialized” versions of its existing ones that were “trained using Muse Wonder.” They also come with two features the company first introduced with Wonder: Active Memo...
article_content:
Starting on Friday, everyone using Meta’s Muse agent and Meta AI gets new models the company trained using Muse Wonder, its frontier model. Subscribers still get Wonder itself for harder tasks.

Meta hasn’t named the new models, though we can assume  their codenames don’t involve fruits . The company calls them “specialized” versions of its existing ones that were “trained using Muse Wonder.” They also come with two features the company first introduced with Wonder: Active Memory and Active Focus.

Meta originally  launched Wonder  and the more capable Wonder Full on Oct. 12. Wonder is currently available through the  Meta Model API  and in Muse Code, the company’s coding agent, while Wonder Full is limited to Muse Code’s two most expensive plans.

Wonder-trained models for everyone

Muse, Meta’s personal agent app , launched in September on the smaller  Muse Spark  model and became somewhat of a breakout hit for Meta and introduced consumers to the idea of personal agents.

Unlike many personal agents, Muse has a free tier, giving it a far lower barrier of entry than OpenAI’s Dots or Anthropic’s Duet, which are only available to subscribers on those vendors’ highest pricing tiers.

What’s maybe most interesting here from a technical perspective is that Meta didn’t simply develop a smaller, general-purpose version of Wonder.

Credit: Meta.

Instead, the company stresses that it trained the new models on the behaviors that matter in a consumer app like Muse. That means the agents have to decide when to work on their own and when to check with the user, for example, and be able to take corrections in the middle of a task without losing track.

Using a large model to train smaller ones is obviously a common way for AI labs to get frontier behavior into products at consumer scale, but Meta sadly hasn’t detailed its method.

It’s also worth noting that Meta is tuning those models for very specific use cases.

A personal agent need to be able to a restaurant table and manage a user’s inbox, but the model that powers that agent doesn’t need to know everything a frontier model knows. But it does need to remember what a user said a week ago, and know how to keep going when a website breaks halfway through a booking.

That’s where features like Active Memory and Active Focus come in.

“Active Memory”

Active Memory helps the models remember details and take them from earlier conversations into new ones.

As Meta writes in its announcement, “We’ve trained our models to recognize what type of information is temporary versus permanent, to reason across time, and to distinguish between what is still relevant and what has become stale.”

On Meta’s internal evaluation, the new models in Muse correctly use critical context in 90% of tasks, up from 76% for the previous model.

Credit: Meta.

“Active Focus”

Active Focus is focused on keeping the models working on a task when something goes awry.

“We’ve trained our models on a variety of bottlenecks reflective of the real world,” Meta writes, “so that they can try harder, recover, or find alternatives on your behalf.” I

In Muse, the company reports a 67% improvement in finishing routine tasks when these new models run into unexpected problems, but it didn’t share the baseline.

Meta says the models are also better at deciding when to work on their own and when to check with the user, and they handle corrections in the middle of a task.

Two tiers of models

On the API, Wonder costs $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, while Muse also has a free tier and Meta AI runs inside WhatsApp, Instagram, Facebook, and Messenger.

Training lighther-weight models with Wonder is likely a cheaper way to reach that many users than serving Wonder itself to all of them.

title: “Most apps never make it off localhost”: Cursor takes on Lovable and Replit with fully managed app deployment
author: The New Stack
description:
AI coding agents have certainly made it easier to transform an idea into a working application. However, getting that application off a local machine and into the hands of real users remains a hurdle, requiring essential infrastructure steps spanning everything from hosting and database provisioning, to critical security checks.

Cursor, the AI coding platform acquired by Elon Musk’s SpaceX for  $60 billion  back  in August ,  acknowledged the problem  in an X post published on Thursday.

&ldquo...
article_content:
AI coding agents have certainly made it easier to transform an idea into a working application. However, getting that application off a local machine and into the hands of real users remains a hurdle, requiring essential infrastructure steps spanning everything from hosting and database provisioning, to critical security checks.

Cursor, the AI coding platform acquired by Elon Musk’s SpaceX for  $60 billion  back  in August ,  acknowledged the problem  in an X post published on Thursday.

“Agents have made it easier to write code, but most apps never make it off localhost,” the company notes.

To address this, Cursor  is introducing  new  app-building and deployment functionality , designed to take AI-generated applications from development to a live, shareable URL, without users having to even think about the underlying infrastructure themselves.

“Agents have made it easier to write code, but most apps never make it off localhost.”

Built on cloud agents

The new feature is built around  cloud agents , which Cursor  introduced last year  as a way for developers to run multiple AI coding agents remotely without having to keep their laptops engaged. At the time, the company highlighted their ability to fix bugs, handle smaller coding tasks and implement some complex features.

With this latest update, those same agents can now take applications all the way through to deployment, handling the important steps needed to make them accessible to other users. The functionality is only available through cloud agents, though, which means it can’t be used with agents running locally.

Users start by describing the application they want to build in natural language, with Cursor managing the code generation and development process as usual.

1. Prompt Cursor as usual

From there, the agent creates the application and sets up the underlying project, including the necessary components to get it running.

2. Cursor’s agent builds the application

Once the application is ready, users can preview the result before deciding whether to hit publish.

3. Preview the app before publishing

Publishing makes the application accessible through a live URL, allowing users to share it with colleagues or other users without having to configure hosting themselves.

4. Share the app via a live link

It’s worth noting that there are two ways to get started. Users building an application from scratch will automatically have a new repository created on  Cursor Origin , the company’s  Git-based code-hosting platform launched in August  as an agent-centric alternative to GitHub.

Alternatively, users can deploy applications from an existing GitHub repository. This means developers who already have an application under development can use Cursor’s cloud agents to prepare and publish it, without having to move their code to Origin or set up deployment infrastructure manually.

Judging by Cursor’s  own examples , the feature seemingly targets employees who need to create internal business applications, such as sales dashboards, onboarding programs, customer presentations and developer portals. So in that regard, it could prove a boon for non-developers who have an idea for a tool but  lack the technical nous to get it running themselves.

Of course, there’s nothing restricting the feature to business applications. An aspiring vibe coder could just as easily create a neighbourhood football league tracker or interactive family holiday planner. And because individual subscribers can publish apps publicly, those creations can be shared with anyone who has the link.

Under the hood: hosting, databases and security

Cursor had actually begun closing this gap, when in August  it introduced the ability  to preview cloud-agent projects and publish them to a live URL. However, users still needed to connect their own Vercel accounts.

Cursor’s earlier app-building feature, introduced in August 2026.

The latest release removes that requirement while introducing various new smarts to the mix.

Behind the scenes, Cursor now takes care of several infrastructure requirements, including hosting, databases, and authentication.

For hosting, Cursor automatically creates a dedicated account for each team or individual subscriber, isolated from other customers. While Cursor’s announcement doesn’t identify the underlying hosting provider, Vercel  revealed in a separate response  on X that the new functionality is built on its  Vercel for Platforms infrastructure . This basically allows users to deploy applications without having to create their own Vercel accounts or configure hosting themselves.

Deploy apps in one click with  @cursor_ai .

• No account to create

• No deployment configuration

• Database provisioning included

Built on Vercel for Platforms →  https://t.co/09OAnq0Q7W   https://t.co/SiMHJlOIvD

— Vercel (@vercel)  November 5, 2026

If an application needs a database, Cursor provisions one using PostgreSQL, while private and team applications are protected by Cursor’s existing sign-in system. Individual subscribers can also make their apps publicly accessible.

Applications can connect to external services, such as company databases or data warehouses, with users supplying the necessary credentials. Cursor says these secrets are managed separately, meaning the AI agent never sees their actual values.

Then there’s the thorny issue of security. When users choose to publish an application, Cursor says it runs “a series of deterministic and agentic security checks” before allowing it to go live. These include mandatory checks for exposed credentials, secrets and sensitive files, alongside an AI-powered review intended to identify more serious vulnerabilities.

However, it’s unclear how reliably these automated checks can identify more complex problems, such as incorrectly configured database permissions or application-level access controls. This is an important consideration for organisations contemplating connecting AI-generated applications to sensitive internal systems, where additional security scrutiny would still be advisable.

There is precedent for such concerns, too. In May last year,  Semafor reported  that two Replit employees examined 1,645 Lovable-built applications and discovered that 170 of them exposed sensitive information. The problems involved incorrectly configured database permissions, highlighting the difficulties of securing applications created through AI tools. Lovable says it  subsequently introduced  further security checks to identify potential vulnerabilities before applications are published.

Cursor moves onto Lovable and Replit’s turf

Of course, Cursor is entering territory already occupied by the likes of  Lovable  and  Replit , which allow users to create and publish applications through natural-language prompts.

While Cursor’s latest announcement emphasizes internal business tools, Lovable and Replit have traditionally appealed to a broader audience of aspiring application creators. Still, the overlap is clear, and Cursor’s move into deployment has already caught the attention of developers.

“Cursor just came for the localhost graveyard.”

One software engineer  writes on X  that “ cursor just came for the localhost graveyard ,” riffing on Cursor’s own messaging about AI-generated applications that never make it beyond local development.

There’s also an interesting overlap with  Grok Build , particularly given SpaceX’s acquisition of Cursor in August.

SpaceXAI introduced  Grok’s Build Mode in July , before expanding it to all Grok plans the  following month . The feature allows users to create apps, games and websites directly inside a Grok conversation, then publish them to shareable grok.me links.

That bears something of a resemblance to Cursor’s latest offering, although Cursor is approaching it through its established coding environment and cloud agents, and with a stronger emphasis on business applications and managed infrastructure.

The overlap hasn’t gone unnoticed though. One X user  responded to Cursor’s announcement  by asking, “ so cursor is now properly replacing grok build ?”

There’s no indication that Grok Build  is  being replaced, but the two offerings now cover some notably similar ground, raising questions about how SpaceXAI intends to distinguish them going forward.

For those wanting to check out Cursor’s new functionality, it’s available on  all  paid Cursor plans with cloud agents enabled.

With deployment increasingly becoming part of the AI coding experience, Cursor’s latest move could put further pressure on dedicated app-building platforms as the distinction between tools aimed at professional developers and those targeting aspiring vibe coders continues to narrow.

However, getting that application off a local machine and into the hands of real users remains a hurdle, requiring essential infrastructure steps spanning everything from hosting and database provisioning, to critical security checks.
