title: Postgres and ClickHouse can share tables. EnterpriseDB wants one set of rules to govern them.
author: The New Stack
description:
If you have built anything that needs both a system of record and fast analytics , you know the shape of the problem. Postgres ®  holds the orders, the accounts, the state your application cannot afford to get wrong. ClickHouse software answers the questions.

A row store tuned for transactions was never built to answer at speed: what happened across a billion events in the last hour, which cohort is churning, what the agent should do next. Both engines are excellent at their jobs. The miser...
article_content:
If you have built anything that needs both a system of record and fast analytics , you know the shape of the problem. Postgres ®  holds the orders, the accounts, the state your application cannot afford to get wrong. ClickHouse software answers the questions.

A row store tuned for transactions was never built to answer at speed: what happened across a billion events in the last hour, which cohort is churning, what the agent should do next. Both engines are excellent at their jobs. The misery lives entirely in the gap between them.

“Both engines are excellent at their jobs. The misery lives entirely in the gap between them.”

EnterpriseDB (EDB) has  acquired  Altinity, the independent company behind Altinity Stable Builds, the Altinity Kubernetes Operator, and Altinity.Cloud.

The headline is corporate. The reason a developer should care is narrower:  The #1 contributor to Postgres  and the  people who have run ClickHouse software  in production for nearly a decade now work on one roadmap, and that roadmap is aimed at three pains you live with every week.

Pain 1: The CDC job is the product nobody asked for

Count the moving parts between a committed Postgres transaction and the same row being queryable in ClickHouse software. A replication slot. A connector with its own failure modes. A message broker you size, secure, and patch. A sink that must survive schema changes without silently dropping columns. A dedup strategy, because at-least-once delivery means duplicates.

Monitoring on every hop, because lag in any one of them turns a “real-time” dashboard into a lie. None of that code is your product. All of it is on your on-call rota, and it is the reason the page comes at 3 a.m.

Pain 2: Your agent is reasoning over last night’s data

Agentic workloads changed the economics of staleness. A dashboard 20 minutes behind is annoying. An agent that approves a refund, reprices inventory, or flags a transaction on a 20-minute-old aggregate is wrong, and wrong at machine speed, thousands of times before anyone notices.

“An agent that approves a refund, reprices inventory, or flags a transaction on a 20-minute-old aggregate is wrong, and wrong at machine speed…”

So developers building agents write the same awkward code: Query Postgres for current state, query ClickHouse software for the trend, stitch the two in the application, and hope the clocks agree. You have become the integration layer, and the integration layer is where the bugs live.

Pain 3: You run the stack twice

Every row-level rule, masked column, and “analysts see aggregates, not customer IDs” policy exists once in Postgres and again in ClickHouse software, and the two drift the first time someone updates one and forgets the other. Operating ClickHouse software on Kubernetes is its own job: Keeper, storage classes, replica placement, backups, upgrades, and one or two engineers who have quietly become “the ClickHouse people.”

And if you took the shortcut of a managed analytics service, your data lives where the vendor says and your bill scales with their pricing model, not with your infrastructure. Two engines, two permission models, two operators, two support contracts, and a lock-in you did not choose.

Read against those three pains, the deal starts to make sense: Each one maps to a pillar of what EDB and Altinity now plan to build together.

Pillar 1: One shared layer, not a pipeline

Today, Postgres,  WarehousePG  (EDB’s MPP warehouse), and ClickHouse software can read the same Apache Iceberg tables and query each other. Postgres writes the record and ClickHouse software reads it through the same open table format, with less data movement and integration effort between them. What is planned is one shared catalog and one governance model across all three engines, and one sovereign control plane for Postgres and ClickHouse software.

The organizing architecture is Iceberg as the shared layer today, with EDB’s control plane to follow as the shared operation. Treat the shared catalog as what is being built, not what you can download today. But the design goal is the one you would set yourself: fewer hops, one catalog, no bespoke reconciliation code. The CDC job is meant to stop being something you own.

Pillar 2: Live data for agents, governed where it lives

EDB Postgres AI pairs a sovereign  multi-model data layer  with an agentic runtime and governance enforced in Postgres at the data layer—at the point of action and with an audit trail. For an agent, the goal is that it asks for business context and gets the record and the analysis from one system, rather than your code orchestrating two databases and a queue.

For permissions, one governance model across all three engines is part of the plan. Today, Postgres enforces purpose-bound access for agents, and ClickHouse software enforces its own role-based access. The plan is to define the policy once, where the data lives, and let every engine enforce it instead of re-implementing it in application code or a second permission model. That allows your agents to reason over what is true now without the security review blocking your release.

Pillar 3: The operators, the experts, and the choice of where it runs

Altinity’s answer to running ClickHouse software in production has been the  Kubernetes Operator , with more than 100 million pulls, and Altinity Stable Builds maintained for three years with security and bug-fix backports. That knowledge now sits inside the #1 contributor to Postgres, which also created CloudNativePG and donated it to the open source community, where it is now a CNCF project and the Postgres operator many teams already run. One vendor understands both operators.

The plan is one sovereign control plane that runs Postgres and ClickHouse software, with one support organization behind it on the night they interact badly. Where it runs is yours to decide: bring-your-own-cloud, self-hosted on your own Kubernetes or OpenShift, air-gapped, or fully managed. Altinity.Cloud already deploys into customers’ own cloud accounts, and EDB Postgres AI runs in your own account or on-premises. So if your regulator, your CFO, or your latency budget says the data stays here, the stack follows you rather than the other way round.

The one answer

Three pains, three pillars, one conclusion: The application layer should stop being the place where two databases are reconciled. Postgres keeps the record. ClickHouse software answers the hard questions on the same live data. Everything you delete from the middle is code you no longer debug, monitor, or explain to an auditor.

“The best pipeline is the one you never have to write.”

The best pipeline is the one you never have to write. For developers who have spent years keeping two databases in agreement by hand and explaining the drift to auditors, product managers, and themselves, that is the promise worth watching. And it is the first thing to test as each planned piece lands.

title: Anthropic found a way to prove which AI model answered you — but there’s a costly catch
author: The New Stack
description:
Developers using AI APIs have little way of knowing whether the model answering their requests is actually the one they’re paying for. A provider could route requests to a cheaper model, or an attacker could interfere with responses, without customers having an obvious way to detect the switch.

Now, Anthropic wants to change that. The company’s Frontier Red Team has released  FlashProve , an open-source cryptographic system designed to verify which AI model produced a response witho...
article_content:
Developers using AI APIs have little way of knowing whether the model answering their requests is actually the one they’re paying for. A provider could route requests to a cheaper model, or an attacker could interfere with responses, without customers having an obvious way to detect the switch.

Now, Anthropic wants to change that. The company’s Frontier Red Team has released  FlashProve , an open-source cryptographic system designed to verify which AI model produced a response without exposing its underlying weights.

Announced Tuesday , the research could eventually help developers verify third-party AI services and detect compromised inference systems. But FlashProve remains a research prototype, and the cost of generating proofs makes it impractical for routine API traffic.

But FlashProve remains a research prototype, and the cost of generating proofs makes it impractical for routine API traffic.

How FlashProve proves the model

FlashProve uses  zkSNARKs  to verify that a response came from a specific set of model weights without revealing those weights. The commitment still has to come from a trusted source, or the proof means little.

Anthropic has released  FlashProve on GitHub , where developers can download the code and test the system themselves. It’s still a research prototype, however, and isn’t available as a feature of the Claude API.

The cost of every proof

Anthropic tested FlashProve on Meta’s Llama 4 Maverick, a 400-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model, rather than Claude.

According to Anthropic’s  benchmarks , FlashProve processed roughly 110 prompt tokens per second while generating proofs on a single Nvidia H100 GPU. Each proof was about 18.78 MB and took around 21 seconds to verify on a single CPU thread. Generating the proof is far more expensive than checking it.

Compared with standard inference using vLLM, FlashProve needed 70 to 95 times more GPU time to generate proofs. It also generates them in batches after requests are completed, rather than verifying tokens as they’re delivered.

FlashProve cuts proof sizes to roughly 19 MB and verification times to seconds

FlashProve cuts proof sizes to roughly 19 MB and verification times to seconds, although generating those proofs remains expensive and less practical for applications that need immediate verification of every response.

For developers already  watching every token of their inference spend , adding that much GPU overhead would be difficult to justify for routine API traffic.

Still, Anthropic says FlashProve is substantially faster than previous open-source systems. An earlier system called  VerInf  needed 14.3 hours to generate a proof covering 1,000 tokens. The resulting proof was 93.6 GB and took almost a day to verify.

Claude built it, humans verified

Anthropic credits Claude with much of FlashProve’s development, including optimizations that made its cryptographic proofs substantially faster. But the researchers still had to verify that those improvements hadn’t compromised the protocol’s security guarantees.

The team used  Lean  to formally verify the protocol’s mathematical properties, including that it accepts valid proofs, rejects forged proofs with overwhelming probability, and doesn’t reveal the model’s weights beyond what the responses disclose.

FlashProve includes two verifiers: a faster C++ implementation and a Lean version backed by formal proofs. The C++ verifier passed Anthropic’s comparison tests, but it hasn’t been formally verified. Neither has the GPU prover.

Anthropic says the C++ verifier and GPU prover have been tested against the formally defined protocol, but neither has the same mathematical guarantees as the Lean implementation.

Why FlashProve isn’t production-ready

FlashProve is still limited to 1,024 tokens of context. It also uses integer-based inference and greedy decoding, while production models typically rely on floating-point calculations and sampling.

There’s no indication of when, or whether, FlashProve will make its way into the Claude API.

There’s no indication of when, or whether, FlashProve will make its way into the Claude API. Anthropic describes the  GitHub release  as a research artifact that isn’t being maintained or accepting contributions.

A provider could route requests to a cheaper model, or an attacker could interfere with responses, without customers having an obvious way to detect the switch.

title: Render just removed its AI sandbox time limit — and Vercel still has a 24-hour cap
author: The New Stack
description:
Render is taking on Vercel with AI sandboxes that can run indefinitely, along with new tools for managing long-running agent workflows and shared storage.

Announced Wednesday, the launch removes  Render ’s previous 30-day continuous runtime limit on paid workspace plans. Vercel caps individual sandbox sessions at 24 hours, while Render says its environments can suspend when idle and resume with their files, memory and running processes intact.

Render founder and CEO  Anurag Goel , a form...
article_content:
Render is taking on Vercel with AI sandboxes that can run indefinitely, along with new tools for managing long-running agent workflows and shared storage.

Announced Wednesday, the launch removes  Render ’s previous 30-day continuous runtime limit on paid workspace plans. Vercel caps individual sandbox sessions at 24 hours, while Render says its environments can suspend when idle and resume with their files, memory and running processes intact.

Render founder and CEO  Anurag Goel , a former Stripe engineer and head of risk, built the platform as an alternative to AWS without the same infrastructure complexity. Now he’s extending that approach to AI agents, combining sandboxes, durable workflows, and shared storage with the applications and databases they depend on.

Not everything is ready yet. Credential brokering will initially be available only to selected customers, private networking for sandboxes is still in development, and Render has yet to settle how its shared storage will handle simultaneous writes to the same file.

Sandboxes that resume mid-task

With this launch, Render sandboxes can stay active through a multi-day codebase migration or while an agent tests an entire application.

The bigger difference comes when a sandbox needs to resume work. Vercel  limits uninterrupted sessions to 24 hours , and while persistent sandboxes can restart, their running processes start over.

Render takes a different approach. A sandbox “suspends when it goes idle and wakes on the next command with its files and memory intact, so the agent picks up mid-task instead of rebuilding its state,” the company tells  The New Stack .

“suspends when it goes idle and wakes on the next command with its files and memory intact, so the agent picks up mid-task instead of rebuilding its state.”

Credentials that never enter

One of the launch’s security features is credential brokering, which attaches credentials to an agent’s outbound requests as they leave the sandbox so that secrets never enter it.

Pressed on whether that sets Render apart from Vercel, which already offers scoped credentials for agents through its Connect service and has  been pushing its own vendors toward short-lived credentials , the company does not claim an edge.

Credential brokering “is not a competitive differentiator” and “is rapidly becoming table stakes,” Render tells  The New Stack , calling it “a feature we believe users of Render will appreciate having access to, rather than one users of other platforms will migrate for.”

Render tells  The New Stack , it is “turning credential brokering on for small groups of customers first to make sure the experience meets our quality bar” before expanding in the coming weeks, while every developer in the beta gets outbound controls that can “block all traffic from a sandbox or allow only the domains you list.”

The company’s larger argument is that the sandbox matters less than everything around it. Developers choose Render over Vercel, the company contends, because an agent usually has to run inside a larger product and do heavy background work that needs an API staying up and holding its database connections, along with background workers, cron jobs, and the database itself.

Compute flexibility, less complexity

Vercel started with the frontend and serverless functions and is strong there; Render allows, but the company tells  The New Stack  that Vercel’s “underlying ‘fluid compute’ model is inflexible and inefficient for running the compute-heavy backend workloads that agentic applications depend on,” noting that a single function “tops out at 2 CPUs and 4 GB of RAM,” a ceiling that applies to Vercel Functions rather than its sandboxes.

Render tells  The New Stack , it “gives developers the compute flexibility of AWS but takes the complexity off their plate.”  Cristian Herrera , CTO of OCMI, which considered Vercel while moving away from AWS, tells Render that “Vercel is a different story,” adding that “if you need to do anything outside of Next.js, you’re fighting the platform.”

“if you need to do anything outside of Next.js, you’re fighting the platform.”

Vercel acknowledged  The New Stack’s  request for comment but had not provided a statement by publication time.

Workflows that survive crashes

Render’s new Durable Workflows let developers resume long-running jobs after a failure without starting over. Developers can write workflows in Python or TypeScript, with individual tasks running for up to 24 hours. Render “saves the result of every step as it finishes,” the company tells  The New Stack . If a process crashes, the workflow can resume on a new machine using those saved results, so “model calls, payments, and database writes that have already succeeded don’t run again.”

A risk remains if a process crashes after a payment goes through but before the result is saved. Render recommends using idempotency keys to prevent duplicate charges or database writes. Shared Filesystems let sandboxes and workflow tasks access the same persistent files, even after the compute that created them shuts down.

Render says the feature is designed for “many agents reading the same repo or dataset, with each one writing its own output.” But handling “concurrent writes to the same file, including locking and conflict resolution, is something we’re still studying,” the company tells  The New Stack .

Render says AWS and Vercel are “the two platforms new users most often tell us they’re leaving today, citing complexity and  cost  as major factors,” the company tells  The New Stack . Render doesn’t yet have figures showing how many customers have migrated from Vercel.

Render says AWS and Vercel are “the two platforms new users most often tell us they’re leaving today”

One failed transfer took 50 minutes to figure out

Kath tells  The New Stack  that most failed transfers he sees come down to a connection or login problem with an outside trading partner. The log usually shows one of four error types: authentication, network, permissions, or a missing file. He mostly works in GoAnywhere and said the pattern holds on Globalscape and other MFT platforms. 

He points to an example of a financial services company that sends a daily settlement file to a trading partner over SFTP, a secure way to move files between servers. And one day, the partner reports the file never arrived.

So the admin searches logs to find the right one, which shows an authentication failure. The admin then checks the SFTP connection settings and tests the password. When that doesn’t work, the admin asks the partner to inspect its own server logs.

And that’s where the answers are found. The partner had rotated its SSH keys without notifying others, so GoAnywhere was signing in with a key the partner no longer accepted. The team deployed the right key, tested the connection, and reran the job. The file went out as expected.

Kath’s tally:

Forty minutes of the 50 were spent investigating the problem. The fix took only 5 to 10 minutes.

“The opportunity isn’t simply making file transfers faster,” Kath says. “It’s reducing the administrative friction around managing them.”

Guided Diagnostics points to the likely cause and leaves the fix to the admin

Guided Diagnostic lives in GoAnywhere’s admin console. So when a job fails, it reads the failure and lays out a ranked list of things to check. The admin can skip the set that matches logs, settings, and help articles. 

On the settlement-file failure, it would flag “Authentication failure detected,” list the likely causes, and suggest next steps. It doesn’t change any setting, Kath says. “It would reduce the effort required to identify the likely cause and determine the next appropriate action.”

The admin can still make the change, and that’s the right call for software that handles a bank’s settlement files.

This online event will also cover three related features: Anomaly detection, log insights, and AI-generated documentation of how to build each workflow.

160 hours of troubleshooting

The 160 hours is one part of a bigger number. Fortra MFT asked dozens of customers how long routine MFT tasks take by hand, then compared that with the same tasks using the AI features. Across each task it asked about, the estimate reached 571 hours a year per user. Troubleshooting spent up to 160 of the 571 hours. 

Here’s how Kath splits the troubleshooting estimates.

In Kath’s own example, the root cause was on the partner’s own server. The time spent waiting for the partner to respond was not part of the estimate.

Repeat errors get the most help

Kath expects Guided Diagnostics to help with the common failures that leave an error message behind. It helps less with intermittent network drops, problems found on the partner’s side, complex workflow failures, performance bottlenecks, or custom integrations. 

A good admin should still take over when the cause sits outside GoAnywhere, when several things break simultaneously, when a fix carries security or operational risk, or when no one on the team has experienced the specific error. 

Kath will take questions on all of this during the live Q&A on November 19.  Register here  to join the discussion. The research behind the number will also appear in  The Next Era of MFT: How AI Transforms Managed File Transfer , an upcoming ebook from Fortra.  Sign up to get an advance copy here.

title: “Signing in to your company’s plugins one by one is annoying”: Anthropic’s fix puts Claude in the identity business
author: The New Stack
description:
Anthropic is now letting businesses automatically connect employees to approved Claude plugins, saving staff from having to sign in to and authorize each service individually. The feature also allows Claude to verify users’ organizational membership directly, making it easier for companies to manage access to workplace applications.

The feature builds on the Enterprise-Managed Authorization ( EMA ) extension to the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which debuted back in June. As  The New Stack   re...
article_content:
Anthropic is now letting businesses automatically connect employees to approved Claude plugins, saving staff from having to sign in to and authorize each service individually. The feature also allows Claude to verify users’ organizational membership directly, making it easier for companies to manage access to workplace applications.

The feature builds on the Enterprise-Managed Authorization ( EMA ) extension to the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which debuted back in June. As  The New Stack   reported at the time , this ushered in a way for companies to manage MCP connections centrally through their existing identity providers, with Okta becoming the first to support it.

Anthropic also  announced support  for the extension in Claude, Claude Code and Cowork on the same day, and  published implementation guidance  for developers building compatible MCP servers.

In its original guise, the approach relied on the company’s identity provider being compatible with EMA. Okta was the first to support the extension, and adoption among other providers remains limited, meaning many organizations have still had to authorize connections individually.

“Claude itself can issue the signed identity assertions that participating MCP services use to recognize employees.”

On the ClaudeDevs X account on Tuesday, Anthropic  introduced another option : Claude  itself  can issue the signed identity assertions that participating MCP services use to recognize employees. This effectively means businesses can enable automatic connections without requiring their identity provider to support the extension.

“If you’re building plugins for Claude, add support so users get started faster and stay connected without re-authorizing,” the company writes.

The new Claude authorization feature is available in beta now, for Team and Enterprise customers.

Claude takes over the identity check

Taking to X on Tuesday,  Boris Cherny , head of applications at Anthropic, points to the frustration of employees having to repeatedly authenticate workplace applications.

“Signing in to your company’s plugins one by one is annoying.”

“Signing in to your company’s plugins one by one is annoying, so we let Claude auto-connect to them now,” Cherny  writes .

Signing in to your company's plugins one by one is annoying, so we let Claude auto-connect to them now.

Team and Enterprise admins can set them up, and teammates are connected automatically the first time they use the plugins.  https://t.co/w2oxw0bKOZ

— Boris Cherny (@bcherny)  November 3, 2026

Administrators can choose which supported services to enable, and which employee roles should receive access. For example, a company might be comfortable giving all employees access to a general-purpose productivity tool, while restricting access to more sensitive systems, such as company databases, to specific roles because of the risks associated with exposing confidential information or making unauthorized changes.

When an eligible user opens a plugin, Claude sends a signed assertion identifying them as a member of the organization. The receiving service checks that assertion before providing an access token.

The process also handles subsequent connections automatically, so users don’t have to repeatedly authorize the same service when tokens expire.

The initial rollout spans a broad array of more than a dozen services, including Amplitude, Apollo.io, Atlassian, Datadog, Dropbox, Figma, Granola, HubSpot, Linear, Mixpanel, Notion, PagerDuty, Semrush, and Supabase.

14 services have signed up to Claude’s auto-connect plugins at launch.

In a November 3  blog post , Supabase explained that customers can now use Claude to authenticate employees accessing its MCP server, even if their identity provider lacks EMA support.

Indeed, the company points specifically to the limited adoption of the extension among enterprise identity providers as a key obstacle that the new feature addresses.

“Okta was the only identity provider that supported the extension at launch and most still don’t,” Supabase writes. “Organizations on those providers no longer have to wait because Claude can now be the issuer instead.”

To configure the connection, a Supabase administrator first approves Claude for the organization. An administrator then selects Claude-issued authorization in Claude’s connector settings, registers the unique issuer URL in Supabase, tests the connection and enables access for the relevant employee roles.

Authorizing Claude to access Supabase.

It’s worth noting that employees must already have a matching Supabase SSO account, and their existing permissions determine what they can access. The company also cautions that removing someone from the company’s identity provider alone will not revoke Claude-issued access, and administrators must remove departing employees from both Claude and Supabase.

Claude as an identity provider?

The upshot of all this is that Claude is now taking on a role traditionally handled by enterprise identity providers, vouching for users when they access third-party services. While it’s still early days, and the feature is currently limited to those in the business realm, the announcement has already prompted some positive reactions.

“Tired of reauthorizing in every other session.”

“This is soo good, tired of reauthorizing in every other session,” one user  writes on X .

Others are keen to see more companies support the feature, with one eager for payments giant Stripe to join the party. “I spend more time reconnecting Stripe than every other plugin combined,” the user  writes .

The implications for enterprise authentication also caught people’s attention. “Claude becoming an identity provider,” one  user remarked , raising a broader question about Anthropic’s growing role in verifying user identities.

Technically, Claude is acting as a trusted issuer for participating MCP services, verifying that users belong to a particular Claude organization. It doesn’t provide the full range of functions associated with a traditional identity provider, and connected services remain responsible for enforcing their own access permissions.

So for now, Claude’s identity ambitions extend only as far as the services willing to take its word for who you are.

title: A developer opened Postman. Then two AI coding agents changed without their permission.
author: The New Stack
description:
A developer says Postman’s desktop app installed plugins into Claude Code and OpenAI Codex without their permission. The app also tried to approve its own startup hook, which tells Codex to use Postman’s tools for API development tasks.

The developer, known as “indicava” on GitHub,  reported the issue on October 25  after Codex began showing authentication errors and repeatedly loading Postman skills without being asked.

It’s raised concerns about how easily third-party application...
article_content:
A developer says Postman’s desktop app installed plugins into Claude Code and OpenAI Codex without their permission. The app also tried to approve its own startup hook, which tells Codex to use Postman’s tools for API development tasks.

The developer, known as “indicava” on GitHub,  reported the issue on October 25  after Codex began showing authentication errors and repeatedly loading Postman skills without being asked.

It’s raised concerns about how easily third-party applications can change how AI coding agents work, especially when those changes happen without a clear opt-in.

Plugins installed without permission

According to the report, opening Postman desktop version 12.33.4 on macOS triggered an installation process affecting both Claude Code and Codex.

Postman’s application logs, included in the GitHub issue, show an installation event on October 24 marked auto-existing-upgrade, with results indicating that plugins for both coding agents had been installed.

The developer also found changes to Codex’s user-level configuration file,  ~/.codex/config.toml , including an enabled Postman plugin, a new plugin marketplace, and a trusted session-start hook.

The report also found a Postman CLI executable on the machine, with timestamps matching the installation.

Claude Code’s configuration similarly showed an installed Postman plugin. The report also found a Postman CLI executable on the machine, with timestamps matching the installation.

The developer says they had not explicitly authorized these changes. The report documents one macOS installation, and the behavior has not been independently reproduced across other systems.

The self-approving startup hook

But perhaps even more interesting is how Postman gets Codex to trust its plugin in the first place. According to Postman’s  own documentation , its installer can automatically approve a session-start hook on the user’s behalf.

According to Postman’s own documentation, its installer can automatically approve a session-start hook on the user’s behalf.

Developers who install the plugin directly through Codex, however, must review and approve the hook themselves. The  installer’s source code  shows exactly what happens.

Postman checks whether Codex already trusts the hook. If it doesn’t, the installer uses  config/batchWrite  to add the hook’s trusted hash to Codex’s configuration. It checks that the hook hasn’t changed before approving it, and if approval fails or can’t be confirmed, it logs a message telling the developer to review the hook in Codex.

Session-start hooks can  give coding agents instructions automatically , even when the developer hasn’t asked for them. Postman’s  startup instructions  tell Codex to load the  postman:api-engineer  skill before handling most API development tasks.

Codex is still supposed to follow the developer’s instructions first. But for many API tasks, it’s also being told to use Postman’s tools by default, whether the developer asked for them or not.

That might be useful for developers who chose to install the plugin. The concern here is that Postman’s desktop app reportedly added those instructions to an existing coding environment without the developer’s permission.

Developers raise security concerns

The findings have drawn criticism from developers on GitHub and X. Security researcher  Frank Denis   called the integrations “junk” on X  and pointed out that Postman’s installer attempts to trust its own startup hook.

Siddharth Garimella  went further,  claiming that Postman’s hooks intercept API data  and send it back to the company. However, the GitHub report provides no evidence that Postman collected or transmitted API data. It documents changes to agent settings and a remote MCP connection, not data theft.

The developer also found that Postman had configured a connection to its remote MCP server at  https://mcp.postman.com/mcp , but Codex repeatedly failed to authenticate.

The criticism has also spread to GitHub, where one commenter  calls the behavior  “unacceptable, even creating risk in corporate environment.” Another  urges Postman  to be transparent and ask for permission.

Who controls the agent

The developer wants Postman to stop installing plugins for existing users without their permission and leave hook approval up to Codex. They also want a way to fully undo the changes.

Postman  provides an uninstall command , but the developer says that isn’t enough. Removing the integration should also clear any changes to agent settings, trusted hooks, MCP connections, and installed CLI tools.

For now, developers can check their Claude Code and Codex settings for unfamiliar plugins, hooks, or MCP connections.

Postman’s installer can approve its own Codex hook without the usual manual review.

The complaint comes as developers are  pushing for more control over their coding agents . Postman’s installer can approve its own Codex hook without the usual manual review. What remains unanswered is why an existing desktop installation reportedly triggered that process without the user’s permission.

The New Stack  reached out to Postman to ask about the automatic installations, hook approvals, and user consent. The company had not responded by the time of publication.

The post  A developer opened Postman. Then two AI coding agents changed without their permission.  appeared first on  The New Stack .

title: Can agent standards keep up with the companies building them?
author: The New Stack
description:
Mazin Gilbert, executive director of the Linux Foundation’s Agentic AI Foundation , left Google earlier this year to lead the new AAIF, and he recently shared with  The New Stack  a truth central to its mission: The  AAIF  has to move faster than its members.

Gilbert , speaking in an interview at AGNTCon + MCPCon North America in San Jose last month, said on  The New Stack  podcast, “If this foundation does not move at the speed of light, it becomes irrelevant.”

H...
article_content:
Mazin Gilbert, executive director of the Linux Foundation’s Agentic AI Foundation , left Google earlier this year to lead the new AAIF, and he recently shared with  The New Stack  a truth central to its mission: The  AAIF  has to move faster than its members.

Gilbert , speaking in an interview at AGNTCon + MCPCon North America in San Jose last month, said on  The New Stack  podcast, “If this foundation does not move at the speed of light, it becomes irrelevant.”

He also talked about how he gets OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google to agree on standards — even though they compete on products. Those companies are going to build products “with and without the standards,” he says.

All of this is happening while the foundation’s own members are often still figuring out how to build and use agents themselves. Some contribute to protocols and ship products, but others are still trying to get their agents out of the lab and into production. Gilbert says a third group of companies “frankly are panicking,” because they don’t have an agent strategy yet.

The San Jose event drew 4,300 registrants, he says, double the size of the foundation’s previous largest event in Amsterdam earlier this year.

How MCP gets built

Before our recording, Gilbert had just met with a group of maintainers from “very fiercely competing companies” who were working on the protocols together. All of those companies depend on these standards, he says, so they have a reason to get the work done.

“These protocols are the air you breathe.”

—Mazin Gilbert, executive director, AAIF.

“These protocols are the air you breathe. These protocols are the plumbing,” Gilbert says. “They may not be that sexy, maybe, but if we don’t get those right, that entire agentic AI space will be a mess, expensive and prohibitive basically for any company to deploy this at scale.”

As an example, he points to the  July release  of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) specification, which made the protocol stateless. “Every one of those companies not only contributed to it, but they ended up completely updating their entire stack to the stateless MCP,” he says.

MCP downloads grew tenfold in the protocol’s first 10 months at the foundation, according to Gilbert, after  Anthropic donated it  last December. Today, fewer than 15 percent of its maintainers work at Anthropic, and more than 1,000 organizations contribute 75 percent of the pull requests, he says. Those contributors include U.S. retailers and companies around the world.

At the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), many projects started at startups before they were donated. At the AAIF, Gilbert says, large companies tend to contribute the protocols, and smaller companies extend them and build businesses on top.

Some of those startups were doing something “very different” six months or a year ago, he says, and some didn’t exist yet. Now they’re building enterprise products on MCP and the foundation’s gateway projects to connect agents to companies’ back-end systems.

Getting members to contribute

The AAIF now has 305 members, and Gilbert said in his keynote that about one new company joins every business day. He calls it the fastest-growing foundation in the Linux Foundation’s history. About 40 percent of its members are startups, and 19 percent are nonprofits, national labs, and academic institutions.

“None of us have done this before, so I just want to be very clear about that. We are learning this as we go,” he says.

Part of the job is making membership worth enough that companies actively contribute. “It’s not about the money. Their time is far more valuable than their money. Their people are far more valuable than the money,” Gilbert says.

He’d like every member to contribute, but also acknowledges that’s not the case yet. He knows who does, because he uses his own agents to track contributions across the foundation.

Some companies are still trying to understand what agents can do for them and what they’d get back on the investment. Others don’t know how to contribute. Gilbert encourages them to start by joining a working group and listening, and says they don’t have to arrive as experts. For companies still learning, the foundation launched its first certification in September: the  Model Context Protocol Associate  (MCPA).

The  Gates Foundation , which joined in September, now sits on the AAIF’s board. Gilbert says it’s helping developers in parts of Africa and South Asia get the training and certification they need to contribute, and to attend events they couldn’t otherwise afford.

Pressed on whether nonprofits and for-profit companies clash inside the foundation, Gilbert says he hasn’t seen it yet. “Whether you are a nonprofit, for-profit, small, large, your value, your impact, your power in this foundation really depends on contributions,” he says.

How many gateways do you need?

The foundation is also choosing which projects to accept. The community has submitted 65 projects through its public intake process, Gilbert says, and the AAIF has declined some. The first 10 to 20 projects “really define the DNA of this foundation,” he says.

With the four projects it announced in San Jose (Agent Skills from Anthropic, Open Responses from OpenAI, OpenEnv from Hugging Face, and OpenSandbox from Alibaba), the AAIF now hosts 10.

In some cases, the foundation is taking in technologies that are already widely adopted, like MCP and Agent Skills. In others, nobody agrees yet on what a standard should look like.

Gateways are one example. The AAIF approved two gateway projects this year, Solo.io’s  agentgateway  and  Agent Router , which moved over from the CNCF’s Envoy project in September. Gilbert says five or six more companies want to contribute their own. Does the community need “six gateways or 10 gateways,” he asks, “or do we need to harmonize those together?”

He doesn’t have an answer yet, and says the community doesn’t either. The foundation gives those companies neutral governance to work it out together, he says.

The technical committee and governing board evaluate each proposal, including whether the AAIF is the right home for it, Gilbert says. They look at every layer of the stack, including agent frameworks, execution harnesses, gateways, guardrails, memory, protocols, observability, and identity. Not every project the foundation accepts will become the standard, he notes.

Agents that can transact

Gilbert wants the foundation to work on identity, security, trust, and observability. He also wants it to take on agent commerce.

“These agents, the internet of agents, must be transactional,” he says. An agent making a purchase would need to discover a catalog, talk to a merchant’s agent, negotiate, pay, and handle returns or disputes, and Gilbert says each step still needs a protocol.

He’s also excited about physical AI, meaning protocols for agents that talk to machines and appliances instead of databases. “Your refrigerator, your washing machines. It’s so cool,” he says. “It’s like science fiction, but it’s happening now.”

Wherever the protocols fall short, Gilbert says, companies will write custom code, and customers will end up paying to support it. A standard that arrives after a customer has built and deployed its own integration still leaves that customer with code to maintain.

article_content:
In this article

Mitigation and protection guidance

Microsoft Defender detections

Hunting queries

Indicators of compromise

In October 2026, the financially motivated threat actor Storm-3358 began targeting organizations in the financial sector using the agentic AI offensive framework ARTEX. The threat actor that Microsoft Threat Intelligence tracks as Storm-3358 is a Cambodia-based intrusion cluster that primarily targets financial organizations in Southeast Asia, in addition to a smaller number of large financial organizations globally.

Microsoft has observed Storm-3358 use ARTEX in combination with conventional automated tools to scan systems connected to the public internet, exploit security flaws including anonymous file upload and server-side request forgery (SSRF), and install open-source remote access trojans (RATs). Storm-3358 has used the WISP, vshell, and AdaptixC2 RATs for persistence and lateral movement. Microsoft has observed ARTEX agents using utilities like netcat and curl to download these RATs to compromised systems, as shown in Figure 1.

Figure 1. Example commands that ARTEX agents used to download RATs to compromised systems.

In recent ARTEX-related attacks, threat actors have used ARTEX agents to scan and exploit vulnerabilities in web applications, use web shells for persistence on compromised web servers, compromise  credentials from public sources  and compromised systems, and  use compromised cloud identities  for persistence and data exfiltration. ARTEX agents can also perform brute-force password attacks, password spraying, API enumeration and abuse, and database dumping. Agentic tools like ARTEX can leverage compromised credentials and systems at machine speed to move laterally, escalate privileges, and exfiltrate data.

This activity illustrates an ongoing trend of threat actors accelerating all stages of the attack chain with agentic AI penetration testing frameworks, including ARTEX. As these capabilities evolve, defenders must similarly use AI to investigate and respond across large environments.

While threat actors regularly use proxies and virtual private networks (VPNs) to change the source IP address of malicious traffic and bypass static detections, Microsoft is providing indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help defenders detect related activity.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Microsoft’s research into threats involving agentic frameworks informs security detections and investigative context across its products. The capabilities available to customers depend on the source of the activity and the products and protections deployed in their environment.

Several behavioral signals can help organizations determine that they are being targeted by threat actors using agentic AI. Agentic AI frameworks scanning a target send a wide variety of requests in a brief time and retry variations on the same technique or move on to next-stage actions at machine speed. Agentic AI frameworks use existing penetration testing tools. For example, ARTEX by default uses Nmap, curl, wget, Python HTTP clients, Norma SDK WebFetch, and headless Chromium through Playwright, among others. These tools may send network traffic with distinctive characteristics, such as default user agent strings. While blocking network traffic with these characteristics will not stop an attack by an AI agent, which will quickly change them, identifying them can alert defenders to the activity.

Defensive honeypots , decoys, tarpits, and fake wins can pull autonomous AI attacks away from legitimate targets. Honeypots and decoy surfaces such as  Microsoft Sentinel Deception  give the agent attractive but worthless targets to pursue. Tarpits consume the agent’s time and budget. Fake wins present convincing evidence that the agent’s objective is complete, which can cause it to stop on a false success. In Microsoft’s testing, these controls helped reduce the attack traffic reaching real assets and produced high-confidence, attribution-quality signal.

For additional information on the evolution of threat actors’ use of ARTEX please see Microsoft’s recent blogs:  AI-driven, large-scale nation-state campaign using ARTEX enables supply chain compromise  and  Threat actors use agentic AI tooling to find and abuse exposed secrets .

Microsoft’s continuous research into threat actors leveraging agentic frameworks integrates directly into the following products:

Identity and sign-in activity — Microsoft Entra ID Protection

Microsoft analyzes sign-in activity and other signals to identify potential identity risk. Customers can investigate risk detections and risky sign-ins, and configure Conditional Access policies that use sign-in or user risk to require multifactor authentication or block access when specified conditions are met. Identity and sign-in activity from known threat actor infrastructure, including from agentic frameworks like ARTEX, generate Verified threat actor IP risk detections delivered at high risk. See:

Investigate risk with Microsoft Entra ID Protection

Risk-based user sign-in protection in Microsoft Entra ID

What are risk detections? – Microsoft Entra ID Protection

Endpoint activity — Microsoft Defender for Endpoint

Endpoint alerts help security teams identify and investigate suspicious activity on devices. Indicators of compromise can support detection and, when configured, blocking. Customers can review related alerts in the Microsoft Defender portal. See:

Review alerts in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint

Activity across security domains — Microsoft Defender portal

The portal brings together alerts and incidents from Microsoft security solutions and provides relevant threat intelligence to support investigation, threat hunting, and response. This helps customers assess suspicious activity in the context of their own environment. See:

Investigate alerts in Microsoft Defender XDR

Security Dashboard for AI

Threat actor misuse of AI accelerates risk across enterprise environments by amplifying existing threats such as exploitation of vulnerabilities, phishing, malware threats, and insider activity. To help organizations stay ahead of AI-enabled threat activity, Microsoft has introduced the Security Dashboard for AI. The dashboard provides users with a unified view of AI security posture by aggregating security, identity, and data risk across  Microsoft Defender ,  Microsoft Entra , and  Microsoft Purview . See:

Security Dashboard for AI

Microsoft Defender detections

Microsoft Defender  customers can refer to the list of applicable detections below. Microsoft Defender coordinates detection, prevention, investigation, and response across endpoints, identities, email, apps to provide integrated protection against attacks like the threat discussed in this blog. These alerts may trigger on unrelated activity. Customers should investigate to determine if the alert is related to the activity outlined in this blog.

Microsoft Security Copilot

Microsoft Security Copilot  is  embedded in Microsoft Defender  and provides security teams with AI-powered capabilities to summarize incidents, analyze files and scripts, summarize identities, use guided responses, and generate device summaries, hunting queries, and incident reports.

Customers can also  deploy AI agents , including the following  Microsoft Security Copilot agents , to perform security tasks efficiently:

Threat Intelligence Briefing agent

Phishing Triage agent

Threat Hunting agent

Dynamic Threat Detection agent

Security Copilot is also available as a  standalone experience  where customers can perform specific security-related tasks, such as incident investigation, user analysis, and vulnerability impact assessment. In addition, Security Copilot offers  developer scenarios  that allow customers to build, test, publish, and integrate AI agents and plugins to meet unique security needs.

Threat intelligence reports

Microsoft Defender XDR customers can use the following  threat analytics  reports in the Defender portal (requires license for at least one Defender XDR product) to get the most up-to-date information about the activity and techniques discussed in this blog. These reports provide intelligence, protection information, and recommended actions to prevent, mitigate, or respond to associated threats found in customer environments.

Activity profile: ARTEX abuse expands as cybercriminals target financial sector

Microsoft Security Copilot customers can also use the  Microsoft Security Copilot integration  in Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence, either in the Security Copilot standalone portal or in the  embedded experience  in the Microsoft Defender portal to get more information about this threat.

Hunting queries

Microsoft Defender XDR

Microsoft Defender XDR customers can run the following  advanced hunting  query to find related activity in their networks:

Download of new files using curl

Threat actors might use tools such as curl to download additional files, communicate with C2 infrastructure, or exfiltrate data. This query looks for new files being downloaded using curl. curl also has legitimate uses, so files and hosts should be reviewed to identify potentially malicious activity.

| where TimeGenerated between (ago(7d)..ago(1d))

| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "curl"

| extend url = extract("http[s]?:\\/\\/(?:[a-zA-Z]|[0-9]|[$-_@.&+]|[!*\\(\\),]|(?:%[0-9a-fA-F][0-9a-fA-F]))+", 0,InitiatingProcessCommandLine)

| extend ip = extract("(\\b25[0-5]|\\b2[0-4][0-9]|\\b[01]?[0-9][0-9]?)(\\.(25[0-5]|2[0-4][0-9]|[01]?[0-9][0-9]?)){3}[^ ]*", 0, CommandLine)

| extend remote_file = iif(isnotempty(url), url, ip))

| summarize by remote_file;

| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "curl"

| extend url = extract("http[s]?:\\/\\/(?:[a-zA-Z]|[0-9]|[$-_@.&+]|[!*\\(\\),]|(?:%[0-9a-fA-F][0-9a-fA-F]))+", 0,InitiatingProcessCommandLine)

| extend ip = extract("(\\b25[0-5]|\\b2[0-4][0-9]|\\b[01]?[0-9][0-9]?)(\\.(25[0-5]|2[0-4][0-9]|[01]?[0-9][0-9]?)){3}[^ ]*", 0, InitiatingProcessCommandLine)

| extend remote_file = iif(isnotempty(url), url, ip)

| union (SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688

| extend url = extract("http[s]?:\\/\\/(?:[a-zA-Z]|[0-9]|[$-_@.&+]|[!*\\(\\),]|(?:%[0-9a-fA-F][0-9a-fA-F]))+", 0,CommandLine)

| extend ip = extract("(\\b25[0-5]|\\b2[0-4][0-9]|\\b[01]?[0-9][0-9]?)(\\.(25[0-5]|2[0-4][0-9]|[01]?[0-9][0-9]?)){3}[^ ]*", 0, CommandLine)

| extend remote_file = iif(isnotempty(url), url, ip))

| where remote_file !in (known_files)

Microsoft Sentinel

Microsoft Sentinel customers can run the following  advanced hunting  query to find related activity in their networks:

Detect network IP indicators of compromise using ASIM

The following query checks IP address across data sources in the past 30 days supported by ASIM network session parser.

let lookback = 30d; let

ioc_ip_addr = dynamic(["199.19.95.66", "199.19.95.67", "199.19.95.68", "91.92.240.238", "85.11.168.45", "178.15.54.129", "31.77.229.35", "85.11.167.52"]);

| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), EventCount=count() by SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstDomain, Dvc, EventProduct, EventVendor

Indicators of compromise

Note:  Threat actors regularly use proxies and virtual private networks (VPNs) to change the source IP address of malicious traffic and bypass static detections. Microsoft is providing the following sample indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help defenders detect related activity.

title: Threat actors use agentic AI tooling to find and abuse exposed secrets
author: Microsoft Security Blog
description:
In this article

From exposed secrets to cloud compromise

Follow-on actions

Mitigating application credential abuse activity

Defending against agentic AI attacks

Microsoft detections

Advanced hunting queries

Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed threat actors using an agentic AI offensive framework to search public GitHub repositories for exposed secrets, including credentials, application credentials, and AI inference-related API keys across multiple applications and cloud services. ...
article_content:
In this article

From exposed secrets to cloud compromise

Follow-on actions

Mitigating application credential abuse activity

Defending against agentic AI attacks

Microsoft detections

Advanced hunting queries

Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed threat actors using an agentic AI offensive framework to search public GitHub repositories for exposed secrets, including credentials, application credentials, and AI inference-related API keys across multiple applications and cloud services. These threat actors can then use the secrets for further malicious activity against the compromised organization.

Searching open code repositories for exposed credentials, secrets, keys, and other authentication material is a well-documented technique that has historically been limited by the time required for human operators to find code repositories, review the data in the repositories, and leverage authentication material for further action. However, agentic tooling like ARTEX allows threat actors to not only scan for secrets across multiple repositories at a quicker pace but also use the agents to analyze the output and conduct follow-on attacks, cutting down on the need for the threat actor to have hands-on-keyboard interactions throughout the attack chain. In at least one case, Microsoft observed an AI agent advance from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from Azure Key Vault in just five minutes.

Microsoft has also investigated follow-on activity involving the misuse of valid application credentials. As early as October 28, 2026, Microsoft began observing successful service principal sign-ins from the IP address 199.19.77[.]84 involving multiple application IDs across some impacted customers, including cases where a multitenant application credential was compromised at the source (vendor-owned application) and used to access multiple downstream tenants. The threat actor used the compromised credentials for cloud resource discovery, and credential and data exfiltration, including from Azure Key Vaults and Storage Accounts, and abuse of Azure AI services consistent with the activity described above. Additionally, Microsoft observed malicious activity originating from two IP addresses potentially associated with this campaign. We identified malicious operations from 65.87.223[.]26, including indications of vulnerability exploitation by embedded shell commands in a user agent and attempts to obtain App Service authentication tokens. A similar campaign involving the same IPs addressed was also reported by  Todyl . Separately, Microsoft observed reconnaissance operations from 157.22.126[.]128 targeting AI workloads deployed by victims on Azure AI services.

Microsoft encourages organizations to scan their code in GitHub and determine where any secrets are present. In addition to removing the secrets from the code base, affected organizations should immediately rotate any exposed keys or credentials. GitHub monitors public repositories by automatically scanning for secrets. In addition to scanning their own repositories, organizations can  enable public monitoring  through GitHub to detect secrets leaked in secondary public repositories across GitHub. This extends secret scanning beyond the repositories an enterprise owns to follow potential secret exposure across the platform.  GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps  scans for credentials and other sensitive content in source code. Push protection can also block supported secrets before they’re pushed. Organizations need either GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps or, for organizations using the standalone experience, GitHub Secret Protection for Azure DevOps enabled.

Secrets are exposed in public repositories when code containing the secret is committed to GitHub. Developers might store secrets in configuration files, scripts, or other code to quickly operationalize the OAuth application or avoid configuring more modern authentication flows. Organizations can reduce exposure by protecting workload identities and secrets, enforcing least privilege, safeguarding recovery resources, and enabling relevant  Microsoft Defender for Cloud  protections. Publicly exposed credentials remain usable until revoked or rotated; removing the original disclosure alone does not remediate the exposure. Microsoft recommends that developers  migrate OAuth applications away from secret-based authentication . While storing long-lived application client secrets in code is a common practice, using managed identities for application authentication eliminates the possibility of secret exposure in code, manual processes associated with secret management, and barriers to securely scaling applications.

This activity illustrates an ongoing trend of threat actors  accelerating all stages of the attack chain with agentic AI  penetration testing frameworks, including ARTEX. As these capabilities evolve, defenders must similarly use AI to investigate and respond across large environments.

From exposed secrets to cloud compromise

Starting in August 2026, Microsoft observed threat actors using an agentic AI offensive framework to submit large volumes of queries to GitHub for secrets. The queries submitted by the AI framework often included the name of a target organization, keywords for secrets, a keyword linked to cloud services, or a keyword linked to another AI service provider. Organizations that find their secrets exposed in public repositories must assume that the exposed secrets and associated applications are compromised.

Follow-on actions

Credential abuse via Entra ID

In one follow-on attack that began as early as October 28, 2026, an agentic framework used valid leaked or stolen application credentials to access Microsoft Entra ID tenants of certain organizations and connected Azure and Microsoft 365 resources. The sign-ins primarily came from two IP addresses: 199.19.77[.]84 and 199.19.77[.]18. The latter IP address is a Tor exit node, which might be associated with unrelated malicious activity, including from unrelated sources. The agent successfully conducted service principal sign-ins on dozens of associated applications across multiple tenants.. Service principals are the identities that applications use to authenticate and give direct, programmatic access to whatever the application is authorized to reach.

The threat actor targeted operations that return credentials, including storage account keys, App Service settings, connection strings and publishing credentials, AI and machine learning (ML) connections and datastores, and Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) user credentials. The compromised applications subsequently accessed SharePoint and OneDrive in the targeted organization tenants, including file downloads and mailbox-item access. In some tenants, the threat actor sent Microsoft Graph API requests, which were mostly searches to find content of interest. The threat actor enumerated subscriptions, resource groups, permissions, AI model deployments, and service configurations in Azure to map the environment.

Additionally, the threat actor attempted to validate stolen Azure resources, including compromised Azure AI services, as identified using Defender for Cloud’s AI threat protection. Observed activity suggests that the threat actor might have attempted to abuse some of these compromised AI resources to facilitate their broader attack activity.

Figure 1. Tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) observed across the credential abuse attack chain

Cloud API adjustments indicative of adaptive behavior

Additionally in this attack the agent’s operations on a victim’s Azure Resource Manager (ARM) instance originating from 199.19.77[.]84 demonstrated sequences consistent with adaptive troubleshooting, where failed cloud API requests were followed by changes to HTTP methods or API versions and subsequent HTTP 200 responses:

A batch of ARM requests attempting to enumerate secret metadata across multiple Azure Key Vault resources returned HTTP 400 (Bad Request). These requests specified a version associated with Key Vault’s data-plane APIs against ARM (control-plane) APIs. Approximately 28 seconds after the first failed response, a batch rerun began against the same vault resource paths using the ARM API version 2023-07-01 and returned HTTP 200.

A GET request to enumerate an Azure SQL server’s firewall rules specified an outdated API version and returned HTTP 400. Approximately 60 seconds after that request, a matching GET began using a supported version and subsequently returned HTTP 200. The URL changed only in its api-version parameter.

An ARM POST request to an Application Insights query endpoint returned HTTP 400 because an outdated API version was specified. Approximately 80 seconds after the failed request, another POST began against the same endpoint, specifying a supported API version, and subsequently returned HTTP 200.

OAuth application abuse

In multiple cases, Microsoft observed the same agentic AI tools subsequently obtain a token for a  single-tenant OAuth application  in the same target organization, then use the compromised OAuth application to enumerate other cloud resources within the organization. In some cases, the agents exfiltrated secrets from the organization’s Azure Key Vault. The agents once authenticated have also searched Azure DevOps for secrets. Until the secrets are revoked or rotated, they can allow a threat actor to maintain persistence in the organization, compromise additional identities, or hijack resources. In one observed case, an AI agent progressed from searching for the client secrets in GitHub to exfiltrating data from Azure Key Vault in five minutes.

The agents also used the compromised OAuth application to use the  Run Command , which runs scripts in Azure VMs. With access to this functionality on a VM, a threat actor can access unsecured credentials and other stored data, compromise associated workload identities, or run code that provides persistence or lateral movement.

During this activity, the AI agents repeatedly demonstrated a focus on credentials that provide access to AI services, such as API keys for major AI service providers and OAuth applications with access to Foundry Tools (previously known as Azure Cognitive Services). Multiple public reports have documented threat actors using agentic AI tools to compromise credentials for AI services, sometimes to run the same agentic AI workflow.

Mitigating application credential abuse activity

Microsoft recommends the following mitigation steps to contain, detect, and investigate this threat.

Containment

Block 199.19.77[.]84/32 as a named location in a Conditional Access policy targeting workload identities, assigned directly to service principals, and in a user-scoped block policy to cover replayed sessions. Note that workload identity policies require Workload ID Premium licensing and cover only single-tenant apps registered in your tenant. Block the exact IP rather than the whole ASN.

For affected users, revoke Entra sessions, Azure DevOps PATs and SSH keys.

For any affected application, remove all client secrets, certificates and federated credentials, including those added by the threat actor and disable the service principal if needed. Tokens already issued remain valid until expiry.

Rotate everything stored in any Key Vault the affected application could read, and any credentials found in accessed documents.

MSPs: Review Partner Center access, GDAP relationships, and customer tenants, and notify affected customers per your agreements.

Detection and hunting

Review Entra service principal and non-interactive sign-in logs for 199.19.77[.]84 and 199.19.77[.]18 including failed attempts. Sign-in errors AADSTS7000215 (invalid secret) or AADSTS7000222 (expired secret) indicate someone holds a credential for your app; a failure followed by a success is urgent.

Review Azure Activity, Key Vault and Storage diagnostics, Entra audit, Azure DevOps audit and Microsoft 365 unified audit logs for the address, including secret reads, blob and file downloads, and changes to apps, permissions or pipelines.

In Azure DevOps auditing, review PAT creation and first use, federated service connections, pipeline runs and edits, and unfamiliar user agents. Enable auditing if it is off.

Look for behavior as well as the IP: one address authenticating to three or more service principals with mixed success, or one app requesting tokens across Azure Resource Manager, Key Vault, Storage and Graph in a short window. Search as far back as retention allows.

Defending against agentic AI attacks

Threat actors can and do change the source IP address, user agent strings, and other fingerprints left by the agentic AI penetration testing tools they use. This can make identifying and blocking malicious network traffic early difficult for defenders.

Several behavioral signals can help organizations determine that they are being targeted by threat actors using agentic AI. Agentic AI frameworks scanning a target send a wide variety of requests in a brief time and retry variations on the same technique or move on to next-stage actions at machine speed. Agentic AI frameworks use existing penetration testing tools. For example, ARTEX by default uses Nmap, curl, wget, Python HTTP clients, Norma SDK WebFetch, and headless Chromium through Playwright, among others. These tools may send network traffic with distinctive characteristics, such as default user agent strings. While blocking network traffic with these characteristics will not stop an attack by an AI agent, which will quickly change them, identifying them can alert defenders to the activity.

Defensive honeypots , decoys, tarpits, and fake wins can pull autonomous AI attacks away from legitimate targets. Honeypots and decoy surfaces such as  Microsoft Sentinel Deception  give the agent attractive but worthless targets to pursue. Tarpits consume the agent’s time and budget. Fake wins present convincing evidence that the agent’s objective is complete, which can cause it to stop on a false success. In Microsoft’s testing, these controls helped reduce the attack traffic reaching real assets and produced high-confidence, attribution-quality signal.

Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat.

Protect and continuously assess application credentials and secrets. Avoid storing service principal credentials, storage keys, connection strings, and other secrets in source code, configuration files, public repositories, issues, or other locations where they might be inadvertently exposed. To find credentials in source code, consider using tools like  GitHub Advanced Security  or other  OWASP source code analysis tools .

Rotate compromised or exposed credentials immediately and establish credential lifecycle practices. Treat credentials that have been publicly exposed as compromised, even if the original location has subsequently been edited or deleted. Removing the content does not invalidate the credential or eliminate copies retained in edit history, caches, archives, logs, or other systems. Immediately revoke or rotate the affected credentials and investigate their historical use. Where supported, organizations should favor mechanisms that reduce reliance on long-lived credentials. Learn more about  protecting secrets with Defender for Cloud .

Enable appropriate Microsoft Defender for Cloud plans for critical Azure workloads. Consider enabling workload protections relevant to the resources in your environment, including Defender for Resource Manager, Defender for Storage, Defender for Key Vault, Defender for App Service, and Defender for Databases. Learn more in the  Microsoft Defender for Cloud overview .

Apply least privilege to service principals and other workload identities. Review the Azure role-based access control (RBAC) permissions assigned to service principals and restrict their privileges to the resources and operations required by their applications. Learn more about  best practices for Azure RBAC .

Protect backup and recovery infrastructure as part of resilience. Restrict access to backup and recovery resources and closely monitor attempts to modify or remove their protection controls. Learn more about  Azure Backup security best practices .

Hardening OAuth applications against compromise involves managing the permissions of the applications in your organization and securing application secrets. To triage applications in your environment, enforce security policies with new applications as they are created, and address existing applications over time beginning with the most recent ones.

Identify and catalog applications running in your cloud environment. The  Cloud app catalog  page in Defender for Cloud Apps is one service that can help accomplish this.

Use Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps  Cloud Discovery  tools to identify unmanaged apps, and prioritize the most frequently used apps to migrate and integrate.

Use  Conditional Access policies for workload identities . Consider augmenting identity signals with  workload identity risk protection .

Set permission restrictions to limit who can create an application in the tenant. This can be achieved by setting the ability for users to register apps to “No” and limiting the  application developer  role to privileged users.
