On October 29, 2026, Cursor reported that a tampered copy of Claude Code extension (anthropic.claude-code, versions 2.1.313 and 2.1.312) was available and served in the Cursor extension marketplace for a few hours to attempt a supply-chain attack on Cursor users. Cursor reports that it was live from about 2:27 AM to 1:35 PM Pacific Daylight Time (PDT). We have confirmed that the malicious packages found on Cursor marketplace were never published nor distributed from Microsoft Visual Studio Marketplace and from npm @anthropic-ai/claude-code, which were not affected by this incident. Anthropic confirmed to Microsoft that their systems were not compromised and they did not develop the malicious package posted in Cursor marketplace. At this time, all evidence suggests that the incident is limited to Cursor marketplace.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence analyzed the injected JavaScript embedded in the malicious extension package. The injected loader runs when the extension module loads and attempts to add an attacker-controlled Secure Shell (SSH) key, enable the local SSH service, establish reverse SSH forwarding, configure persistence, and report host details. Successful remote access depends on host privileges, SSH configuration, and the attacker’s server configuration; however, the loader may still write keys and persistence artifacts even when tunnel access fails.

Organizations should identify systems that installed or automatically updated to this version from the Cursor marketplace, preserve evidence, remove confirmed malicious artifacts, review endpoint and network telemetry, and rotate credentials or revoke sessions when investigation indicates exposure. Microsoft customers can use the detections and hunting guidance in this post after the listed coverage and query validation gates are complete.

Attack chain overview

A malicious artifact associated with the Cursor Marketplace incident included a JavaScript function that executed before the extension’s expected code. When the module loads, this function can use Node.js APIs to collect host information, modify files, and execute operating-system commands. The following sections describe capabilities and attempted actions based on our analysis of the injected code.

Attack chain

The loader first collects host reconnaissance. It then attempts to install an SSH key, enable SSH, create a reverse tunnel, and configure persistence. A delayed callback subsequently attempts to send host details. The following sequence reflects code execution order; it does not prove that every step succeeded on every host.

Module loading and reconnaissance collection.  The injected function executes before normal extension initialization and collects host and user information.

SSH access preparation.  The loader appends an embedded public key and attempts to enable the local SSH service.

Reverse forwarding.  An embedded tunnel identity authenticates an outbound connection that requests forwarding to the workstation’s SSH port.

Platform-specific persistence.  Scripts and startup configuration are written to relaunch the connection.

Host reconnaissance reporting.  After the access and persistence setup attempts, a delayed callback attempts to transmit the previously collected host details and selected environment-variable names.

Figure 1. Attack chain reconstructed from the injected code.

The loader uses embedded components and built-in system tools to establish persistent access without downloading another executable. It suppresses command output and silently catches errors to conceal failures and malicious activity, while the extension continues functioning normally to avoid alerting users.

Host reconnaissance collection

The loader collects the hostname, username, operating system, architecture, home directory, working directory, and global Git email. It also looks for environment-variable names containing terms such as  KEY, TOKEN, SECRET, PASS, AWS, or GCP,  keeping up to forty matches.

The callback sends matching environment-variable names, not values. This reveals potentially sensitive configuration categories but does not demonstrate theft of the secrets stored in those variables.

Collection occurs during module loading. The collected details are retained for the delayed reporting callback described after the persistence stage.

SSH authorization and tunnel identities

The loader uses two SSH identities with distinct roles. One public key authorizes access to the workstation’s user account, while a separate private key authenticates the outbound connection to the tunnel server. First, the loader checks the user’s authorized_keys file for the comment svc-telemetry. If the marker is missing, it appends an embedded Ed25519 public key. That creates an authorization entry for whoever holds the corresponding private key, subject to the local SSH server’s configuration.

Next, it decodes a separate private key for the outbound connection. The initial copy is written to a hidden temporary file named .stk_ followed by ten hexadecimal characters derived from the hostname and home directory. SSH receives that file through its -i option and connects using the remote account tunnel.

The public-key material is redacted but the format is similar to the following:

ssh-ed25519 [REDACTED PUBLIC KEY] svc-telemetry

Protocol Tunneling (T1572): reverse SSH forwarding

The tunneling SSH process is launched with the command line containing the following arguments:

-N -R '*:0:localhost:22'

It requests a listening port on the remote SSH server and forwards connections through the tunnel to port 22 on the victim’s loopback interface. The remote port value 0 asks the server to allocate a port; it does not change the local target from port 22. The -N option tells SSH not to run a command on the tunnel server.

This design starts with an outbound connection from the workstation rather than waiting for a direct inbound connection to it. The loader disables ordinary host-key checking, bypasses the normal known-hosts file, sets keepalives, and avoids interactive prompts. On Unix-like systems it prefers autossh, falling back to ssh; on Windows it uses a hidden PowerShell loop. The loops wait sixty seconds after SSH exits before retrying.

Figure 2. Terminal-style SSH command configuring an outbound reverse tunnel from a server-assigned remote port to the workstation’s local SSH service on port 22. Host-key verification is disabled, and the identity-file path is redacted.

A running SSH process does not necessarily mean the attacker gained access. Both the attacker’s server and the victim’s workstation must allow the connection, and server settings determine whether the tunnel is publicly reachable. Cursor reports that errors and administrator-permission requirements blocked SSH access on most macOS and Windows hosts. However, the malware could still attempt to plant its SSH key, establish persistence, and report host information.

Platform-specific startup persistence

The loader writes platform-specific scripts and startup configuration outside the extension directory. The following table summarizes these mechanisms and their associated artifacts. The code attempts to configure persistence, but the presence of an artifact alone does not establish that the startup mechanism ran successfully.

Platform    Startup mechanism    Key artifacts     macOS  User LaunchAgent with RunAtLoad and KeepAlive  ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist, ~/.config/.smt,

~/.config/.smtk    Linux  User-crontab @reboot entry  ~/.config/.smt, ~/.config/.smtk    Windows  Attempted SysMon scheduled task requesting SYSTEM execution  %USERPROFILE%\.config\smt.cmd, %USERPROFILE%\.config\smtk    Windows fallback  Batch file in the user’s Startup folder  %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\sysmon.cmd

On Unix-like systems, the .smt script reconstructs the persistent .smtk identity when it runs, then starts its own SSH retry loop. On Windows, the loader writes the identity and batch script directly.

The startup objects use names such as SysMon and com.apple.sysmond, which resemble monitoring components. Behind these names, their configured actions invoke the generated scripts that maintain reverse SSH forwarding.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Immediate actions

Run advanced hunting queries below to identify affected systems and investigate systems where users installed or automatically updated anthropic.claude-code version 2.1.313 and 2.1.312 through the Cursor Extension Marketplace. Review extension-installation records and correlate endpoint, network, file, process, and authentication telemetry with the published indicators. Preserve the extension package, modified SSH authorization files, generated keys and scripts, and startup configuration before cleanup. Isolate devices with evidence of loader execution or backdoor installation.

Remediation actions

After evidence collection, check the affected user’s ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on macOS and Linux for the attacker-controlled key labeled svc-telemetry. On Windows, check both %USERPROFILE%\.ssh\authorized_keys and C:\ProgramData\ssh\administrators_authorized_keys, where present. Confirm the key against the fingerprint in Indicators of Compromise before removing the exact unauthorized entry. Preserve unrelated SSH keys and legitimate remote-development configuration. A missing marker alone should not replace review of the installation, process, network, and persistence evidence.

Remove the trojanized extension and confirmed malicious persistence after evidence collection. Inspect each startup object’s configured action before removal; names alone are not sufficient to distinguish malicious objects from legitimate monitoring software.

macOS:  Unload and remove the malicious user LaunchAgent at ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist and remove its associated ~/.config/.smt script and ~/.config/.smtk identity.

Linux:  Remove the malicious user-crontab @reboot entry referencing ~/.config/.smt, preserving unrelated entries, and remove the associated script and ~/.config/.smtk identity.

Windows:  Remove the malicious SysMon scheduled task, the Startup-folder sysmon.cmd fallback, and associated %USERPROFILE%\.config\smt.cmd and %USERPROFILE%\.config\smtk files.

All applicable platforms:  Stop confirmed malicious SSH and retry processes and remove their temporary .stk_ identity files after collection.

Cursor published platform-specific checks and remediation scripts in its  security notice . Review the scripts and execution requirements before use, then verify that no listed artifacts remain. Cleanup does not replace investigation of device activity during the exposure window.

Removing or updating the extension does not remove artifacts written outside its installation directory. Remove confirmed unauthorized SSH keys, tunnel identities, scripts, and startup entries separately. Cursor’s reported server takedown does not remove artifacts already present on a device.

Follow-up Investigation and recovery

Review telemetry after the extension loaded for SSH key acceptance, tunnel processes, local SSH sessions, command execution, and file activity. Rotate credentials and revoke sessions from a known-clean device when telemetry indicates credential access or when device trust cannot be restored. Rebuild the device when required by the investigation and verify that the tunnel and startup artifacts do not return after login or restart.

To reduce the risk of malicious extensions and extension-based supply chain attacks, organizations using Cursor should apply the relevant controls in  Cursor’s security-hardening guidance , including restricting extensions to approved publishers and configuring an extension installation cooldown to delay installation of newly published versions. These measures can help limit exposure to malicious releases.

Microsoft Defender XDR detections

Microsoft Defender XDR customers can refer to the list of applicable detections below. Microsoft Defender XDR coordinates detection, prevention, investigation, and response across endpoints, identities, email, and apps to provide integrated protection against attacks like the threat discussed in this blog.

Customers with provisioned access can also use  Microsoft Security Copilot in Microsoft Defender  to investigate and respond to incidents, hunt for threats, and protect their organization with relevant threat intelligence.

Threat intelligence reports

Microsoft customers can use the following reports in Microsoft products to get the most up-to-date information about the threat actor, malicious activity, and techniques discussed in this blog. These reports provide intelligence, protection information, and recommended actions to prevent, mitigate, or respond to associated threats found in customer environments.

Microsoft Defender XDR Threat analytics

Activity Profile: Malicious Claude Code branded extension v2.1.313 contains a persistent SSH backdoor

Advanced hunting queries

The following queries use the Microsoft Defender XDR advanced hunting schema and the time range selected in the portal. A result is an investigative lead, not proof of compromise.

Connections to the reported infrastructure

Find network events involving the reported IP address during the last 30 days, including the process responsible for each connection.

or RemoteUrl has "134.209.82.225"

Find file events matching the reported SHA-256 hash, artifact filenames, or filename prefix during the last 30 days. Filename matches are hunting leads and require investigation.

".smt",

Possible Windows scheduled-task persistence

Find scheduled-task creation events whose additional fields contain both reported terms, SysMon and smt, during the last 30 days.

MITRE ATT&CK techniques

The following mappings describe behaviors implemented or attempted by the analyzed loader, not confirmed execution on every affected host. They do not establish attribution to a particular threat actor.

T1572 – Protocol Tunneling   Requests reverse SSH forwarding to the workstation’s local SSH service.     T1053.003 – Cron   Attempts a Linux user-crontab @reboot entry.     T1053.005 – Scheduled Task   Attempts a Windows startup task requesting SYSTEM execution.

Indicators of compromise (IOCs)

The following indicators are associated with the publicly analyzed JavaScript sample. The remote address is defanged. Contextual strings and paths require behavioral correlation and should not be treated as conclusive evidence of compromise on their own.

article_content:
In this article

Activity overview

Attack chain overview

Portable runtime staging and execution variants

Host discovery and AD CS assessment

Case 1: ESC1 abuse and the cost of an identity exclusion

Case 2: PetitPotam and ESC8 turn a workstation into a domain-controller identity

Why the response outcomes differed

Actionable investigation methods

References

Learn More

Microsoft Threat Intelligence investigated two human-operated intrusions in which threat actors used Microsoft Teams messages and calls to impersonate IT or help desk personnel and socially engineer users into granting interactive remote access, primarily through Quick Assist. Once connected, the threat actors staged portable Python, Bun, or Java runtimes, performed host and network discovery, and assessed Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) for certificate-based authentication paths.

Although the incidents began with the same social-engineering and remote-access pattern, they diverged at the certificate layer. In Case 1, the threat actor abused an Enterprise CA Security Configuration 1 (ESC1) -vulnerable certificate template to obtain authentication certificates for privileged accounts and performed DCSync. In Case 2, the threat actor used PetitPotam, a technique that causes a Windows server to authenticate to an attacker-controlled system. The attacker relayed the domain controller’s New Technology (NT) LAN Manager (NTLM) authentication to AD CS Web Enrollment (ESC8), obtained a certificate for the domain-controller account, and used it for certificate-based Kerberos authentication (PKINIT – Public Key Cryptography for Initial Authentication).

This intrusion pattern is high impact because a user-approved remote session can become certificate-backed access to privileged identities and domain infrastructure. In Case 1, Microsoft Defender attack disruption restricted covered identities and blocked substantial follow-on activity, but a privileged identity excluded from automated containment remained usable and later supported data exfiltration. In Case 2, Defender generated ESC8-related alerts, after which the customer isolated the associated workstation and no further progression was observed. The activity did not exploit a vulnerability in Microsoft Teams; instead, it relied on social engineering and insecure or overly permissive AD CS configurations.

In this blog, we analyze the shared attack chain, the ESC1 and ESC8 certificate-abuse paths, and the different response outcomes. We also provide investigation methods, mitigation recommendations, Microsoft Defender detection guidance, and advanced hunting queries to help defenders identify and interrupt this access path. The activity described here is not attributed to a specific threat actor.

Activity overview

Risk to enterprise environments

AD CS can turn a certificate request into a durable authentication path. An attacker who obtains an authentication certificate for a privileged user or machine account can use that certificate independently of the initially compromised password. Resetting the user’s password or reimaging the first workstation does not revoke an issued certificate or invalidate Kerberos tickets that have already been issued.

Two AD CS abuse techniques are central to these incidents:

ESC1 – certificate template abuse:  A low-privileged requester abuses a misconfigured authentication-capable template that permits requester-supplied identity information and broad enrollment, allowing the requester to obtain a certificate for a privileged account.

ESC8 – NTLM relay to Web Enrollment:  An attacker relays a user or machine account’s NTLM authentication to an AD CS web enrollment endpoint that lacks relay protections, then requests a certificate as the relayed identity.

Attackers can use Microsoft Teams to impersonate IT support personnel and persuade users to approve a remote session, gaining hands-on-keyboard access without a conventional malware attachment.

Portable or renamed runtimes such as Python, Bun, and Java can execute attacker-controlled scripts from user-writable locations while retaining legitimate file metadata.

Automated disruption is most effective when every compromised identity and device remains eligible for containment; exclusions can preserve the attacker’s path.

Attack chain overview

Both incidents followed the same initial sequence: help desk impersonation through Teams, a user-approved Quick Assist or other remote-support session, archive transfer and extraction, portable runtime execution, and host and AD CS discovery. The certificate technique and response outcome then split into two distinct branches.

Figure 1. Both incidents followed a shared entry and execution pattern before diverging into two AD CS abuse paths. Case 1 used an ESC1-vulnerable certificate template to obtain certificates for privileged identities. Case 2 used PetitPotam to coerce domain-controller authentication and relay it to AD CS Web Enrollment through ESC8. The response outcomes differed based on containment coverage and removal of the active execution point.

Shared initial access and execution pattern

Teams helpdesk impersonation and remote access

Both incidents began with Teams phishing messages and calls that impersonated support personnel. The social engineering  persuaded a user to establish an attacker-controlled remote session , primarily by guiding the user to open Quick Assist and provide the connection code. This gave the attacker hands-on-keyboard access to the workstation. Across the broader activity, organization-themed onmicrosoft.com tenant names and support-oriented display names were used to make the external contact appear familiar.

Figure 2. Example Teams call displaying External and Scam suspected indicators. These labels are important user-facing signals during support impersonation attempts.

The remote session was the decisive transition in the attack. Immediately after the user granted control through Quick Assist, the attacker used the session to place an archive in the victim’s Downloads folder. Commands launched during the session created a KB-prefixed staging directory under the user’s profile, extracted the archive into that directory, and started the included payload with a portable Python, JavaScript, or Java runtime. The payload then performed host and network discovery and began assessing AD CS.

Portable runtime staging and execution variants

The runtime and packaging varied between deployments, but the execution pattern remained consistent: an archive was placed on the device during the remote session, extracted into a newly created user-profile directory, and used to launch attacker-controlled code. In one JavaScript variant, a renamed executable retained version metadata identifying it as the Bun runtime and launched the staged loader. A separate variant used a staged Java runtime to launch a Java source file.

Figure 3. Sanitized Bun staging command. The update-themed path, renamed runtime, script operand, and remote-session context form the useful investigation pattern.

File names alone are weak indicators. The actionable pattern is a portable runtime launched from a newly created, user-writable staging directory after an unauthorized remote session, followed by script execution, discovery commands, or connections to identity infrastructure.

Figure 4. Sanitized Java staging variant. The campaign could substitute runtime and packaging choices while keeping the broader access pattern.

The Java variant confirms that runtime choice can change between deployments. The AD CS behavior in each incident should be validated through the initiating process, account, device, and certificate records rather than assumed from the presence of Bun or Java alone.

Host discovery and AD CS assessment

The staged components queried Windows version information, network configuration, and running processes. These commands are common in administration, but they become high-value signals when it is launched by a renamed runtime from an uncommon location and follow an unexpected remote-support session.

Figure 5. Host-discovery commands from the first draft. Their value comes from the initiating staged runtime, user-writable path, and preceding unauthorized remote session.

The compromised workstation also connected to domain infrastructure using LDAPS and SMB.

From this shared workstation foothold, the incidents followed different certificate-abuse paths. In Case 1, the attacker exploited an ESC1-vulnerable certificate template. In Case 2, the attacker used PetitPotam to coerce domain-controller authentication and relay it to AD CS Web Enrollment through ESC8.

Case 1: ESC1 abuse and the cost of an identity exclusion

ESC1 certificate requests expand privilege

The first Teams-phishing wave targeted three user accounts and compromised one workstation. From the shared foothold described above, the attacker examined AD CS for a privilege-escalation path.

Figure 6. Case 1: Help desk impersonation led to ESC1 certificate abuse. Attack disruption restricted most compromised identities, but an excluded privileged account remained usable and later supported data exfiltration.

The attacker found a certificate template vulnerable to ESC1. ESC1 describes a template configuration in which a requester can supply identity information in the certificate request and obtain a certificate that supports authentication. When broad enrollment rights and weak issuance controls are combined with that setting, a low-privileged account can request a certificate representing a privileged identity.

In the first wave, the attacker obtained certificates for three highly privileged accounts. Microsoft Defender attack disruption targeted the initially compromised user and those three certificate-compromised identities. Remote logons and Server Message Block (SMB) access were restricted and active sessions were disconnected. One privileged account was excluded from automated response, so containment did not apply to that identity.

Renewed phishing and ESC1 privilege expansion

About 90 minutes after the first disrupted session, the attacker launched a larger Teams-phishing wave targeting 16 users and compromised another workstation. The attacker again abused the ESC1-vulnerable template, this time obtaining certificates for eight additional privileged accounts.

Attack disruption targeted the newly compromised user and the eight certificate-compromised identities. More than 1,000 subsequent SMB file-access attempts and additional logon attempts were blocked, limiting the attacker’s ability to reuse those accounts for lateral movement.

DCSync, the excluded account, and data theft

Within seconds of obtaining one privileged certificate, the attacker authenticated to a domain controller and performed DCSync while containment was taking effect. Attack disruption limited additional replication and follow-on use, but the operation had already begun.

The privileged account excluded during the first disruption remained available. The attacker continued to use it for network and remote-interactive logons, reached a file server, and launched a renamed copy of Rclone using the filename SearchApp.exe. The command recursively copied data from a file-server share to an external Secure File Transfer Protocol (SFTP) destination, used 20 concurrent transfers, selected files up to three years old, and excluded several executable, database, virtual-disk, media, temporary, and log file types.

Figure 7. Sanitized Rclone command used to copy data from a file-server share to an external SFTP destination.

The incident demonstrates that partial identity containment can reduce attack activity while still leaving a viable privileged route.

Case 2: PetitPotam and ESC8 turn a workstation into a domain-controller identity

PetitPotam coerces domain-controller authentication

The ESC1 path used in the first case was not available in this environment. Instead, the attacker used PetitPotam to send requests over the Encrypting File System Remote Protocol (EFSRPC), causing the domain controller to authenticate to an attacker-controlled system using its machine account. The attacker then relayed that NTLM authentication to AD CS Web Enrollment without knowing the domain controller’s password.

Figure 8. Case 2: Help desk impersonation led to PetitPotam authentication coercion, ESC8 relay to AD CS, certificate-based Kerberos authentication, and customer-led device isolation.

NTLM relay reaches AD CS Web Enrollment

The attacker relayed the domain controller’s NTLM authentication to AD CS Web Enrollment. This technique is known as ESC8. It targets an enrollment web endpoint that accepts NTLM without sufficient relay protection, allowing the attacker to submit a certificate request as the relayed account.

The AD CS server authenticated the domain-controller machine account even though the connection originated from another device. That identity-to-source mismatch is a strong investigation pivot: correlate the machine account, source device, Web Enrollment request, Certification Authority (CA) issuance record, and subsequent Kerberos activity.

After authenticating to Web Enrollment as the domain controller, the attacker requested and retrieved a certificate using the Domain Controller template. The important service paths are the certificate submission and retrieval endpoints under /certsrv; isolated URL access is not malicious by itself and must be correlated with the authenticated identity, source device, process, and CA request.

Figure 9. Sanitized view of AD CS Web Enrollment activity involving certificate submission and retrieval through /certsrv, used during ESC8 certificate issuance for a relayed domain-controller identity.

Certificate-based Kerberos authentication

The attacker used the newly issued domain-controller certificate for Kerberos PKINIT and obtained a ticket-granting ticket (TGT) for the domain controller. This step converted a relayed NTLM authentication into a certificate-backed Kerberos identity.

PKINIT success is the response threshold: responders should investigate the requesting device, authenticated account, issued certificate, active Kerberos sessions, and any service-ticket use. Certificate revocation and Kerberos ticket review are separate containment actions.

Customer-led device isolation and observed outcome

Microsoft Defender generated ESC8-related alerts, after which the customer isolated the workstation associated with the certificate-enrollment and Kerberos activity. The documented containment action in this case was customer-led device isolation. No further attack progression was observed following isolation.

Why the response outcomes differed

In Case 1, an exclusion left a compromised privileged account available to the attacker despite disruption of other identities. In Case 2, customer-led device isolation followed Defender alerts, and no further attack progression was observed.

Response element    Case 1: ESC1    Case 2: ESC8     Response mechanism  Microsoft Defender automated attack disruption targeting compromised identities.  Microsoft Defender alerts followed by customer-led device isolation.    Measured effect  Covered identities were restricted; more than 1,000 SMB attempts and additional logons were blocked; further DCSync activity was limited.  The workstation associated with certificate enrollment and Kerberos activity was isolated.    Containment follow-up  One privileged account was excluded from automated response and remained available to the attacker.  No further progression was observed after isolation;    Observed outcome  The excluded identity was later used for file-server access and data exfiltration.  No subsequent attack progression was documented after customer isolation.

Actionable investigation methods

The most useful artifacts are not individual commands or ports in isolation. Investigators should reconstruct the chain across collaboration, endpoint, identity, and certificate systems.

Teams and remote access:  identify the external tenant, user interaction, call or chat timing, remote-session start, approved remote monitoring and management (RMM) process, and child processes created during the session.

Runtime staging:  inspect newly created KB-prefixed or application-like folders, archive extraction, runtime metadata, script operands, parent-child relationships, and subsequent network activity.

Directory interaction:  use network data to identify LDAPS and SMB connections, then use endpoint and directory logs to determine what the initiating process did. TLS intentionally hides LDAP query content from passive network inspection.

ESC1:  review certificate request and issuance events, requester identity, subject and Subject Alternative Names (SAN) values, template name, enrollment permissions, and the first authentication performed with the issued certificate.

PetitPotam and ESC8:  correlate EFSRPC activity, outbound authentication by the domain controller, the device that relayed the authentication, Web Enrollment access, CA request and issuance records, and PKINIT from the originating workstation.

Disruption and containment:  enumerate every compromised identity and device, review exclusions before and during response, revoke unauthorized certificates, and assess active Kerberos tickets separately

Reduce support impersonation and unauthorized remote access

Require users to verify unsolicited support requests through a known internal channel before joining a call, sharing a screen, or starting a remote-control session.

Encourage users to pay attention to warnings in incoming messages and calls when impersonation is detected.

Review Teams external-access and federation policies. Limit external domains to business requirements and investigate newly observed organization-themed or helpdesk-themed tenants in context.

Restrict remote-support software to approved products, operators, and workflows. Alert when approved RMM tools extract archives, create interpreters, or launch scripts from user-writable paths.

Constrain runtime-based execution

Use App Control for Business or equivalent application control to restrict unapproved portable runtimes and script execution from user-writable locations.

Evaluate file identity through signer, original filename, product metadata, path, parent process, and behavior. A renamed executable can retain legitimate version information.

Test relevant attack surface reduction rules and endpoint protection policies. Do not assume controls for Windows script hosts automatically cover JavaScript executed through Bun or source files launched through Java.

Harden AD CS against ESC1 and ESC8

Follow Microsoft’s secure configuration guidance for mitigating NTLM relay against AD CS:  https://support.microsoft.com/help/5005413

Review authentication-capable templates for requester-supplied subject information, broad enrollment permissions, weak issuance requirements, and excessive certificate purpose. Remove unnecessary enrollment rights and require approval where appropriate.

Inventory AD CS Web Enrollment and Certificate Enrollment Web Service endpoints. Remove endpoints that are not required.

Require HTTPS and enforce Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA) on enrollment web endpoints. HTTPS protects confidentiality; EPA provides the channel binding needed to resist NTLM relay.

Disable NTLM on enrollment services where operationally feasible and validate Kerberos-only authentication before broad enforcement.

Use Defender for Identity AD CS security posture assessments to identify ESC1-related template exposure and insecure enrollment Internet Information Services (IIS) endpoints associated with ESC8:  https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-for-identity/security-posture-assessments/certificates

Enable certificate auditing and prepare certificate-aware response

Enable the Certification Services advanced audit subcategory for success and failure, and configure the Certification Authority audit filter to record request and issuance activity.

Preserve CA security events, CA database records, IIS or Web Enrollment logs, endpoint process lineage, identity alerts, and Teams interaction records.

If an unauthorized certificate was issued, identify its serial number and thumbprint, revoke it, publish updated revocation information, and confirm that relying systems can obtain the update.

Review certificate-based Kerberos activity and active tickets. Revoking a certificate does not retroactively invalidate TGTs or service tickets that were already issued.

Treat containment exclusions as incident decisions. If an account or device cannot be automatically contained, assign a compensating manual action and verify completion.

This threat has exhibited use of the following attack techniques. For standard industry documentation, refer to the MITRE ATT&CK framework.

Initial Access

T1566.003 Phishing: Spearphishing via Service  | Teams messages used for support impersonation.

T1566.004 Phishing: Spearphishing Voice  | A Teams call formed part of the social-engineering interaction.

Command and Control

T1219 Remote Access Software  | An attacker-controlled remote monitoring and management session provided interactive access.

Execution

T1059.003 Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell  | Shell commands staged archives, launched the runtime, and initiated native discovery commands.

T1059.007 Command and Scripting Interpreter: JavaScript/JScript  | Bun executed attacker-supplied JavaScript modules.

Defense Evasion

T1036 Masquerading  | The activity used update-themed staging and a renamed Bun executable.

Discovery

T1082 System Information Discovery  | The runtime initiated a Windows version registry query.

T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery  | The runtime initiated ipconfig /all.

T1057 Process Discovery  | The runtime initiated tasklist.

Credential Access

T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle  | Certificate authority telemetry showed a domain-controller identity authenticating from another device, supporting NTLM relay; no name-resolution poisoning was established.

T1649 Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates  | The activity involved abusive machine-certificate issuance through Certificate Services Web Enrollment and subsequent certificate-based authentication.

article_content:
New-age tech stocks extended their rally this week, with 54 of the 69 companies under Inc42’s coverage posting gains ranging from 0.4% to 23.3%.

CarTrade led the gainers, rebounding 23.3% after last week’s steep decline to close at ₹2,699.30. Awfis followed with a 20.4% rise to ₹281.65, while ixigo climbed 19.1%.

Recently listed Tonbo Imaging and Zetwerk touched fresh highs during the week. Lenskart, Ather Energy, Eternal, and Nykaa were also among the stocks that hit 52-week highs.

The gains lifted the combined market capitalisation of the 69 companies to $169.3 Bn from $160.9 Bn last week, an increase of 5.2%.

Among the losers, RateGain fell the highest by 9.19% to close the week at ₹725.90.

Here are some key developments from listed new-age tech companies during the week:

Kissht’s AUM Crosses ₹10,000 Cr:   Kissht’s assets under management (AUM) crossed ₹10,000 Cr, driven by growth in personal loans and its expansion into loans against property. The company attributed the growth to its AI-led underwriting and digital collections infrastructure, adding that its recent ₹832.2 Cr preferential issue strengthened its capital base.

MobiKwik Secures NBFC Licence   :   MobiKwik received an RBI licence to operate as an NBFC, following in-principle approval in April 2026. It plans to begin operations within three to six months and disburse ₹5,000 Cr in consumer and MSME loans over three to four years through an asset-light co-lending model.

Pine Labs Partners With Stripe   :   Pine Labs partnered with Stripe to offer Singapore retailers a unified platform for online and in-store payments, combining Stripe’s online infrastructure with Pine Labs’ terminals and merchant tools. The companies plan to expand the offering to other Southeast Asian markets in 2027. Pine Labs served 11.6 Lakh merchants across more than 22 markets at the end of Q2 FY27.

Here’s a look at the performance of the broader markets this week.

Benchmarks Jump Over 8%

Indian equities recorded a sharp weekly recovery, with the Nifty 50 gaining 8.6%, or 1,977 points, to close at 25,030.35. The Sensex rose 8.8%, or 6,568 points, to 81,028.02. Both benchmarks advanced in all five sessions, with the Nifty ending at its weekly high.

The broader market’s gains were smaller, with the Nifty Midcap 100 and Nifty Smallcap 100 rising 5.8% and 2.8%, respectively.

Renewed foreign investor buying, strong Q2 FY27 earnings, easing geopolitical concerns, and lower crude oil prices supported sentiment. Lower bond yields and a softer dollar also helped.

Foreign institutional investors (FIIs) bought a net ₹45,960 Cr of equities across the five sessions, marking their second consecutive week of buying after a 10-week selling streak. The inflows exceeded the ₹45,162 Cr they sold during October.

Domestic institutional investors (DIIs) sold a net ₹24,197 Cr, ending an 11-week buying streak. Together, the two investor groups remained net buyers of approximately ₹21,763 Cr.

Geojit Investments’ head of research Vinod Nair attributed the improved sentiment to strong Q2 earnings, healthy October auto sales, and firm GST collections, alongside easing concerns around the Iran conflict and tariffs following the US midterm election verdict.

He also pointed to foreign investors rotating out of crowded AI trades. The Indian market’s rally coincided with a selloff in global AI and semiconductor stocks.

Private banks led the gains following renewed foreign investor interest in a segment previously weighed down by concerns over net interest margins. Automobile and consumption stocks benefited from festive demand, while IT and PSU banks recorded relatively modest gains.

The sustainability of foreign inflows, crude oil prices, and developments in West Asia will remain key market triggers. Remaining Q2 results, US inflation and jobs data, and India’s inflation print will also influence trading.

Nair cautioned that intermittent profit booking could follow the sharp gains, although the near-term outlook remains constructive. He favours large-cap companies with earnings visibility and a buy-on-dips approach.

Meanwhile, the stock market will open for a special Muhurat trading session tomorrow, from 14:20 IST to 15:30 IST, on the occasion of Diwali.

Now, let’s take a detailed look at the performance of Awifs and RateGain this week.

Awfis Rallies After Q2 Results

Awfis shares gained 20.4% this week to close at ₹281.65, following a near-doubling of its consolidated net profit in Q2 FY27. Net profit rose 92.8% to ₹30.8 Cr from ₹16 Cr a year ago and increased 28.5% from ₹24 Cr in the preceding quarter.

Operating revenue grew 19.6% YoY and 3.2% QoQ to ₹438.7 Cr. Awfis reported normalised revenue of ₹451 Cr, including an adjustment of around ₹13 Cr for actual rent received under finance lease arrangements. On this basis, coworking and allied services contributed approximately ₹376 Cr, while construction and fit-out projects under its Transform vertical generated ₹75 Cr.

Awfis added six centres during the quarter, taking its network to 254 centres with approximately 1.74 Lakh seats across 18 cities. Portfolio occupancy stood at 76.2%, rising to 84.1% at centres operational for more than 12 months.

Its premium portfolio comprised 29 Gold and 10 Elite centres. The company said incremental premium seats were being signed at prices around 35% higher than its flagship offerings.

Awfis plans to prioritise occupancy, client renewals, and capital-efficient expansion, while adding premium workspaces in Pune, Bengaluru, Mumbai, and Delhi NCR.

RateGain Falls Despite Growth

RateGain shares declined 9.2% this week to close at ₹725.90, despite reporting a 46.5% YoY increase in    consolidated net profit to ₹74.7 Cr in Q2 FY27   . The company’s stock plunged by over 11% on Friday, the next trading session after its quarterly disclosures.

Operating revenue surged 152.6% YoY to ₹745.4 Cr, largely reflecting the consolidation of travel marketing platform Sojern, acquired for $250 Mn in November 2025.

Sequentially, however, revenue fell 5% from ₹785 Cr, while net profit declined 21.3% from ₹94.9 Cr.

Excluding expenses related to deferred deal consideration for Sojern, adjusted net profit rose 78% YoY to ₹90.8 Cr. Adjusted EBITDA more than tripled to ₹169.1 Cr.

The acquisition has reshaped RateGain’s business mix. Marketing technology accounted for 80.2% of revenue, followed by data-as-a-service at 13.2% and distribution at 6.6%.

Its customer base stood at 14,538 at September-end, around 4.5 times the 3,224 customers reported at the end of FY25. Customers include hotel chains, online travel agencies, airlines, car rental companies, and destination marketing organisations.

RateGain’s UK subsidiary repaid another $46.3 Mn of acquisition-related debt during the quarter. Cumulative repayments reached $93.8 Mn, or 75% of the original $125 Mn facility from HSBC and Citibank, leaving outstanding debt of $31.3 Mn.

The company reported a sales pipeline of ₹660 Cr and new contract wins worth ₹277.7 Cr. Chairman and MD Bhanu Chopra said its second-half priorities included expanding the combined RateGain-Sojern offering and increasing customer adoption of its AI products.

article_content:
IPO-bound hospitality chain PRISM, the parent entity of OYO, reported a consolidated profit after tax (PAT) of ₹353 Cr in the first quarter (Q1) of the fiscal year 2026-27 (FY27), up 17.3% from ₹301 Cr in the year-ago period.

According to PRISM’s audited financials seen by Inc42, the profitability came largely on the back of a deferred tax credit of nearly ₹244 Cr in the quarter under review.

Nevertheless, PRISM continued to grow its top line and generated an operating revenue of ₹2,814 Cr in Q1 FY27. This was nearly 35% higher than ₹2,078 Cr reported in the year ago quarter.

The IPO-bound startup also managed to improve its EBITDA by 24.3% to ₹760 Cr in the quarter under review as against ₹611 Cr in Q1 FY26. On the operational front, PRISM’s gross booking value (GBV) stood at nearly ₹9,600 Cr in the quarter ended June 2026, up nearly 30% from ₹7,408 Cr in Q1 FY26.

This is largely in line with what PRISM founder and CEO Ritesh Agarwal had said during the company’s extraordinary general meeting (EGM) in October this year.

“Our performance (in Q1 FY27) across segments on hotels or on vacation homes has demonstrated improving gross margins, higher operating earnings, even as we invest in expanding our brands and strengthening customer demand,” Agarwal had said then.

During the EGM, Agarwal also attributed PRISM’s performance to investments made in technology, brands and distribution capabilities over the past few years.

Founded in 2012 by Agarwal, OYO initially operated a budget hotel chain. It has since grown into a hospitality giant that offers holiday homes, coworking spaces, motels and corporate stays in more than 35 countries. The startup’s parent Oravel Stays rebranded to PRISM last year ahead of its initial public offering (IPO).

The startup has raised about $3.5 Bn in funding to date and counts the likes of SoftBank, Lightspeed India, Peak XV Partners and Microsoft among its backers.

The Q1 FY27 performance comes as PRISM is gearing up to list on the bourses. The hospitality giant first filed its draft red herring prospectus (DRHP) with the SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route in December last year.

It then received the market regulator’s approval for its IPO  in June this year. Right after,  the startup filed its updated DRHP with SEBI for a ₹6,650 Cr IPO , which will comprise entirely of a fresh issue of shares.

The Ritesh Agarwal-led startup is said to be eyeing a valuation of $7 Bn to $8 Bn for the public issue.

title: ED Searches CoinDCX & Delta Exchange Over Alleged Illegal Cross-Border Transfers
author: Inc42

“ED Bengaluru has conducted search(es) at th...
article_content:
The Enforcement Directorate (ED) conducted searches at three premises linked to crypto exchanges CoinDCX and Delta Exchange India (DEI) over alleged unauthorised cross-border transactions involving crypto derivatives and tokenised foreign stocks.

In a statement, the agency said the searches were conducted between November 4 and November 5 across Bengaluru. The crypto trading transactions in question run into thousands of crores of Rupees, as per ED.

“ED Bengaluru has conducted search(es) at three premises linked to Neblio Technologies Pvt. Ltd. (CoinDCX parent) and Excelium Technologies Pvt. Ltd.(which operates Delta Exchange India) under FEMA 1999 in the case of large scale unauthorised cross-border financial transactions involving crypto token derivatives and real world asset tokens,” said ED in a statement.

As per the directorate, ED began its probe into the matter after receiving information of alleged forex violations by CoinDCX and Delta Exchange India.

The agency alleged that CoinDCX and Delta Exchange India facilitated spot trading, futures and options (F&O) trading and trading in tokenised shares of foreign companies – all through cryptocurrencies.

ED also claimed CoinDCX advertised these products despite not being authorised to offer them.

While CoinDCX is yet to issue a statement on the matter, Delta Exchange India said that it cooperated “fully” with the officials and furnished the information sought. In a post on X, the crypto exchange further claimed that it is not involved in “any cross-border transfer of VDAs (virtual digital assets) in any form or manner”.

“We acknowledge the Enforcement Directorate’s statement regarding their visit to our premises on 4th & 5th November… We cooperated fully with the officials and provided the information that they sought. We remain committed to extending our support and cooperation as may be required…,” said Delta Exchange India.

CoinDCX’s Alleged Modus Operandi

According to the ED, user funds (deposited in Rupees) were allegedly converted into stablecoins, primarily USDT, and then transferred to overseas crypto platforms including Binance, KuCoin, Gate.io and Bybit. The agency alleged that these transfers circumvented forex rules governing cross-border money transfers.

For spot trades, the ED alleged that CoinDCX used an account, opened in the name of a Costa Rica-based entity, to send the USDT to foreign crypto platforms. Describing the Costa Rican company as a mere “paper entity”, the agency alleged that the transactions were allegedly actually executed directly through CoinDCX APIs.

The directorate also made similar allegations for CoinDCX’s F&O product. ED said that the homegrown platform allegedly opened matching positions via APIs on foreign platforms after users placed orders, with settlements occurring overseas when positions were closed.

The ED also claimed that tokenised-stock trading on CoinDCX was routed through Hyperliquid, an overseas decentralised crypto trading platform. It said that user funds were converted into USDT to open positions, with settlements completed on the overseas platform.

The alleged volumes of spot, derivatives and tokenised-stock transactions were described as running into thousands of crores of rupees. The ED also alleged that CoinDCX paid hundreds of crores in transaction fees to foreign platforms in stablecoins. This, the agency said, contravened forex rules.

Delta Exchange India Under ED Radar

Just like CoinDCX, the Enforcement Directorate also alleged that Delta Exchange India offered spot trading, crypto derivatives and tokenised foreign stocks via cryptocurrencies.

It alleged that a large volume of DEI’s derivatives and tokenised-stock transactions was routed through CoinDCX, which in turn executed them on foreign platforms.

The agency alleged that Delta Exchange India also transferred hundreds of crores of Rupees to overseas associate entities. These transfers are under investigation, added the ED.

In a statement, the ED said the fintech products offered by both crypto exchanges appear to have prima facie contravened norms under the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956, the SEBI Act, 1992 and the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934. The investigation remains ongoing.

The searches are part of ED’s broader clampdown on forex violations involving crypto platforms. Just days ago, the  directorate launched a probe into alleged FEMA violations involving crypto platforms  Mudrex and Saber.money as well as decentralised finance (DeFi) protocol Instadapp and its associated platform, Fluid, over alleged unauthorised cross-border fund transfers worth more than ₹4,940 Cr.

Prior to this in June this year, the  ED had also searched six premises linked to five platforms , namely Transak, Carret, Xpat, Onramp.money and Onmeta, over alleged unauthorised cross-border crypto transfers.

title: Stockal’s US Trading Row: Missing Consent, A Chinese Microcap, And Unanswered Questions
author: Inc42
description:
Indian investors who held Apple, Amazon, Tesla, and NVIDIA, shares allege they logged into their Stockal accounts to find those investments replaced with shares of a thinly traded Chinese microcap.

Nearly 30 investors say their portfolios were altered without consent on October 15. Their established US stock holdings were allegedly liquidated and the proceeds used to buy Nasdaq-listed Zhibao Technology shares.

One investor told Moneycontrol that securities worth $3.1 Mn, or around ₹29 Cr, were...
article_content:
Indian investors who held Apple, Amazon, Tesla, and NVIDIA, shares allege they logged into their Stockal accounts to find those investments replaced with shares of a thinly traded Chinese microcap.

Nearly 30 investors say their portfolios were altered without consent on October 15. Their established US stock holdings were allegedly liquidated and the proceeds used to buy Nasdaq-listed Zhibao Technology shares.

One investor told Moneycontrol that securities worth $3.1 Mn, or around ₹29 Cr, were sold within two minutes, followed by purchases of 30.5 Lakh Zhibao shares within 15 minutes. Another reported that holdings worth $335,768 were sold and 3 Lakh Zhibao shares purchased.

Media reports put investor-reported losses above ₹100 Cr. Inc42 has not independently verified this aggregate or authenticated the investors’ account details and alleged transactions.

An FIR has reportedly been registered in Bengaluru. The dispute now centres on how the accounts were accessed, whether safeguards failed, and who bears responsibility across Stockal, its parent Borderless Investing, and US brokerage partner DriveWealth.

How The Trades Unfolded

Founded in 2016 by Sitashwa Srivastava and Vinay Bharathwaj, Stockal enables Indians to invest overseas through US stocks, exchange-traded funds, and curated portfolios. It has    raised over $15 Mn    from investors like ScaleX Partners, Arc Ventures, July Ventures, HDFC Securities, and Cadenza Ventures. The startup partners with DriveWealth to facilitate US stock investments.

Bharathwaj left Borderless in 2022 and is currently the founder and CEO of “AI-first money intelligence and advisory platform” Cruise Money, as per his LinkedIn profile.

Investors allege the October 15 transactions replaced holdings in companies including Alphabet and AMD with Zhibao shares, leaving them exposed to a thinly traded microcap.

Borderless said DriveWealth notified it on October 16, India time, of suspicious trading across 13 accounts. Its assessment indicated an unauthorised third party had accessed 26 accounts using valid login credentials.

In 13 accounts, large-cap US equities were liquidated to acquire thinly traded microcap securities. Borderless said it restricted access shortly after receiving the notification.

An investor told Moneycontrol that Borderless contacted him on October 18, acknowledged suspicious activity, and said DriveWealth had restricted transactions in his account.

Zhibao’s subsequent decline deepened investors’ reported losses. Against an average purchase price of around $1.05 cited in investor accounts, the shares closed at $0.42 on October 23 — a fall of approximately 60%.

Differing Accounts Of Access

In an October 30 letter to an investor, DriveWealth reportedly said the unauthorised access occurred through the Stockal interface and attributed responsibility for associated security lapses to Stockal. It reportedly said it froze the account on Stockal’s instructions.

Responding to Inc42’s questions, DriveWealth said, “The Stockal incident is unrelated to DriveWealth’s systems. It occurred on Stockal’s app, not our platform. DriveWealth does not have a customer-facing app through which trades are placed, and our systems and client data were not affected by this incident.”

Borderless’s public statement offered a possible explanation – social engineering involving information exposed in another company’s data breach several weeks earlier. It stressed that this connection remained unverified and under investigation.

Borderless said its investigation found no evidence of a breach or compromise of its platform, interface, infrastructure, or internal systems. It also said no funds were withdrawn from affected accounts, based on findings available so far.

This distinction leaves the disputed trades themselves central to investors’ concerns – their allegation concerns changes to their holdings without consent, irrespective of whether money left the accounts.

Safeguards Under The Spotlight

The precise access method remains under investigation. However, the incident raises questions about whether possession of valid credentials could have been sufficient to execute the disputed trades.

Yash Kadakia, founder and CTO of cybersecurity firm Security Brigade, told Inc42 that stolen credentials are a common entry point, but platforms cannot shift responsibility entirely to customers when compromised passwords enable financial transactions.

He said layered safeguards should include two-factor authentication, SIM binding, device and geographical checks, and separate transaction-level authentication.

Behavioural monitoring is also critical. Multiple accounts accessed from one IP address, or similar trading patterns across accounts within a short period, should trigger scrutiny, he said.

Such monitoring could explain DriveWealth’s detection of suspicious activity, Kadakia suggested, although the actual detection mechanism remains unclear.

He added that implementation and enforcement remain challenges despite stronger SEBI cybersecurity requirements for regulated entities.

Borderless Sets Out Its Position

Borderless said it had engaged independent cybersecurity specialists, introduced additional authentication and account-protection measures, and found no evidence of a wider threat to its platform, products, or other customer accounts.

It maintained that unauthorised trading identified so far was restricted to 13 accounts.

The company said it had been engaging affected customers and working with DriveWealth to reconstruct events, examine disputed transactions, and explore avenues for a fair resolution. However, it said assistance should not be construed as an admission of liability, negligence, wrongdoing, or responsibility. It said it was cooperating with authorities and regulators.

Borderless also maintained it had provided substantive responses to media enquiries before publication and cautioned that its public account could change as the investigation progressed.

Inc42 has separately sought answers on the transactions, investigation, and investor concerns. The story will be updated upon receiving a response.

Who Bears The Responsibility?

The controversy has also drawn attention to Stockal’s former partnership with HDFC Securities. Launched in 2019 through globalinvesting.in, their operational association ended in July 2024.

HDFC Securities has clarified that it is not named among the accused in the FIR and said it would cooperate with regulators and law enforcement authorities.

While HDFC Securities has clarified its position, questions about the disputed trades remain unresolved. How were the accounts accessed, why were the transactions not intercepted, and what recourse do affected investors have to restore their holdings or recover losses?

Cross-border investing divides responsibilities across the customer interface, trade execution, and custody of securities. Establishing each intermediary’s obligations and the safeguards applied will be central to determining accountability.

For affected investors, the immediate issue remains whether the investigation will explain the disputed trades and deliver a resolution. For now, neither the source of the alleged compromise nor responsibility for the claimed losses has been conclusively established.

With the regulatory clearance in place, MFSPL intends to commence operations over the next three to six months. It intends to operate on...
article_content:
MobiKwik’s wholly owned subsidiary, MobiKwik Financial Services Pvt Ltd (MFSPL), has received a Certificate of Registration (CoR) from the RBI to operate as a non-banking financial company (NBFC).

The certificate was issued on November 5, following the RBI’s in-principle approval in April 2026. The dedicated NBFC was officially incorporated on March 13, 2025.

With the regulatory clearance in place, MFSPL intends to commence operations over the next three to six months. It intends to operate on an asset-light co-lending model, partnering with banks and other NBFCs.

In a statement, the company said that it plans to complement its existing lending service provider (LSP) business with the ability to originate credit directly through its NBFC.

“This will provide greater flexibility in product development, faster go-to-market execution and opportunities to improve lending economics, while allowing the group to continue leveraging its partnerships with established lenders,” the company said.

MobiKwik aims to disburse loans worth ₹5,000 Cr over the next three to four years, covering secured and unsecured credit for consumers and MSMEs.

Cofounder and CFO Upasana Taku said that the NBFC extension would allow MobiKwik to build on its existing lender partnerships and technology infrastructure while participating more actively in the lending value chain. The company plans to focus on responsible lending, prudent underwriting and sustainable growth.

During its Q2 earnings call, the CFO noted that MobiKwik could initially route around 10% of its digital lending disbursals through the NBFC. If the company disburses ₹6,000 Cr through its digital lending business next year, it would aim to route ₹600 Cr through MFSPL.

Under a proposed 10:90 co-lending arrangement, MobiKwik would contribute 10% of the loan amount, while its lending partner would fund the remaining 90%. This would require around ₹60 Cr in capital from MobiKwik to support ₹600 Cr in disbursals, allowing it to limit its on-book exposure while leveraging its existing underwriting and collections capabilities.

The NBFC launch comes amid an uptick for MobiKwik’s business.  MobiKwik reported a consolidated net profit of ₹11.8 Cr in Q2 FY27  against a net loss of ₹28.6 Cr in the year-ago quarter.

Operating revenue increased 9.4% YoY to ₹295.7 Cr from ₹270.2 Cr. The company said it recorded its highest-ever quarterly net profit, marking its fourth consecutive profitable quarter.

During the quarter, MobiKwik’s financial services business segment, which includes its ZIP EMI credit offering, increased 41.8% YoY to ₹86.9 Cr.

Loan disbursals through its lending partners rose 34.1% YoY to ₹1,082.6 Cr, up 46.9% sequentially from ₹736.7 Cr. The sequential recovery followed a temporary dip linked to technology infrastructure migration during the transfer of its lending business.

MobiKwik increased its major lending partners to 11 from six a year earlier. It classifies partners with quarterly disbursals exceeding ₹5 Cr as major lenders. Of the total disbursals, 21% came through its distribution model, while the remaining 79% were under its first-loss default guarantee (FLDG) model, under which it shares credit risk with lending partners.

Lending-related expenses, including operational and financial guarantee costs, declined 16.4% YoY to ₹29.8 Cr. The company attributed the reduction to improved credit quality and better commercial terms with lending partners.

MobiKwik expects lending disbursals to maintain strong double-digit growth as newer partnerships mature and it introduces additional product categories, although management cautioned that the growth rate may moderate.

Shares of MobiKwik ended today’s trading session 2.3% higher at ₹224.75 apiece on the BSE.

article_content:
Indian stockbrokers’ combined total active user base shrunk by 0.5% to 4.59 Cr in October, dropping from 4.61 Cr users in September. Despite the broader market plateau, user consolidation accelerated in favour of newer players.

Groww continued to cement its market-leading position with 1.38 Cr active users in October, commanding a 30% market share. Notably, it added 3.04 Lakh users in the month, more than any other competitor in the top 10.

To note, Groww’s net active client additions in October were approximately 1.5X the combined additions of the next four largest brokers by active client base, Angel One, Zerodha, ICICI Securities and Upstox, which collectively added around 2.02 lakh active clients.

But the positions below saw an intriguing shakeup.

Zerodha, after losing clients in many months over the past year, slipped from second place.

Angel One overtook Zerodha, adding around 2.4 Lakh users to take its active user count to 69.99 Lakh and its market share to 15.3%. It grew at a 3.3% rate over the past month to overtake Zerodha.

“During the quarter, Angel One acquired nearly 15 lakh new clients, up 11.6% from the previous quarter, taking its client base to 3.99 Cr by September before it crossed 4 Cr in October. Its wealth management business continued to scale, with assets under management rising 19.1% quarter-on-quarter and 160.5% year-on-year to ₹16,000 Cr,” the company said in a statement.

Meanwhile, more than 32K users or around 0.5% of Zerodha’s active user base turned inactive over the previous month. It ended the month with 67.59 Lakh users, compared to 67.92 Lakh users in the previous month, although its market share remained nearly unchanged at 14.7%.

ICICI Securities held its fourth place with 21.64 Lakh active users, adding 3.7 Lakh users in October to take its market share to 4.7% market share.

In fifth place, Upstox shed 0.6% of its user base as the startup saw 11.3 Lakh users leave to bring its active user count down to 18.43 Lakh with a market share of just 4%.

Kotak Securities occupied sixth position with 14.05 Lakh active users while HDFC Securities finished seventh with 13.61 Lakh active users. The two bank-linked brokerages grew their user base by 0.9% and 0.5% respectively.

Meanwhile, Dhan, in eighth place, added nearly 26K users over the past, as its user base increased 2.3% to 11.47 Lakh from 11.21 Lakh in September. It was able to match Groww in terms of growth rate to become the second fastest growing brokerage among the top 10 after Angel One.

SBI Securities lost the most users after Zerodha, with an exodus of 17K users or 1.7% of its user base. The retail stockbroking subsidiary of SBI Capital Markets saw its active user count decline to 10.04 Lakh compared to 10.21 Lakh in September.

Rounding off the top 10, Motilal Oswal’s active user count grew 0.8% to 9.16 Lakh from 9.09 Lakh.

Beyond the top 10, Sahi added 34,372 active clients during October, adding to its bid to solidify its name in the discount brokerage space.

Markets Recover In The Month Of October

October marked a modest recovery for Indian equities after September’s sharp correction, although foreign investor selling remained elevated. The Nifty 50 rose 2.81% while Sensex gained over 3%. The gains ended the benchmarks’ two-month losing streak, but the recovery was not broad-based, with mid- and small-cap stocks continuing to face pressure.

As per data shared by Bajaj Broking, foreign institutional investors (FIIs) were net sellers of ₹45,162 Cr in October, while domestic institutional investors (DIIs) bought shares worth ₹62,220 Cr on a net basis. However, foreign selling eased in the second half of the month, with FPIs turning net buyers and investing ₹13,112 Cr between October 16 and 31, after pulling out nearly ₹47,955 Cr in the first fortnight.

“Going ahead, the reversal in FII flows is an encouraging signal for sentiment, though elevated crude and global event risk could temper the momentum,” Pabitro Mukherjee, Deputy Vice President-Research, Bajaj Broking had noted.

The post  Brokers In October: Angel One Climbs To The Second Spot With 2.4 Lakh New User Additions  appeared first on  Inc42 Media .

title: AvenuesAI Q2 Net Profit Rises 6% YoY To ₹72 Cr, Revenue Up 47%

description:

The fintech company’s operating EBITDA, excluding other income, grew just 3% Y...
article_content:
AvenuesAI (formerly Infibeam Avenues) reported a 6% growth in its net profit to ₹71.7 Cr in the quarter ended September (Q2 FY27) from ₹67.7 Cr a year earlier.  On a sequential basis , net profit declined 15.4% from ₹84.8 Cr.

Meanwhile, its operating revenue grew 46.5% YoY and 7.4% QoQ to ₹287.9 Cr during the quarter under review. Including other income of ₹2.8 Cr, total income during the quarter stood at ₹290.7 Cr.

The fintech company’s operating EBITDA, excluding other income, grew just 3% YoY to ₹9.9 Cr. This came as its total expenses rose 49.4% YoY and 7.7% QoQ to ₹282.5 Cr in Q2 FY27, outpacing the growth in operating revenue.

At the same time, its consolidated net revenue, after accounting for payment processing and other costs, declined 1% YoY to ₹151.3 Cr in Q2 FY27.

AvenuesAI attributed the decline to its ‘competitive pricing strategy’ amid efforts to deepen merchant relationships and increase transaction volumes. As a result, its net take rate moderated 4% to 5.06 bps despite a 19% sequential increase in its total payments volume to ₹1.77 Lakh Cr.

The company generated ₹282.2 Cr in revenue from its payment business, which includes its CCAvenue payment gateway, payment infrastructure services to banks (CPGS), and credit and lending-related services, accounting for nearly 98% of its operating revenue during the quarter. The remaining ₹5.7 Cr was derived from its ecommerce platform business, Rediff.

AvenuesAI Looks To Unlock Value Across Subsidiaries

Alongside its financial performance, AvenuesAI outlined its plans to expand its AI capabilities, with advanced technology development and AI software-related work remaining among the key objectives of its rights issue.

In June last year,  the company had raised ₹700 Cr via a rights issue , primarily for the repayment of outstanding loans, expansion of its IPO-bound digital content and ecommerce marketplace Rediff and further investments in its AI arm, Nueromind, for which it had earmarked ₹294 Cr.

Almost 42.7%, or ₹297.2 Cr, of the net proceeds remained unutilised at the end of the September quarter.

AvenuesAI has now announced that it will directly utilise the funds for AI development and software-related activities instead of routing the investment through Nueromind. It clarified that the change was limited to the mode of implementation, with no alteration to the end use of the proceeds.

In the June quarter, AvenuesAI announced plans to amalgamate Nueromind with itself, subject to NCLT approval.

It is also developing its Transaction Intelligence Score (TISco), an AI-led initiative that will use permitted transaction and merchant-behaviour signals for risk assessment, fraud prevention, merchant intelligence and financial services workflows.

The company aims to use its transaction infrastructure to build an intelligence layer that can support merchant and enterprise services.

On the investment front, AvenuesAI said it made investments in two financial services companies during the September quarter. It acquired a stake of up to 7% in Online PSB Loans Limited for a consideration of up to ₹65 Cr. It also invested up to ₹34.5 Cr to acquire a stake of up to 1.38% in Ratnaafin Capital Private Limited.

The company also reiterated its plans to expand CCAvenue’s international payments business, particularly in the US, by leveraging its payment technology, enterprise relationships and regulated infrastructure.

Meanwhile, its ecommerce arm, Rediff, is on its way to the bourses for a separate listing. After  filing for an IPO confidentially  earlier this year, the markets regulator  SEBI approved the draft papers in August .

However, the Q2 disclosure did not provide an update on Rediff’s proposed IPO. As per sources, Rediff would look to raise in between ₹600-800 Cr via the IPO

AvenuesAI outlined that unlocking value from Rediff is one of its three strategic priorities for FY27. It plans to integrate Rediff’s consumer and enterprise digital ecosystem with its payments and AI capabilities. This includes RediffOne,  which offers digital commerce and communication services , and RediffPay, which is intended to expand consumer payment engagement.

AvenuesAI has maintained its FY27 consolidated revenue guidance of ₹1,100-1,300 Cr.

The company said its focus for the remainder of FY27 will remain on expanding merchant relationships, improving operating discipline and creating additional monetisation opportunities through Rediff, enterprise technology and applied AI.

It is also  monitoring potential changes to the merchant discount rate (MDR) policy  for eligible UPI transactions, with any introduction, timing or scope remaining subject to government and regulatory decisions.

Shares of AvenueAI ended today’s trading session 3.72% lower at ₹129.25.

title: MakeMyTrip Acquires Majority Stake In Quick Ride To Enter Ride Pooling
author: Inc42
description:

In a statement, MakeMyTrip said that the acquisition will allow it “to establish a presence in the ride pooling segment, which is complementary to the group’s existing ground transportation portfolio.”

As part of the transaction, Quick Ride’s brand and ride-pooling business have been transferred to a newly formed ent...
article_content:
Nasdaq-listed traveltech major MakeMyTrip has expanded into the carpooling segment via the acquisition of a majority stake in Bengaluru-based Quick Ride for an undisclosed amount.

In a statement, MakeMyTrip said that the acquisition will allow it “to establish a presence in the ride pooling segment, which is complementary to the group’s existing ground transportation portfolio.”

As part of the transaction, Quick Ride’s brand and ride-pooling business have been transferred to a newly formed entity, Co Ride Mobility Private Limited, in which MakeMyTrip has acquired a majority stake. Quick Ride’s promoters will continue to lead the business.

However, Quick Ride’s erstwhile electric vehicle (EV) taxi business will remain with its predecessor entity, iDisha Info Labs Pvt Ltd.

Founded in 2014 by KNM Rao, Quick Ride offers a ride-sharing application that connects passengers to riders. It connects the commuters travelling in the same direction.

It also offers an enterprise solution for shared mobility and counts IT companies such as Wipro, TCS, Infosys, IBM and Cognizant, among others as its clients. Its services are available in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Chennai, Pune, Kochi, Delhi NCR, Mumbai, and Kolkata.

The startup has raised over $14 Mn from investors like Sequoia, Prosus and Venture Highway. Sequoia exited the startup in 2021.

MakeMyTrip’s Acquisition-Led Expansion

The Quick Ride acquisition is part of MakeMyTrip’s broader strategy to expand its presence across adjacent travel and mobility segments through strategic investments and acquisitions.

Commenting on the acquisition, MakeMyTrip group CEO Rajesh Magow said that the investment would help the company establish a presence in daily intra-city commutes while strengthening its intercity travel offerings.

“As part of our expansion strategy, we have pursued selective strategic partnerships, investments and acquisitions that complement and strengthen our existing business and expand the breadth and depth of our offerings. Ride pooling gives us a presence in high-frequency daily commutes within cities, as well as intercity travel,” he added.

The company plans to leverage its experience in building redBus across India and overseas markets to scale Quick Ride’s ride-pooling business.

In the past few years, MakeMyTrip has acquired Savaari to strengthen its car rental services, Happay in corporate travel and expense management, and  Flamingo Transworld  in regional group holiday packages. It has also made a strategic minority investment in visa processing platform Atlys.

The development comes as MakeMyTrip looks to deepen its presence across the travel value chain, moving beyond conventional travel bookings towards a broader set of transportation and ancillary services.

On the financial front, the travel tech major’s consolidated net profit for the three months ended June 30, 2026 (Q1 FY27)  plunged 65% to $9.1 Mn  from $25.8 Mn in the year-ago period. MakeMyTrip’s revenue grew 6% YoY to $285.6 Mn.

title: Delhi HC Upholds BharatPe’s Veto Rights In Unity SFB Shareholding Dispute
