article_content:
For years, India’s best scientists left for the US. Now they are staying, and more of them are choosing startups over corporate labs. For Nicolas Sauvage, Founder and President of TDK Ventures, those two shifts are the biggest changes in Indian deeptech over the past five to 10 years.

“The best talent starts to go into the startups in deeptech, and they try things that they would not have tried 10 years or even five years ago,” Sauvage said in a fireside chat with Shivani Muthanna, Senior Director – Strategic Content & Video at YourStory, at  TechSparks 2026 .

TDK Ventures  is the corporate venture capital arm of Japanese electronics company TDK Corporation. Set up in Silicon Valley in 2019, it opened its  Bengaluru innovation hub  in 2023, its first office outside the US. India is its second largest market by number of investments, Sauvage said.

The  ecosystem he is betting on  is growing. India is home to more than 4,200 deeptech startups, which raised $2.3 billion in 2025, up 37% from the year before, according to a Nasscom–Zinnov report.

During the session titled ‘Global by design: What Indian deeptech needs to become globally iconic’, he laid out what Indian founders need to get right to build companies that compete globally, from picking a first customer and the right investors to planning for scale before it becomes expensive to do so.

Where India has the right to win  Speaking on investing in SpaceTech, Sauvage named the US, China, and India as the three countries where he would consider investing as a VC. Space is one area where he believes India has a clear advantage, built on decades of institutional investment through the Indian Space Research Organisation. The government’s space promotion agency, IN-SPACe, projects that India’s space economy will grow from $8.4 billion to  $44 billion by 2033 , raising its share of the global market from 2% to 8%.

TDK Ventures  co-led a $20.5 million Series A  in Bengaluru-based spacetech startup Ethereal Exploration Guild (The Guild), which is developing a fully reusable medium-lift launch vehicle.

Sauvage also pointed to a shift in AI. The conversation, he said, has moved from tokens and compute to electrons and gigawatts, which means everything involved in delivering power to chips now matters. TDK Ventures invested in C2i Semiconductors, a Bengaluru startup founded in 2024 by former Texas Instruments engineers that builds power management technology for AI data centres. Germany’s Infineon Technologies announced the acquisition of C2i in August 2026 and completed it in October, about two years after the startup was founded.

Beyond individual sectors, Sauvage credited a cultural trait:  jugaad , or resourcefulness under constraint.

“Think about the entrepreneurship journey. It means going from an idea with massive constraints and creating something that’s valuable and does a job. That sounds like  jugaad  to me,” he said.

That resourcefulness shows up in the numbers, he added. Capital efficiency among Indian portfolio companies is world class. “I’m from Europe, but don’t talk about Europe when we think about capital efficiency,” he said.

" align="center">

Let the first market shape the product  When asked what founders building from India for the world should think about first, Sauvage pointed to Exponent Energy. Founded in 2020 by former Ather Energy executives Arun Vinayak and Sanjay Byalal, the company offers 15-minute fast charging. In June 2026,  TDK Ventures co-led a Rs 200 crore  ($21.1 million) round in Exponent, taking the company’s total funding since 2020 to $65.7 million.

Exponent’s long-term goal was megawatt-scale fast charging for intercity buses. It could not start there. Instead, it began by supplying battery management systems (BMS) to three-wheeler makers, a fragmented market with more than 70 manufacturers at the time.

“There was no way a German startup would convince BMW to take their solution. No way a US startup would convince General Motors to take their BMS solution,” Sauvage said.

India’s fragmented market let Exponent deploy across many manufacturers in Bengaluru and beyond, giving it  a base to build from .

Founders need superpowers, and so do their investors  Sauvage described founders as superheroes. Each needs a superpower: something they know or can do that no one else can. That is what draws investors in. But, like any superhero film, there are many battles before the end, and founders need allies.

“You want to make sure that the investors you pick as an entrepreneur bring the right superpower at the right time,” he said.

Corporate VCs can bring a go-to-market channel, an early anchor customer, a hard-to-access supplier, or help reducing scientific risk, depending on who they are. He urged founders to choose investors based on what they add that the cap table does not already have.

For TDK Ventures, that means drawing on TDK’s work in energy, sensing, passive components, and power supplies. Sauvage said electric motorcycle maker  Ultraviolette now gets components  typically reserved for TDK’s largest customers, while TDK is working with The Guild on future component requirements and roadmaps.

Alongside seeking venture-capital financial returns, he said, TDK Ventures looks for ways TDK’s capabilities, or “superpowers”, can accelerate and de-risk a founder’s journey towards building a globally significant company.

First principles over trade-offs  Sauvage traced several portfolio wins back to first-principles thinking. TDK Ventures invested in AI chip company Groq in 2020. During an interview with founder Jonathan Ross before investing, Sauvage noticed that every answer, from setting company values to hiring, firing, and designing the compiler, came back to first principles.

That approach produced a chip architecture designed around the compiler, which allowed for fully predictable, low-latency inference. Sauvage said he was convinced inference was the future before the ChatGPT moment, when he estimated the market for inference alone at more than $60 billion. In December 2025,  NVIDIA signed a non-exclusive licensing deal  for Groq’s technology, reportedly worth about $20 billion, and hired Ross and several members of his team.

He applied the same lens to engineering decisions that look like trade-offs. Ultraviolette, he said, uses first-principles engineering to pursue improvements in performance, weight and cost together. The company now sells its bikes in Germany, France, Switzerland, the UK, and other European markets, bringing its products into markets served by established manufacturers such as BMW. Ultraviolette recently  raised $85 million  in a round led by Yali Capital and TDK Ventures.

Patience and impatience at the same time  Deeptech founders, Sauvage said, need both. “Overnight success takes 10 years,” he said, noting that Groq took 10 years and SpaceX took 17. At the same time, founders need urgency and a sense of contribution to society.

Before investing, he looks for four things: a founder with a superpower, a category-defining product, a large enough market, and evidence the company can win one customer and then the next while staying capital-efficient. Markets worth $1 billion to $2 billion can be too small for the venture returns TDK Ventures seeks, he said, because the firm looks for each investment to have the potential to return the entire fund.

He cited SPAN, a Silicon Valley company led by Indian-origin founder Arch Rao. SPAN began by redesigning the home electrical panel, a product largely unchanged for a century.

As AI infrastructure demand surged, SPAN extended its power-management technology into distributed compute through partnerships, which Sauvage said changed the company’s trajectory.

Longer cycles also explain why India needs more corporate investors now, he argued. Using a roughly four-year journey to success in SaaS and fintech as an illustration, Sauvage described an ecosystem that can recycle entrepreneurial experience about 2.5 times a decade, as founders and employees carry what they have learned into new companies. A ten-year deeptech journey allows only one such cycle over the same period. Networks of repeat founders and alumni-founded businesses, like those associated with PayPal and SpaceX, therefore take longer to develop. Corporate investors can help bridge that gap with technical expertise, suppliers and customer relationships.

“I want global companies, corporates, and their corporate VCs to know this is the time to invest in India for deeptech,” he said.

Build for scale before it gets expensive  Sauvage emphasised thinking about scale and international expansion early, because shortcuts taken to win the first market in India can become expensive to reverse later.

When TDK Ventures met Ultraviolette, the team was already deliberate about Europe while focused on winning in India first, with customers riding its bikes as far as the Himalayas.

His advice to founders: find what is specific to India that a global customer would trust. India’s wide temperature range, for example, could favour energy storage that performs across extremes, such as sodium-ion or thermal batteries.

“Try to think about what makes you being in India a proof point that because you’re successful in India, you will win everywhere,” he said.

For Sauvage, India’s deeptech opportunity rests on more than talent. The founders most likely to build iconic companies are those who treat India as a starting point rather than a boundary, pick investors who fill specific gaps, and design for international markets before shortcuts become costly to undo. It is a long game that demands patience and impatience at once, and in his view, the moment for global capital to back it in India has arrived.

main_event: If it works in India, it can work anywhere: TDK Ventures’ Nicolas Sauvage on building deeptech for the world

title: Why operational excellence will define the next phase of India’s startup growth

article_content:
Growth rarely announces itself. It arrives as a signed term sheet on a Friday evening, a large client wanting to go live in three weeks, or an investor doubling a commitment.

But the win is rarely the hard part. The hard part is the Monday after.

That Monday tells you whether you have built a company or simply had a good quarter.

When operations become a competitive advantage  In most startups, operations sit in the back seat. It is the team that asks for approvals, slows down contracts, and says “not yet” when sales say “yes”. Founders tolerate it the way one tolerates a seatbelt.

I have never accepted that framing. Bain & Company’s long-running research on growth found that 85% of the barriers to profitable growth are internal, with revenue outgrowing talent at the top of the list. Companies rarely lose to the market. They lose to their own machinery, and that machinery is operations.

Build it before you need it   Early on, operations feel optional. A small team, a founder who knows everything, a spreadsheet that works. Why design controls for a business that fits in one room?

Because by the time you feel the need, you are already late. Operations built in the middle of a growth spurt is built under pressure: rushed hires, patched processes, controls bolted on after something breaks. Worse, it takes bandwidth from growth itself. The team that should be closing the next client is busy repairing the last one. You slow down precisely when you meant to accelerate.

Nobody lays the tracks after the train has left the station.

This is not a case for bloat. It is a case for sequencing. Build the backbone one stage ahead of where you are, lean and proportionate, so the organisation absorbs growth instead of buckling under it.

The companies that scale most smoothly are rarely the ones scrambling when growth arrives; the reporting, controls and people for the next stage are already in place. Investors notice the difference.

In due diligence, a clean data room and a well-documented control environment often say more about a company's readiness than its growth curve does.

Run on data, not opinions  Operations is also where a company's data lives, or should. Every onboarding, approval, and report generates information. Most startups treat it as exhaust. The better ones treat it as instrumentation. When operations own clean, consistent data, leadership stops arguing about whose number is right and starts debating what to do about it. You see a bottleneck forming before a client complains. And automation and AI, which nearly every board is now asking about, only work on data you can trust.

Automate a messy process and you simply get the mess faster.

If your founders and your operations team are looking at different numbers, you do not have a data problem. You have an operations problem.

Never pay for the same lesson twice  The same discipline applies to mistakes. A mistake made once is a lesson; made twice, it is a choice.

Every error in a growing firm should leave something behind, whether a changed control, a clearer owner, or a better checklist.

The corollary matters as much. If the same method keeps producing the same disappointing result, the problem is rarely effort. It is the method. Operations should be the function that notices, asks why, and has the licence to change how the work gets done. Processes are not scripture. They are hypotheses, and good operators keep testing them.

Bring operations in before growth is sold, not after  For founders and boards redrawing their organisation charts this year, one test is telling. Do operations hear about a new product, market, or client after it is sold, or while it is being designed? If it is after, operations will always be firefighting, and firefighters rarely get to build anything.

Put operations where growth is planned, not at the end of the line where growth is processed. Give it a seat in strategy reviews, a voice in pricing and launches, and a mandate to say "here is how", not just "not yet".

Three questions are worth asking every quarter:  ●	If our business doubled next quarter, what would break first?

●	Which decisions still need the founder, and should they?

●	Would our records survive an investor's due diligence this week?

Will your growth last, or was it just a good quarter?  There is an old military line: amateurs talk strategy, professionals talk logistics.

India's startup story so far has been told in the language of strategy: rounds, valuations, category creation. The next chapter will be about sustaining growth rather than merely achieving it, and it will be told in the language of execution and governance. Momentary growth is an event. Sustained growth is a capability. And capability, in the end, is what operations builds.

(Sandesha Jaitapkar is the COO at Artha Group)

title: How Satin Group’s Sankalp plans to empower India’s next wave of founders
author: YourStory
description: India’s startup ecosystem is witnessing a growing wave of innovation in climate action and sustainability. From students developing affordable technology solutions for micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) to early-stage entrepreneurs tackling circular economy challenges, the ideas are promising. But turning a climate-focused idea into a scalable business requires more than passion. Founders need access to capital, industry networks and structured mentorship to translate their vision into ...
article_content:
India’s startup ecosystem is witnessing a growing wave of innovation in climate action and sustainability. From students developing affordable technology solutions for micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) to early-stage entrepreneurs tackling circular economy challenges, the ideas are promising. But turning a climate-focused idea into a scalable business requires more than passion. Founders need access to capital, industry networks and structured mentorship to translate their vision into viable enterprises.

Recognising these gaps, Satin Group, based in Gurugram, Haryana, launched Sankalp this September. It is a platform designed to nurture sustainability-focused ideas from students and early-stage entrepreneurs. In an exclusive interaction with YourStory, Pramod Marar, CEO of Satin FinServ Limited, discussed the thinking behind the initiative, the importance of non-financial support alongside funding, and the role financial institutions can play in scaling climate innovation.     

Sankalp operates through two distinct tracks: student-led business ideas and early-stage startups. The student track encourages college students to develop technology-driven solutions to climate and environmental challenges. The startup track focuses on young businesses working in areas such as clean mobility, circular economy, waste management, and sustainable supply chains. Sankalp winners stand a chance to win Rs 32 lakh, with Rs 10 lakh for students and Rs 22 lakh for startups.

Applications for the first cohort closed on October 4. Sankalp says the response has been encouraging, with more than 17,000 registrations and over 1,000 teams taking part. Student innovators, it adds, showed a notable interest in technology-led solutions for climate challenges.

“We were pleasantly surprised to see a strong focus among students on creating technology-led solutions in the climate space,” Marar said. 

The genesis of Sankalp  Marar brings more than two decades of experience across banking, microfinance, and sustainability-focused entrepreneurship. Having started his own venture early in his career, he experienced firsthand the challenges faced by entrepreneurs seeking initial funding, particularly those from salaried or service-sector families without access to financial backing.

“Startup wasn’t a cool term at that time; it wasn’t even a term that existed. I come from a middle-class service background family. There was a lot of moral support, but there was no financial support. That’s when I realised how difficult it was to access early-stage capital,” Marar recalled.

While founders may have the passion and business acumen to develop an idea, scaling it requires a broader support system. Capital is only one part of the equation; access to expertise, networks and institutional support can be equally important.

“Most startup founders are very passionate about their ideas and have the acumen to scale them. But scaling requires a lot of elements beyond capital. That’s why we started Sankalp — to help build the ecosystem around sustainability and climate innovation,” Marar said.

Satin Group, which was founded in 1990, comprises three non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) focused on  microfinance , housing finance, and corporate and SME lending. Its broader ecosystem also includes Satin Growth Alternatives, a debt fund, and Satin Technologies, its technology arm. This combination of financial and technological capabilities provides the group with multiple avenues to support emerging sustainability-focused businesses.

University incubators play an important role in nurturing early-stage ideas, but Sankalp aims to go further by helping entrepreneurs bridge the gap between developing a concept and preparing it for the market.

“I wouldn’t call it a scaled-down version because we actually try to go beyond the conventional model of incubation. We want to understand whether we can support founders through experienced mentorship, both at an individual level and through institutions, as well as through debt and equity,” Marar said.

With applications closed, Sankalp has moved from a wide pool of ideas to a tighter evaluation. KPMG is the programme’s assessment partner. It is independently evaluating every application against a predefined framework, helping with shortlisting and identifying the most promising ventures. Satin says this keeps the selection objective and based only on merit.

Thirty teams have made it to the virtual jury round, where they will present to a panel of practitioners, venture capital (VC) fund managers and lenders. The shortlisted ventures cover climate tech, circular economy, clean energy, sustainable cities, waste management, water management and sustainable agriculture. 

According to Satin, what stood out was not just the range of ideas but the depth applicants showed in their chosen areas. Judges will look at the strength of the idea, innovation, feasibility, scalability and potential for meaningful impact.

Based on the jury’s assessments, select finalists will go on to the in-person Grand Finale, where they will present before a jury and industry leaders for final evaluation and recognition.

The jury rounds are also meant to open doors beyond the prize money. Both the virtual round and the Grand Finale will have representatives from VC funds, incubation centres and institutional investors, who can evaluate the ideas and explore funding possibilities. Satin has also signed formal arrangements with certain incubation centres to offer institutional mentoring to the selected founders. In addition, Satin Growth Alternatives, the group’s Category II alternative investment fund (AIF), will look at the ideas from an investment angle.

Satin is careful about what this means for funding. At this stage, it says, Sankalp is not an announced debt-and-equity programme. Any financing would be considered case by case, depending on the business model, stage of development, funding needs and suitability, with the aim of finding viable opportunities and exploring ways to support their growth.

For Satin, the programme fits in its wider ambition to help build a more sustainable and climate-resilient economy. Financing remains central to its business, the company says, but Sankalp gives it a chance to engage with emerging innovators and understand how climate-focused business models are evolving, along with the opportunities and challenges in the space. It also helps Satin spot solutions that may, over time, match its own financing capabilities. 

The group has already been building towards this. Satin Finserv set up its Sustainable & Emerging Businesses (SEB) vertical in August 2025 to offer financing to sustainability-oriented and emerging enterprises, with a streamlined process and dedicated relationship support. In the last 12 months, it has disbursed loans of roughly Rs 400 crore to businesses focused on sustainability, either as users or providers of sustainability-focused solutions.

Sankalp complements that effort, Satin says, by helping it discover promising entrepreneurs and innovations.

Why Sankalp matters for India’s green transition   India’s transition towards a low-carbon economy will require more than technological breakthroughs. It will also depend on whether promising innovations can secure funding, find customers, and scale sustainably. Financial institutions, established businesses, and entrepreneurs all have a role to play in building this ecosystem.

Sankalp seeks to bring these stakeholders together, combining access to finance with mentorship and industry connections. Its approach reflects the idea that supporting climate innovation should extend beyond funding a promising idea or awarding a one-time prize.

“Rather than just waiting for institutions to put their money on the table, can financial institutions come together to create a platform that helps founders go beyond simply raising capital?” Marar said.

By seeking to connect entrepreneurs with financing, expertise, and potential commercial partners, Sankalp aims to create a longer-term support system for sustainability-focused businesses.""

From students developing affordable technology solutions for micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) to early-stage entrepreneurs tackling circular economy challenges, the ideas are promising.

article_content:
The government has approved a new tranche of 12 applications, worth over Rs 7,500 crore, under the Electronics Components Manufacturing Scheme, IT Secretary S Krishnan said on Friday.

The latest round of approvals also covers projects related to materials and capital goods, widening the scheme's reach across the electronics supply chain.

This round of approvals adds to the momentum behind the scheme, which aims to build a domestic ecosystem for components and reduce India's dependence on imports.

The government is keen to strengthen upstream segments such as raw materials and manufacturing equipment, alongside component production.

The government also launched the Semicon 2.0 web application portal under the ambitious Semicon India Programme.

author: YourStory

article_content:
Launched in 2014,        PhotoSparks    is a weekly feature from  YourStory,  with photographs that celebrate the spirit of creativity and innovation. In the earlier 1,030 posts, we featured an    art festival,       cartoon gallery.       world music festival   ,    telecom expo   ,    millets fair,       climate change expo,       wildlife conference,       startup festival,       Diwali rangoli,    and    jazz festival.

The Namma Art Bengaluru national festival was held at Karnataka Chitrakala Parishath (KCP) for the second time this year (see our coverage of earlier exhibitions at this popular cultural hub  here ). KCP’s flagship event is the annual  Chitra Santhe , regarded as India’s largest street fair for art.

India’s artistic landscape is as vast and varied as the country itself. It spans intricate visual languages of Madhubani, Warli, Gond and Pattachitra; sculptural traditions of Channapatna, Dhokra and Thanjavur; miniature painting and textile traditions, and much more.

The worlds of contemporary painting, photography, installation, and new media add new perspectives and vocabularies for art lovers. The beauty of this artistic panorama truly emerges when these creative forms are showcased together.

“Art has always served as a powerful medium of expression that transcends boundaries, connects communities, and reflects the spirit of society,” explains Shashidhara Rao, General Secretary, KCP.

A pan-India exhibition that brings traditional and contemporary art into one shared space can create a powerful visual and cultural conversation. Instead of presenting India’s art traditions as isolated regional categories, such an exhibition reveals the connections between them.

Also Read

2026 Outlook: AI, robotics, biotech, unicorns and the road ahead

As seen in this photo essay, there are recurring ideas of nature, spirituality, community, identity, mythology, and everyday life. The differences are equally important: they demonstrate the extraordinary plurality of Indian experience and the many ways in which communities have interpreted and expressed their worlds.

Bringing traditional and contemporary practices together also allows the exhibition to move beyond the idea of heritage as something belonging only to the past. Traditional art forms are living practices, continually evolving through artists, artisans and new generations.

Contemporary artists, meanwhile, frequently draw upon inherited visual languages and stories while questioning, reinterpreting and transforming them for the present. Placing these works side by side makes this continuity visible.

“In an increasingly dynamic world, the role of art in preserving heritage, encouraging dialogue, and inspiring fresh perspectives has become more significant than ever,” KCP’s Rao adds.

The Namma Art festival is thus more than a showcase of beautiful objects, as shown in this photo essay. It serves as a map of India’s cultural imagination — one in which a folk painting from one region can resonate with a contemporary installation from another, and where regional identities can coexist within a larger national story.

The experience of seeing many art forms together is also deeply democratic. It invites audiences to discover unfamiliar traditions and appreciate the knowledge embedded in craft. It creates opportunities for dialogue between artists, craftspeople, designers, collectors, students, and the wider public.

Also Read

Year in review: startups that raised big from VCs in 2025

“Our festival represents a wide spectrum of artistic approaches, mediums and regional sensibilities. Their works collectively reflect the dynamism of contemporary practice in India,” says KCP president BL Shankar.

Such a national exhibition celebrates an idea that is central to India itself: unity does not require uniformity. Its strength lies in the coexistence of many languages, histories, materials, communities and ways of seeing.

By bringing traditional and contemporary art together, the exhibition can offer audiences not simply a view of Indian art, but an experience of India — diverse, layered, evolving, and connected.

Featured artists at the KCP festival include Vivek Vadkar, AG Nellagi, Ashok Mansur, Sunil Barman, Dhiraj Balchandra Patil, and Sudha Sridhar.

Vivek Vadkar is a contemporary Indian artist renowned for his powerful and emotive oil paintings of horses in motion. His popular  Seven Horses  compositions draw on traditions where running horses symbolise success, victory and positive energy.

AG Nellagi is known particularly for his expressive paintings of bulls. His work draws deeply on his personal experience as a farmer and on the cultural symbolism associated with the bull, which represents strength, determination, fertility, and confidence. He has received awards and recognition from the Karnataka Lalit Kala Academy and other cultural institutions.

Also Read

How IIT Madras Incubation Cell is powering India’s next-gen deeptech startups

Ashok Mansur is a visual artist and photographer with an interest in art, history and cultural imagery. A farmer by profession, he is also known for his beautiful landscapes along with people portraits.

Sunil Barman is a self-taught artist whose paintings focus on the quiet beauty of village life in Bengal. He works primarily with fine pen-and-ink drawing layered over delicate watercolour washes. His paintings evoke nostalgia for rural life where people and nature coexist in an unhurried rhythm.

“This edition has proudly presented 150 invited artists from across India. They showcase the diverse ideas, mediums and voices that reflect the spirit of traditional and contemporary art today,” festival convener SA Vimalanathan signs off.

Now what have  you  done today to pause in your busy schedule and harness your creative side for a better world?

title: Aina launches Rs 47,000 ring to bring AI agents to your fingertips
author: YourStory
description: What if booking a cab, sending a message or managing a meeting required nothing more than a flick of your thumb? Bengaluru- and San Francisco-based startup Aina believes the next phase of artificial intelligence will be less about asking machines questions and more about letting them anticipate what people need. At a private launch event in Bengaluru, the startup unveiled an AI-powered smart ring that combines a colour display, voice commands and gesture-based controls. Priced at $499 (Rs 47,000...
article_content:
What if booking a cab, sending a message or managing a meeting required nothing more than a flick of your thumb? Bengaluru- and San Francisco-based startup Aina believes the next phase of artificial intelligence will be less about asking machines questions and more about letting them anticipate what people need. At a private launch event in Bengaluru, the startup unveiled an AI-powered smart ring that combines a colour display, voice commands and gesture-based controls. Priced at $499 (Rs 47,000), the device is available for pre-order at a limited early-bird price starting at $399 (Rs 37,700), with shipments expected to begin in January 2027. Unlike conventional smart rings, which largely focus on health and fitness tracking, Aina wants its device to become an everyday interface between users and AI agents. The premise is simple: AI agents are getting smarter, but using them still involves unlocking phones, navigating apps and approving individual actions. Aina wants to reduce that friction. Its proposition revolves around a question displayed during the launch presentation: What if AI didn't wait to be asked?

An AI ring that anticipates your next move  To simplify these interactions, Aina has built its ring around three features: Cues, Voice and Remote.

Cues uses contextual information, including routines and connected applications, to anticipate what users might want to do next. For instance, if someone regularly books a cab around the same time each morning, the ring could suggest booking a ride without waiting for an explicit request. At the launch event, Aina demonstrated a ride-booking interaction that illustrated how everyday transactions could be completed through minimal gestures.

The ring can be operated using a five-way joystick-like control, allowing users to approve or reject suggestions with their thumb without reaching for a smartphone. Aina says its context-aware intelligence can learn users' routines and anticipate relevant actions over the next 15 minutes, drawing on information from the iPhone, Mac and connected services. The company showcased integrations involving Uber, Apple Music, Spotify, phone calls, calendar meetings, smart home controls and email actions.

The second interaction method, Voice, allows users to dictate notes, set reminders, send messages and issue commands. Aina also showcased use cases involving WhatsApp and Telegram, alongside Mac dictation through Wispr Flow. The third feature, Remote, turns the ring into a controller for connected devices. According to the company, users can manage music, phone calls, smart home appliances and meeting controls without picking up another device.

What goes into the $499 ring?  According to specifications presented at the Bengaluru launch, the ring weighs less than 13 grams and features a titanium body, full-colour display, haptic feedback and directional audio. The company claims up to 18 hours of battery life and plans to offer the device in four colours: Eclipse Black, Amber Gold, Mercury Silver and Slate Titanium, across seven sizes. Aina also highlighted a five-way control mechanism called the Shifter, which works alongside its gesture-based interface.

The startup says the ring will come with an open developer platform, allowing third-party developers to build new interactions and integrations. It also showcased support for AI agent platforms including Muse, Grokbot and Instinct. The company currently supports iOS and Mac, with further integrations expected to be announced later. Whether its open platform translates into a substantial developer ecosystem will become clearer once the device reaches customers.

From Ultrahuman to Aina  Aina was founded by Apoorv Shankar, who previously served as vice-president of hardware at Bengaluru-based wearable technology company Ultrahuman. Shankar founded Aina in May 2025 as a human-computer interaction lab, focusing on how people could interact with intelligent software beyond conventional screens and keyboards. The startup  raised $5.5 million in seed funding in July 2026 , as previously reported by YourStory. The round was led by Redstart Labs and 360 ONE Asset, with participation from MIXI Global Investments, Antler, Blume Founders Fund and angel investors including CRED founder Kunal Shah and Razorpay co-founders Harshil Mathur and Shashank Kumar. The funding was earmarked for commercialising its AI-first hardware interface and expanding its engineering and product teams.

Aina says it spent around 15 months developing the technology and began testing the ring with a limited group of users in October 2026.

Can a ring replace everyday smartphone interactions?  Aina's launch comes as technology companies experiment with new ways of bringing AI into daily life. While smartphones remain the dominant interface for digital services, the rise of AI agents is prompting startups to rethink how people give instructions, approve actions and receive information. Aina's approach is to make that interface smaller and more contextual, with users retaining control over whether suggested actions are executed.

However, at $499, the ring is a premium purchase, particularly when smartphones and smartwatches already perform many of the functions it promises. Its usefulness will depend on how accurately its AI anticipates user needs, how reliably it works with third-party services and whether the thumb-based controls become intuitive enough for daily use. Battery life, voice recognition and application support will also matter when the product moves beyond controlled demonstrations. For now, Aina's claims remain to be tested at scale, with commercial deliveries planned for January 2027.
ai_summary: What if booking a cab, sending a message or managing a meeting required nothing more than a flick of your thumb. Bengaluru- and San Francisco-based startup Aina believes the next phase of artificial intelligence will be less about asking machines questions and more about letting them anticipate what people need.
main_event: Aina launches Rs 47,000 ring to bring AI agents to your fingertips

The startup track focuses on young businesses working in areas such as clean mobility, circular economy, waste management, and sustainable supply chains. article_content:
Honasa Consumer, the parent company of beauty & personal care brand Mamaearth, registered an 87% year-on-year (YoY) rise in net profit for the second quarter of the current fiscal, while revenue rose 36% driven by strong growth across categories.

The company reported a net profit of Rs 73.24 crore in Q2FY27, compared with Rs 39.22 crore in the similar period of FY26. Revenue during the quarter was Rs 731.18 crore, compared with Rs 538.06 crore a year ago.

According to Honasa Consumer, the second quarter revenue growth is the highest it has recorded since its public listing in November 2023.

However, sequentially, profit fell from Rs 90.44 crore in the first quarter. Revenue in the first quarter was Rs 755.94 crore.

Honasa also operates the brands Dermacare and Aqualogica.

CEO Varun Alagh said, “At the brand level, each business is writing its own growth story. Mamaearth has sustained its high-teens growth, The Derma Co. continues to grow profitably. Our Younger Brands grew over 45% YoY, reflecting highlighting the potential of our emerging portfolio.”

He added that each brand has a distinct consumer, proposition and opportunity and the goal is to build a sustainable business in each category.

The omnichannel channel retailer noted that its offline business saw growth, with general trade expanding to over 3.2 lakh outlets and modern trade (large-format retail outlets) recording a 40% YoY growth in offtake.

“As we enter the next phase of growth, we will continue to push the boundaries of innovation, deepen our presence in core categories, and make our products accessible to more consumers across channels,” said Ghazal Alagh, CIO & Co-founder, Honasa Consumer.

For the six months of the fiscal year, the company reported a revenue of Rs 1,487.13 crore, a YoY growth of 31%. The net profit for the period was Rs 163.69 crore, a YoY rise of 103%.

title: When code is cheap, trust is not: Inside the AI-era engineering roundtable

The roundtable, moderated by  Ipshita Basu , brought t...
article_content:
AI has made writing code faster than ever, but the harder question for engineering leaders is what happens after the code is written. At a roundtable on operating engineering in the AI era, leaders from logistics, food tech, healthcare, telecom, fintech, ecommerce and higher education compared notes on scaling with AI without losing reliability, security or control. The shared view was that speed is no longer the hard part. Governing it is.

The roundtable, moderated by  Ipshita Basu , brought together  Manjunath Nakshathri , Head of Engineering, Mojro;  Shobhit Suman , CPO, HungerBox;  Pavan Kumar A T , CTO, Digii (DigiiCampus);  Pranjal Nadhani , Co-founder and CTO, Cautio;  Kenil Paul , VP, Technology and Solutions, 6D Technologies;  Rimjhim Agrawal , Co-founder and CTO, BrainSightAI;  Dhruv Rastogi , Chief AI Officer, MediAssist;  Chandrakesh Pandey , Senior Vice President of Technology, Niyo Solutions Inc.;  Achal Sharma , CTO, TechnoSport;  Sunil Kumar , Director Engineering, Meesho; and  Anshul Sharma , Director Engineering, Scaler.

The session was hosted by  groundcover  and  Data Signals  in partnership with  YourStory , and was led on the host side by  Paul Trebe , Head of Sales and Partnership, groundcover, and  Satish Dange , Founder, Data Signals.

Where the bottleneck has moved  Participants agreed that AI has compressed build time, but the pressure has shifted downstream. When agents generate large volumes of code, the questions become who reviews it, who tests it and who monitors dozens of deployments a day. Several leaders said their teams now spend more time on design, context and governance than on writing components. Agents are only as effective as the context they receive, and few organizations yet have repository knowledge, documentation and templates in a form an agent can reliably use.

Drawing the line on autonomy  The room converged on a progressive approach. Reversible, read-only work, such as fetching data or generating reports, can go to agents with little friction. Irreversible actions, such as deleting data or running database updates, stay behind human review. Blast radius matters as much as reversibility. If a wrong call could affect end users or production systems, a person makes it.

One of the participants described a ‘ four eyes’  model in which AI does the maker work of reading and analyzing, deterministic rules deliver clear yes or no outcomes, and a human signs off. Another speaker described risk scoring based on severity and occurrence, which focuses human review on medium and high criticality items. Others drew the line by specialization, letting engineers use agents freely in their own domain while production ownership stays with people who can debug at 2 AM.

That scenario also surfaced in a hopeful form. Instead of waking an engineer, an agent can investigate an incident and hand over a report by morning, leaving the decision with a human. Trust, participants said, will build gradually, much as it did with online payments, and the line will keep moving.

Accountability and the skills question  Accountability drew firm agreement: it cannot be delegated to a model. Leaders remain answerable for what agents do. AI works as an intelligence multiplier, one participant noted, which means mistakes are amplified as quickly as good decisions.

Skill erosion sparked livelier debate. Some saw a shift in skills, much as calculators changed arithmetic. Others, particularly in healthcare, worried about losing the expertise needed to judge AI output at all. One practical answer was to decide deliberately where AI drafts and where humans do.

Data control as a design decision  For telecom and healthcare leaders, data control is settled at design time. Models cannot simply run in a public cloud when regulators, tenancy separation, and residency rules apply, and one mistake can bring heavy penalties. Others stressed governance from the first stage, covering what data is ingested, what is used for training versus inference, and how it is masked or de-identified. Concerns about intellectual property and bias also led to a call to vet AI tools as rigorously as new hires.

Observability for an agentic world  Observability ran through every topic. Teams described tracing agent inputs, decisions, and handoffs so they can see why an agent acted as it did and correct it. One ecommerce team learned the cost of underinvesting: a ranking change left every dashboard green while business impact surfaced days later, and the root cause analysis took more than a week. It has since built a change ledger, lineage, a system graph, and a debugging agent that proposes ranked hypotheses.

The observability view was that it can no longer sit apart from development. Paul Trebe put it plainly: “You can no longer decouple observability from development.” Agents need context-rich data to act well, he noted, and the agents themselves must be monitored, since AI traces can run to 500,000 lines that only other agents can realistically parse.

What comes next  No one claimed a finished playbook. Open questions remain on measuring agent reliability and return on investment, protecting data and IP, and keeping engineers sharp enough to challenge what AI produces.

Still, the conversation pointed to a common direction. Give developers room to move fast, but build the guardrails first. Keep humans in charge of irreversible and high-impact calls, and widen automation as trust is earned. Several participants argued that standing still is not an option, since competitors will not wait. The real test of the AI era is less about how quickly teams can build and more about how confidently they can run what they have built.
ai_summary: AI has made writing code faster than ever, but the harder question for engineering leaders is what happens after the code is written. At a roundtable on operating engineering in the AI era, leaders from logistics, food tech, healthcare, telecom, fintech, ecommerce and higher education compared notes on scaling with AI without losing reliability, security or control.
main_event: When code is cheap, trust is not: Inside the AI-era engineering roundtable

article_content:
November began on a positive note for the Indian startup ecosystem with venture capital funding seeing a sharp rise, after four weeks of tepid inflow of funds.

The total funding for the first week of November was $263 million across 23 deals, compared to just $115 million in the  previous week .

This week saw two key breakthroughs.

First, the total funding amount was well above $200 million. This is significant as the funds raised in the preceding four weeks were below $200 million. Second, after four weeks, the Indian startup ecosystem saw a $100-million transaction from jewellery brand GIVA.

These developments provide a big boost to the startup ecosystem, which has been struggling to raise large amounts of capital. Additionally, a potential investor slump in AI companies in the aftermath of the US mid-term elections could benefit Indian startups.

This is because much of the money is concentrated in the AI segment in the US. Now one can expect some sort of rebalancing in capital distribution with certain funds flowing into India. However, it is early days to comment on how the capital will flow into the country.

Key transactions  Jewellery brand  GIVA  raised $100 million led by Multiples Alternate Asset Management.

Consumer AI startup  EloElo Group  raised $80 million from Hornbill Capital, NBCUniversal, MIT Investment Co, Play Ventures, Kalaari Capital, Waterbridge Ventures and Griffin Gaming Partners.

Healthtech startup  Clinics On Cloud  raised $12.5 million from Model42.

Peppermint Robotics  raised Rs 100 crore (~$10.5 million) from pi Ventures, Crane Venture Partners and Asiana Fund.

Speciality chemicals startup  altM  raised $10.3 million from Rainmatter by Zerodha, Mela Ventures, Omnivore, Theia Ventures, Aureolis Ventures and Spectrum Impact.

Cleantech startup  Two Point O Capital (TW.O)  raised $10 million from Transition Venture Capital, Omnivore and angel investors.

Wealthtech startup  PowerUp Money  raised $10 million from Flourish Ventures, Peak XV Partners, Accel, Blume Ventures, Kae Capital, 8i Ventures and DeVC.

Spacetech startup  Cosmoserve Space  raised $6 million from Rebright Partners, Aranya Holdings, Naandi Ventures, AUM Ventures and Shakti VC.

author: YourStory
description:
MakeMyTrip on Friday announced it has acquired a majority stake in 'Quick Ride', a technology-led shared mobility platform, for an undisclosed sum.

The investment provides an opportunity for MakeMyTrip to establish its presence in the shared mobility/ride pooling segment, complementary to the group's existing ground transportation portfolio, the company stated.

Bengaluru-headquartered Quick Ride is a technology-led, asset-light shared mobility platform that connects people travelling along sim...
article_content:
MakeMyTrip on Friday announced it has acquired a majority stake in 'Quick Ride', a technology-led shared mobility platform, for an undisclosed sum.

The investment provides an opportunity for MakeMyTrip to establish its presence in the shared mobility/ride pooling segment, complementary to the group's existing ground transportation portfolio, the company stated.

Bengaluru-headquartered Quick Ride is a technology-led, asset-light shared mobility platform that connects people travelling along similar routes, enabling affordable ride pooling for everyday commutes.

The 'Quick Ride' brand and its ride pooling business underwent an internal restructuring and are now housed under a new entity, Co Ride Mobility Private Limited. MakeMyTrip has acquired the Quick Ride brand and its ride pooling business with a majority stake in this entity.

Quick Ride's promoters will continue to lead the business. Its erstwhile EV taxi business will remain with the predecessor entity, iDisha Info Labs Private Limited, MakeMyTrip stated.

Rajesh Magow, Co-Founder & Group Chief Executive Officer, MakeMyTrip, said, "As part of our expansion strategy, we have pursued selective strategic partnerships, investments and acquisitions that complement and strengthen our existing business and expand the breadth and depth of our offerings. Ride pooling gives us a presence in high-frequency daily commutes within cities, as well as intercity travel".

Quick Ride will be housed under our ground transport business, and we will bring the learnings from building redBus in India and overseas markets to grow and scale the business, he added.

KNM Rao, Founder and CEO, Quick Ride, said, "Becoming part of the MakeMyTrip group is an important milestone for our team and for the community of users who have placed their trust in us. We look forward to drawing on MakeMyTrip's reach and experience in travel to further scale the business".

In recent years, MakeMyTrip has made acquisitions across travel segments, including Savaari in car rental services, Happay in corporate travel and expense management, Flamingo Transworld in regional group holiday packages and through strategic minority investment in Atlys in visa processing.

article_content:
Bihar Museum in Patna was recently ranked ahead of New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Louvre in Paris. The museum has secured the ninth place on The World's 100 Best Museums 2026, published by German travel guide Worth a Journey. The Met stands tenth and the Louvre 31st. It is the only Indian institution on the list and the highest-ranked museum in Asia. For a museum that opened barely a decade ago, it is a significant achievement. More so because there was a time when the project itself faced serious opposition, with questions raised about its cost, relevance and the way it was being executed.

Reflecting on the recognition in a recent LinkedIn post, YourStory Founder and CEO Shradha Sharma recalled the roles played by two people in getting the museum built: Nitish Kumar, who championed the project as Bihar's Chief Minister, and 1992-batch IAS officer Chanchal Kumar, who was entrusted with its execution. When the state government proposed spending nearly Rs 500 crore on a world-class museum in Patna, the decision attracted criticism. Why should a state struggling with basic infrastructure invest so much in a museum? Who would visit it? Could the money have been better spent elsewhere? According to Sharma, even people within the political establishment questioned the proposal. Nitish Kumar, however, stood by the project, convinced that Bihar needed an institution worthy of its historical and cultural heritage.

This Diwali, this one is for everyone who has ever been written off.

A museum in Patna now ranks above the Met in New York and the Louvre in Paris. The Bihar Museum is 9th on the World’s 100 Best Museums list for 2026 put out by the German travel guide Worth a Journey. The Met is…  pic.twitter.com/1sUAvkUqfh

— Shradha Sharma (@SharmaShradha)  November 6, 2026

" data-type="tweet">   This Diwali, this one is for everyone who has ever been written off.

A museum in Patna now ranks above the Met in New York and the Louvre in Paris. The Bihar Museum is 9th on the World’s 100 Best Museums list for 2026 put out by the German travel guide Worth a Journey. The Met is…  pic.twitter.com/1sUAvkUqfh

— Shradha Sharma (@SharmaShradha)  November 6, 2026

Getting the museum built  The challenges began with the land. According to Sharma, the proposed 13-acre site had seven government bungalows, some occupied by senior officials and a state minister. Getting the occupants to vacate required considerable administrative effort and legal intervention. She also recounted an incident in which men allegedly linked to local politicians entered the construction site demanding subcontracts, prompting police intervention. The museum was designed by Pritzker Prize-winning Japanese architect Fumihiko Maki in collaboration with Mumbai-based architectural firm Opolis, while Larsen & Toubro was selected to construct it. But appointing internationally recognised architects and an established construction company was only part of the challenge. Getting the project completed was another matter.

The museum also faced judicial scrutiny. In June 2015, the Patna High Court, hearing a public interest litigation, criticised the expenditure of approximately Rs 500 crore and questioned the transparency of the contracting process. The court held that the project was not in the public interest but declined to halt construction because the building was nearing completion. Those findings remain an important part of the museum's history. Its international recognition does not erase the questions raised about public spending and governance, although the institution has since gained recognition well beyond Bihar.

Sharma credits much of the execution to Chanchal Kumar, who held the dual responsibility of Secretary of Art and Culture and Secretary of the Building Construction Department.

The arrangement meant that both the museum's cultural vision and its construction came under the same officer. Sharma said she recently read his account of how the museum came together and was struck by how little he spoke about his own contribution. Behind the finished building were years of navigating approvals, land disputes, administrative resistance and the many complications that accompany a large public project. In Sharma's telling, Nitish Kumar's political backing and Chanchal Kumar's persistence were crucial to seeing it through.

A reminder of Bihar's strengths  For Sharma, who grew up in Bihar, the recognition carries a more personal meaning. Few places in India can claim the kind of historical and intellectual inheritance that Bihar possesses. Bodh Gaya is where the Buddha attained enlightenment. Vaishali is closely associated with Mahavira. Ancient Pataliputra was the capital of the Mauryan Empire under Ashoka, while Patna is the birthplace of Guru Gobind Singh. Nalanda and Vikramshila were among the great centres of learning in ancient India. Yet Bihar's present-day image often has little to do with this extraordinary history. Its achievements are celebrated in textbooks, but the state has struggled to build contemporary institutions that attract the same admiration.

Sharma drew on an episode from the Ramayana to explain what the museum means to her. Before Hanuman makes his leap across the ocean to Lanka, Jambavan reminds him of the strength he has forgotten. Bihar, she suggested, needed a similar reminder of what it is capable of achieving. The museum offers one. Its galleries house sculptures, coins, manuscripts and artefacts that bring the region's history to life, including the celebrated Didarganj Yakshi. And now, a German travel publication has placed it among the world's ten best museums, ahead of institutions with far longer histories and international reputations. The ranking is one publication's assessment, but it is nevertheless a significant moment for a museum that faced so many questions during its creation.
ai_summary: Bihar Museum in Patna was recently ranked ahead of New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Louvre in Paris. The museum has secured the ninth place on The World's 100 Best Museums 2026, published by German travel guide Worth a Journey.
main_event: How a Rs 500 Cr bet put Bihar Museum ahead of the Met and Louvre

article_content:
Eternal founder Deepinder Goyal has posted a series of updates and clarifications on X amid backlash from some Indian doctors who criticised his brain-monitoring wearable Temple. Describing Temple as “an ambitious project”, Goyal gave a detailed explanation on what the team is building.

“The team is delusional enough to think we can build this. And we will,” he wrote on Friday. He also later added that the first 10,000 orders will not have to pay a subscription to use Temple.

Criticising the doctors, he said, "All my emotion last night was directed at a few influencer doctors, who are more influencers than doctors. They did not read our research in detail, and spread twisted facts to call something new a scam. They get views by piling on us."

The open debate started on Thursday when Goyal took to X to defend the device. He said, “First and foremost, a business lesson: if Temple were a scam, and any of what we said weren't true, people would know it in just a few days of using Temple.”

He also said the device features a 14-day no-question return policy. “If the product doesn't work, it fails out of the gate and the company dies before recovering a tenth of its R&D," he said.

Goyal is currently Vice Chairman and Non-Executive Director of Eternal (parent company of Zomato). He is also the founder of healthtech wearable startup Temple and LAT Aerospace.

In the post, Goyal highlighted that $30 million was invested in building the device, including $20 million of his personal money. 

Calling this his purpose, he said it's not about the money. “I have enough of it to last for generations. My incentives are fully aligned with getting the science right. I am not staking a reputation earned over 20 years on making a quick buck.”

Goyal argued that most wearable companies start with internal studies. He referred to Whoop which shipped its fitness band in 2015 but the first published validation happened a few years later. He also added that Temple had a higher standard. "Pre-prints are a step prior to peer reviewed publications, and they are coming up."

Reposing confidence in the product, he said, “We stand by our science and our methods. Each of our claims is easily verifiable by individuals and institutions alike, and you will see a lot of independent studies come up on their own when the device becomes available to use.”

Moreover, he added that this device is a fitness tracker, and wellness device, not a medical device. “If at some point, we clinically validate any of our metrics, we will let you know.”

title: Northern Arc's diversified debt fund hits first close at over Rs 400 Cr
author: YourStory
description:

article_content:
Northern Arc Investment Managers, the asset management arm of Northern Arc Capital, has announced the first close of its Northern Arc Diversified Debt Fund with commitments of more than Rs 400 crore from institutions, family offices, ultra-high-net-worth individuals (UHNIs) and high-net-worth individuals (HNIs).

The fund is the firm's 15th private credit vehicle. It is a sector-agnostic Category II Alternative Investment Fund (AIF) focused on performing private credit, rated AA (SO) by CareEdge Ratings. It targets a corpus of Rs 1,500 crore, with a greenshoe option of Rs 500 crore that could take it to Rs 2,000 crore. The fund has a five-year tenure and targets a 16% XIRR.

The announcement coincides with the maturity of the Northern Arc India Impact Fund, which channelled global capital into financial inclusion opportunities across India. Over its tenure, the fund supported 60 businesses across credit cycles, with gross deployment of over Rs 1,398 crore at the fund level, backed by UHNIs, family offices, and domestic and global institutional investors.

Commenting on the announcements, Ashish Mehrotra, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer, Northern Arc Capital, said, "The first close of the Northern Arc Diversified Debt Fund reflects continued investor interest in private credit and its evolving role in sophisticated investment portfolios. The maturity of our Northern Arc India Impact Fund further demonstrates our experience in managing private credit investments across credit cycles. Together, these milestones reinforce our focus on disciplined credit selection, portfolio diversification and risk management.”

He added, “Over the past decade, we have built a diversified private credit platform that has deployed over Rs. 16,500 crores across 15 AIFs and two PMS offerings and served more than 1,500 investors across institutional and wealth segments. As private credit becomes an increasingly strategic allocation for investors, we remain focused on connecting capital with businesses across sectors while creating opportunities for risk-adjusted returns."

Since its inception in 2014, Northern Arc Investment Managers has launched 15 funds, of which seven have fully matured, delivering returns at a weighted average XIRR of over 14.5%, in line with targeted returns, without any extension or principal loss to investors, the company said. It has cumulatively distributed over Rs 10,000 crore of principal and coupon since inception.

Separately, Northern Arc Capital reported a 41% year-on-year growth in consolidated profit after tax to Rs 129 crore in Q2 FY27, while net interest income rose 32% to Rs 425 crore. Lending assets under management grew 34% to Rs 19,003 crore, supported by a 64% rise in direct lending AUM to Rs 12,502 crore, which now accounts for 66% of the overall portfolio. Credit costs improved by 11 basis points to 2.66%."

The fund is the firm's 15th private credit vehicle.

title: VibeCode30 2026: The 30 AI-built products to watch from India
author: YourStory
description:
The next generation of technology builders may not all be software engineers. They could be students, product managers, marketing professionals, small business owners or simply individuals who understand a problem well enough to solve it.

article_content:
The next generation of technology builders may not all be software engineers. They could be students, product managers, marketing professionals, small business owners or simply individuals who understand a problem well enough to solve it.

With AI-powered coding tools lowering the technical and financial barriers to software development, more people are turning ideas into working products without conventional development teams or large budgets.

Recognising this shift, YourStory launched VibeCode30, a new initiative presented by Hostinger, at the 17th edition of TechSparks 2026 in Bengaluru. The inaugural cohort celebrates 30 AI-native products built to solve real-world problems, from simplifying house hunting and improving financial literacy to supporting healthcare professionals and making everyday business operations more efficient.

Unlike traditional startup showcases, Vibecode30 focuses on products and their builders, whether they work independently or in small teams, with or without formal coding experience.

The inaugural edition received 207 applications from across the country, including smaller centres such as Ajmer, Silvassa, Sugauli, and Thoothukudi. The final 30 products represent 19 industries and 11 cities, reflecting the range of problems that AI-native builders are addressing. Importantly, every selected product had moved beyond the prototype stage and was accessible to real users.

The cohort demonstrates that while AI can accelerate software development, understanding the problem, validating the output, and improving the product remain essential. It also shows how smaller, highly specific problems can now become viable opportunities for innovation.

Meet the VibeCode30 2026 cohort:

AjmerAstro  Built by Himanshu Dadhich in Ajmer,  AjmerAstro  is an AI-powered astrology platform offering personalised Vedic and KP astrology guidance in English and Hindi, with a system that remembers previous conversations.

AlgoTrips  Delhi-based Tushar Garg built  AlgoTrips , an AI travel planner that creates day-by-day itineraries with live pricing for flights, hotels, activities, and transfers, allowing users to plan and book trips.

Arena  Developed by Bengaluru-based Prathik Arunkumar and Arun Kumar,  Arena  helps schools manage house competitions through live leaderboards, digital scoring, and real-time updates.

Beet.Health  Built by Vatsl Goswami and Shivanshi Shukla,   Beet.Health  helps nutrition clinics manage appointments, payments, and meal plans while enabling clients to track their progress through a mobile app and WhatsApp assistant.

Bengaluru.rent  Created by Bengaluru-based Harshit Anand,  Bengaluru.rent  is a free platform where tenants anonymously share rental prices and connect directly with property owners and prospective flatmates without brokers.

Benki.tech  Developed by Sonam Rao, Avinash Narsimah, and Kumaraswamy BV in Bengaluru,  Benki.tech  uses a simulated panel of customers to help businesses pressure test business ideas, marketing messages, and product offerings.

Bloom UPSC  Built by Bengaluru-based former banker Guru Sasidhar Pattem,  Bloom UPSC  provides civil services aspirants with study materials, practice questions, answer evaluation, and video lessons in English and Telugu.

Boolean Beyond  Coimbatore-based  Boolean Beyond  developed BeyondSave, a WhatsApp-based platform that enables local jewellery businesses to manage customer savings schemes, payments, and balances.

ElderNest  Bengaluru-based Shubham Jain created  ElderNest  to help families discover and compare senior care homes across India, with information on services, pricing and admission support.

Gold Investment Monitor  Created by Surendhran Sivalingam in Coimbatore,  Gold Investment Monitor  analyses 24 market signals and combines them into a single verdic to help Indian households assess whether to buy gold or wait.

Holt  Built by Bhubaneswar-based Debashis Nayak,  Holt  is an open-source memory tool for AI coding assistants that runs locally on a developer’s machine, helping them retain project context across sessions.

IndianCoffeeBeans.com  Hyderabad-based Abhishek Thrilok built  IndianCoffeeBeans.com , a searchable directory tracking more than 90 Indian specialty coffee roasters and 1,200+ coffees.

Indiccore  Developed by Sahil Gulati and his team in Gurugram,  Indiccore  helps civil services aspirants analyse mock-test performance, identify weaknesses, and improve examination strategies.

Madhav.live  Built by Ashish Singh Shekhawat in Bengaluru,  Madhav.live  lets users talk to Krishna about everyday problems and receive guidance rooted in the Bhagavad Gita, in the language they are most comfortable with.

MagicSlides.app  Created by Bengaluru-based Sanskar Tiwari,  MagicSlides  instantly converts topics, documents, web links, and YouTube videos into presentations, supporting more than 100 languages.

Mira  Developed by Shagun Verma and Abhaya Trivedi in Mumbai,  Mira  is an AI voice assistant that helps short-term rental hosts handle guest enquiries and check property availability, giving small hosts the kind of front desk usually only hotels can afford. 

NextDoor.Company  Built by Sankalp Sinha in Bengaluru,  NextDoor.Company  helps jobseekers discover startups hiring nearby through a map-based platform with company and employment information.

Nomira  Created by Bengaluru-based Prernaa Agarwal,  Nomira  is a women-first travel platform combining safety information, offline maps, travel communities, and group trips.

Orbit Research  Developed by Silvassa-based student Aditya Singh,  Orbit Research  combines academic research tools into a single platform for discovering papers, checking references, preparing manuscripts, and creating presentations.

Penfight  Built by Amarjeet Sarma and his Bengaluru-based team,  Penfight  recreates the popular school desk pen-flicking game as an online multiplayer experience.

Pretend AI  Pune-based Kareena Rogers developed  Pretend AI , an iPhone app that allows users to rehearse conversations with custom AI personas through realistic text exchanges.

RayAI  Created by Reshma Budhia and Swetha Sree Kannan at Chennai-based agency Toss The Coin,  RayAI  helps marketing teams create campaigns, content and design assets using shared brand knowledge and workflows.

Soma  Built by Gurugram-based Saurav Singhal,  Soma  brings together health reports, wearable data, nutrition, and fitness information to provide personalised health insights.

TofuBofu  Hyderabad-based Arnav Neil developed  TofuBofu  to help B2B companies measure and improve how often AI recommends them, as buyers increasingly turn to AI for product research and decision making. 

Vitfinity  Created by Bengaluru-based Pranay Reddy and his team,  Vitfinity  teaches financial literacy to school children through interactive simulations and a 180-lesson curriculum.

Voqalize  Built by Sripathi Krishnan and his Bengaluru-based team,  Voqalize  enables enterprises to integrate multilingual conversational voice AI into software applications.

Whitefield Womania  Developed by Rakshita Dwivedi and Abhishek Dwivedi in Bengaluru,  Whitefield Womania  is a digital directory connecting residents with women-led local businesses.

Youdemy  Created by Bengaluru-based Rohit Ranjan Singh,  Youdemy  organises free YouTube lectures into structured courses with learning streaks, points, and leaderboards.

Zespan  Built by Udupi-based Abhishek N,  Zespan  monitors AI agents operating in enterprise environments, identifies incorrect decisions and helps prevent recurring errors.

Zoku  Developed by Bengaluru-based Priyanshu Dangi,  Zoku  is a voice-first development application that allows software developers to manage multiple AI coding agents simultaneously.

title: AI’s ability to find cyber flaws outpacing firms’ capacity to fix them: Palo Alto Networks' Nikesh Arora
author: YourStory
description:
Nikesh Arora, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Palo Alto Networks, has raised concerns about the growing use of frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models to identify software vulnerabilities and link them into potential attack paths. 

While these capabilities can help strengthen cybersecurity, they could also give attackers faster ways to exploit weaknesses in enterprise systems. The bigger challenge, Arora notes in a LinkedIn  post , is ensuring that organisations can verify, pr...
article_content:
Nikesh Arora, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Palo Alto Networks, has raised concerns about the growing use of frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models to identify software vulnerabilities and link them into potential attack paths. 

While these capabilities can help strengthen cybersecurity, they could also give attackers faster ways to exploit weaknesses in enterprise systems. The bigger challenge, Arora notes in a LinkedIn  post , is ensuring that organisations can verify, prioritise and fix vulnerabilities at the same pace at which AI can discover them.

“Most organizations do not have capacity to patch at the speed needed, especially the smaller ones,” Arora wrote. Smaller businesses often lack security specialists, while larger ones must test fixes against existing applications. He also says models identify different weaknesses, so one model cannot provide complete coverage.

Finding a flaw is only the start. Teams must confirm it, assess the risk, develop a fix, test for disruption and deploy it. False positives, or incorrect alerts, waste time, while untested patches can disrupt services.

The scale is growing. The US National Institute of Standards and Technology said submissions to its National Vulnerability Database rose 263% between 2020 and 2025. It enriched nearly 42,000 records in 2025, but this was still insufficient. In April 2026, it adopted risk-based prioritisation, focusing on exploited flaws and critical software.

AI developers are linking discovery with repair. Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, launched in April 2026 with Palo Alto Networks among its partners, gives selected organisations access to Claude Mythos Preview for defensive security. Anthropic said partners had identified more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity flaws by June and expanded the programme to around 150 additional organisations. 

On November 4, OpenAI reported that a controlled Linux-kernel pipeline generated candidate patches for 948 local privilege-escalation vulnerabilities, which allow a user to gain higher access rights. Human researchers reviewed the findings before reporting them to maintainers.

In India, CERT-In’s November 4 advisory warned of an AI-assisted threat actor targeting non-bank lenders, fintech firms, payment providers and cryptocurrency platforms through machine intelligence and payment APIs. The agency has also issued 2026 guidance on AI-assisted vulnerability defence and AI security auditing.

Arora advocates virtual patching as an interim measure. “The most obvious solution is virtual patching. This is a time tested technology that is currently available with cyber vendors for endpoints, WAF, cloud, network use cases.” 

WAF is a web application firewall, which filters website and application traffic. A virtual patch is a security rule that blocks a known method of exploiting a flaw without changing the affected software. It buys time while a permanent update is tested, but does not remove the weakness. The Open Worldwide Application Security Project cautions that it protects only the traffic the system inspects and attacks variations its rules recognise.

Arora calls for a shared vulnerability clearing house and faster development of protective signatures, or detection rules. He also highlights operational technology, systems that monitor or control physical processes such as energy, water and transport. Patching them can be difficult because downtime may affect safety or essential services.

title: Delhi HC upholds interim protection for BharatPe’s shareholder rights, dismisses Unity Bank’s appeal
author: YourStory
description:
A division bench of the Delhi High Court has dismissed an appeal by Unity Bank, upholding the interim protection granted to BharatPe's parent company RIPL (Resilient Innovations Private Limited) under the Shareholders’ Agreement and affirming the order of a single judge.

The court has now, on two occasions, declined to let the bank and its promoter proceed on reserved matters without the prior written consent of RIPL, as the Shareholders’ Agreement (SHA) requires.

Rejecting the bank’s explanat...
article_content:
A division bench of the Delhi High Court has dismissed an appeal by Unity Bank, upholding the interim protection granted to BharatPe's parent company RIPL (Resilient Innovations Private Limited) under the Shareholders’ Agreement and affirming the order of a single judge.

The court has now, on two occasions, declined to let the bank and its promoter proceed on reserved matters without the prior written consent of RIPL, as the Shareholders’ Agreement (SHA) requires.

Rejecting the bank’s explanation that it had sought RIPL’s consent on Reserved Matters through an “inadvertent error”, the bench called the plea an “argument of desperation and nothing more”. It noted that Unity had expressly sought RIPL’s consent in writing, which showed it knew of the contractual requirement.

The bench reaffirmed that Unity cannot take decisions on Reserved Matters without the prior written consent of RIPL and Centrum, observing that Clause 8 of the SHA explicitly bars any action on such matters without it. It endorsed the single judge’s findings, describing the matter as “elementary”.

The court also rejected Unity’s contention that the Reserve Bank of India had turned down the SHA. It observed that the RBI had never objected to the agreement, which had been submitted to it for approval, and held that the injunction does not obstruct any RBI directive and merely requires enforcement of Clause 8.

Turning down the argument that the SHA cannot override the Articles of Association, the bench noted that Clause 8 opens with a non obstante clause, giving it precedence over the relevant provisions of the Articles.

BharatPe welcomed the decision. A spokesperson said, “The Board must ensure that the Bank complies with the Court’s directions in letter and spirit. We expect the Board to exercise independent judgment, free from undue influence, and act in the interests of the Bank and all its stakeholders, including minority shareholders. Governance processes followed since the Bank’s inception must be respected and applied consistently. They cannot be set aside to favour one shareholder group at the expense of another.

“We expect the Board to guide the Bank in honouring its contractual obligations and ensuring that its actions comply with the Court’s directions. We believe the Hon’ble Division Bench’s decision reinforces the importance of the agreed governance framework and the shareholder rights that formed the basis of the joint venture in 2021. Respect for these commitments is essential to maintaining trust between shareholders and protecting the institution’s long-term interests.”

The ruling reinforces that Unity Bank is bound by the Reserved Matter provisions of the SHA and cannot dismiss its own written requests for shareholder consent as inadvertent errors to avoid its contractual obligations.

The court has now, on two occasions, declined to let the bank and its promoter proceed on reserved matters without the prior written consent of RIPL, as the Shareholders’ Agreement (SHA) requires.
main_event: Delhi HC upholds interim protection for BharatPe’s shareholder rights, dismisses Unity Bank’s appeal
