article_content:
Finnish deeptech company

Vensum Power  has raised €9 million in a Series A funding round co-led by

Lifeline Ventures ,  Larsen & Toubro Group  and  Eviny Ventures . The investment

will support the mass production of its power conversion technology and its expansion

into AI data centres. The new funding brings Vensum Power's total capital

raised to €15.2 million.

Vensum Power develops a

software-defined power conversion platform designed to improve energy

efficiency by reducing electricity losses during power conversion. Its

technology is intended for applications including electric vehicle (EV)

charging, energy storage systems and DC microgrids.

As electricity demand

continues to grow, reducing energy losses during power conversion is becoming

increasingly important. Vensum Power aims to address this challenge through its

software-defined approach, which enables its converters to maintain high efficiency

even when electrical loads change rapidly, helping make more effective use of

available power capacity.

The company is also

targeting AI data centres, where rising electricity requirements and limited

power availability are creating additional challenges. Its technology aims to

improve the efficiency of electricity delivery to computing infrastructure, helping

data centres make better use of their existing power capacity.

According to  Peter Nisula ,

CEO of Vensum Power, the funding marks the company's transition from technology

development to industrial-scale production, while opening opportunities to

apply its technology in AI data centres.

The question in data

centres is no longer only how powerful the chips are, but how efficiently the

used electricity actually reaches them. Thanks to the software-defined

approach, our converters operate consistently at extremely high efficiency even

with rapidly changing loads,

explains Nisula.

With the new capital,

Vensum Power plans to move its power conversion platform into mass production

in 2027, targeting EV charging, energy storage and DC microgrids, while

extending its technology into the AI data centre market.
ai_summary: Finnish deeptech company Vensum Power has raised €9 million in a Series A funding round co-led by Lifeline Ventures , Larsen & Toubro Group and Eviny Ventures . The investment will support the mass production of its power conversion technology and its expansion into AI data centres.
main_event: Vensum Power raises €9M to cut power losses in AI data centres, EV charging and energy storage

author: Tech.eu

article_content:
A London-based startup building AI infrastructure for scientific drug discovery has received backing from the UK government’s Sovereign AI fund and Stripe CEO Patrick Collison.

Potential Sciences  leverages AI, machine learning and quantum chemistry simulations to help researchers understand how molecules behave and interact.

It is pioneering a new approach, with an AI model focused on the fundamental laws of physics, rather than previous experimental data, the startup says.

It says this could make the AI calculations needed to design chemicals 100 times cheaper than at present.

The government’s Sovereign AI fund today confirmed it was backing Potential Sciences, as part of a raise in the tens of millions of dollars. The Sovereign AI fund is also committing compute capacity to Potential Sciences, which was founded in November last year.

It marks the latest bet by the UK government's Sovereign AI fund, whose mission is to ensure that the UK develops, owns and scales key AI firms. Its other bets include chip startup Olix and AI startups Ineffable Intelligence and Callosum.

The seed funding round also includes backing from Twin Path Ventures, Odyssey, Portfolio Ventures, Blue Wire Capital, rule30, Nauta Capital and Lightfield Equity, as well as angel investment from Collison and other angel investors.

Potential Sciences declined to disclose exactly how much was raised or its valuation.

Potential Sciences was founded by doctor Hatem Helal, a former Graphcore executive, the chip designed acquired by SoftBank, in 2025.

Sovereign AI Investment Partner Joséphine Kant said: "I first met Hatem in Cambridge, and he immediately struck me as a formidable founder. He combines technical excellence with low ego and unapologetic ambition. He knows the science in extraordinary detail, but he’s also deliberate about bringing in people who are exceptional in areas different from his own.

"Potential Sciences have the ambition to become a true frontier lab for chemistry, with the potential to fundamentally change how the field works."
ai_summary: A London-based startup building AI infrastructure for scientific drug discovery has received backing from the UK government’s Sovereign AI fund and Stripe CEO Patrick Collison. Potential Sciences leverages AI, machine learning and quantum chemistry simulations to help researchers understand how molecules behave and interact.
main_event: UK Sovereign AI fund and Stripe CEO back Potential Sciences in multi-million-dollar raise

title: Five UK startups secure eight patents from Panasonic, Nokia, NEC and DENSO
author: Tech.eu
description:

The five winners of IPHatch UK 2026 have secured eight patents originating from Panasonic,  Nokia, NEC and DENSO, giving them access to innovations that would ordinarily be far beyond the reach of young businesses.  The achievement follows a highly competitive selection process for the fourth annua...
article_content:
Five UK startups have won the rights to patented technologies developed by some of the world's largest corporations, a prize that could transform their ability to compete at home and internationally.

The five winners of IPHatch UK 2026 have secured eight patents originating from Panasonic,  Nokia, NEC and DENSO, giving them access to innovations that would ordinarily be far beyond the reach of young businesses.  The achievement follows a highly competitive selection process for the fourth annual UK  competition.

Twenty-one startups were shortlisted for the final pitch day at City of Glasgow  College, and five were selected.  Winners also gain a direct relationship with the corporations behind the technology, which could open doors to future collaboration, investment and international markets.  The five successful companies are:

•  CALMS International  (West Midlands), an enterprise software company, awarded  an NEC patent

• Cyber Nandhini (Aberdeen), a cybersecurity business, awarded a Nokia patent

•  The Discourse AI  (Suffolk), an education technology and AI company, awarded two  Panasonic patents

•  Mixd Reality  (Staffordshire), an augmented reality and education technology  company, awarded a Panasonic patent

• RS9 Technologies (West Midlands), a cybersecurity and AI business, awarded three  DENSO patents

As AI accelerates, patents could become an even bigger competitive advantage  AI is rapidly cutting the time and cost of building software, making it harder for businesses to rely on their technology alone to stay ahead of competitors.

Building on an existing, granted patent can reduce R&D time and cost for a startup, and give it patented technology developed by a global corporation.

For major corporations, the model puts valuable but underused patents to work through ambitious startups, rather than leaving them sitting in corporate portfolios.

For smaller businesses, it offers a rare chance to build on years of corporate R&D,  strengthening their technology, competitive position and potential for international growth.

Deepak Pathak, European Ambassador for Piece Future /IPHatch, said:

"Britain has some extraordinary entrepreneurs, but imagine what more they could achieve if we connected them directly with the technology, expertise and resources of the world's largest companies.

We're opening doors that would ordinarily be closed to smaller businesses, giving them valuable technology, stronger protection against competition and opportunities for future partnerships with global giants.“

Operated by  Piece Future, IPHatch has commercialised more than 350 patents and welcomed more than  100 startups through 14 competitions across 12 markets, connecting entrepreneurs with technologies developed by multinational corporations.

Lead image: Deepak Pathak, now European Ambassador for Piece Future / IPHatch, presenting at the IPHatch UK launch event.  Photo: IPHatch.

The five winners of IPHatch UK 2026 have secured eight patents originating from Panasonic, Nokia, NEC and DENSO, giving them access to innovations that would ordinarily be far beyond the reach of young businesses.

article_content:
Aftersales product resolution platform  Claimlane  has raised €5.6

million in a Series A funding round led by  Verb Ventures , with participation

from  Skagerak Capital  and  Vendep Capital . The investment will support the

development of customer-specific AI agents and the company's expansion in the

United States.

Claimlane develops a platform that helps brands

and retailers manage product-related issues, including warranty claims,

repairs, replacements, refunds and supplier coordination. Its customers include

Skechers, Black Diamond, tonies and Hummel.

Handling faulty or damaged products often

involves multiple parties across the supply chain, from retailers and

manufacturers to suppliers and repair partners. These processes can be complex

and time-consuming, particularly when businesses rely on disconnected systems

to assess claims, determine responsibility and coordinate resolutions.

Claimlane aims to simplify these operations by

bringing the different stages of aftersales product resolution into a single

platform. The system connects customers, retailers, brands and service

partners, allowing them to share information, assess product issues based on

warranty conditions, supplier agreements and case histories, and coordinate the

actions needed to resolve them. These actions can include arranging repairs,

initiating replacements, processing refunds or issuing credit notes through

connected systems.

By reducing manual administration and improving

access to case information, Claimlane also aims to help businesses identify

recurring product issues, improve supplier relationships and recover value from

products that might otherwise be lost.

We see an opportunity to change the economics of

aftersales across both customer and business relationships. Resolve issues in a

way that earns customer trust, recover more value from products and give teams

time to improve the business. This investment will help us bring AI deeper into

that work and further accelerate our growth in the US,

said  Anders Sommer , CEO

and co-founder of Claimlane.

The new funding will support Claimlane's

development of AI agents tailored to customers' products, policies, supplier

agreements and workflows. These agents are designed to help aftersales teams

assess relevant information, reduce repetitive tasks and manage cases more

efficiently, while maintaining human involvement in decisions that require

judgement.

The company also plans to develop

industry-specific capabilities for sectors including electronics, furniture and

outdoor equipment.

Alongside

product development, Claimlane will use the investment to expand its US

operations and work more closely with brands and retailers in the market. North

America has become the company's largest market for new customers so far this

year.
ai_summary: Aftersales product resolution platform Claimlane has raised €5.6 million in a Series A funding round led by Verb Ventures , with participation from Skagerak Capital and Vendep Capital . The investment will support the development of customer-specific AI agents and the company's expansion in the United States.
main_event: Claimlane bags €5.6M to turn product claims into business value

The fintech, which offers loans, a BNPL product, and a debit card, saw revenues come in at £147.5m for...
article_content:
Zilch , the UK fintech reportedly gearing up for an IPO, has reported a 36 per cent increase in full-year revenues to £147.5m, but losses swelled almost three-fold to £35.9m, its latest financial figures show.

Zilch CEO Philip Belamant heralded the year a “foundational" one for the fintech, which provides various lending products and said this year it had hit $300m (£224m) in annual run rate.

The fintech, which offers loans, a BNPL product, and a debit card, saw revenues come in at £147.5m for the year ending March 2026, helped by customers spending more through their Zilch accounts.

Gross merchandise value (GMV), the value of goods sold through its platform, rose 28 per cent to £2.4bn.

But losses swelled from £12.5m to £35.8m in the period, as it was hit by customer acquisition costs, brand building costs as well as an increased credit loss provision as it took on longer term loans.

Active user numbers increased 21 per cent to 970,000 while average annual spend per active customer rose six per cent to £2,500, Zilch said.

Zilch, which is backed by Goldman Sachs and eBay, was valued at $2bn in a 2021 funding round.

It makes money by fees and its services being advertiser-subsidised.

Zilch is reportedly lining up investment banks for an IPO as early as next year.

Belamant, CEO and co-founder, Zilch, said: “FY26 was a foundational year for Zilch. We delivered strong financial growth while making deliberate investments in our products, technology

and infrastructure to strengthen the business and position ourselves for the next phase of expansion.

“We’re confident in the strength and profitability of our business model, and we’re now seeing the results of those investments. Reaching a $300m annual run rate and delivering two consecutive quarters of adjusted profit before tax demonstrates how the foundations we built during FY26 are translating into accelerated growth and stronger financial performance.”
ai_summary: Zilch , the UK fintech reportedly gearing up for an IPO, has reported a 36 per cent increase in full-year revenues to £147.5m, but losses swelled almost three-fold to £35.9m, its latest financial figures show. Zilch CEO Philip Belamant heralded the year a “foundational" one for the fintech, which provides various lending products and said this year it had hit $300m (£224m) in annual run rate.
main_event: Zilch sees revenues uplift but losses increase

Beyond the...
article_content:
European healthtech investment in  H1 2026  was driven by

large funding rounds, with continued interest in biotechnology, medical devices

and AI-powered healthcare solutions.

The UK attracted significant investment, led by major rounds

for Isomorphic Labs and Oviva. The ten largest transactions totalled

approximately €2.59 billion, with Isomorphic Labs accounting for around 69 per

cent of that amount, highlighting the concentration of capital among a small

number of companies.

Beyond these major deals, funding supported a range of

technologies, including AI-driven drug discovery, automated diagnostics,

robotic blood collection and digital chronic disease management.

For further insights into funding trends across the European

technology ecosystem, check out Tech.eu's  Funding Explorer , free and open to

everyone.

Here are the companies that raised the most in H1 2026.

Amount raised in H1 2026: $2.1B

Isomorphic Labs  is an AI-driven drug discovery company developing computational technologies to improve the design and development of medicines.

The company uses advanced AI models to study molecular structures and interactions. Its Isomorphic Labs Drug Design Engine (IsoDDE) builds on advances in protein structure prediction to support the identification and development of potential treatments, including for cancer and immune disorders.

In May 2026, Isomorphic Labs raised  $2.1 billion  in Series B funding to support further development and deployment of IsoDDE, expansion of its therapeutic pipeline and recruitment across AI, engineering, drug design and clinical teams.

Amount raised in H1 2026: €200M

Combining digital technology with clinical expertise,  Oviva  provides personalised programmes for managing obesity and other chronic health conditions.

Its platform integrates a medical app with remote support from healthcare professionals, including dietitians and doctors. AI is used to personalise treatment pathways and support clinical teams, while its services are integrated into healthcare systems across several European markets.

In January 2026, Oviva announced a  €200 million  Series D transaction, comprising new investment and secondary share sales. The financing is intended to support the expansion of its digital healthcare programmes, including treatments for hypertension and type 2 diabetes, and broaden access to chronic disease management.

Amount raised in H1 2026: €100M

Specialising in biosimilar medicines,  Alvotech  develops and manufactures biological treatments designed to provide alternatives to existing approved biologic drugs.

Based in Reykjavík, the company operates across research, development and manufacturing, with products targeting conditions including autoimmune disorders, eye diseases, osteoporosis and cancer. Its activities cover the development of biosimilars through to their production and commercialisation in international markets.

In January 2026, Alvotech secured a  €100 million  senior term loan facility from GoldenTree Asset Management. The debt financing will strengthen liquidity, support research and development, and provide operational flexibility as the company expands manufacturing capacity and prepares additional product launches.

Amount raised in H1 2026: $100M

CeQur  develops wearable medical devices designed to simplify insulin delivery for people living with diabetes. Its main product, CeQur Simplicity, is a discreet, wearable patch that allows patients to administer mealtime insulin without repeated injections. The technology is intended to make daily diabetes management more convenient while supporting adherence to prescribed insulin treatment.

In June 2026, CeQur closed a  $100 million  Series E funding round to accelerate commercial expansion, including growing its sales team and strengthening relationships with healthcare providers and diabetes specialists. It will also support wider adoption of CeQur Simplicity as the company introduces additional dosing and wear-duration options.

Amount raised in H1 2026: €84M

Using AI to support orthodontic care outside traditional clinical settings,  DentalMonitoring  develops software that enables dental professionals to remotely monitor patients throughout treatment.

Its technology analyses images captured by patients using their smartphones, helping orthodontists assess treatment progress, identify potential issues and determine when in-person appointments may be necessary. The platform is designed to improve communication between patients and practitioners while supporting more efficient treatment management.

In February 2026, DentalMonitoring announced  €84 million  in investment to support international expansion and product development. The funding will strengthen its presence in existing markets, support entry into new regions and advance its AI capabilities, integrations and partnerships across the dental technology sector.

Amount raised in H1 2026: €83M

FineHeart  is a French medtech company developing implantable medical devices for the treatment of advanced heart failure.

Its main technology, FlowMaker, is a fully implantable cardiac output accelerator designed to support the heart's natural pumping function. The company focuses on developing cardiovascular technologies that address the needs of patients with severe heart conditions, combining clinical research with medical device engineering.

In January 2026, FineHeart announced  €83 million  in financing to support the clinical development and industrialisation of FlowMaker and the development of Europe's active implantable medical device sector.

Amount raised in H1 2026: $86.6M

Ona Therapeutics  is a Barcelona-based biotechnology company developing treatments for advanced cancers. Its research focuses on tumour biology and the mechanisms that enable cancer cells to survive, spread and resist existing therapies.

The company is developing antibody-based treatments targeting proteins associated with tumour progression, with the aim of addressing cancers for which current treatment options remain limited.

In June 2026, Ona Therapeutics raised  $86.6 million  in Series B funding. The investment is intended to advance its oncology drug development programmes, including clinical development activities and further research into its therapeutic pipeline.

Amount raised in H1 2026: €62.5M

Neurent Medical  develops minimally invasive medical technology for treating chronic inflammatory conditions affecting the nasal passages.

The company's NEUROMARK system uses proprietary radiofrequency technology to target overactive nerves associated with chronic rhinitis, a condition characterised by persistent nasal congestion, runny nose and other symptoms. The treatment is designed to provide lasting symptom relief through a procedure that can be performed by healthcare professionals without extensive recovery time.

In February 2026, Neurent Medical closed a  €62.5 million  Series C funding round. The capital will support commercial expansion of NEUROMARK, strengthen clinical evidence and advance the company's product development and additional treatment indications.

Amount raised in H1 2026: $70M

Automating blood collection is the focus of Dutch medtech company  Vitestro , which develops robotic systems for diagnostic procedures. Its Aletta device combines robotics, imaging technology and AI to perform blood draws autonomously.

Designed for use in hospitals and laboratories, the system aims to standardise blood collection, reduce the workload of healthcare professionals and improve the efficiency of clinical workflows.

In March 2026, Vitestro raised  $70 million  in Series B funding. The investment will support further development of its Aletta robotic blood collection system, integration into high-volume clinical workflows and preparations for wider commercial deployment.

Amount raised in H1 2026: €60M

Tissium  is a French medical technology company developing biomorphic programmable polymers for tissue reconstruction.

Its materials are designed to bond with biological tissues and support surgical repairs without conventional sutures. The technology can be adapted to different clinical applications, including nerve repair, hernia treatment and cardiovascular procedures. Its COAPTIUM CONNECT system is designed to reconnect damaged peripheral nerves while minimising trauma to surrounding tissue.

In June 2026, Tissium announced a  €60 million  financing package to support commercial expansion in the US, clinical programmes and further development of its polymer technology platform.
ai_summary: European healthtech investment in H1 2026 was driven by large funding rounds, with continued interest in biotechnology, medical devices and AI-powered healthcare solutions. The UK attracted significant investment, led by major rounds for Isomorphic Labs and Oviva.
main_event: Healthtech: Europe’s 10 most-funded companies in H1 2026

title: Battle Truck: A startup sandbox on wheels for Ukraine's front lines
author: Tech.eu
description:

But there’s just one problem.

Most donated ambulances are poorly suited to Ukrainian roads and conditions, with mechanical failures leaving vehicles out of service when medics need them most.

Now, a group of European and US medtech and defence technology companies is developing a rugged medical evacuation vehicle for Ukraine, combining battlefield medical equipment, protective technologies a...
article_content:
You’ve no doubt seen fundraisers online to donate funds to send emergency service vehicles to Ukraine.

But there’s just one problem.

Most donated ambulances are poorly suited to Ukrainian roads and conditions, with mechanical failures leaving vehicles out of service when medics need them most.

Now, a group of European and US medtech and defence technology companies is developing a rugged medical evacuation vehicle for Ukraine, combining battlefield medical equipment, protective technologies and digital triage systems.

Spearheaded by startup entrepreneur and volunteer medic Howard Hunt, Battle Truck aims to address two challenges: the shortage of reliable evacuation vehicles that can handle Ukrainian roads and frontline conditions, and the difficulty early-stage medical technology companies face in testing and demonstrating their innovations in real-world environments.

Check out our  earlier interview  with Howard Hunt, co-founder of volunteer evacuation team, The AO.

According to Hunt, donating vehicles without considering Ukrainian road conditions and frontline requirements can leave medics with equipment that is difficult to maintain and unreliable when casualties need evacuating.

Another factor is ensuring medics and their patients are safe.

Hospitals and ambulances in Ukraine are increasingly coming under Russian drone and missile attack, despite the Geneva Conventions (the international rules of war) requiring all parties to protect them.

At least 515 healthcare workers have been killed in Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion on 24 February 2022, according to the latest tally displayed by the   Attacks on Health Care in Ukraine   monitoring project. There is no official data on the number of medics killed or injured during the war.

Building an ambulance that can survive Ukraine's front lines

The Battle Truck project is seeking a donated van, ideally a Fiat Ducato or similar heavy transit vehicle, to convert into a durable evacuation platform with upgraded suspension, tyres and protective equipment. Rather than developing another conventional ambulance, the team wants to create a shared testing platform for technologies that could improve casualty survival and protect frontline medical personnel.

“The vehicle is basically a trojan horse of products. We drive it into Ukraine and prove it works,” Hunt explained.

The proposed vehicle would combine technologies from several companies across Europe and the US, allowing Ukrainian medics to assess them under realistic conditions:

NIXXEN  (Netherlands) would contribute vehicle engineering and modular evacuation capabilities, including adaptations to the van's suspension, chassis and other components to help it withstand damaged roads, potholes and uneven terrain. The aim is to improve stability, durability and mobility when transporting casualties.

Molecular Products  (UK) is contributing its Rugged Oxygen Generator (ROG), designed to provide oxygen without relying on conventional compressed gas cylinders or an external power supply.

Velico  (US) is developing FrontlineODP, a spray-dried plasma technology designed to bring potentially lifesaving blood products closer to casualties suffering severe bleeding.

AO-Med  (Estonia) would provide digital triage management and Tactical Combat Casualty Care (TCCC) reporting technology, enabling medics to record and communicate casualty information during evacuation.

Phoenix Denmark , a manufacturer of tactical and protective equipment for military and security personnel, has been identified as a potential supplier of a specialised protective covering for the Battle Truck.

Protecting medics from incendiary weapons and drone detection

Beyond making the vehicle more durable, Battle Truck's partners are exploring technologies to protect medics and patients from some of the deadliest threats on Ukraine's front lines.

The proposed blanket would cover the vehicle and is intended to provide protection against explosive fragments and burning white phosphorus particles, while also reducing its thermal signature.

The dangers facing frontline medical teams in Ukraine extend beyond conventional shelling and drone strikes. Incendiary weapons can ignite vehicles, destroy medical equipment and cause devastating burns, while white phosphorus presents particular risks because its burning particles can adhere to surfaces and reignite when exposed to oxygen.

Human Rights Watch has documented incendiary attacks in Ukraine, including a November 2024 drone attack that set fire to two ambulances at the Kherson Regional Oncology Centre, although the weapons used in that incident were not identified. By reducing the vehicle's infrared visibility, the covering could potentially make it harder to detect and target during casualty evacuation.

Velico: Bringing lifesaving plasma closer to the front line

Conventional plasma typically requires frozen storage and thawing before transfusion, making it difficult to transport and administer in frontline environments.

Velico's technology converts donated plasma into a dry product that can be stored in lightweight packaging and rehydrated with sterile water in under three minutes, potentially enabling earlier treatment during medical evacuation.

The company is also developing decentralised manufacturing systems that would allow regional blood centres to produce their own dried plasma. Its technology is undergoing evaluation by France's Armed Forces Blood Transfusion Centre, while a 2026 clinical trial involving 24 healthy volunteers reported encouraging initial safety results.

For Battle Truck, the potential benefit is access to plasma during casualty evacuation without the conventional frozen-plasma supply chain.

Molecular Products: Oxygen without cylinders or electricity

I spoke to Hitesh Raval, Defence Business Development Manager at Molecular Products, about the company's involvement. Raval explained that conventional compressed oxygen cylinders can present additional hazards in environments exposed to gunfire and explosions.

Damage to pressurised cylinders can endanger medics and patients. Molecular Products' ROG is designed to provide a non-compressed, power-independent oxygen supply for frontline medical use.

According to Raval, the system can provide approximately 15 minutes of oxygen, potentially helping medics treat casualties before they can be transferred to more comprehensive care.

The company has been discussing the technology with Ukrainian medics and military medical personnel. Raval says the response has been encouraging, but obtaining equipment remains a significant challenge.

The medtech procurement problem: When saving lives takes a back seat

For early-stage defence and medtech companies, gaining traction in Ukraine can be essential to securing investment and procurement opportunities. However, demonstrating new technologies under operational conditions is expensive and logistically challenging, especially when military procurement priorities focus on drones and other battlefield equipment.

For Raval, Battle Truck builds on his experience with Ukrainian medical personnel and his desire to improve casualty evacuation from the front line.

“Through my work, I've met Ukrainian medics, doctors and brigade commanders. Hearing directly from people dealing with those conditions makes you ask what you can do to help.

At Molecular Products, we've been developing a battlefield oxygen generator for frontline medics based on 40-year-old technology in submarines, and I immediately recognised its potential for frontline medical care. When I met Howard and heard about the Battle Truck project, the appeal was almost instantaneous.

I felt I had enough experience and industry connections to help bring together the equipment and partners needed to make it happen.”

While medics introduced to the Rugged Oxygen Generator have received it enthusiastically, one of the biggest problems is procurement.

Raval recounts:

“I had a meeting with medical personnel connected to the Azov Brigade — a Ukrainian military unit that began as a volunteer battalion in 2014 before joining the National Guard — including a staff sergeant, a medical trainer and a combat medic.

They were very interested in the product, but the question was how they could obtain it. Even when frontline medics identify equipment that could help them, there isn't necessarily a straightforward route to purchasing and deploying it.”

Competing priorities also matter, especially when military resources are needed for drones and other equipment. The team has had encouraging discussions with vehicle manufacturers. However, a vehicle deployed in a war zone may not return intact.

“Potential partners need to understand that from the outset,” said Raval.

“My approach is to be direct about what we're trying to achieve and what we need. The priority is getting suitable equipment to the people who need it, rather than creating a marketing exercise.”

Crucially, the Battle Truck team wants frontline medics involved in evaluating the vehicle and its equipment rather than assuming that technologies developed elsewhere will automatically be suitable.

Raval has also been exploring links with stabilisation points and medical evacuation networks in Ukraine, potentially allowing the vehicle to operate as part of a wider casualty evacuation system.

From prototype to the front line: Proving Battle Truck works

Potential testing routes include Dark Star bootcamps and Brave Tech programmes, alongside Ukrainian military testing facilities in Rivne and Lutsk.

The team has identified the Rivne Interregional Medical Cluster as a potential route to accessing those facilities. If successful, the team hopes to secure a formal requirement or procurement request from Ukrainian military medical authorities, including brigade commanders or the Ukrainian Ministry of Defence's medical structures.

That request could potentially support procurement discussions with German or Dutch authorities.

“We've been exploring this fast-track procurement opportunity for the past four months, and believe it might be possible if we are able to prove viability in battlefield conditions,” said Hunt.

The proposed collaboration is non-exclusive, with participating companies expected to cover the costs of their own prototype technologies. If the project eventually secures a purchase order, the partners would negotiate how to distribute proceeds. A memorandum of understanding is among the proposed next steps.

The €500,000 challenge: Turning Battle Truck into reality

The immediate priority is securing a suitable van and the funding needed to integrate the technologies. Raval estimates that approximately €500,000 could potentially support three or four vehicles, depending on the final configuration and contributions from partners.

The team is exploring support from NGOs and humanitarian organisations, alongside potential contributions from vehicle manufacturers and technology companies.

Raval has suggested assembling the initial vehicle in Germany to simplify coordination between European suppliers, although Poland is also under consideration.

The timetable remains dependent on securing funding, equipment and a suitable vehicle. Once assembled, the prototype would be taken to Ukraine for testing. If successfully validated, the project's presentation identifies the 92nd Brigade in Lyman as its intended recipient.

The longer-term ambition is to establish a repeatable model for supplying similarly equipped evacuation vehicles, combining practical medical support with opportunities for participating startups to demonstrate their technologies.

Edwin Mélotte, founder of Dutch vehicle engineering company NIXXEN, believes the project addresses an imbalance in defence innovation, where investment in offensive capabilities often overshadows technologies designed to keep wounded soldiers alive.

“While everyone is focused on offensive capabilities, we're focused on saving lives. Getting injured soldiers medical attention quickly is critical, but so is ensuring they receive the right treatment.

That's why we've turned our attention to medical technology. By bringing these technologies together in one vehicle, we hope to give more of the brave men and women on the front line a better chance of survival.

If the first Battle Truck proves successful, our ambition is to help deliver another 500 vehicles and more medical equipment, not only to the front lines but also to cities further from the fighting, where civilian casualties are increasing.”

Raval stresses:

“Ultimately, the people operating these vehicles are putting themselves at considerable risk to evacuate casualties. Anything that can improve their protection deserves serious consideration.

But the immediate motivation is much simpler. We want to give combat casualties a better chance of survival and help protect the medics who are trying to evacuate them.”

Can you help get Battle Truck on the road?

Battle Truck is seeking a suitable van, funding and industry partners to help turn the concept into a working medical evacuation vehicle for Ukraine.

Whether you're a vehicle manufacturer, medtech company, humanitarian organisation or potential donor, the team is keen to hear from those who can contribute equipment, expertise or financial support.

Get in touch with the Battle Truck team  europe@ao-med.com

Or visit the Battle Truck page on the  AO website .
ai_summary: You’ve no doubt seen fundraisers online to donate funds to send emergency service vehicles to Ukraine. But there’s just one problem.

Finall...
article_content:
It's a cold and wet London day and the queue of entrepreneurs snakes outside the Cholmondeley back entrance to the Houses of Parliament.

The Thames flows adjacently, turbulent as the weather, as the crowd awaits the 8am opening of this particular entrance. There are no Black Rods here to summon attention and open the door, just shivering wonks and wannabes hoping their ill-fitting clothes don't chafe and nobody compares their dress sense to the horrors of Sam Altman or Elizabeth Holmes.

Finally the locks are unopened and the people go slowly through security, laptop bags scrutinised, passes checked and directions given. The entrepreneurs are here to hear the AI minister and his shadow counterpart talk about the country's future and to network.

Invited by the  UK think tank,  The Entrepreneurs Network  for the launch of  Starting Out and Starting Up: Making self-employment a route into work for young people,  I'm not just here for the impressive 'continental' breakfast and human politicians espousing AI, I'm here to see what young entrepreneurs think about the upcoming budget and whether their efforts at setting up businesses and startups will receive the support it deserves.

The energy in the room, unlike the dress sense, is vibrant and cool, this is no country for tech bros. It was a diverse audience, and not everybody was from London either. I wade through the pastries and berries to listen to optimistic conversations and the feeling that the budget might deliver for them.

While I'm yet to meet a depressed or pessimistic entrepreneur, the vibe does feel positive although a recent  report  published before the Budget told a slightly different story.

According to new polling of UK entrepreneurs by Public First for The Entrepreneurs Network, run in partnership with Blick Rothenberg, more than 75% of UK founders expected the taxes they personally pay or on their business to go up.

What founders fear

Nearly 90% of founders took a negative view on the level of taxation in the UK and the same amount disagreed that the government understands the needs of entrepreneurs and almost 80% said life as an entrepreneur had become harder after they'd started their business.

There were other fears about rising employer National Insurance contributions and raising Capital Gains Tax as well as dividend tax, but the truly damning of the damned statistics  was that 23% of founders expected to leave the UK in the next 12 months.

Moreover, unlike the conversations I wigged on to in the Cholmondeley Room and on the Thames terrace, there was also true pessimism, not optimism, for the  UK economy outlook with almost 80% saying they feared for it. These fears were summed up by Philip Salter, founder of The Entrepreneurs Network:

Founders are going into this Budget expected to pay more. Nine in ten take a dim view of the level of tax and nearly a quarter expect to leave the UK within a year. That should worry anyone who wants the UK to grow.

The message from entrepreneurs is loud and clear. Cut the cost and complexity of employing people and don't hike taxes. This would do more than anything else to show founders that the UK wants them to build here and stay here.

AI will save the day

Not that the speakers mentioned any of that, not least Rt Hon Kanishka Narayan MP, Minister for AI or Dr Ben Spencer MP, Shadow Minister for AI. Narayan was brisk and all about business, talking as if he had a private jet waiting to whisk him to Mar-A-Lago and a meeting with Trump, while Spencer looked and spoke as if he had just arrived in an overdue Uber after a night meeting with Boris Johnson.

Different strokes for different folks, but the story was the same. UK entrepreneurs and their businesses were going to be saved and heavily assisted by AI, not particularly by political parties' policies, just that AI was great and the UK was great at AI and had always been great at AI.

The humans in the room nodded their heads while Narayan's PR ushered him away, looking as if he was in rehearsals for a new version of the TV satire  In The Thick Of It,  all strutting peacock and the usual hideous dress sense. Stephens meanwhile stayed, bestowing handshakes and advice to all who approached him as if he had nothing better to do that morning, such is being in the Opposition.

As the stage emptied and networking reached the second level, I spoke instead to one of the caterers when I reached for my final pastry, thanking him for his service. In return, he told me of a secret covered passageway that went from the House of Lords to Westminster Tube station meaning I wouldn't get drenched by the rain on departure.

Thinking this was the best advice I'd had all morning, I hid my visitor's badge and naturally followed his instructions, but I was nabbed at the entrance and told to go the normal way. I wondered why the guard had cottoned on to me so easily and then I knew... I was too well-dressed for this crowd. I should have worn trainers.
ai_summary: It's a cold and wet London day and the queue of entrepreneurs snakes outside the Cholmondeley back entrance to the Houses of Parliament. The Thames flows adjacently, turbulent as the weather, as the crowd awaits the 8am opening of this particular entrance.
main_event: The UK needs its entrepreneurs more than anything else

title: German aerospace startup VÆRIDION raises €30M for zero-emission regional fights
author: Tech.eu
description:
A Munich-based aerospace startup on a mission to make affordable, zero-emission regional flights an everyday reality has raised €30m in a new funding round, it said today.

VÆRIDION  is developing an electric nine-seater aircraft, which operates entirely on battery-powered electric propulsion and is designed to travel up to 400km, serving passengers and cargo.

The startup aims to replicate what electric cars have done for road transport, replacing fossil-fuelled vehicles with battery-powered al...
article_content:
A Munich-based aerospace startup on a mission to make affordable, zero-emission regional flights an everyday reality has raised €30m in a new funding round, it said today.

VÆRIDION  is developing an electric nine-seater aircraft, which operates entirely on battery-powered electric propulsion and is designed to travel up to 400km, serving passengers and cargo.

The startup aims to replicate what electric cars have done for road transport, replacing fossil-fuelled vehicles with battery-powered alternatives.

It was founded in 2021 by two former Airbus managers, Ivor van Dartel and Dr Sebastian Seemann.

Its patented prototype Microliner is starting as a nine-seater aircraft, with plans to scale the technology to offer pan-European flights.  It is targeting 2030 for the Microliner to enter commercial service.

It says the Microliner emits less noise than conventional aircraft, making it well-suited to smaller airfields and easy to roll out in underserved areas.

The Series A2 funding round was led by SHIFT Invest, the Netherlands-based VC, and Invest-NL, the Netherlands' national investment institution, with participation from existing investors World Fund, Project A and Vsquared Ventures.

VÆRIDION has raised approximately €60 million to date and the new funding will be geared toward developing the first prototype of the Mircroliner.

The startup also said it has been selected by the EU for a €94.5 million Innovation Fund grant as it looks to develop its Microliner aircraft to manufacture it at industrial scale.

Ivor van Dartel, founder and CEO of VÆRIDION, said: “Over the past year, we have

turned the Microliner from a validated design into hardware, with exceptional capital

efficiency. Our propulsion and battery technology is now being tested at our own facility in

Oberpfaffenhofen. This equity round enables us to build our first conforming aircraft."

VÆRIDION is developing an electric nine-seater aircraft, which operates entirely on battery-powered electric propulsion and is designed to travel up to 400km, serving passengers and cargo.

article_content:
UK-based

healthcare AI company  Nayara  has closed a pre-seed funding round led by  SFC Capital , an early-stage investor in the UK. The funding will support the

development and expansion of its AI-powered platform designed to improve

communication and support for patients between clinical appointments.

Nayara

develops AI companions for hospitals, healthcare systems and medical technology

companies, providing personalised guidance and helping healthcare professionals

stay informed about patients' needs outside clinical settings.

While

much of healthcare takes place outside hospitals, patients often face medical

questions, uncertainty and concerns between appointments without immediate

access to professional support. At the same time, clinical teams must manage

routine enquiries alongside their existing responsibilities, with limited

visibility into patients' progress between visits.

Nayara

aims to address these challenges through AI-powered companions that answer

routine questions, provide personalised guidance and emotional support, and

proactively check in with patients. The platform also identifies concerns and

requests that require attention from healthcare providers and directs them to

the appropriate teams.

By

automating routine communication and providing information about patients'

needs, the technology is intended to reduce administrative workloads and help

healthcare professionals prioritise follow-up care.

According

to  Gal Moore , co-founder and CEO of Nayara, advances in medical technology have

expanded the possibilities of healthcare, while patient support has not evolved

at the same pace.

We

started Nayara with a simple belief: no patient should feel alone in their

healthcare journey. No warning sign should go unaddressed because the clinical

team lacked the information, or the time, to act,

said Moore.

The

company's approach combines input from medical professionals, patients, people

with experience supporting loved ones through illness and AI engineers. These

clinical, personal and technical perspectives inform the development of its

platform.

Nayara's

technology is already being used across clinical pathways, including oncology,

where its AI companion for breast cancer patients has supported hundreds of

people.

The

new funding will be used to accelerate product development, support clinical

validation and expand the company's commercial activities.
ai_summary: UK-based healthcare AI company Nayara has closed a pre-seed funding round led by SFC Capital , an early-stage investor in the UK. The funding will support the development and expansion of its AI-powered platform designed to improve communication and support for patients between clinical appointments.
main_event: SFC Capital backs Nayara's AI platform for patient care

article_content:
The Estonian government has today approved draft legislation paving the way for 24/7 robotic pharmacies, allowing patients to obtain prescription and over-the-counter medicines without a pharmacist physically present on site. The proposed amendments to the Medicinal Products Act would enable automated self-service pharmacies equipped with digital identity verification, remote video consultations with licensed pharmacists and robotic medicine dispensing.

The bill must still pass through parliament, with implementation targeted for 1 March 2027.

If enacted, Estonia could become the first European country to introduce remote prescription medicine dispensing through automated pharmacies, going beyond existing collection lockers and systems limited to non-prescription products.

At the centre of the initiative is Estonian technology company  Grab2Go , whose co-founders Mart Viilipus and Reio Orasmäe encountered legislation requiring pharmacists to be physically present when dispensing medication. Rather than abandoning the project, they approached  Accelerate Estonia , a government-backed innovation programme run by the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications.

Working with the Estonian Medicines Board and Ministry of Social Affairs, the programme helped identify the regulatory changes needed to bring the technology to market while maintaining patient safety.

I spoke to Reio Orasmäe, co-founder and CSO of Grab2Go, and Olari Püvi, Head of Accelerate Estonia, to learn more.

A pharmacy at 2 am

Automated pharmacies could improve access to medication outside conventional opening hours. As Orasmäe notes:

“Whether you're a parent with a sick child, an elderly person or someone who suddenly needs medicine, accessing a pharmacy late at night, early in the morning or on a Sunday can be difficult.

Online pharmacies are becoming more popular, but delivery may take a day or two. That doesn't solve the problem when someone needs medication immediately.”

As for how it works, Orasmäe likens the customer experience to self-service ordering at McDonald's. Customers select their medication using a touchscreen before connecting with a licensed pharmacist via video consultation. The pharmacist reviews the request and authorises dispensing.

“During our six-month pilot in Estonia, a mandatory video consultation with a pharmacist was part of the process. The pharmacist could ask questions about the intended use of the medication and verify that it was appropriate for the customer,” shared Orasmäe.

Estonia has a highly developed digital identity infrastructure, allowing identification through an ID card or other digital solutions.

The robotic system handles product storage and dispensing within a secure steel enclosure accessible only to authorised personnel. No robots malfunctioned during the pilot, but Orasmäe says helping customers become comfortable with digital identity verification proved more challenging.

“In many ways, the robotics is the easiest part. Some people are very familiar with digital services, while others need more assistance.

We even had an 82-year-old woman using the system. Having someone available to help customers during the first few months when introducing a new service can make a significant difference.”

The regulatory catch-22: How do you test something that's illegal?

The Grab2Go project exposed a broader problem facing startups developing technologies that existing legislation does not accommodate. Regulators often require real-world evidence before changing the law, but companies cannot legally collect that evidence without permission to test their products.

“The Ministry of Social Affairs needed data before it could consider changing the law. But we couldn't collect that data because we weren't allowed to test the technology. It's a circular problem,” Püvi explained.

The experience prompted Accelerate Estonia to develop an experimentation framework allowing companies to test innovative products and services under controlled real-world conditions, even where existing regulations would otherwise prohibit them.

Rather than introducing permanent legislative changes before knowing whether a technology works, regulators could authorise limited trials and use the findings to assess safety, practicality and economic value.

“We regularly encounter entrepreneurs who are frustrated because regulations prevent them from testing new ideas. Some projects succeed, and others fail, but without experimentation, potentially valuable innovations can remain stuck for years.

If we'd had this framework when Grab2Go first approached us, robotic pharmacies might already have been on the market.”

Püvi believes the framework could benefit other startups facing similar regulatory barriers, extending its impact well beyond automated pharmacies.

Can robotic pharmacies solve Estonia's pharmacist shortage?

Beyond convenience, automated pharmacies could help address workforce shortages and improve access to medication in underserved communities.

“Estonia has rural communities and islands where access to pharmacies can be difficult. Automated pharmacies could improve access to medicines for people living in those areas,” explained Püvi.

Accelerate Estonia and PwC conducted an impact analysis examining the economic and societal implications of introducing self-service pharmacies. The study highlighted an ageing workforce, with 53 per cent of pharmacists and 43 per cent of pharmaceutical technicians over 50, raising concerns about staffing as more professionals approach retirement.

Automation could let pharmacists serve customers remotely across multiple locations, improving staff allocation. Püvi also sees potential to reduce pressure on emergency healthcare services.

“People sometimes seek emergency medical assistance for relatively minor problems because they cannot access medication or pharmacy services when they need them.

If someone can obtain appropriate medication from a pharmacy operating 24 hours a day, seven days a week, that could help reduce some of that pressure.”

The business case for automated pharmacies

For pharmacy operators, Grab2Go is targeting a return on investment of approximately two to three years.

“One of the biggest factors is labour costs, which continue to increase. As those costs rise, the potential payback period for automation becomes shorter. At the same time, the cost of robotics and associated components has been declining as the technology becomes more widely adopted,” Orasmäe explained.

Grab2Go intends to operate primarily as a technology provider, supplying hardware and software to pharmacy operators, with commercial arrangements tailored to individual requirements.

The company also sees international opportunities. According to Püvi, countries including Canada, Sweden, Norway and Austria have shown interest in Estonia's approach

The proposed legislation is intended to be technology-neutral, allowing other companies to develop competing automated pharmacy systems.

“We work with pioneering companies to identify regulatory barriers and create opportunities for entirely new markets to emerge. Grab2Go may be the first, but we hope other companies will follow,” Püvi said.

However, developing a product for a market that does not legally exist presents significant investment challenges.

“We sometimes joke at Accelerate Estonia that you have to be a little crazy to start a business whose product is initially illegal under existing regulations.”

Orasmäe points out that while considerable expertise already exists in warehouse automation, robotic logistics and pharmaceutical storage, customer-facing automated pharmacies require different capabilities.

“The processes, customer interactions and even the robotics themselves have different requirements.

We've invested in developing our technology to the point where we have a third version ready, but until the regulatory framework changes, customers cannot actually operate it commercially. That's a significant barrier to investment.

Once the market becomes legally accessible, other companies will have a reason to start developing competing solutions.”

Changing the law without compromising patient safety

For regulators, the central question was whether automated pharmacies could deliver the same standard of care as conventional pharmacies.

According to Püvi, the impact analysis examined approximately 30 to 40 issues, including patient safety, professional responsibilities and whether the technology addressed a genuine need.

“One important finding was that automation could actually improve the quality of the pharmacist's interaction with customers. Pharmacists do much more than hand over medication.

They're responsible for inventory, ordering products, managing the pharmacy and, in some cases, preparing or compounding medications for individual patients.”

Automating dispensing could let pharmacists focus on consultations rather than managing operational tasks. Crucially, the pharmacist retains final authority over dispensing, including for common over-the-counter medicines.

“Demonstrating that the system was safe, beneficial and could improve existing services took considerable time. In a democratic country, regulatory change requires consultation and evidence.

You need to demonstrate that the proposed changes genuinely improve the system.”

Following parliamentary approval, Estonia's Ministry of Social Affairs will need approximately three to four months to prepare the necessary digital and administrative systems and inform pharmacy operators about the new framework. Grab2Go is targeting deployment in March 2027.

According to Püvi, there was discussion about allowing the changes to take effect earlier, but that would have placed unnecessary pressure on regulators and pharmacy operators.

“There was discussion about allowing the changes to take effect as early as January, but that would have created unnecessary pressure for everyone involved.

We've been working on this for approximately two and a half years, so a few additional months to ensure everything is properly implemented makes sense. It gives regulators, pharmacy operators and Grab2Go time to prepare.”

Grab2Go's technology could potentially be applied to other regulated products requiring secure storage, identity verification and professional authorisation, such as medical cannabis, subject to applicable regulations.

Orasmäe believes automated pharmacies also improve inventory management through AI-based forecasting, stock monitoring and automatic replenishment.

“Customers shouldn't routinely have to visit a pharmacy only to discover that a common medication is unavailable and needs to be ordered.

For people managing chronic conditions, such as asthma or allergies, reliable access to medication is particularly important. The goal is not simply to automate dispensing. It's to make the entire process of accessing medication more convenient, reliable and efficient.”

For Accelerate Estonia, the broader lesson is that governments need mechanisms to evaluate emerging technologies without allowing existing regulations to prevent experimentation altogether. Püvi asserts:

“We need ways to test new solutions responsibly, gather evidence and determine whether they can deliver genuine benefits.

Grab2Go is an important example of what becomes possible when entrepreneurs and the government work together to address those barriers.”
ai_summary: The Estonian government has today approved draft legislation paving the way for 24/7 robotic pharmacies, allowing patients to obtain prescription and over-the-counter medicines without a pharmacist physically present on site. The proposed amendments to the Medicinal Products Act would enable automated self-service pharmacies equipped with digital identity verification, remote video consultations with licensed pharmacists and robotic medicine dispensing.
main_event: Estonia approves 24/7 robotic pharmacies, paving the way for a European first

article_content:
AI-powered learning platform  Mindmax  has raised £2.5

million in venture capital funding in a round led by  Concept Ventures , with

participation from  Redrice Ventures ,  Daybreak Ventures  and  Lerer Hippeau . The

round also attracted angel investors, including former Depop CEO  Maria Raga  and

Helsing co-founder  Torsten Reil .

Founded by  Ed Cooke  and  Daniel Zohar , Mindmax is developing

AI-powered learning tools designed to help people acquire new skills, retain

information and prepare for professional qualifications.

The founders were previously part of the team behind

Memrise , a language learning platform that has attracted more than 80 million

users worldwide. Their experience developing Memrise has informed Mindmax's

approach to personalised, AI-powered learning.

Mindmax's first product is an AI tutor focused on

professional exam preparation and upskilling. The platform uses real-time

conversations to create personalised learning experiences, allowing users to

ask questions, interrupt explanations and direct lessons towards topics they

find difficult. Users can also access visual explanations and illustrations

during each session, with lessons adapted to their existing knowledge, learning

goals and individual approaches to learning.

The company is developing its technology amid growing

concerns about the impact of AI on learning and independent thinking. As AI

tools become more widely used in education and professional settings, questions

have emerged about the potential effects of relying on technology to perform

tasks that previously required active learning and problem-solving.

Mindmax aims to address these concerns by using AI to

encourage active participation in the learning process rather than simply

providing answers. Its approach focuses on interactive conversations, allowing

users to explore subjects through questions and receive explanations tailored

to their needs.

Curiosity has always been the greatest fuel for learning.

Which means you need to be able to ask questions. When you’re in a one-to-one

conversation with an expert, you’ll ask 20-30 questions per hour. You can’t do

that in a classroom. It’s why our approach is so powerful,

said Daniel Zohar,

co-founder of Mindmax.

According to the company, its interactive approach is

designed to improve learning and information retention compared with more

passive formats. Mindmax plans to continue developing the capabilities of its

AI models to support more personalised learning experiences.

The funding announcement follows the launch of Mindmax's

platform, which builds on the founders' experience developing language learning

platform Memrise, which has attracted more than 80 million users worldwide.

The round also attracted angel investors, including former Depop CEO Maria Raga and Helsing co-founder Torsten Reil .

article_content:
Spanish AI accounting

platform  Kabilio  has raised €10 million in a funding round led by  Picus Capital

and  Visionaries , with participation from CDTI, Spain's public agency for

technological innovation. The investment brings the company's total funding

since launch to €14 million. Picus Capital and Visionaries also led Kabilio's

pre-seed  round.

Founded by  Jose Ojeda

and  Álex Valls , Kabilio develops an AI-powered platform

designed to help accounting firms and their small business clients automate

administrative and financial processes.

In Spain, as in much of

Europe, small businesses typically outsource their bookkeeping and tax-related

work to external accounting firms. These firms often manage large volumes of

invoices, bank transactions and financial documents, with many processes still

requiring manual input and reconciliation.

Kabilio aims to reduce

this administrative workload by automating repetitive accounting tasks while

keeping accountants responsible for reviewing and approving the results.

Its platform uses AI to

read invoices, suggest accounting entries, match bank transactions and prepare

reconciliations, while identifying cases that require professional attention.

The system works alongside firms' existing software, allowing accountants to

review and approve information rather than enter it manually.

According to the

company, its technology reduces the time spent on bookkeeping and

reconciliation by approximately 60 per cent. The platform also structures

financial documents, transactions and accounting entries as data, recording

firms' rules and decisions to support further automation.

Kabilio is introducing

an AI accounting agent designed to automate workflows such as retrieving

invoices, reconciling transactions, validating entries and requesting missing

documents through email and WhatsApp. Accountants can assign tasks using

plain-language instructions and control the agent's level of autonomy. Several

firms are already piloting the technology.

The company has also

launched Kabilio Empresas, a platform that allows small businesses to issue

invoices, connect bank accounts and monitor cash flow while sharing financial

data with their accounting firms in real time. Fiscalidad Inteligente and

Alemany Assessors are already using the platform to manage a large part of

their client portfolios.

An agent is only as

good as the data it works on. That is why we are bringing the firm’s clients

onto the same platform: the moment a business issues an invoice or a payment

hits its bank, the firm has it and the agent will be able to act on it. The

firm is freed from busy work, and its clients feel the difference,

said Álex

Valls, co-founder and co-CEO of Kabilio.

In a later phase,

Kabilio plans to extend its AI agent to small business clients, enabling it to

issue invoices, follow up on overdue payments, request missing receipts and

answer routine accounting and tax questions.

Kabilio currently works

with nearly 500 accounting firms, compared with 100 a year ago. Its customers

include Adlanter, Solfico and Gemap, with the latter two belonging to the

iusTime group. The company has also expanded its team to 80 employees, more

than half of whom work in product and engineering.

The new funding will

support Kabilio's next development phase, including the rollout of its AI

accounting agent, further automation of accounting workflows and the expansion

of its shared platform for accounting firms and small businesses.
ai_summary: Spanish AI accounting platform Kabilio has raised €10 million in a funding round led by Picus Capital and Visionaries , with participation from CDTI, Spain's public agency for technological innovation. The investment brings the company's total funding since launch to €14 million.

title: Sort A Brick is turning forgotten LEGO into a multibillion-euro circular economy market
author: Tech.eu
description:
Billions of LEGO bricks are sitting unused in homes worldwide. While the bricks themselves can last for generations, rebuilding original sets from mixed collections can require hours of painstaking manual sorting.

Lithuanian startup  Sort A Brick  is developing automated technology to make that process commercially viable, turning collections of used bricks into complete, ready-to-build sets.

According to the company, the global secondary LEGO market is worth approximately €800 million, but on...
article_content:
Billions of LEGO bricks are sitting unused in homes worldwide. While the bricks themselves can last for generations, rebuilding original sets from mixed collections can require hours of painstaking manual sorting.

Lithuanian startup  Sort A Brick  is developing automated technology to make that process commercially viable, turning collections of used bricks into complete, ready-to-build sets.

According to the company, the global secondary LEGO market is worth approximately €800 million, but only €80 million comes from sales of complete used sets.  Sort A Brick  estimates that a market for certified refurbished sets could grow to €4.7 billion by 2036 if automated sorting makes large-scale restoration commercially viable.

In October, Sort A Brick unveiled its second-generation automated sorting machine, capable of scanning and sorting up to 3,600 bricks an hour, four times faster than its predecessor. The launch coincides with the company's expansion into direct sales of refurbished sets.

More than 75 per cent of its listed inventory sold during the online store's first week, and the company reports that customers across 20 EU countries have purchased more than 1,100 sets.

Sort A Brick has also received nearly 2,000 restoration requests from 41 countries and processed more than 700 kilograms of mixed bricks, with Germany emerging as a key market.

I spoke to Ilya Malkin, CEO of Sort A Brick, to learn more.

From restoring childhood collections to selling refurbished sets

I've been following Sort A Brick's progress for several years. The company originally focused on restoring customers' existing LEGO collections, so I was curious about what prompted the move into selling refurbished sets.

According to Malkin, the company had always considered direct sales, but legal complexities and higher customer expectations meant it needed to improve its technology first.

“We decided to wait until our technology improved enough to deliver the quality and consistency we wanted.

We now have two business lines: restoring customers' existing collections and selling refurbished sets that we've assembled ourselves.”

The company is positioning its refurbished sets as a more reliable alternative to conventional second-hand purchases, where missing or incorrect pieces can be a problem.

“The sets are cleaned, checked for completeness and made entirely from genuine LEGO bricks. If a customer discovers a missing or non-genuine piece, we'll replace it. Customers can also scan a QR code to access the building instructions.”

Demand for restoration services has been strong, but processing capacity has been the biggest limitation. Malkin says some customers are willing to wait years to have their collections restored.

“The average order value is around €500, which is quite high. Customers often send us 14 or 15 kilograms of mixed bricks. “

Although the cost per restored set can be relatively low, paying €500 in one instalment is a significant barrier.”

Some customers find that the cost of restoring their entire collection exceeds what they are prepared to spend.

“That's one reason why selling individual refurbished sets makes sense. Instead of spending hundreds of euros restoring a collection, someone can buy a single set for €10 or €15, depending on the model.

We're targeting prices around half those of equivalent new sets, although older and rarer sets may be more expensive.”

Scaling LEGO sorting through computer vision and automation

The automated sorting system uses computer vision to identify LEGO bricks and match them against a database of sets. Software then determines which sets can potentially be reconstructed from the available pieces. The process begins with pre-sorting and cleaning. The second-generation machine scans bricks from all sides, while a redesigned distribution system and ten times more output containers allow hundreds of sets to be processed simultaneously.

Overall capacity has increased fivefold with approximately three times the physical footprint. Pieces the system cannot recognise are directed to a semi-manual sorting station, while completed sets undergo final inspection before delivery.

“We use computer vision to support that process, but we still have a human checking each set because we want to guarantee completeness,” Malkin explained.

The improvements extend beyond the sorting hardware to the software and supporting equipment.

“Our original machine was essentially a prototype. We were operating it in three shifts, running around 22 hours a day, but we were still limited in how much we could process,” Malkin recalled.

Improving recognition without chasing AI vanity metrics

The computer vision technology has evolved from identifying shapes to recognising colours and printed pieces, each introducing additional complexity.

“We're very pragmatic about what we invest in when it comes to AI. We don't want to chase vanity metrics. We introduce new capabilities when they significantly increase the proportion of bricks we can recognise,” Malkin said.

The system now automatically identifies more than 93 per cent of pieces, with the remaining seven per cent directed to manual sorting stations. Transferring those capabilities between machines presents another challenge, as even small hardware differences can affect recognition accuracy.

“When you build a machine and calibrate everything, the computer vision system works. But even if you replicate the machine, transferring those capabilities isn't straightforward,” Malkin explained.

The team is experimenting with using data from the original machine to train its successor, particularly for shape recognition. Colour recognition is more difficult because it requires machine-specific calibration.

“However, because we've already gone through that process once, it should be easier with the next generation.”

The challenge of making circularity commercially viable

Hardware-intensive businesses can be difficult to finance because companies must invest in machinery before they can properly test the market. For Malkin, another challenge is achieving sufficient scale to determine whether the business model is economically viable.

“At a very small scale, the results of an experiment can be misleading. The demand we've seen is encouraging, but we still need to demonstrate that the business works at scale.”

The second-generation machine is therefore a critical step towards making the operation commercially sustainable.

“We expect this new generation to make the operation profitable, which would allow us to start replicating the system. You can't scale something that's losing money every time you operate it.”

LEGO's durability makes it particularly suited to reuse, but reconstructing sets from thousands of mixed pieces is difficult without automation.

“So in a way, we're helping make that promise of reuse more practical.”

The legal complexities of refurbishing LEGO

Sort A Brick has been developing intellectual property around its sorting technology, filing a patent application in Sweden for its original machine.

“We received confirmation much faster than we expected, after around nine months,” Malkin explained.

However, the development of its second-generation machine, which incorporates additional innovations, has introduced challenges around patent protection.

“One unexpected challenge was coordinating the timing of the patent applications. If the first application becomes public before the second is filed, it can potentially create problems for protecting the newer technology.”

Protecting its own technology is only part of the legal challenge. Sort A Brick must also navigate intellectual property and resale rules surrounding LEGO products.

“We have to be careful about the images we use commercially,” Malkin explained.

“That's why we've organised building events where people come and build LEGO models, and we photograph those completed models ourselves.”

Establishing the provenance of second-hand bricks is another consideration, as resale rules can depend on where products were originally placed on the market.

"When we buy mixed bricks from individuals, we don't necessarily have the original receipts. So we identify the sets in their collections and ask sellers to confirm that they owned them.”

Malkin said the company is taking a cautious approach as it scales.

“Our lawyers have warned us that intellectual property disputes could arise as we grow, so it's something we take seriously.”

Beyond LEGO: Expanding automated sorting to other toys, Sort a Brick’s tech could eventually be adapted to other products, although their components would need to retain sufficient value to justify automated sorting.

“There are more than 100,000 different types of parts to identify,” Malkin shared.

“For our technology to make economic sense in another industry, there needs to be a large variety of parts, those parts need to retain enough value to justify sorting them, and there needs to be a way to identify and organise them.”

Other durable, modular toys could offer similar opportunities, including Playmobil and BRIO wooden railway sets. However, Malkin sees considerable room for growth in the company's existing market.

“There's so much LEGO in circulation that we could be working on this market for another decade.”

Scaling globally through sorting centres and partnerships

The company plans to open pilot sorting centres in Europe and the US in 2027, with ambitions to establish up to 40 sorting lines worldwide by 2030. Beyond processing second-hand LEGO, Malkin sees an opportunity to turn these facilities into educational spaces.

“We already have visits from schools and kindergartens because children find the technology fascinating,” said Malkin.

"When we open larger facilities, we'd like people to be able to see the machines working. It demonstrates recycling and reuse in a very tangible way.”

author: Ars Technica

article_content:
It’s not easy to extract iron from its ore. But the peoples of the ancient city of Great Zimbabwe—the capital of a thriving kingdom in southern Africa between 1000 to 1700 AD—were masters.

At sites near the city’s stone ruins, clusters of iron-smelting furnaces survive today as mounds of rubble. At Mashava, a village 25 miles northwest, fragments bear fingermarks of those who long ago smoothed the structures’ clay interiors.

Some of the furnaces were nearly an adult’s arm span in width, with walls thick and strong to contain the heat of more than 2,100° Fahrenheit needed to smelt iron. Unlike other furnaces that required workers to force air into them with bellows, these were designed to suck air in, then out through a chimney, no human labor required. This would have made it significantly easier to produce the iron, which was fashioned into hoes, axes, and arrowheads.

article_content:
An  Estonian newspaper recently revealed  that a British soldier disobeyed a direct order to remove the SIM card from his cellphone before being deployed to a part of Estonia, approximately 90 miles west of the Russian border.

As a result of his refusal to engage in this element of operational security (opsec), the soldier, Daniel Barton-Kennedy, had his phone hacked, and nude photos of himself were stolen and used as blackmail against him.

Eventually, Barton-Kennedy was court-martialed for disobeying a lawful command, pled guilty, was reduced in rank, and ordered to serve 10 months in detention.
