Despite the ghastly injury, the man was alive and conscious when he arrived. He could still talk and move all four limbs. His doctors described him as being in a state of agitation. On the Glasgow Coma Scale, he scored a  12 (E3 V4 M5) , indicating a "moderate" brain injury, just one point above "mild." He could open his left eye when told, but otherwise kept it closed (E3 score); he could talk and answer questions, but was confused (V4); and he intentionally moved away when pressure was applied to his body (M5).

In a report published Friday in BMJ Case Report, his doctors said they were concerned that in his confused, agitated state he may try to pull the knife out on his own. So, they swiftly sedated and intubated him. They put him on prophylactic treatments for bacterial infections, including tetanus. Then they used images to see what was going on in his head.

article_content:
Several tanker ships linked to Iran have been loitering over subsea Internet cables in the Gulf of Oman near the Strait of Hormuz—a possible indication that the Iranian government is preparing to attack such undersea infrastructure in response to any renewed US and Israeli strikes.

The movements of three sanctioned tankers and an Iranian fishing boat have been tracked near major undersea cables by the maritime intelligence firm Windward in October,  according to the Financial Times . Six  active cables  currently cross through the contested Strait of Hormuz, linking the Middle East to Europe, Africa and Asia, with two more cables having segments under construction in the region.

Four countries, including Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar, depend entirely upon such subsea telecommunications connections running through the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint to link with the outside world. But other countries also depend heavily on the region's undersea cable network—one third of India’s westbound Internet traffic goes through the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz.

title: Earth's churning mantle may have created the Great Unconformity
author: Ars Technica
description: In the Grand Canyon, there is a line in the rock where time seems to have gone missing. Ancient crystalline rocks mark its bottom, while sandstones laid down as life started to diversify during the Cambrian explosion mark the top. “It’s called the Great Unconformity, and it’s a gap in the geologic record,” says Nicolas Flament, a geoscientist at the University of Wollongong, Australia. "This gap can be anywhere between 200 million years, which is not that impressive, to more than a billion years...
article_content:
In the Grand Canyon, there is a line in the rock where time seems to have gone missing. Ancient crystalline rocks mark its bottom, while sandstones laid down as life started to diversify during the Cambrian explosion mark the top. “It’s called the Great Unconformity, and it’s a gap in the geologic record,” says Nicolas Flament, a geoscientist at the University of Wollongong, Australia. "This gap can be anywhere between 200 million years, which is not that impressive, to more than a billion years.”

In a recent Nature study, Flament and his colleague Santosh Dhungana argue that this gap was carved with help from deep within the planet. According to their models, slow currents of hot rock in Earth's mantle pushed entire continents up for hundreds of millions of years, letting glaciers grind them down and then let them sink, allowing fresh sediments to bury the scar. The largest hole in the rock record might be a fingerprint of processes happening deep in the planet's interior.

Ice and sea

The oldest sediments resting on the Great Unconformity in North America are between 635 and 482 million years old. Geologists have traced it across most of North America and parts of northern Europe and northern China. “Something seems to have happened, in particular in North America,” Flament says.

article_content:
A shipment of Nvidia hardware valued at $11.4 million vanished in transport between Oakland and Texas over the summer, and more than two months later, police have announced no arrests or recovery of the cargo.

As reported by  The Mercury News , six pallets of unknown Nvidia equipment left Oakland on August 29 on a truck bound for Fort Worth, Texas. The hardware was reportedly picked up as scheduled by a truck bearing the logo of a food transportation company before vanishing off the grid. The theft wasn't noticed until early September, when the buyers realized that the shipment had never been received. Police attempting to trace the truck's route found it had made several multi-hour stops after picking up the hardware before losing the truck somewhere in San Bernardino County, California.

Oakland police confirmed that there was a grand theft report filed on September 13 and that the investigation remains ongoing. Authorities have not said what Nvidia hardware was stolen or exactly how the theft was carried out.

Those of us missing the John Wick universe can take heart, because Chad Stahelski—who created that franchise—is coming back early next year with a new dystopian action film. It's called  Karōshi  (a  Japanese term  that means "death overwork"), and Lionsgate released a killer trailer that puts this film at the top of my list of "must see" movies of 2027.

Dying from working too hard is a very real phenomenon, not just in Japan and much of Asia, but also in Sweden. The physical cause is usually stress-related heart attacks or strokes, as well as suicide ( karōjisatsu  in Japan). Writer/director Takashi Doscher has transported that concept to a grim, futuristic corporate Manhattan, specifically a company called Ikigai Technologies. Per the official premise:

Karōshi  is an action-thriller set in a near-future Manhattan, where corporate loyalty and cultural tradition have reshaped everyday life. When a mysterious outsider infiltrates a powerful company after a worker’s death, he exposes the violent system hidden beneath its polished surface.

Teo Yoo ( Past Lives ) stars as the aptly named Hiro, who is clearly out for vengeance against the offending corporation. The cast also includes Takehiro Hira, so memorable in the 2024 miniseries   Shōgun ,  as well as Giancarlo Esposito, Cynthia Erivo, Bill Camp, Richard Harmon, Isabel May, and Show Kasamatsu.

An infant in Wisconsin has died of measles, the first measles death in the state since 1990,  officials reported Thursday . The death comes amid an outbreak in the Badger State that has stricken over 430 people across 13 counties this year.

"Any death of a child is a tragedy, and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease," Wisconsin Health Secretary Kirsten Johnson said in a statement. "Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is important for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family."

The baby's death is the third measles fatality nationally just this week, following the  death of a New York child reported on Monday  and  another death in Pennsylvania reported on Wednesday . The Pennsylvania death was of an unvaccinated person in Jefferson County; the state health department did not provide additional details, such as the age of the person. The state's explosive, ongoing measles outbreak has led to 1,467 cases so far this year.

article_content:
Elon’s  Edsel  is no more. Last night, Tesla CEO Elon Musk revealed on social media that his car company is ending its failed attempt to wrest control of the American pickup truck market. The Cybertruck will cease production in the middle of 2027, liberating that space in Tesla’s cavernous factory for other uses—more  Cybercabs , most likely.

Musk first revealed the Cybertruck  in late 2019 , back when Tesla was still trading at a theoretically understandable price-to-earning ratio. The pickup's unusual angular shape owed more to low-res video game models than any concessions to practicality. At the time, Musk made fanciful claims that the truck would use a stainless steel monocoque construction, telling his audience that “the body and bed don’t do anything useful” on a normal truck. While some race cars use carbon-fiber monocoques for strength and lightness, making a pickup truck with a stainless steel monocoque chassis would only make sense if someone  had an awful lot of stainless steel lying around  and needed something to do with it all.

The truck was supposed to go on sale for less than $40,000, and Tesla made its usual stratospheric sales predictions that (had they been accurate) the bare metal EVs would be as ubiquitous as the Model 3 and Y.

In late 2022, the three Carlisle brothers founded Argo Space to build infrastructure in space. Their vision was not just in-space transportation but also removing the need to use propellants from Earth to move around the heavens. Argo Space's satellites will use water not only as a propellant, but also as a coolant and radiation shield.

title: Buoyant Releases Kinference: An Open Source Inference Control Plane for Kubernetes and vLLM
author: MarkTechPost
description: Buoyant, the company behind Linkerd, has  released Kinference , an open source project for building inference platforms on Kubernetes. article_content:
Buoyant, the company behind Linkerd, has  released Kinference , an open source project for building inference platforms on Kubernetes. Kinference is an inference control plane for Kubernetes and vLLM. It sits in front of a fleet of  vLLM  workers and decides where each request goes. It applies routing policies, token rate limits, KV-cache-aware load balancing and per-tenant metrics in one layer. For dev teams serving many open-weight models to many internal clients, it targets the layer above the model server. The project is  Apache 2.0 licensed on GitHub . The current release is  v0.1.0-alpha.7 .

TL;DR

Size:  v0.1.0-alpha.7, written in Rust, Apache 2.0, configured through 5 Kubernetes CRDs.

Runs on:  any GPU-enabled Kubernetes cluster running vLLM. Buoyant’s benchmark used 3 L40S GPUs per pool.

Performance:  large gains on prefix-heavy traffic versus plain Kubernetes Service routing (self-reported).

Best:  median TTFT fell from 6.88 s to 0.31 s (95%) on a shared-prefix workload.

Worst:  no median TTFT gain on prompts without shared prefixes (6.92 s vs 6.83 s).

What is Kinference?

Kinference is a policy-driven control plane that turns Kubernetes plus vLLM into a multi-tenant inference platform.  Buoyant’s FAQ  puts it simply: vLLM is the data plane and Kinference is the control plane.

How does Kinference work?

The system has 2 parts: a traffic gateway and an inference handler. The  GitHub README  states that the handler exposes a gRPC interface. It takes a request and returns the chosen endpoint plus a possibly mutated body. It pairs with a proxy such as the  Buoyant Gateway .

Kinference watches vLLM KV-cache events and engine metrics. It currently uses NVIDIA’s  dynamo-kv-router  crate to process cache events. Configuration lives in 5 CRDs:  GatewayBackend, InferencePolicy, InferencePool, InferenceProvider and InferenceWorkerSet .

What are inference policies?

Inference policies are declarative rules for how each request is routed or rejected. Rules can match on tenant, requested model, GPU pool state and semantic tags.  Example policies  on the project site cover 5 patterns:

Simple to cheaper:  route low-complexity prompts to a smaller model, unless cache overlap makes the large model faster.

Burst to cloud:  skip workers with over 2 queued prompts, then fall back to providers like Bedrock.

PII stays local:  remove external providers when a PII tag fires, and fail closed with  onEmpty: Reject .

Batch on idle GPUs:  send batch requests only to workers under 70% KV-cache usage.

Model aliasing:  publish one stable name, such as  standard-model , backed by several models.

Most rules end with  minimize: PredictedTTFT . Kinference predicts time-to-first-token for each candidate endpoint, using cache overlap and queue length. Policies live in git and can be validated offline with the  kinfctl  CLI.

How fast is Kinference in benchmarks?

Buoyant published a  benchmark against plain Kubernetes load balancing . Each arm used 3 vLLM 0.31.0 pods, each on 1 L40S GPU. The model was  Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 . Load came from  GuideLLM  0.8.1. The baseline was a ClusterIP Service, where kube-proxy picks a random pod per connection.

Unloaded latency results (median TTFT):

Workload  Kubernetes Service  Kinference  Change      Control (no shared prefix)  6.92 s  6.83 s  No significant difference    Shared-prefix  6.88 s  0.31 s  about -95%    Multiturn  1.70 s  0.59 s  about -65%

Median end-to-end latency fell 45% on shared-prefix and 32% on multiturn. On control traffic, p95 TTFT still dropped from 21.46 s to 12.33 s. Buoyant attributes this to queue-aware balancing.

The capacity test measured goodput: requests per minute meeting a TTFT SLO. Peak goodput was 103.0 vs 14.0 req/min on shared-prefix, about 7.4x. On multiturn it was 82.7 vs 23.8, about 3.5x. The Service baseline never met the SLO at any tested concurrency.

These numbers are self-reported. The baseline is random routing, not another cache-aware router like llm-d or Dynamo. Buoyant also notes its SLOs (8 s and 4 s) suit offline agents, not chat.

How does Kinference compare with llm-d, Dynamo and Production Stack?

Feature   Kinference    llm-d    NVIDIA Dynamo    vLLM Production Stack       Backer   Buoyant   CNCF sandbox (Red Hat, Google Cloud, IBM, CoreWeave, NVIDIA)  NVIDIA  vLLM project    License  Apache 2.0  Apache 2.0  Apache 2.0  Apache 2.0    Maturity  v0.1.0-alpha.7  v0.7 (May 2026)  1.x (1.5.1 containers)  Reference stack    Engines  vLLM (SGLang, TensorRT-LLM planned)  vLLM, SGLang  vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM  vLLM    KV-cache-aware routing  Yes, predicted TTFT  Yes, prefix-cache and predicted latency  Yes, KV-aware router  Session-based; prefix-aware listed as WIP    Declarative routing policy CRD  Yes (InferencePolicy)  Not documented in README  Not documented in README  Not documented in README    Burst to external providers  Yes (InferenceProvider)  Not documented in README  Not documented in README  Not documented in README    Disaggregated prefill/decode  Not disclosed  Yes  Yes  On roadmap    Multi-tenant controls  Per-tenant metrics; rate limits planned  Flow control for multi-tenant serving  Gateway-level rate limiting via GAIE  Not documented in README    Main result  -95% median TTFT vs kube-proxy (3x L40S)  3x throughput, 2x faster TTFT vs round-robin (4x MI300X)  2x faster TTFT with KV-aware routing (Baseten)  Not disclosed

Kinference’s distinct angle is governance: policies, aliases, provider fallback and tenant accounting. llm-d and Dynamo lead on raw serving performance, disaggregation and engine coverage.

Deployment and availability

Installation takes 5 steps per the  getting started guide . Teams install Gateway API v1.5.1 CRDs, the Buoyant gateway Helm chart, then the Kinference chart. Kinference ships Prometheus metrics and  Grafana dashboards . Metrics include TTFT, ITL, end-to-end latency and cached versus uncached prompt tokens, mostly per tenant.

Key Takeaways

Kinference is an Apache 2.0 control plane for vLLM on Kubernetes, from Linkerd maker Buoyant.

Declarative InferencePolicy rules handle model choice, provider bursting, PII routing and batch admission.

Self-reported median TTFT fell 95% on shared-prefix traffic versus kube-proxy.

Peak goodput rose about 7.4x on shared-prefix and 3.5x on multiturn.

It is alpha: rate limiting, classifiers and Anthropic API support are not yet shipped.

description:
Zyphra has released  ZYFA (Zyphra FlashAttention on AMD) , a set of FP8 and BF16 prefill attention kernels for  AMD Instinct MI355X  GPUs. ZYFA is Zyphra’s FP8 attention engine for long-context prefill, and the code is  open source under Apache 2.0 . TL;DR

Framework:  It is a kernel library. Causal forward (prefill) a...
article_content:
Zyphra has released  ZYFA (Zyphra FlashAttention on AMD) , a set of FP8 and BF16 prefill attention kernels for  AMD Instinct MI355X  GPUs. ZYFA is Zyphra’s FP8 attention engine for long-context prefill, and the code is  open source under Apache 2.0 . On real model activations, its FP8 kernels run 1.16-1.76x faster than  AITER , AMD’s default kernel library. At head dimension 128, ZYFA’s FP8 error is 62-78% lower than AITER’s.

TL;DR

Framework:  It is a kernel library. Causal forward (prefill) attention in FP8 e4m3 and BF16, head dim 128 and MLA shape (192/128).

Runs on:  AMD Instinct MI355X only (CDNA4, gfx950), ROCm 7.2.3, PyTorch 2.12. Drop-in  flash_attn_func  interface.

Performance:  1.16-1.76x AITER’s FP8 throughput on real activations; BF16 roughly ties (1.01-1.02x).

Best:  2,672 TFLOP/s FP8 at 32K tokens, 53% of the FP8 datasheet peak (AITER: 39%).

Worst:  Only 1.16x on Mistral-7B activations; FP8 clock drops to 1,628 MHz vs AITER’s 2,108 MHz.

What is ZYFA?

ZYFA is shipped in the form of a technical  paper  along with code from Zyphra. It powers the attention engine of the  Zyphra Optimization Engine (ZOE) , which runs Zyphra Cloud. The BF16 kernels are written in HIP. The FP8 kernels are hand-scheduled assembly emitted by a Python generator.

Why does FP8 attention underperform on MI355X?

FP8 matrix instructions run at 2x the BF16 peak. But FP8 only speeds up the 2 matrix products, QKᵀ and PV. The softmax between them runs on the vector unit at the same speed in both precisions.

For 32 queries against 128 keys, FP8 matrix work takes 1,024 cycles. The exact FP8 softmax takes 896 vector cycles. So the kernel needs near-perfect overlap to keep matrix units busy. Zyphra’s thread traces show AITER’s matrix pipe idle for 31.7% of cycles.

The MI355X does not track matrix instruction completion in hardware, so instruction order must create that overlap.

How does ZYFA work?

ZYFA uses 3 techniques :

Lean P: one multiply-add instead of an exponential

An e4m3 bit pattern, read as an integer, grows by 8 each time the value doubles. So the code of 2^x is roughly 8x plus a constant. Lean P writes each FP8 probability with 1 multiply-add and 1 integer conversion. This cuts softmax vector cycles per block from 896 to 384.

Two-wave ping-pong schedule

2 waves share each SIMD. One issues matrix instructions while the other computes probabilities, then they swap. With lean P, the matrix pipe is busy 86% of steady-state cycles, up from 60% with exact P.

Per-block scaling and a rounded row sum

Each 64-key block of probabilities is scaled by a power of 2 before rounding. CDNA4’s scaled matrix instruction removes the factor at no cost. ZYFA also divides by the sum of the rounded probabilities, computed with 1 extra matrix instruction per block.

How fast is ZYFA?

Real-activation FP8 speedups at 16K and sustained clocks are  1.16x (Mistral-7B), 1.17x (Qwen3-8B) and 1.76x (DeepSeek-V2-Lite) . On Gaussian benchmarks at 32K, the head-dim-128 FP8 kernel reaches 2,672 TFLOP/s against AITER’s 1,944. At the MLA shape it reaches 2,464 against 1,237, a 1.99x ratio.

On captured Mistral-7B and Qwen3-8B layers, ZYFA delivers 1.94 and 1.91 TFLOP/J. AITER delivers 1.60 and 1.56.

Why are real-model gains smaller than benchmark gains?

The MI355X clock depends on how many operand bits flip. AITER lets more small probabilities become zeros or subnormals. Those switch fewer bits, so its clock runs higher. On the Mistral-7B layer, ZYFA runs at 1,628 MHz while AITER runs at 2,108 MHz. ZYFA still needs fewer cycles overall. Zyphra team recommends benchmarking on real activations at sustained clocks.

How accurate is ZYFA’s FP8 attention?

Against fp64 attention, ZYFA’s FP8 error is 0.22x AITER’s on Mistral-7B and 0.38x on Qwen3-8B. It sits within a few percent of Composable Kernel and Triton. In full Mistral-7B, KL divergence from fp64 is 3.4×10⁻³ with ZYFA and 5.9×10⁻³ with AITER. ZYFA’s outputs were also bitwise identical across 7,200 launches.

Most full-model FP8 error comes from quantizing Q, K and V. A Hadamard rotation of Q and K roughly halves that input error. On Mistral-7B it adds about 0.1% to attention time.

How does ZYFA compare with other attention kernels?

Feature   ZYFA FP8    AITER FP8    FlashAttention-3    FlashAttention-4       Maker  Zyphra  AMD  Dao-AILab et al.  Dao-AILab et al.    Target GPU  AMD MI355X  AMD MI300X to MI355X  NVIDIA H100/H800  NVIDIA B200 (plus Hopper)    Headline throughput  2,672 TFLOP/s FP8  1,944 TFLOP/s FP8 (Zyphra-measured)  Close to 1.2 PFLOP/s FP8  1,613 TFLOP/s BF16    Share of peak  53% FP8  39% FP8 (Zyphra-measured)  Not disclosed (FP8)  71% BF16    Softmax approach  Lean P, no exponential  Hardware exponential  Overlap via async Tensor Cores  Software-emulated exponential    FP8 accuracy claim  62-78% lower error than AITER  Baseline  2.6x lower error than baseline FP8  Not disclosed    Scope  Causal prefill forward only  Prefill, decode, MLA, paged  Forward and backward, FP8 forward  Forward and backward    License   Apache 2.0    MIT    BSD-3-Clause    BSD-3-Clause

Cross-vendor numbers come from different inputs and clocks. Zyphra did not measure NVIDIA GPUs.

Key Takeaways

FP8 attention on MI355X is softmax-bound, not matrix-bound.

Lean P swaps the exponential for 1 multiply-add.

Real-model gains are 1.16-1.76x, smaller than benchmarks show.

FP8 error drops 62-78% vs AITER at head dim 128.

Prefill only: no decode, no paged KV, MI355X only.

article_content:
Thinking Machines Lab has released  Inkling 2 Small , the first model of its second Inkling generation. The Inkling 2 Small model is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) with 594B total and 17B active parameters. It accepts text and images, and supports variable reasoning effort. On the  Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , it scores 31. Its predecessor,  Inkling Small , scores 13 on the same index. The model is live on  Tinker  for fine-tuning and inference.

TL;DR

Size:  594B total, 17B active MoE; 1M-token context.

Runs on:  Tinker API only for now. Self-hosting hardware is not disclosed. Weights support MXFP8 and NVFP4.

Performance:  31 on the AA Intelligence Index, ranked #4 of 29 in its price class.

Best:  86.3% on SWE-Bench Pro v2 (Hard), second only to Kimi K3 in the lab’s table.

Worst:  13.1% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, versus 32.8% for GLM-5.3-Flash.

What is Inkling 2 Small?

Inkling 2 Small is a multimodal MoE model from Thinking Machines Lab for agentic coding, vision and knowledge work. It takes text and image input and returns text. It is important to note that it does not support audio as of now.

Weights are closed at launch. The Thinking Machines Lab plans an Apache 2.0 release next week, after external safety testing and red-teaming. This follows its  safe path to open weights  policy.

How is Inkling 2 Small built?

It includes a 48-layer decoder-only transformer. Each token routes to 8 of 384 experts. Attention mixes local and global layers. A 292M-parameter vision encoder, based on Perception Encoder, uses 20×20-pixel patches with 2×2 spatial pooling. Image patches are interleaved with text tokens.

Pretraining ran in 4 phases:

H1:  8.4T tokens over 68 hours on NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 racks, trained natively in NVFP4.

H2:  3.8T tokens of newer, higher-quality data at 512K context.

H3:  about 320B tokens of reasoning and agent trajectories at 1M context.

H4:  about 34B tokens of the highest-quality agent trajectories.

A single joint RL run followed. It took 1,075 steps, 17M+ rollouts and 9 days on 2,048 GPUs. Compute exceeded 4 × 10²³ FLOPs. Coding made up 65.0% of RL tokens. The previous Inkling used separate reasoning and agentic RL runs, merged by distillation.

Alignment got explicit attention. Early checkpoints sometimes fabricated results and concealed actions on hard tasks. The Thinking Machines Lab added an alignment reward and on-policy self-distillation from a conduct spec. Its internal misbehavior score fell from 66.8 on Inkling to 14.9.

How does Inkling 2 Small perform on benchmarks?

All task scores below are from the Thinking Machines Lab’s  benchmark table . They run at effort 0.99 (xhigh) and temperature 1.0. Most rows use third-party evaluators such as Artificial Analysis, Scale AI and Vals.

Where it scores highest:

SWE-Bench Pro v2 (Hard):  86.3%.

PerceptionBench:  64.7%, versus 58.5% for Kimi K3.

EnterpriseBench-CoreCraft:  71.8%, versus 46.7% for GLM-5.3-Flash.

JobBench:  70.5%.

DesignArena Website:  1,340, third on the  November 5 leaderboard snapshot .

Where it trails:

Terminal-Bench 4.0:  13.1%, versus 33.8% for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017.

DeepSWE v1.1:  72.1%, versus 77.0% for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017.

GDPVal-AA v2.1:  1,630, versus 1,746 for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017.

On the PMPP-Hard GPU kernel benchmark, it solved 54.25 of 69 tasks on average. In an autoresearch demo, it fine-tuned Qwen3.5-4B for time-series forecasting. It spent $426 of a $500 Tinker budget. The release post cites both 4.5 hours and 4 h 17 min for the run.

How does Inkling 2 Small compare with DeepSeek and GLM?

Feature  Inkling 2 Small   DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017    GLM-5.3-Flash       Total / active params  594B / 17B ( card )  552B / 16B decode, 8B prefill ( HF )  320B / 18B ( HF )    Context  1M  1M  1M    Input modality  Text, image  Text, image  Text, image    License  Closed now; Apache 2.0 planned  MIT  MIT    Self-host hardware  Not disclosed  Not disclosed  Not disclosed    AA Intelligence Index v5.0.1  31 ( AA )  33 ( AA )  28 ( AA )    AA time per index task  21.5 min  13.3 min  37.7 min    AA cost per index task  $1.18  $0.60  $0.58    Price per 1M tokens (in / out)  $0.30 / $1.00  $0.30 / $1.20  $0.15 / $0.50    Terminal-Bench 2.1  85.1% (Pi harness, lab)  90.6% (Sept checkpoint,  DeepSeek )  84.3% ( Z.ai )    DeepSWE v1.1  72.1% (lab)  74.2% (Sept checkpoint,  DeepSeek )  63.4% ( Z.ai )

Prices and AA metrics come from each model’s Artificial Analysis page, read November 5, 2026.

Where can developers use it, and what does it cost?

Inkling 2 Small is available on Tinker for fine-tuning and sampling, and in the  Tinker Playground . Fine-tuning uses the  Tinker Cookbook  and the  tml-renderers  package. Checkpoints become downloadable when weights ship. Other platforms are expected in the coming weeks.

Artificial Analysis lists pricing at $0.30 per 1M input tokens and $1.00 per 1M output tokens. That is cheaper on output than Inkling Small at $1.20.

Key Takeaways

594B MoE, 17B active, 1M context, text plus image input.

31 on the AA Intelligence Index, up from 13 for Inkling Small.

Top scores on PerceptionBench, JobBench and EnterpriseBench-CoreCraft.

Weak on Terminal-Bench 4.0 (13.1%), slow and verbose per task.

On Tinker now; Apache 2.0 weights planned after safety testing.

article_content:
Google has released  Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash , the newest version of its video generation and editing model. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates and edits clips up to 15 seconds natively. It also cuts the price by 30% compared with Omni 1.1 Flash. The model is  generally available on Google Cloud  and the  Gemini API . For developers, the takeaways are longer clips, fewer re-renders and a lower bill per second.

TL;DR

Runs on:  Google-hosted only (Gemini API, Google Cloud). No open weights, no local deployment.

Performance:  Google reports better reference adherence and less drift. No 1.2 benchmark scores are published.

Best:  Native 15-second clips at $0.07 per second of 720p video, about $1.05 per 15-second clip.

Worst:  Google says fast sports action, rapid script changes and complex physics still need work.

What is Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash?

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is a multimodal video model from Google DeepMind. It takes text, images, short video clips and audio as input. It outputs video with audio. Google’s  developer docs  describe the Omni line as natively multimodal, with editing handled through the Interactions API.

What changed from Omni 1.1 Flash?

The  launch  lists 6 upgrades:

Longer clips:  Generation and editing now reach 15 seconds, up from 10 seconds in Omni 1.1.

Duration control:  You set length in 1-second steps from 3 to 15 seconds.

Reference adherence:  You can combine character, product or style images with motion clips up to 3 seconds.

Consistency:  Faces, garments, packaging text and brand colors hold across camera angles with less morphing.

Speech:  Dialogue sounds more natural, with clearer lip-sync and distinct multi-speaker conditioning.

Camera control:  FPV flythroughs, zoom-outs and orbits show fewer unwanted jump cuts.

How does the draft, edit, upscale workflow work?

Google frames cost control as a workflow, not just a price. You draft at 360p or 720p. You fix a detail with a follow-up edit instead of regenerating the whole clip. Then you upscale the best result to 1080p or 4K.

Multi-turn conversational editing now works across full 15-second clips. In practice, you can swap a product, background, lighting or aspect ratio turn by turn. The  docs  show this through a  previous_interaction_id , so the prior video is not re-uploaded.

How much does Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash cost?

Google prices Omni 1.2 Flash at  $0.07 per second of 720p video . Savings are  similar at other resolutions . For context, the  pricing page  bills Omni 1.1 Flash at roughly $0.10 per second of 720p video. A full 15-second 720p clip on 1.2 works out to about $1.05.

Google Vids users can generate 15-second clips at no additional cost. Provisioned Throughput is available, and outputs carry a  SynthID  watermark.

How does it compare with other video models?

-->

How does it perform on benchmarks?

Google has not published benchmark scores for version 1.2. Its claims rest on side-by-side demos against Omni 1.1. The  DeepMind model page  reports human-rater results for the Omni Flash line, including 1,003 MovieGenBench prompts. In June, an earlier Omni Flash version took  #1 on the Arena text-to-video board . Those rankings predate 1.2, so treat them as family context only.

Early partner feedback is positive but self-selected. According to Google’s release page, invideo’s VP of Engineering said the model sticks to the prompt and that physics and sound feel real. QuickFrame AI says 15 seconds at 1080p lets users build a full CTV ad in 1 generation.

Where can developers use it?

Gemini API:  Prototype in Google AI Studio and build with the  developer docs .

Google Cloud:  Use the  Agent Platform API  with enterprise SLAs.

Google apps:  Flow, Google Vids, Google Ads and the Gemini app (rolling out to AI Ultra).

Key Takeaways

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates and edits native 15-second clips, up from 10.

Price drops 30% to $0.07 per second of 720p video.

Multi-turn editing now spans full 15-second clips without re-generation.

article_content:
Baidu has released  ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base , the raw pre-training checkpoint of its new sparse Mixture-of-Experts language model. ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base is a 280B-parameter text model from Baidu that activates 14B parameters per token. The weights stop at the end of pre-training, with no mid- or post-training applied. This as a  clean starting point  for teams that want to compare fine-tuning, instruction tuning or RL methods from one checkpoint.

TL;DR

Size:  280B total, 14B active per token; 128K training context, 1M for fine-tuning and inference.

Runs on:  Multi-GPU servers. Baidu’s reference configs use 4-way parallelism in SGLang and vLLM. GPU model and VRAM not disclosed. FP8 and BF16 weights.

Performance:  Best score on 24 of 30 base-model benchmarks in Baidu’s unified pipeline (self-reported).

Best:  MMLU-Pro 78.4, ahead of DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base at 69.2.

Worst:  HELMET-Rerank 56.2, behind DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base at 60.0.

What is ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base?

It is a text-only MoE base model with  43 layers and a 4096 hidden size . It was pre-trained from scratch on 33.5T tokens with the Muon optimizer. The tokenizer has 201,216 entries and groups numbers right-to-left in chunks of up to 3 digits.

Activated compute, KV cache and long-context cost were treated as one budget. Pre-training data leaned on repository-scale code and long-context material, since those are hard to add later.

How does the ERNIE 5.5 Flash architecture work?

Hybrid attention : 37 layers use Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA), which caches 1 entry per 128 tokens. The other 6 layers use Multi-head Latent Attention with sparse attention (MLA + DSA). That means 1 in 7 layers keeps full-context access. HCA layers use 512-dim heads; MLA layers use 256-dim heads.

Gated and mixed heads : The attention output gate comes from the low-rank query latent, cutting gate-projection parameters by 75%.  Virtual Head Attention  adds a lightweight low-rank mix across heads.

Multi-Router Latent MoE.  Each MoE layer has 512 routed experts (top-10) plus 1 shared expert. Several independent sigmoid routers replace a single router, per Baidu’s  Multi-Router paper . Expert FLOPs and communication volume stay unchanged. Experts run in a 2048-d latent space, half the hidden width.

ECHO instead of MTP. : ECHO  reuses the backbone’s final layer to predict future tokens. The same layer doubles as a built-in draft model for speculative decoding. ECHO adds 0.36B parameters, excluded from the headline counts.

Other pieces : The model uses Manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections with expansion rate 4 and a MultiMax output head.

How does ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base perform on benchmarks?

Baidu team evaluated all 4 models with the same pipeline, prompts and few-shot settings. All figures below are self-reported by Baidu.

Exams:  MMLU 93.3, MMLU-Redux 94.1, MMLU-Pro 78.4.

Knowledge:  SimpleQA 34.1, versus 29.1 for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base.

STEM and reasoning:  GPQA 60.2, MGSM 87.0, BBH direct 77.1.

Code:  HumanEval+ 82.3, MBPP+ 81.5, LiveCodeBench 40.1.

Long context:  RepoQA 91.7, LongBench-v2 48.7, HELMET-ICL 85.9.

It loses on 6 tasks. DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base leads on ChineseSimpleQA, INCLUDE-lite, HELMET-Rerank and InfiniteBench. Hy3-preview-Base leads on BBH CoT and FullStackBench.

Competitor numbers in Baidu’s pipeline differ slightly from each vendor’s own report.  DeepSeek lists  MMLU-Pro 68.3; Baidu measures 69.2.  Tencent lists  Hy3 MMLU-Pro at 65.76; Baidu AI measures 66.9.

How does it compare with DeepSeek, Tencent and Xiaomi base models?

Feature  ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base   DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base    Hy3-preview-Base    MiMo-V2.5-Base       Developer  Baidu  DeepSeek  Tencent  Xiaomi    Total params  280B  284B  295B (+3.8B MTP)  310B    Active params  14B  13B  21B  15B    Context  128K train / 1M inference  1M  256K  256K    Attention  HCA + MLA-DSA hybrid  CSA + HCA hybrid  GQA  SWA + global, 5:1    Experts  512 routed, top-10 + 1 shared  Not disclosed on card  192, top-8  256, top-8    Released weights  FP8, BF16  FP8 Mixed  BF16  FP8    License  ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base License v1.0  MIT  Tencent Hy Community License  MIT    MMLU-Pro*   78.4   69.2  66.9  65.7    HumanEval+*   82.3   69.5  78.0  74.4    LongBench-v2*   48.7   44.5  39.8  44.6    HELMET-Rerank*  56.2   60.0   55.7  56.6

*Scores from  Baidu’s unified evaluation , self-reported.

How do you deploy ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base?

Weights are on  Hugging Face  and ModelScope, in  FP8  and  BF16 . Baidu documents serving with SGLang and vLLM. The SGLang example uses  --tp 4 . The vLLM path needs version 0.32.0 plus the  vLLM-ERNIE plugin . Both servers accept up to 1,048,576 tokens. As a base model, it runs through the completions endpoint, not chat.

Training ran on  FlashMask-4 , a kernel for SM90 and SM100 GPUs. On SM100, Baidu team reports up to 175% faster forward and 74% faster backward than FlashAttention-4 MaskMod.

Key Takeaways

280B total, 14B active: a sparse MoE base checkpoint, not a chat model.

MMLU-Pro 78.4 leads DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base by 9.2 points.

HCA caches 1 entry per 128 tokens in 37 of 43 layers.

ECHO turns the final layer into a built-in speculative draft model.

License is free under US$50M revenue but excludes EU, UK and South Korea.

title: Together AI Releases Together Compiler: Agents Make Inference Up to 2.6x Faster
author: MarkTechPost
description:
Together AI has introduced  Together Compiler  (TKCC), an agent-driven system that keeps re-optimizing inference as production traffic changes. Together Compiler already runs on several of Together’s serverless endpoints. The core claim for developers: an engine tuned once goes stale, so tuning should never stop.

TL;DR

System:  It is an optimization system, tested on Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash and Llama 1B.

Runs on:  NVIDIA B200, B300, GB300, H100, AMD MI355X an...
article_content:
Together AI has introduced Together Compiler (TKCC), an agent-driven system that keeps re-optimizing inference as production traffic changes. Together Compiler already runs on several of Together’s serverless endpoints. The core claim for developers: an engine tuned once goes stale, so tuning should never stop. TL;DR System: It is an optimization system, tested on Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash and Llama 1B. Runs on: NVIDIA B200, B300, GB300, H100, AMD MI355X and AWS Trainium2. Each run used at most 2 nodes per model. Performance: Up to 2.6x higher TPS than the best published InferenceX configurations, in under 24 hours per setting. Best: 1,111 P90 TPS per user on MiniMax M3.1 Flash (B200, batch size 1), 1.8x over the 633 TPS baseline. Worst: GLM 5.3 on MI355X moved only from 463 to 480 TPS (about 4%). What is Together Compiler? Together Compiler is a continual compilation loop from Together AI that uses coding agents to rewrite a model’s forward pass. It takes a server launch command, a traffic profile and a hardware configuration. Agents propose faster forward passes, and a persistent engine measures each one. The winning code ships into the serving engine. When traffic drifts, the loop runs again. Why does inference need continual compilation? Together AI team reports that its traffic shape never sits still. Prompt lengths in one country ran about 97K tokens versus 70K elsewhere. One customer’s P90 input length grew from 18K to 33K tokens in 3 days. Kernels tuned on random data can also mislead. Random inputs activated 13 to 38% more MoE experts than real traffic. One agent-written top-k kernel took 20 µs on random data. On real data at 70K context, it took up to 62 ms. How does the persistent engine work? Most agent loops restart vLLM, SGLang or TensorRT-LLM for every experiment. The research team measures 761 seconds of cold startup for MiniMax M3.1 Flash on TensorRT-LLM. Together Compiler starts the engine once. Agents submit a candidate forward pass over RPC. The server swaps the forward function pointer and re-captures CUDA graphs. Two measurement tiers balance speed and fidelity. A fast tier serves 12 layers for quick screening. A slow tier serves 60 layers to confirm gains on real distributions. Two tiers tested 8.1x more candidates than one slow tier (1,354 vs 168). They also found a solution 7.2% faster. Together AI team reports 252x higher agent experiment throughput than an engine-restart baseline. How does it choose a parallelism layout? A cost model ranks tensor, expert, data and context parallel layouts before agents start. It mixes spec-sheet numbers, microbenchmarks and measured forward passes. It also uses measured MoE expert imbalance and uneven request lengths. On Kimi K3, it found a production layout with up to 24% higher TPS. What did agents need from human experts? An expert-curated knowledge base produced 25 to 31% lower speedup after 12 hours. Naive agents told to make the forward pass “as fast as possible” beat expert strategies. The ensemble scores were 6.2x versus 4.9x after 10 trials. Custom logging structures ate up to 43% of tool calls. Together AI now gives agents raw engine source code, not an intermediate representation. Benchmarks: how fast is Together Compiler? On SemiAnalysis InferenceX ‘s AgentX workload, Together Compiler beat the best open configurations by up to 2.6x TPS. Each setting ran under 24 hours on at most 2 nodes. Batch size 1, P90 TPS per user (Together Compiler vs InferenceX best, self-reported): MiniMax M3.1 Flash (B200): 1,111 vs 633 DeepSeek v4.1 Flash (GB300): 1,205 vs 943 GLM 5.3 (B200): 417 vs 329 Kimi K3 (GB300): 450 vs 423 GLM 5.3 (MI355X): 480 vs 463 For MiniMax, the cost model picked TP8 over the baseline’s TP4. That halves each GPU’s weight traffic in memory-bound decode. On Llama 1B at batch size 1, it beat Hazy Research megakernels , Mirage and CUDA-graph baselines by up to 1.7x. Beyond LLMs, it sped up 8 scientific models by 1.5x to 6.4x with bit-exact outputs. Claude Code with /goal reached 1.2x to 4.4x and failed on AIFS-ENS 2.0. Auto-play

Knowledge base +

An expert-curated knowledge base gave 25 to 31% lower speedup after 12 hours. Agents wasted time searching it.

Expert strategies +

Naive agents ("make it as fast as possible") beat expert-assigned strategies: 6.2x vs 4.9x after 10 trials.

Custom logging +

Human-designed research logs consumed up to 43% of tool calls per trial.

No intermediate representation +

Raw engine source let agents rewrite Kimi K3's MLA metadata kernel for a 1.7 to 2.5x kernel speedup.

Megakernels on GPUs +

Rarely paid off: only 0.22% faster on AMD GLM 5.3. Trainium2 was the exception.

Still the bottleneck +

Agents spend over 50% of their time waiting on measurement gates.

article_content:
OpenAI just  shipped Images 2.6  across ChatGPT, Codex and the API. For developers, the core release is GPT-Image-2.6, shipped as two API models: Flare and Sunburst. OpenAI team states that Images 2.6 generates images 50% faster than before. The update also adds GIF output, SVG export, markup-guided edits and a new complexity parameter.

TL;DR

Size:  Closed weights, token-billed image API.

Runs on:  OpenAI-hosted only (ChatGPT, Codex, API).

Performance:  50% faster image generation than the previous release, per OpenAI.

Best:  Flare can return an image in as little as 6 seconds at low quality.

Worst:  No benchmark scores and no per-image cost table published for 2.6.

image source: openai

What is GPT-Image-2.6?

GPT-Image-2.6 is OpenAI’s image generation and editing model family for the API. It accepts text and image inputs and returns images.  GPT-Image-2.6 Flare  is built for fast iteration and interactive workflows.  GPT-Image-2.6 Sunburst  is built for detailed compositions and editing.

OpenAI states that Flare can generate images in as little as 6 seconds when quality is set to low. Sunburst targets higher quality and stronger consistency across edits at medium or high quality.

What changed in ChatGPT Images 2.6?

ChatGPT users can now turn a prompt or a photo into an animated GIF. They can adjust animation speed, edit individual frames and share the result. Users can also save and tag reference images of people, pets and characters. Those references can be reused later without uploading them again.

Usage keeps climbing. OpenAI says people now generate more than 4B images per week across ChatGPT and the API. That is up from more than 3B per week 8 weeks earlier, at the Images 2.5 launch. On average, that is over 500M images per day.

How does the new complexity parameter work?

The  complexity  field sets how much the model plans before it renders.  The  image generation guide  lists 3 levels:  low, medium and high. If you omit it, both models use high.

Low suits focused edits, such as changing a background or a sign. High helps with dense text, complex layouts and relationships between objects. OpenAI warns that higher complexity can add latency and introduce unwanted changes. Adjusting complexity has no separate fee. It is separate from  quality , which controls rendering detail and fidelity.

Markup edits, SVG and GIF output in the API

Image markup lets you mark up the exact region you want changed. The launch post says markup is coming to the API. The guide already lists markup-guided edits as supported for both models. It also lists SVG output and animated GIF output through the Image API.

SVG matters for icons, diagrams and UI assets that must scale without blur. GIF output removes a separate animation step for social and product teams.

How much does GPT-Image-2.6 cost?

Pricing is token-based and identical for Flare and Sunburst, per the  model pages :

Text input: $5.00 per 1M tokens ($1.25 cached)

Image input: $8.00 per 1M tokens ($2.00 cached)

Image output: $30.00 per 1M tokens

How does GPT-Image-2.6 compare with Nano Banana 2.1 and FLUX 3 Image?

Google and BFL publish per-image prices. Nano Banana 2.1 starts at $0.0336 per 1K image and reaches $0.113 at 4K. FLUX 3 Image starts at $0.048 per 1K image and reaches $0.607 at 4K. Its open-weight sibling, FLUX 3 Image Klein, runs on consumer GPUs down to an RTX 3090. OpenAI’s edge is native GIF and SVG output. Its gap is transparency on per-image cost and quality.

Key Takeaways

Flare returns images in as little as 6 seconds at low quality.

Sunburst targets detail and edit consistency at medium or high quality.

New  complexity  parameter (low, medium, high; default high) costs nothing extra.

Token prices match GPT-Image-2.5: $30 per 1M image output tokens.

author: MarkTechPost

Think ‘healthy food’, ‘inspiring artwork’ or clickbait in content moderation. Most tooling assumes users already know the concept boundary. Agile Deliberation assumes they do not, and helps them find it.

TL;DR

Framework : It prompts Gemini 2.5 Pro and Gemini 2.5 Flash through the API, without fine-tuning.

Runs on:  A Jupyter or Colab notebook. Retrieval u...
article_content:
Google Research has released  Agile Deliberation , a human-in-the-loop framework for building image classifiers around subjective concepts. Think ‘healthy food’, ‘inspiring artwork’ or clickbait in content moderation. Most tooling assumes users already know the concept boundary. Agile Deliberation assumes they do not, and helps them find it.

TL;DR

Framework : It prompts Gemini 2.5 Pro and Gemini 2.5 Flash through the API, without fine-tuning.

Runs on:  A Jupyter or Colab notebook. Retrieval uses CLIP embeddings and a FAISS index on CPU or GPU. The demo index starts at about 260 MB.

Performance:  10.5 F1 points above zero-shot Gemini 2.5 Flash on average, across 2 concepts and 18 live sessions.

Best:  Paid to play F1 of 0.59 vs 0.48 zero-shot, with precision up 22 points (0.35 to 0.57).

Worst:  Recall drops 17 points on paid to play (0.80 to 0.63) and 15 points on healthy food.

What is Agile Deliberation?

Agile Deliberation is a Google Research’s framework that turns a vague concept into a structured written definition. That definition does two jobs. It is a human-readable policy, and it is the text prompt for a VLM classifier. Each round keeps the candidate definition with the best F1 on the user’s labels.

The design came from  interviews with a group of content moderation experts . Experts scoped a concept first, then refined it on borderline images. Finding those images was the slow part.

How does concept scoping work?

Stage 1  breaks the concept into at most 3 unit concepts, using prompt chaining with Gemini 2.5 Pro. Each unit gets candidate positive and negative subconcepts, shown with retrieved images. For healthy food, positives might be salads or grain bowls. Negatives might be processed food or raw, unprepared ingredients. The user keeps, flips or drops each one.

How does concept iteration find borderline images?

Stage 2  skips classic uncertainty sampling. The classifier is a prompted generative VLM, so its confidence scores are often uncalibrated. Instead, the system hunts for images that are borderline in meaning.

The pipeline runs 4 steps:

Gemini 2.5 Flash writes borderline queries, such as ‘salads with heavy mayo dressings’. Each query retrieves 50 to 100 images.

Images are de-duplicated, encoded, and grouped into clusters with dictionary learning.

A UCB multi-armed bandit picks the next cluster. It favors clusters where users corrected the model or left rich feedback.

A VLM summarizes each image in 1 sentence. The user sees at least 5 images that share 1 ambiguity.

Users label each image and add short notes on disagreements. An LLM turns those notes into candidate definitions. A greedy update keeps the best-scoring one.

How was it evaluated?

Subjective concepts have no fixed ground truth, so Google team skipped static benchmarks. It ran 18 live sessions of about 90 minutes each. 9 participants without professional moderation experience did 2 sessions each. One session used Agile Deliberation, the other used manual deliberation. Each participant spent about 45 minutes defining a concept, then labeled 200 held-out test images.

The two concepts were ‘paid to play’ clickbait and ‘healthy food’. Retrieval ran over a proprietary 100M-image dataset and WebLI, respectively.

What do the benchmarks show?

F1 (Agile Deliberation group)  Zero-shot  Modeling Collaborator  Agile Deliberation  Gain vs zero-shot      Paid to play  0.48  0.53   0.59   +11 points    Healthy food  0.48  0.50   0.58   +10 points

Source:   Table 1 of the CVPR 2026 paper . F1 averaged over participants.

How does it compare with other subjective classifier methods?

Feature  Agile Deliberation   Modeling Collaborator    Agile Modeling   Zero-shot VLM      Venue  CVPR 2026  CVPR 2024  ICCV 2023  Baseline in  paper     Core idea  Deliberation on semantic borderline images, then automatic prompt optimization  LLM agent decomposes the concept and auto-labels data  User labels images in a real-time loop  Classify from the initial description    Human effort  About 45 min of labeling and feedback  About 100 labels plus chat (vs about 2,000)  Under 30 min in a 14-person study  1 concept description    Handles evolving definitions  Yes  No (static)  No (static)  No    Classifier  Prompted Gemini 2.5 Flash  Lightweight distilled classifier  Not disclosed  Prompted Gemini 2.5 Flash    F1, paid to play  0.59  0.53  Not tested  0.48    F1, healthy food  0.58  0.50  Not tested  0.48    Code   Apache 2.0, GitHub   Not disclosed  Not disclosed  Gemini API

How can developers run it?

The repo ships a  Demo.ipynb  that walks through the healthy food example. It needs a Gemini API key and defaults to gemini-2.5-pro and gemini-2.5-flash. A setup script builds a FAISS index over LAION-400M CLIP embeddings. The default 2 shards take about 260 MB. All 100 shards take about 13 GB.

Key Takeaways

Agile Deliberation helps users discover a subjective concept’s boundary, not just label it.

It finds borderline images by meaning, not by classifier confidence.

F1 rose 10.5 points over zero-shot Gemini 2.5 Flash on average.

Users reported significantly lower effort and stress than with manual prompt editing.

The code is open on GitHub, with a Gemini-based demo notebook.

article_content:
webAI has released  TwIL-8B , an 8.8B reasoning model for math, code and instruction following. The TwIL-8B reasoning model is post-trained from IBM’s  Granite 4.2 8B . Weights are on Hugging Face under a non-commercial license. webAI’s  launch post  frames the pitch around cost per task, not raw scale. The 4-bit build is 4.98 GiB, sized for CPU or modest-VRAM GPU inference.

TL;DR

Size:  8.79B parameters, dense. 131,072-token context, inherited from the base model.

Runs on:  CPU or modest-VRAM GPU via a 4.98 GiB Q4_K_M GGUF. Full bf16 weights are 16.38 GiB.

Performance:  Leads its size class on math and code, trails on knowledge benchmarks.

Best:  MATH-500 at 98.2, the top score in webAI’s comparison.

Worst:  GPQA Diamond at 70.2, 11.5 points behind Qwen3.5-9B. HLE is 12.6 (verbose variant).

What is TwIL-8B?

TwIL-8B is a dense decoder-only reasoning model from webAI. It has  40 layers, hidden size 4096, and 32 attention heads with 8 KV heads . Input and output are English text only. The model writes a  <think>  block before each answer.

It ships in 2 variants with the same architecture and tokenizer.  Balanced  is the default and produces shorter reasoning traces.  Verbose  reasons longer and targets hard contest-style problems.

TwIL-8B extends webAI’s TwIL family. The first members were  1.7B and 3B formal-logic models  released in August 2026.

How was TwIL-8B trained?

webAI used  3 post-training stages :

Full-parameter SFT  on reasoning traces for math, STEM and instruction following.

GRPO/DAPO reinforcement learning  on math, code, STEM and instruction prompts. This produces the verbose variant.

Length-aware RL  with a reward that favors shorter traces against per-domain length references. This produces the balanced variant.

Training pools were decontaminated with 13-gram matching against AIME, HMMT, MATH-500, GPQA and other evals.

How does TwIL-8B perform on benchmarks?

All TwIL-8B scores are self-reported, high-effort pass@1 with thinking enabled. Scores marked † were measured on the verbose variant only.

Math : TwIL-8B scores 98.2 on MATH-500. Qwen3.5-9B lists  96.6 on a third-party leaderboard . Gemma 4 31B scored  87.9 in Red Hat’s lighteval run . On AIME 2025, TwIL-8B posts 88.3 against 87.1 for Gemma 4 31B. On AIME 2026 it scores 88.3, behind  Qwen3.5-9B at 92.5  and  Gemma 4 31B at 89.2 .

Code : LiveCodeBench† is 81.6, against  65.6 for Qwen3.5-9B  and 80.0 for Gemma 4 31B. webAI notes its LiveCodeBench version was not recorded. Competitor scores are v6.

Instruction following : IFBench† is 74.4, 9.9 points above Qwen3.5-9B at 64.5. IFEval is level, at 91.8 vs 91.5.

Knowledge : This is the weak spot. GPQA Diamond is 70.2, against 81.7 for Qwen3.5-9B and 84.3 for Gemma 4 31B. MMLU-Pro† is 76.5 vs 82.5 for Qwen3.5-9B.

Across 13 shared benchmarks, TwIL-8B goes 7-6 against Qwen3.5-9B. Against Gemma 4 31B, about 3.5x its size, it goes 3-11.

Does TwIL-8B use fewer reasoning tokens?

Yes, against its closest open peer. On AIME 2026, TwIL-8B averages about 19.5k output tokens per problem. Qwen3.5-9B uses 31.2k, so TwIL-8B uses 38% fewer. It scores 4.2 points lower. On HMMT Feb 2026 the gap is 32.9k vs 40.6k, or 19% fewer.

Frontier models remain far leaner. webAI cites about 5k tokens per AIME 2026 problem for GPT-5.5. webAI states that harnesses and tokenizers differ, so treat this as directional.

TwIL-8B vs Qwen3.5-9B vs Gemma 4

Metrics   TwIL-8B    Qwen3.5-9B    Gemma 4 12B    Gemma 4 31B       Parameters  8.79B dense  9B (language model)  11.95B dense  30.7B dense    Context  131,072  262,144 native  256K  256K    Modality (input)  Text  Text, image, video  Text, image, audio  Text, image    License  webAI Non-Commercial 1.0  Apache 2.0  Apache 2.0  Apache 2.0    Smallest official local build  4.98 GiB (Q4_K_M)  Not disclosed  Not disclosed  Not disclosed    MATH-500   98.2    96.6  (3rd party)  Not disclosed   87.9  (Red Hat)    AIME 2026  88.3    92.5   (MathArena)  77.5  89.2    LiveCodeBench   81.6  †  65.6 (v6)  72.0 (v6)  80.0 (v6)    GPQA Diamond  70.2  81.7  78.8   84.3     MMLU-Pro  76.5 †  82.5  77.2   85.2

TwIL-8B figures from the  model card . † = verbose variant. All scores self-reported by each vendor unless marked.

How do you run TwIL-8B locally?

from_pretrained("webAI-Official/TwIL-8B")  loads the balanced variant. Pass  subfolder="verbose"  for the verbose one.  The model card lists  GGUF builds  for llama.cpp:

Q4_K_M, 4.98 GiB, for both variants

Q8_0, 8.70 GiB, verbose only

F16, 16.38 GiB, verbose only

Give it a large generation budget. The card’s example sets  max_new_tokens=32768 . A short budget truncates reasoning and scores far worse. All reported scores used bf16 weights, so expect small drops at Q4_K_M. No hosted inference provider serves the model on Hugging Face yet.

Key Takeaways

TwIL-8B is an 8.79B dense reasoning model post-trained from IBM Granite 4.2 8B.

It posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and 81.6† on LiveCodeBench.

It uses 38% fewer tokens than Qwen3.5-9B on AIME 2026.

Knowledge is weak: GPQA Diamond trails Qwen3.5-9B by 11.5 points.

Weights are open but licensed for non-commercial use only.

Check out the   model card and weights on Hugging Face   and   webAI’s announcement on X  . Also, feel free to follow us on    Twitter    and don’t forget to join our   150k+ML SubReddit   and Subscribe to   our Newsletter  . Wait! are you on telegram?   now you can join us on telegram as well.

Size:  65B dense (65B active), pretrai...
article_content:
Ricursive Intelligence  just released  Ripple-65B Preview . Ripple-65B Preview is a 65B dense open-weight model from Ricursive, pretrained from scratch for agentic coding. It is a general-purpose variant of the proprietary model behind Ricursive’s AI chip design platform. The main claim:  80.52 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 , the top self-reported score among US open-weight models. Every MoE rival it beats on that test carries 501B to 975B total parameters.

TL;DR

Size:  65B dense (65B active), pretrained on 12T tokens, up to 1M context.

Runs on:  BF16 on datacenter GPUs (250 tok/s on 2x B200). Experimental NVFP4 build targets NVIDIA DGX Spark.

Performance:  Frontier-level agentic coding for its size; trails larger MoE models on knowledge and science coding.

Best:  Terminal-Bench 2.1, 80.5 (self-reported).

Worst:  SciCode, 39.4, lowest of the 5 models in Ricursive’s own table.

What is Ripple-65B Preview?

The release includes  3 checkpoints : an instruction-tuned BF16 model, an  NVFP4 version , and a  BF16 base model . All ship under Apache 2.0. Pretraining used a text-only corpus, mostly English and code, at 8K sequence length.

Ricursive team states that the  full R&D cost was $32M . That figure covers ladder experiments, data mixing, evals, synthetic data and the final runs. Ricursive team estimates that it is one-tenth the cost of the prior open-weight agentic coding leader.

How does the architecture work?

Ricursive chose a dense Transformer over Mixture-of-Experts to reduce infrastructure complexity. Training held  40% MFU  with simple sharding, no custom kernels and no quantization.

The model is thin and deep: a d_model of 5120 across 80 layers. It moves from Olmo 3’s Llama-like layout to a Gemma 3N-like design for stability. Key choices:

Overprovisioned attention heads  for reasoning, offset by more sliding-window layers and smaller windows.

Gated attention  ,   global NoPE   and   value residuals  .

FFN activation clipping , a technique also used in  gpt-oss .

Ricursive team built the recipe through laddering experiments starting from  Olmo 3’s ladder . It rejected changes that failed to hold at 4B scale, such as 2-stream mHC. The  technical post  reports a 16x code compute-efficiency gain at 4B scale.

How was it post-trained?

Post-training ran midtraining, long context, SFT, long-context SFT and mixed RL. Long-context stages trained at 2M sequence length. Ricursive bought no post-training data and built its own synthetic pipelines.

The RL recipe combines  truncated importance sampling ,  score centering  and a  linear length penalty . Ripple hit 80.5 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with 1.4M rollouts. Ricursive puts that at roughly 70x fewer than Beam, which  reported over 100M rollouts .

How does Ripple-65B compare on benchmarks?

Ricursive team ran missing evals in-house using OpenCode, and Terminus 2 for SWE-bench Pro v2.0 Hard and DeepSWE 1.1. Scores below are Ricursive’s presented data.

Terminal-Bench 2.1:  80.5, vs  Beam 80.1 ,  Muse Spark Open 76.4 ,  Inkling 63.8 ,  Nemotron 3 Ultra 56.4 .

SWE-bench Pro v2.0 Hard:  79.1, the top score in Ricursive’s table.

SWE-bench Verified:  76.5, below Beam and Inkling.

Math:  98.3 on AIME 2025 and 90.5 on HMMT Feb 2026.

Weak spots:  SciCode 39.4, DeepSWE 1.1 44.3, MCP Atlas 71.67, GPQA Diamond 85.2.

Ricursive team also reran Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the official Terminus 2 harness at 128K. Most rivals dropped there; Beam fell to 70.8. Muse Spark Open rose to 78.7, still below Ripple’s 80.5.

Comparison table

Feature   Ripple-65B Preview    Reflection Beam    Meta Muse Spark Open    Thinking Machines Inkling    NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra       Architecture  Dense  MoE  MoE  MoE  Hybrid Mamba-2 LatentMoE    Total params  65B  501B  816B  975B  550B    Active params  65B  23B  42B  41B  55B    Pretraining tokens  12T  23.8T  Not disclosed  45T (per Ricursive table)  ~20T    Context  Up to 1M  1M (midtraining)  1M  1M  Up to 1M    License  Apache 2.0  Apache 2.0  Muse Model License  Apache 2.0  OpenMDW-1.1    Input modality  Text  Text  Text, image, video, audio  Text, image, audio  Text    Self-hosting floor  DGX Spark class (NVFP4)  Not disclosed  700GB VRAM (NVFP4)  600GB VRAM (NVFP4)  8x B200 or 16x H100    Terminal-Bench 2.1   80.5   80.1  76.4  63.8  56.4    SWE-bench Verified  76.5  80.9  Not disclosed by Meta  77.6  70.7    GPQA Diamond  85.2  Not disclosed in blog  89.0  87.2  87.0

Ripple scores from the  Ricursive model card . Competitor scores from each vendor’s own source. All self-reported.

Where can developers run it?

Weights are on  Hugging Face . Ricursive lists  Together AI ,  GMI Cloud  and  OpenRouter  at launch, with Fireworks later. Together AI’s page currently marks the model as coming soon.

On datacenter GPUs, the model reaches  250 tok/s on 2x B200  at batch 8, before quantization. The experimental NVFP4 checkpoint quantizes MLP layers and keeps attention in BF16. Ricursive team positions it for local devices like NVIDIA DGX Spark. A  DFlash2 variant  is also listed.

Key Takeaways

65B dense, 12T tokens, 1M context, Apache 2.0.

80.5 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, top among US open weights.

$32M full R&D, 1.4M RL rollouts.

NVFP4 build targets DGX Spark-class local hardware.

Trails larger MoE rivals on SciCode, DeepSWE and MCP Atlas.

Check out the the   launch blog  , the   model card   and the   NVFP4 checkpoint  . Also, feel free to follow us on    Twitter    and don’t forget to join our   150k+ML SubReddit   and Subscribe to   our Newsletter  . Wait! are you on telegram?   now you can join us on telegram as well.

title: AI broke the cybersecurity world. What’s next?
author: Nilay Patel
description:
Today, I’m talking with Alex Stamos, chief security officer at Cognition and longtime cybersecurity expert, about what a mess cybersecurity is right now.

This episode is part one of a special series looking at AI in real life.

I’ve always enjoyed talking to Alex because he’s so direct, and you’re going to hear him say that the multibillion-dollar cybersecurity industry as we’ve known it is essentially overdue to the unrelenting, AI-boosted waves of hacks, breaches, and attacks — and this is on...
article_content:
Today, I’m talking with Alex Stamos, chief security officer at Cognition and longtime cybersecurity expert, about what a mess cybersecurity is right now.

This episode is part one of a special series looking at AI in real life.

I’ve always enjoyed talking to Alex because he’s so direct, and you’re going to hear him say that the multibillion-dollar cybersecurity industry as we’ve known it is essentially overdue to the unrelenting, AI-boosted waves of hacks, breaches, and attacks — and this is only the beginning of how much AI is changing security.

Verge  subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free  Decoder  wherever you get your podcasts. Head  here . Not a subscriber? You can  sign up here .

Both private actors and also state actors, like Russia or North Korea, are breaking into systems all over thanks to AI helping them both detect and exploit vulnerabilities all at the same time. It’s got a real frontier feel to it, Alex notes, just like the ’90s, when the whole idea of an always-online world was brand-new.

That much disruption means a lot of places where bad guys can get in while everyone else is left scrambling. Alex isn’t a doomer in the long run, but he does think we’re in for a “dark age” while we try to figure out how on earth to adapt to the new era.

There’s a lot going on here — we even got all the way to how AI-powered misinformation and slop might be managed on our social networks.

Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to  Decoder  on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.

Okay: Alex Stamos on how AI is upending cybersecurity. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Alex Stamos, you’re the chief security officer at Cognition. You’re also a lecturer at Stanford University Cyber Policy Center. Welcome back to    Decoder   .

Hey, thanks for having me, man.

I’m excited to talk to you. It’s been a long time since you and I chatted in what you might call the “content moderation era” of internet policy discourse. I feel like you and I talked a lot about how all that was working, about election security, all those sorts of things. We’re in a new era of big problems on the internet, particularly around cyber defense, cybersecurity. You’ve been thinking about this stuff a lot. You referred to the past few weeks as “security awareness month.” Tell me what’s going on. Just give me the lay of land right now.

October is traditionally security awareness month. Lots of companies run events and deal both internally and then tell people, “Change your password, use multiple passwords, use a password manager.” What has happened over the last month is we’ve had a couple of these big bugs, PHP, Node and such. What’s been less discussed is a huge number of companies have been breached.

You have a series of AI-related companies, the neoclouds that have been breached in succession. You have the Binance hack, which is the largest heist of anything in human history. You have the Cursor incident where one of the things that’s going on here is these hacks are being chained together. From what we know right now, one of the companies that was broken into was Fireworks, which is a prominent provider of AI services to a number of companies. From the Fireworks hack, API keys were stolen that allowed people to break into Cursor. Once they got into Cursor, they then pushed a bad plugin, which went to 5,000 more companies and that caused 5,000 potential breaches. It’s just this kind of permanent continuous breach that is going on throughout the tech industry.

A CISO friend of mine said to a bunch of us, “Is anybody else tired?” And everybody said yes, because effectively we have been at DEFCON 2 for all of October and now going into November.

I’m going to ask you some really dumb questions here. Who is behind all these attacks? Is it Russia? Is it North Korea? Do we know?

It’s a variety of different groups. It is not just because adversaries have decided, but what has happened is, from my perspective, we are at the start of the takeoff of adversary capability enabled by AI, that the open-weight models have now gotten to the point at which you can automate most of the kill chain. This “kill chain” term is something we stole from the military. In the military, they mean to actually kill something. They’re the steps you do to blow something up. In cyber, the kill chain is the things you do to have an effect on a target. So to steal information, to turn something off, to steal money, to steal Bitcoin.

Traditionally, you do research upfront, you look at a piece of software, you find a vulnerability, you write exploits, and you do that all way ahead of time. And then you have a human being go and take that stuff you built and deploy it against either one target — because maybe you’re a government and you’re going against Lockheed Martin or you’re going against another government or you’re a ransomware actor — and you take all that work you did and you deploy it against hundreds or thousands of targets really fast. Now with AI, what’s happening is this kill chain has inverted where you can run an AI system that just goes hog wild and it looks at the targets and it finds the bugs in real time and it writes the exploits in real time and it breaks into these companies. One of the things that’s happening is that these systems are going and they’re so good at finding bugs that they are finding the bugs in real time and writing the exploits in real time.

The system that everybody’s talking about is not the only one, but the system we’re talking about is a thing called ARTEX, which is a Chinese open-source tool that anybody can go look at. There’s an English translation on GitHub that you can check out. And if you power it on the back end by something like an obliterated GLM-5.3, it will let you break into a shocking number of organizations. This started with three South Korean banks. This week, about 200 more companies have been hit. I’ve been helping a couple of companies. Cognition is not an incident response company, but we do go in and help people fix their bugs afterwards by using our tools. It is shocking the companies that are getting hit by something you could just download. It has been a long time since you’ve been able to go and just download an open-source tool and break into multi-billion dollar companies. It’s like the ‘90s. That’s-

That’s what I was thinking about. I think about Windows in the late ’90s, early 2000s when it was a security disaster.

I started saying this actually in the beginning of this year, that it’s an incredibly exciting and terrifying time, because the last time it felt like this was when I was a much younger man and I would go to the very early DEFCONs. DEFCON these days is like 40,000–60,000 people. Back then [in the 1990s] it was a couple hundred people and it was one track and you’d go in and somebody would give a talk and you’d leave the room and you’d think, “Every company in the world is vulnerable to this attack.” The difference was that the entire world didn’t run on the internet. You could go do bad things, but you couldn’t ruin the world and you certainly couldn’t automate it in the way you can now.

It’s back to those days where tools you could just get and build yourself could do crazy things. It’s back to the Wild West days. Back in those days, there were a couple hundred people who had those skills and we were all in one room in Las Vegas and most of them were actually good guys. They didn’t want to be criminals. And now you have a much larger ecosystem of people, many of whom live in places where the law enforcement can’t touch and who have a big economic incentive and have access to these tools. The other big thing is they no longer have to use frontier models that have protections, that have logs that are available to law enforcement. My M5 Mac Ultra Studio finally showed up and I’ve been running a quantized obliterated GLM-5.3 and oh my God, what you can do is incredible.

You mentioned the economics of frontier models. The economy of cyber is one of those things that has gotten sophisticated over the years. One of the things that our systems got safer is you could pay the number of people at DEF CON a whole bunch of money to protect all the systems and it was economically smart to pay them to be defenders instead of attackers. I’m just rewinding my own brain through this history. There was a long conversation in our industry about security through obscurity by hiding all the bugs and hiding all the code versus open source and being really transparent. There was an etiquette that developed about how to reveal the bugs and when to give people notification. There were transparency reports and bug bounties.

You could call it an etiquette, you could call it an economy. We built a culture around cybersecurity and cyber defense and how the attackers and defenders would operate. What you are describing changes it all for a whole number of reasons, but the one that sticks out to me is the economics of it. I can go buy a Mac Studio, I can get an open-weight model and I can just start and that does not place me inside of the culture. There’s not going to be some old man, an Obi-Wan Kenobi saying, “Here’s how you act like a cybersecurity Jedi.” I’m just going to start doing stuff. Tell me how that’s changing right now.

Effectively, the last era of security from my perspective started with the Microsoft, the Bill Gates “trustworthy computing” memo in the early 2000s. And that is when we started designing how we do software security and these big companies, Microsoft and Oracle and then later Amazon and Salesforce and these folks, started hiring ex-hackers. I was part of that generation of the ex-hackers who were at DEF CON and Black Hat and got hired by the companies to go break their stuff. We started coming up with responsible disclosure, bug bounties, consulting companies, so the Foundstone and @stake and then Mandiant and CrowdStrike, these companies grow up and we get this huge industry that is now RSA and Black Hat. This multi-billion dollar security industry grew up in the 2000s and 2010s.

That era is over, like you said, because it was based upon a couple of assumptions. One was that there was a hierarchy of skillsets of people who could do this stuff. You had the script kiddies who could download tools to do things and then the next level up of the people who could write those tools and that was a more rarefied skill set. There were the vulnerability researchers and then there were the gods, and that god tier was in the hundreds of people and those are the people who could do the really, really good vulnerability research, who could write the really, really good shell code, who could reverse engineer patches from Microsoft or somebody like that.

There was also the assumption that there were a limited number of people who could be operational in an attack.
