title: Doubling down on solar power density with the Arduino® GIGA R1™ WiFi board
author: Arduino
description:
As global adoption of solar energy continues to accelerate, researchers and engineers face a fundamental spatial challenge: how do you generate more electricity without consuming more land?

Cosimo Borrello and Ferdinando Gioia – co-founders of the Italian photovoltaic technology startup  A.M.P.S.  – together with a team of researchers from the “Mediterranea” University of Reggio Calabria developed and field-tested  a dynamic double-layer photovoltaic prototype   designed to maximize solar power...
article_content:
As global adoption of solar energy continues to accelerate, researchers and engineers face a fundamental spatial challenge: how do you generate more electricity without consuming more land?

Cosimo Borrello and Ferdinando Gioia – co-founders of the Italian photovoltaic technology startup  A.M.P.S.  – together with a team of researchers from the “Mediterranea” University of Reggio Calabria developed and field-tested  a dynamic double-layer photovoltaic prototype   designed to maximize solar power output  per square meter of ground area. 

The challenge: overcoming land constraints

Conventional single-layer solar farms require significant spacing between rows to avoid mutual shading during solar tracking. While tracking raises energy yields per module, the extra space reduces overall energy production per unit of land. 

To solve this, the innovators at A.M.P.S. and the university stacked two vertically aligned layers of bifacial solar mini-modules within the exact same ground footprint as a single-layer setup. Rather than accepting the inevitable shadows cast by the top layer onto the bottom layer,  the team implemented independent solar tracking  for the stacked panels. By dynamically controlling panel rotation, the system is built to actively manages mutual shading while harvesting direct, diffuse, and reflected sunlight across both active surfaces. 

The brain behind the setup: GIGA R1 WiFi

At the core of the experimental testbed in Reggio Calabria, Italy, is a   GIGA R1 WiFi  . Installed on a custom-designed control PCB, it acts as the central embedded manager for the entire installation: 

Automated motion control:  It is structured to coordinate twelve Nema23 stepper motors via dedicated DM542T drivers to independently adjust the rotation angles of twelve bifacial mini-modules across both layers.

Independent current sensing:  It is engineered to acquire real-time current measurements from twelve INA260 sensors attached to each module to track energy performance.

Remote data logging:  It is constructed to process the synchronized current sweeps and uploads the experimental data directly to a remote server for analysis.

“We chose the GIGA R1 WiFi because it brings together everything a prototype like ours needs, with lots of I/O, a fast dual-core microcontroller and built-in Wi-Fi on a single board,” Cosimo told us. “We had to drive twelve stepper motors independently, read twelve limit switches and twelve current sensors, and send the data to a remote server, and very few boards can handle all of that on their own. Having used an Arduino Mega    board in many past projects, GIGA R1 was the natural next step, with the same familiar format and far more power and connectivity. It gave us a reliable control platform quickly, so we could focus on the photovoltaic research rather than on the electronics.”

Real-world results and future applications

In field testing under clear-sky conditions, with the top layer tracking the sun and the bottom layer fixed, the researchers reported the following increases in short-circuit current, a test measurement that is not the same as total energy production, compared with a fixed single-layer installation occupying the same ground area:

About  +42%  relative to a monofacial single-layer installation.

About  +27%  relative to a bifacial single-layer installation.

About  +39%  and  +25%  respectively with a simplified open-loop tracking model based on a five-parameter sigmoid function, which the researchers reported were close to the results obtained using closed-loop control.

The researchers identify potential applications ranging from compact rooftop modules for space-constrained urban environments to utility-scale plants and agrivoltaics. In agricultural settings, the dynamic rotation of both layers may also allow operators to adjust the amount of natural sunlight reaching crops, although these applications were not evaluated in the reported field test.

By serving as a reliable control platform, GIGA R1 WiFi helped enable the team to  move rapidly from concept to field validation  – demonstrating how accessible open-source hardware can support advanced research in clean energy and land-use efficiency. 

Want to explore the mathematical models, control algorithms, and complete test data? Read the coverage on   PV Magazine   or dive into the  full published paper in  Renewable Energy  .

article_content:
You have an idea. Maybe it’s a smart home device that solves an everyday annoyance, a robot you’ve been sketching for months, or an experiment that becomes something bigger. Now comes your first major decision: what hardware will you use to bring it to life?

With so many development boards available, choosing the right one isn’t always straightforward. But there’s more to the decision than specifications or price. The hardware is only the beginning. What truly makes a difference is the community and resources behind it.

And with the holiday season bringing   discounts of up to 50%     on selected Arduino ®  boards, there’s an added incentive to explore what the original Arduino has to offer.

The original Arduino advantage is more than the hardware

An Arduino board may be small enough to fit in your hand, but what comes with it extends far beyond the hardware.  Choosing a genuine Arduino means having access to an ecosystem built to help you turn ideas into working projects.   Official documentation  , ready-to-use libraries, tutorials, projects, demos, and development tools take much of the guesswork out of the process — whether you’re writing your first lines of code or tackling a sophisticated prototype.

And let’s not forget about the community. Millions of makers, educators, and developers around the world share their knowledge, troubleshoot challenges, and inspire one another through projects that push the boundaries of innovation.

That’s the advantage of the original Arduino. You’re not just purchasing a board. You’re tapping into years of engineering expertise, trusted resources, and a global community that helps you make the best of it.

A board for every ambition — a few favorites to explore

How you bring your projects to life often depends on the tools you choose. Whether you’re experimenting with electronics, connecting devices, or developing a sophisticated prototype, Arduino has a board to match your ambitions. Here are six solid options for the makers, developers, and builders in your life.

Start building. Keep exploring

There’s a reason the  Arduino ®    UNO      Rev3 board  continues to be a favorite among makers and educators. Its reliability, approachable design, and extensive  learning resources  make it an excellent tool for exploring electronics, coding, and interactive projects. 

Ready for more processing power? The  UNO R4 Minima  brings 32-bit performance to the familiar UNO form factor, opening up new opportunities for experimentation.

Build your own   retro-style MP3 player   with the  UNO R4 Minima , perfect for music lovers and makers.

Give your projects a smarter edge

Want to make your projects smarter and more connected? The  UNO R4 WiFi  combines 32-bit processing with Wi-Fi and Bluetooth ®  wireless connectivity, along with a 12×8 LED matrix, making it a compelling choice for connected devices, automation, and interactive builds.

For projects where space matters, the compact Arduino ®   Nano        ESP32 board  delivers wireless connectivity and support for MicroPython, giving developers plenty of flexibility for IoT applications.

Build a  keypad password lock system  with the  UNO R4 WiFi,  which replaces the physical key with a secure digital interface.

Think bigger. Build bolder

Some ideas demand more room to grow. With a generous selection of input/output pins, the Arduino ®   Mega        2560  board is well suited for projects involving multiple sensors, motors and other components. 

And for developers tackling more computationally demanding applications, the Arduino ®   GIGA      R1 WiFi  board brings dual-core processing, wireless connectivity, and advanced peripherals to the workbench.

Keep an eye on the ever changing cryptocurrency value on this   cryptocurrency tracker   with the GIGA R1 and GIGA Display Shield .

Six boards. Different strengths, and one shared purpose: give makers and developers the freedom to experiment, solve problems, and bring ambitious ideas to life.

Big ideas deserve great hardware. And a great deal!

Whether it’s your first experiment or you’re building more sophisticated prototypes, Arduino hardware opens the gates to all kinds of creative and innovative possibilities. And this holiday season, there’s an added reason to explore them. 

If you’ve been waiting to get started with Arduino, expand your collection, or tackle a project that’s been in the planning stages for a while,  we’ve got the perfect incentive for you; selected hardware available at discounts up to 50% during our holiday promotion. So what will you build next?

Explore the holiday deals  .

title: How Techno Sky and Arduino Opta brought an industrial visual emergency signaling solution to air traffic management
author: Arduino
description:
When you’re developing systems that support air navigation services, the margin for compromise is essentially zero. Reliability isn’t a “nice to have,” it’s the baseline. That’s the world in which Techno Sky operates, and it’s what makes their decision to build around the  Arduino® Opta  RS485 microPLC  responsive to the project’s identified requirements.

Techno Sky  is an ENAV Group company that manages and maintains hardware and software systems supporting air navigation services, and develop...
article_content:
When you’re developing systems that support air navigation services, the margin for compromise is essentially zero. Reliability isn’t a “nice to have,” it’s the baseline. That’s the world in which Techno Sky operates, and it’s what makes their decision to build around the  Arduino® Opta  RS485 microPLC  responsive to the project’s identified requirements.

Techno Sky  is an ENAV Group company that manages and maintains hardware and software systems supporting air navigation services, and develops innovative technologies for the Air Traffic Management (ATM) sector. Their R&D department works on solutions for air navigation service providers (ANSPs), airports, aviation authorities, and organizations worldwide – systems designed for use under demanding operational conditions.

The challenge: a compact, reliable visual emergency signaling system

The project that brought Techno Sky to Arduino was the development of a visual emergency signaling system for integration within ENAV’s Digital Tower environment. The requirements were unambiguous: industrial-grade reliability, compact form factor, continuous operating capability, Ethernet and industrial communication interfaces, integrated I/O, and the ability to develop and maintain the system without building dedicated custom electronics from scratch.

A fully custom hardware design was on the table, but it would have added significant time and complexity – hardware design, integration, and validation cycles that would delay the project without necessarily improving the outcome. The team needed a platform that would let them focus on application logic and system integration, not on reinventing the controller underneath it.

Opta: a non-conventional, but versatile and effective path to innovation

The R&D team evaluated conventional PLCs, custom embedded electronics, and single-board computers before landing on Opta. It selected Opta based on its combination of industrial characteristics and software flexibility in a single package. The team determined that the conventional PLCs it evaluated offered less development agility for this project. Custom electronics would have added hardware design overhead. The single-board computers evaluated by the team did not meet the project’s identified specifications.

The Opta RS485 offered integrated Ethernet and RS485 communications, relay outputs, and the flexibility of the Arduino programming environment and library ecosystem – all in a compact, DIN rail-mountable form factor designed for industrial applications. Critically, it allowed new functionality to be implemented through software without adding dedicated hardware, a quality that would prove important as the system evolved.

An architecture for in-house deployment within the year

In the deployed system, Opta acts as the main embedded controller, managing signaling outputs, Ethernet communication, RS485 communication with external equipment, operating modes and timing, supervision functions, and communication integrity and security. The system currently implements eight signaling modes on a single controller – functions that the Techno Sky team determined could otherwise have required additional hardware or a more complex architecture.

The main engineering challenge during development was coordinating communications, physical outputs, signaling sequences, and supervision in parallel. The team addressed this through a modular software architecture and the use of watchdog and communication-validation mechanisms – approaches intended to support a manageable codebase and consistent system behavior. Development was carried out internally by Techno Sky’s R&D team using Arduino documentation, libraries, and development resources.

According to Techno Sky, the project started in October and reached operational deployment in under 12 months. One Opta controller integrating more than ten main control functions, designed for continuous operation, with the same architecture carried through from R&D prototype to operational system.

From prototype to production on the same platform

That last point deserves emphasis. R&D teams may prototype on one platform and later transition hardware when moving toward deployment. Techno Sky didn’t need to make that transition. The architecture based on Opta developed during R&D was the architecture retained for operational use – a decision that they report was based on its assessment of the platform for this application.

Techno Sky summarized their experience: “Opta enabled us to move rapidly from an R&D concept to an operational solution. Its industrial hardware, combined with the Arduino programming environment and library ecosystem, allowed us to integrate and expand multiple functions without increasing hardware complexity. The fact that we are retaining Opta in the operational system reflects our positive assessment of its effectiveness and reliability for this application.”

More ideas, more innovation

The Techno Sky team has been working with Arduino platforms across their R&D activities for several years, and this project showcases their reinforced confidence in their chosen Arduino product line. Future applications under consideration include monitoring systems, remote control, sensor integration, robotics, automated test equipment, and ATM infrastructure – a range of potential uses that Techno Sky is evaluating.

For teams facing similar integration challenges – multiple control and communication functions, demanding reliability requirements, and pressure to move quickly from concept to deployment – Techno Sky’s assessment is direct: Opta is well suited, in Techno Sky’s assessment, when those functions need to come together in a compact system, without the overhead of custom hardware design.

Ready to explore options for your industrial application? Find out more about  the Opta family  and Arduino’s industrial-grade range at  arduino.cc/pro .

title: How about a Hallowuino half-dozen?
author: Arduino
description:
It’s almost that time of year again! No chance to 3D print your Arduino®-powered pumpkin project? Didn’t get around to animating the LEDs on your costume? There’s still time, and here’s a half-dozen Hallowuino-themed projects to get you inspired.

Spooky, Sassy Pumpkin

You’ve heard of  Spooky, Scary Skeletons , well  here’s a Spooky, Sassy Pumpkin  that is built to use a USB webcam to identify visitors as they approach, then answer their questions about what it sees using the  Arduino App Lab  ...
article_content:
It’s almost that time of year again! No chance to 3D print your Arduino®-powered pumpkin project? Didn’t get around to animating the LEDs on your costume? There’s still time, and here’s a half-dozen Hallowuino-themed projects to get you inspired.

Spooky, Sassy Pumpkin

You’ve heard of  Spooky, Scary Skeletons , well  here’s a Spooky, Sassy Pumpkin  that is built to use a USB webcam to identify visitors as they approach, then answer their questions about what it sees using the  Arduino App Lab  Vision-Language Model (VLM) Brick. This jack-o’-lantern packs a whole lot more smarts than your average fruit thanks to the dual-brain  VENTUNO  Q  concealed underneath it. All processing is designed to be handled offline, on-device without sending users’ faces and voices  across networks or to the cloud.

Arduino-Powered Animatronic Supergroup

Bands break up for all kinds of reasons, so we were pleased to see Arduino Project Hub member nerdabilly figure out a way to  sync the Costco Skeleton Punk Rocker animatronic with the Lowe’s Reaper Band . The band members are centered around a Bluetooth speaker, while the rocker is triggered by a timer or motion sensor. Not wanting to permanently alter these expensive displays, nerdabilly used the existing analog signal from the band leader to trigger the pink in place of its motion-sensing trigger, so the whole crew can rock out with their skulls out. Nerdabilly, we salute you for keeping this spooky symphony in sync!

Simple Spookiness with Modulinos and MP3s

Here’s some  simple steps to sprinkle some spookiness into your season  from our own team. Using the UNO  R4-based  Plug and Make Kit , plus a DFRobot DFPlayer MP3 player module, we show you how to trigger spooky lights and sounds when the Modulino® Distance sensor detects a presence. You can even connect to the  Arduino Cloud  to activate, customize, and monitor your project remotely. And that’s just the start – the seven included modules and built-in Wi-Fi give you plenty of options for creating your own frightful projects!

Ultrasonic Spider

Everyone has to start their Arduino journey somewhere, and for Project Hub member ParzivalUK, that place was a half-decade old project video demonstrating a fake spider dropping on unsuspecting passers-by. Unfortunately, ParzivalUK found that the accompanying code no longer worked for their project, and there weren’t detailed steps on how to recreate it. Driven by a desire to delight their son with a fun Halloween prank, ParzivalUK pushed on, combining a servo with an ultrasonic sensor to  drop a toy spider on anyone who comes within approximately 40cm of the trap , with a continuous rotation servo to wind it back up, ready for the next victim!

Portal Sentry Turret

We love seeing projects shared on the  unofficial Arduino Discord server . User jaysicks’  Aperture Science Sentry Turret costume  really caught our eye, and we asked for a little more detail. The resulting Instructable is a detailed step-by-step guide for recreating the iconic tripod robot from one of the most beloved puzzle platformers of all time. With no 3D printer at hand, the costume relies on cardboard construction but comes out looking great. A red LED in the eye responds to the audio output from the incorporated GD380D-M audio playback module when a button is pressed, and the whole thing is controlled by an ATtiny85V microcontroller, programmed using the  Arduino IDE . We think jaysicks’ son will be the envy of the neighborhood this Halloween, or at least among those with a solid appreciation of classic video games!

Cyber Research Systems T-1-7 Warrior Robot

The T-800 and T-1000 may get most of the screen time, but  Redditor u/parsupo recreated the more niche T-1-7 Warrior Robot  for their annual Halloween project. Built around an electric wheelchair base, the bot uses an Arduino Mega 2560 to receive and process commands from a remote control, and the same ATmega328 chips found in the UNO to control lights, gun movement, and the head. It may not be made of mimetic polyalloy, but we wouldn’t want to run into it in a dark alley!

What will you make?

Got a spooky Arduino-based project to share? Or need help realizing your creation? Be sure to  add it to Arduino Project Hub . Then head over to the  Arduino subreddit  and  let us know !

article_content:
Arduino, Qualcomm Technologies, and Edge Impulse recently teamed up with Hackster to host the   Invent the Future   competition. The competition attracted  4,028 registrants  and  1,202 hardware applications , culminating in  153 final project submissions  across a wide range of real-world applications.

There were several categories in the competition, all unified by the  UNO Q board  and Arduino® App Lab. The judging is officially complete and the winners have been announced, which means we get to show you the top projects that most impressed the judges and took home the awards!

These winning creations illustrate a range of uses for the UNO Q – and stay tuned, because we’ll also be shining the spotlight on many other fantastic contest submissions in the coming days.

Best Social Impact

While sustainability was a consideration for every category, the Best Social Impact award went to a project built explicitly to make the world a better place. The winning project was the   Smart Water Guardian AI  , built by KOCHONI Biaou David Barthélémy.

This project puts the edge AI capabilities demonstrated by UNO Q to good use, by monitoring water-quality indicators in real time. Through a host of sensors, it is designed to measure everything from temperature and pH to turbidity and dissolved solids content, allowing for detection of anomalies that correlate with poor water quality – detection that could save lives.

Best in Home Automation

Home automation is a thriving industry, and there are all kinds of tech products you can use to build the smart house of your dreams. But what about your chickens’ house? That’s what Coders Cafe’s   Smart Coop 2.0   is for.

Smart Coop 2.0 is a system design, driven by an UNO Q, for intended to support routine chicken care. It is built to handle the basics, like dispensing feed on a schedule and heating the space, using local AI models designed to detect eggs and potential predators. The creator designed Smart Coop 2.0 to make certain chicken-care tasks more convenient and to detect potential predators, including coyotes and foxes.

Best in Gaming

RollerCoaster Tycoon  was a popular video game generally among two types of people: those who enjoy creative building and those who like maximizing metrics. Kevin Loeffler is the latter type, and he wondered how real-life roller coasters might stack up. The result is   RCT IRL  , which is a wearable sensor system for classifying and quantifying roller coaster rides.

“Wearable” here means an UNO Q, a SparkFun 9DoF IMU (inertial measurement unit), and a battery stuffed into a fanny pack. During a coaster ride, the dual-brain board from Arduino is structured to collect movement data through the IMU. Afterwards, three Edge Impulse models are designed to process the data and generate model-based scores labeled Excitement, Intensity, and Nausea. Together with interesting stats like ride time and maximum g-forces, those values populate a report card for the roller coaster, just like in the game.

Best in Industrial IoT

HaloSense V1   is pasquale887’s attempt to give humans new senses via neuroplasticity. In short, neuroplasticity is your brain’s ability to accommodate new functions. Of course, there isn’t anything supernatural or superhuman about that, and your brain can only work with the sensory input it receives. HaloSense V1 provides new information through the senses you already have.

Or, to put it another way, HaloSense V1 is a haptic feedback headset. Through an array of 13 haptic feedback motors, it pulses and buzzes to convey information gathered through sensors connected to an UNO Q. The project is intended to explore whether, over time, a wearer can learn to interpret the haptic patterns as information.

Best in Robotics

We’re in the midst of a shift in robotics towards human-friendly designs. Mohammed Akramuddin’s   Curie   is engineered to be as friendly as it gets. This little desktop robot is cute, with facial expressions displayed on an OLED screen. The creator designed it to help users, including those with ADHD, manage tasks. 

Like all of the other projects in this competition, Curie contains an UNO Q board. It connects to various APIs, including Groq (a cloud interface that is built to let developers run open-source artificial intelligence models at high speeds), to help its owner manage their workload. It is designed to do that in the usual digital assistant ways, by taking notes and setting reminders, but also by providing more tailored assistance. It can, for example, break a complex task up into small pieces that are more approachable. It is also designed to identify potential distraction and provide a nudge to help users return to their task.

Best in Show

The Best in Show award went to the overall competition winner, regardless of category. The winner was Jorge Eldis González for his work on the  Edge-AI Spectrophotometer , which is, as its name indicates, a spectrophotometer that integrates AI on the edge.

A spectrophotometer measures the wavelength of light, in order to detect the properties of sampled materials. That is a non-destructive analysis and can, for instance, tell you if a sample contains contaminants.

The Edge-AI Spectrophotometer is built using commercially available components, using an UNO Q and a SparkFun Electronics AS7343 Triad Spectroscopy Sensor. It then runs a machine learning inference model on the edge, which detects deviations from known baselines. The creator designed the project to make its testing workflow more accessible to less-experienced operators and to explore additional spectrophotometry applications.

Congratulations to all the winners!

article_content:
Linux mascot Tux the penguin was created by Larry Ewing using GIMP

The idea that changed how we build technology

Happy Linux Day, Arduino Fans!

Since 1991, Linux has helped popularize open-source software. And then Arduino, inspired by that, extended that open source concept to hardware with its own launch in 2005. The open-source movement did not stop at the screen; it also influenced the development of physical computing. As we celebrate Linux Day, we honor the collaborative ethos that helped shape the internet and the Arduino movement. Just as Linux democratized software by opening the kernel, Arduino liberated hardware from corporate labs, proving that when we freely share our blueprints from C++ to circuit schematics, we empower a global community to build the future together.

Linux meets the physical world

Imagine building an autonomous robot where the engineering challenge isn’t just running computer vision, but seamlessly bridging that user-space intelligence with bare-metal physical execution. The  Arduino ®  UNO    Q board  solves this by unifying a Qualcomm Dragonwing    QRB2210 microprocessor running a full Debian Linux environment with an STM32U585 microcontroller for real-time, deterministic hardware control. This dual architecture gives developers the established capabilities of Debian’s package ecosystem and networking stack for AI workloads, while the bare-metal microcontroller supports real-time control of motors, sensors, and actuators, including sub-millisecond operations where supported by the applicable configuration and workload.

This integrated architecture is designed to reduce the friction associated with bridging separate computing and control hardware.By unifying real-time control with Debian’s robust software ecosystem, the UNO Q can help developers focus on building applications across robotics, computer vision, and industrial automation.The platform illustrates how advanced computing and bare-metal execution can be combined in an open, collaborative development environment.

From ideas to real world builds

The real power of open source comes to life in what people can create with it. Across the Arduino community, makers and developers can explore a broad range of possibilities, from desktop companion robots to autonomous systems that tackle everyday problems, and beyond. Whether they’re experimenting with the UNO Q or  Arduino ®  VENTUNO    Q board , sharing their ingenuity through competitions and hackathons, or inspiring others with creative builds, these projects turn bold ideas into working solutions. Here are a few builds that caught our attention, built by community members using Arduino hardware and Linux-based capabilities.

Curie: An AI companion for ADHD and cognitive focus grounding

Curie is an open-source desk companion built on UNO Q, intended to interact through audio and vision features to help users begin tasks and maintain focus.   Learn more  .

Autonomous pantry assistant

An autonomous edge AI assistant that identifies pantry products and reads their labels aloud for people with low vision.   Learn more.

A robot arm that sees you

Imagine a robot arm designed to detect configured users and deliver selected objects. The arm runs on Feetech digital servo motors with a Waveshare control board, and a camera on the head handles the recognition.   Learn more.

Depth multitool on the VENTUNO Q

One ordinary webcam, a depth model on the VENTUNO Q NPU, and four visualization modes for estimating the distance of objects within the camera’s field of view.   Learn more.

Building on open foundations

Many community projects build on open-source software and hardware. Arduino continues to strengthen that foundation with new hardware, software, and tools that give developers more ways to experiment, create, and solve difficult problems. The 2026   Arduino Open Source Report   highlights this motion and key contributions from our vibrant, passionate community. Here are just a few of the highlights, reported by Arduino as part of its open-source ecosystem:

6 new open source hardware boards

11 new official libraries

Arduino ®  App Lab for UNO Q

The community led with:

1,218 new libraries, bringing the total to 8,754

6,602 new versions of libraries

420 new open source projects

The next chapter

As AI descends from the cloud to power the next generation of autonomous robots and edge devices, open-source development continues to play an important role in this area. The convergence of Linux, Arduino, and edge intelligence is helping enable new physical-computing applications, and it is the global community that will define what is possible.  That is the true spirit of Linux Day: a brilliant, decentralized future we are building together.

title: Arduino® App Lab 0.11 is here
author: Arduino
article_content:
You build something great on your Arduino ®  UNO    Q board. Now what? Arduino App Lab 0.11 is about taking your project further, whether that means shipping it to another board, getting help while you code, or teaching your device to recognize a tennis swing. 

Here is what’s new!

App Release: deploy to production, at scale

App Lab 0.11 deepens our integration with the  Works with Arduino    program . 

App Lab now supports exporting production grade “Apps Releases,” so your project built in App Lab can be packaged for deployment without leaving the tool. 

How does it work?

1. Package an app into a ready-to-run file.

2. Install it on another board.

3. Run it on compatible third-party hardware included in the Works with Arduino    program.

What’s the difference between this new App Release and the export feature?

Export is great for sharing a project. An App Release is designed to provide a consistent, ready-to-run package. An App Release is a frozen, immutable package with locked dependencies to support consistent behavior across compatible devices. Sketches are pre-compiled, which can reduce startup times. Remote dependencies like AI models are downloaded at install time, which can streamline setup across multiple boards.

Check our documentation to learn more:

Create an App Release

Install an App Release

Agent Panel right inside the editor

Chat with an Agent Panel next to your code to build, troubleshoot, and brainstorm ideas. 

Agent Panel uses the app, files, and code open in your workspace as context, which can reduce the need to copy and paste or switch tabs. It will update files in your workspace as you chat with it in plain-language, and it keeps your chat history organized by app.

What’s the difference between the Agent Panel and Agent Mode?

Agent Mode, introduced in  App Lab 0.10 , is a full-window experience centered on the agent. You describe what you want and the agent creates and works on your app for you. The Agent Panel is a side chat that stays open while you work in your app. It uses the app and files you have open as context, updates them as you chat, and you run your app right there as usual.

New Pose Estimation Brick: teach your board the moves

The new Pose Estimation Brick runs locally on your Arduino ®  VENTUNO    Q and comes with two features: one with preconfigured capabilities and one that supports custom poses. 

Preconfigured skeleton tracking and pose detection

The Brick tracks a 17-point body skeleton at up to 10 frames per second and draws a live overlay on your video stream. It also recognizes standard poses like standing, sitting, or arms up and down, without a separate model-training step. The demo app is just six lines of code.

Make it yours: teach it a custom pose

Need something more specific? Give the Brick a folder of photos of the pose you want, plus a folder of photos that are not that pose. No separate model-training step or additional tool is required. The photos are the whole input, and App Lab performs a recognition check before the app starts.

Want to recognize a tennis stroke? Provide representative photos to configure the custom pose.

Bring your own model

Add language models for the LLM Brick straight from Hugging Face, using a model ID or URL. App Lab checks that the model is compatible and selects a support quantization based on the model. 

Check out the documentation at this link:  Custom model import documentation

Your phone is now a sensor board

The Mobile Companion App now streams  more than the camera . 

Microphone and IMU data now flow into App Lab through a new remote sensor peripheral, at high frequency over WebSocket, with password protection and encryption options. Data is sent as JSON, so you can define your own keys. Because it is built on WebSockets, compatible external devices can stream data to your board using the supported WebSocket interface, which can support remote-control and IoT use cases.

Know where you are, even when GPS struggles

In this short demo,   Anthony   Hebert and   Stefano Implicito   show how easy it is to get started and put TPS to the test by finding   Andy   in the middle of a crowded show floor.

We showed the  Qualcomm Terrestrial Positioning Service  (TPS) running on UNO Q at  The Things Conference 2026  on September 28th. It uses nearby Wi-Fi, cellular, and Bluetooth LE signals to support positioning while managing power consumption. A new TPS brick and example provide a way to evaluate the service.

Also in Arduino App Lab 0.11

VENTUNO Q flashing:  flash your board from the built-in flasher in Settings.

Board extensions:  select and configure the carriers and JHAT add-ons attached to your board from the Settings page.

Publish to Arduino Project Hub:  upload your app as a project draft from the App menu.

Editor improvements:  Find All References for Python and C++, YAML syntax checking, any file or folder name, and a separate console tab for each Brick container.

Get started

Download  Arduino App Lab 0.11  today and tell us what you build!

For the full list of changes,  see the release notes .

article_content:
STEMpedia and Arduino bring block-based coding to the Arduino®   UNO  R4 WiFi and UNO R4 Minima boards as well as the Arduino® Alvik  robot.

Every maker remembers the moment something they built first came to life: an LED blinking, a servo sweeping, a sensor reacting to a hand wave. Today, that moment gets a lot easier to reach thanks to a new collaboration between   STEMpedia   and  Arduino!

We’re excited to reveal that PictoBlox 10.0, STEMpedia’s coding and technology creation platform, has expanded its Arduino compatibility to include the  UNO R4 WiFi ,  UNO R4 Minima , and  Alvik robot .

And what better place to celebrate this news than at   Maker Faire Rome 2026  ? Join us from October 23rd–25th to explore the new integration and try PictoBlox for yourself! 

From first-time coder to confident creator

Arduino has long been a starting point in electronics for makers, students and educators.PictoBlox brings a visual, drag-and-drop programming experience that helps users to focus on programming concepts without having to start with coding syntax. Together, they can help beginners go from “I’ve never coded” to “I built a working project” in a single session.

But PictoBlox isn’t just for beginners – or just for programming. Beyond block-based coding and Python, the platform is designed to let users explore AI and machine learning, experiment with tinyML and intelligent systems, program compatible robotics and electronic hardware, and develop IoT projects. It also supports game and animation development, opening up even more opportunities for hands-on creativity and experimentation.

Announcing the collaboration, Dhrupal Shah, CEO and Co-Founder of STEMpedia, said:  “Great innovations begin with the freedom to experiment. By expanding Arduino board support in PictoBlox, we are making it easier for learners and makers around the world to turn their ideas into working projects. 

“Students can create AI-powered projects and train their own Machine Learning models, making complex technologies more accessible. We’re excited to see how this collaboration inspires the global maker community to explore, build, and innovate.”

What you can do with PictoBlox and Arduino

Combining visual programming with Arduino hardware opens up all sorts of creative possibilities:

Program with blocks:  snap together scripts instead of typing code, and see how your Arduino responds right away.

Work with sensors:  read inputs such as an IR sensor and use them to trigger actions.

Control actuators:  drive LEDs and servo motors from your scripts.

Go wireless:  control your projects from a smartphone using Dabble, a project interaction and Bluetooth controller app.

By bringing together Arduino’s hardware ecosystem and PictoBlox’s versatile coding environment, the collaboration aims to make technology creation more approachable and open up new possibilities for the global maker community to learn, build, share, and innovate. 

Built for classrooms, clubs and makerspaces

Whether you’re teaching in a classroom, running a coding club or experimenting in a makerspace, this expanded integration is all about trying to lower the learning barrier and open up new possibilities for creative exploration.

By helping reduce the need to manage syntax, block-based coding means learners can focus on developing essential skills like logical thinking, problem-solving and understanding how code works. And as their confidence grows, they can build on these foundations, explore text-based programming and take on increasingly ambitious projects within the Arduino ecosystem.

For educators, it’s a compelling combination: an approachable software environment and a familiar, well-supported hardware platform, with plenty of room for students to learn, experiment and grow – all in one workflow! 

Get hands-on at Maker Faire Rome! 

Heading to Maker Faire Rome this year? Be sure to stop by  booth N.02 , where you can see PictoBlox and Arduino in action, try out the new integration for yourself and chat with the team. We’d love to see you there!

Download PictoBlox at:    https://thestempedia.com/product/pictoblox/download-pictoblox/

Through approximately five to six ho...
article_content:
Want real-world experience developing AI models and deploying applications using cutting-edge technologies such as the  Arduino ®  UNO    Q board ? Qualcomm Academy has a new second-level program for you! The  AI Associate Certification: Model to App  is a hands-on, online, and self-paced program designed to provide experience with the end-to-end ML workflow, including data preparation, model creation, optimization, deployment, and on-device inference. 

Through approximately five to six hours of build-along training, you’ll enjoy a combination of technical depth and practical application, helping you develop the confidence to create accurate, efficient, and production-ready AI solutions at the edge.

Three projects. One complete edge AI journey.

To achieve their certification, participants use a learning-focused development kit based on UNO Q to complete three real-world projects that span voice, vision, and sensor-based AI:

Wake Word Detection:  Create and optimize a voice-enabled application that recognizes predefined wake words.

Person Recognition:  Build a computer vision application that processes image data and performs real-time inference on an edge device.

Gesture Recognition:  Train a model using IMU sensor data to detect and classify movements in real time.

Each project connects model architecture, training, validation, quantization, deployment, and application integration so learners can explore the ML lifecycle in practice.

Build skills for real-world edge AI development

By completing the certification, you will gain  hands-on experience with developing ML models , preparing data, quantizing and optimizing models to explore tradeoffs among accuracy, latency, power consumption, and performance, and visualizing model graphs. You will also gain experience with AI development toolchains, explore MCU and MPU capabilities, develop real-time applications, and work with FastRPC communication for AI workloads.

The program is designed for developers and engineers, embedded systems professionals, IoT and robotics developers, students, and industry professionals interested in gaining practical experience with ML and edge AI. Learners should have basic Python skills, familiarity with an IDE, introductory knowledge of PyTorch and ML concepts, and prior hands-on experience equivalent to the Qualcomm Academy foundational AI certificate programs.

Flexible learning, practical results

The AI Associate Certification: Model to App is available online and can be completed at each learner’s own pace. You may purchase the program via  Qualcomm Academy . After successfully completing the certification requirements, you will receive a Qualcomm Technologies certificate and badge that can be displayed on your CV and LinkedIn profile.

Start building – from model to app!

Take the next step in your AI development journey. Enroll in the  AI Associate Certification: Model to App  and gain hands-on experience applying ML concepts to applications running at the edge.

Enroll now    !

Visiting  Maker Faire Rome (October 23rd–25th) ? Make sure to stop by the Arduino booth to talk to the team about how you can get your AI Associate Certification: Model to App.

Avocado OS gives SECO customers a production-ready Linux foundation from the first dev kit, so robotics and Physical AI teams can move from prototype to deployed fleet without building and maintaining their own OS, with a p...
article_content:
Arezzo (Italy) and Nashville (USA), November 5th, 2026 –   SECO  S.p.A. (“SECO” or the “Company”) and Peridio, creator of  Avocado OS , today announced a collaboration to make Avocado OS available across SECO’s portfolio of solutions based on  Qualcomm Dragonwing   platforms. Avocado OS gives SECO customers a production-ready Linux foundation from the first dev kit, so robotics and Physical AI teams can move from prototype to deployed fleet without building and maintaining their own OS, with a particular focus on robotics and Physical AI applications. The initial rollout covers the  SOM-COMe-CT6-Dragonwing-IQ-X ,  SOM-SMARC-Dragonwing-IQ8 , and the  SOM-SMARC-QCS6490  following the launch of the  SOM-COM-HPC-A-Dragonwing-IQ10  and the  SBC-Dragonwing-IQ-2390 .

SECO and Peridio are both focused on deploying physical AI at scale. With Avocado OS, customers – particularly those building robots, autonomous machines and other Physical AI systems – gain access to a further production-grade, commercially backed industrial Linux distribution, fully validated on SECO hardware. Teams that have already built  standards on Avocado OS  can bring their software stack to SECO’s Dragonwing platforms easily and confidently.

Customers choosing SECO hardware together with Peridio’s Avocado OS will benefit from preferred support from both companies, with coordinated engineering assistance covering hardware, BSP and operating system, reducing integration risk and shortening time-to-market.

“SECO and Peridio share the same vision to provide customers with everything they need to build and scale Physical AI products. With Avocado OS we’re giving more choices to developers by providing and supporting one of the fastest growing Linux distributions in the market centered around Physical AI use cases. This further reinforces our commitment to an open ecosystem centered around our System on Modules.”  said Dario Freddi, Chief Strategy Officer & Managing Director, USA at SECO.

“Robotics teams don’t ship one board, they ship a matrix of them. SECO has built that matrix on Dragonwing, from SMARC to COM-HPC, from QCS6490 to IQ10. Avocado OS lets a team define its system once and carry it across that range, from dev kit to fleet, with SECO and Peridio both standing behind the BSP.”  said Bill Brock, CEO at Peridio.

title: STM32 Summit 2026: STMicroelectronics Announces its Unified MCU Platform, Addressing Technology Convergence Across Industrial, Automotive and Physical AI Applications
author: Edge AI and Vision Alliance
description:
One unified STM32 platform enables customers to reuse architectures, IP, software and tools across industrial, automotive, and robotics applications

The new STM32A family extends the STM32 platform into high-safety and automotive systems, supporting software-defined systems and physical AI

Geneva, Switzerland, Nov 4, 2026 –   STMicroelectronics (NYSE: STM) , a global semiconductor leader serving customers across the spectrum of electronics applications, today announced a major strategic evolut...
article_content:
One unified STM32 platform enables customers to reuse architectures, IP, software and tools across industrial, automotive, and robotics applications

The new STM32A family extends the STM32 platform into high-safety and automotive systems, supporting software-defined systems and physical AI

Geneva, Switzerland, Nov 4, 2026 –   STMicroelectronics (NYSE: STM) , a global semiconductor leader serving customers across the spectrum of electronics applications, today announced a major strategic evolution of its STM32 portfolio: a unified STM32 microcontroller platform spanning industrial, automotive, and robotics applications.

As part of this strategy, the new STM32A family extends the platform into automotive and safety-critical systems. Building on more than 20 years of STM32 development, this cross-domain platform will help developers bring advanced embedded systems to market faster by enabling greater continuity and reuse across application domains, including emerging physical AI systems, while supporting each market’s specific requirements for safety, security, qualification and product longevity.

“Embedded innovation should not require developers to start again with every new product. With the unified STM32 platform, we are creating a foundation they can trust across markets and generations. The industry needs less fragmentation and a stronger focus on helping MCU technologies converge around a common foundation, while maximizing software reuse. This is how we intend to make STM32 the reference MCU platform across industries,”  said Remi El-Ouazzane, President, Microcontrollers, Digital ICs and RF Products Group, STMicroelectronics.

One platform for converging technology needs

As intelligence moves to the edge, industrial and automotive systems increasingly share requirements for real-time control, secure operation, functional safety, connectivity and AI processing. The unified STM32 platform gives development teams a consistent architecture and software foundation, enabling them to reuse proven assets while selecting products tailored to the performance, qualification, and lifecycle requirements of each application.

–  Continuity across the portfolio : Arm® Cortex®-M cores and shared architectural principles give developers a familiar path between STM32 MCU families, making it easier to carry proven software and IP into new designs.

–  A common development ecosystem : STM32Cube, the world largest MCU software ecosystem, and the broader Arm ecosystem provide a consistent development environment backed by software resources, technical support, and the ST developer community and help customers retain established workflows.

–  Shared process technologies : ST’s 40nm Flash technology and 18nm FD-SOI technology with embedded phase-change memory, augmented by TSMC eNVM technologies, provide a scalable manufacturing foundation for future STM32 products.

Arm, ST’s longstanding partner, shares this vision of a unified microcontroller platform. ST is a lead partner in shaping the future of the Arm Cortex-M portfolio, the architecture of choice for more than 100 billion devices already, and in building the high-performance MCU foundation required for physical AI. This collaboration is helping developers reuse more code across applications, from cars and robots to automated industrial systems.

“The next major frontier for computing is bringing intelligence into the machines that move, manufacture and operate in the physical world,”  said Drew Henry, Executive Vice President, Physical AI, Arm.  “Building on more than two decades of collaboration, Arm and STMicroelectronics are advancing Cortex-M together to meet the demands of intelligence at the edge, where the physical world is sensed and controlled, helping unlock the next generation of physical AI systems.”

STM32A extends the platform into high-safety and automotive markets

The new STM32A family brings the STM32 platform into high-safety and automotive systems. It enables customers to reuse software while meeting the qualification and performance requirements of each application. The first three STM32A microcontrollers are sampling to customers, with broader availability planned in 2027:

•  STM32A4  targets entry-level automotive local control nodes and safety systems

•  STM32A5  addresses mid-range safety-critical applications in industrial automation, robotics, and energy systems, as well as automotive applications.

•  STM32A9  addresses safety-critical multi-domain control where real-time control, low latency, Ethernet, and deterministic communication become essential.

Hear more from our customers and partners on the benefits of a unified microcontroller platform  https://www.st.com/content/st_com/en/campaigns/unified-stm32-mcu-platform-z11.html

title: Infineon Redefines Real-Time Compute and Control for Software-Defined Vehicles and Physical AI with New AURIX™ RC1
author: Edge AI and Vision Alliance

article_content:
Fundamentally new automotive microcontroller platform is Infineon’s first to leverage the open-standard instruction set architecture RISC-V

Platform simplifies development of software-defined vehicles by providing one common, highly scalable microcontroller basis across domains instead of point solutions

High-end product lineup within the family will extend microcontroller domain with additional microprocessor capabilities to support further integration of functions

Advanced processing, safety, cybersecurity, and integrated networking capabilities provide future-ready foundation for evolving requirements throughout vehicle lifecycles

Complementing software ecosystem reduces migration efforts and accelerates software development for customers

Munich, Germany – 4 November 2026 –  Infineon Technologies AG (FSE: IFX / OTCQX: IFNNY) is taking a strategic step forward to expand its portfolio for software-defined vehicles (SDV) as well as other software-defined (SDX) and Physical AI applications, reinforcing its position as global market leader in microcontrollers (MCU). The company is introducing a fundamentally new MCU platform within its industry-leading AURIX  series for real-time control in automotive and beyond. AURIX RC1 is Infineon’s first MCU platform that leverages the benefits of RISC-V. Scaling from traditional microcontrollers to hybrid microcontroller/microprocessor devices, it provides a new level of power-efficient real-time intelligence to enable safe and secured future SDV, SDX and Physical AI. Infineon will present the AURIX RC1 family concept at the electronica trade fair in Munich, Germany (10-13 November) and targets to provide samples in the first half of 2027.

“Delivering vehicles and other physical systems that become smarter, safer and more efficient over time through new software fundamentally changes the requirements for the computing hardware,”  said Peter Schiefer, President of the Automotive Division at Infineon.  “Microcontrollers need to become more configurable, scalable, and adaptable while maintaining highest safety and security levels as applications evolve. AURIX RC1 combines the flexibility of the open standard RISC-V with decades of Infineon expertise in providing dependable execution of safety-critical tasks in real-time. Our ambition is to redefine real-time compute and control for software-defined vehicles and extend this to Physical AI.”

Accelerating SDV development with a common RISC-V foundation

In SDV, functions and software that used to be distributed in many control units around the car are increasingly integrated into central car computers and zone controllers. AURIX RC1 simplifies the development of such architectures by providing engineering teams with one common MCU basis rather than a point solution for every domain. Complementing Infineon’s existing MCU portfolio, it integrates the strengths of AURIX as well as Infineon’s TRAVEO  T2G family for body, connectivity and display applications into one joint next MCU generation. As a result, AURIX RC1 spans applications from zone, body, and chassis control, battery management systems, powertrains, and safety management for driver assistance to cockpit applications, providing further scalability towards cross-domain computing.

The modular nature of RISC-V allows Infineon to optimize individual lineups of the AURIX RC1 family for specific applications while simultaneously leveraging the advantages of a common foundation across the entire family. Processing resources can be tailored to the specific needs of each application. Combined with application-specific power management capabilities, this helps to balance performance requirements and energy consumption. At the same time, software, tools, and expertise developed for one domain can be reused and scaled across others, helping shorten development cycles and accelerate innovation.

Extending MCUs to hybrid MCU/MPU architectures

Depending on the application, AURIX RC1 will integrate up to 12 32-bit processing cores, an advanced parallel processing unit for edge AI and up to 40 megabytes of embedded memory. Furthermore, Infineon is planning to introduce a product lineup within the AURIX RC1 family that extends the traditional microcontroller domain with additional 64-bit microprocessor capabilities. This will allow Infineon to further scale computing performance as the trend to consolidate more functions in central computers continues.

In addition to higher computing performance, functional safety, future-proof cybersecurity and high-speed in-vehicle networking are foundational requirements in software-defined vehicles. AURIX RC1 is designed to support applications up to the highest automotive safety level (ASIL D) and features cybersecurity mechanisms that meet global standards and regulations such as ISO/SAE 21434 and the Cyber Resilience Act. The microcontroller platform provides hardware mechanisms for a high level of physical protection and crypto-agility and is ready to support also evolving security requirements of the future such as post-quantum cryptography.

To efficiently move data across the vehicle, the product family supports state-of-the-art communication standards such as CAN-XL, 10BASE-T1S and multi-Gigabit Ethernet. On selected devices, this includes integrated BRIGHTLANE  Ethernet switching technology and hardware-accelerated data routing. Bringing together control and communication, this helps to reduce the number of necessary external components as well as workload on application processors.

Infineon supports AURIX RC1 with a complementary scalable portfolio of matching OPTIREG  power supply solutions, providing a seamless and optimized power management offering across the platform.

Software ecosystem helps accelerate adoption and simplify migration

AURIX RC1 is supported by the most comprehensive software ecosystem in AURIX history, the DRIVECORE ecosystem. Combining software from Infineon and from ecosystem partners into pre-integrated software bundles, DRIVECORE helps customers accelerate software development and reduce migration effort when transitioning from existing AURIX and TRAVEO T2G platforms to AURIX RC1.

DRIVECORE provides support for AUTOSAR, open-source software, functional safety and cybersecurity. Virtual prototyping allows teams to begin software development and validation before hardware availability, while AI-assisted migration tools simplify software porting and help preserve existing software investments.

Over the past years, Infineon has established a leading position in advancing automotive RISC-V. The company fosters industry collaboration to accelerate ecosystem readiness and adoption of open standards for automotive real-time compute. As a premium member of the RISC-V International association and a founding member of the joint venture Quintauris, Infineon is working closely with industry leaders across software, tooling, middleware, virtualization, and system development to help establish common industry foundations, improve interoperability, and accelerate the availability of production-ready automotive RISC-V solutions. This provides customers with greater software portability, ecosystem choice, and long-term scalability.

Further information about AURIX RC1 is available at  www.infineon.com/RC1 .

Infineon at electronica 2026

At this year’s electronica in Munich, Germany, Infineon showcases semiconductor innovations and system solutions for the AI era. As intelligence moves beyond the cloud and into machines, vehicles, industrial systems and everyday devices, technology from Infineon helps machines sense, process, connect and act in a safe, secure and energy-efficient way. At electronica 2026, Infineon will show technologies for Physical AI in robotics, for intelligent edge devices, software-defined electric vehicles, and future power supply from renewable power generation to AI data centers. Infineon will present innovative and energy-efficient solutions for an increasingly intelligent and connected world from November 10 to 13 in Hall C3, Booth 502. More information is available at  www.infineon.com/electronica .

About Infineon

Infineon Technologies AG is a global semiconductor leader in power systems and IoT. Infineon drives decarbonization and digitalization with its products and solutions. The Company had around 57,000 employees worldwide (end of September 2025) and generated revenue of about €14.7 billion in the 2025 fiscal year (ending 30 September). Infineon is listed on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange (ticker symbol: IFX) and in the USA on the OTCQX International over-the-counter market (ticker symbol: IFNNY).

title: Rethinking FPGA-Based Vision Architectures for the Physical AI Era
author: Edge AI and Vision Alliance

article_content:
This blog post was originally published at  Lattice Semiconductor’s website . It is reprinted here with the permission of Lattice Semiconductor.

Thanks to the continued expansion of artificial intelligence (AI), today’s devices are only getting smarter. Physical AI is expanding automated capabilities beyond digital applications, operating in robots, drones, industrial automation platforms, autonomous vehicles, and other devices. It’s even reached the dental hygiene space in the form of a  $500 AI-powered toothbrush .

Whether a toothbrush, drone, or otherwise, these devices rely heavily on sensors to perceive the world around them. And while AI can help enable more autonomous and responsive devices, synchronizing, transporting, and processing sensor data at the edge is no simple task. System designers must create efficient pathways between sensors and compute if they want physical AI applications to help rather than hinder their devices.

In our latest  LinkedIn Live panel , experts from Lattice,  Arrow Electronics ,  Citrobits ,  Tecphos , and  tinyVision.ai  discussed why the future of physical AI depends on rethinking the architecture that connects perception to processing power.

The Complexity of Sensor-Rich Systems

As smart robotics, autonomous systems, and other AI-enabled devices continue to proliferate our lives, they drive increased demand for sensors. These sensors – cameras, lidar, radar, and others – serve as critical perception inputs for physical AI systems, providing the data required to understand and respond to the device’s surroundings in real time.

The richer the perception data required for these smart devices, the more sensors are needed throughout the system design. While additional sensors help improve coverage and situational awareness, they also increase demands. Each source adds to the bandwidth demands, data streams, and synchronization requirements needed within limited device infrastructure.

At the same time, processor vendors are expanding AI compute capabilities in increasingly compact devices, leaving system designers with the need to support more input with limited connectivity options. This has created a growing mismatch between the amount of sensor data being generated and the I/O resources available to ingest it. Designers must manage bandwidth and latency requirements, limited power budgets, thermal constraints, wiring complexity, and overall system costs, all while trying to incorporate more distributed sensors.

With only so many available I/O interfaces and potentially significant wiring costs, it is incredibly difficult to create edge systems that can transport data efficiently from sensors to processors. Doing so in a manner that maintains performance and efficiency without exacerbating bandwidth and power constraints requires a more intentional design.

Building Sensor-to-Compute Pipelines

Traditional centralized edge architectures are increasingly strained by high-volume, multi-sensor data movement. Edge vision systems, for instance, cannot simply route raw sensor data streams directly into a CPU, GPU, or NPU without creating bandwidth, latency, and power challenges. As sensor counts rise, centralized architecture is becoming increasingly difficult to scale.

Designers hoping to address this challenge are reconsidering how vision pipelines ingest and transport data from the sensor to the primary compute platform. Rather than relying on a single processor to accommodate every sensor connection, the architecture can use flexible interface devices to aggregate inputs, synchronize data streams, and adapt multiple sensor interfaces to the connectivity available on the host processor. This creates a more efficient path for data to move through the system while allowing designers to support different sensor types and interface requirements.

This is particularly important in multi-sensor systems, where accurate timestamping and synchronization help perception algorithms correlate data collected from different sensors at different times. Cameras, lidar, radar, and other sensors may use different connections and generate data with different bandwidth and timing requirements. A flexible ingestion layer can bring these inputs together and deliver them to the host through the interface best suited to the application, creating a more scalable foundation for additional sensors.

Different connectivity options, including MIPI, PCIe, Ethernet, and USB, each bring trade-offs around bandwidth, latency, reach, synchronization, driver complexity, and power. The right architecture depends on the application, but the broader design challenge remains the same: moving high-volume sensor data into compute efficiently while preserving performance, scalability, and system responsiveness.

However, the solution brings with it another challenge: finding hardware that’s flexible and capable enough to handle the job.

How FPGAs Address Sensor and Interface Challenges

This is where  field programmable gate arrays (FPGAs)  play a critical role. As vision systems become more distributed, designers need a flexible way to connect different sensor types and deliver their data through the interfaces available on the host processor. FPGAs provide that adaptability, serving as an intermediary connectivity layer that can:

Aggregate inputs from cameras, lidar, radar, and other sensors.

Bridge sensor and host connectivity standards.

Synchronize data streams.

Route data to CPUs, GPUs, NPUs, and other host processors.

Just as importantly, FPGAs can provide a flexible ingestion layer between sensors and host processors. They can accept inputs from multiple sensor types, align and synchronize data streams, and bridge those inputs to host interfaces such as MIPI, PCIe, Ethernet, or USB. This allows designers to connect the right sensors to the right compute platform without requiring the host processor to natively support every sensor interface.

FPGAs can also help overcome I/O limitations at the edge by bridging and expanding connectivity between sensors and compute, enabling support for a wider range of sensor and host interfaces. Their reconfigurable nature allows systems to adapt as sensor requirements, interface standards, and host platforms continue to evolve without requiring designers to replace the broader hardware architecture.

Ultimately, FPGA-based architectures can simplify sensor integration and data movement, creating a scalable connectivity foundation for physical AI systems with diverse sensors and host processors.

The Path to More Effective Physical AI

As physical AI systems continue to evolve, success will be rooted in the efficient ingestion, organization, and movement of sensor data at the edge. By enabling sensor aggregation, synchronization, and connectivity across diverse sensor and host interfaces, FPGAs can help provide the infrastructure required to support the next generation of robotics, industrial automation, machine vision, and beyond.

To learn more about the sensor-rich evolution of physical AI deployments, watch our full  LinkedIn Live panel discussion . To explore how FPGAs can better enable smart, multi-sensor devices,  contact our team today .

Hussein Osman

Segment Marketing Director, Lattice Semiconductor

title: Why Reliability Matters More Than Ever in Edge AI Vision Systems
author: Edge AI and Vision Alliance
description:
This blog post was originally published at  Arducam’s website . It is reprinted here with the permission of Arducam.

 

AI Demos Are Easy. Production Deployment Is Hard.

Artificial intelligence has dramatically lowered the barrier to building sophisticated computer vision systems. Today, developers can run complex object detection, classification, and tracking models directly on edge devices—often within hours of unboxing new hardware.

Getting an AI camera to perform flawlessly for a bri...
article_content:
This blog post was originally published at  Arducam’s website . It is reprinted here with the permission of Arducam.

 

AI Demos Are Easy. Production Deployment Is Hard.

Artificial intelligence has dramatically lowered the barrier to building sophisticated computer vision systems. Today, developers can run complex object detection, classification, and tracking models directly on edge devices—often within hours of unboxing new hardware.

Getting an AI camera to perform flawlessly for a brief demonstration has never been easier.

Getting it to work reliably for months—or even years—in the field is an entirely different challenge. As Edge AI transitions from experimental prototypes to mission-critical production deployments,  reliability is becoming just as vital as intelligence.  In fact, it is often the single factor that determines whether a commercial AI project succeeds or quietly fails.

 

The Massive Gulf Between a Demo and a Product

Most AI vision systems begin their life cycle in highly controlled, forgiving environments:

A development board sits comfortably on an office desk.

Ambient temperatures remain strictly regulated by HVAC systems.

Airflow around the components is entirely unrestricted.

Engineers are on standby to monitor every frame and reboot the system if needed.

Under these pristine conditions, almost any system can appear stable. Production environments, however, are rarely so accommodating.

Whether deployed inside a busy logistics warehouse, a heavy industrial factory, a remote security installation, or an autonomous mobile robot (AMR), an AI camera must operate continuously while absorbing relentless environmental stress:

Elevated Ambient Temperatures:  Confronting baking summer heat or factory floor thermal spikes.

Choked Airflow:  Sealed tightly inside compact, dust-proof enclosures.

Environmental Pollutants:  Accumulating layers of dust and grime over lenses and heatsinks.

Mechanical Vibrations:  Sustaining constant shocks from nearby machinery or robotic movement.

Continuous Heavy Workloads:  Running intensive model inference cycles 24/7 without a break.

The harsh reality of hardware engineering is that critical limitations often emerge weeks or months after a prototype has been approved.

When Heat Becomes the Enemy of Intelligence

Thermal management is arguably one of the most overlooked bottlenecks in modern Edge AI design.

Every AI workload is computationally expensive and inherently generates heat. As continuous inference processes run, system temperatures steadily climb. Without a sophisticated, proactive thermal architecture, these elevated temperatures trigger a domino effect of system degradations:

Thermal Throttling:  The processor automatically cuts clock speeds to protect itself, causing frame rates to drop.

Inference Fluctuation:  Dropped frames lead to lagging pipelines and erratic AI model behavior.

System Stalls:  Extreme heat accumulation results in unpredictable freezes or unexpected reboots.

Hardware Wear:  Prolonged exposure to high thermal stress drastically reduces the lifespan of delicate electronic components.

The Hardware Paradox:  In many failed deployments, the AI model itself is blamed for inconsistent accuracy, when the true culprit is silent, unmanaged thermal instability.

For production-ready systems, thermal performance cannot be measured by peak benchmark bursts alone. It must be evaluated by how consistently the system maintains its cooling efficiency under a relentless, compounding workload over long-term operations.

 

Reliability Is a Multi-Dimensional Metric

While managing heat is paramount, field reliability extends far beyond a simple temperature reading on a datasheet. A truly deployable vision system must maintain stable operation across a spectrum of unpredictable real-world variables.

Before moving from a prototype to a commercial rollout, product teams must ask harder deployment questions:

Can the hardware architecture sustain maximum inference loads indefinitely?

How does the system’s power consumption and accuracy curve change after hundreds of hours of non-stop operation?

Can the connection interfaces tolerate constant temperature fluctuations without signal degradation?

Is the physical form factor ruggedized against constant industrial vibration and dust ingress?

These structural considerations rarely make it onto flashy benchmark charts, yet they carry the heaviest weight in real-world deployments.

The Hidden, Compounding Cost of Downtime

In the enterprise and industrial sectors, Edge AI reliability is directly tied to financial and operational outcomes.

A security camera that drops frames due to thermal throttling creates blind spots and liability.

An automated quality inspection line that freezes can instantly halt an entire manufacturing workflow.

A logistics robot that loses its vision pipeline unexpectedly interrupts warehouse operations and demands manual intervention.

The total cost of field maintenance, system downtime, and damaged client trust often far exceeds the initial cost of the vision hardware. This is why industrial users are shifting their evaluation metrics: they no longer buy the fastest chip; they buy the most operationally stable platform.

The most sophisticated AI model in the world delivers exactly zero value the moment the system stops running.

Engineering for Uninterrupted, Long-Term Operation

At  Arducam , we believe that Edge AI hardware should be validated under the exact same unforgiving conditions it will face in the field. That core philosophy directly guided the development of our   IMX500 MIPI AI Camera  .

Rather than engineering strictly for brief bursts of peak performance, our development team prioritized long-term thermal resilience and passive dissipation architecture:

Optimized Thermal Signature:  Under continuous, intensive AI workloads, the camera module maintains a remarkably lean  ~35°C  temperature profile (measured in standard ambient conditions).

Built for the Long Haul:  The module is designed from the ground up to endure  long-duration, non-stop industrial stress testing , validating that stable AI inference and structural integrity remain uncompromised over extended operational cycles.

While no single lab test can replicate every chaotic deployment environment, engineering for continuous, low-temperature endurance provides the baseline confidence required for demanding industrial applications.

The Shift: From “Can It Run AI?” to “Can It Keep Running?”

As the Edge AI ecosystem matures, the industry conversation is undergoing a fundamental shift.

A few years ago, the primary question was proof of capability:  “Can we successfully run an AI model on a compact edge device?”  Today, the industry has moved past that milestone. The defining question of the production era is:  “Can our Edge AI system operate reliably, autonomously, and continuously in a brutal environment when nobody is watching?”

The future of machine vision will not be defined solely by adding more TOPS or larger neural networks. It will be shaped by meticulous thermal engineering, ruggedized hardware form factors, and an absolute commitment to operational stability.

Because successful Edge AI products are not measured by how impressive they look during a 5-minute boardroom demo. They are judged by their ability to run silently, reliably, and indefinitely in the field.

 

Conclusion: Reliability is a Core Requirement

When evaluating an AI camera module for your next commercial rollout, benchmark scores and framework compatibility are only the first few lines of the equation.

Thermal behavior under stress, structural ruggedness, and long-term continuous operation must be treated as primary design constraints from day one. In real-world deployments, operational reliability isn’t a premium feature you add later.

It is the foundational requirement.
