article_content:
LETTER FROM THE EDITOR

Dear Colleague,

This issue looks at two layers of an edge AI system: the model architectures that run on it and the camera and sensor hardware that feeds it. Synopsys explains how transformers work and why they now underpin multimodal AI, while Tel Aviv University presents state-space models as a more efficient alternative for long sequences. Etron and VergeSense offer practical guidance on specifying cameras for computer vision and designing battery-powered edge AI sensors. We also highlight new multimodal MCUs, generative AI processor IP and robotics development tools, along with Nota AI’s award-winning vision agent.

The  2027 Embedded Vision Summit  takes place February 2–4 in San Francisco, now as part of SPIE Photonics West. Explore more than 90 sessions across four tracks, with topics ranging from multimodal models and generative vision AI at the edge to industrial AI deployment. Meet Summit exhibitors in the Vision Tech expo, and explore more than 1,400 Photonics West exhibits, including the AR | VR | MR expo and a diverse range of optics and photonics exhibitors.

Newsletter readers receive 10% off the early-bird price for a full-program pass with code  PW27EVS-EB-NL .  Summit program and registration

Also, mark your calendar for three upcoming webinars:

On  Thursday, November 5 , we’ll present a webinar on Yole Group’s latest edge AI processor market forecast through 2031, split by device class and application, from always-on sensors to consumer devices, vehicles and robots. Yole Group will also present their latest teardowns of edge AI devices, showing which chips are used, how they are integrated at the board level and what they cost. In addition, they’ll assess the processors themselves, looking at NPU architecture, process node, memory and the real cost of on-device inference. Join us for a unique assessment of the competitive field, covering incumbent MCU and SoC suppliers as well as emerging entrants, and exploring which chip characteristics decide design wins.  More info here .

And on  November 17 , Manuel López Roldán of SiMa.ai will discuss what engineers need from their development tools in order to move quickly from prototype to productized system: broad model support and compilation, fast testing and debugging, clean integration, and environments where AI coding agents work efficiently alongside engineers.  Webinar details and registration .

Finally, on  Tuesday, December 15 , Alicia Shapiro, CMO and Editor at  AiNews.com  will moderate a newly announced panel comprised of Anirudh Koul, Senior Manager, GenAI Sciences and GenAI Tech Lead at Pinterest, Brad Chisum, CEO of  EyePop.ai , and Tom Larson, President of Velasea, to discuss key trends shaping the vision AI market, including composable workflows, edge and hybrid deployment, and the growing importance of orchestration and operational efficiency. They’ll explore why the industry is shifting from individual models and experiments toward AI vision platforms built for real-world deployment, and present some practical use cases for businesses and systems integrators looking to build their own computer vision solutions. The panel will present findings from EyePop.ai’s new white paper,  2026: The Rise of AI Vision Platforms , which compares 35 AI vision platforms across 12 attributes.

Webinar details and registration

There is still time to participate in the 2026 Computer Vision and Physical AI Developer Survey. Qualified participants will receive access to an extensive set of survey results, along with an invitation to an exclusive webinar discussing early findings.  Participate before the survey closes .

Erik Peters

Director of Ecosystem and Community Engagement, Edge AI and Vision Alliance

BUILDING AND DEPLOYING REAL-WORLD ROBOTS

TRANSFORMERS AND BEYOND

Understanding Transformers: From LLMs to Context-Aware Multimodal Models

Transformers have become the foundation of modern AI, reshaping how products are built and how businesses operate. In this talk Tom Michiels, System Architect at Synopsys, explains why transformers replaced earlier models, what makes them highly scalable and how they expanded from language systems to multimodal models that reason across text, images, audio and more. He introduces core concepts like attention, embeddings and tokenization, examining how these models learn and generalize. He traces the evolution from GPT-style language models to vision transformers and multimodal systems that enable capabilities such as in-context learning. He explores practical considerations, including latency, memory, cost, KV caching and quantization. And he highlights trends like long-context models, on-device AI and mixture-of-experts. Viewers will gain a practical understanding of how transformers work and how to apply them in product decisions.

Efficient State-Space Models

The transformer architecture revolutionized the field of AI and serves as the basis for current state-of-the-art large language models. Yet, transformer networks struggle with the quadratic complexity of long sequences, a critical bottleneck for high-resolution embedded vision. In this talk, Raja Giryes, Professor at Tel Aviv University, presents structured state-space models (SSMs), specifically Mamba, as a linear-complexity alternative. He shares recent findings from his research and others, including “hidden attention”—a technique to interpret Mamba’s decision-making process—and novel methods like LongMamba and DeciMamba that significantly extend the context length of Mamba in an efficient way. Finally, he discusses the application of these models to language and vision tasks, offering practical strategies to improve their reliability in edge deployments. Viewers will leave with a clear road map for adopting efficient, interpretable and robust SSMs for next-generation embedded AI.

DESIGNING CAMERAS AND VISION SENSORS

Specifying and Designing Cameras for Computer Vision Applications

Designing a camera system requires a deep understanding of the fundamental principles of image formation and the physical characteristics of its components. Translating computer vision-based system requirements into camera system parameters is a crucial step. In this talk, Richard Crisp, Vice President / CTO at Etron Technology America, provides a comprehensive overview of the key concepts involved in designing or specifying a camera system. He covers the basics of image formation and the associated physics. He discusses sensor and lens effects that impact image quality, such as diffraction, circle of confusion and depth of field. He also discusses application-specific requirements, including lighting conditions, frame rate and motion blur. Finally, he presents a detailed example illustrating how to translate application requirements into camera parameters, highlighting cost-performance trade-offs. Viewers will gain a thorough understanding of the key factors influencing camera system design and be able to make informed decisions when selecting or designing a camera system.

Designing Vision-Based, Battery-Powered Edge AI Sensors

Battery-powered wireless vision sensors can reduce installation cost and enable deployments where external power is impractical. But once edge AI is added for on-device image processing—both to protect privacy and to minimize bandwidth—the power budget becomes the central design constraint and the main source of technical risk. In this talk, Larry Arne, Director of Hardware at VergeSense, shares a practical approach to designing battery-powered edge AI sensors, starting with how to build and validate a power budget: choosing battery chemistry, estimating usable capacity, characterizing performance over temperature and age and forecasting consumption across operating modes. He then covers key architectural decisions that determine feasibility, including sensor and regulator selection, memory trade-offs (RAM vs. flash vs. MRAM vs. ReRAM), NPU/accelerator choices, memory sizing, switched power domains, battery end-of-life behavior and wireless connectivity. Viewers will take away a repeatable checklist for reducing risk and avoiding late-stage power surprises.

UPCOMING INDUSTRY EVENTS

Edge AI Silicon: Market Forecasts, System Tear-Downs and Chip Analyses

Yole Group Webinar: November 5, 9:00 am PT

From Demo to Product: What It Really Takes to Ship Physical AI Applications

Intel Webinar: November 19, 10:00 am PT

From Computer Vision Experiments to Production: Building AI Vision Solutions That Scale

EyePop.ai Webinar: December 15, 9:00 am PT

Embedded Vision Summit

February 2–4, 2027, San Francisco, California

FEATURED NEWS

Synaptics has introduced the Astra SR200 Series  of multimodal edge AI MCUs and  has expanded its Coralboard family with Google Research

BrainChip has launched Sequora Core IP , using a state-space architecture to bring generative AI to battery-powered devices

NVIDIA has expanded its Isaac robotics platform  with Isaac OS, Isaac Lab 3.0 and a humanoid reference platform built on Jetson Thor

EyePop.ai has released a white paper comparing 35 AI vision platforms  across 12 attributes to help teams evaluate options for production deployment

Cadence and Analog Devices have developed a Tensilica-based DSP architecture  that adds neural-network inference to next-generation automotive audio processors

More News

EDGE AI AND VISION PRODUCT OF THE YEAR WINNER SHOWCASE

Nota AI Nota Vision Agent (Best Edge AI Large Multimodal Model)

Nota AI’s Nota Vision Agent has been awarded the 2026 Edge AI and Vision Product of the Year Award in the Edge AI Large Multimodal Models category. NVA (Nota Vision Agent) is Nota AI’s flagship generative AI video monitoring solution that transforms traditional video feeds into intelligent, conversational insights. Unlike conventional computer vision (CV)-based object detection focused on predefined objects, NVA leverages a Vision Language Model (VLM) to interpret complex scenarios and generate real-time text descriptions, safety reports, and incident summaries. Serving mission-critical sectors such as transportation, industrial safety, logistics, and national defense, NVA enables organizations to shift from passive monitoring to proactive, AI-driven decision-making.

Please see  here  for more information. The Edge AI and Vision Product of the Year Awards recognize innovation in products that enable or incorporate edge AI and computer vision, as evaluated by independent industry experts.

title: Optimizing the MLIR-Based Torq NPU Compiler
author: Edge AI and Vision Alliance
description:
How ENERZAi reduced the DMA overhead caused by SLICE parallelism in the IREE/MLIR-based compiler for the Torq NPU on Synaptics Astra

 

This blog post was originally published at  ENERZAi’s website . It is reprinted here with the permission of ENERZAi.

Hi, this is ENERZAi. We recently contributed to the backend implementation and model optimization of the Torq compiler, an open-source IREE/MLIR-based compiler for the Torq NPU in the Astra SL2610 product line from global semiconductor comp...
article_content:
How ENERZAi reduced the DMA overhead caused by SLICE parallelism in the IREE/MLIR-based compiler for the Torq NPU on Synaptics Astra

 

This blog post was originally published at  ENERZAi’s website . It is reprinted here with the permission of ENERZAi.

Hi, this is ENERZAi. We recently contributed to the backend implementation and model optimization of the Torq compiler, an open-source IREE/MLIR-based compiler for the Torq NPU in the Astra SL2610 product line from global semiconductor company Synaptics. In this post, we’ll share the challenges we ran into along the way and the insights we gained.

In particular, we’ll take a close look at the hidden data-movement (DMA) cost that arises when an operation is split across the NPU’s two compute blocks (SLICEs) to run in parallel, and at where in the compiler’s layers we reduced it, and how.

Once again, a big thank-you to Synaptics for making this opportunity possible!

An NPU Ecosystem That Is Still Taking Shape

Interest in domain-specific architectures has grown rapidly over the past few years. CPUs and GPUs have already evolved to divide work between general-purpose computation and massively parallel workloads. Deep learning has created a similar need for specialization: much of a model can be expressed as a flow of tensor operations, making architectures tailored to those workloads increasingly important. The rapid growth of model-based services is accelerating this trend.

As a result, many companies are developing and shipping processing units specialized for neural-network workloads: NPUs, or Neural Processing Units. They are particularly important in edge computing, where models need to run directly on-device under tight power and memory budgets while still delivering useful intelligence.

Unlike CPUs and GPUs, however, NPUs do not yet benefit from mature compiler stacks, runtimes, and the thick ecosystem built on top of them. Architectures vary widely across vendors, commercial deployment is still relatively young compared with GPUs, and there is no broadly established agreement on where the hardware/software boundary should sit. APIs and infrastructure therefore differ significantly from one platform to another. In some cases, an NPU may already be in production while the software stack needed to use it effectively is still catching up.

The Optimization That Looked Obvious

One of the first ideas an NPU with multiple compute units suggests is simple: split the work and run the pieces in parallel. The Torq NPU on the Astra SL2619 has two  SLICEs , or compute blocks, so at first glance splitting an operation in half and running one half on each SLICE looks like an obvious optimization.

A few hardware terms are enough to see why the result is not always so simple:

A  SLICE program  operates on data that has already been placed in  LRAM , a small on-chip memory.

XRAM  is a region reserved in the board’s main DRAM for NPU execution.

Data moves between XRAM and LRAM through  DMA . Inputs need to reach LRAM before a SLICE can use them, and results are copied back to XRAM when needed.

Splitting an operation can create more opportunities for parallel execution, but it can also create more data movement. The split is decided while the compiler is still working with tensor-level intermediate representation (IR), before concrete DMA tasks and SLICE programs exist. Once the pieces are lowered, each one may acquire its own loads, stores, and program-code transfers. If two pieces need the same constant or input, that data may be moved more than once.

There is another subtlety: having two SLICE tasks does not mean the two SLICEs actually overlap. The current scheduler assigns work according to the ordering of  start  and  wait  operations in the IR. Both programs need to start before the corresponding waits if we want them to execute concurrently.

# Two SLICEs actually overlap

slice_start(0)

slice_start(1)

slice_wait(0)

slice_wait(1)

# Two tasks, but still sequential

slice_start(0)

slice_wait(0)

slice_start(1)

slice_wait(1)

When an MLIR parallel loop such as  scf.forall  is unrolled into two independent pieces, the first schedule can be produced. Simply creating two operations side by side, however, may still result in the second form: if each operation is immediately followed by its own wait, the second SLICE does not begin until the first has finished.

Data movement adds another complication. DMA can overlap with SLICE execution, so extra traffic is not automatically serialized into latency. But it is still more work for the schedule to absorb, and any part that does not overlap extends the critical path.

This became a recurring pattern in our work on Torq:  an optimization that looked beneficial in tensor IR could expose a new cost only after it reached a lower level of the compiler.  Parallelism was not the hard part by itself. The hard part was making the cost of that parallelism visible soon enough to do something about it.

That observation leads to a compiler-design question: where should each optimization live when the decision is made at one level, but its cost appears at another?

Why Torq Uses Multiple Compiler Layers

Compilers represent a model through a sequence of intermediate representations (IRs) between the original model and the final hardware code. Different optimizations need different information from those representations.

Some transformations are useful across many targets. Others depend on the target’s dataflow, supported operation patterns, or memory hierarchy. The two kinds cannot simply be separated and forgotten about, because their decisions still interact. Operation fusion is a good example: combining operations can avoid materializing intermediate results, but a fused expression may not fit the small set of specialized operations an NPU provides, and the cost of making it fit can outweigh the savings from fusion. Tiling has the same tension. It can be expressed at the tensor level, while the useful tile shape is ultimately constrained by hardware memory and allocation strategy.

Torq handles this by separating concerns across several compiler layers. In MLIR, these layers are organized as  dialects , each representing operations and concepts at a particular level of abstraction.  Torq keeps  tensor semantics and high-level transformations in standard dialects for as long as possible. Torq-specific dialects appear only when concrete information about NPU programs and memory becomes necessary.

Torq Compiler is implemented as an IREE plugin and makes extensive use of MLIR. The main layers are:

The    linalg    layer : MLIR’s builtin dialect for expressing tensor operations primarily in terms of their mathematical semantics. Tensor-level transformations such as tiling and fusion operate on this IR. Some passes may consult target information, but hardware-specific program descriptors and internal data paths are not exposed yet.

The    torq_hl    layer : A dialect that gives operations Torq-specific semantics and represents XRAM/LRAM transfers as well as SLICE-program execution. At this level, it becomes explicit which data needs to move into or out of NPU memory and when NPU programs are launched.

The    torq_hw    layer : A dialect that maps to the descriptors consumed by the hardware. Information such as the D/W/B/Q data paths and ALU/ACT configuration appears directly in the IR that defines an actual SLICE task.

Looking at the same matrix multiplication at each level makes the progression concrete:

// linalg: only the mathematical tensor operation is expressed here.

//         tensor.empty and linalg.fill(0.0) initialize the tensor that

//         becomes the outs operand (output tensor) of the matmul.

%zero = arith.constant 0.000000e+00 : bf16

%e = tensor.empty() : tensor<64x128xbf16>

%f = linalg.fill ins(%zero : bf16) outs(%e : tensor<64x128xbf16>) -> tensor<64x128xbf16>

%m = linalg.matmul ins(%a, %b : tensor<64x64xbf16>, tensor<64x128xbf16>)

outs(%f : tensor<64x128xbf16>) -> tensor<64x128xbf16>

// torq_hl: an execution unit understood by the NPU. linalg.fill is gone;

//          an uninitialized tensor.empty remains as the init operand,

//          and bias / quantization parameters are attached as operands.

//          (%sb = dense<[0, 1]> : tensor<2xi32>, i.e. bias 0 · scale 1)

%init = tensor.empty() : tensor<64x128xbf16>

%q = "torq_hl.matmul"(%init, %sb, %a, %b) {output_zp = 0, shift = 0, ...}

// torq_hw: the hardware descriptor itself.

torq_hw.slice_task {

op : "matmul-fast"

D %arg3 : memref<64x128xbf16, lram>    W %arg2 : memref<64x64xbf16, lram>

B %arg1 : memref<2xi32, lram>          Q %arg0 : memref<64x128xbf16, lram>

CFG {alu_op0_mode = [MUL, ...], alu_op1_mode = [ACC, ...], act_mode = ACT,

weight_format = BF, alu_format = BF, act_format = BF, ...}

}

The arithmetic is the same at every level, but the representation becomes increasingly concrete.  linalg  carries the tensor-level semantics.  torq_hl  adds the information needed to execute the operation as an NPU program. By the time we reach  torq_hw , D (Input Data), W (Weight), B (Bias/Scale), Q (Output), and the ALU/ACT configuration expose something close to the hardware behavior itself.

The lower-level cost becomes even clearer once the surrounding program and data movement are visible:

// torq_hl: the machinery surrounding a single kernel operation.

%a_x = torq_hl.map_binding {binding_index = 0} : memref<64x64xbf16>   // XRAM address

%a_l = memref.alloc() : memref<64x64xbf16, lram>                      // LRAM allocation

torq_hl.load %a_x to %a_l {element_size_bytes = 8192}                 // DMA in (XRAM -> LRAM)

...

%prog = torq_hl.program "slice_program_torq_hl.matmul_0" {

^bb0(%q: ..., %b: ..., %w: ..., %d: ...):

"torq_hl.matmul"(%q, %b, %w, %d) {output_zp = 0, shift = 0, ...}

}

%inv, %code = torq_hl.create_invocation "slice_program_torq_hl.matmul_0"

program(%prog) on 0 : ..., memref<5120xi8>

torq_hl.load %code to %code_l {element_size_bytes = 5120}             // program-code DMA

torq_hl.start_program %inv args(%q_l, %b_l, %a_l, %d_l)

torq_hl.wait_program %inv

torq_hl.store %q_l to %q_x {element_size_bytes = 16384}               // DMA out (LRAM -> XRAM)

What was a single tensor operation in  linalg  has expanded into finding XRAM addresses, allocating LRAM, loading inputs, launching and waiting for a program, and finally storing the result back out. The arithmetic has not changed, but the cost of preparing that computation for execution on the device is now visible.

This is why the layering mattered to our work. A split made at the  linalg  level can turn into additional addresses, DMA, and program launches in  torq_hl . At the same time, some fixes are easiest before those details exist, while others require exactly the information that appears later. Instead of putting every optimization into one layer, we can address each cost where the necessary information becomes available.

The same structure also gives the compiler room to evolve. NPU operations, memory capacity, and data paths may change across hardware generations. Keeping high-level semantics separate from lower-level hardware details limits how much of the pipeline needs to change with the target.

Paying Back the Cost of Slicing

Once we could see where the extra movement appeared, most of our work followed one theme:  keep the parallelism, but remove as much of the movement it introduces as possible.  The fixes landed at different abstraction levels because each one needed a different view of the program.

Keep Elementwise Chains Together in  linalg

At the  linalg  layer, we found cases where consecutive element-wise operations were sliced one operation at a time. Composite activations and post-processing often canonicalize into chains of  linalg.generic  operations. If each operation ends up in a separate loop, intermediate values can cross loop boundaries and later be materialized in XRAM.

We unified the  torq-fuse-group  attached to operations in such a chain. The compiler pulls  linalg  operations in the same group into a single  scf.forall , while operations in different groups are placed in separate loops. By assigning the chain to one group before slicing begins, the compiler can construct one loop for the whole chain from the start rather than trying to merge loops afterward. The example below compresses a longer chain down to three operations for readability.

// [Before change, before slicing]

// The chain still consists of multiple operations, and no loop has been

// created yet. Each operation only carries a marker describing which group

// it belongs to. Those markers are fragmented across the chain.

%a = linalg.generic { ... }          {torq-fuse-group = [3]}

%b = linalg.generic { ... %a ... }   {torq-fuse-group = [4]}

%c = linalg.generic { ... %b ... }   // no marker

// [After change, before slicing]

// Walk the chain and unify the group marker. The operations and their order

// do not change; only the marker does.

%a = linalg.generic { ... }          {torq-fuse-group = [30]}

%b = linalg.generic { ... %a ... }   {torq-fuse-group = [30]}

%c = linalg.generic { ... %b ... }   {torq-fuse-group = [30]}

// [Before change, after slicing]

// Fragmented markers produce one loop per operation.

%a = scf.forall (%i) = (0) to (N) step (N/2) { linalg.generic { ... } }         // %a survives across a loop boundary

%b = scf.forall (%i) = (0) to (N) step (N/2) { linalg.generic { ... %a ... } }  // the next loop consumes %a

%c = scf.forall (%i) = (0) to (N) step (N/2) { linalg.generic { ... %b ... } }  // the boundary repeats at every stage

// [After change, after slicing]

// One loop contains the whole chain, so the intermediates stay inside it.

%c = scf.forall (%i) = (0) to (N) step (N/2) {

%t0 = linalg.generic { ... }

%t1 = linalg.generic { ... %t0 ... }

linalg.generic { ... %t1 ... }

}

On the lowering paths where this problem occurred, intermediates crossing different  scf.forall  loops were materialized in XRAM, creating extra round trips. Keeping the chain inside one loop lets those intermediates stay in LRAM longer and reduces the associated DMA in/out. The point is less “fusion for its own sake” than preserving on-chip residency across the chain.

Compile-time timeline of  erf  (1x1024x64, bf16) with slicing enabled. In each panel the upper group is before the elementwise chain was placed in one fuse group and the lower group is after; the bottom panel enlarges the blue frame, the first 330 µs of each run. ① Stores to XRAM between the ops of the chain: each op writes both SLICE halves out. ② Loads that bring those values straight back into LRAM for the next op. ③ With the whole chain in one fuse group, the intermediates stay in LRAM and the SLICE programs run back to back. Stores drop from 36 (2.6 MB) to 7 (448 KB), and the estimated time from 1834.9 µs to 888.0 µs.

Reorder SLICE Extraction Before Memory Conversion

A different problem appeared after the compiler had reached  torq_hl . Some values were still represented as tensors, but their memory placement was now encoded in their types. In the original IR, the compiler could convert a full value to XRAM first and only then extract the smaller SLICE that was actually needed.

We rewrote that into an equivalent form: extract the SLICE while the value is still in LRAM, then convert only the smaller SLICE. This keeps the large tensor on-chip and exposes a redundant round trip on the smaller SLICE that an existing compiler optimization can fold away.

// Before our change

%x  = torq_hl.convert in(%big) {encoding = xram}   // write the full result to XRAM

%sl = tensor.extract_slice %x [...]                // extract the required part from XRAM

%l  = torq_hl.convert in(%sl) {encoding = lram}    // bring it back into LRAM

// After our change

%sl = tensor.extract_slice %big [...]              // extract directly while still in LRAM

%x  = torq_hl.convert in(%sl) {encoding = xram}    // the large tensor never leaves for XRAM

%l  = torq_hl.convert in(%x) {encoding = lram}     // this round trip on the SLICE is now redundant

// After subsequent cleanup

%sl = tensor.extract_slice %big [...]              // extract directly in LRAM\

max_pool  (5×5, 1x15x20x384, i8) before (upper group) and after (lower group) SLICE extraction was moved ahead of the LRAM-to-XRAM conversion. ① The full 112.5 KB result is converted to XRAM. ② Each SLICE then extracts its 56.2 KB half and loads it back into LRAM. ③ After the change both SLICEs take their halves while the value is still in LRAM, so the round trip disappears. The estimated time drops from 369.3 µs to 312.9 µs.

Neither this change nor the  linalg  grouping above introduced a new operation. In both cases, the useful transformation already existed somewhere in the compiler; the important part was arranging the IR so that it could do the right thing for Torq’s memory model.

Expose Access Semantics Instead of Reimplementing Analysis

At the  torq_hl  layer, LRAM addresses, loads/stores, and program boundaries are explicit, so some redundant movement can be attacked directly. If the same read-only data is loaded separately for two SLICEs, we want to transfer it once and share it. If an intermediate is written to temporary XRAM but will never be read again, we want to remove that store.

The interesting part was that many of the analyses and transformations needed for these cases already existed. The problem was that  torq_hl  is a custom dialect, so the compiler did not automatically know how its operations access memory or whether they are safe to move. Rather than reimplementing the analyses, we exposed those properties through compiler interfaces.

The read/write direction of SLICE-program arguments is described through  AsyncAccessOpInterface , a simplified version of the interface used in IREE. For operation-level memory effects and motion legality, we use  MemoryEffectsOpInterface  and  ConditionallySpeculatable . Once those properties are available, existing MLIR analyses and utilities can reason about  torq_hl  as well.

One immediate benefit is eliminating dead stores. Without read/write information, the compiler has to assume that every SLICE-program argument might be both read and written. Once it knows that a later program overwrites a value rather than reading it, an earlier spill can disappear.

// Before our change

%t_x = torq_hl.map_binding {binding_index = 2}   // temporary location in XRAM

%t_l = memref.alloc() : memref<..., lram>        // location in LRAM

torq_hl.start_program %inv_a args(%t_l, %d_l)    // A writes its result to %t_l

torq_hl.wait_program %inv_a

torq_hl.store %t_l to %t_x                       // spill %t_l because LRAM is tight

torq_hl.start_program %inv_b args(%t_l, %e_l)    // B also writes a result to %t_l

torq_hl.wait_program %inv_b                      // but we cannot tell whether B reads or writes %t_l

torq_hl.store %t_l to %q_x                       // so the earlier store cannot be removed

// After our change: the interface tells us B only overwrites %t_l,

// so the previously spilled copy will never be read again.

%t_l = memref.alloc() : memref<..., lram>

torq_hl.start_program %inv_a args(%t_l, %d_l)

torq_hl.wait_program %inv_a

// one store and the %t_x binding disappear

torq_hl.start_program %inv_b args(%t_l, %e_l)

torq_hl.wait_program %inv_b

torq_hl.store %t_l to %q_x                       // the final result store remains

The same information helps when a buffer is temporarily spilled to XRAM because LRAM is full and loaded again later. If the intervening program only reads the buffer, the previously written XRAM copy is still valid. The compiler can release the LRAM allocation and reuse that copy instead of allocating another XRAM location and storing the same data again.

A conv1d layer (kernel 127, stride 64, 80,000 audio samples to 288 channels) before (upper group) and after (lower group)  AsyncAccessOpInterface . The bottom panel lines up the same loop iteration from both runs (blue frames: 1950–2720 µs before, 1842–2612 µs after), each shifted to start at 0. ① A dead store: a 200 KB value is spilled to XRAM although the next program only overwrites it. ② The matching 200 KB load, which disappears with it. ③ An unchanged 309 KB buffer is stored to XRAM again; after the change the copy already in XRAM is reused. DMA out drops from 22 transfers (4.5 MB) to 13 (2.4 MB), and the estimated time from 5091.1 µs to 4218.8 µs.

A related question is whether an operation can move at all. If an operation produces the same value on every loop iteration, it is better to execute it once outside the loop and reuse the result. Previously, MLIR could not tell whether moving a  torq_hl  operation was legal.

// Before our change: recompute the same value on every iteration

// (or for every SLICE program). We cannot prove it is safe to move out.

scf.forall (%i) ... {

%s = torq_hl.segmentation ... (%w, %sb, %in)   // all three inputs are independent of %i

... computations using %s ...

}

// After our change: the operation is classified as safe to move,

// allowing MLIR's moveLoopInvariantCode utility to process it.

%s = torq_hl.segmentation ... (%w, %sb, %in)

scf.forall (%i) ... {

... computations using %s ...

}

We marked only the operations that were actually safe to move; operations whose meaning depends on their position, such as those that gather values by index, were excluded. This allowed us to reuse MLIR’s  getBackwardSlice  and  moveLoopInvariantCode  instead of writing separate legality logic.

Taken together, these changes removed part of the duplicate movement introduced by slicing. They also changed how we thought about the problem: splitting work well is not enough. If parallelization creates overhead, the compiler needs a way to pay that overhead back before the parallelism turns into real performance.

What We Learned

Looking back, the individual rewrites and interfaces matter less than the pattern behind them.

First, optimization starts with understanding how data moves through the chip. On Torq, each operation has specific input paths, accumulation paths, and post-processing paths available to it, and those constraints determine what can fit inside a single program. Task count and DMA bytes are useful diagnostics, but they are not performance verdicts by themselves. Even when fusion reduces the number of tasks, we still need to ask which kernel path the fused operation selects and what happens to the actual critical path.

Second, tiling, fusion, and slicing are tightly coupled under a constrained LRAM budget. All three affect what stays on-chip, how much of it stays there, and how often it needs to move again. Making those decisions independently can easily make the optimizations work against each other.

The answer is not to collapse everything into one hardware-specific IR. The layered pipeline does not remove the coupling between optimizations; it gives that coupling a place to become visible. High-level transformations can keep working with tensor semantics, while lower layers expose the hardware costs those decisions eventually create. For us, that separation became less about architectural neatness and more about having the right information available at the right time.

What’s Next

The same lesson shapes where we want to take the compiler next. Our goal is to support a broader range of models and future hardware without turning every new target into another set of hard-coded special cases.

1. From EasyKernel to Nadya.

Today, Torq kernels are written in EasyKernel, an internal C++ DSL. Instead of writing low-level hardware descriptors and instruction streams directly, a kernel can be expressed in something closer to ordinary loops and then serialized into descriptors. This is much easier to work with, but the implementation of each tensor operation still lives inside the compiler. That makes new operations and future hardware generations harder to support and also limits opportunities for runtime profiling and tuning of kernel implementations.

One direction we are exploring is moving kernel authoring to Nadya, a kernel programming language we are developing. Nadya is designed to make it possible to write high-performance programs without requiring every author to understand all of the underlying hardware optimization details. The implementation of how the NPU executes an operation could live in external kernel code, while the compiler decides how multiple operations should be scheduled together.

2. Making optimization decisions searchable.

The compilation pipeline contains many decisions driven by heuristics: tile sizes, SLICE partitioning, whether to fuse, and so on. Rather than hard-coding those choices into individual passes, we want to parameterize them so they can be explored systematically by a tuning loop. That loop may live in an external tool or be integrated more tightly with the compiler over time; the important part is to separate the search policy from the transformation logic. This lets the same compiler pipeline evaluate different configurations and adapt to new hardware without rewriting heuristics for every target.

There are still many open problems in making a compiler for a new class of target both powerful and flexible. But that is exactly what makes the project interesting. At ENERZAi, we are still working through those problems one by one.

An Open Project

One of the best parts of this project is that both the hardware specifications and the compiler are public. The compiler is available at  synaptics-torq/torq-compiler Github repo , model examples are available in  torq-examples , and the official documentation is at  synaptics-torq.github.io . Anyone can inspect the kinds of problems we are working on, and contributors who are interested can get involved directly.

If you’d like to learn more about the Torq project or ENERZAi’s other optimization technologies, such as Nadya, feel free to reach out anytime!

ENERZAi – Contact

Jaeho Kim

ENERZAi

HIGHLIGHTS

Cadence Maestro portfolio introduces domain-specialized AI models purpose-built to power agentic chip and system design.

Vertically integrated reinforcement learning environment connects Cadence Maestro models, Cadence AI Super Agents and proven Cadence EDA and SDA tools to continuously improve engineering outcomes and drive faster time to market.

article_content:
HIGHLIGHTS

Cadence Maestro portfolio introduces domain-specialized AI models purpose-built to power agentic chip and system design.

Vertically integrated reinforcement learning environment connects Cadence Maestro models, Cadence AI Super Agents and proven Cadence EDA and SDA tools to continuously improve engineering outcomes and drive faster time to market.

Initial design-workflow results show up to 30% higher quality and up to 5X greater token efficiency versus general-purpose foundation models.

Secure architecture enables the optimal combination of domain-specialized Maestro models, leading frontier and open-weight models with cloud and customer-controlled on-premises deployment.

SAN JOSE, Calif.–( BUSINESS WIRE )–Cadence (Nasdaq: CDNS) today announced the Maestro  AI Model Portfolio, which powers Cadence® AI Super Agents across semiconductor and system design workflows. By integrating these models with reinforcement learning (RL) loops and its proven electronic design automation (EDA) and system design automation (SDA) tools, Cadence delivers a deeply integrated agentic engineering platform designed to improve results, accelerate time to market and continuously enhance performance through recursive self-improvement.

The Maestro technology offers customers a secure, Cadence-managed platform that combines exceptional domain-specialized intelligence and expertise with the control, choice, and flexibility they need to innovate with confidence. The Maestro portfolio spans multiple model sizes and architectures, combining domain-specialized post-trained large language models (LLMs), trained decision models and self-improving agent skills. Integrated with Cadence AI Super Agents—including AuraStack , ChipStack , InnoStack , and ViraStack  AI Super Agents—as well as its proven EDA and SDA tools and reinforcement learning, the Maestro portfolio brings specialized intelligence to complex engineering workflows through an optimal blend of frontier, open-weight and domain-specialized models across cloud and on-premises environments.

“Revolutionizing complex engineering tasks requires deep domain-specialized intelligence,” said Anirudh Devgan, president and CEO at Cadence. “Combining our Maestro portfolio of domain-specialized models with leading frontier and open-weight models enables our AI Super Agents to drive Cadence EDA and SDA tools with exceptional skill and efficiency to transform chip and system design.”

“Agentic chip design requires AI that can generate design content, evaluate tradeoffs and learn from verified engineering results,” said Tim Costa, vice president and general manager of industrial and computational engineering at NVIDIA. “Our collaboration with Cadence brings NVIDIA Nemotron, OpenShell and deep engineering expertise to Maestro’s domain-specialized models. By grounding reinforcement learning in feedback from EDA tools and deterministic solvers, we can teach agents to make better design decisions based on how well their work meets engineering objectives and constraints.”

“We are deploying Cadence’s InnoStack AI Super Agent into our production design environment,” said Hisato Yoshida, COO of Socionext. “By combining agentic AI with advanced EDA tools for physical design, we expect up to 5X overall productivity gains while maintaining design quality. We see the Maestro portfolio as the next step in driving even greater efficiency across our design process.”

“Ultra-low power devices require innovation across disciplines. Agentic AI unlocks new power opportunities,” said Garima Sharda, vice president of engineering at Silicon Labs. “By leveraging the Cadence Verisium Debug as part of ChipStack AI Super Agent, our engineering teams have achieved acceleration in root-cause analysis and end-to-end debug during pre-silicon low power verification. We look forward to realizing further benefits through Cadence’s Maestro domain-specialized models.”

A Self-Improving Learning Environment for Engineering AI

Initial results show up to 30% improvement in quality of results and up to 5X greater token efficiency versus a general-purpose foundation model. These gains come from a vertically integrated learning environment combining Cadence domain knowledge, curated engineering datasets, AI Super Agents, EDA and SDA tools, and evaluation harnesses. Cadence’s principled algorithms and deterministic solvers evaluate outputs against engineering objectives, constraints and ground truth, creating closed and verified feedback loops for reinforcement learning and recursive improvement.

Domain Intelligence with Intelligent Model Choice

The Cadence learning environment unifies complementary AI capabilities in a single workflow. Frontier and open-weight models provide broad language, reasoning and multimodal capabilities; the Maestro AI Model Portfolio provides domain expertise for complex chip and system design. Given a high-level objective, Cadence AI Super Agents interpret design intent, decompose tasks, orchestrate the Maestro portfolio with other leading frontier and open-weight models, and drive Cadence EDA and SDA tools. The combined solution interprets specifications, generates design content, analyzes results, evaluates tradeoffs and guides decisions based on engineering requirements, cost and security. The Maestro portfolio, including NVIDIA Nemotron and other models, can be further post-trained on a customer’s proprietary data, designs, and workflows and, by balancing EDA and SDA tool calls with LLM invocations, it significantly reduces token usage while maintaining execution efficiency.

The complete Cadence agentic environment—including AI Super Agents, Maestro AI Model Portfolio and EDA tools—can run on Cadence’s secure cloud platform, secure public clouds, or in a customer-controlled on-premises environment to meet data privacy, security and deployment requirements. Cadence and NVIDIA are also working together on agent security through integration with the  NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture .

Availability

The first Maestro models are available to select early access customers in the fourth quarter of 2026.

About Cadence

Cadence is a market leader in AI and digital twins, pioneering the application of computational software to accelerate innovation in the engineering design of silicon to systems. Our design solutions, based on Cadence’s Intelligent System Design  strategy, are essential for the world’s leading semiconductor and systems companies to build their next-generation products from chips to full electromechanical systems that serve a wide range of markets, including hyperscale computing, mobile communications, automotive, aerospace, industrial, life sciences and robotics. In 2025, Cadence was recognized by Fortune as one of the world’s top 100 best companies to work for. Cadence solutions offer limitless opportunities—learn more at www.cadence.com.

Contacts

Steve Gartner

sgartner@cadence.com

title: BrainChip Unveils AKD1500 SPI Chip, Bringing Neuromorphic AI to Everyday Edge Devices
author: Edge AI and Vision Alliance
article_content:
AKD1500 SPI pairs with the microcontroller, opening Akida AI to the high-volume MCU market

 

LAGUNA HILLS, Calif. – Oct. 22, 2026 –   BrainChip Holdings Ltd . (ASX: BRN, OTCQX: BRCHF, ADR: BCHPY), a global leader in ultra-low-power, fully digital, event-based neuromorphic AI, today announced the AKD1500 SPI, expanding its AKD1500 family with a co-processor that brings Akida neuromorphic AI to wearables, smart home devices and other microcontroller-based edge products. Using the SPI interface already found in most microcontrollers, AKD1500 SPI lets device makers add AI with a single chip rather than redesign around a new processor.

AKD1500 SPI’s standout feature is edge learning, enabling devices to learn new words, sounds, users or patterns directly on the chip, without sending data to the cloud or retraining the model. Like every Akida processor, it also runs several AI tasks on one chip.

Alongside the AKD1500 PCIe for M.2 and multi-chip designs, the AKD1500 family lets device makers run the same AI in anything from a smartwatch to a multi-chip edge system with a SPI interface.

“Our customers demand reflex-like responsiveness and efficiency. They measure every milliwatt and every millisecond,” said Ivan Projić, co-founder and CEO of Neuromorphyx. “On BrainBoard1500 and NeuroReflex, we’ve seen the AKD1500 run neural networks over SPI within the power and size limits of real embedded products.”

Karlo Mikualco, co-founder and CTO of Neuromorphyx, added, “With its SPI interface, the AKD1500 lets teams bring that efficiency, plus on-chip learning, into robotics, industrial and space-grade systems without replacing the host processor they already trust.”

Add AI without replacing the processor

Most everyday devices, such as smartwatches, doorbells and factory sensors, already have a microcontroller, which is built to control the device. Adding AI usually means moving to a larger, more expensive processor and redesigning the entire product.

The AKD1500 SPI avoids that by using SPI, a standard interface most microcontrollers already have, letting device makers add one chip to their existing design.

The AKD1500 SPI works alongside the MCU as a dedicated AI processor. The MCU controls the device, relaying sensor data to the AKD1500 SPI, which runs the full neural network and sends back the result, such as a recognized word or a detected fault.

Running the model on the device also removes the cloud round trip, including latency, the loss of AI when connectivity drops and the risk of data leaving the product. Voice, sensor and device-health data stay on the device.

“The AKD1500 SPI brings brain-inspired AI into NEXA EEG Glasses, designed for everyday wear,” stated Yazin Al Mandhari, COO at Onsor. “It’s an important step in our work to help people living with epilepsy and their care teams better understand brain activity beyond the clinic.”

Built for the multi-billion-unit microcontroller market

Microcontrollers are among the most widely shipped chips in the world, and until recently almost none of them could learn on-chip once a product shipped. ABI Research forecasts that chipset shipments of TinyML AI, which are lightweight machine learning models deployed directly onto ultra-low-power microcontrollers, will surpass 4.1 billion units by 2031, with dedicated AI processors the fastest-growing part of that segment.

“We built the AKD1500 family around how products are actually designed,” said Steve Brightfield, chief product officer at BrainChip. “The AKD1500 SPI connects to the MCU a team already uses, and the AKD1500 PCIe serves systems that need more performance. Both run the same models with the same tools, so customers can grow without starting over.”

The AKD1500 PCIe serves performance-driven systems and multi-chip designs; the AKD1500 SPI opens the high-volume microcontroller market across consumer, industrial and healthcare products.

The AKD1500 SPI is available now from the  BrainChip Shop , its channel partner  DigiKey  or through sales ( sales@brainchip.com ).

About BrainChip Holdings Ltd.

BrainChip  is the worldwide leader in edge AI on-chip processing and learning. The company’s first-to-market, fully digital, event-based AI processor, Akida , uses neuromorphic principles to analyze only essential sensor inputs at the point of acquisition, processing data with unmatched efficiency, precision and energy economy. BrainChip’s Sequora  is an efficient digital AI processor for GenAI and other large models using state-space architectures. BrainChip’s technology is deployed across industries including aerospace, defense, industrial IoT, healthcare, consumer devices, and wearables. Explore more at  www.brainchip.com .

author: Edge AI and Vision Alliance
description:
New tools joining NVIDIA Cosmos are helping accelerate data pipelines, train, evaluate and optimize world models more efficiently, and improve accuracy at lower cost.

 

To help developers rapidly build  world models , which help  physical AI  systems understand and simulate the real world, NVIDIA has expanded the  Cosmos platform  with new training tools, simulation checkpoints and Cosmos Data Factory blueprints.

Ranking top five on six different open models leaderboards, the NVIDIA Cosm...
article_content:
New tools joining NVIDIA Cosmos are helping accelerate data pipelines, train, evaluate and optimize world models more efficiently, and improve accuracy at lower cost.

 

To help developers rapidly build  world models , which help  physical AI  systems understand and simulate the real world, NVIDIA has expanded the  Cosmos platform  with new training tools, simulation checkpoints and Cosmos Data Factory blueprints.

Ranking top five on six different open models leaderboards, the NVIDIA Cosmos platform gives world model builders the frontier open models — as well as data, training and optimization tools and recipes — to scale training data, adapt models, test behavior and optimize for performance before deployment.

Build Better Training Data

Building world models begins with multimodal, multisensory data.

NVIDIA Cosmos Data Factory  brings together the tools and skills for labeling, curating, augmenting and evaluating data at scale for training physical AI. Cosmos Curator, a GPU-accelerated solution for curating video training datasets, has now added support for multimodal multisensory inputs and processing blocks.

Cosmos Data Factory now offers the following five cloud-native blueprints and is available through  GitHub ,  Microsoft Azure ,  Nebius  and  CoreWeave :

Autonomous Vehicle Dataset Generation:  Curates and labels driving data, then adds synthetic examples of hard-to-capture scenarios to expand training coverage.

Image Attribute Augmentation:  Varies object appearance to improve image search.

Event Video Generation:  Turns still images into synthetic videos of rare or unsafe events.

Defect Image Generation:  Generates printed circuit board, metal and glass defect images for inspection models.

Video Data Augmentation:  Changes weather and lighting in existing footage while preserving scene structure.

Cosmos Data Factory accelerates data curation, processing and synthetic data generation with agentic skills.

Companies are already putting Cosmos Data Factory blueprints to work to speed their physical AI development workflows.

Porsche is leading the development of a shared AV data flywheel across Volkswagen Group brands, using Cosmos Data Factory through Voxel51 on Microsoft Azure. This is expected to reduce repeated physical test drives by up to 90% and shorten development cycle times by up to 85%.

Porsche searching and augmenting autonomous vehicle data footage in Voxel51, powered by Cosmos Data Factory.

ANYbotics generated over 1,500 synthetic video clips with Cosmos Data Factory blueprints, curating real-world data and validating outputs with  Encord’s  platform, to train its industrial-inspection robots to recognize liquid spills and other changes between facility visits.

ANYbotics generating anomaly clips with Encord powered by NVIDIA Cosmos Data Factory.

Ultralytics , a computer vision company, retrained its YOLO model with real images and targeted synthetic defects generated using Cosmos Data Factory, improving defect localization and recall.

Train, Adapt and Optimize Models

With training data prepared, developers may train their own architecture or start with a pretrained model.

At GTC Berlin, NVIDIA extended  Cosmos Framework  training, optimization and deployment tools and recipes as agent skills to more open models, along with Cosmos 3, giving world model builders a faster path from experimentation to deployment.

Developers and agents can now adapt open models like  GR00T ,  Alpamayo , QWEN, Pi0.5 and other compatible Hugging Face models through fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, optimize the model with distillation and quantization, and deploy with high-performing inference.

Cosmos Framework is an open, modular framework of model training and optimization tools and skills to accelerate world model development.

To develop a world model specialized for egocentric manipulation, robotics research lab MicroAGI post-trained Cosmos 3 on videos of humans manipulating objects and distilled its 32-billion-parameter reasoner down to an 8-billion-parameter Nano model with no loss in accuracy.

Developers can label data and post-train Cosmos 3 on  Roboflow  for their specific environments and tasks, then deploy those models to RoboFlow hosted or on-premises NVIDIA GPUs to bring video reasoning into factories and warehouses.

Test Policies and Run Models Faster

Alongside these tools, NVIDIA continues advancing foundational technology through its work on Cosmos models.

New  Cosmos 3 Nano model variants  for simulation enable developers to test autonomous policies in repeatable, hard-to-capture, multiview multisensor scenarios. Accompanying code allows developers to adapt the models to train and evaluate their own policies for autonomous vehicles and bimanual robots in interactive simulations before real-world testing.

Multiview and multisensory video data generation for evaluating policies in closed loop simulation.

Developers can deploy core Cosmos models using updated  NVIDIA Cosmos 3 NIM  microservices, which deliver up to 2x faster inference with no quality loss in validated configurations, while continuous video analysis enables sub-second alerts.

For vision AI developers, the new  NVIDIA Metropolis Blueprint for video search and summarization (VSS) 3.3 , built on Cosmos NIM microservices, turns one prompt into an efficient video AI application and helps teams monitor 40% more video streams with the same GPU.

ADNOC uses Fogsphere’s MistIQ agentic platform, built with Cosmos and the NVIDIA Metropolis VSS Blueprint, to detect safety hazards in real time across 65 sites. For rare events,  Fogsphere  also uses the Cosmos Data Factory to generate synthetic training data, improving detection without needing to physically stage dangerous situations.

The Cosmos platform is fully modular and open. Developers can use  Cosmos Data Factory  to generate training datasets,  Cosmos Framework  to train and adapt world models, then deploy supported  Cosmos models through NIM microservices .

Pranjali Joshi

Product Marketing Manager, NVIDIA Omniverse

article_content:
Falling vehicle costs, end-to-end AI, and hybrid fleet operation are driving the global robotaxi fleet toward two million units.

KEY TAKEAWAYS

The global robotaxi fleet [1]  is expected to reach 331,000 vehicles in 2031, an average annual growth of 78%.

Market drivers: five factors are jointly powering the comeback, led by vehicle BOM and manufacturing cost reductions and by the expansion of commercial services.

End-to-end algorithms, hybrid operation, and L2+/L4 convergence are turning pilot fleets into a scalable business.

Waymo leads in operational fleet size (unsupervised), closely followed by Pony.AI, WeRide, and Apollo Go. The ranking remains highly dynamic, with automotive OEMs such as Tesla, XPeng, and Geely now joining in.

Key enabling semiconductors follow the same curve: the combined robo-X markets for sensors and processors will reach about $4.4 billion and almost $4 billion respectively in 2035.

After the hype and the disillusionment of the last decade, the robotaxi is back, and this time on a steady and rapid growth path. Vehicle costs are falling, commercial services are expanding city by city, and the algorithms behind autonomous driving have reached the point where scaling a fleet is both technically feasible and economically defensible.

Yole Group’ s Principal Analysts, Yu Yang and Pierrick Boulay , identify five factors jointly boosting the market, from a 70% reduction in vehicle bill-of-materials and manufacturing costs to the convergence of L2+ and L4 technology stacks.

Against this backdrop, Yole Group releases its latest report,  Robotaxi 2026 , offering both qualitative and quantitative analysis of this fast-growing industry, an in-depth review of the supply chain with a focus on key players, and an update on the latest technological progress, including AI, cost reduction, and the key enabling semiconductors behind it. Together with Yole Group’s wider automotive and robotics coverage, this new report gives decision-makers a unique ongoing view of the autonomous mobility industry through insightful, actionable analysis.

Thanks to this combination of technical and commercial progress, the global robotaxi fleet is forecast to grow to 331,000 vehicles in 2031, an average annual growth of 78%. The momentum will continue beyond that date, reaching a milestone of two million vehicles at a 57% CAGR. By then, robotaxis are expected to have a measurable impact on new light vehicle sales in the countries leading this transition, with a 4% impact in China and a 1% impact in the US.

Five drivers explain the turnaround

Vehicle BOM and manufacturing costs have fallen by up to 70% on multiple models. The expansion of services is increasing revenue while optimized operations reduce costs. End-to-end algorithms provide a technically feasible and economically efficient path to scaling operations. ‘Hybrid’ mode allows robotaxis and driver-based ride-hailing to serve customers seamlessly, promoting robotaxi rides. The convergence of L2+ and L4 also leverages massive volumes of real-life L2+ data for model training.

Yu Yang, PhD, Principal Lead Analyst, Automotives & Robotics at Yole Group :  “The robotaxi industry has shifted from proving that the technology works to proving that the business works. Removing up to 70% of the vehicle cost is what turns a demonstration fleet into a service that can scale, and a handful of operators have now crossed that line.”

On operational fleet size (unsupervised), Waymo stands out

But it is not alone. Indeed, Waymo is closely followed by Pony.AI, WeRide, and Apollo Go, in a ranking that remains highly dynamic. The survivors of the industry’s dark years are now in the fast lane, each with a distinct model.

Waymo is quickly expanding its commercial fleet in the US while testing in the UK and Japan. Apollo Go runs the largest fleet, with almost full coverage in some Chinese cities. Uber has given up in-house development but cooperates with multiple players across several countries, while DiDi has stopped in-house vehicle development and turned to vehicles co-designed with GAC. WeRide is expanding globally and combining L4 robotaxi and L2+ ADAS stacks, Pony.AI has reached unit economics in two Chinese cities with synergies between robotaxis and robotrucks, and Zoox has its released its purpose-built robovan for commercial operation in the US.

Automotive OEMs, by nature, hold a position in the value chain. Tesla is launching its Cybercab, aiming for a share of the large market potential. XPeng is entering the robotaxi market with a foundation model shared with its AV programs and a dedicated vehicle model. Geely is leveraging vehicle manufacturing, including the base car supplied to Waymo, its own AV capability, and its Caocao mobility subsidiary. Most other OEMs cooperate with robotaxi players by co-developing or manufacturing vehicles, and sometimes by investing in them. Although most businesses start within their domestic market, competition is global: the US and China are both incubating giants, while Europe, the Middle East, and parts of Southeast Asia are the most favorable destinations for robo-X players from both countries.

Pierrick Boulay, Principal Analyst, Automotive Semiconductors at Yole Group :  “The Robotaxi does not create a separate semiconductor supply chain. Instead, it stretches the existing ADAS one. The same processor and sensor suppliers serve both markets, and the real differentiator is vertical integration.”

Behind this momentum, key enabling semiconductors are directly impacted and are growing at a similar pace. The combined robo-X markets for sensors and processors will reach about $4.4 billion and roughly $4 billion, respectively, in 2035. As an extension of ADAS technologies, the supplier landscape largely overlaps with the leading ADAS names, both for processors and for the multiple sensing modalities, with the notable exception of vertically integrated players: Waymo with its own TPU, LiDAR, and radar, Tesla with its own SoC, and XPeng with its own SoC and power modules.

With the global fleet on track to reach 331,000 vehicles in 2031 and two million by 2035, the pace and direction of this new cycle have never been more critical for OEMs, robotaxi operators, semiconductor suppliers, and investors. The  Robotaxi 2026 report  from Yole Group provides the market intelligence and technology insights required to navigate this rapidly evolving landscape and identify future growth opportunities.

For more information about this report or to schedule an interview with Yole Group analysts, please contact us.

Stay connected with Yole Group for more insights!!

[1]  This figure does not include robotrucks and robobuses/shuttles.

Source: Yole Group

article_content:
Seco S.p.A. and Peridio have announced a collaboration to make Avocado OS, Peridio's production-ready Linux distribution, available across Seco's portfolio of systems based on Qualcomm Dragonwing platforms. The partnership targets robotics and physical AI applications, providing developers with a commercially supported operating system validated on Seco hardware and intended to simplify the transition from prototype development to production deployment.

Avocado OS  gives development teams access to an industrial Linux foundation from the first development kit, removing the need to build and maintain their own operating system. This is particularly relevant to companies developing robots, autonomous machines, and other physical AI systems, where maintaining a consistent software environment across development and deployed fleets can add complexity and integration effort.

The initial rollout covers several Seco Dragonwing-based platforms: the  SOM-COMe-CT6-Dragonwing-IQ-X ,  SOM-SMARC-Dragonwing-IQ8 , and  SOM-SMARC-QCS6490 . The collaboration also follows the launch of the  SOM-COM-HPC-A-Dragonwing-IQ10  and the  SBC-Dragonwing-IQ-2390 .

By combining Seco hardware with Avocado OS, the companies aim to provide a validated platform for customers developing and deploying physical AI solutions at scale. Organizations already using Avocado OS can transfer their existing software stacks to the supported Seco Dragonwing platforms, reducing the effort required to adapt applications to new hardware.

The agreement also includes preferred support from both companies for customers selecting Seco systems with Avocado OS. Coordinated engineering assistance will cover hardware, board support packages (BSPs), and the operating system, helping address integration challenges across the software and hardware layers. This joint support model is intended to reduce deployment risks and shorten time-to-market for robotics and other  industrial  AI applications.

Through this collaboration, Seco and Peridio aim to give developers a more direct path from initial development to production-ready deployments on Qualcomm Dragonwing-based systems.

title: Aetina Unveils Rugged Edge AI System for Heavy-Duty Vehicles
author: Embedded.com
description:
Aetina Corporation has announced mass-production availability of the DeviceEdge AIE-VX28/18-IP, a fanless, IP66-rated edge AI platform designed for heavy-duty vehicles, off-highway machinery, and roadside infrastructure. Powered by Nvidia Jetson AGX Orin, the system supports up to 12 simultaneous camera inputs, enabling 360-degree vision analytics for applications such as obstacle avoidance, pedestrian detection, and equipment safety.

Designed for construction, agricultural, mining, and rail ve...
article_content:
Aetina Corporation has announced mass-production availability of the DeviceEdge AIE-VX28/18-IP, a fanless, IP66-rated edge AI platform designed for heavy-duty vehicles, off-highway machinery, and roadside infrastructure. Powered by Nvidia Jetson AGX Orin, the system supports up to 12 simultaneous camera inputs, enabling 360-degree vision analytics for applications such as obstacle avoidance, pedestrian detection, and equipment safety.

Designed for construction, agricultural, mining, and rail vehicles, the platform combines MIL-STD-810H durability with four power over Ethernet (PoE) camera connections and eight GMSL2 inputs. Its sealed enclosure protects against dust and water, while waterproof M12 connectors with threaded locking help maintain reliable connections under vibration. The system operates from -25°C to 70°C and accepts a 9-48 VDC input, with ignition power control for surge protection and safe shutdown. It also carries E-Mark (E24) automotive certification.

The four M12 PoE ports provide a combined 60-W power budget for IP cameras, while eight GMSL2 cameras connect through mini-FAKRA connectors. This combination supports different camera configurations, with PoE simplifying cabling and GMSL2 providing low-latency video transmission over longer distances across large vehicle chassis.

The  Nvidia Jetson AGX Orin  module delivers up to 275 TOPS of AI performance for concurrent deep neural networks and real-time vision processing using  Nvidia JetPack  6.2 or later. With JetPack 7.2 and its Super Mode, the Jetson AGX Orin 32-GB module increases AI performance from 200 to 241 TOPS, providing additional processing capacity without requiring a higher-cost module.

Connectivity includes M12 10 GbE, isolated CAN FD, and RS-232/422/485 interfaces. M.2 expansion supports NVMe storage, Wi-Fi, and Bluetooth, as well as RTK positioning and LTE/5G connectivity modules.

Target applications include blind-spot monitoring and geofence alerts for construction machinery, autonomous agricultural equipment, outdoor autonomous mobile robots, and roadside traffic monitoring. At Smart City Expo World Congress 2026 in Barcelona, Aetina is demonstrating a loading-dock safety application using eight concurrent GMSL2 camera streams and the  Nvidia DeepStream SDK  to identify workers near a truck. The same approach can be applied to forklifts, excavators, and other vehicles with restricted visibility.

The  AIE-VX28/18-IP  is available now for mass-production orders. Aetina also provides an optimized board support package, long-term technical support, and customization services covering chassis design and system validation. Validated peripherals include Innodisk  automotive  GMSL2 cameras, industrial storage, and 4G/5G connectivity modules.
