title: Advancing digital sovereignty with greater control and choice
author: Microsoft Azure
description:
Across my conversations with leaders in government, critical infrastructure and regulated industries, one priority consistently rises to the top: putting technology to work on their most important systems while maintaining the control those systems require.

This challenge is becoming more important as advanced cloud and AI capabilities move into public services, regulated processes and essential operations. Organizations are considering more than where data resides. They also seek to understand...
article_content:
Across my conversations with leaders in government, critical infrastructure and regulated industries, one priority consistently rises to the top: putting technology to work on their most important systems while maintaining the control those systems require.

This challenge is becoming more important as advanced cloud and AI capabilities move into public services, regulated processes and essential operations. Organizations are considering more than where data resides. They also seek to understand who can access and operate their systems, how sensitive digital assets remain protected, which technology dependencies matter most and whether critical services can continue as regulatory, geopolitical, security or network conditions change. Digital sovereignty should give organizations greater control and security over the technology they depend on, while continuing to innovate.

Last year, we introduced Microsoft Sovereign Cloud to give customers more choice in how they address these requirements. Since then, we have continued to turn our commitments into practical capabilities across public cloud and customer-operated environments, while expanding how we enable partners to address sovereignty requirements in their local markets. Today, we are sharing the next stage of that work.

A continuum of control, built around the workload

Microsoft Sovereign Cloud diagram showing a continuum of sovereignty solutions across three areas: Sovereign Public Cloud for control, data protection and regional requirements; Sovereign Private Cloud for critical workloads across connected and disconnected environments; and the Sovereign Partner Ecosystem for trusted, locally operated and specialized solutions.

Our approach to digital sovereignty starts with the workload. Each workload carries different requirements for data, operations, technology dependencies, continuity and risk. Microsoft Sovereign Cloud is designed to make it easier for organizations to apply the appropriate level of control to each workload without forcing every application into the same deployment model.

Those needs can vary widely across organizations. A public-facing digital service may benefit from the scale and pace of innovation in the public cloud. A system supporting essential operations may need to continue running locally if connectivity is disrupted. An AI workload handling highly sensitive data may require models, data and processing to remain within a customer-controlled environment.

Microsoft Sovereign Cloud is designed around this workload-based approach, providing a continuum of management, control and options across Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud and the Sovereign Partner Ecosystem. Organizations can apply the level of control appropriate to each workload while maintaining a consistent approach to governance and operations across their digital estate. Sovereign Public Cloud adds capabilities for workloads that require greater control and transparency while continuing to benefit from the scale and innovation of Azure.

Sovereign Private Cloud extends cloud capabilities into customer-operated environments, including connected and disconnected operations. The Sovereign Partner Ecosystem broadens the continuum through independently operated environments, specialized partners, locally relevant expertise and technologies that support customers’ sovereignty requirements.

These are not isolated destinations. Customers can combine public cloud, private cloud and partner capabilities across their digital estate, applying different levels of control to different workloads as their operating needs evolve.

Making control more visible in Sovereign Public Cloud

For many workloads, the public cloud provides a combination of scale, innovation, integrated security and compliance. Organizations can benefit from these capabilities while applying additional sovereignty controls for residency, confidentiality, operator access, policy and continuity. Our work in Sovereign Public Cloud makes these controls easier to understand, apply and demonstrate.

Sovereign Control Panel, entering public preview at Microsoft Ignite, brings these signals together in a unified Azure portal experience. It helps organizations understand their sovereignty posture, apply and manage controls, identify gaps and risks and take action to address them. It also supports business continuity readiness by helping customers understand workload dependencies and assess portability across operating environments when required.

This visibility complements controls across the operator-access lifecycle. Just-in-time Access and Customer Lockbox give customers additional control over access to their environments. For customers in the European Union (EU) and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), we are rolling out Data Guardian, which adds European-resident oversight by a trusted EU partner for qualifying Microsoft engineer remote access to in-scope production systems. Production Touch Ledger, also launched with phased rollout in the EU and EFTA, creates tamper-evident records of that access and the actions performed.

Azure Key Vault Managed Hardware Security Module (HSM) already gives customers dedicated, single-tenant protection and control over the encryption keys used by supported Azure services. Last year, we committed to extending that control beyond Microsoft infrastructure. External key management with Azure Managed HSM is now generally available, allowing customers to keep the root encryption key in hardware they own and operate on-premises or through a trusted third party. This gives organizations another option for workloads that require physical control of key hardware outside Microsoft infrastructure.

Azure confidential computing helps protect supported data while it is processed in a hardware-based and attested trusted execution environment. We are also increasing transparency into the technologies that underpin that trust. Azure Confidential Clean Rooms, now in limited preview, applies confidential computing to approved multiparty collaboration, allowing participants to analyze shared sensitive data while limiting broader exposure of the underlying information.

Together, these capabilities provide additional technical and operational controls that can support a broader digital sovereignty strategy aligned to an organization’s legal, policy, security, resilience and business requirements.

Designing for resilience and operational independence

For some workloads, digital sovereignty also means maintaining critical operations as connectivity, geopolitical and operating conditions change. Resilience must be designed from the start so essential workloads can continue operating through disruption.

To help customers prepare for these scenarios, we are publishing new sovereign business continuity guidance and architecture patterns. These resources help organizations translate resilience requirements into architectures they can plan, implement and test before they are needed.

For many workloads, the scale and geographic reach of the public cloud provide a strong foundation for resilience across locations and operating conditions. For workloads that require greater operational independence, Sovereign Private Cloud extends that continuum into customer-operated environments. It supports connected and disconnected operating models. The ability to transition workloads from connected to disconnected operations is entering public preview, giving organizations greater flexibility to sustain critical services as connectivity and operating requirements change.

Bringing more of the application lifecycle under local control

Operational independence requires more than infrastructure. Increasingly, organizations need data, development tools, model capabilities and productivity services their applications depend on to operate within the same customer-controlled environment.

Sovereign Private Cloud, built on Azure Local, extends Microsoft cloud capabilities into environments that customers operate and control. SQL Server on Azure Local is already generally available for connected and disconnected deployments. DocumentDB and Blob Storage on Azure Local are both entering public preview, giving organizations more choice in how they run and manage critical data within customer-controlled environments.

GitHub Enterprise Local will become generally available at Microsoft Ignite as a validated GitHub Enterprise Server appliance on Azure Local, helping organizations keep repositories, code and development artifacts under local control. Developers can also use GitHub Copilot with locally hosted models for inference, bringing AI-assisted development closer to their code and data within the environments they control.

The local application environment is expanding with Foundry Local. At Ignite, Foundry Local will become generally available for connected and disconnected operations on Azure Local, with an expanded model catalog that includes Microsoft, partner, open-weight and open-source models. Local inference and agentic retrieval will also enable users to interact with local enterprise data using natural language and receive responses grounded in that data. Integration with Microsoft 365 Local, available in preview for approved customers, extends this functionality to locally operated Microsoft SharePoint and Exchange servers.

Confidential virtual machines on Azure Local are generally available, extending confidential computing capabilities to customer-controlled infrastructure. Hardware-encrypted memory and hardware-based isolation help protect sensitive data while it is being processed. Workload attestation adds assurance before sensitive data or keys are released. For regulated, sensitive and mission-critical workloads, these safeguards provide another layer of protection while giving organizations greater control over where their data and applications run.

Azure Local will support multitenancy, allowing organizations to separate resources, governance and management across multiple tenants while sharing the underlying infrastructure. This significantly expands what customers with distinct business units or security boundaries can achieve with Sovereign Private Cloud. Multitenancy also creates new opportunities for local operators and service providers to deliver differentiated sovereign cloud services on Azure Local infrastructure.

These additions bring more of the application lifecycle under local control, spanning data, development, productivity, AI and operations. Organizations can determine what runs locally based on the requirements of each workload.

Extending the continuum through partners

Graphic titled “Sovereign Partner Ecosystem” with the subtitle “National clouds · Software · Services · Platform co-innovation,” showing 31 partner logos: Accenture, AMD, Armada, Avanade, base-it, Bleu, Capgemini, Cirrus Data, CloudCasa by Catalogic, Cronos Groep, cTelecoms, DataON, Delos Cloud, Dell Technologies, F5, Felo, Fortinet, HPE, Inspark, Intel, Mattermost, Mistral, NVIDIA, Qualidev, Qumulo, RiverMeadow, Rubrik, Supermicro, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Veeam and WSO2.

Navigating sovereignty is increasingly complex. Regulatory, security, operational and business requirements vary across countries, industries and workloads. Organizations must translate these needs into technology and operating models that work in their local context. Meeting these needs often requires a combination of technology, local operating authority, sector expertise and specialized solutions.

The Sovereign Partner Ecosystem broadens the ways customers can address these requirements. National Partner Clouds, including Bleu Cloud in France and Delos Cloud in Germany, provide independently operated environments for customers that require a different ownership and operating model. Software partners can enhance Azure Local environments with capabilities across security, identity, observability, backup and recovery, migration, data, networking and applications. Digital sovereignty specialized partners combine Microsoft technologies with local knowledge and implementation expertise. Platform co-innovation partners expand infrastructure choice from datacenter to the edge.

This ecosystem gives customers the flexibility to combine technology, operating models and trusted expertise based on the requirements of each workload.

The next chapter of digital sovereignty

AI is amplifying both the opportunity and the impact of technology choices. As AI systems and agents interact with sensitive data, business processes and essential infrastructure, they also expand the security considerations organizations need to manage. Organizations need clear control over where these systems run, who can operate them, what actions they can take and how critical services continue when conditions change.

Microsoft Sovereign Cloud brings these choices together as a continuum of control across the public cloud, customer-operated environments and our partner ecosystem. It gives organizations the flexibility to apply the appropriate level of control to each workload while continuing to benefit from cloud capabilities and ongoing innovation.

We will continue to expand this continuum so organizations can innovate with cloud and AI while maintaining the control, confidentiality, resilience and operational authority their most important workloads require.

Douglas Phillips leads global engineering efforts for Microsoft’s specialized, sovereign and private clouds. He is responsible for Microsoft’s global strategy, products and operations that bring Microsoft’s industry-leading solutions, including Azure, our adaptive cloud portfolio and Microsoft 365 collaboration suite, to customers with additional sovereignty, security, edge and compliance requirements.

Learn more

title: Designing for sovereign AI: A shared foundation from edge to cloud
author: Microsoft Azure
description:
As organizations apply AI to more business-critical and data-intensive workloads, AI processing is moving closer to where data is created, decisions are made, and operations take place.

Manufacturers can analyze confidential production data next to the systems that generate it.

Pharmaceutical companies can apply AI to clinical trials within controlled environments.

Government agencies can run AI applications on sensitive information while maintaining established security and operational bound...
article_content:
As organizations apply AI to more business-critical and data-intensive workloads, AI processing is moving closer to where data is created, decisions are made, and operations take place.

Manufacturers can analyze confidential production data next to the systems that generate it.

Pharmaceutical companies can apply AI to clinical trials within controlled environments.

Government agencies can run AI applications on sensitive information while maintaining established security and operational boundaries.

This shift reflects ongoing innovation across the technology ecosystem to give organizations greater flexibility in where they run AI and process sensitive data, and it is changing the  digital sovereignty  conversation. It now encompasses where data is stored and processed, where workloads run, who can access and operate the systems around them, and how those systems remain secure and operational as requirements change. The next phase of digital sovereignty will take shape across the technology ecosystem, through closer alignment among silicon, infrastructure, cloud, security, data, and AI.

Learn more about digital sovereignty

As AI extends into more sensitive and mission-critical workloads, sovereignty must be designed across the stack, from silicon and infrastructure to cloud, data, and AI. Microsoft and Intel® are working together to help organizations create a more consistent foundation for innovation, while retaining greater choice over where workloads run and how they are controlled.

A flexible sovereign architecture allows organizations to place each workload in the right environment, apply the controls it requires, and maintain a more consistent technology and operating foundation as requirements evolve.

Sovereignty must work across the technology stack

Sovereignty requirements vary by workload. The right level of control depends on factors such as data sensitivity, regulation, latency, connectivity, operational access, and resilience requirements. This creates a continuum, where organizations can apply different levels of control across public cloud, customer-controlled environments, and trusted partner solutions.

Delivering that flexibility requires the underlying technology layers to work together. The controls that shape where a workload runs, how data is protected, who can access it, and how the environment is verified extend across silicon, infrastructure, cloud, security, data, and AI.

This is where the Microsoft and Intel partnership comes into focus. Together, we are working to create a more consistent foundation across these layers, giving organizations greater choice in where workloads run and how they are controlled. This principle is central to the work between Microsoft and Intel.  Azure Local , running on Intel® Xeon® 6 processors, brings distributed Azure infrastructure together with a common compute foundation for customer-controlled environments. Organizations can extend cloud and AI capabilities closer to their data and operations while maintaining consistent approaches to security, management, and governance.

Trust must be designed for and verified

For sensitive workloads, trust must be supported by technical protections and verifiable evidence. Organizations need to protect workloads across the technology stack and verify that systems are operating under the security conditions they have established.

That starts at the compute layer and extends through identity, encryption, governance, policy, and operations. For supported  Azure Confidential VM  configurations, Intel® Xeon® processors provide hardware-based protections, including  Intel® Trust Domain Extensions (Intel TDX) , which can help isolate workloads while they are in use. Hardware-backed attestation can provide evidence that helps organizations verify relevant security properties of the environment against their requirements. Microsoft extends this foundation through security and governance controls across cloud and customer-controlled environments.

Together, these capabilities can help organizations verify relevant security properties of the environment against their requirements. This is particularly important as AI brings regulated, proprietary, and mission-critical data into new workloads.

Each workload should receive protections proportionate to its risk. Isolation, encryption, attestation, and operational controls can be applied where they provide meaningful value while preserving a manageable operating model across the broader environment.

Digital sovereignty requires trust across the technology stack. Together, Intel and Microsoft are combining hardware-based security and confidential computing with cloud, AI and distributed infrastructure to help customers protect sensitive workloads and verify the environments in which they run. This shared foundation gives organizations greater control, confidence and choice, with the performance and scale to continue innovating as AI moves into more regulated and mission-critical environments.

— Anand Pashupathy, Vice President and General Manager, Intel Product Assurance and Security

Sovereign AI brings intelligence closer to data

Much of the data with the greatest potential for AI must remain within defined operational, regulatory, or security boundaries. This includes data tied to industrial operations, government services, clinical environments, intellectual property, and proprietary research.

Workload placement has therefore become a practical AI decision. Organizations need the flexibility to run AI closer to their data, applications, and operations. Delivering that flexibility requires infrastructure, cloud platforms, AI software, and security capabilities to work as a connected foundation.

Microsoft Foundry  helps organizations build and deploy AI applications and models, with options for where AI runs based on their requirements.  Foundry Local  enables organizations to run AI inference in their own environments, closer to the data and applications those models rely on. On the same infrastructure, Intel Xeon 6 processors with Intel® Advanced Matrix Extensions (Intel AMX) can accelerate AI workloads directly on the CPU.  Intel® OpenVINO™  helps developers optimize and deploy models across supported infrastructure.

This approach extends across the broader application environment. Organizations may need to manage AI, applications, data, development, and productivity workloads within the same governance and operational boundary.  Microsoft 365 Local  and GitHub Enterprise Local extend customer-controlled options to collaboration, source code, and software development workflows.

Sovereign AI brings models, data, applications, development tools, and infrastructure together under the controls each workload requires. This approach allows organizations to apply AI within the operational and governance boundaries established for their most sensitive data.

Organizations want to apply AI to their most valuable data while maintaining the controls that data requires. On supported Azure confidential VM configurations, Intel TDX helps make that possible by running AI workloads in hardware-isolated trust domains, protecting models and data while in use and isolating them from the host and hypervisor. Hardware-backed attestation then gives organizations evidence they can check against their own requirements, so they can move from trusting their environment to verifying it.

—Anand Pashupathy, Vice President and General Manager, Intel Product Assurance and Security

Sovereignty architecture must be adaptable

Sovereignty requirements will continue to change. A workload that runs in a connected environment today may face different regulatory, resilience, or connectivity requirements tomorrow. AI models, applications, and infrastructure will also continue to evolve.

A sovereign architecture must therefore provide control without creating rigidity. Organizations should be able to adapt where workloads run, how they are secured, and how they connect without rebuilding their management and security model each time requirements change.

This is another reason partnership across the technology stack matters. Alignment across silicon, infrastructure, cloud, security, and AI software can give organizations a more stable foundation even as individual technologies and workload requirements evolve.

A well-designed sovereign architecture gives organizations room to respond as regulations, technologies, and operating conditions change.

Explore Microsoft Sovereign Cloud in Europe

Discover how Microsoft Sovereign Cloud in Europe helps organizations address evolving data sovereignty, security, and compliance requirements while accelerating cloud and AI innovation.

Learn more

Three questions leaders should ask

Digital sovereignty can become abstract quickly. A better place to start is the workload.

1. What must remain under your control?

Consider the data, infrastructure, administrative access, software operations, and connectivity on which the workload depends. The answer may differ by application, even within the same organization.

2. Can you verify that those controls are working?

Policies and contractual commitments are important, but sensitive workloads may also require technical evidence. Consider how your architecture supports encryption, isolation, identity and access control, policy enforcement, attestation, and operational transparency.

3. Will the architecture leave you room to adapt?

AI capabilities, regulations, operating conditions, and workload requirements will continue to change. Your architecture should allow you to adopt new models, move processing closer to data, and adjust where workloads run without creating an entirely separate technology environment each time.

Digital sovereignty depends on cloud, infrastructure, security, AI, and silicon working together. Our collaboration with Intel gives customers a more consistent foundation across these layers, so they can apply stronger controls where needed while retaining the flexibility to innovate.

—Bernardo Caldas, CVP, Azure Edge Product Management

The strongest sovereignty strategy preserves choice

Digital sovereignty should give organizations greater control over the technology and data they depend on while preserving their capacity to innovate.

Achieving that outcome requires collaboration across the technology ecosystem. Microsoft and Intel are connecting silicon, infrastructure, cloud, security, and AI to give organizations greater flexibility in where workloads run, how they are protected, and how they evolve.

A shared foundation across these layers allows organizations to apply the right controls to each workload and benefit from advances across the broader technology ecosystem.

A strong sovereignty strategy meets today’s requirements while preserving tomorrow’s options.

Resources to learn more

Dive deeper into digital sovereignty  to learn how Microsoft is helping organizations address data residency, operational control, security, and regulatory requirements across cloud and customer-controlled environments.

Learn more about Microsoft Sovereign Private Cloud .

Join us at Microsoft Ignite  in November to hear the latest on  Microsoft Sovereign Cloud,  Azure Local, AI, security, and infrastructure innovation.

Azure Local

Learn how organizations can run distributed infrastructure and applications with a consistent Azure experience

title: Managing open-weight model risk in enterprise deployments
author: Microsoft Azure
description:
The growing AI landscape is giving enterprises more choice in how they build, customize, and deploy increasingly capable models. Open-weight models are an important part of that landscape. They give enterprises access to model weights and greater flexibility to inspect, evaluate, modify, and run models within their own environments.

While that flexibility can be valuable, it also affects how enterprises evaluate models, where they implement safeguards, and who is responsible for maintaining tho...
article_content:
The growing AI landscape is giving enterprises more choice in how they build, customize, and deploy increasingly capable models. Open-weight models are an important part of that landscape. They give enterprises access to model weights and greater flexibility to inspect, evaluate, modify, and run models within their own environments.

While that flexibility can be valuable, it also affects how enterprises evaluate models, where they implement safeguards, and who is responsible for maintaining those safeguards over time.

As enterprises choose which models to deploy, the relevant question is broader than whether a model is open-weight or closed-weight. Enterprises need to understand what they are using the model for, what could go wrong in that context, and what evidence and controls they need to manage risks.

Today, Microsoft and NVIDIA are publishing Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise, the first in a planned series of joint resources intended to help enterprises address those questions. The paper introduces a shared risk taxonomy and an approach to managing model risks grounded in established standards and frameworks, including International Organization for Standardization (ISO) standards and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) AI Risk Management Framework.

The paper reflects a core idea: weight openness alone does not determine an AI system’s risk. Risk depends on the model, use case, deployment, and safeguards.

Read the whitepaper: Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise

Understanding risk in the deployment context

Open- and closed-weight models can share many of the same underlying risks, but how those risks materialize depends on the deployment. A model used to help an employee draft a document presents different considerations than the same model used in a customer-facing workflow, just as a standalone inference endpoint differs from a system connected to external data or tools.

The architecture matters too. A risk may originate in the model, while the most effective control may sit in the inference environment, application, or surrounding operational processes. The joint guidance looks beyond the model label to factors including provenance, intended use, users, deployment conditions, and surrounding controls. This first paper focuses primarily on model-layer risks. Evaluating a model alone does not establish the safety of an agent or application: teams must also assess its permissions, data access, tools, runtime, and operational controls.

Establishing a common language

Managing these risks consistently also requires a common vocabulary across engineering, security, legal, safety, and business teams.

The initial Microsoft and NVIDIA taxonomy organizes risks into five broad categories: Cybersecurity, Data Protection, Content, Human-AI Interaction, and Bias. It is not a policy or deployment checklist, but instead it should be used by enterprises to adapt it to their own systems, use cases, and risk criteria, then connect relevant risks to evaluations, mitigations, and accountable owners.

Using evaluations as risk evidence

Evaluations help turn the taxonomy into something enterprises can use. The paper maps evaluations to a selection of risks across the five categories, giving teams a way to start with a risk that matters for their deployment and identify evaluations that can produce relevant evidence about it.

Microsoft Foundry helps enterprises assess quality, groundedness, and safety with built-in and custom evaluations and automated red teaming. Its configurable content-safety controls help detect and mitigate harmful inputs and outputs and prompt attacks. Teams should validate control availability for their model and deployment, including preview status, and combine these capabilities with application-specific testing, monitoring, and human oversight.

Evaluations still need to be interpreted in the context of a particular deployment and the goal is to make it easier for teams to connect the risks they identify with useful evidence, while building a broader set of evaluation resources that can evolve alongside models, deployment patterns, and emerging risks. Microsoft and NVIDIA plan to use the joint repository to share additional evaluations and point to existing resources that can help enterprises assess specific risks.

Accounting for changes in control and responsibility

Open-weight access gives enterprises greater control over how a model is evaluated, modified, and deployed. Model access and deployment are separate choices: open-weight models can also be used through managed platforms. Responsibility for safeguards depends on the service and deployment configuration; enterprises that operate their own model deployments may take on controls otherwise provided by a managed service.

Those safeguards can operate at different layers, and (depending on the risk) enterprises might use model changes, access controls, input and output filtering, monitoring, or human review. The important step is connecting each identified risk to controls that can effectively address it within the deployed system. Those decisions need to be revisited as models and deployments change.

Building on this work

Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise focuses primarily on the model layer. Future work from Microsoft and NVIDIA is intended to extend this approach across the runtime, harness, and application layers, with additional technical guidance on evaluation and mitigation.

We also expect the resources supporting this work to evolve as new models, evaluations, and deployment patterns emerge. The joint repository will provide a place to share additional evaluation resources, including contributions from the broader community.

For enterprises deploying open-weight models today, the paper provides guidance they can begin applying to their own use cases. We encourage developers, security practitioners, researchers, and others working in this space to read the paper, explore the evaluations, and contribute evaluations that can help strengthen this shared body of work.

Read the joint Microsoft-NVIDIA paper, Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise.

Explore the joint repository and technical resources.

Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise was developed jointly by Microsoft and NVIDIA, with Andrew Berkley and April Chen of Microsoft and Michael Boone, Eileen Long, and Arun Rao of NVIDIA leading the development and editing of the paper.

Explore Microsoft Foundry evaluations and content-safety controls for implementation guidance.

To learn more about Microsoft Security solutions, visit our website. Bookmark the Security blog to keep up with our expert coverage on security matters. Also, follow us on LinkedIn (Microsoft Security) and X (@MSFTSecurity) for the latest news and updates on cybersecurity.

title: Evolving the cloud-native foundation for the next generation of AI
author: Microsoft Azure
description:
Building a cloud-native foundation for AI

The relationship between model innovation and AI infrastructure has never been more clear; as AI becomes more capable, the platform underneath it matters even more. Agents are fundamentally changing how applications work, and with that, what organizations need from the cloud.

Learn how to build a cloud-native AI foundation

Cloud-native practices gave organizations the scale, flexibility and resilience  to build a generation of distributed applications...
article_content:
Building a cloud-native foundation for AI

The relationship between model innovation and AI infrastructure has never been more clear; as AI becomes more capable, the platform underneath it matters even more. Agents are fundamentally changing how applications work, and with that, what organizations need from the cloud.

Learn how to build a cloud-native AI foundation

Cloud-native practices gave organizations the scale, flexibility and resilience  to build a generation of distributed applications. Agents build on that foundation, but they work differently, placing new demands on it. Unlike applications designed around more predictable workflows,  agents behave in entirely new ways, gathering information and deep intelligence from across the business , using tools, making decisions, and coordinating work across long-running processes. To complete complex tasks, they pause for approval, respond to new information in real time and change course as conditions evolve. All this changes what the platform needs to deliver.

Customers need infrastructure that adapts as demand changes, applications that remain reliable as work becomes more dynamic, and the visibility and control to understand what is happening across the system. Meeting those needs doesn’t mean starting over, but it does require that the cloud-native foundation organizations already rely on, to evolve.  Compute, storage and networking need to work together . Application platforms need to make it easier to build and run AI workloads. Open technologies need to give customers flexibility without adding unnecessary complexity.

The platform decisions organizations make today are increasingly strategic, shaping how effectively they can put AI to work for their business. Evolving the cloud-native foundation is essential to helping organizations get more from AI today while giving them the flexibility to take advantage of new capabilities as they emerge.

Optimize infrastructure for AI workloads

The true measure of AI infrastructure is the useful work it enables. AI workloads rarely place the same demands on infrastructure from beginning to end.  Different parts of the work may need accelerated compute, CPUs, fast access to data or connectivity  across applications and environments. The answer isn’t simply more capacity, but rather, to  match the right resources to the right work at the right time .

That makes coordination across the infrastructure extremely important. Compute, storage and networking need to work together as demands change. When they do, teams can spend less time managing infrastructure and more time focused on the applications and outcomes that matter to their business.

Economics matter, too. Infrastructure needs to be tuned to the demands of the application and the business value it delivers,  with the right balance of performance, reliability and cost  across the complete workload.

Basecamp Research  is one example. The company used Azure to assemble 9.7 trillion nucleotides for EDEN, its therapeutic-design models, and reported laboratory validation across three therapeutic applications within about three weeks. In this example, AI didn’t simply require more infrastructure, it needed AI infrastructure that was coordinated and designed around the outcome – bringing together the compute, data and platform capabilities needed to move complex work forward.

As Glen Gowers, co-founder of Basecamp Research put it: “To really be successful here, we need those three ingredients to come together. We need someone scaling the data; that’s us. But someone who really knows how to scale models and scale compute is Microsoft.”

Leadership takeaway: Measure success by the useful work AI completes. Judge infrastructure investment by the performance, reliability and cost of delivering those outcomes, with compute, storage and networking operating as one system.

Turn open-source innovation into production capability

Open technologies have long helped drive cloud innovation, and AI is accelerating that pace. New models, frameworks and cloud-native technologies give organizations more choice in how they build and adapt applications.

That opportunity builds on an established cloud-native foundation. Gartner forecasts that by 2028, 95% of new AI agent deployment will use Kubernetes. 1  Reusing established components can shorten the path to production, allowing developers to focus on differentiated business capabilities rather than rebuilding the foundation.

More choice can also bring more complexity. Taking advantage of open-source innovation often requires specialized expertise to integrate, manage and maintain technologies in production. That expertise is hard to find and even harder to scale. We need to make these capabilities accessible to more businesses, without requiring every organization to build and maintain that expertise themselves.

Azure helps reduce that burden. Services like  Azure Kubernetes Service  give teams access to open-source innovation while helping manage the complexity and risk of running it in production. This makes it easier for more businesses to take advantage of open technologies while preserving the flexibility to adapt with changing needs.

Leadership takeaway: Choose a platform that helps turn open-source freedom into business advantage.  Preserve the ability to adapt and optimize while reducing the expertise and operating effort  required to sustain those choices in production.

Align AI infrastructure costs with business value

As more organizations put AI into production, understanding the economics becomes increasingly important. AI investment starts with an expectation of business value: faster decisions, more responsive services or greater capacity to get useful work done. Then, it’s evaluating whether the value justifies the investment to deliver it.  FinOps  can help teams understand that return and make more informed decisions in this area.

For customers, that starts with understanding the full investment required to run AI applications and how to optimize it as workloads scale. Models represent a significant expense, with token usage and agent behavior influencing spending. Compute, storage, networking and operations also factor into the equation. Considering these together helps customers make more informed decisions about where to optimize.

Learn FinOps best practices for compute

Teams can’t simply place their bets on spending less. They need to carefully consider that a more capable model or additional infrastructure that costs more may be the right choice if it produces greater value long-term. Teams need to understand the full cost, establish ownership and put guardrails in place as they scale. From there, they can use business outcomes to decide where to optimize and where to invest.

Leadership takeaway: Manage AI investment against the business return it needs to deliver. Evaluate model and platform costs together, then use evidence of outcome value to decide where to optimize and where to invest.

Transform cloud operations with agentic AI

Operations teams are already stretched thin, keeping critical services running while balancing competing priorities and constant change. AI adds new complexity, and it also creates an opportunity to change how those environments are managed.

Cloud-native operations gave teams a new model for managing infrastructure, bringing increased automation, visibility and resilience.  Agentic operations build on that foundation , bringing deeper intelligence across applications and infrastructure by connecting signals from otherwise disconnected systems. This helps teams identify issues earlier and resolve them faster, while increasing automation and continuously improving how their environments perform; all within the tools they already use.

Over time, AI can help operations teams move from reacting to problems toward anticipating and addressing them before they disrupt the business. As these capabilities mature, more actions can be automated within defined controls, with people remaining in the loop and accountable for critical decisions. When operations teams have greater reach without additional manual effort, reliability, performance and cost are continuously improved while critical services remain uninterrupted.

Leadership takeaway: Invest in operations that can anticipate problems and coordinate action across the environment. Expand autonomy as capabilities are validated, with clear controls and human accountability protecting critical business services.

Automate operations with Azure SRE Agent

Build a cloud-native AI foundation on Azure

Azure serves as the foundation customers need to put AI to work at scale. That means infrastructure designed around the complete workload, access to open innovation without unnecessary complexity, and a clear view of cost and business value. Greater intelligence across cloud operations helps teams anticipate issues and continuously improve how their environments perform as application needs evolve.

We’re continuing to invest in capabilities across Azure  that give customers greater flexibility in how they build and run AI applications. From  secure, isolated environments for agents  to simpler application deployment and the ability to run workloads across cloud and edge environments, these investments help customers take advantage of new capabilities without adding unnecessary operational complexity.

Get started with Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)

AI is changing what applications can do, and Azure has already evolved to support that shift. The cloud platform has to evolve with them. Years of focused engineering investment have built the foundation for some of the most advanced AI workloads running today, with continued innovation to support what comes next.

Build for the next generation of AI

Platform value compounds when improvements reinforce one another: faster information access keeps compute productive, operational insight exposes waste, and open technologies preserve room to adapt. The leadership task is to make those gains work together. That is the next chapter of cloud native: a foundation that turns advances in AI into dependable business value.

To learn more about the recent Azure innovations and how Azure is evolving the cloud-native foundation for AI applications and agents, explore:

Flex Nodes for AKS

Azure SRE Agent

Azure Container Apps Sandboxes

Azure Container Apps Express

Explore what this means for your organization.  Register for our upcoming discovery session  to learn how to put a cloud-native foundation for AI applications and agents into practice.

Build your AI foundation

Learn how to put a cloud-native foundation for AI applications and agents into practice in our upcoming discovery session.

author: Microsoft Azure

article_content:
We’re proud to share that Microsoft has been named a  Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Server Virtualization Platforms . We believe this recognition comes at an important moment for enterprise infrastructure. The question is no longer simply which hypervisor to run. It is how to create a consistent operating model across cloud, datacenter, edge, and sovereign environments. Microsoft addresses that challenge at two levels: operational consistency through Azure and  Azure Arc , and infrastructure consistency through  Hyper-V .

Read the report

From choosing a hypervisor to choosing an operating model

For years, the primary virtualization decision was which hypervisor to run. Today, the more consequential decision is how infrastructure will be operated across every environment the business depends on. Virtualization remains a critical foundation, but the value of the platform increasingly depends on how infrastructure is managed, governed, secured, updated, and connected across environments. As infrastructure becomes more distributed, how it is operated becomes as important as where it runs.

Microsoft delivers that consistency at two complementary levels:

Operational consistency:  Azure provides common management, governance, and security across cloud, datacenter, and edge environments. Azure Arc extends those capabilities to distributed infrastructure, giving organizations a unified way to operate diverse environments.

Infrastructure consistency:  Hyper-V provides a common virtualization foundation across Azure, Azure Local, and  Windows Server , helping organizations maintain a consistent infrastructure layer wherever workloads run.

Together, these layers help organizations preserve choice without multiplying operational models. Workloads can move, environments can evolve, and new technologies can be adopted without requiring a separate operating model for every environment.

Ready for what comes next

Operational and infrastructure consistency will become even more important as AI reshapes enterprise IT. Models, agents, applications, and data will increasingly span cloud, datacenter, edge, and sovereign environments. AI alone will not reduce the complexity of distributed infrastructure; in many cases, it will increase the need for common management, governance, security, and infrastructure foundations.

Being named a Leader in this Magic Quadrant is an honor for us. More importantly, we believe it reflects a direction many organizations are pursuing: operational consistency across increasingly distributed environments. We remain committed to helping customers combine the flexibility to run workloads where they choose with the consistency required to manage them as one environment.

Recognized as a Leader

title: Advancing hardware security with open-source Integrated HSM technology
author: Microsoft Azure
description:
At this year’s  OCP Global Summit , Microsoft announced Project Tessera, the evolution of the  Azure Integrated Hardware Security Module (HSM),  into a fully open-source initiative developed in collaboration with Marvell®, Oracle, and  Open Compute Project (OCP) . Project Tessera advances our broader commitment to open, industrywide standards for platform security.

The motivation behind Project Tessera is straightforward: the entire industry benefits when we collaborate and advance hardware sec...
article_content:
At this year’s  OCP Global Summit , Microsoft announced Project Tessera, the evolution of the  Azure Integrated Hardware Security Module (HSM),  into a fully open-source initiative developed in collaboration with Marvell®, Oracle, and  Open Compute Project (OCP) . Project Tessera advances our broader commitment to open, industrywide standards for platform security.

The motivation behind Project Tessera is straightforward: the entire industry benefits when we collaborate and advance hardware security together.

Project Tessera carries forward the workload directly attached to the HSM architecture introduced by Azure Integrated HSM,  making the architecture, specifications, protocols, drivers, software, firmware, and reproducible build environments open source  for the broader community. Over time, the initiative will advance toward a fully open-source silicon implementation, while making hardware broadly available, enabling organizations across the ecosystem to adopt, integrate, and contribute to the platform.

Explore the Tessera Integrated HSM GitHub

This approach builds on the model Microsoft established with other industry collaborators on  Caliptra , a fully open-source  silicon root-of-trust that has since been broadly adopted  across the hardware ecosystem. Through Project Tessera, industry leaders including Microsoft, Marvell®, Oracle, and the Open Compute Project will apply that same model of transparency and collaboration to advance hardware key protection with the industry.

The cybersecurity landscape is rapidly changing, and protecting keys and credentials has never been more important. We are now facing two generational transformations that are fundamentally reshaping how we view the cybersecurity landscape:

AI is increasing the speed and scale of cyberattacks

AI-orchestrated attacks are increasing the scale, speed, and sophistication of attacks, giving adversaries new ways to operate and compressing the time between vulnerability discovery and exploitation. These capabilities amplify risks such as credential theft, key exfiltration, and signing abuse.

Keys and credentials are high-value control assets . When compromised, they can enable attackers to impersonate trusted entities, bypass security controls, authorize malicious operations, expose sensitive data, and undermine software security defenses. Protecting these assets requires infrastructure with layered, hardened protections capable of withstanding sustained attacks across multiple concurrent attack vectors.

Quantum computing is changing the cryptographic risk horizon

Quantum computing promises transformative advances, but it also presents a risk to many of today’s cryptographic algorithms.  A sufficiently powerful quantum computer could break widely used public-key cryptography , undermining digital signatures, authentication, and identity verification.

Post-quantum cryptography was once viewed as an important but distant technology shift. Advances in quantum computing have changed that perspective as organizations recognize the urgency, scale, and complexity of the transition.  HSM-backed signing infrastructure will be among the first critical systems to migrate , requiring HSMs that support post-quantum cryptography and are interoperable with classical HSMs to support migration.

These emerging threats motivated the development of  Azure Integrated HSM , which was designed to meet rigorous security standards for hardware-based key protection, while also accelerating Microsoft’s transition to post-quantum cryptography through scale deployments of quantum resilient integrated HSMs.

Azure Integrated HSM  introduced a workload-attached HSM that performs cryptographic operations closer to the workload while keys remain continuously protected within the HSM security boundary. This architecture strengthens key protection, improves cryptographic performance, offers crypto-agility, and provides a simpler operational model.

Tessera is an evolution of Azure’s first integrated HSM model, incorporating insights gained from deploying Azure Integrated HSM at scale, and advances the technology through collaboration in the Open Compute Project, with the goal of broadly addressing the challenges of key and credential management in the era of AI and quantum computing.

Eliminating key management anti-patterns

In central HSM deployment models, HSM infrastructure is separate from compute resources, requiring cryptographic operations to traverse the network. The resulting latency and operational dependencies can lead enterprises to adopt workarounds that improve performance or availability but unintentionally weaken key protections. Some of these common key-management anti-patterns include:

HSM keys may act as certificate authorities and endorse externally generated keys. These keys can then serve as trusted delegates without receiving the same hardware protection.

HSM generated keys may be created as extractable and exported from the HSM in wrapped form.  When used outside of the HSM the keys may not receive assurance levels equivalent to a FIPS 140-3 Level 3 HSM and become more susceptible to exfiltration or misuse.

Other anti-patterns include caching keys outside of HSMs for resilience, using software-held keys to reduce network latency to remote HSMs, sharing keys and security domains to simplify governance, and relying on proprietary protocols for interoperability.  These practices intend to prioritize operational flexibility but can make key protection, policy enforcement, and auditable provenance less consistent across environments, undermining the security value HSMs are designed to provide.

The goal of Project Tessera is to advance the integrated HSM model to address these challenges in the industry, without compromising on security. The project will deliver Tessera Integrated HSM, a fully open-source integrated HSM designed to consistently enforce FIPS 140-3 Level 3 key protection throughout the key’s lifecycle.

By combining strong hardware-rooted protection with an open-source implementation and open protocols, Tessera Integrated HSM creates a path toward greater transparency, interoperability, and  innovation across the HSM ecosystem . The native support for quantum-resilient cryptography will help ease the industry’s transition to post-quantum cryptography.

Figure 1: Tessera Integrated HSM

Demonstrating an open, interoperable HSM ecosystem

Today at the Open Compute Project Global Summit, Microsoft and Marvell® demonstrated the Tessera Integrated HSM transfer protocols establishing HSM partition cloning and resiliency rings across a Tessera Integrated HSM and a Marvell® LiquidSecurity® 2 HSM. The demonstration showed how two heterogeneous HSMs can operate in a resilient and unified security domain. Non-extractable keys within the security domain always remain protected within the HSMs and are available only to the authorized HSM partitions participating in the security domain and remain under the sole control of the partition owner.

The Tessera Integrated HSM protocols use post-quantum cryptography to protect communication between HSMs. This enables authorized workloads with a Tessera Integrated HSM to use both classical cryptography and post-quantum cryptographic services while their keys remain secured within the HSM boundary and can only be authorized for use by the key owner.

Figure 2: Partition cloning example

The Project Tessera specifications, protocols, software libraries, drivers, firmware, and hardware are available through the  Tessera Integrated HSM GitHub . Going forward, this repository will add more open-source silicon, new hardware designs, and enhancements developed with the community.

Expanding Project Tessera through confidential computing

The early collaborators working on Project Tessera within the OCP community are exploring how the Tessera Integrated HSM key protection architecture can extend beyond systems with dedicated integrated HSM hardware. As part of this work, the project is making a minimal, unikernel-based Tessera firmware stack open source, designed to run within hardware-isolated  confidential computing environments .

This implementation uses the same firmware stack as the hardware integrated HSM, extending a common security architecture across HSMs and confidential computing environments. In this model, cryptographic keys are protected within a confidential computing container, which provides cryptographic services to securely bound workloads, including worker containers and virtual machines. The initial implementation leverages AMD SEV-SNP and integrates with open-source virtualization technologies such as  OpenVMM , with the Open Compute community working to extend support to other confidential computing architectures.

The complementary deployment models in Project Tessera extend strong key protection across systems with different hardware capabilities and assurance requirements. For platforms without dedicated integrated HSM hardware, confidential computing provides broadly deployable, hardware-isolated key protection with a minimal trusted computing base.

Project Tessera provides the highest level of hardware assurance, protecting keys within a dedicated, tamper-resistant security boundary designed to meet demanding certification requirements, including FIPS 140-3 Level 3 and Common Criteria.

Figure 3: Protection profiles for assurance levels

The deployment models share the same Project Tessera firmware and programming model, giving organizations a consistent foundation for cryptographic security across their infrastructure while providing a natural path to integrated HSM and higher levels of assurance in newer systems.

Together, these models make strong key protection accessible across a broad range of systems with different security assurance needs, all built on a common, open architecture. As the Open Compute Project community continues to advance Tessera Integrated HSM, we see an exciting opportunity for broader industry collaboration to strengthen key protection, expand secure key management, and accelerate innovation across the ecosystem.

Explore the Tessera Integrated HSM GitHub

For more information, visit the Microsoft booth at the Open Compute Project Global Summit for live demonstrations,  explore Tessera Integrated HSM implementation on GitHub , and read the Microsoft Infrastructure Community blog for additional hardware security announcements:  OCP2026 Hardware Security Updates .

Check out Microsoft’s presence at OCP Summit this year:  aka.ms/OCP2026

Learn more about Azure Infrastructure:  aka.ms/silicontosystems

title: Infrastructure for the frontier era: Scaling intelligence through open industry collaboration
author: Microsoft Azure
description:
At Microsoft, our vision is to build a  Frontier Firm : one where people and technology work together, combining human expertise, context, and judgment with technology that can extend intelligence throughout everyday work. The potential is significant: helping people create, solve complex problems, and make progress on some of society’s most consequential challenges.

But realizing that potential requires frontier infrastructure . The next phase of Super Intelligence needs a unified infrastructu...
article_content:
At Microsoft, our vision is to build a  Frontier Firm : one where people and technology work together, combining human expertise, context, and judgment with technology that can extend intelligence throughout everyday work. The potential is significant: helping people create, solve complex problems, and make progress on some of society’s most consequential challenges.

But realizing that potential requires frontier infrastructure . The next phase of Super Intelligence needs a unified infrastructure engine that delivers more intelligence with greater efficiency, making AI more available, reliable, and sustainable across science, healthcare, education, and the economy. This is the work of an entire ecosystem, and precisely the vision we have advanced for years through our industry collaboration within the Open Compute Project Foundation.

Designing silicon in the loop with real workloads

As we enter the next phase of Super Intelligence, inference is becoming the dominant workload and that’s where efficiency, latency, and cost really matter.  Azure Maia 300 , our next generation AI accelerator from our Maia family, advances the inference efficiency frontier. Maia 300 is a complete system designed for the new types of AI workloads emerging today: long-context reasoning, latency-sensitive conversational experiences, and sustained, multi-step agentic tasks. By improving efficiency across the system, we expect Maia 300 to deliver 40% more tokens per watt compared to leading GPU-based systems. And in a full 96-accelerator configuration, it delivers up to seven times the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200.

Learn more about Maia 300

Maia  reflects our system co-design approach. It is designed alongside Microsoft infrastructure and production workloads, bringing models, application frameworks, kernels, communication libraries, systems software, and custom silicon into one optimization loop. Maia 200 is deploying across the United States, Europe and Australia and delivering up to 1.7x more tokens per watt for built-in AI capabilities in Microsoft Teams,  Copilot  and Cowork experiences compared with leading GPU infrastructure.

Azure Maia 200 systems in a datacenter

AI is not only about accelerators. Agentic workloads create entirely new demands on CPUs. Every agent interaction generates orchestration, data retrieval, memory management, and service calls that must occur quickly and efficiently. That is why we designed Cobalt 200 as an agent-native CPU.  Cobalt 200  delivers more than 50% performance improvement over Cobalt 100 and reduces agent call latency by 33%, while providing 23% higher throughput on agentic workloads.

Azure Cobalt 200 systems in a datacenter

Maia and Cobalt are designed in the loop  with our largest enterprise workloads. That gives Microsoft a unique advantage in tuning performance, reliability, and cost to exactly what customers need in production.

We are applying the same principle to storage and security. The  Azure Boost Data Processing Unit  moves compression, networking transactions, and security functions away from the CPU onto purpose-built silicon, enabling us to deliver four times more performance while using significantly less power.

And  Azure Integrated HSM  makes security part of the hardware foundation, with our in-house security chip in all new datacenter servers. It brings cryptographic operations closer to the workload while keeping keys protected inside the hardware security boundary—not exposed in application memory.

Building an open, resilient AI fabric

Compute creates intelligence  and networks make it usable at scale.

Working with industry partners, Microsoft developed  Multipath Reliable Connection (MRC) , rethinking Ethernet for AI. Its multi-plane architecture scales beyond 100,000 GPUs with two network tiers, reducing power, complexity, failure points, and cost. By intelligently distributing traffic across multiple paths and through packet spraying, MRC limits congestion and maintains reliable performance for frontier-scale training.

We are also advancing open scale-up connectivity through Optical Compute Interconnect Multi-Source Agreement ( OCI MSA ). OCI, the first optical specification for multi-rack scale-up systems, enables high-bandwidth, power-efficient, multi-vendor infrastructure. Moving forward, we will continue to work with the industry to expand participation in OCI MSA.

In parallel, The  Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking  (ESUN) workstream brings together more than 175 organizations to define requirements for Ethernet-based scale-up networking. The group has released specification version 1.0 and is developing version 1.1 for later this year. Read more about our  networking innovations with the open community .

Rethinking power from grid to silicon

AI infrastructure is also forcing a fundamental redesign of power delivery. Through OCP and the Open Systems for AI initiative, Microsoft is helping  advance the industry’s transition  toward 800 volt direct current (VDC) infrastructure.

Mt. Diablo, Microsoft’s disaggregated high-voltage datacenter (DC) sidecar architecture, separates power conversion from the compute rack so each can scale independently. It includes a modular design supporting approximately 100 kilowatts (kW) to beyond one megawatt (MW), with redundant feeds, telemetry and optional energy storage. Microsoft, together with OCP partners, contributed Mt. Diablo specifications v0.7 and v1.0 to OCP.

Microsoft and its partners are advancing solid-state transformer-based architectures to make power conversion more efficient, responsive, and scalable for next-generation 800 VDC datacenters. Through OCP’s Clean Backup Power initiative, we are developing open requirements for reliable backup systems that reduce reliance on diesel. In parallel, Microsoft collaborated with partners to release a common grid-interface specification to align utilities, operators, and equipment vendors as hyperscale power architectures evolve. Read more about  Microsoft’s approach to 800VDC transition and scaling power infrastructure sustainably .

Cooling as a first-class design consideration

Microsoft approaches cooling as a datacenter-wide challenge, driving innovation from DC facility design to rack-level liquid cooling technologies.

Our third-generation Azure Heat Exchanger Unit, Mt. Atlas, nearly doubles cooling capacity compared to the previous generation while maintaining the same operational footprint. We are also contributing public reference architecture through OCP to help accelerate industry adoption.

At the datacenter level, Microsoft is advancing a  zonal cooling  strategy in its next-generation AI datacenters to handle the growing mix of liquid-cooled accelerators and traditional air-cooled systems .  By tailoring cooling to the specific needs of each workload, and introducing multiple independent water loops, each supplying coolant at different temperatures, we aim to increase efficiency and performance while supporting Microsoft’s energy, carbon, and water reduction goals.

Open hardware security innovation

Microsoft believes strong cloud security is built through openness , transparency, and industry collaboration. This principle is reflected in  our founding role in the Confidential Computing Consortium , our work to establish Caliptra as an open-source silicon root of trust, and our contributions to the OCP S.A.F.E. security conformance framework. As AI reshapes the cybersecurity landscape and advances in quantum computing introduce new cryptographic risks, protecting the keys and credentials at the foundation of digital trust has never been more important.

To address these challenges, and building on our commitment to security transparency and industry collaboration, Microsoft, Marvell, and Oracle are introducing  Tessera Integrated HSM , an open-source initiative for integrated hardware security modules. Tessera Integrated HSM carries forward the workload direct attached HSM architecture introduced by Azure Integrated HSM,  open-sourcing  its architecture, specifications, protocols, drivers, software, firmware, and silicon to the broader community.  Learn more about Tessera Integrated HSM .

Fleet resiliency at scale

As AI infrastructure scales, fleet reliability is essential to protecting customer workloads, capacity, and service quality. Through OCP, Microsoft has published common RAS, debugging, telemetry, and diagnostics specifications, while contributing work on hardware fault management, CPU and GPU management, and fleet memory fault management. We are using years of fleet data and using AI to validate, predict, and drive fleet actions aimed at preventing faults, pinpointing issues, and recovering more autonomously. Learn more about how  Microsoft is advancing fleet reliability through industry collaboration .

Advancing sustainability across the infrastructure stack

Scaling AI responsibly means considering the full datacenter lifecycle to help reach our 2030 commitments to be carbon negative, water positive, and zero waste. As a company, we are committed to incorporating sustainability into how we design, build, and operate our datacenters extending to the communities where we build them. Through OCP, Microsoft is collaborating with partners on low-embodied-carbon steel and concrete—with pathways to reduce concrete emissions by more than 50% per cubic yard.

We are advancing waste-heat reuse, and helping develop Cloud Services Product Category Rules for consistent, auditable lifecycle-carbon reporting. Inside our datacenters, closed-loop liquid cooling, intelligent power management, and renewable-energy agreements help reduce resource use, while Circular Centers reuse or recycle more than 90% of servers and components. Beyond the datacenter, we are investing in local skills, partnerships, and infrastructure so the communities hosting this growth can grow with us.  Read Microsoft’s 2026 Environmental Sustainability report .

Building the frontier together

Our vision is to help every organization become a Frontier Firm, uniting human expertise with AI in a continuous learning loop that turns knowledge and ingenuity into scalable intelligence. Realizing that vision requires full-stack co-design: silicon, compute, memory, networking, power, cooling, models, and applications working as one secure, reliable, efficient, and sustainable platform while giving customers choice without passing complexity on to them.

Such a future cannot be realized by a single organization. Through OCP, we are advancing open interfaces, sharing lessons from operating infrastructure at global scale, and collaborating across the industry so innovation moves faster, and the ecosystem stops solving the same problems repeatedly. Together, we can transform frontier innovation into infrastructure that makes intelligence accessible and affordable for every organization, in every industry, and across every region of the world.

At OCP Global Summit 2026, we invite the community to build that future with us.

Build for what’s next

Learn more about Microsoft’s systems approach to infrastructure.

Start here

author: AWS Architecture Blog
