article_content:
When your food-ordering platform doubles its brand count, dedicated clusters become your biggest cost problem, and every failed request during a traffic surge is a lost sale.

Here is how Cognizant and AWS Professional Services solved it.

Cognizant is a global services company that helps organizations modernize technology, reimagine processes, and transform customer experiences. Its OrderServ service is an omnichannel ordering solution for the food services industry that supports ordering across devices and integrates with point-of-sale, kitchen display, payment, loyalty, and other enterprise systems. Cognizant is an AWS Premier Tier Services Partner with multiple AWS Competencies and a member of the AWS Managed Service Provider (MSP) and AWS Well-Architected Partner Programs.

In 2022, Cognizant published how OrderServ 2.0 reimagined digital food ordering by migrating from a monolith to microservices on AWS Fargate, achieving 30 percent cost savings over traditional hosted architectures.

Since then, the service grew from serving a single quick-service restaurant (QSR) brand to powering multiple brands across markets. Each brand ran as a dedicated Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with 21 microservices. This provided hard isolation, but cost scaled linearly with every brand onboarded, and scaling speed could not keep up with promotional traffic surges that spike 5–10× within minutes.

In this post, we describe how AWS Professional Services partnered with Cognizant to transform OrderServ into a multi-tenant software as a service (SaaS) offering, achieving 47–64 percent compute cost reduction, scaling time reduced from 5–7 minutes to 30–60 seconds, and authentication costs cut by 80 percent.

The problem: Dedicated clusters don’t scale with brands

OrderServ 2.0 ran 21 microservices per brand on dedicated AWS Fargate clusters. For five brands, this meant:

  • 105 ECS services (21 × 5), each with idle capacity during off-peak hours.
  • 315 sidecar containers for observability, configuration, and log routing, duplicated per brand.
  • Linear cost growth, because onboarding a new brand required provisioning an entire cluster.
  • 5-minute scaling gap, because large container images increased image-pull and task startup times on AWS Fargate, delaying the addition of capacity during promotional traffic surges.

In QSR, every failed request during a surge is a lost sale and users may switch to competitor services immediately. The service needed to serve over 10 brands cost-effectively while handling unpredictable traffic patterns: lunch rushes, promotional events, and festival surges.

Solution overview

We addressed these challenges through four architectural changes:

  • Shared ECS cluster with a tenancy library: Application-level isolation replaces per-brand infrastructure.
  • EC2 warm pools with Bottlerocket: Sub-minute scaling replaces AWS Fargate cold starts.
  • Crash observability pipeline: Zero-loss logging and 90-day forensics at $10/month per service.
  • Passkeys for multi-tenant authentication: Biometric login reduces recurring SMS costs.

Solution 1: Shared cluster with application-level isolation

As OrderServ scaled from one to five brands, the cost of replicating 21 microservices per tenant made the economics unsustainable. We needed to consolidate infrastructure while preserving the data isolation guarantees each brand required.

Why we moved away from dedicated clusters

The dedicated-cluster model provided strong isolation but no economy of scale. With the platform growing from five brands, onboarding a new brand needed to become a configuration change, not an infrastructure provisioning exercise.

Model Pros Cons
Dedicated cluster per brand (status quo) Hard isolation, simple AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) Linear cost, idle capacity, slow onboarding
Shared cluster with opt-out Aggregate scaling, config-only onboarding Requires application-level isolation, wider IAM scope

We chose the shared cluster as the default, with the ability to place high-volume brands on dedicated clusters when needed.

Figure 1 illustrates this transformation, from five dedicated ECS clusters (105 services, 315 sidecar containers) to a single shared cluster with 21 services and an opt-out path for high-volume brands. The tenancy library handles tenant resolution, resource routing, and context propagation, while per-tenant data stores (Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon Aurora, Valkey) maintain strict data isolation.

Figure 1: Evolution from dedicated clusters per brand to a shared cluster model with opt-out for high-volume brands

The service uses AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) keys to encrypt every data store at rest, and the architecture implements Transport Layer Security (TLS) to protect all service-to-service and client-to-service communication. Amazon DynamoDB automatically encrypts tables by default. Customers enable encryption when creating Amazon Aurora Clusters and the Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system, and customers configure both at-rest and in-transit encryption for the Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey cluster.

The tenancy library as primary isolation

Most multi-tenant architectures enforce isolation at the infrastructure level: separate accounts, separate IAM roles, or separate compute. We took a different approach: a shared .NET Core library as the primary enforcement point for tenant isolation. IAM and resource policies are the backstop that contains the blast radius when the library has a defect.

Every request carries an X-Tenant-Id header injected by the Amazon API Gateway authorizer. The tenancy library:

  • Resolves tenant context per request using request-scoped storage (AsyncLocal), never static or singleton state.
  • Routes all data access: Amazon DynamoDB table names, Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey key prefixes, Amazon Aurora schema selection, and S3 paths.
  • Refuses to construct resource IDs without a tenant prefix, so a missing tenant context fails closed instead of reading another tenant’s data.
  • Propagates tenant context on service-to-service calls and asynchronous messages (SQS/SNS attributes).
  • Enriches every log line and distributed trace with the tenant ID.

This design means the same service binary runs identically in a shared cluster or a dedicated cluster. The compute model becomes a deployment decision, not an architectural constraint.

Application-level isolation moves the isolation boundary into code, and code could potentially have defects. Because an Amazon ECS task role is granted per task rather than per request, a task in the shared cluster necessarily holds permissions spanning every brand it serves. To narrow that scope, the tenancy library acquires tenant-scoped credentials at run time: it calls sts:AssumeRole with the tenant ID as a session tag, and the role’s policies reference that tag so the credentials reach only that tenant’s DynamoDB tables, S3 prefixes, and Aurora schema. Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey enforces its own layer, with per-tenant role-based access control (RBAC) users restricted to the tenant’s key pattern, so the cache engine itself refuses a cross-tenant key access rather than trusting the library to have built the key correctly.

Impact

The following table compares key operational metrics (service count, sidecar overhead, onboarding time, and capacity utilization) before and after the migration to a shared cluster model.

Metric Before (dedicated) After (shared + library)
ECS services to deploy 21 × N brands 21 total
Sidecar containers 315 (for 5 brands) 63 total
Onboarding a new brand Provision full cluster (days) Configuration change (minutes)
Idle capacity Per-brand (wasted) Aggregate (efficient)

Solution 2: EC2 warm pools with Bottlerocket for sub-minute scaling

With all brands now sharing a single cluster, traffic spikes from any one brand could impact the others. We needed a scaling strategy that could absorb sudden surges in seconds, not minutes.

Why we moved away from AWS Fargate

AWS Fargate removes infrastructure management, but OrderServ required additional capacity in under a minute during unpredictable demand surges. New tasks took 5–7 minutes to become healthy, primarily because Fargate had to download and extract the workload’s large container image before starting the application. Task provisioning, application initialization and health checks added to the delay, but image retrieval was the largest contributor. During this interval, existing ECS tasks become saturated, latency increased and some orders started failing.

The solution: EC2 Auto Scaling groups with warm pools

We migrated to Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling groups with Bottlerocket (the AWS purpose-built container OS) and warm pools:

  • The system pre-initializes and stops warm pool instances, and you pay only for Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) storage (~$3/month per instance).
  • When ECS needs capacity, the Auto Scaling group (ASG) starts a stopped instance (image pre-cached, ECS agent registered) in 30–60 seconds.
  • We set capacity headroom (target utilization at 80 percent), so that the first wave absorbs instantly.
  • Bottlerocket provides atomic auto-updates, eliminating the Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) patching burden.

Five-layer scaling strategy

Rather than relying on a single scaling mechanism, we implemented five complementary layers, each targeting a specific traffic pattern to remove gaps between detection and response.

Layer Mechanism Traffic pattern solved
Predictive ECS predictive scaling (machine learning, 14-day history). Scheduled scaling for specific known events (New Year, Christmas) was already handled manually via ASG scheduled actions Daily lunch/dinner peaks, scheduled scaling
Reactive Target tracking on ALBRequestCountPerTarget (60s) Unexpected moderate spikes
Headroom EC2 ASG target capacity at 80% First wave of any spike
Downstream ECS Service Connect RequestCount metric Bottleneck shifting
Throttling API Gateway per-tenant rate limits via AWS Lambda authorizer Extreme surges (noisy neighbor)

Figure 2 illustrates how the five scaling layers work together with the EC2 warm pool. Pre-initialized warm pool instances launch in 30–60 seconds versus 5–7 minutes for an AWS Fargate cold start, at a cost of approximately $3/month per stopped instance.

Figure 2: Five-layer scaling strategy

Cost and performance impact

In addition to improving scaling performance, the move from AWS Fargate to Amazon EC2 reduced the projected monthly cost of running 21 services in the Asia Pacific (Mumbai) AWS Region (ap-south-1). Two instruments do different jobs here: On-Demand Capacity Reservations is designed to make sure capacity is available in the Availability Zone when a surge activates the warm pool, and Compute Savings Plan supply the discount. The reservation carries no term commitment and can be resized or released as the fleet changes, so the following one-year and three-year terms apply to the Savings Plan alone.

Approach Monthly cost (21 services) versus AWS Fargate
AWS Fargate On-Demand (before) ~$1,568 Baseline
EC2 ASG with 1-year Compute Savings Plan and warm pool ~$832
  • ~47%
EC2 ASG with 3-year Compute Savings Plan with warm pool ~$568
  • ~64%

The reservation covers the steady-state fleet, while you stop warm pool instances, adding approximately $30 per month in Amazon EBS storage costs. Scaling time falls from 5–7 minutes to 30–60 seconds.

Solution 3: Crash observability pipeline

When containers crash in production, the support team needs three things: what happened, the root cause, and the container’s execution state at the time of failure. In the prior state, OrderServ used the awslogs driver to send container output to CloudWatch Logs. Although this captured normal application output, it did not provide durable task-stop metadata, cross-service request correlation or persistent crash artifacts.

  • Potential loss of final logs records during crash: When a task terminates abruptly, records still in the log driver’s delivery buffer might not reach Amazon CloudWatch Logs.
  • Short lived task metadata: Amazon ECS makes stopped-task information available through the API for a limited period of 1 hour, reducing the investigation window.
  • No cross-service correlation: Plain-text logs lacked trace IDs and consistent task, container, and service identifiers needed to follow a failed request across services.
  • No persistent crash artifacts: The ephemeral task storage of AWS Fargate disappeared when the task stopped, taking local crash dumps and diagnostic files with it.

The solution: FireLens sidecar + Amazon EventBridge persistence

Figure 3 shows the crash observability pipeline, where the application container emits structured JSON logs with X-Ray trace IDs to a FireLens (Fluent Bit) sidecar. The sidecar survives container termination and routes logs to CloudWatch Logs with Infrequent Access class and 30-day retention, as well as to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) with gzip partitioning and 365-day retention. Amazon EventBridge captures task-stop events with full metadata, while the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) collector provides auto-instrumented traces to X-Ray and EFS persists crash dumps across availability zones, all at approximately $10/month per service.

Figure 3: Crash observability pipeline. FireLens operates at the container runtime level, surviving application container crashes. Amazon EventBridge persists task metadata for 90 days

FireLens (Fluent Bit) as a sidecar is the key architectural choice. ECS redirects the application container’s stdout at the container runtime level. If the app container receives an out-of-memory (OOM) kill, Fluent Bit still has the logs.

For hard crashes where application logs are not sufficient (stack overflow, native code fault), the .NET Core runtime automatically writes a mini dump to an Amazon EFS mount at /tmp/dumps/. Because Amazon EFS writes are immediately durable and the mount survives container death, the process state (thread call stacks, heap objects, loaded modules) helps preserve diagnostic information after a SIGKILL. An AWS Lambda function copies dumps to S3 for analysis without VPC access. Cost: ~$0.02/month.

Amazon EventBridge to Amazon CloudWatch Logs persists the complete Amazon ECS task state change event with 90-day retention. No AWS Lambda function is required.

Every log line is structured JSON with the AWS X-Ray trace ID. The support workflow: search for an error, find the trace ID, open X-Ray, and see the full request flow across all 21 services.

We also use CloudWatch Logs Infrequent Access class with FireLens dual output (CloudWatch + S3), reducing observability costs by 62 percent per service.

Cost: approximately $10/month per service for the complete pipeline.

Solution 4: Passkeys for multi-tenant authentication

QSR mobile apps need instant login. Every second of friction is a lost order. The service previously relied on SMS one-time password (OTP) for every login, which at millions of monthly active users meant significant costs and user friction.

Passkeys with per-brand cryptographic isolation

We implemented passkeys (WebAuthn) using the native support in Amazon Cognito:

  • First-time registration: Phone number + OTP verifies identity, then the device registers a passkey bound to the Secure Enclave.
  • Every subsequent login: Face ID or fingerprint, which completes in about 2 seconds with no SMS cost.
  • New device or stale profile: Because carriers reassign phone numbers, possession of a number is treated as a claim rather than proof of identity. Registering a passkey on a new device repeats the OTP verification, and a profile whose last verification predates our revalidation window is re-verified before any registered credential is honoured.
  • Per-brand isolation: Each brand operates its own Cognito User Pool with a distinct Relying Party ID that is cryptographically isolated at the OS level.

A Post-Authentication Lambda (about 60 lines) maintains a customer authentication profile in DynamoDB, keyed by a hash of the brand/tenant id and the customer’s phone number. Because the brand ID is part of the key, the same customer registering with two brands produces two unrelated records, and the system cannot locate any record without the brand context. The profile stores only authentication state, such as which devices were registered and when each was last verified. It holds no order history, loyalty balance, or other brand-specific data. Passkey credentials are isolated by the same principle: because each brand uses a distinct Relying Party ID, the authentication flow prevents presenting a credential registered for one brand to another brand, and the device enforces that boundary. The implementation required about 95 lines of custom code to integrate with Amazon Cognito’s authentication logic.

Metric Before After
Cost per login ~$0.03 (SMS OTP) $0 (passkey)
Login latency 15–30 seconds ~2 seconds
SMS cost reduction — 80%+ at steady state
Phishing resistance None Cryptographic (device-bound)

Overall results

The architectural evolution delivered compounding savings:

Dimension Before After Improvement
Compute cost AWS Fargate On-Demand EC2 + Warm pools + ODCR + Compute Savings Plan 47–64% reduction
Scaling speed ~ 5-7 minutes 30–60 seconds 5–10× faster
Observability cost Standard CW Logs IA + FireLens + S3 62% reduction
Authentication cost SMS OTP every login Passkeys 80%+ reduction
Tenant onboarding Manual, multi-day Configuration-driven Days → minutes
Crash diagnosis “Exit Code: 1” Full trace + stack trace Blind → full visibility

For a service serving over 5 brands, the combined annual savings exceed 60 percent of the previous infrastructure cost, while simultaneously improving scaling speed, operational visibility, and user experience.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how Cognizant OrderServ evolved from a single tenant microservices service to a multi-tenant SaaS service by making four architectural changes: shared compute with a tenancy library, Amazon EC2 warm pools for sub-minute scaling, a crash observability pipeline, and passkeys for frictionless authentication. The architecture addresses key failure modes through tenant validation, capacity headroom, per-tenant throttling and dedicated-cluster for high-volume brands. These capabilities introduce trade-offs, including greater application-level isolation, EC2 capacity management and compute Savings Plan commitments.

The key insight is that multi-tenancy does not require infrastructure isolation for every tenant. A well-designed tenancy library with strict resource-routing conventions provides application-level isolation while sharing compute, making the isolation model a deployment decision rather than an architectural constraint.

If you operate a multi-brand or multi-tenant service on Amazon ECS and face similar challenges with cost scaling or surge handling, consider these patterns:

  • Evaluate whether your isolation requirements truly need per-tenant infrastructure, or whether application-level isolation with per-tenant data stores is sufficient.
  • For workloads with unpredictable surges, compare the total cost of AWS Fargate over-provisioning against EC2 warm pools with compute Savings Plan.
  • Use FireLens sidecars for log delivery in any environment where container crashes are possible.

To learn more, explore these resources:

  • AWS Well-Architected SaaS Lens – Best practices for multi-tenant SaaS architectures on AWS
  • SaaS Tenant Isolation Strategies – Patterns for isolating tenants in pooled and siloed models, including run-time policy-based isolation with IAM
  • Amazon ECS documentation – Container orchestration and service connect
  • EC2 Auto Scaling warm pools documentation – Configuration and cost guidance
  • Bottlerocket documentation – Container-optimized OS for Amazon ECS
  • Best practices for resilience and availability on Amazon ECS
  • Let’s Architect! Building multi-tenant SaaS systems
  • Contact Cognizant | Partner Overview

title: How TUI scales threat modeling for 100+ teams with Amazon Bedrock
author: AWS Architecture Blog
description:

article_content:
When your security team has four engineers and your organization has over 100 digital product teams, threat modeling becomes a bottleneck fast. That was the challenge TUI faced. TUI operates across the travel and tourism industry with airlines, hotels, cruise ships, and local travel experiences. Our Platform & Engineering division needs security assessments to keep pace.

At TUI, each threat modeling session took 4–6 hours of manual work: reviewing architecture diagrams, mapping threats to internal standards, researching security issues, and documenting findings in Confluence. The team could complete only 3–4 sessions per month, leaving a constant backlog.

TUI needed threat modeling to become mandatory for every new service, not a luxury TUI reserved for the highest-priority projects. TUI built an AI-powered threat modeling system using Amazon Bedrock, collaborating with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center during a 10-week proof of concept (PoC) to develop and validate the architecture. Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed service for building generative AI applications, and TUI used the Claude Sonnet 4.5 foundation model from Anthropic. TUI chose Amazon Bedrock for managed access to Claude Sonnet 4.5 without operating model infrastructure, its extended thinking support that the workflow uses for deeper analysis, and its integration with the AWS services already in TUI’s stack. TUI deployed the agentic workflow on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, part of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. AgentCore runtime hosts the agent in production without provisioning or scaling infrastructure. After the PoC, TUI took the system to production within 30 days.

In this post, we describe how TUI built an agentic AI workflow for threat modeling, the iteration process that shaped the architecture, and the results after deployment.

The challenge

TUI’s security engineering team followed a thorough but manual process: for each application, an engineer reviewed the architecture, identified threats using STRIDE methodology, mapped them to TUI Technology Standards, P&E-specific standards, and ISO 27001 controls, and documented findings in Confluence with Jira tickets.

With 100+ digital product teams and only 3–4 sessions possible per month, most teams waited weeks for their review. Security engineers also had varying levels of expertise across technology stacks, and there was no automated way to verify these standards were consistently applied to every assessment.

Solution overview

The solution extends AWS Threat Designer with TUI-specific capabilities through a serverless architecture deployed in the eu-central-1 (Frankfurt) AWS Region. Model availability varies by Region. For model availability by Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock. Together, these services replace the manual review process with an automated workflow that applies TUI Technology Standards and P&E-specific standards consistently. The system uses the following key services:

  • Amazon Bedrock for threat analysis and generation using Claude Sonnet 4.5 from Anthropic, with configurable extended thinking budgets.

  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime for hosting the agentic workflow as a managed, serverless runtime. It runs the containerized LangGraph agent without provisioning or scaling infrastructure, supports long-running sessions that exceed typical function timeouts, and provides per-session isolation for concurrent threat models.

  • AWS Lambda for serverless backend compute with LangGraph workflow orchestration.

  • Amazon DynamoDB for workflow state management with resume capability.

  • Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) for architecture diagram storage, TUI knowledge base, and web search cache.

  • AWS Amplify for the React front end with Amazon Cognito authentication.

Figure 1: TUI Threat Designer system architecture. Users authenticate through Amazon Cognito and interact with the React front end hosted on AWS Amplify. Requests flow through Amazon API Gateway to AWS Lambda, which orchestrates the LangGraph workflow through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The agent uses Amazon Bedrock (Claude Sonnet 4.5 from Anthropic) for threat analysis, with Amazon DynamoDB for state management and Amazon S3 for architecture diagram storage and caching.

The core is a LangGraph-based agentic workflow that processes architecture diagrams through several specialized nodes. Engineers upload one or more diagrams (for example, a high-level architecture alongside a detailed network topology), which the workflow converts to base64 to identify components and data flows. It then loads relevant security standards and generates threats with iterative refinement. The workflow runs gap analysis, optionally compares against a subject matter expert (SME) assessment, and assembles the final threat model with export options (PDF, JSON, or Confluence).

The following screenshot shows the submission wizard. Engineers provide a title, upload architecture diagrams, add optional context and assumptions, and select a reasoning depth based on architecture complexity. The entire setup takes approximately two minutes.

Figure 2: The submission wizard guides engineers through a six-step process. The iterations slider controls the reasoning budget, from None for quick scans to High for complex architectures with 20 or more components.

Once submitted, the system processes the architecture through each workflow node with real-time progress tracking. Engineers can monitor which phase is active and return to review results when processing completes.

Figure 3: Real-time progress tracking shows the current workflow phase. The Thinking indicator on the Threats node reflects the extended thinking capability of Claude analyzing the architecture against TUI security standards.

The iteration journey: from brute force to intelligent selection

TUI’s team didn’t arrive at the final design on day one. They iterated through several approaches, and each failure pointed toward the next improvement.

Attempt 1: Load everything into the prompt. The first approach loaded all 192 TUI security standards (338 KB) directly into the foundation model context. This failed immediately. Some individual standard documents run 20+ pages, and the combined content exceeded token limits before the foundation model could begin threat analysis.

Even with a subset of standards, the foundation model struggled to follow structured instructions. When asked to recommend only TUI-approved tools for mitigations, it would ignore the approved tool list and suggest generic alternatives. Too much contradictory information from different standards confused the model.

Attempt 2: Metadata-driven selection. The breakthrough came from treating the problem as a search and selection challenge rather than a prompt-loading exercise. Instead of loading all standards, the team pre-generated lightweight metadata for each document: keywords, component types, STRIDE categories, and a relevance score.

At runtime, the foundation model reviews this metadata (about 60 KB) and selects only the 16 most relevant standards for the specific architecture being analyzed. This reduced context from 338 KB to 21 KB, a 94% reduction, while maintaining coverage. The reduction is calculated from the metadata approach versus loading all standards directly.

The metadata approach fits the structure of TUI’s knowledge base: some documents are always mandatory (security guidelines, approved tools), while others apply only to certain architectures. The team also evaluated retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), but with a bounded corpus of 192 standards, some mandatory regardless of the query, metadata-driven selection proved more predictable and easier to debug. RAG may complement it as the knowledge base grows.

Agentic threat generation: a self-correcting workflow

The threat generation node is where the agentic behavior matters most. Rather than generating threats in a single pass, the system uses a Reason and Act pattern with a LangGraph subgraph. The agent has four tools at its disposal: adding threats, deleting threats, reading the current threat catalog, and running gap analysis.

The agent autonomously decides which tools to call and in what order. It generates an initial set of threats using STRIDE methodology, then reviews its own output against the loaded TUI standards. Each threat includes a title, description, affected component, and threat vector. It also assigns likelihood and impact scores using TUI’s risk matrix. Threats include recommended mitigations with TUI-approved tools and mapped ISO 27001 controls.

A tool budget system helps prevent the agent from generating indefinitely. After three threat-generation calls, the system forces a gap analysis. The agent must step back and assess what’s missing before generating more. This mimics how human security experts work: generate, review, identify gaps, fill them.

A validation node checks three conditions before the workflow can proceed: the threat catalog isn’t empty, all six STRIDE categories are covered, and gap analysis has been performed at least once. If a check fails, the agent receives specific feedback and loops back.

Based on TUI’s production data, the combination of iterative generation and gap analysis typically produces 40–60 threats per architecture, compared to the 30–40 that manual sessions identified. It also supports configurable extended thinking budgets, from 24K reasoning tokens for standard architectures up to 64K for complex systems.

Web search for current threat intelligence

Security threats evolve regularly. A threat model generated today needs to account for issues disclosed last week. The workflow integrates web search to fill gaps where TUI’s internal standards don’t cover specific technologies.

For every technology identified in the architecture (Keycloak, Kong, Redis, and so on), the system generates two search queries: one for known issues and one for hardening best practices. These queries target authoritative sources such as OWASP, NIST, and CWE databases. Before making an API call, it checks an Amazon S3-based cache with a 7-day time-to-live (TTL). Only technology component names are used for external searches. Architecture details and customer data are not included in queries.

The cache key uses a hash of the sorted component names, deliberately excluding foundation model-generated descriptions. Those descriptions vary slightly between runs even for the same diagram, which would reduce cache effectiveness.

Based on TUI’s monitoring data, the cache achieves a 70–80% hit rate because many TUI applications share core technologies. A cache hit returns results in under 100 milliseconds, compared to 2–3 seconds for a live search. TUI’s team evaluated multiple search providers during the PoC and designed the system with a pluggable provider architecture, allowing provider switching as capabilities evolve.

SME comparison: human-in-the-loop validation

TUI’s security engineers don’t just use the system. They validate it. The workflow includes an optional node where engineers upload their own manually created threat assessment as a PDF. The workflow extracts threats using Claude, normalizes risk ratings to a standard scale (LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL), and matches them against the AI-generated threats using semantic similarity.

When the AI and the SME disagree on a threat’s severity, the system flags the discrepancy with both ratings and the SME’s rationale. For example, the AI might rate a credential stuffing event (automated login attempts using unintended disclosure of credential databases) as HIGH while the SME rates it MEDIUM. Over time, these comparisons calibrate the system’s risk scoring and surface areas where the AI consistently over- or under-estimates risk.

The following screenshot shows an SME Comparison Alert for a credential stuffing threat. The system matched the AI-generated threat with a similar SME threat, compared both ratings (AI: High, SME: HIGH), and provided the SME’s rationale alongside a recommendation.

Figure 4: An SME Comparison Alert for a credential stuffing threat. The system displays both the AI and SME ratings, the matched SME threat, the expert’s rationale, and a recommendation. In this case, ratings are consistent. When they disagree, the alert highlights the discrepancy for human review.

Path to production: 30 days from handover to live

After the PoC handover, TUI’s team took the system from prototype to production-ready deployment in 30 days. The following results reflect the system’s performance in production.

Results

Metric Before After
Time per assessment 4–6 hours Up to 70% reduction*
Sessions per month 3–4 10–12 (300% increase)*
Standards applied Varies by engineer 100% consistent
Threats identified 30–40 40–60 per architecture
Mandatory for all teams No (backlog too large) Yes (feasible at scale)

*Based on TUI’s internal measurements comparing pre- and post-deployment performance.

The solution processes each architecture in the eu-central-1 Region, with data encrypted at rest using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) and in transit with TLS. Architecture diagrams and threat models are processed within the AWS infrastructure, helping TUI meet its data residency and security requirements.

The following screenshot shows the threat catalog, a card view of completed threat models. Each card displays the original architecture diagram, an AI-generated description, completion status, and threat counts by severity (red for high, yellow for medium, green for low).

Figure 5: The threat catalog provides an overview of completed threat models. Each card shows the architecture diagram, an AI-generated summary, and threat counts grouped by severity.

Engineers can select a threat model to view a dashboard with four analytical views: threats by likelihood, threats by STRIDE category, threats by target asset, and threat sources.

Figure 6: The insights dashboard for a completed threat model. This example shows 40 identified threats (6 high, 24 medium, and 10 low) distributed across all six STRIDE categories and mapped to specific architecture components.

“In the first four weeks after launch, 64 users registered and 19 unique creators produced 34 threat models with Threat Designer. What previously took one to two weeks per assessment is now available on demand. As of October 2026, adoption has grown to 255 registered users, 86 threat models, and 43 active creators, demonstrating that teams are embracing self-service security as part of their development workflow.”

— Marvin Jordan, Head of Technology for Security Platform and Practices, TUI

Conclusion

TUI’s experience shows that agentic AI workflows can address a real operational challenge in enterprise security: making thorough threat modeling fast enough to be mandatory. The combination of metadata-driven context selection, self-correcting threat generation, and intelligent caching allowed a four-person security team to support over 100 digital product teams. TUI achieved consistent, standards-aligned assessments at scale.

Looking ahead, TUI plans to expand the system with automated Jira ticket creation for mitigation tracking and integration with CI/CD pipelines for pre-deployment security checks.

You can get started with Amazon Bedrock to build AI-powered security workflows and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to deploy agentic applications in production. For hands-on guidance with your specific use case, connect with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center. To explore the open source foundation that this solution extends, see the Threat Designer project on GitHub and the AWS blog post Accelerate threat modeling with generative AI.

We welcome your feedback and questions in the comments.

title: How to run a DR readiness engagement
author: AWS Architecture Blog
description:
Part 3 of 3

The framework from Part 1 (three business decisions) and Part 2 (progressive validation) works at any pace. You can apply it over months as part of normal operation...
article_content:
Part 3 of 3

The framework from Part 1 (three business decisions) and Part 2 (progressive validation) works at any pace. You can apply it over months as part of normal operations, or compress it into a structured engagement that moves from undefined targets to a validated recovery commitment in weeks. This post walks through how to run that engagement yourself, with concrete steps, outputs, and a before-and-after example from a real enterprise engagement.

Step 1: Kickoff (define the scope)

Bring three groups into one room: the application owner who knows the technical architecture, the business owner who understands the consequence of downtime, and the platform team that owns the shared services your application depends on. If a dependency is owned by a team not represented in the room, that’s your first action item before proceeding.

Ask these questions in order:

  • What does the user need to be able to do for this function to count as “recovered”?
  • Which applications, shared services, and accounts are in the path of that user journey?
  • Who owns each piece, and have they confirmed their recovery timeline?

The output artifact is a boundary map: a document listing every service and account in the recovery path, with an owner assigned to each and their stated recovery timeline recorded. This single artifact becomes the foundation for every subsequent step.

Step 2: Assessment (surface the gaps)

Run a structured review of each component in the boundary map. For each dependency, ask: does it recover in the target AWS Region, does it recover within the stated recovery time objective (RTO), and does an upstream service’s recovery target cap the RTO you can actually commit to?

  • A Well-Architected Framework Review against the Reliability pillar gives you a systematic way to surface single points of failure, missing health checks, and unverified quotas.
  • An Operational Readiness Review checks whether the runbook’s assumptions hold: are the resources pre-provisioned, do upstream dependencies recover within the target, and are there any manual steps that depend on a specific person being available?

The output is a prioritized list of dependency gaps with owners assigned and a target fix date for each. “Done” at this step means every gap has an owner, a planned fix, and a committed date. Gaps without owners don’t get fixed.

Step 3: Validation plan (structure the tests)

Build a test calendar that progresses through the levels from Part 2. A practical sequence for a first engagement:

  • Week 2: Tabletop exercise on the highest-consequence function. Confirm ownership, escalation path, and expected duration per step.
  • Week 4-6: Planned failover after gap remediation. Measure actual recovery time against the committed RTO. Verify data consistency against the recovery point objective (RPO).
  • Week 8-10: Surprise drill (if the planned failover passed). Test coordination without advance notice.

Don’t schedule a game day with fault injection until you’ve passed a planned failover cleanly. Each level builds confidence for the next. Attempting a higher level before the lower one passes cleanly wastes effort and produces noisy findings that obscure the real gaps.

Step 4: Execute and learn (close the loop)

Each test produces findings. Document them in a format that maps each finding back to the decision it informs:

  • Boundary findings (a shared service discovered mid-test that wasn’t in the recovery scope) → feed back into Decision 1.
  • Consequence findings (recovery took longer than the business can tolerate) → feed back into Decision 2, where the business owner either accepts the longer timeline or invests in a faster architecture.
  • Dependency findings (an upstream service whose recovery target capped the application’s own, a resource that wasn’t pre-provisioned) → feed back into Decision 3.

The output is an updated recovery commitment that reflects what you actually measured, not what you assumed. This document replaces the prior version and becomes the baseline for the next cycle.

Step 5: Ongoing cadence (prevent drift)

Recovery posture drifts as applications change. A new microservice adds a dependency nobody mapped. A team deploys a configuration change that shifts traffic routing. A quota that covered peak load 6 months ago no longer does. Schedule a quarterly review that checks: has the boundary changed (new shared services, new accounts)? Has the business owner confirmed they still accept the RTO/RPO targets? Have any dependencies changed their recovery behavior?

A trigger for re-engagement outside the quarterly cycle: any architecture change that adds a cross-account dependency or changes the failover path.

What this looks like in practice

In the enterprise engagement referenced throughout this series, the team applied this pattern across its portfolio of applications and accounts. The first exercise missed a contractual recovery commitment of 5 hours, taking more than twice that long. Root causes mapped to all three decisions: the boundary excluded a shared authentication platform (most downstream applications couldn’t authenticate users), the dependency chain included an upstream service whose recovery target capped what the applications calling it could achieve, disaster recovery (DR) resources weren’t pre-provisioned, and DNS failover depended on a manual step that took over 3 hours under coordination pressure.

Over 4 months, the team redefined the boundary to include shared platforms, documented the full dependency chain per application, reconciled each application’s target against its slowest dependency, pre-provisioned the recovery environment, and replaced manual DNS failover with automated routing built on Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC) routing controls. ARC routing controls are on/off switches on a data plane that shifts traffic without depending on the Amazon Route 53 control plane, so a cutover doesn’t rely on modifying DNS records mid-event. This follows the Well-Architected guidance to rely on the data plane, not the control plane, during recovery (REL11-BP04), the same static-stability principle behind pre-provisioning. The second exercise passed. The organization operated a live customer-facing system from the recovery Region for the first time. Senior leadership cited the structured engagement as the factor that connected the two different outcomes.

Accelerating the timeline

You can run every step in this post with your own teams. If you want to compress the timeline, AWS Enterprise Support provides specific mechanisms that map to each step: a Technical Account Manager to facilitate the kickoff and maintain engagement momentum between sessions, Well-Architected and Operational Readiness Reviews for the assessment, specialist Solutions Architects for deep dependency analysis, and AWS Countdown for coordinated operational-readiness and engineering support during critical events, including planned failovers and DR game days. These are acceleration options, not prerequisites. The steps and outputs are the same either way.

The AWS Resilience Lifecycle Framework and AWS Resilience Analysis Framework provide the detailed practices behind each decision, and AWS Resilience Hub helps you assess applications against your defined RTO and RPO targets.

title: Validating your DR commitment: From controlled test to real-world readiness
author: AWS Architecture Blog
description:
Part 2 of 3

In Part 1 of this series, you defined three business decisions that shape your disaster recovery (DR) commitment: the recovery boundary, the business-anchored target, and the dependency-reconciled commitment. Those decisions give you a target on paper. Testing tells you whether it holds under real conditions.

This pos...
article_content:
Part 2 of 3

In Part 1 of this series, you defined three business decisions that shape your disaster recovery (DR) commitment: the recovery boundary, the business-anchored target, and the dependency-reconciled commitment. Those decisions give you a target on paper. Testing tells you whether it holds under real conditions.

This post covers a progressive approach to DR validation. Each level of testing surfaces a different class of gap, and each gap feeds back into the three decisions from Part 1 so your commitment gets stronger with every cycle.

Why a single test isn’t enough

A scheduled DR exercise with advance notice proves that the failover mechanism works. That’s a necessary starting point. You can confirm that traffic shifts correctly, data remains consistent in the recovery Region, and the application functions as expected after the transition.

A scheduled exercise doesn’t test the assumptions that only surface under pressure. It doesn’t show whether teams who haven’t rehearsed together can coordinate, or whether everyone agrees on who declares the failover and under what conditions. It also can’t confirm that you provisioned and validated your recovery environment before you triggered the failover. These are the conditions where real recoveries stall, and they’re invisible to a test where every team knows it’s coming and watches closely.

In the same engagement from Part 1, several applications had DR instances in a stopped state. The failover automation assumed it could launch instances, create database replicas, and scale container fleets on demand during the exercise. That approach worked only if the team confirmed two things in advance: that the recovery AWS Region had capacity for the requested instance types, and that the account quotas could absorb the full production load. The team didn’t verify these assumptions in advance.

The architecture was correct. The team didn’t verify those assumptions in advance, and it didn’t pre-provision the recovery environment. To close this gap, the team needs to pre-provision the recovery environment and configure auto scaling groups, confirm that its account quotas match production capacity requirements, and remove any runbook step that assumes your team needs to create resources during the event.

Four levels of progressive validation

The AWS Resilience Lifecycle Framework treats testing as a practice you deepen over time. The four levels below are a maturity model you can apply yourself, ordered from lowest-cost awareness to highest-fidelity validation. We’ve drawn it from patterns across the DR exercises we’ve seen. Each surfaces a different class of gap.

Level 1: Tabletop exercise. A facilitated walkthrough of the recovery plan without touching production. The goal is shared awareness and ownership clarity.

Questions to ask during the tabletop:

  • Who declares the failover, and under what conditions?
  • For each step in the runbook, who owns it and what’s their backup?
  • What’s the expected duration of each step, and what’s the total end-to-end timeline?
  • Which steps depend on a specific person being available?

In the same case study from Part 1, the first tabletop surfaced three boundary gaps: the shared authentication platform wasn’t in the recovery scope, a networking account owned by a different team had no failover runbook, and the DNS update step listed a generic team alias with no named owner.

Level 2: Planned failover. A scheduled failover with advance notice. The goal is confirming the mechanism works under known conditions.

What to measure:

  • Actual recovery time per application compared to the stated recovery time objective (RTO).
  • Data consistency validation in the recovery Region to confirm the recovery point objective (RPO).
  • Any step that requires manual intervention (potential automation candidate).
  • Any dependency that recovered later than expected.

In the same case study, the planned failover revealed the DNS misconfiguration: the shared platform’s Amazon Route 53 records still resolved to the primary Region 45 minutes into the test. Most downstream applications appeared healthy but couldn’t serve users. Actual recovery took more than twice the 5-hour target.

A successful planned failover produces a measured gap (or confirmation) between the RTO target you defined and your actual recovery time. That number is the starting point for every subsequent conversation with the business owner about whether the target is realistic.

Level 3: Surprise drill. A failover triggered without advance notice to the responding team. The goal is testing execution readiness, not capability.

This level finds the gaps that preparation hides: the runbook that only its original author can interpret, the step that depends on a specific person’s tribal knowledge, and the escalation path that nobody has practiced. In the case study, a later surprise drill revealed that only one engineer understood how to validate database consistency in the recovery Region. With that person unavailable, the team lost 90 minutes locating and interpreting the procedure.

Level 4: Game day with fault injection. An exercise where you inject specific dependency failures using AWS Fault Injection Service, which ships purpose-built scenarios such as “AZ Availability: Power Interruption” and “Cross-Region: Connectivity”. The goal is testing resilience under conditions you didn’t fully script.

You discover the dependency you assumed would be healthy, the monitoring gap that delays detection, and the cascade that your tabletop didn’t model. This is the closest approximation to a real event without waiting for one to happen.

What each level reveals

The tabletop finds the step no team owns. The planned failover finds the misconfiguration. The surprise drill finds the coordination failure. The game day finds the unmodeled dependency. Each level surfaces a different class of gap.

Run only the calm, scheduled test and you validate the mechanism while leaving the conditions that cause real recovery failures untested. The point isn’t to skip levels. You build confidence at each level before increasing realism. But stopping at the planned failover, a pattern we often see once the mechanism works, leaves team, process, and dependency gaps invisible until an event exposes them.

Closing the loop

Each test produces specific findings that map directly to the three decisions from Part 1.

  • A boundary gap (a shared service discovered mid-test that wasn’t in the recovery scope) feeds back into Decision 1.
  • A recovery that exceeds the time the business can tolerate feeds back into Decision 2, where the business owner either accepts the longer timeline or invests in a faster architecture.
  • A dependency that recovered slower than the target assumed feeds back into Decision 3 for a revised commitment that reflects what was actually measured.

In the same engagement, the first exercise surfaced all four patterns described across this series: a boundary gap (shared platform not in scope), a dependency gap (an upstream service whose recovery target capped the application’s own), a stability gap (resources not pre-provisioned), and a coordination gap (manual DNS failover). The team mapped each finding to a specific decision and a specific fix. Four months later, the second exercise passed. The organization operated a live customer-facing system from the recovery Region for the first time.

The value of progressive testing is not passing a single exercise. It’s building a practice where each cycle tightens the recovery commitment, and each finding has a clear path back to the decision it informs.

Where to start

If you haven’t run a tabletop yet, start there. Gather the owners of one critical business function and walk the recovery plan together. Ask: who declares the failover, what’s the first action, who owns each step, and what’s the expected duration of each. If the room disagrees with any answer, this indicates an opportunity to clarify and strengthen your recovery plan before touching production.

If you’ve passed a planned failover, consider whether a surprise drill would surface coordination gaps that preparation masks. In this engagement, the surprise drill cost the team 90 minutes that the planned failover never surfaced. Whatever level you’re at, document what each test reveals and feed it back into the three decisions. A posture that improves every test cycle is worth more than one that passes a single exercise and never evolves. In Part 3, we walk through how to structure a full DR readiness engagement: who to involve, what to produce at each step, and how to compress the timeline from months to weeks.

title: Three business decisions that define your DR success
author: AWS Architecture Blog
description:
Part 1 of 3

article_content:
Part 1 of 3

A disaster recovery (DR) strategy is only as strong as the business decisions behind it. The architecture and failover mechanisms matter, but they execute against targets that you define. In our experience facilitating enterprise DR exercises, the difference between teams that meet their recovery targets and teams that don’t often comes down to three decisions made (or deferred) before the first architecture diagram: what you’re actually recovering, what the business needs from that recovery, and what your dependencies allow you to commit to.

This post helps you validate whether your current approach accounts for each one. It draws on a pattern from a real engagement where revisiting these decisions turned a missed recovery target into a successful test four months later.

This is Part 1 of a three-part series. It walks through those three decisions and shows how to make them before you choose an architecture pattern. Part 2 covers progressive validation testing. Part 3 covers how to run a DR readiness engagement. The approach builds on the AWS Resilience Lifecycle Framework and the AWS Resilience Analysis Framework.

Define the recovery boundary

The first decision is drawing the line around what “recovered” means. You cannot meaningfully define a recovery time objective (RTO) until you specify precisely what you need working for you to consider that objective met.

The Resilience Lifecycle Framework defines a business function as the end-to-end capability a user depends on (completing a transaction, filing a report, accessing an account). A single business function often spans multiple applications, accounts, and teams. When you set a recovery target at the application level without accounting for the shared services that the application calls, you might define the boundary too narrowly to deliver the capabilities your users require.

Here’s a pattern we observed in a DR exercise for a large enterprise customer. The customer tested dozens of applications across many AWS accounts. Each application had its own failover automation, and each one failed over correctly. But a shared authentication platform (running in a separate account, managed by a different team) used Amazon Route 53 simple routing pointed at the primary AWS Region. It had no health checks and no failover configuration. Because the team didn’t include it in the recovery scope, the platform remained in the primary Region while everything else moved. The result: Most of the downstream applications that depended on it couldn’t authenticate users. Although the team had successfully failed over the applications themselves, the business function (user login, transaction, confirmation) did not work. This single boundary gap, not the individual application architectures, was the primary driver of the missed recovery target.

The solution involved redefining the recovery scope rather than changing the architecture. The organization redefined recovery boundaries around business functions (what capabilities must you deliver to your users?) rather than individual applications (is this service running?). That single change pulled the shared authentication platform inside the scope and helped the team discover the dependency. A business impact analysis is the structured starting point for this work.

Anchor the target to business consequence

The second decision is settling what recovery means in terms the business owns. Business stakeholders strengthen RTO and recovery point objective (RPO) when they help set them. In organizations where these targets are defined by engineering alone, they can become disconnected from what the business actually tolerates. A 4-hour RTO means something different for a payments platform that clears interbank settlement than it does for an internal reporting dashboard, even when both share the same database engine and replication setup.

In the same engagement, the business carried a contractual recovery commitment of 5 hours. The business treated it as a firm commitment to their regulator. The engineering team treated it as a stretch goal based on the architecture’s theoretical capability. Neither side had validated whether 5 hours was achievable given the dependency chain. That disconnect only became visible when the first exercise took 9–11 hours. The target had never been tested against the actual recovery path, and the business stakeholder who owned the penalty had never been asked whether the engineering team’s assumptions matched theirs.

RPO is a statement about data loss. For a payments platform clearing interbank settlement, an RPO of 5 minutes might still be too wide if those minutes contain transactions that can’t be reconstructed. The question for the business owner is: Which records must survive a Regional impairment, and can you prove they will? The business owner uses that framing to decide whether asynchronous replication (with its window of in-flight data loss) is acceptable. The alternative is synchronous writes, with the latency cost that comes with them.

RTO is a statement about downtime tolerance. A 4-hour recovery time is a technical figure until someone attaches a consequence to each hour. For regulatory filings, the fourth hour might mean a missed deadline with financial penalties. For a storefront, every minute carries lost orders.

The AWS Resilience Lifecycle Framework recommends defining objectives around business outcomes directly (for example, the percentage of successful orders maintained when a component degrades). A service-level agreement (SLA) is a contract with a financial penalty. A service-level objective is a target you manage toward. Raising an SLA doesn’t make an application more resilient.

The output of this decision is a recovery requirement stated in language the business recognizes and engineering can build against: the function, the consequence of losing it, the data that must survive, and the tolerable downtime before the consequence lands.

Account for the dependency chain

The third decision is confirming that your recovery target accounts for everything in the critical path, not just the components you own. Your application recovers only as fast as its slowest dependency. If a service you call takes 4 hours to recover in the recovery Region, your achievable RTO is 4 hours regardless of your own architecture.

In the same engagement, one customer-facing application had committed to a 1-hour recovery target and had the architecture to meet it on its own. But it called a shared identity service, owned by a different team, to validate every user session. That identity service carried a 4-hour recovery target. No matter how fast the customer-facing application recovered, users couldn’t do anything until the identity service came back. The application’s real, achievable RTO was 4 hours, set entirely by a dependency its own team didn’t own and hadn’t accounted for when they committed to 1 hour.

This is why the dependency chain, not the application in isolation, defines the commitment you can make. Identify and document every service your business function calls, note the recovery target each one holds, and set your own target against the slowest link you depend on. Where another team owns a dependency, its recovery target becomes a commitment you need from them, in writing, not an assumption. The AWS Fault Isolation Boundaries whitepaper helps you reason about which dependencies hold during a Regional impairment, and which introduce risk. The distinction that matters is what your runbook asks a service to do. Reading existing data keeps working during an impairment: existing credentials still authenticate, and existing DNS records still resolve. Changing things is what carries risk, because creating or modifying AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles and Route 53 records runs through control planes that live in a single Region. A recovery path that only reads existing state holds up. One that must create or change resources mid-event might not. That’s the case for settling those changes ahead of time.

Where you can, reduce the chain itself. When you pre-provision and run a dependency in the recovery Region before the event, you reduce how many services need to recover before you can restore your application. The shorter the chain of things that must recover in sequence, the closer your achievable target gets to the one you want to commit to.

Where to start

Start your validation by examining one business function. Assess whether: Is the recovery boundary drawn around the full user journey, including shared services in other accounts? Has a business stakeholder confirmed the consequence-per-hour attached to the current RTO and RPO? Does the target account for every dependency in the path, including global endpoints and any runbook step that assumes resource creation during failover?

If you can answer yes to all three with evidence, your targets are well-founded. If any answer is uncertain, you’ve identified where to focus next. In Part 2, we cover how to validate your answers through progressive testing that closes the distance between a controlled exercise and real-world readiness.
