title: Automating the full AWS DRS agent lifecycle: Install, heal, and offboard
author: AWS Architecture Blog
description: If you protect a large Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) fleet with AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (AWS DRS), you manage the AWS Replication Agent across its whole lifecycle. You install it, keep it healthy and registered, and remove it cleanly when a server leaves disaster recovery (DR) scope. An enterprise IT customer with mor...
article_content:
If you protect a large Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) fleet with AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (AWS DRS), you manage the AWS Replication Agent across its whole lifecycle. You install it, keep it healthy and registered, and remove it cleanly when a server leaves disaster recovery (DR) scope. An enterprise IT customer with more than 300 Linux and Windows instances in DR scope ran into two of these problems while planning and validating a scheduled DR drill. Some agents had stalled after a network change, and some descoped servers were still replicating and adding to the bill. A server with a stalled agent can’t meet your recovery point objective (RPO), the maximum data loss you can accept after a disruption. The customer’s team checked replication status in the AWS DRS console before each drill, so a problem that started between drills could go unnoticed until the next one.

Working with that customer, we automated the install, heal, and offboard phases of the lifecycle. Most of the design choices in this post came from fixing those two problems. Each phase runs as an AWS Systems Manager (SSM) Automation document, started by Amazon EventBridge or on a schedule. A single EC2 tag decides which phase applies to an instance. Because the logic lives in the Automation documents, there are no AWS Lambda functions to maintain. When you take an instance out of scope, the automation records whether replication billing actually stopped.

You can find the SSM Automation documents, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies, and deployment scripts in the aws-samples/sample-drs-agent-lifecycle-automation GitHub repository.

Solution overview

You apply a DR tag to each EC2 instance, and its value (yes, pause, or no) tells the automation what to do. Three SSM Automation documents divide the work. Onboarding installs and repairs the agent and keeps registration healthy. Healing responds when replication stalls, and offboarding runs teardown when you descope an instance.

AWS Systems Manager State Manager runs onboarding on a 30-minute schedule against tagged instances. Amazon EventBridge triggers healing when AWS DRS reports a stalled server, and offboarding when the DR tag changes. The automation runs primarily in your source AWS Region and calls the DR Region only where AWS DRS requires it.

Prerequisites

To deploy this solution, you need:

  • An AWS account with administrative access.
  • Two AWS Regions configured: a source Region (where your EC2 instances run) and a DR Region (where AWS DRS replicates to).
  • AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery initialized in both the source Region (for failback) and the DR Region (for replication).
  • Network connectivity between Regions with TCP 443 (AWS DRS API and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3)) and TCP 1500 (replication data) open. For private connectivity, use AWS Transit Gateway or VPC peering. Public endpoints are also supported.
  • (Optional) Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) endpoints for AWS DRS and Amazon S3 in the DR Region, if using private connectivity.
  • IAM permissions to deploy AWS CloudFormation stacks that create named IAM roles (CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM), Amazon EventBridge rules, and a State Manager association, and to register SSM Automation documents. You also need iam:PassRole on DRS-Automation-Role, because the Amazon EventBridge rules and the State Manager association use that role.
  • AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) installed and configured.
  • An instance profile on each source EC2 instance with the AWSElasticDisasterRecoveryAgentInstallationPolicy and AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore managed policies, so that each instance is managed by Systems Manager. If your instances already have an instance profile, attach both policies to its role.
  • An existing Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic for notifications.
  • (Optional) An existing Amazon S3 bucket for audit reports.
  • Git, Bash 4 or later, and yq. The deployment scripts use yq to read config.yaml. macOS includes Bash 3.2, so install a newer version, for example with Homebrew.

You don’t need to create the automation’s IAM roles yourself. The CloudFormation templates create DRS-Automation-Role (which runs every lifecycle action) and DRS-EventBridge-Forward-Role (deployed with the DR Region stack), along with the Amazon EventBridge rules in both Regions and the State Manager association. Amazon CloudWatch metrics are published automatically.

One tag controls the entire lifecycle

After you deploy the solution, the value of the DR tag on each EC2 instance determines what the automation does:

DR value State What happens
yes Protected Agent is installed, failback tag applied, health maintained every 30 minutes
pause Quiesced Agent stays installed, stalled alerts suppressed, offboarding blocked
no or deleted Descoped Replication stopped, source server deleted, agent uninstalled
Anything else (for example, DR=maybe, DR=true) Misconfigured Fail-safe: automation skips the instance and logs a SKIPPED_MISCONFIGURED status. No install, no heal, no teardown, preventing an unrecognized value from triggering the wrong action

The tag value is normalized (trimmed and lowercased) before evaluation. A value like DR=Yes normalizes to DR=yes and matches correctly.

Three SSM Automation documents divide the lifecycle:

  • DRS-Agent-Onboard runs every 30 minutes through State Manager against tag:DR=yes instances. It installs or repairs the agent, applies the AWSDRS:AllowLaunchingIntoThisInstance tag, and validates AWS DRS registration. The tag tells AWS DRS to launch recovery onto the original instance during failback and acts as the drift-correction backstop. State Manager re-evaluates tagged instances every 30 minutes. Each run catches instances that lost the Replication Agent, newly tagged instances that aren’t onboarded yet, and earlier runs that failed silently.
  • DRS-Agent-Heal fires when Amazon EventBridge receives a replication-stalled event (cross-Region forwarded from the DR Region). The rule filters on the STALLED state, so recovery transitions don’t trigger unnecessary runs. It inspects the replication error to distinguish agent-side failures from infrastructure issues. For agent problems, it restarts the service first, then reinstalls in place only if the restart doesn’t fix it. For infrastructure-caused stalls, it escalates to operators through Amazon SNS.
  • DRS-Agent-Offboard fires when Amazon EventBridge detects a DR tag change or deletion. The offboarding document first verifies safeguards: a tag re-check, a terminated-instance guard, and an optional approval gate. After those pass, it records replication state and stops replication. It then disconnects the source server, deletes it, uninstalls the Replication Agent, and removes the tags.

How the components connect

The solution operates primarily in the source Region. Cross-Region calls happen only where AWS DRS requires them (registration checks and teardown API calls target the DR Region).

The following diagram shows how the automation components connect across the source and DR Regions. State Manager and Amazon EventBridge operate in the source Region; AWS DRS replication and the stall-forwarding rule run in the DR Region.

Figure 1: AWS DRS agent lifecycle automation architecture across the source and DR Regions

In the source Region, State Manager runs the onboarding document every 30 minutes, and Amazon EventBridge rules start the heal and offboarding documents when their events arrive. AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store holds the DR-event stand-down flag (/drs/control/event-in-progress). The DRS-Automation-Role IAM role runs every automation step. Amazon SNS delivers alerts, Amazon S3 stores per-event audit reports, and Amazon CloudWatch captures outcome metrics.

In the DR Region, AWS DRS manages source server registration and ongoing replication. AWS DRS emits replication events only in the DR Region, where the source servers are registered. An Amazon EventBridge forwarding rule filters replication-stalled events by the STALLED state. It then sends them to the source Region for healing. Staging subnets and Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes, managed by AWS DRS, support the replication infrastructure.

For networking, AWS Transit Gateway (which connects VPCs across Regions) carries TCP 443 (AWS DRS API and S3) and TCP 1500 (replication data) between Regions. Amazon VPC endpoints for AWS DRS and S3 keep traffic on the AWS backbone without internet exposure. An Amazon Route 53 Private Hosted Zone (for DNS resolution within your VPC) resolves endpoint names to private IPs. This removes the need for --endpoint installer flags and protects failback compatibility.

Tag and rule examples

Run these commands after you deploy the solution. Tag an instance for protection:

aws ec2 create-tags --resources i-0abc123def456 --tags Key=DR,Value=yes

Descope an instance (triggers offboarding):

aws ec2 create-tags --resources i-0abc123def456 --tags Key=DR,Value=no

Or remove the tag entirely (also triggers offboarding):

aws ec2 delete-tags --resources i-0abc123def456 --tags Key=DR

The Amazon EventBridge rule that triggers offboarding matches this pattern:

{

"source": ["aws.tag"],

"detail-type": ["Tag Change on Resource"],

"detail": {

"changed-tag-keys": ["DR"],

"service": ["ec2"],

"resource-type": ["instance"]

}

}

The Amazon EventBridge rule that triggers healing filters on the STALLED state so recovery transitions are ignored:

{

"source": ["aws.drs"],

"detail-type": ["DRS Source Server Data Replication Stalled Change"],

"detail": {

"state": ["STALLED"]

}

}

Three layers protecting the RPO

The 15-minute RPO referenced throughout this post is a customer-configured target, not an AWS service guarantee. The architecture helps protect it with three complementary layers, each covering a different failure mode.

Layer 1: OS service auto-restart (seconds). The agent service uses systemd Restart=always on Linux and Windows Service Recovery. When the process stops, the OS brings it back automatically. On Linux, systemd restarts the service almost instantly. On Windows, the first recovery action fires after a configurable delay (30 seconds by default). This layer handles agent process crashes without any automation running.

Layer 2: Amazon EventBridge heal (minutes, not seconds). If the agent disappears or can’t maintain registration, AWS DRS detects the stall and emits a replication-stalled event in the DR Region. A forwarding rule filters on the STALLED state and sends it cross-Region to the source Region’s event bus. A matching receive rule triggers the heal document.

The heal document restarts the agent first (most stalls are transient). If restart fails, it re-runs the installer in place, preserving driver state to avoid a full-disk rescan. The restart path is the faster of the two, and total time depends on your environment and on AWS DRS stall-detection latency. The reinstall path takes longer because the agent must re-establish block-level tracking. Stall-detection latency also counts against the window, because lag must accumulate before the service marks a server as stalled.

Layer 3: State Manager backstop (up to 30 minutes). The onboarding document re-evaluates DR=yes instances every 30 minutes, catching drift and edge cases that faster layers miss. This exceeds the 15-minute RPO target, so it functions as a safety net rather than the primary defense.

Layer 2 requires the Amazon EventBridge data plane in both Regions to be operational, while Layers 1 and 3 run entirely in the source Region.

Onboarding: How ongoing convergence works

State Manager targets tag:DR=yes. Instances that already have the tag and instances you tag later are included automatically, without manual registration.

The onboarding document is idempotent. It skips healthy, registered instances. For instances that need work, it checks the stand-down flag and instance state, validates the operating system (Linux or Windows), and flags unsupported architectures as TAGGED_UNSUPPORTED. If AutoInstallEnabled is false, the run is audit-only.

For actual installs, a concurrency lock (flock on Linux, a named mutex on Windows) prevents races when multiple automation runs overlap on the same instance. This lock is built into the documents and needs no configuration. The State Manager association sets MaxConcurrency to 10 and MaxErrors to 100% in templates/state-manager-association.yaml. MaxConcurrency limits how many instances are processed at once. With MaxErrors at 100%, a failure on one instance doesn’t stop the run for the rest of the fleet. For larger fleets, raise MaxConcurrency gradually and watch for AWS DRS API throttling.

The failback tag (AWSDRS:AllowLaunchingIntoThisInstance) is applied only when the agent is confirmed present. Registration is assessed cross-Region, and if an instance stays in PENDING_REGISTRATION beyond a configurable threshold (default: 3 runs), the document escalates through Amazon SNS. Each execution writes an S3 audit record and emits a CloudWatch metric.

Healing agent issues within RPO

The heal document reads the source server ARN from the event and looks up the matching EC2 instance ID with drs:DescribeSourceServers in the DR Region. It then checks the stand-down flag and the tag state. Values other than yes suppress the heal with no action and no alert.

If restart doesn’t resolve the issue, the automation re-runs the installer in place as a fallback. It doesn’t uninstall first, so the existing replication driver stays intact where possible. Reinstallation can trigger a block-level rescan whose duration scales with total disk size. On large volumes, this might temporarily exceed the RPO window while the rescan completes.

Not every stall is an agent problem. Bandwidth throttling, undersized replication servers, or staging-area disk issues can also cause stalls. The automation escalates these non-agent stalls to your operators through Amazon SNS rather than attempting agent remediation. If the Replication Agent is still not functioning after reinstall, you receive a HEAL_FAILED notification with diagnostic details.

Only the AWS DRS agent service is restarted, not the EC2 instance itself. Your workloads keep running without interruption.

Offboarding with honest billing status

When you set DR=no or delete the tag, Amazon EventBridge fires a Tag Change on Resource event. The offboarding document applies several safeguards before teardown.

Terminated-instance guard: EC2 termination strips tags, generating the same event as a deliberate descope. The document sends an alert and stops. It doesn’t delete the source server, which contains the recovery point.

Tag re-check: If the tag has been restored, the document exits.

Approval gate: If AutoOffboardEnabled is false, the document sends a notification and stops.

State recording: Before modifying resources, it captures replication state, lag duration, and last snapshot time.

Recovery-instance check: Before completing teardown, the offboarding document checks for active recovery instances. If found, it flags them in the audit report and sends an SNS alert. Recovery instances incur separate EC2 billing that persists after source server deletion.

Adaptive retry: A maximum of 10 attempts with exponential backoff handles API throttling during bulk descope.

After teardown, the document checks what actually succeeded:

Outcome Meaning
COMPLETED Source server deleted, billing halted
BILLING_STOPPED_ORPHAN Replication stopped but delete didn’t succeed. Operator must manually delete.
FAILED stop_replication didn’t succeed. Billing might still be active. Operator review recommended.
NO_SERVER Instance was not registered as an AWS DRS source server. Clean no-op.

Because each outcome reflects what actually succeeded, you know whether replication billing has stopped or whether a source server needs manual follow-up.

Security: Least-privilege IAM roles

The solution creates two IAM roles and relies on one that you provide. SSM Automation and Amazon EventBridge assume the DRS-Automation-Role to run all lifecycle actions. Its permissions cover SSM, EC2 tags, cross-Region AWS DRS calls, SNS, S3, Parameter Store, and iam:PassRole on itself. The iam:PassRole permission only allows passing this role to Systems Manager. Run Command is limited to instances tagged DR=yes. In the DR Region, the DRS-EventBridge-Forward-Role can only put events on the source Region’s default event bus.

On each EC2 instance, the instance profile from the prerequisites lets the Replication Agent and SSM Agent reach their services. The automation stores no long-lived credentials. Each role receives temporary credentials when it’s assumed. When you use private connectivity, cross-Region traffic stays on Transit Gateway and VPC endpoints.

Deploy the solution

Start in audit mode, where the onboarding document reports what it would install without changing any instance and offboarding sends a notification instead of running teardown. Review the audit reports, then turn on installation for a small set of instances before you scale to the full fleet.

To configure config.yaml

Clone the repository and change to its directory:

git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sample-drs-agent-lifecycle-automation.git

cd sample-drs-agent-lifecycle-automation

The deployment scripts read your settings from config.yaml in the root of the repository. Set the values in the following sample before you deploy. The file in the repository also sets document names and stack names. Keep those at their defaults, because the commands in this post use the default names.

# Region configuration

source_region: us-west-1        # Region where your EC2 instances run

dr_region: us-east-2            # Region where AWS DRS replicates to

account_id: "111122223333"      # Your AWS account ID

# Observability

sns_topic_name: drs-alerts      # Existing SNS topic for notifications

amzn-s3-demo-audit_bucket: ""           # Existing S3 bucket for audit reports; empty turns off audit reports

cloudwatch_namespace: DRSAutomation

# Automation toggles (start in audit mode)

auto_install_enabled: "false"   # false = report only; true = install and repair agents

auto_offboard_enabled: "false"  # false = notify only; true = tear down on descope

# Tag configuration

dr_tag_key: DR

dr_protected_value: "yes"

dr_descope_value: "no"

# Stand-down control and schedule

stand_down_parameter: /drs/control/event-in-progress

schedule_rate: "rate(30 minutes)"

The following table describes the values you’re most likely to change.

Parameter Required Description
source_region Yes Region that hosts your EC2 instances and the automation
dr_region Yes Region where AWS DRS replicates to
account_id Yes AWS account that hosts the automation
sns_topic_name Yes Name of an existing SNS topic in the source Region
amzn-s3-demo-audit_bucket No Existing S3 bucket for JSON audit reports. Leave empty to skip them
auto_install_enabled No Set to false to report only, or true to install and repair agents
auto_offboard_enabled No Set to false to notify only, or true to run teardown when you descope an instance
dr_tag_key No EC2 tag key that controls the lifecycle (default DR)

To deploy the solution

The following steps deploy each component separately so you can see what each one creates. Run the commands from the root of the cloned repository. Replace the example account ID (111122223333) and Regions (us-west-1 and us-east-2) with your own values.

To deploy everything in one command instead, run ./scripts/deploy.sh after you edit config.yaml, and then go to the confirmation commands after step 6. The script prints the status of every stack when it finishes. Without yq, it falls back to built-in defaults, including a placeholder account ID. Use either the script or the individual steps, not both.

  1. Deploy the IAM role stack. The template creates a role with an explicit name (DRS-Automation-Role), so CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM is required. 
    aws cloudformation deploy \

--template-file templates/iam-roles.yaml \

--stack-name drs-automation-iam \

--capabilities CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM \

--region us-west-1 \

--parameter-overrides \

AccountId=111122223333 \

SourceRegion=us-west-1 \

DRRegion=us-east-2 \

SNSTopicName=drs-alerts
  2. Register the three SSM Automation documents. The script reads source_region from config.yaml and creates the documents from the documents/ folder on the first run. On later runs, it publishes a new default version of any document that changed. 
    ./scripts/register-documents.sh
  3. Deploy the Amazon EventBridge rules in the source Region. This stack creates the tag-change rule that starts offboarding and the rule that starts healing. It uses the existing DRS-Automation-Role, so it doesn’t need CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM. 
    aws cloudformation deploy \

--template-file templates/eventbridge-source.yaml \

--stack-name drs-eventbridge-source \

--region us-west-1 \

--parameter-overrides \

AutomationRoleArn=arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/DRS-Automation-Role \

TargetRegion=us-east-2 \

SNSTopicArn=arn:aws:sns:us-west-1:111122223333:drs-alerts \

AutoOffboardEnabled=false
  4. Deploy the forwarding rule in the DR Region. This stack creates DRS-EventBridge-Forward-Role, which lets the rule send stalled events to the source Region’s event bus, so CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM is required. 
    aws cloudformation deploy \

--template-file templates/eventbridge-dr.yaml \

--stack-name drs-eventbridge-dr \

--capabilities CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM \

--region us-east-2 \

--parameter-overrides \

SourceRegion=us-west-1 \

AccountId=111122223333
  5. Create the stand-down flag in Parameter Store with a value of false. The script reads the parameter name and Region from config.yaml and doesn’t overwrite an existing value. 
    ./scripts/init-parameters.sh

    If you prefer not to use the script, run the following command instead:

    aws ssm put-parameter --name /drs/control/event-in-progress \

--value false --type String --region us-west-1
  6. Deploy the State Manager association in audit mode. The association runs once as soon as it’s created and then every 30 minutes. 
    aws cloudformation deploy \

--template-file templates/state-manager-association.yaml \

--stack-name drs-state-manager \

--region us-west-1 \

--parameter-overrides \

AutomationRoleArn=arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/DRS-Automation-Role \

TargetRegion=us-east-2 \

AutoInstallEnabled=false \

SNSTopicArn=arn:aws:sns:us-west-1:111122223333:drs-alerts

To confirm the deployment, run the following commands:

aws cloudformation describe-stacks --region us-west-1 \

--query "Stacks[?starts_with(StackName, 'drs-')].[StackName,StackStatus]" --output table

aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name drs-eventbridge-dr --region us-east-2 \

--query "Stacks[0].StackStatus" --output text

aws events list-rules --name-prefix DRS- --region us-west-1 --query "Rules[].Name"

aws events list-rules --name-prefix DRS- --region us-east-2 --query "Rules[].Name"

aws ssm list-documents --filters Key=Owner,Values=Self --region us-west-1 \

--query "DocumentIdentifiers[?starts_with(Name, 'DRS-Agent-')].Name"

aws ssm get-parameter --name /drs/control/event-in-progress --region us-west-1 \

--query "Parameter.Value" --output text

A successful deployment shows the following results:

  • All four stacks show CREATE_COMPLETE, or UPDATE_COMPLETE after a re-run.
  • The source Region lists the DRS-Tag-Change-Offboard and DRS-Stalled-Heal-Receive rules.
  • The DR Region lists the DRS-Stalled-Forward rule.
  • The source Region lists the DRS-Agent-Onboard, DRS-Agent-Heal, and DRS-Agent-Offboard documents.
  • The stand-down flag returns false.
  • In the AWS Systems Manager console, State Manager lists DRS-Agent-Onboard-Association.

When you’re ready to turn on installation, set auto_install_enabled: "true" in config.yaml and deploy the State Manager stack again with AutoInstallEnabled=true:

aws cloudformation deploy \

--template-file templates/state-manager-association.yaml \

--stack-name drs-state-manager \

--region us-west-1 \

--parameter-overrides \

AutomationRoleArn=arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/DRS-Automation-Role \

TargetRegion=us-east-2 \

AutoInstallEnabled=true \

SNSTopicArn=arn:aws:sns:us-west-1:111122223333:drs-alerts

To turn on teardown, set auto_offboard_enabled: "true" and deploy the source Region Amazon EventBridge stack again with AutoOffboardEnabled=true:

aws cloudformation deploy \

--template-file templates/eventbridge-source.yaml \

--stack-name drs-eventbridge-source \

--region us-west-1 \

--parameter-overrides \

AutomationRoleArn=arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/DRS-Automation-Role \

TargetRegion=us-east-2 \

SNSTopicArn=arn:aws:sns:us-west-1:111122223333:drs-alerts \

AutoOffboardEnabled=true

Safety guards prevent unintended actions

The following table lists the safety guards across the three automation documents. The stand-down flag and the tag value allow-list apply to every document. The terminated-instance guard and honest billing status protect offboarding, and the remaining guards protect onboarding and healing.

Guard Prevents
DR-event stand-down Acting during failover/failback
Terminated-instance guard Deleting a recovery point on instance termination
Reverse-direction detect Overwriting an AWS DRS-managed failback agent
Concurrency lock Race conditions from overlapping runs
AutoInstallEnabled gate Unintended installs in audit-first deployments
OS pre-check Running installer on incompatible operating system
Honest billing status Reporting “billing stopped” when teardown partially completed
Tag value allow-list A typo triggering the wrong lifecycle action
Agent-presence-gated tagging Applying failback tag to an agent-less instance

To pause the automation during a declared DR event:

aws ssm put-parameter --name /drs/control/event-in-progress \

--value true --type String --overwrite --region us-west-1

To resume after the event:

aws ssm put-parameter --name /drs/control/event-in-progress \

--value false --type String --overwrite --region us-west-1

Monitoring and observability

The three SSM Automation documents produce telemetry across three channels, each tuned for a different audience.

Amazon SNS notifications go to the on-call team. Onboarding stays quiet unless an instance needs intervention. Heal notifies on both success and intervention-needed, because a successful auto-heal still tells you a real issue occurred and was resolved. Offboarding sends a notification at each stage: start, complete, orphan, incomplete, and approval-needed.

Amazon S3 audit reports serve compliance and troubleshooting. One JSON object per lifecycle event at s3:///drs///-.json captures instance ID, host name, platform, source server ID, status, and pre-teardown replication state. To control storage costs, add a lifecycle rule to the bucket (for example, expire objects under drs/ after 90 days).

Amazon CloudWatch metrics power fleet dashboards. An Outcome metric (1=handled, 0=needs attention) dimensioned by event type provides at-a-glance fleet health.

Clean up

Removing the automation doesn’t stop replication. Instances tagged DR=yes keep replicating until you stop replication through the AWS DRS console or API. To remove the automation infrastructure, run the following commands:

  1. Delete the State Manager association and the source Region Amazon EventBridge stacks. 
    aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name drs-state-manager --region us-west-1

aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name drs-eventbridge-source --region us-west-1
  2. Delete the Amazon EventBridge forwarding stack in the DR Region. 
    aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name drs-eventbridge-dr --region us-east-2
  3. Delete the SSM Automation documents and the stand-down parameter. 
    aws ssm delete-document --name DRS-Agent-Onboard --region us-west-1

aws ssm delete-document --name DRS-Agent-Heal --region us-west-1

aws ssm delete-document --name DRS-Agent-Offboard --region us-west-1

aws ssm delete-parameter --name /drs/control/event-in-progress --region us-west-1
  4. After the other stacks are deleted, delete the IAM role stack. 
    aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name drs-automation-iam --region us-west-1
  5. (Optional) If you created the SNS topic and S3 bucket only for this solution, delete them.

Conclusion

With a DR=yes tag in place, onboarding keeps the agent installed and registered, and healing restarts or reinstalls it when replication stalls. When you descope an instance, offboarding stops replication, removes the source server, and writes a JSON audit record to Amazon S3. That record tells you whether billing stopped or whether a partial teardown needs an operator’s follow-up. The whole lifecycle runs from one tag, without function code for your team to maintain.

The June 2023 post Deploying AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery at scale with AWS Systems Manager covered the initial install. This solution builds on it with ongoing health checks and offboarding.

Next steps

Start by cloning the repository and deploying it in audit mode in a test account. Tag a few instances with DR=yes and let onboarding run for a day. The audit reports in Amazon S3 show what the automation would install or repair on each instance, without changing anything. When the reports match what you expect, turn on installation for those instances. Then set DR=no on one of them to check the offboarding notification before you turn on teardown. If you have questions or improvements, open an issue in the GitHub repository.

Additional resources

  • AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery User Guide
  • AWS Systems Manager Automation
  • Amazon EventBridge cross-Region routing

About the authors

Manisha Yadav

Manisha is a Delivery Consultant with AWS Professional Services in Gurugram, India. She helps enterprise customers move workloads to AWS and then keep them recoverable, mostly with AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery and AWS Systems Manager. The automation in this post started as her answer to managing Replication Agents one instance at a time.

Danish Shamim

Danish is a Senior Delivery Consultant at AWS Professional Services, where he focuses on disaster recovery and large migrations. He helps enterprise customers protect and move their workloads, and he builds the automation and runbooks that keep those solutions running in production.

Vimal Bhati

Vimal helps AWS customers move workloads to AWS as a Delivery Consultant at AWS Professional Services. He works mostly on Infrastructure as Code with AWS CloudFormation, and he contributed the deployment tooling for this solution.
ai_summary: If you protect a large Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) fleet with AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (AWS DRS), you manage the AWS Replication Agent across its whole lifecycle. You install it, keep it healthy and registered, and remove it cleanly when a server leaves disaster recovery (DR) scope.

title: How BMW Group accelerated connected vehicle workloads on AWS Graviton
author: AWS Architecture Blog
description:
This post is co-written with Tomislav Lozancic, Hrvoje Lukavski from BMW Group, and Hugo Cardoso from CTW.

article_content:
This post is co-written with Tomislav Lozancic, Hrvoje Lukavski from BMW Group, and Hugo Cardoso from CTW.

BMW Connected Company, a division within BMW Group, develops and operates premium digital services for BMW’s connected vehicle fleet of more than 24.5 million vehicles worldwide. Critical TechWorks (CTW), established in September 2018, focuses exclusively on developing software for BMW Group’s future connected vehicle fleet.

In 2024, BMW Connected Company began migrating its Connected Vehicle platform, known internally as Orbit, from x86 to Arm-based compute as part of a broader modernization strategy to advance BMW Group’s economic and environmental goals.

In this post, we share the methodology behind the migration, tooling and patterns that helped application teams move to AWS Graviton at their own pace, without service disruption.

Laying the groundwork

Before applications could adopt a new processor architecture, the platform needed a more flexible provisioning layer. The team adopted Karpenter, replacing fixed Managed Node Groups with dynamic, policy-driven node pools that could provision the right instance type automatically. You can read more about this migration in Transforming the BMW Connected Vehicle Backend with Karpenter.

With the compute foundation in place, the next challenge was supporting multi-architecture builds. Building, testing, and deploying the same application for two architectures without slowing teams down required extending the continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) platform. Build runners needed to target both x86 and Arm while producing dual build pipelines, as described in the following section.

Introducing Graviton-based CI/CD runners

The Connected Vehicle CI/CD platform facilitates over 130,000 builds and deployments daily through self-hosted GitHub Actions runners. You can read more about the evolution of this platform in An Engine of Efficiency: BMW Group’s CI/CD Modernization Journey with AWS.

To surface potential issues early and minimize disruption, the team first validated Graviton on a set of self-contained services. Dedicated Graviton runners operated alongside the existing x86 fleet during this phase. The price-performance advantage of Graviton was confirmed immediately, with lower cost per build minute and faster build times, justifying the business case for wider adoption.

Building on these initial results, the team designed the wider platform rollout around two complementary tracks.

  1. Dual build pipelines: Building and shipping both CPU architectures in parallel, giving applications a non-disruptive path to transition independently.
  2. Container hosting: Extending support into the centralized container platform, so applications could be hosted on Graviton.

The following figure shows the six-stage journey to adopt AWS Graviton. The stages are grouped into two phases: a build-foundation phase and a workload-migration phase.

Figure 1: AWS Graviton adoption journey across the Connected Vehicle platform

Supporting adoption

Getting teams onto Graviton depended less on policy than on removing friction. The following practices lowered the barrier to entry, beginning with the build pipeline.

1 – Multi-architecture builds

As outlined earlier, every container image needed to support both architectures before workloads could run on Arm-based instances. To achieve this, two complementary build approaches were used: emulated builds using Docker Buildx with QEMU, and native builds on Graviton-based runners.

Both approaches produce multi-arch images by publishing a manifest list (OCI image index) alongside the architecture-specific images. When a container runtime pulls a tagged image, it reads the manifest and automatically selects the correct variant for the node’s architecture. This means a single image tag serves both arm64 and amd64 nodes transparently.

2 – Mirroring base images

Public images are mirrored into a private Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) to achieve availability, immutability, and CVE compliance. To preserve multi-arch support during mirroring, the team uses Google’s Crane. Crane transfers images directly between registries and filters the manifest to only the required platforms, which avoids wasted storage from unused architectures.

Besides public images, custom application workloads also needed support for both architectures. Most Dockerfiles required no changes, because their base images and dependencies already supported multiple architectures. In some cases, an alternative or dependency with Arm support needed to be found. For the builds, two approaches were considered:

  1. Native build per architecture: Each architecture is built and pushed separately on a runner with the matching architecture, followed by a final job that creates and pushes the image index. In GitHub Actions, this means one runner per architecture plus one index-creation step. This approach is more reliable but requires a dedicated runner for each target architecture.
  2. Emulated builds from a single machine: Using Docker Buildx with QEMU, all architectures can be built and pushed from a single x86 or Arm runner. This streamlines the pipeline but introduces emulation overhead, often making builds significantly slower for compute-intensive workloads.

The team opted to support both approaches. For platform-scale adoption, Graviton runners were preferred because they ran arm64 builds natively. This avoided the QEMU emulation overhead and surfaced architecture-specific issues earlier in the pipeline. With GitHub Actions reusable workflows, teams can select the right fit for each use case. Dockerfiles use the QEMU path to avoid spinning up additional runners. Those with significant complexity, large dependency downloads, or long build times use native builds, where the overhead becomes problematic.

Graviton runner labels mirror the existing x86 labels, so adoption involves swapping x64 for arm64 in a single label.

3 – Defining Graviton NodePools

The following diagram shows the mixed-architecture Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) cluster, including how on-premises systems connect and how the Graviton and x86 node pools coexist.

Figure 2: Mixed-architecture Amazon EKS cluster with dedicated Graviton node pools and opt-in scheduling

Dedicated Graviton node pools let teams adopt without friction across each environment. The pools are shared and general-purpose by default, not tailored to individual workloads. This keeps the underlying infrastructure model consistent and predictable while still allowing teams to migrate on their own schedule. Karpenter’s automatic scaling foundation supports efficient resource allocation and rapid provisioning for both Arm and x86 workloads.

To avoid accidental scheduling, the Graviton node pools use taints. Workloads must explicitly opt in using a node selector and matching toleration. This supports controlled rollout and predictable behavior:

nodeSelector:

bmw.de/stateless-arm: supported

tolerations:

- key: "bmw.de/stateless-arm"

operator: "Equal"

value: "supported"

effect: "NoSchedule"

With this in place, only Arm-ready workloads are scheduled on Graviton nodes, while other workloads continue to run on amd64 nodes without disruption.

4 – Phased rollout

Before supporting broad adoption for application workloads, the team first validated the migration path by running core platform services (Karpenter, Prometheus, and operational tooling). This platform-first approach identified compatibility gaps early, refined node pool configuration, and established rollback patterns. Teams had a proven reference model before they were encouraged to opt in.

A key design principle was minimizing rollback risk by keeping both architectures viable simultaneously. Dual-arch images and a dedicated NodePool mean every application can run on both CPU architectures. If issues arise, workloads fall back to x86 without image rebuilds or pipeline changes.

Kubernetes node affinity rules prefer Arm without forcing it, so workloads naturally gravitate toward Graviton instances:

{{/*

Workload node affinity

*/}}

{{- define "common.nodeaffinity" -}}

preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:

- weight: 100

preference:

matchExpressions:

- key: kubernetes.io/arch

operator: In

values:

- arm64

{{- end -}}

{{/*

Workload node tolerations

*/}}

{{- define "common.tolerations" -}}

- key: bmw.de/arm

operator: Equal

value: supported

effect: NoSchedule

{{- end -}}

If a full rollback is needed, the GitOps-based ArgoCD deployment model makes recovery straightforward by reverting to the previous version in Git and letting ArgoCD reconcile the cluster state.

Results

The migration delivered approximately $600,000 in annualized infrastructure savings and measurable performance improvements. After moving the NGINX-based ingress controller from x86 to Graviton, key results included:

  • CPU consumption decreased by approximately 57 percent, while maintaining the same ingress profile.
  • Price-performance improved by around 40 percent, as lower CPU consumption per request increased throughput capacity per dollar spent.
  • Scaling efficiency improved at peak loads, with workloads requiring less compute capacity to handle equivalent traffic volumes.

Today, more than 65 percent of the platform runs on Graviton across production environments, a shift that supports BMW Group’s sustainability goals by reducing compute energy demand.

Lessons learned

Migrating a platform of this scale surfaced practical lessons that shaped the team’s approach and would benefit others considering a similar transition:

  • Opt-in scheduling: Use taints, selectors, and tolerations to make sure that only ready workloads migrate.
  • Multi-architecture images: One manifest-based tag for both architectures keeps releases straightforward and rollback instant.
  • Platform-first adoption: Validate on shared infrastructure first to reduce risk before teams opt in.
  • Optimization of emulated builds: This approach is useful for straightforward pipelines. Compute-heavy builds should use native or cross-compilation paths instead, which avoids unnecessary QEMU overhead and long build times.

Conclusion

BMW Group migrated its Connected Vehicle platform to AWS Graviton, achieving over $600,000 in annual cost savings and a 40 percent improvement in price-performance. The more than 130,000 daily builds and deployments that power more than 24.5 million connected vehicles continued without disruption.

The migration succeeded because of deliberate, incremental choices: taint-based node isolation, multi-arch container builds, and Karpenter’s ability to provision the right instance at the right time. Each layer reduced risk while keeping the rollout optional for individual teams. What started as a platform experiment is now the default compute path.

To get started with Graviton-based workloads on Amazon EKS, see the AWS Graviton Getting Started guide. To learn how BMW Group adopted Karpenter at scale, read Transforming the BMW Connected Vehicle Backend with Karpenter.

About the authors

Tomislav is Lead Cloud Solution Architect at BMW Group, responsible for the Connected Vehicle platform overseeing more than 400 Amazon EKS clusters supporting 24.5+ million connected vehicles. With a degree in Computer Science, he specializes in cloud-native technologies and Kubernetes at scale. Tomislav focuses on optimizing cloud infrastructure for performance, cost efficiency, and reliability, playing a key role in BMW Group’s cloud strategy and mission-critical services.

Brendan Jones

Brendan is a Senior Solutions Architect at AWS for BMW Group. He is passionate about helping automotive customers build innovative, highly scalable, and resilient cloud architectures which maximize business impact for their customers.

Akshay is a Cloud Infrastructure Architect at AWS with over 14 years of experience in designing and implementing scalable, secure, and cost-efficient cloud solutions. He leads cloud transformation initiatives across multiple industries, helping customers modernize their infrastructure and optimize cloud operations. Akshay specializes in DevOps automation, FinOps strategies, and infrastructure-as-code frameworks to drive efficiency and innovation. In his free time, Akshay enjoys contributing to the cloud and DevOps community through technical writing, open-source projects, and mentoring professionals in their cloud journey.

Hrvoje is Lead Product Manager at BMW Group, driving the development of the Connected Vehicle Platform and ensuring its quality and future-readiness. A FinOps Champion and Chaos Engineering pioneer, he advises executive leadership on cloud strategy and believes the best engineering disappears into the product.

Hugo is a DevOps Engineer at Critical TechWorks. With a background in software engineering, he applies a developer’s mindset to platform and infrastructure challenges by connecting systems and extending them with software when needed. He focuses on breaking down complex problems while maintaining strong security and tenancy boundaries, delivering solutions that keep platforms simple and intuitive for both their users and maintainers.

title: How boAt delivers personalized fitness coaching with Amazon Bedrock
author: AWS Architecture Blog
description:
This post is co-written with Sridhara Seshadri from KaHa Technologies Pvt Ltd, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Imagine Marketing Limited (IML).

Recognizing that users need more than raw fitness data, boAt launched the “AI Coach” feature. It uses a combination of user history, preferences, and generative AI to deliver personalized coaching plans in real time. Using AWS, boAt built a solution that delivers personalized AI coaching. The AI Coach feature has been in production for o...
article_content:
This post is co-written with Sridhara Seshadri from KaHa Technologies Pvt Ltd, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Imagine Marketing Limited (IML).

Recognizing that users need more than raw fitness data, boAt launched the “AI Coach” feature. It uses a combination of user history, preferences, and generative AI to deliver personalized coaching plans in real time. Using AWS, boAt built a solution that delivers personalized AI coaching. The AI Coach feature has been in production for over six months, reliably serving millions of boAt smartwatch users across India. In this post, we explore how boAt built the AI Coach on Amazon Bedrock and AWS Lambda, and the design choices that made it scalable and cost-effective.

Imagine Marketing Limited primarily operates under the brand boAt, launched in 2015 in the consumer electronics industry, focused on mass-premium, lifestyle-oriented products for India’s young, tech-savvy consumers at accessible price points. Starting with audio, boAt has expanded into adjacent categories such as wearables and charging solutions, selling through online marketplaces, D2C, and offline retail. In FY 2025, boAt led India’s branded personal audio with strong value and volume shares, sold over 34 million units in India as reported in FounderPin, and ranked among the top global audio brands by volume. Its agile, digital-first model drives rapid innovation, wide reach, and faster time-to-market aligned with evolving consumer preferences.

Opportunity

With the emergence of advanced AI capabilities, boAt saw an opportunity to deliver a highly personalized fitness coaching experience for its smartwatch users. The core objective was to help users build and sustain fitness and wellness habits aligned with their lifestyles. These recommendations needed to be straightforward for users to follow while clearly communicating their value.

The three primary design principles were personalization, affordability, and scalability.

Solution architecture

The following shows a simplified high-level architecture of the AI Coach components deployed on AWS.

Figure 1: High-level architecture of the boAt AI Coach on AWS

The following sections provide a brief overview of the architecture and its key components.

  1. Data source: The boAt smartwatch serves as the primary data source, capturing metrics such as steps, user activities (for example, running or yoga), and sleep data. All data is encrypted at rest and in transit. The boAt Crest companion app for iOS and Android also captures additional data points, such as the user’s preferred communication style and fitness goals for a predefined period.
  2. Historical data: Historical user data, when available, plays a key role in personalizing plans. These data points are transmitted by the companion application to backend servers and stored in Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for MySQL and Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility). When the AI coach creates a plan, this historical data provides important context about what the user has done earlier.
  3. AWS Lambda: This component plays several roles:
    • It acts as a translation layer, transforming input data into a format suitable for large language models (LLMs) and converting model outputs into a format the companion application can parse and interpret. This layer also abstracts the underlying AI coach implementation.
    • On the input side, the data sent through the API is in a legacy format optimized for database operations. This is mapped to a more verbose format so that LLMs can better interpret what each key means.
    • On the output side, the system handles missing keys in the generated plan by substituting safe defaults and verifying that the response format remains consistent with the companion application’s requirements.
    • For production deployments, consider placing the Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance in a private subnet and exposing it through an Amazon API Gateway private integration using a VPC link.

The AI Coach feature has two main logical pieces:

  1. Personalized plan generation.
  2. Nudges to aid adherence to the plan.

We use the Meta Llama 3.3 70B Instruct model on Amazon Bedrock to implement the AI Coach feature. For model availability by Region, see Region availability at a glance.

AWS Lambda retrieves historical user data for a predefined period in accordance with applicable privacy laws from the boAt Crest Companion app (full historical data is stored in Amazon RDS and Amazon DocumentDB), supplies it as context to the LLM for personalized plan generation, and parses the model response for the client. The team uses Amazon Bedrock on-demand inference exclusively, with structured data retrieval and prompt construction handled within Lambda. As adoption grows, they plan to transition to Amazon Bedrock batch inference to optimize costs at scale.

The plan is personalized to each user based on the inputs provided by the user during onboarding to this feature and historical user data patterns. The architecture was designed in such a way that future changes in user inputs don’t need a change in the backend components.

Relevant nudges are sent to the user at different times of each day, based on their actual metrics compared to the recommended ones. The style and tone of the nudges are offered as a configuration for the end user. These range from informational and objective to pop-culture and sarcastic, with a wide variety of style packs to choose from.

After evaluating options, the team selected the AWS Lambda and Amazon Bedrock combination for three reasons:

  1. Model-agnostic access: The unified API in Amazon Bedrock let the team evaluate multiple foundation models (including Meta Llama 3.3) through a single integration. This avoided the need to build separate pipelines for each LLM and accelerated model selection.
  2. Built-in observability and cost governance: Amazon Bedrock publishes per-invocation metrics (token counts, latency, and error rates) directly to Amazon CloudWatch, and it supports application inference profiles with cost allocation tags to attribute usage by tenant, feature, or environment. Combined with the average Lambda execution-time metrics, this gave the team precise per-user unit economics from day one, without building custom metering infrastructure.
  3. Serverless scalability with zero infrastructure overhead: The on-demand inference mode in Amazon Bedrock requires no provisioned compute. It scales automatically with usage and charges only per token processed. As AI Coach adoption grows, the team can extend throughput through cross-Region inference profiles that dynamically route requests across AWS Regions, without changes to their Lambda-based backend or impact to the end user experience.

Throughout development, the team applied responsible AI practices—including output validation, safe default substitution for missing response keys, and prompt constraints limiting recommendations to watch-supported activities—to deliver a trustworthy and safe user experience.

The following screenshots illustrate the AI Coach onboarding experience, where users set their fitness goals, preferred activities, workout frequency, sleep schedule, and stress levels to generate a fully personalized coaching plan.

Beyond the user-facing experience shown in the preceding screenshots, the development journey involved several technical and design challenges worth highlighting. The following are notable challenges the team encountered during development and real-world testing.

  1. Personalizing plans effectively: During the initial testing phase, the generated plans were not personalized enough to meet our expectations. The data the companion app provides is in JSON format, made of key-value pairs. We found that the keys needed to be more descriptive for the LLM to interpret the data effectively. For example, weight became weight_in_kg, and target became step_goal. We spent considerable time verifying that each legacy key was expanded and made as descriptive as possible. This higher level of descriptiveness significantly improved plan personalization.
  2. Smartwatch capability matching: Recommended activities in the plan, such as swimming, had to align with the user’s onboarding preferences, their overall goals, and the smartwatch’s capability to support those activities. We added a dedicated section to the prompt that lists watch-supported activities, which reduced the likelihood of unsupported recommendations. However, because of the non-deterministic nature of LLMs, prompt optimization alone did not eliminate all errors. We therefore added a parsing layer and suitable defaults to handle exception cases.

Conclusion

The boAt AI Coach demonstrates how generative AI can transform raw smartwatch data into personalized, actionable wellness guidance at scale. By combining Amazon Bedrock, AWS Lambda, and thoughtful prompt engineering, the team shipped a production-grade feature that serves millions of users without sacrificing personalization or reliability. To learn more about the boAt AI Coach and explore the technologies behind it, check out the following resources:

  • Read about how the AI Coach in boAt smartwatches can improve your fitness
  • Explore Amazon Bedrock for building generative AI applications
  • Explore the boAt Chrome Eon smartwatch featuring AI Coach

About the authors

Natasha Sah

Natasha is a Solutions Architect based in the APAC region, where she collaborates with customers across IT/ITeS industry to architect scalable, cost-effective solutions on AWS. With expertise spanning generative AI and agentic developer productivity, she focuses on turning emerging AI capabilities into measurable results by helping teams weave AI into their workflows and products to accelerate how they build and ship.

Sridhara Seshadri

Sridhara is the Solution Architect at KaHa Technologies Pvt Ltd, the technology partner powering the boAt smartwatch application. With over 25 years of experience spanning networking, connected devices, mobile platforms, cloud technologies and artificial intelligence, he designs and delivers scalable products from ideation to production. His work spans solution architecture, software engineering, and data science where he partners with cross-functional teams to build intelligent, user-centric experiences.

title: How Revinate accelerated API adoption with Amazon API Gateway
author: AWS Architecture Blog
description:
Accelerating API adoption while reducing operational overhead is a challenge that every growing organization faces. For Revinate, a hospitality provider serving over 12,500 hotels worldwide and powering more than 1.25 billion guest profiles, Amazon API Gateway became the foundation of their solution.

Revinate empowers hoteliers to connect directly with guests at every touchpoint, driving $24 billion in li...
article_content:
Accelerating API adoption while reducing operational overhead is a challenge that every growing organization faces. For Revinate, a hospitality provider serving over 12,500 hotels worldwide and powering more than 1.25 billion guest profiles, Amazon API Gateway became the foundation of their solution.

Revinate empowers hoteliers to connect directly with guests at every touchpoint, driving $24 billion in lifetime direct revenue through an AI-powered Customer Data Platform (CDP) that helps reduce reliance on online travel agencies (OTAs) and deliver data-driven insights.

With the expansion of CDP capabilities, Revinate needed to expose rich guest data through APIs, so that hotel properties and partners can programmatically access guest profiles, reservation data, and other critical hospitality information.

This post explores how Revinate used Amazon API Gateway and the newly released Amazon API Gateway Portal to create a scalable, secure, and developer-friendly API program.

Business need: Evolving API infrastructure to match growth

As Revinate expanded its CDP capabilities and began exposing guest profile and reservation data through APIs, the limitations of managing API infrastructure in-house became clear. Each new partner integration required manual provisioning, custom security configuration, and ongoing maintenance. The team needed an API gateway solution that could scale with growing partner demand without adding operational burden. Rather than building and maintaining a self-hosted solution, Revinate wanted an approach that would open up engineering time, streamline partner integrations, and align infrastructure costs with actual usage. The team identified four key business drivers:

  • Operational efficiency and agility – Accelerate API deployment cycles and reduce time spent on infrastructure maintenance so the engineering team can focus on building features that directly serve customers.
  • Faster partner and developer onboarding – Helping external developers and partners to discover and adopt Revinate’s APIs required a faster, more self-service experience.
  • Growth aligned costs – Infrastructure costs needed to scale proportionately with revenue generation. An on-demand pricing model, where costs flex with actual API usage rather than fixed overhead, was essential to support sustainable growth. Equally important was the ability to attribute API costs per consumer, enabling transparent cost allocation across hotel properties and partners.
  • Enhanced security and compliance – API security controls including authentication, authorization, rate limiting, and threat protection. Meeting compliance requirements and maintaining customer trust demanded strong security without adding complexity to the development workflow or requiring the team to build and maintain custom security infrastructure.

These requirements shaped the team’s evaluation of available solutions.

Evaluating alternatives

When evaluating API gateway solutions, the team translated the business drivers into four core technical requirements. On-demand pricing was essential to align infrastructure costs with actual API usage and enable per-consumer cost attribution. Authentication federation allows integration with Revinate’s existing identity provider, so partners can onboard faster without building custom auth infrastructure. Rate limiting was needed to protect backend services and enforce fair usage across hotel properties and partners as the API program scales. Finally, strong security, including threat protection, audit logging, and access controls, was required to meet compliance requirements for protecting sensitive guest data.

The engineering team evaluated three approaches. Each approach came with distinct tradeoffs across cost, flexibility, and operational burden.

Self-managed API management

Deploying a self-managed API gateway would provide flexibility and avoid licensing fees, but requires ongoing infrastructure management, security patching, scaling, and monitoring. The team would also need to build a custom developer portal from scratch.

Custom-built

Building a proprietary API gateway tailored to Revinate’s exact needs offers maximum control but demands significant upfront development investment and ongoing maintenance. Every capability, including routing, authentication, rate limiting, and documentation, would need to be built and maintained in-house, diverting engineering resources from core hospitality platform features.

Enterprise API management platforms

Enterprise platforms offer comprehensive out-of-the-box features, but introduce vendor dependencies, higher costs, and fixed-term licensing models where costs misalign with revenue growth.

All three approaches shared a common drawback: they would divert resources, whether engineering time, budget, or both, toward capabilities that don’t differentiate Revinate’s product, delaying time-to-market for features that directly serve hotel customers.

The solution: Amazon API Gateway with Developer Portal

Revinate needed the comprehensive capabilities of an enterprise API management platform without the fixed-term licensing, vendor dependencies, and operational overhead. Amazon API Gateway, combined with the newly released Amazon API Gateway Portal, delivered exactly that, aligning with both the technical requirements and business objectives that shaped the evaluation.

Fully managed infrastructure

Amazon API Gateway removes the need to manage underlying infrastructure, so the engineering team can focus on the core hospitality solution rather than API gateway operations.

Native AWS integration

Amazon API Gateway provides native integration with other AWS services, including Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) for backend services and AWS Lambda authorizers for federated authentication with an external identity provider. This allows Revinate to authenticate API consumers against the existing identity provider infrastructure with minimal development effort.

Infrastructure as code with Terraform

The team maintains strict infrastructure-as-code practices, using Terraform exclusively for all production deployments. The AWS provider for Terraform enables defining the Amazon API Gateway configuration, including REST APIs, stages, usage plans, and authorizers as version-controlled code. This approach verifies consistency across environments, enables peer review of infrastructure changes, and provides complete audit trails for compliance requirements. The declarative nature of Terraform enables rapidly iterating on the API Gateway configuration during development while maintaining confidence in production deployments.

Cost-effective pay-per-use model

Amazon API Gateway’s pay-per-use pricing model aligned perfectly with Revinate’s growth strategy. During the initial rollout phase, costs remained minimal and scaled naturally as new API consumers onboarded. Usage plans allow Revinate to track and attribute costs per consumer, providing clear visibility into which hotel properties and partners drive API usage. This per-consumer cost attribution, combined with tiered pricing that scales from tens to hundreds of customers, replaced fixed annual licensing fees that required upfront investment regardless of actual usage.

Managed Developer Portal

The November 2025 release of Amazon API Gateway Portal provided a fully managed, AWS-native Developer Portal that served as the central hub for API discovery, documentation, and governance. This removes months of custom development work that building a comparable solution would require.

Developers can use the managed portal to:

  • Set up a branded Developer Portal in minutes rather than months.
  • Provide hotel property developers with self-service API discovery and interactive documentation.
  • Maintain centralized control over API documentation freshness and access governance.
  • Deliver a professional developer experience that accelerates customer onboarding from weeks to days.

Strong security

API Gateway provides built-in security features that meet stringent requirements for protecting sensitive guest data:

  • OAuth2 client credentials for machine-to-machine (M2M) authentication.
  • Authorization logic using AWS Lambda authorizers integrating with an external identity provider of choice.
  • Request throttling and quota management to prevent abuse.
  • Integration with AWS WAF and Amazon CloudFront for layered protection against common web exploits and DDoS threats.
  • Comprehensive audit logging through AWS CloudTrail for compliance and access tracking.
  • Real-time observability through Amazon CloudWatch metrics and dashboards, with support for streaming to third-party observability platforms.

Architecture overview

The solution uses a modern, scalable AWS architecture designed to serve hotel properties globally. Hotel properties access the platform as API consumers through Amazon CloudFront for edge caching and low-latency responses, with AWS WAF providing comprehensive protection against common web threats and bots. Requests flow through Amazon API Gateway, which serves as the unified entry point for API operations. Lambda authorizers handle authentication and authorization by integrating with an identity provider (IdP) to provide secure, token-based access control for each request. After authentication, API Gateway routes traffic to backend services running on Amazon EKS, providing the flexibility and scalability needed for containerized microservices. The EKS application layer orchestrates requests to the Customer Data Platform.

Figure 1: Architecture diagram showing the end-to-end flow from hotel property consumers accessing the Amazon API Gateway Portal, through Amazon API Gateway, to backend services running on Amazon EKS.

Connecting API Gateway to EKS

A critical design decision emerged: how to securely and efficiently connect API Gateway to backend services in Amazon EKS while keeping traffic within the AWS backbone network using VPC Link. The team evaluated four options:

Option 1: NGINX ingress controller: Route traffic through a Kubernetes-native NGINX Ingress Controller with a Load Balancer service.

Pros: Highly customizable routing, flexible header manipulation, consistent with common Kubernetes patterns.

Cons: Adds extra latency hop, requires manual lifecycle management (upgrades, configs, scaling), non-AWS-native monitoring.

Option 2: AWS load balancer controller: Use the AWS Load Balancer Controller to manage LB resources as Kubernetes Ingress objects.

Pros: Bridges AWS and Kubernetes natively, supports path-based routing, AWS-managed Load Balancer (LB) lifecycle.

Cons: Introduces an additional hop (Amazon API Gateway → LB → service).

Option 3: Target group binding: Directly bind Amazon EKS pods to Network Load Balancer (NLB) Target Groups using the AWS Load Balancer Controller’s TargetGroupBinding feature.

Pros: Removes ingress controller overhead, lowest latency, native AWS integration, cost-efficient (shared NLB across multiple Target Groups), fine-grained control over health checks and scaling.

Cons: More complex initial setup, less Kubernetes-native (more AWS-specific), different applications will need individual NLB.

Option 4: LoadBalancer service: Expose each service directly via a Kubernetes LoadBalancer service (NLB/ALB).

Pros: Most straightforward setup, minimal routing complexity, no ingress controller needed.

Cons: No path-based routing, costly at scale (each service requires its own load balancer), limited observability, requires TLS offloading configuration, different applications will need individual NLB.

The team selected Target group binding because it effectively balances performance, cost-efficiency, and AWS-native integration. By removing the extra hop introduced by traditional ingress controllers, this approach provides direct control over Target Groups and health checks while maintaining sub-second latency at scale.

Security implementation

The API Gateway implementation uses OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow with an external identity provider, delivering strong authentication for machine-to-machine (M2M) communication. This approach provides secure, scalable access control as Revinate onboards new hotel properties and partners.

API Gateway enforces usage plans with configurable throttling and quota limits, for fair usage and protection against abuse.

Figure 2: Sequence diagram illustrating the OAuth 2.0 authentication flow using AWS Lambda authorizers.

AWS Lambda authorizers take the caller’s identity as the input and return an IAM policy as the output. This architecture provides flexibility to implement sophisticated authorization logic while maintaining the simplicity of the API Gateway managed infrastructure. The team also deploys and manages the Lambda authorizer functions through Terraform, maintaining infrastructure as code (IaC) standards.

Developer Portal experience

The Amazon API Gateway Portal serves as the central hub for the API operations, providing developers using APIs with a streamlined experience.

Figure 3: User interface flow showing the developer journey through the Amazon API Gateway Portal, including API discovery, interactive documentation with try-it-now functionality, and subscription management.

Developers can:

  • Browse available REST APIs with comprehensive documentation.
  • Test API endpoints directly in the portal with interactive examples.
  • Access code samples and integration guides.

This self-service model reduced burden on support while accelerating customer time-to-value.

Results and benefits

The implementation of Amazon API Gateway and the Developer Portal delivered significant qualitative benefits across operational efficiency, developer experience, and business scalability.

Reduced operational overhead

By choosing a fully managed API gateway, the engineering team avoided the burden of maintaining, scaling, and troubleshooting self-hosted infrastructure. With the fully managed API gateway, the team can focus on core platform innovations that directly benefit hotel customers rather than undifferentiated gateway operations.

Improved developer experience

The centralized Developer Portal transformed the integration experience for hotel properties and partners. Self-service API discovery and interactive documentation reduced onboarding time from weeks to days. Developers consistently praised the professional portal experience and comprehensive documentation.

Accelerated customer onboarding

With the Developer Portal’s self-service capabilities, new customers can discover APIs and begin integration without waiting for manual provisioning or support intervention. This self-service approach positions Revinate to scale API access to hundreds of hotel properties and partners as demand grows.

Enhanced governance and control

The solution centralized control over API documentation, versioning, and access policies, verifying consistency across customer integrations. A single source of truth for API specifications removes documentation drift and reduces integration errors. Managing infrastructure through Terraform verifies changes follow proper review and approval processes.

Cost optimization

The pay-per-use pricing model aligns costs with actual usage and revenue generation. Usage plans and API keys provide per-consumer cost attribution, giving Revinate clear visibility into infrastructure spend by customer. As usage scales, tiered pricing verifies predictable cost growth that tracks with business value, replacing fixed licensing models that require upfront investment regardless of adoption.

Positioned for growth

The API layer, from Amazon API Gateway to the Developer Portal, scales automatically to meet demand without capacity planning or operational intervention. The team can confidently pursue growth targets knowing the API infrastructure will scale automatically.

Enhanced security posture

Amazon API Gateway provides strong security capabilities built into the platform, including centralized authentication and authorization mechanisms, request throttling and rate limiting to protect against abuse, and automatic threat protection through AWS Shield integration. Built-in security capabilities remove the need to build and maintain custom infrastructure while verifying consistent security policies across API endpoints. The centralized approach reduces the attack surface and provides comprehensive audit trails through CloudWatch integration, so the team can maintain robust security without additional operational overhead.

Key takeaways

The successful implementation of Amazon API Gateway and the Amazon API Gateway Portal offers valuable lessons for organizations exposing APIs to external customers and partners:

Managed services accelerate time-to-market – By using fully managed infrastructure and the new Amazon API Gateway Portal, the team avoided months of custom development work and launched the API program faster than would have been possible with self-managed alternatives.

Developer experience drives adoption – The professional, self-service Amazon API Gateway Portal significantly reduced friction in the customer onboarding process, so API access can rapidly scale as new hotel properties and partners onboard.

Infrastructure as code verifies consistency – Using Terraform for all production deployments provided the infrastructure team with version control, peer review, and audit trails while maintaining deployment consistency across environments.

Pay-per-use aligns costs with value – For organizations in growth mode, pay-per-use pricing removes the risk of overcommitting to fixed costs before achieving product-market fit with API offerings.

OAuth 2.0 delivers strong security at scale – Implementing OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow with an external identity provider enables a robust, scalable authentication foundation that grows securely alongside its expanding customer base.

Native AWS integration reduces complexity – For organizations already running on AWS, API Gateway’s native integration with services like EKS, Lambda, and CloudWatch minimizes architectural complexity and operational overhead.

Future enhancements

With the outbound API program successfully launched, the team is planning to extend API Gateway to inbound APIs, where partners push data into Revinate’s service. This will provide consistent security, monitoring, and governance across API traffic.

The team is also exploring advanced API Gateway features including request and response transformation, caching for improved performance, and deeper integration with AWS WAF for enhanced security against evolving threats.

Conclusion

Choosing Amazon API Gateway with the Developer Portal demonstrates how fully managed services can accelerate innovation while reducing operational complexity. By embracing AWS-native solutions and infrastructure-as-code practices, Revinate built a scalable, secure API program that supports growth as more customers get onboarded.

As the hospitality industry continues its digital transformation, this API-first approach positions them to empower hoteliers with the data and integrations needed to deliver exceptional guest experiences and drive direct revenue growth.

Next steps

Whether you’re in hospitality, software as a service (SaaS), healthcare, or any industry where partners and customers need programmatic access to your service, the pattern Revinate followed is broadly applicable. Start by mapping your business drivers to concrete technical requirements. This grounds your API gateway choices in outcomes, not only features. From there, explore Amazon API Gateway’s REST and HTTP API options to find the right fit for your traffic patterns and integration needs. Use the Amazon API Gateway Portal to give your developers a self-service onboarding experience from day one. If you’re already running workloads on AWS, the native integration with services like EKS, Lambda, and CloudWatch means you can build on your existing architecture rather than introducing new operational complexity. For teams that follow infrastructure as code practices, the Terraform AWS Provider for API Gateway helps you to define your entire API configuration as version-controlled code. To get started, visit the Amazon API Gateway documentation or reach out to your AWS account team for architecture guidance tailored to your use case and scale.
