title: Data governance with annotations in Amazon S3
author: AWS Architecture Blog
description: If you run data governance in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), the context that matters most probably lives somewhere other than S3. Think of how an object is classified, which retention policy applies to it, where the data may reside, and whether it holds personally identifiable information (PII). You typically keep that context in a separate database, one system away from the objects it describes.
article_content:
If you run data governance in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), the context that matters most probably lives somewhere other than S3. Think of how an object is classified, which retention policy applies to it, where the data may reside, and whether it holds personally identifiable information (PII). You typically keep that context in a separate database, one system away from the objects it describes.

Amazon S3 annotations closes that gap. You can attach the governance context directly to the S3 object, without rewriting the object. A single object version can carry up to 1,000 annotations. Each one is a UTF-8 payload between 1 byte and 1 MB, in a format such as JSON, XML, YAML, or plain text. That’s room for a complete governance record rather than a few key-value pairs.

Annotations give you five properties that are hard to get from a separate metadata store:

  • Context that travels with the data – S3 stores annotations with the object version rather than in a separate system. When you copy or replicate an object, S3 moves the annotations with it, so a classification or residency label accompanies a disaster-recovery copy.
  • Context you can revise in place – Updating an annotation doesn’t rewrite the object or change its ETag, so a record’s classification can be corrected, or a generated label promoted from proposed to reviewed, as the context is validated.
  • Governance answers without reading the data – A consumer with read-only annotation access can answer a question such as “which objects hold PII and have an expired retention policy” per object through the annotation APIs, or across the bucket through an S3 Metadata annotation table.
  • Context stays readable in any storage class – Even when an object is archived in a cold storage class, its annotations stay directly readable. You can retrieve the governance context for an object in Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive without restoring the object first. You pay S3 Standard rates for annotations regardless of the parent object’s storage class.
  • SQL at scale – An S3 Metadata annotation table, which is an Apache Iceberg table, makes the same context queryable with Amazon Athena or any Iceberg-compatible engine across a large object population.

This post walks through the pattern end to end, then the handful of S3 behaviors that determine whether the design is correct. Each behavior comes with the documented rule and a working example: an annotation payload, an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policy statement, or an AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) call.

Prerequisites

To follow along and adapt the examples, you need the following:

  • An AWS account with an S3 bucket that has versioning enabled.
  • An AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal with permission to configure bucket policies and annotation actions.
  • The AWS CLI installed and configured.

Familiarity with S3 annotations concepts, object versioning, and IAM identity-based policies is assumed.

The governance record

Consider a governed bucket where each object is a business record such as a contract, policy document, or customer record. You build an enrichment pipeline that reads each new object and records a governance annotation. That annotation captures the classification, the applicable retention policy, the jurisdiction and data residency, a PII inventory, and a short rationale. Annotations aren’t limited to governance context. The same mechanism can attach other object context, such as a short content summary or a processing date. In this pattern, the annotation is written after the upload completes, through the annotation API operations. The same process backfills objects that predate the pipeline, through the separate path shown in the architecture section.

A PutObjectAnnotation call writes exactly one uniquely named annotation on a given object version, and an object version can hold up to 1,000 annotations. How you distribute a governance record across them is a design choice. With granular annotations, you can update one aspect of the context without rewriting the rest, keep an accidental overwrite scoped to a single field, and query finer-grained units in an S3 Metadata annotation table, which you optionally enable for richer queryability. A single annotation that holds the whole record keeps each write and each read to one operation, and keeps the record internally consistent. There’s no partial state across several names to reconcile. This post uses one annotation, named governance-context, because the record here is authored and consumed as a unit.

The payload looks like the following.

{

"schema_version": "1.0",

"classification": "confidential",

"retention": {

"policy": "contracts-7y",

"effective_date": "2026-06-01",

"expires_on": "2033-06-01",

"status": "active"

},

"jurisdiction": "EU",

"data_residency": "eu-west-1",

"pii": {

"present": true,

"categories": ["name", "email", "national_id"]

},

"rationale": "Signed customer contract containing personal data of EU data subjects; classified confidential under the 7-year contracts retention policy.",

"generated_by": "enrichment-process",

"generated_at": "2026-06-29T10:15:00Z",

"review_required": true

}

When a record is reviewed or reclassified, the enrichment process updates the annotation in place with PutObjectAnnotation. The classification changes without rewriting the object or changing its ETag. That in-place update is itself replicated, so a later re-classification on the source keeps a cross-Region copy’s context current without recopying the object. This works as long as the replication role carries the annotation-replication permission described later in this post.

Objects that predate the pipeline need the same context. A backfill pass annotates existing object versions in bulk with the same PutObjectAnnotation call, so the write path covers new objects as they arrive while the backfill path brings the existing population up to the same standard. Both paths appear in the architecture that follows.

On the read side, a consumer with read-only annotation access answers the governance question by listing and retrieving annotation context. There are no object reads and no separate governance database.

At scale, you activate an S3 Metadata annotation table with a bucket metadata configuration that names an IAM role S3 assumes to read your annotations. S3 then provisions and maintains a table in Amazon S3 Tables, a capability of Amazon S3, backed by Apache Iceberg, that you query with SQL. The role trusts the metadata.s3.amazonaws.com service principal. That turns the same question into one Athena statement across a large object population. S3 populates the table asynchronously, and the initial backfill can take minutes to hours depending on how many objects and annotations the bucket holds. Query results reflect annotations as of the most recent table refresh, which typically happens within about an hour, so treat them as eventually consistent rather than real time.

SELECT object_key, object_version_id

FROM "s3tablescatalog/aws-s3"."b_amzn_s3_demo_governance"."annotation"

WHERE name = 'governance-context'

AND json_extract_scalar(text_value, '$.pii.present') = 'true'

AND json_extract_scalar(text_value, '$.retention.status') = 'expired';

Reference architecture for the pattern

The pattern sits inside an event-driven system with S3 at the center, shown in Figure 1. It carries four paths. A write path enriches new objects, a maintenance path keeps context current, a backfill path annotates existing objects, and a read path serves consumers from annotation context alone.

Figure 1: Event-driven architecture for authoring, maintaining, backfilling, and reading S3 annotation governance context.

The numbered steps in Figure 1 trace the four paths:

  1. A producer uploads an object to the governed S3 bucket with PutObject.
  2. S3 emits an object-created event to Amazon EventBridge. When you route through Amazon EventBridge rather than invoking AWS Lambda directly from S3, you can filter on event attributes such as prefix or object size. You can also route the same event to multiple targets without changing the bucket configuration. A direct notification or an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue is a reasonable simpler choice if you don’t need that routing.
  3. Amazon EventBridge invokes the enrichment Lambda function.
  4. The function calls the Amazon Bedrock enrichment agent to classify the object and extract retention, jurisdiction, and PII context. The agent returns the structured context to the function (dashed return arrow). Have the function validate that the output parses as JSON and conforms to your schema before it writes anything. Models often wrap JSON in a Markdown code fence, and an annotation payload must be the raw structured document.
  5. The function writes the context to the object with PutObjectAnnotation. The write emits an s3:ObjectAnnotation:Put event notification that downstream consumers can subscribe to, which fits the event-driven design.
  6. On a schedule, Amazon EventBridge Scheduler re-invokes the enrichment function to re-assess and update annotations in place.
  7. To annotate objects that predate the pipeline, S3 Batch Operations invokes a backfill Lambda function.
  8. The backfill function writes context with PutObjectAnnotation.
  9. A consumer asks the Bedrock consumer agent a governance question, and the agent returns a grounded answer (dashed return arrow).
  10. The consumer agent lists and retrieves the relevant annotations with ListObjectAnnotations and GetObjectAnnotation. S3 returns annotation context only, never the object body (dashed return arrow).
  11. For queries across many objects, the consumer agent queries Athena.
  12. Athena reads the S3 Metadata annotation table, which S3 maintains automatically from the object annotations (dashed “maintains” relationship).

The scheduled update in step 6 needs one guard: a conditional write on the object’s ETag. Pass the ETag with the --object-if-match CLI parameter, which maps to the x-amz-object-if-match request header.

An ETag is the identifier S3 returns for an object version’s content. The function reads it when it fetches the object and passes it back on the write. If the object was overwritten in the meantime, the ETag no longer matches and the annotation write fails. That guards against overwriting context that belongs to a version the function never evaluated.

The behaviors that decide your design

The plumbing is straightforward. The behaviors in this section are where teams most often get a governance design wrong. Each behavior appears in the documentation, and each has a governance implication that becomes clear only when you trace it through. One principle predicts most of them:

An annotation is caller-authored context bound to a specific object version. S3 stores it and moves it, but it doesn’t interpret or validate its meaning. The annotation’s lifecycle follows the object version’s lifecycle.

Two consequences follow. Because an annotation is bound to an object version, versioning behavior governs whether your context stays or disappears: delete markers, version-specific deletes, and overwrites all change what remains attached. And because S3 doesn’t interpret the content, a classification your agent writes is only as trustworthy as the process that produced it. For each behavior, ask what the annotation is bound to, and what the object version’s lifecycle does in that situation.

Deletion is scoped to the object version

A common governance requirement is to delete a data subject’s records on request. The annotation is bound to a specific object version, so it disappears only when that version disappears. Deleting the object and assuming its context goes with it is correct only in a non-versioned bucket.

In a versioned bucket, a DELETE request without a version ID creates a delete marker and leaves the underlying version, along with its annotations, in place. The object no longer appears in a ListObjectsV2 response, so it looks gone. It’s still returned by ListObjectVersions, and the PII context you recorded still exists on that prior version.

To actually remove the annotations, delete the specific version.

aws s3api delete-object \

--bucket amzn-s3-demo-governance \

--key contracts/acme-msa.pdf \

--version-id

To expire noncurrent versions on a schedule instead, apply an S3 Lifecycle configuration such as the following. It permanently deletes noncurrent versions 30 days after they become noncurrent.

{

"Rules": [

{

"ID": "expire-noncurrent-governed-records",

"Filter": { "Prefix": "contracts/" },

"Status": "Enabled",

"NoncurrentVersionExpiration": { "NoncurrentDays": 30 }

}

]

}

A lifecycle rule expires versions on a time schedule. It can’t read annotation values. If you want an object’s classification or retention status to trigger expiration or deletion, your own automation has to read the annotation and issue the delete. If the trigger you need is an event rather than a value, such as a contract closing or an audit completing, Object Lock event holds handle that natively and you don’t need to build the automation.

Don’t rely on a plain delete for a right-to-be-forgotten workflow in a versioned bucket. Decide up front whether you will issue version-targeted deletes or expire noncurrent versions, make that the only supported path in your tooling, and test it against a real object. The failure mode is silent. Version-targeted deletion is also permanent, so tooling that deletes the wrong version destroys data that is recoverable only from a separate backup.

Object Lock freezes annotations

Governance buckets frequently use S3 Object Lock, and annotations count as modifications to the object version, which Object Lock blocks. While a version is under an active Object Lock retention, PutObjectAnnotation and DeleteObjectAnnotation are both denied with AccessDenied and the message “object protected by object lock retention,” in both Governance and Compliance mode. Reading annotations still works, so consumers are unaffected. What you can’t do is add or update a governance annotation on a version whose retention has already started.

That makes sequencing a design rule: Annotate the object first, then apply the retention period. An annotation written before the lock survives and remains readable, but it’s frozen until retention expires. If your agent re-assesses classifications over time, plan the retention duration and the enrichment cadence together. Where retention starts on a future event rather than at write time, there’s no known end to that frozen window when you annotate, so write the complete governance record before the hold goes on.

The retention mode also changes the right-to-be-forgotten path. In Governance mode, a version-targeted delete of a locked version is denied unless the caller holds s3:BypassGovernanceRetention and passes --bypass-governance-retention. That workflow therefore needs the permission and an approval step around it. In Compliance mode, no one can delete the version, including the root user, until retention expires, so a request may not be satisfiable before then.

Event holds add a third case. A version under an event hold is protected while the hold is in place. Releasing the hold starts the retention period rather than ending protection, so releasing it moves a deletion request further away rather than closer. IAM and bucket policy condition keys govern who may set or release a hold and can enforce minimum and maximum durations, which is where the approval gate belongs.

Object Lock and annotations do different jobs. Object Lock enforces retention, including event-based retention through event holds. The annotation records which policy applies and why, which is context Object Lock doesn’t store. One protects the object, the other explains the decision.

Multipart copies drop annotations unless you opt in

Governance labels are only useful if they stay attached as data moves. For a CopyObject request (objects up to 5 GiB), S3 copies annotations along with the object by default.

For larger objects copied with multipart upload, annotations aren’t copied unless you opt in. Multipart upload is what the AWS CLI and SDKs use through their transfer managers above roughly 8 MB. The default is easy to overlook, because the behavior changes with object size rather than with the command you run. A copy that carries its labels on a small object silently drops them once the object crosses the multipart threshold, with no error or warning. With the multipart opt-in, the SDK writes the annotations after the copy completes, so the destination object exists briefly without all its annotations.

aws s3 cp \

s3://amzn-s3-demo-governance/contracts/acme-msa.pdf \

s3://amzn-s3-demo-governance-dr/contracts/acme-msa.pdf \

--copy-props all

When you call CopyObject directly, the x-amz-annotation-directive header gives explicit control. COPY includes the source annotations on the destination object, and EXCLUDE omits them. Reach for EXCLUDE when you deliberately want a reduced-sensitivity copy.

Set this once as a default rather than deciding per call. Standardize on the copy-props opt-in in every annotation-dependent copy path. Confirm it with a test that copies an object larger than the multipart threshold, because a small-object test would pass while hiding the problem.

Annotation deletion and overwrite are irreversible

Object versioning gives you a safety net. Annotations don’t have one. There’s no delete marker and no version history for an annotation, even in a versioned bucket, so after you delete one it’s gone. The same is true of an update: writing a new payload to an existing annotation name overwrites the previous content in place. That makes an accidental overwrite as destructive as a delete.

Treat annotation deletion as a deliberate, gated action rather than routine cleanup. Restrict s3:DeleteObjectAnnotation to a dedicated administrative role, with an approval step. If a record’s context might be needed for an audit, subscribe to the s3:ObjectAnnotation:Put and s3:ObjectAnnotation:Delete event notifications, or use the S3 Metadata journal table, to keep an audit trail of annotation changes, so that removing the annotation doesn’t erase your only copy of the governance decision.

SSE-C objects can’t have annotations

S3 encrypts annotations using the same configuration as their parent object. That covers server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3), with AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) keys (SSE-KMS), and dual-layer SSE-KMS (DSSE-KMS). One exception matters at design time: Objects encrypted with server-side encryption using customer-provided keys (SSE-C) can’t have annotations. The following AWS CLI call attempts to annotate an SSE-C object and shows the error you get back.

aws s3api put-object-annotation \

--bucket amzn-s3-demo-governance \

--key contracts/acme-msa.pdf \

--annotation-name governance-context \

--annotation-payload governance-context.json \

--sse-customer-algorithm AES256 \

--sse-customer-key  \

--sse-customer-key-md5 

An error occurred (InvalidRequest) when calling the PutObjectAnnotation operation:

Adding metadata to object with CUSTOMER_MANAGED encryption is not supported

If you build a governed bucket on SSE-C and plan to layer annotation-based context on top, the pattern won’t work. This aligns with the broader direction for SSE-C: in April 2026, S3 disabled SSE-C by default for new buckets and select existing buckets. If you use or are considering SSE-C, plan to move to SSE-S3, SSE-KMS, or DSSE-KMS, all of which support annotations.

Scope read, write, and delete access separately

Governance context shouldn’t be writable by everyone who can read it. S3 exposes distinct IAM actions for annotation reads and writes, so an enrichment process can write context while consumers only read it. The following identity-based policy allows an enrichment role to write and read annotations on a governed bucket. On buckets that use SSE-KMS, annotations use the object’s KMS key, so both the enrichment and consumer roles also need kms:Decrypt, and the enrichment role needs kms:GenerateDataKey.

{

"Version": "2012-10-17",

"Statement": [

{

"Sid": "EnrichmentRoleMayWriteAnnotations",

"Effect": "Allow",

"Action": ["s3:PutObjectAnnotation", "s3:GetObjectAnnotation", "s3:GetObjectVersionAnnotation"],

"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-governance/*"

}

]

}

A consumer role receives read-only access to the same context.

{

"Version": "2012-10-17",

"Statement": [

{

"Sid": "ConsumerRoleReadsAnnotations",

"Effect": "Allow",

"Action": ["s3:GetObjectAnnotation", "s3:GetObjectVersionAnnotation","s3:ListObjectAnnotations"],

"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-governance/*"

}

]

}

Keep the destructive action separate. Grant s3:DeleteObjectAnnotation only to a dedicated administrative role, not to the enrichment or consumer roles, so a routine process can’t permanently remove governance context. For defense in depth, add an explicit Deny on s3:DeleteObjectAnnotation to the enrichment and consumer role policies, as shown in the following statement.

{

"Version": "2012-10-17",

"Statement": [

{

"Sid": "DenyAnnotationDeletion",

"Effect": "Deny",

"Action": "s3:DeleteObjectAnnotation",

"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-governance/*"

}

]

}

An explicit deny overrides any allow that might reach the role through another policy, so even a future permission change can’t let those roles delete annotations. The deny covers deletion only. The enrichment role can still overwrite governance-context with PutObjectAnnotation, so rely on the audit trail described earlier to detect an unintended change.

Replication has its own controls. To keep classification and residency labels attached to a cross-Region copy, grant s3:GetObjectVersionAnnotationForReplication on the source objects and s3:ReplicateObjectAnnotation on the destination objects.

{

"Version": "2012-10-17",

"Statement": [

{

"Sid": "ReadSourceAnnotationsForReplication",

"Effect": "Allow",

"Action": "s3:GetObjectVersionAnnotationForReplication",

"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-governance/*"

},

{

"Sid": "ReplicateAnnotationsToDestination",

"Effect": "Allow",

"Action": "s3:ReplicateObjectAnnotation",

"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-governance-dr/*"

}

]

}

Annotations replicate independently of the object and complete after it, so treat replicated annotations as eventually consistent. The object can show a completed replication status while its annotation is still in transit. You can verify annotation replication through the per-annotation replication_status column in the annotation table. To replicate objects while holding their annotations in the source Region, deny s3:ReplicateObjectAnnotation in the replication role policy. Object replication continues, and only annotation replication is blocked.

Generated labels are proposals, not decisions

When an application or agent generates the classification, the second consequence of the mental model becomes a control rather than a footnote. S3 stores whatever label you write and doesn’t check whether it is correct. If a generated PII flag or retention status feeds an automated expiration or deletion, an incorrect label becomes an incorrect deletion.

Keep a validation boundary between authoring context and acting on it. Use generated annotations to inform and prioritize, and require a verification step before any label drives an irreversible lifecycle operation. That step can be an automated policy check or a human review.

The review_required field in the payload shown earlier encodes this boundary. It starts as true and is set to false only after validation, so downstream automation keys off a reviewed label rather than a raw prediction. The generated_by and generated_at fields give you the audit trail to trace which process produced a label when a decision is later questioned.

Treat the enrichment agent as a proposer, never an approver. For reversible or low-impact actions, the approving step can be an automated rule check. For irreversible or high-impact actions such as deletion, expiring retention, or a cross-border transfer, require explicit human approval regardless of how confident the model is.

When annotations are not the right tool

Annotations occupy a specific niche: larger, structured, mutable context that travels with the object. S3 offers other ways to attach information to objects, and they are not interchangeable.

Object tags are limited to 10 small key-value pairs, but they integrate with IAM policy conditions, S3 Lifecycle rules, and cost allocation. User-defined metadata is fixed at upload time and can’t change without copying the object. An external data source offers rich or specialized queries, but it adds a system to operate and keeps context separate from the data it describes.

Tags and user-defined metadata are also queryable at scale through S3 Metadata live inventory tables, so querying isn’t what makes annotations distinct. The larger, richer, mutable payload is. Annotations are the wrong tool in three cases:

  • Your access pattern is relational or join-heavy.
  • You need policy-condition or lifecycle filtering on the values themselves.
  • You have a very high write rate on the same object.

One more constraint shapes the design. Because annotations are written after the object exists, there is a short window between upload and enrichment during which the object carries no governance context. If your controls can’t tolerate that gap, the context can arrive with the upload itself, through user-defined metadata or a pre-registration step. The following table summarizes the comparison.

Design decision S3 annotations Object tags User-defined metadata External data source
Maximum per object version 1,000 10 Fixed set at upload Not applicable
Maximum size 512-byte name + 1 MB payload 128-char key + 256-char value Up to 2 KB total Effectively unbounded
Data format Any UTF-8 text (JSON, XML, YAML, plain text) Key-value strings Key-value strings Any
Mutable after write Yes Yes No (requires object copy) Yes
Set during upload No (after upload only) Yes Yes Not applicable
IAM condition / lifecycle filtering No Yes No Not applicable
Query at scale S3 Metadata annotation table S3 Metadata live inventory table S3 Metadata live inventory table Rich / relational

Production guidance

Three operational points complete the design:

  • Apply least privilege by separating the enrichment role that writes annotations from the consumer roles that read them, and control annotation replication explicitly.
  • Follow the annotation naming rules. Names are 1–512 bytes, limited to letters, digits, underscore, period, and hyphen, and they can’t begin with the reserved aws or s3 prefixes.
  • Version your payload schema so consumers can evolve with it, and encode any binary content with Base64, because payloads must be valid UTF-8.

When you compare cost, account for each component:

  • The storage that the annotation payloads consume.
  • The request charges for PutObjectAnnotation and the read operations.
  • If you enable an S3 Metadata annotation table, that table’s storage and request costs, plus the Athena scan charges when you query it.

Two points are worth highlighting. You pay S3 Standard rates for annotation storage regardless of the parent object’s storage class, so an annotation on an S3 Glacier Deep Archive object still costs Standard-tier storage. And when an object is copied or replicated, each annotation is copied too and metered as a separate PUT. Bulk-copy and replication paths on objects that carry many annotations therefore incur a request cost proportional to the annotation count.

Weigh the total against the cost of running and querying a separate metadata data source, and against the object reads you avoid by keeping context with the object. Confirm current pricing on the S3 pricing page (see Annotations under Management & Insights) and on the S3 Metadata and Athena pricing pages.

Conclusion

With S3 annotations, you can keep governance context with the data it describes: attached to the object, revisable in place, carried across copies and replication, and queryable with SQL through an S3 Metadata annotation table.

Getting that right depends on a small number of behaviors: version-scoped deletion, Object Lock sequencing, annotation preservation across multipart copies, irreversible annotation deletion, the SSE-C constraint, IAM scoping, and the trust boundary around generated labels. The mental model holds that an annotation is caller-authored context bound to an object version, which S3 stores and moves but doesn’t interpret. With that model, you can reason about each behavior before you build.

To get started, adapt the governance annotation schema in this post to your own classification and retention model, and apply the IAM separation and lifecycle handling described here. Each payload, policy statement, and AWS CLI call is inline, so you can copy it directly into your own environment.

About the author

Aditya Jain

Aditya is a Delivery Consultant on the migration team at AWS Professional Services, where he helps customers move on-premises workloads to AWS through infrastructure automation. He focuses on building scalable, automated solutions for cloud-native storage and compute, and on applying AI and machine learning to strengthen those workloads. Connect with him on LinkedIn.
ai_summary: If you run data governance in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), the context that matters most probably lives somewhere other than S3. Think of how an object is classified, which retention policy applies to it, where the data may reside, and whether it holds personally identifiable information (PII).

title: Recommended resilience testing in the next generation of AWS Resilience Hub
author: AWS Architecture Blog
description: Organizations that have defined resilience policies and assessed their applications face a common next step: verifying those applications behave as expected when failures occur. Designing fault injection experiments manually requires deep expertise. You need to know which faults to inject, which resources to target, and how to judge whether the outcome counts as success. Many teams do not know where to start, and experiments built by hand can drift out of date as architectures evolve.
article_content:
Organizations that have defined resilience policies and assessed their applications face a common next step: verifying those applications behave as expected when failures occur. Designing fault injection experiments manually requires deep expertise. You need to know which faults to inject, which resources to target, and how to judge whether the outcome counts as success. Many teams do not know where to start, and experiments built by hand can drift out of date as architectures evolve.

Recommended resilience testing in the next generation of AWS Resilience Hub addresses this. It’s a new capability that helps you validate how your services respond to and recover from failure scenarios. The tests are pre-configured and powered by AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS).

Recommended resilience testing uses what AWS Resilience Hub already knows about your service, including its resources, dependencies, and resilience policy. With this information, AWS Resilience Hub automatically creates FIS experiments, injects faults, and evaluates the results against your success criteria and recovery time objective (RTO). It uses that evaluation to determine a pass or fail outcome. What used to be manual experiment design becomes an out-of-the-box test with built-in success evaluation based on your policy. Each test run auto-generates a report, accessible through the Resilience Hub console.

Customers frequently ask which failure modes to test for and what prescriptive testing guidance we can offer. AWS Resilience Hub answers this by providing four tests at launch, selected based on your service’s architecture and resilience policy.

Availability Zone: recovery – Validates your service can detect and recover from an Availability Zone impairment. The test injects the symptoms of a power interruption in a single Availability Zone, affecting compute, networking, storage, and database resources within that AZ. It confirms your service detects the impaired AZ, continues operating in the healthy AZs, and returns to a healthy state within your defined RTO. It can also help surface single-AZ dependencies you might not be aware of.

Dependency validation – Validates how your service responds when its dependencies within the AWS Region are impaired. If you have enabled dependency discovery, the discovered soft dependency with the highest query volume is pre-selected by default. You can adjust the selection to target individual dependencies or specific groups. The dependency validation test blocks dependencies within the Region to see how your service behaves when they are unavailable. It can help you validate that your service remains healthy when soft dependencies are impaired, and surface dependencies you might not have known were hard. You can also include known hard dependencies to understand their impact and confirm your service detects and responds when they are unavailable. We recommend starting with a single soft dependency and expanding from there.

Multi-Region: isolation – Validates your service can operate independently from a Region when connectivity to another Region is unavailable. The test blocks connectivity between the two Regions, including network traffic, cross-Region data replication, and selected dependencies. This test applies to both active-active and active-passive architectures, and is also a useful precursor to the Multi-Region: recovery test.

Multi-Region: recovery – Validates that your service can recover and serve clients within your defined RTO after a Region is impaired. The test introduces failures into dependencies in the selected Region. Through success alarms, it confirms that your service recovers within your defined RTO in the recovery Region and remains healthy for the duration of the test. You perform the recovery action yourself, such as triggering a failover or executing an Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC) Region switch plan.

Each test works at three levels. A test template is the pre-configured recommendation, specifying the fault actions, target resource types, and parameters. A test is your configured instance of a template for your service, with your success alarms, stop conditions, and settings. A test run is a single execution that scopes to your current resources and produces a pass/fail outcome with results and a report. You can run the same test quarterly, monthly, or on demand. To get to that pass/fail outcome you can use success criteria in the test.

Choose success criteria that reflect your service’s health and customer experience, such as order success rate or end-to-end availability, rather than the state of individual resources. The impaired resources are expected to be unhealthy. What you are validating is whether your service as a whole absorbed the failure. Combined with your resilience policy, these criteria determine the pass/fail outcome.

For recovery tests (Availability Zone recovery and Multi-Region recovery), the test passes when all success criteria return to a healthy state within the RTO defined in your policy and hold until the test ends. This validates not just that your service recovered, but that it recovered fast enough to meet your stated objectives.

For sustained tests (Dependency validation and Multi-Region isolation), the test passes when all success criteria hold their thresholds from fault injection through the end of the test, proving your service remained healthy throughout the impairment.

You can also select additional alarms for observability only, such as watching the impaired Region degrade. These appear in results and reports without affecting the outcome.

Deep dive: Dependency validation

Of the four recommended resilience tests, dependency validation was one of the most requested capabilities by our customers, and for good reason. Modern applications depend on dozens of services, and understanding which of those dependencies your application can function without is the key to building a resilient application. The dependency validation test determines whether your application continues to work when a given dependency becomes unavailable.

How dependency validation works

The dependency validation test blocks connectivity to your selected dependencies within an AWS Region to observe how your service behaves when they are unavailable. It validates that your service remains healthy when soft dependencies are impaired and surfaces dependencies you might not have known were hard. You can also include known hard dependencies to understand their failure impact.

This is a sustained test. Unlike recovery tests that measure whether you meet your RTO, the dependency validation test passes when all success alarms remain in OK state from the moment faults are injected through the end of the test.

Dependency discovery

You can define dependencies in two ways:

  1. Turn on dependency discovery. This uses DNS query log analysis with a 35-day look-back window and continuous polling to automatically identify the AWS services, internal endpoints, and third-party endpoints your service calls. Dependency discovery surfaces dependencies you might not be aware of, including unexpected cross-Region calls, critical third-party dependencies, and infrequently accessed services that could cause failures during incidents.
  2. Manually enter DNS endpoints directly when configuring the test.

After you define your dependencies, we recommend classifying each one as a soft or hard dependency.

Classification When to use Example What the test validates
Soft Your service degrades but continues operating without this dependency Analytics API, notification service, feature flags, recommendation engine Application handles absence gracefully. Test should pass
Hard Your service fails if this dependency is unavailable Primary database, authentication service, credential exchange Application detects failure and handles it gracefully. Test might fail (this is expected and informative)

Prerequisites

Before you begin, make sure you have at least one service created and assessed in the next generation of Resilience Hub. You would also require an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) service role for the next generation of Resilience Hub to assume when running a resilience test. This role can either be created in the next generation of Resilience Hub console or you can specify an existing one.

Configuring the test

From your service dashboard in the next generation of Resilience Hub, choose the Testing tab. You will see four recommended resilience tests. Select Dependency validation, and then choose Edit test configuration.

The configuration page walks you through six sections:

1. Basic settings

Test duration: The length of time fault actions run. Set any value from 1 minute to 12 hours (default: 30 minutes). After the duration, the test takes a few additional minutes to evaluate success before it ends.

Dependency Region: The AWS Region where your service is deployed that you want to test for dependency failures.

2. Dependencies to block

This is where the distinction between soft and hard dependencies directly drives your test.

Default behavior:

The discovered soft dependency with the highest query volume is pre-selected. If no dependencies have been classified as soft, none are pre-selected.

  • Discovered dependencies: A selection box pre-populated with dependencies found in your service in the selected AWS Region. You can choose up to 10 dependencies to test.
  • (Optional) Additional dependencies: Expand this section to include hard dependencies or dependencies not listed in the primary selection. If you didn’t run any dependency discovery, you can use this field to enter a DNS address that will be blocked as a dependency.

Best practice: Start with a single soft dependency and expand from there, progressively building confidence in your application’s failure handling before including hard dependencies.

3. Test actions (fault actions)

The next generation of Resilience Hub uses AWS FIS actions to block connectivity to your selected dependencies, automatically targeting resources discovered in your service. The fault actions inject 100 percent packet loss at the compute layer, dropping traffic to the selected dependencies:

Fault action What it does
aws:ssm:send-command Drops traffic from Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instances to the selected dependencies
aws:ecs:task-network-packet-loss Drops traffic from Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) tasks (EC2 and AWS Fargate) to the selected dependencies
aws:eks:pod-network-packet-loss Drops traffic from Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) pods to the selected dependencies

When the test starts, it matches actions to resources discovered in your service. If no resources match an action’s target type, that action is skipped. This means the test automatically adapts to your compute environment, whether you are running on Amazon EC2, Amazon ECS, Amazon EKS, or a combination.

Additional setup required: The setup for these actions depends on your compute type. You need an AWS Systems Manager Agent container in your Amazon ECS task definition, a Kubernetes service account for Amazon EKS pods, or AWS Systems Manager Agent installed on your Amazon EC2 instances.

4. Test alarms

Alarms determine whether the test passes or fails. Select alarms discovered from your service that reflect service performance and customer experience. For example, order success rate for an ecommerce service or transactions processed for a payments system.

  • Success alarms: The next generation of Resilience Hub uses these to validate whether your service passed or failed the test. Choose alarms that measure your service’s health across the AWS Region.
  • (Optional) Additional alarms: Tracked during the test run and shown in the report, but don’t affect the test outcome. Use additional alarms for observability to monitor how these alarms behave during the dependency impairment.

How to pass: The test passes if all success alarms remain in OK state until the test actions end.

Success criteria and additional alarms share a limit of 5 per configuration update.

5. Stop conditions, reports, and logs

Stop conditions: Amazon CloudWatch alarms that act as guardrails. If breached, they stop the test automatically to protect your workloads. Choose up to five alarms. They must be in the account where the test runs and the AWS Region where the faults are injected.

(Optional) Reports: If you configure an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket as a report destination on your service, the next generation of Resilience Hub generates a report after each test run that includes the test configuration, alarm status, timeline, and results.

Logs: Optionally send test logs to an Amazon S3 bucket or Amazon CloudWatch Logs for deeper analysis. The next generation of Resilience Hub doesn’t charge for sending logs, though ingestion and storage charges apply.

6. Test permissions

The test requires an IAM role to grant access to AWS services and resources. For single account setups, you need one execution role. For multi-account setups, you need an orchestrator role in the account running the test and a target role in each account containing targeted resources. You can create the role directly from AWS Management Console with required permissions pre-configured or use an existing role. Once saved, the role is used by default for future runs.

Note: Updating test settings might change required IAM permissions. Required permissions vary based on the trust policy, fault actions, and test options selected. Always review the IAM role instructions to confirm correct permissions.

Running the test: What success and failure look like

The value of the dependency validation test becomes clear when you compare results across dependency classifications. We walk through two test runs on the same service with the same success alarms: one blocking soft dependencies, one blocking hard dependencies.

Test run: Soft dependencies blocked — PASSED

Dependencies blocked:

  • Payment Gateway.
  • Notification Service.

Success alarms:

  • canary-heartbeat-canary-failure-us-east-2: Monitors service health check availability.
  • canary-order-flow-canary-failure-us-east-2: Monitors end-to-end order processing.

Figure 1: Soft dependency test run with both success alarms holding in OK state for the full test duration

What the results show: Both alarms remained in OK state (solid green) from the moment test actions started through the end of the test. The application continued functioning normally without Payment Gateway and Notification Service. The order flow kept processing. The heartbeat kept responding. The service handled the absence of its soft dependencies gracefully, exactly as designed.

What this proves: These dependencies are correctly classified as soft. Your application can tolerate the loss of these dependencies, suppressing notifications without impacting the customer-facing order flow.

Test run: Hard dependencies blocked — FAILED

Dependencies blocked:

  • Amazon Cognito.
  • AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS).

Success alarms:

  • canary-heartbeat-canary-failure-us-east-2: Monitors service health check availability.
  • canary-order-flow-canary-failure-us-east-2: Monitors end-to-end order processing.

Figure 2: Hard dependency test run with the order-flow alarm entering alarm state while the heartbeat alarm stays healthy

What the results show: The heartbeat canary stayed green throughout. The application did not become unavailable. But the order-flow canary transitioned to alarm state (red) immediately after faults were injected and remained there until the test ended. Without Amazon Cognito (authentication) and AWS STS (credential exchange), the application couldn’t complete the business-critical order flow.

What this proves: Amazon Cognito and AWS STS are correctly classified as hard dependencies. The test confirms that their absence impacts critical functionality, but importantly, it also shows the failure was contained. The application did not cascade into a complete failure. It continued responding (heartbeat passed) while the specific business flow that required authentication failed gracefully.

Interpreting results: A decision framework

Test results aren’t simply pass or fail. A passing test can still surface a misclassified dependency, and a failing test can confirm that a dependency is genuinely critical. What matters is reading the outcome against how you classified the dependency, so you know whether your architecture behaved as intended and what to do about it.

The following decision framework helps you interpret the results of each test, understand what they mean, and decide what to do next.

Scenario Expected Outcome What it means What to do next
Soft dependency blocked → test passes Yes Graceful degradation is working. Classification is accurate. No action required. Your architecture handles this failure correctly.
Soft dependency blocked → test fails No The dependency might be misclassified as soft when it’s actually hard. Or your degradation logic has a gap. Review application behavior. Reclassify as hard, or fix the degradation path.
Hard dependency blocked → test fails Yes Confirms the classification. Critical functionality is impacted without this dependency. Verify the failure is graceful (no cascading failures, no data corruption, no hung connections). Consider whether you can add retry/fallback to reclassify as soft in the future.
Hard dependency blocked → test passes No The dependency might be misclassified. It could actually be soft. This could also indicate the dependency isn’t being called as intended. Investigate whether your application is more resilient than expected, or whether the dependency is not being exercised. Reclassify if appropriate or fix the application logic.

Summary

Recommended resilience testing in the next generation of AWS Resilience Hub removes the barrier between knowing your architecture and proving it holds under failure. It provides four AWS recommended tests built on AWS FIS, covering Availability Zone recovery, dependency validation, Multi-Region isolation, and Multi-Region recovery. You can move from policy definition and failure mode assessment to evidence-backed validation without building experiments from scratch.

You can start with the dependency validation test to understand how your application handles the loss of its dependencies. Expand to AZ recovery and multi-Region tests as your program matures. Each test run captures a point-in-time snapshot of your current resources, produces a pass/fail outcome evaluated against your resilience policy, and feeds results into your compliance and reporting workflows over time.

Recommended resilience testing is available today in all AWS commercial Regions where the next generation of AWS Resilience Hub is supported. To learn more and get started, visit the AWS Resilience Hub User Guide and the AWS Resilience Hub product page.

 

About the authors

Jennifer Moran

Jennifer is a Principal Resilience Specialist Solutions Architect at AWS, where she helps customers architect resilient cloud solutions that improve their resilience posture and operational excellence. She is the co-author of Engineering Resilient Systems on AWS (O’Reilly Media). Her interests include fault-tolerant design, scalable architectures, and high-availability systems.

Imran Sadiq

Imran is a Senior Solutions Architect at Amazon Web Services, working with financial services customers across New Zealand. As a resilience specialist, he is passionate about helping organizations prepare for, respond to, and recover from the unexpected. With deep expertise in resilience testing, disaster recovery, and cloud-native resilience patterns, Imran partners with customers to build resilient systems.

title: Automate medical coding with Step Functions and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
author: AWS Architecture Blog
description:

article_content:
With AI agents, you can automate medical coding while keeping the workflow deterministic, auditable, and subject to human approval. The key is division of labor: the workflow engine owns sequencing and approval gates, while agents reason within individual, bounded steps. Handing the entire workflow to an agent would make the runtime path a property of the model’s reasoning, which is difficult to review and replay.

Medical coding makes this concrete. Teams must translate free-text clinical terms like “migrane” (a typo) or “flutters in my chest sometimes” into standardized codes before they can analyze or report the data. The target vocabularies include controlled medical dictionaries such as MedDRA for adverse events and WHODrug for medications. This work is safety-critical because a coding error can send an adverse event to the wrong safety signal. Yet it’s mostly repetitive work, with skilled coders reviewing terms one by one. The opportunity is to code the confident cases automatically and route only the ambiguous ones to a human.

In this post, we show you how to combine deterministic orchestration with bounded agentic reasoning using AWS Step Functions and the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness integration, a managed capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. We walk through a medical coding workflow that escalates cheapest-first: a safety block-list, then exact matching, then an AI agent only for the terms that need judgment. We also explain the design decisions that keep the model bounded. The complete sample, including infrastructure code and a seeded test dataset, is available in the aws-samples GitHub repository.

Note that MedDRA is a registered trademark of the International Federation of Pharmaceutical Manufacturers and Associations (IFPMA), managed by the MedDRA Maintenance and Support Services Organization (MSSO). WHODrug is maintained by the Uppsala Monitoring Centre (UMC). Both are proprietary, licensed dictionaries. Deploying against them requires a valid subscription. The sample dataset contains generated study identifiers and verbatims with a de minimis illustrative set of dictionary entries, and no patient data. The AWS services used in this sample, including Amazon Aurora and Amazon Bedrock, are HIPAA-eligible when used under a signed AWS Business Associate Addendum (BAA). Before processing protected health information, see the HIPAA Eligible Services Reference and the AWS HIPAA Compliance overview.

Solution overview

The design follows one principle: spend the cheapest, most deterministic mechanism that can code a term with confidence and escalate only when it can’t. A large language model (LLM) agent is powerful but expensive and non-deterministic, so it isn’t the default. Even then, the workflow, not the model, owns every routing decision. The agent might choose which medical code and how confident it is. It doesn’t decide what happens next. A compliance reviewer can read the state machine definition and understand the execution path independent of any agent’s runtime reasoning.

The solution uses AWS Step Functions to orchestrate the coding decision, AWS Lambda for the deterministic steps, and the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness for the agentic step. An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, exposes the agent’s tools. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition (Serverless v2) with the pgvector extension serves as a single store for the reference data and its embeddings, so there is no separate vector store to synchronize.

Figure 1 shows the architecture.

Figure 1: Medical coding workflow solution architecture

Each Step Functions execution codes one verbatim: a deterministic direct lookup, an agentic semantic search that runs only on a miss, score-threshold routing on the agent’s confidence, and a write-back onto the same study record. The state machine is deliberately a standard workflow. Executions are exactly-once, and the queryable history is a per-term audit trail. For a regulated coding process, answering “why was this term coded this way, by what, and when” is a requirement. Error paths in this sample end with the term left open, so every record gets a terminal status. In production, send errors that survive the retries to a Fail state instead. The execution then shows as failed in Amazon CloudWatch, and you can redrive it after fixing the cause.

The write-back step stores every symptom entry’s full medical family tree, not just an isolated code. For example, a symptom like ‘muscle spasms’ links all the way up to its overarching category, ‘musculoskeletal and connective tissue disorders’. Safety teams can then roll up signals at any level, not just the lowest one. Additionally, the agent logs a one-sentence explanation for its decision. This makes sure that if similar symptoms (like cramps) end up categorized differently across studies, teams can trace the exact study context that caused the variance. They don’t need to guess based on a generic confidence score.

Figure 2 shows the coding decision flow in Unified Modeling Language (UML) activity notation.

Figure 2: Medical coding decision flow with the three terminal outcomes in UML activity notation

Note: This sample is for demonstration purposes only and is not intended for clinical use. Before using this pattern in production, validate it against a known-correct dataset and measure coding precision and the incorrect autocode rate.

Walkthrough

The walkthrough follows one verbatim through the state machine, focusing on the architectural decision each stage encodes.

Prerequisites

Before you begin, make sure that you have the following:

  • An AWS account with permissions to create Step Functions state machines, Lambda functions, an Aurora PostgreSQL cluster, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore resources, and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles.
  • Access to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore in a supported AWS Region. The harness uses Claude Sonnet 5 (us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5), and the dictionary search uses Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 (amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0). Both models are enabled by default, but Anthropic models require a one-time usage form before first use, which you can submit from the Amazon Bedrock playground. For model availability by Region, see Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.
  • Node.js 24+, the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) CLI, and a bootstrapped target account.

Estimated cost

The largest cost is the Aurora Serverless v2 cluster. It keeps a minimum capacity of 0.5 Aurora Capacity Units (ACUs), so it’s billed for every hour it runs, even when idle. For current rates, see Amazon Aurora pricing. To stop the charges, delete the stack as described in Clean up.

Step 1. Resolve the deterministic cases first

The first task state invokes a Lambda function that makes two checks, in a deliberate order. It first checks a terms-not-to-autocode block-list. These are real dictionary terms, like “HAEMORRHAGE,” that are too broad to auto-assign because the code changes depending on where the bleeding occurred. A hit ends the workflow with the term left open for a human. Because this runs before any model call, it’s a hard control: a safety rule placed ahead of the model cannot be prompted away, and costs nothing to enforce.

The same function then runs a case-insensitive exact match against the dictionary and a curated synonym list (“Hypothyroid” maps to “Hypothyroidism”). A match is accepted only if it resolves to exactly one distinct code. On the sample workload, five of twelve cases finish here: one safety block and four auto codes at score 1.00, each for the cost of an indexed query. More than a third of the workload never reaches the agent at all.

Step 2. Declare the coding agent in the workflow definition

We use an agent for this step because deciding when to pull in study context is judgment, not a fixed rule. In our test run, the agent called the study-info tool only for ambiguous terms and skipped it for a clear typo and for gibberish input. That kind of judgment is hard to encode as a threshold, and the agent can take on new tools later without a workflow redesign. This is also why the agent sits last in line, after two cheaper, deterministic checks.

Only on a miss does Step Functions invoke the agent, using the AgentCore harness optimized integration. The harness resource declares only the model. The system prompt, tools, and allowed tool names are supplied per invocation from the task state. The agent’s full contract is therefore readable in the workflow definition, and there is no container to build or operate. The following abbreviated excerpt shows the shape. See the sample for the full definition. The InvokeHarness Task state has a hard 15-minute execution cap regardless of TimeoutSeconds, so a term needing many tool round-trips could hit it. The sample’s two-tool, single-turn design stays well under that limit.

CodingAgent:

Type: Task

Resource: arn:aws:states:::bedrockagentcore:invokeHarness

Arguments:

HarnessArn: "${CodingHarnessArn}"

RuntimeSessionId: "{% $uuid() %}"

Messages:

- Role: user

Content:

- Text: >-

{% 'Code this verbatim term: "' & $verbatim & '". Dictionary='

& $dictionary & ' version=' & $dictionaryVersion

& ' study=' & $study & '.' %}

Tools:

- Type: agentcore_gateway

Name: gateway

Config:

AgentCoreGateway:

GatewayArn: "${GatewayArn}"

AllowedTools:

- "@gateway/search-dictionary___search_dictionary"

- "@gateway/study-info___get_study_info"

SystemPrompt:

- Text: |-

You are a clinical medical-coding expert...

The agent has exactly two tools, exposed as Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools through an AgentCore Gateway. search_dictionary embeds the verbatim with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 and runs a pgvector similarity search. It searches the verbatim exactly as given, because the misspelling is the signal. get_study_info returns the study’s free-text protocol description. It exists because similarity search can return several clinically plausible candidates it can’t separate on text alone. A human coder breaks that tie using knowledge of the study. This tool gives the agent the same context and nothing else: it returns prose only, not codes.

The clearest illustration is the same verbatim coded in two different studies. “cramps” returns an identical candidate list in both. Only the study description differs. In an oncology study that monitors muscle spasms as adverse events of special interest, the agent coded it to “muscle spasms.” In a reflux study where abdominal cramping is expected and musculoskeletal events aren’t an endpoint, it coded the same verbatim to “abdominal pain.” In this run, the oncology result scored 0.92 and was autocoded, and the gastrointestinal (GI) result scored 0.85 and went to a coder for review. In both cases the agent’s job was to bring the right candidate to the top with a reason a coder can check. That’s how a coder who knows the protocol would decide.

Step 3. Route on coding confidence, not retrieval similarity

The most important design decision is what the threshold routes on. Routing on retrieval similarity, the distance between the two embeddings, is measurably wrong. Table 1 illustrates this with an example.

Verbatim Selected term Retrieval similarity Agent confidence
migrane Migraine 0.37 0.97
flutters in my chest sometimes Cardiac flutter 0.65 0.75

Table 1. Retrieval similarity and agent confidence for sample terms (one run, Claude Sonnet 5)

Table 1 shows the problem. The typo “migrane” looks very different from “Migraine” as text, so its similarity score is low, but the right code is obvious. “Flutters in my chest sometimes” shares more words with “Cardiac flutter,” so its similarity score is higher, but the right code is less certain. Similarity ranks these two cases the wrong way round, and no threshold can fix that. So instead, the agent reports how confident it is in its own choice, using three bands set in the system prompt. It reports 0.95 to 1.00 when the match is clear, 0.70 to 0.94 when the verbatim is vague or the agent needed study context to choose between candidates, and below 0.70 when nothing fits. For example, “cramps” in the GI study could mean muscle cramps or stomach cramps. The agent checked the study description to choose, and reported 0.85, in the middle band. The bands describe the model’s confidence. The 0.90 autocode gate is a separate, fixed rule in the workflow, applied by the Choice state that comes next.

ScoreThreshold:

Type: Choice

Choices:

- Condition: "{% $agentScore >= 0.9 %}"

Next: WriteBack

- Condition: "{% $agentScore >= 0.7 %}"

Next: MarkForReview

Default: MarkOpen

Note that the routing number is authored by the model. The block-list runs before any model call, and the thresholds are auditable configuration in the state machine definition. The write-back checks the code exists, and anything below the autocode gate reaches a human. Note also that the agent is instructed never to abstain. For gibberish it still returns the top candidate at low confidence, and the gate discards it. The agent scores the candidate, and the workflow decides what happens to it.

Step 4. Write back with a fabrication guard

The terminal task persists the outcome onto the same study record: status, code, hierarchy, score, and a status_changed_by marker that distinguishes machine coding from human action. Before writing, it checks that the chosen code exists in the target dictionary and version. The prompt tells the agent not to invent codes, and this check enforces it. It matters because the agent reads free-text study metadata, which is the kind of input that invites copying a plausible number out of a protocol description. A code that fails the check leaves the term safely open, with the reason recorded. This check has one limit. It can’t tell whether the code was one of the search results, because the workflow only gets the agent’s final response, not what the tools returned. To verify that, look at the agent’s tool calls in AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

Deploy and test the solution

The sample deploys with three commands and seeds twelve verbatims that exercise every branch:

npm install && npm run build

npx cdk deploy

npm run seed

Each verbatim runs as one Step Functions execution (the repository README shows the exact CLI calls). The following table shows a live run:

Verbatim Route Score Outcome
HAEMORRHAGE block-list n/a open (safety block)
Dislocated shoulder exact match 1.00 autocoded
Hypothyroid synonym match 1.00 autocoded
ibuprofen exact match (WHODrug) 1.00 autocoded
FULVESTRANT exact match, derivation-only 1.00 autocoded
migrane agent 0.97 autocoded (Migraine)
nexiuum agent 0.95 autocoded (NEXIUM)
cramps (oncology study) agent + study context 0.92 autocoded (Muscle spasms)
cramps (GI study) agent + study context 0.85 review (Abdominal pain)
flutters in my chest sometimes agent 0.75 review (Cardiac flutter)
heart races when I stand up agent 0.80 review (Tachycardia)
asdfghjkl agent < 0.70 open

Table 2. Score and outcome for sample terms (same run as Table 1)

Derivation-only (FULVESTRANT row): a WHODrug ingredient-level exact match, where the write-back updates only the generic-name derivation and ATC hierarchy fields. No new dictionary term is assigned.

The agent skipped the study-info tool for the unambiguous typo and the gibberish and called it only for the ambiguous cases. Every execution’s graph is inspectable in the Step Functions console, and AgentCore Observability records the agent’s tool calls and token usage in Amazon CloudWatch.

Note: Across repeated runs of identical inputs in this sample, the selected code was stable every time, but the confidence score moved within a band. Cases that land near the 0.90 autocode gate can therefore autocode on one run and route to review on another. In our testing, the oncology cramps case scored between 0.75 and 0.92 over six runs. It was autocoded twice and sent to review four times, and Muscle spasms was selected every time. Assert your tests on the selected code, not the exact score, and set your own autocode threshold with margin below 0.90 rather than directly on it.

Scaling beyond one verbatim: This walkthrough codes one verbatim per execution so each decision stays straightforward to inspect. To code a full study, wrap the workflow in a Step Functions Distributed Map state that reads verbatims from an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) manifest, and set MaxConcurrency based on your account’s Amazon Bedrock quota. To size MaxConcurrency, divide your model’s tokens-per-minute quota by the tokens one agent run burns (model calls * (input tokens + 10 * output tokens) for Sonnet 5). Then multiply by the runtime duration in minutes, divide by the share of verbatims that reach the agent, and apply a safety margin. In our testing, 12 concurrent executions against a cluster that had scaled to zero failed 8 of 12 while still reporting SUCCEEDED, which is why the sample keeps a 0.5 ACU minimum and retries the resume errors. Most verbatims resolve in the two deterministic steps, so only a small share ever reaches the agent. For the quotas that apply to your model, see Quotas for Amazon Bedrock.

Clean up

To avoid future charges, delete the deployed resources with npx cdk destroy. All sample data is reseedable, so nothing needs to be retained.

Recognizing the pattern

This pattern fits when the execution path must be reviewable independently of model reasoning, most of the workload is deterministic, only a judgment-heavy minority needs a model, and “escalate to a human” is a first-class outcome rather than an error. It is not limited to clinical trials: the same pattern applies to medical summaries, case narratives, registry intake, study data, and other adjudication workflows such as laboratory test coding, claims triage, and document classification.

You can extend the AgentCore harness with AgentCore Memory to carry context across invocations, Skills to provide task-specific instructions on demand, and AgentCore Gateway to connect MCP servers, knowledge bases, and other tools. Models, tools, and system prompts can also be selected per invocation from the Step Functions task state. Treat a model change like any other release. Rerun your evaluation set, compare the selected codes and confidence scores with the current model’s, and recalibrate the thresholds before you switch. Through all of this, the workflow remains responsible for sequencing and the audit trail.

This isn’t a pattern for open-ended conversations. If the agent must decide what happens next, a workflow engine that owns sequencing is the wrong boundary. Retrieval quality also constrains the agent: if a term isn’t surfaced, it can’t be chosen. In the sample, “flutters in my chest sometimes” would normally be coded to Palpitations, but vector search ranks Palpitations 19th, so the agent does not see it and selects Cardiac flutter instead. The confidence gate still sent it to a coder, but no prompt or study context can recover a term that retrieval never returns. For production dictionaries, use hybrid retrieval, such as lexical search or curated synonym expansion alongside vectors, and calibrate thresholds against your own verbatim distribution.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how deterministic orchestration and agentic reasoning become complementary when the boundary between them is explicit. AWS Step Functions owns sequencing, thresholds, and the audit trail. The agent owns bounded judgment inside one step and reports a confidence the workflow routes on. The result is a pipeline that codes the common cases for the cost of a query, focuses skilled coders on the ambiguous minority, and routes terms below the confidence gate to a human. The execution history shows exactly which mechanism made each decision. The declarative harness integration keeps the agent inside that boundary as configuration a reviewer can read, not code inside a container.

Next steps

Deploy the sample solution with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK), run the twelve golden cases, then swap in your own reference data and calibrate the thresholds from measured precision. For background, see the AWS Step Functions service integrations, the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation, and pgvector on Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL.

To learn more, see how Step Functions invokes an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness from a Task state, the AgentCore harness developer guide, and transforming data with JSONata in Step Functions. To run at study scale, see Distributed Map for large-scale parallel workloads and quotas for Amazon Bedrock. For service details, see AWS Step Functions and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
