description:
You can now use Amazon MSK Replicator in the AWS GovCloud (US-East, US-West) Regions to replicate streaming data across Amazon MSK clusters and from external Apache Kafka clusters including on-premises, self-managed on AWS, or other cloud providers to Amazon MSK Provisioned clusters.

MSK Replicator is a feature of Amazon MSK that automates data replication between Kafka clusters, eliminating the need to manage custom replication infrastructure...
article_content:
You can now use Amazon MSK Replicator in the AWS GovCloud (US-East, US-West) Regions to replicate streaming data across Amazon MSK clusters and from external Apache Kafka clusters including on-premises, self-managed on AWS, or other cloud providers to Amazon MSK Provisioned clusters.

MSK Replicator is a feature of Amazon MSK that automates data replication between Kafka clusters, eliminating the need to manage custom replication infrastructure or configure open-source tools. With MSK Replicator, you can easily build regionally resilient streaming applications for increased availability and business continuity. MSK Replicator provides automatic asynchronous replication across Kafka clusters, eliminating the need to write custom code, manage infrastructure, or setup cross-region networking. MSK Replicator automatically scales the underlying resources so that you can replicate data on-demand without having to monitor or scale capacity. MSK Replicator also replicates the necessary Kafka metadata including topic configurations, Access Control Lists (ACLs), and consumer group offsets. If an unexpected event occurs in a region, you can failover to the other AWS Region and seamlessly resume processing.

You can get started with MSK Replicator from the Amazon MSK console or the Amazon CLI. To learn more, visit the MSK Replicator documentation, product page, and pricing page.

title: Amazon Redshift expands SUPER data type to store strings up to 16 million bytes
author: aws@amazon.com
description: Amazon Redshift now supports individual strings up to 16 million bytes within SUPER data types. Once you opt in through a database parameter, this enhancement applies when ingesting structured or semi-structured data from JSON, PARQUET, TEXT, and CSV source files, and when transforming data through extract load and transform (ELT) processes. Previously, individual stri...
article_content:
Amazon Redshift now supports individual strings up to 16 million bytes within SUPER data types. Once you opt in through a database parameter, this enhancement applies when ingesting structured or semi-structured data from JSON, PARQUET, TEXT, and CSV source files, and when transforming data through extract load and transform (ELT) processes. Previously, individual strings within SUPER data types were limited to 65,535 bytes.

Storing large individual strings in the SUPER data type helps avoid complex pre-loading transformations needed to store the source data in Amazon Redshift. You can now directly ingest large individual strings greater than 65,535 bytes without extra processing (for example, lengthy documents like terms and conditions and contracts), making them queryable using SQL. Once the data is in Amazon Redshift, you can use the flexibility of PartiQL language to explore and navigate through the data or use string functions to transform the data. Functions such as JSON_PARSE, CONCAT, and LISTAGG can now take input strings and return output strings up to 16 million bytes in length.

This enhancement is available in all AWS Regions, including the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, where Amazon Redshift is available. See the AWS Region Table for more details. To learn more, please visit our documentation or blog.

Once you opt in through a database parameter, this enhancement applies when ingesting structured or semi-structured data from JSON, PARQUET, TEXT, and CSV source files, and when transforming data through extract load and transform (ELT) processes.
main_event: Amazon Redshift expands SUPER data type to store strings up to 16 million bytes

Glue Data Catalog already federates to external Iceberg REST catalogs through an AWS IAM role that you configure with access to your Amazon S3 buckets. This enhancement in Glue Data Catalog provides another way to connect to an external Iceberg catalog and read only the tables that the external catalog authorizes. AWS Lake Formation manages access control when you query an external table using any AWS analytics engine, letting you restrict access further down to specific rows and columns and share external Iceberg tables across AWS accounts.

article_content:
Today, we are announcing the general availability of Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Web Answer is a managed tool that returns a synthesized, grounded, cited answer to a natural-language question in a single call, so agent builders can attach it to an agent and get back a finished answer grounded in current web sources, without building and maintaining their own search, retrieve, synthesis, and citation pipeline. 

Web Answer builds on Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which launched in June, extending it from "find the web content" to "return the finished answer," a capability customers have been asking for. With Web Answer, your agent sends a question and receives a synthesized cited answer in one tool call. Web Answer works like an agent; it plans its own searches, runs several in parallel, and decides when it has gathered enough evidence to answer. You stay in control of the boundaries, with domain include, deny lists and publish-date filters that scope where it looks. It attaches as a target on an AgentCore Gateway and is called over MCP, authenticated with IAM, with zero data egress. 

Web Answer is available in the US East (N. Virginia) Region, with per-tool call pricing. 

To learn more about Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, see Web Answer’s documentation page and Web Answer’s website. For Region availability, see the AWS Region table.

article_content:
AWS Network Load Balancer is now available in the Phoenix Local Zone (us-west-2-phx-2a). AWS Local Zones is a type of AWS infrastructure deployment that places AWS compute, storage, database, and other select services closer to large population, industry, and IT centers where no AWS Region exists today.

With this launch, you can create an AWS Network Load Balancer directly in the Phoenix Local Zone. Previously, if your targets ran in the Phoenix Local Zone, you had to place the load balancer in an Availability Zone in the parent Region, so connections and their traffic had to travel to the parent Region and back. This added latency and routed traffic outside the zone where your application runs. Now, connection routing stays local to your targets, delivering lower and more consistent latency to end users in the Phoenix metro area and keeping traffic within the Local Zone. This is especially valuable for latency-sensitive workloads such as real-time gaming, media streaming, and live financial applications serving users in the region.

To learn more about Network Load Balancer, visit the documentation. For more information on AWS Local Zones, visit the AWS Local Zones website. The Locations webpage lists the available and announced Local Zones. You can enable AWS Local Zones from the Local Zones tab in the AWS Global View console, or the ModifyAvailabilityZoneGroup API.

AWS Local Zones is a type of AWS infrastructure deployment that places AWS compute, storage, database, and other select services closer to large population, industry, and IT centers where no AWS Region exists today.

author: aws@amazon.com
description: Today, AWS announces the general availability of bulk put items for Amazon DynamoDB, a fully managed feature that writes data from Amazon S3 into your existing DynamoDB tables. Many DynamoDB applications use data that other systems produce and store in Amazon S3. Writing this data into existing DynamoDB tables has typically meant building custom pipelines and managing table capacity. With bulk put items, developers and data engineers can write this data without impacting existing workloads or...
article_content:
Today, AWS announces the general availability of bulk put items for Amazon DynamoDB, a fully managed feature that writes data from Amazon S3 into your existing DynamoDB tables. Many DynamoDB applications use data that other systems produce and store in Amazon S3. Writing this data into existing DynamoDB tables has typically meant building custom pipelines and managing table capacity. With bulk put items, developers and data engineers can write this data without impacting existing workloads or building a custom ingestion pipeline, in a cost-efficient way.

You point bulk put items at the S3 location of your input files, and DynamoDB handles the rest. Each item supports its own condition expression, so you can enforce insert-only or version-guarded writes. The Standard tier fits most workloads, and the Accelerated tier is for more time-sensitive workloads. Common use cases include daily refreshes, large catalog enrichments, backfills, and migrations.

Bulk put items with Standard tier is available in all commercial AWS Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, to see the list where the Accelerated tier is available see the regional availability. To learn more, visit the Introducing bulk put items for Amazon DynamoDB blog and the Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide.

title: IAM Roles Anywhere now supports automatic certificate revocation checking
author: aws@amazon.com
description: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) Roles Anywhere now supports automatic revocation checking using certificate revocation list (CRL) distribution points (CDPs). This helps keep revocation checks in sync with your certificate authority (CA) and can help improve your security posture. When you enable this capability on a trust anchor, IAM Roles Anywhere reads the CDP URLs embedded in authenticating certificates, downloads the corresp...
article_content:
AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) Roles Anywhere now supports automatic revocation checking using certificate revocation list (CRL) distribution points (CDPs). This helps keep revocation checks in sync with your certificate authority (CA) and can help improve your security posture. When you enable this capability on a trust anchor, IAM Roles Anywhere reads the CDP URLs embedded in authenticating certificates, downloads the corresponding CRLs, and denies credential requests that use revoked certificates.

Previously, to check revocation status, you had to import CRLs into IAM Roles Anywhere and re-import them each time your CA published an update, which added operational overhead. With this launch, IAM Roles Anywhere downloads CRLs from your CDPs and refreshes them periodically, so you no longer need to re-import them. You can use this capability with AWS Private Certificate Authority or your own public key infrastructure (PKI), provided your certificates include publicly accessible CDP URLs that meet the distribution point requirements. To enable it on a trust anchor, use the IAM Roles Anywhere console, AWS SDKs, or AWS CLI.

This feature is available at no additional cost in all commercial AWS Regions. To learn more, see Automatic revocation checking with CRL distribution points in the IAM Roles Anywhere User Guide.
ai_summary: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) Roles Anywhere now supports automatic revocation checking using certificate revocation list (CRL) distribution points (CDPs). This helps keep revocation checks in sync with your certificate authority (CA) and can help improve your security posture.

article_content:
Today, the Amazon OpenSearch Service optimized engine adds support for agent traces, including OpenTelemetry traces. Your traces and logs now live in the same place. You can follow a request or an agent session from start to finish, find the step that failed or slowed down, and check the related logs without switching tools. 

The optimized engine maps OpenTelemetry logs and traces to object, nested, and flat object fields, with support for multi-valued arrays. Span events, span links, prompts, and tool calls retain their nested structure, allowing field-level queries without flattening data during ingestion.

On hot-tier data, the engine supports update, delete, and upsert operations by document ID. When data arrives late or with errors, you can correct it in place, so your dashboards and alerts work from accurate data. In OpenSearch UI, you can analyze this data with Discover Traces, application performance monitoring, the service map, and the agent traces and sessions views.

These features are available on OpenSearch 3.7, at no additional charge in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), and Europe (Spain).  To get started, send OpenTelemetry data to your domain, for example by using Amazon OpenSearch Ingestion. To learn more, see the documentation.

article_content:
Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for Oracle (Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for Oracle) now allows customers to join their RDS for Oracle DB instances directly to their self-managed Microsoft Active Directory (AD) domain. Your self-managed AD can run on premises, on Amazon EC2, or with another cloud provider. Users in your AD domain can authenticate to RDS for Oracle DB instances using Kerberos.

Previously, in order to use Kerberos authentication with self-managed AD for their RDS for Oracle instances, customers were required to deploy AWS Managed Microsoft AD and establish trust between AWS managed domain and self-managed domain. Now, customers can join their existing self-managed AD directly to authenticate and authorize users without setting up an additional directory or trust relationship. You can set this up using the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDK. You can use self-managed AD without any additional charge.

Kerberos authentication with self-managed Active Directory in Amazon RDS for Oracle is available in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon RDS for Oracle is available. To learn more about Kerberos authentication with self-managed Active Directory, visit Working with self-managed Active Directory with an Amazon RDS for Oracle DB instance in the Amazon RDS User Guide.

title: AWS Security Hub Network Scanning now available in AWS GovCloud (US)
author: aws@amazon.com
description:
AWS Security Hub Network Scanning feature is now supported in AWS GovCloud (US).

Network Scanning probes your resources from the internet to detect actual reachability, not just what could be reachable based on security group rules and route tables. It discovers public IP addresses, virtual machines, and load balancers across your AWS environments, identifies reachable ports, and determines what services are running behind them. This complements Security Hub's existing network reachab...
article_content:
AWS Security Hub Network Scanning feature is now supported in AWS GovCloud (US).

Network Scanning probes your resources from the internet to detect actual reachability, not just what could be reachable based on security group rules and route tables. It discovers public IP addresses, virtual machines, and load balancers across your AWS environments, identifies reachable ports, and determines what services are running behind them. This complements Security Hub's existing network reachability findings, which identify configurations that could make a resource reachable from the internet. Network Scanning confirms that configurations do exist which make a resource reachable from the internet. Each reachable port generates a Security Hub finding with evidence of the port and service discovered. Security Hub Exposures then automatically correlates these findings with other findings and resource configurations to determine broader risk.

Existing customers can enable Network Scanning in individual accounts and regions, or across an organization via a configuration policy. For new Security Hub customers, Network Scanning is on by default. Network Scanning is included with Security Hub Essentials at no additional cost in all AWS commercial and GovCloud (US) Regions that support Security Hub. To learn more, see the AWS Security Hub User Guide and the AWS Security Hub product page. For the full list of Regions, see the AWS Regional Services List.

AWS Security Hub Network Scanning feature is now supported in AWS GovCloud (US).

Network Scanning probes your resources from the internet to detect actual reachability, not just what could be reachable based on security group rules and route tables. article_content:
AWS Lambda durable functions has increased default quotas for running executions and API request rates. The new quotas below apply in all AWS Regions except US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), and Europe (Ireland), which have twice these quotas.

  • Running durable executions per account (1 million to 5 million)
  • Function invocation rate to start durable executions (300 to 3,000 requests per second)
  • CheckpointDurableExecution and GetDurableExecutionState (1,000 to 10,000 requests per second)
  • SendDurableExecutionCallbackSuccess, SendDurableExecutionCallbackFailure, and SendDurableExecutionCallbackHeartbeat (300 to 3,000 requests per second)
  • GetDurableExecution and StopDurableExecution (30 to 300 requests per second)
  • GetDurableExecutionHistory and ListDurableExecutionsByFunction (15 to 150 requests per second)

AWS Lambda durable functions helps you build resilient multi-step applications and AI workflows that execute for up to one year, with built-in checkpointing, automatic retries, and waits that suspend execution without incurring compute charges. With this increase, workloads such as order processing and document pipelines can run more executions in parallel without requesting quota increases. When many executions wait on external work, such as payment confirmations or batch jobs, more can resume together. If you monitor and manage executions with your dashboards or scripts, they can now check status, list executions, read history, and stop executions at least ten times as often.

The new quotas apply in all AWS Regions where AWS Lambda durable functions is available. To learn more, see Lambda quotas in the AWS Lambda Developer Guide.

article_content:
Amazon SageMaker AI now supports IAM Identity Center (IdC) multi-region replication, enabling you to deploy SageMaker AI Studio domains in different regions from your IdC instance's primary region. Previously, the primary IdC instance had to reside in the same region as the SageMaker AI Studio domain; now customers can replicate their primary IdC instance into the region where they wish to use SageMaker AI Studio domains. This capability helps customers maintain compliance while utilizing centralized workforce identity management.

As an Amazon SageMaker AI Studio administrator, you can deploy SageMaker AI domains that align with your workforce's location and data residency requirements, independent of where your primary IdC instance is set up. Organizations can retain their primary IdC instance in one region while operating SageMaker AI Studio workloads in compliance-mandated regions, support global operations through centralized identity management, and satisfy data sovereignty requirements without compromising single sign-on (SSO) capabilities.

To get started see the SageMaker AI documentation and to learn about setting up IAM Identity Center multi-region support see the IAM Identity Center User Guide.

Multi-region IdC replication is available in all standard AWS Regions where Amazon SageMaker AI Studio is supported, including: Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Europe (Ireland), US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), South America (São Paulo), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Canada (Central), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Europe (Paris), Europe (Stockholm).

article_content:
AWS WAF AI traffic monetization now integrates with Stripe. Publishers, content owners, and API providers can collect stablecoin payments from AI bots and agents that settle in local currency directly to their Stripe balance. With this launch, customers can monetize agent access without holding stablecoins or managing a crypto wallet. Stripe is now available as a new payout method alongside existing stablecoin payouts.

To get started, connect your Stripe account to AWS WAF through Stripe Connect in the AWS WAF console. Your existing pricing and agent policies work unchanged. When an agent requests protected content, AWS WAF returns an HTTP 402 response with the valid payment credential types that it accepts. Once the agent returns with a valid payment credential and makes the request again, the content is returned ungated. Revenue from all payment providers appears in the AWS WAF console revenue analytics.

The Stripe integration is available at no additional charge to all AWS WAF customers using Amazon CloudFront, in all edge locations where AWS WAF web ACLs are associated with CloudFront distributions. Standard AWS WAF and Stripe processing fees apply. See AWS WAF pricing for details.

To get started, visit the AWS WAF console or explore the AWS WAF Developer Guide.

title: AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store now allows organization and validation with built-in data types
author: aws@amazon.com
description: AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store now supports 13 new parameter data types that automatically validate parameter values when you create or update a parameter. With built-in validation, you can stop malformed configuration values, such as an invalid IP address, AWS account ID, or JSON document, before your applications read them, without writing your own validation logic. These types allow you to better organize your parameters across your workloads. You can filter by type when calling ...
article_content:
AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store now supports 13 new parameter data types that automatically validate parameter values when you create or update a parameter. With built-in validation, you can stop malformed configuration values, such as an invalid IP address, AWS account ID, or JSON document, before your applications read them, without writing your own validation logic. These types allow you to better organize your parameters across your workloads. You can filter by type when calling the DescribeParameters API or when browsing parameters in the Parameter Store console.

The following data types are available for both standard and advanced parameters:  aws:region, aws:account:id, boolean, integer, float, binary, hostname, email, ipv4-address, and ipv6-address. Three more data types, url, json, and jsonc, are available for advanced parameters. Parameter Store checks the value when you call PutParameter and rejects any value that doesn't match its data type. New data types work with String and SecureString parameters, and several also support StringList parameters, where each item in the list is validated. You can combine a data type with an AllowedPattern for additional constraints, and you can change the data type of an existing text parameter.
ai_summary: AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store now supports 13 new parameter data types that automatically validate parameter values when you create or update a parameter. With built-in validation, you can stop malformed configuration values, such as an invalid IP address, AWS account ID, or JSON document, before your applications read them, without writing your own validation logic. These types allow you to better organize your parameters across your workloads.
main_event: AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store now allows organization and validation with built-in data types

title: Amazon ECS Managed Daemons can now collect json-file logs from application containers on Amazon ECS Managed Instances
author: aws@amazon.com
description:
Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) introduces json-file log driver support for Amazon ECS Managed Instances and log driver volumes for Amazon ECS Managed Daemons. Together, these features let you collect application logs with the observability agent of your choice and forward them to any destination you choose.

With this launch, your application containers on ECS Managed Instances can write their logs as local files in standard Doc...
article_content:
Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) introduces json-file log driver support for Amazon ECS Managed Instances and log driver volumes for Amazon ECS Managed Daemons. Together, these features let you collect application logs with the observability agent of your choice and forward them to any destination you choose.

With this launch, your application containers on ECS Managed Instances can write their logs as local files in standard Docker json-file format, which most observability agents read natively. Your managed daemons can directly read these files through a volume mount, without specifying host bind mount paths or requiring root privileges. As a result, one managed daemon on each instance can collect logs from every application container that uses the json-file log driver. Amazon ECS keeps each container's logs in a dedicated directory named with the container ID and retains them until the container is removed, so your managed daemon can use native file-based log collection and trace every log back to the container that produced it.

To get started, set the log driver to json-file in the logConfiguration of your application task definition. Next, register a daemon task definition that specifies a volume with logDriverVolumeConfiguration, and mount the volume into your daemon container using mountPoints. You can configure this using the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, API, AWS SDKs or AWS CloudFormation. This feature is available in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon ECS Managed Instances and Managed Daemons are available, at no additional cost. To learn more, refer to our documentation page and visit Amazon ECS Managed Instances.

Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) introduces json-file log driver support for Amazon ECS Managed Instances and log driver volumes for Amazon ECS Managed Daemons. Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) is now available in the Asia Pacific (Taipei) and Asia Pacific (New Zealand) Regions, adding to the list of available Regions where you can use Amazon DocumentDB.

Amazon DocumentDB is a fully managed, native JSON database that makes it simple and cost-effective to operate critical document workloads at virtually any scale without managing infrastructure. Amazon DocumentDB is designed to give you the scalability and durability you need when operating mission-critical MongoDB workloads. Storage scales automatically up to 128 TiB without any impact to your application. In addition, Amazon DocumentDB natively integrates with Amazon CloudWatch, AWS CloudTrail, AWS Lambda, AWS Backup, and more. Amazon DocumentDB supports millions of requests per second and can be scaled out to 15 low-latency read replicas in minutes with no application downtime.

To learn more about Amazon DocumentDB, please visit the Amazon DocumentDB product page and pricing page. You can create an Amazon DocumentDB cluster from the AWS Management Console, AWS Command Line Interface (CLI), or AWS SDKs.

title: The Pentagon wants to know who checks code when AI writes it
author:
Elisabeth Burrows
            https://about.gitlab.com/blog/authors/elisabeth-burrows/
description: The Department of War now treats AI-generated code as unverified until it’s proven otherwise.  DoW Instruction 8430.01 , “Accelerated Mission Software,” took effect September 8, 2026, and is the department’s latest guidance on modernizing and managing software. If you build or buy software for the DoW, the instruction changes what’s required of you for every line AI writes. You have to review and test it to the same standard as human-written code, show where AI touched it, and keep it on systems...
article_content:
The Department of War now treats AI-generated code as unverified until it’s proven otherwise.  DoW Instruction 8430.01 , “Accelerated Mission Software,” took effect September 8, 2026, and is the department’s latest guidance on modernizing and managing software. If you build or buy software for the DoW, the instruction changes what’s required of you for every line AI writes. You have to review and test it to the same standard as human-written code, show where AI touched it, and keep it on systems the department has approved. Here’s what the instruction asks of your team, and how GitLab helps you address it.

What is DoW Instruction 8430.01?  Issued by DoW CIO Kirsten Davies, DoW Instruction 8430.01 applies to every DoW organization and to any acquisition program that includes software, regardless of cost. The instruction sets policy and procedures for modernizing and managing software, with an emphasis on delivering capabilities faster. It directs teams to automate testing and security scanning, reuse what already works, and produce evidence as software is built.

The instruction also encourages teams to use AI, calling AI-assisted development a major force multiplier for speed and quality. However, it attaches three conditions: AI’s role is traceable, its code is verified so developers stay accountable, and government data stays within approved boundaries. Each condition changes what a software platform has to do.

Three requirements that shape AI in delivery  While DoW Instruction 8430.01 covers a wide scope, the three conditions mentioned above show how software platforms must adapt. Here they are in more detail.

1. Traceability: Know what AI touched  Software on DoW networks needs proof of what’s in it and how it was built. When AI is involved, the proof has to cover AI, too: which models, which versions, and which datasets were used to write or test the code.

In GitLab, that record lives beside your code.  Dependency Scanning  produces your software bill of materials, and  audit events  and deployment records are generated as part of delivery. Agents in  GitLab Duo Agent Platform  act through  their own service account , tied to the developer who started them, so a commit shows up as the agent acting on behalf of a named person. The commit then lands in the same audit log as everything else, where your SIEM can filter it as AI activity. Because the evidence stays in the platform, you can change models under managed policy without erasing the history.

2. Verification: Check what AI writes  Accelerated delivery cannot compromise security, safety, or supply chain integrity. AI-generated or AI-modified code is unverified input, and a person must approve changes to security-critical functions (a flaw that lets an attacker in) or safety-critical ones (a flaw that can cost lives or platforms). As the instruction states, “Developers and development teams remain fully accountable for the security, functionality, and integrity of any code generated or modified using AI.”

In GitLab, your scans, tests, and approval rules run in the same pipeline for every change, whether a developer or an agent writes the code.  Merge request approval policies  can require a named reviewer whenever a change touches protected paths or introduces a vulnerability, and  protected branches  mean an agent can propose but can’t merge past the people you’ve designated.

Dependency Scanning Auto-Remediation  (currently in beta) is one example of an agent doing the work while your reviewers still sign off. It proposes dependency upgrades and build fixes, and those proposals wait at your existing approval gates like any other merge request. When  GitLab orchestrates agents  across several steps, a flow can carry a change through review, tests, scans, and approvals on its own, pausing for a human to sign off before a merge or deploy. Every flow runs under the same identity, policy, and evidence chain as the rest of GitLab, so speed doesn’t mean skipped steps. For teams deciding how much autonomy to give agents, the  GitLab Security Standard  defines five stages (authorize, isolate, verify, release, and respond) that agents must clear before that autonomy is granted. Those stages are mapped to  NIST Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF)  and  SP 800-53 controls .

3. Data boundaries: Control where AI runs  AI systems must respect data boundaries without compromising intellectual property or classified context. Approved AI services must guarantee that government data and prompts aren’t used to train external models, and non-public DoW information stays on approved DoW systems. That means controlling which models are used and where they are hosted.

GitLab Duo Agent Platform Self-Hosted  runs on infrastructure you control, including air-gapped networks. You choose the supported models, on premises or in a private cloud, and can swap them without rebuilding workflows. Requests route through an  AI Gateway you deploy yourself , so prompts and responses stay in your environment. For  GitLab Dedicated for Government  customers, this is the standard setup: You run the AI Gateway in your  own environment , connected to the model provider of your choice.

Comply with DoW Instruction 8430.01 today  AI will keep getting faster at writing code. The harder job is showing the code can be trusted, and DoW Instruction 8430.01 asks your team to do exactly that. GitLab keeps that proof with the work: Every AI-assisted change carries its own evidence and audit trail, passes the same gates as human-written code, and runs on models you host and control. Your developers get the same guardrails for AI and non-AI work, without extra tools to learn.

See how  GitLab Duo Agent Platform  helps defense teams keep AI-generated code governed, auditable, and under human control.

author:
Bryan Ross

GitLab submitted  its own comment on CADA  because we share the goal of strengthening Europe’s digital sovereignty and security. We believe this important work should prioritize customer ...
article_content:
Sovereignty is moving from buzzword to buying criterion. The European Commission’s proposed  Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA)  would set assurance levels for the cloud and AI services public authorities buy, defining where data should live and who can access it. Parts of it could reach private entities too.

GitLab submitted  its own comment on CADA  because we share the goal of strengthening Europe’s digital sovereignty and security. We believe this important work should prioritize customer control, portability, interoperability, provider diversity, and risk-based safeguards. You can also view GitLab's submission on the  European Commission's Have Your Say portal .

But regulation is only one lever. Many vendor conversations still don’t address sovereignty with enough depth. If this is a priority for your organization, here are ten questions I’d put to any software vendor, GitLab included. Use them as a simple assessment to confirm if a vendor takes sovereignty seriously:

10 questions to ask your vendors  1. Which layers of the stack do you operate yourself?  This question gets at ownership and accountability. A cloud provider and a software vendor control different risks, and a good vendor can help its customers appropriately distinguish between the controls it operates from those it inherits from the infrastructure beneath it.

2. Can I choose where and how the software runs?  Look for a vendor that offers flexibility around how you handle your data and architecture.  Sovereignty needs to vary by workload, and the architecture should be able to meet your requirements. For example, self-managed deployments let you run software on your own infrastructure, whether on-premises, in a private cloud, or in a hybrid setup, so your data stays within boundaries you define.

3. Can I choose the AI models I use, and change them later?  Frontier models change fast, and your vendor should not lock you to one. Look for platforms that are model agnostic and draw on a diverse set of models and hosts. That gives your business the flexibility to use the best model for each use case as new ones are released. Open-weight models can often run in your own environment while offering strong price-performance.

4. Does my data train anyone’s model?  Data is valuable for training AI models, so ask for an official written policy around model training and request it includes sub-processors too. Consider it a great sign if the vendor can confidently point to resources that affirm they do not train generative AI models on your data and restrict AI model sub-processors from using both model inputs and outputs for training.

5. What data leaves my region, and why?  Personal data of identifiable users remains subject to regional regulations, like GDPR, regardless of its origin. However, some data and operational signals need to cross boundaries to keep service secure and available. The right vendor offers local hosting and can otherwise explain what types of data cross borders and justify why.

6. Who can reach my data, and from where?  Ask which roles can reach your infrastructure and customer data, from which regions, and under what safeguards. A vendor that offers deployment options with customer-managed encryption keys and private network connectivity adds further control over that access.

7. How do you handle data and risk classifications?  Ask how the vendor classifies different data and what governance mechanisms and incident response activities are in place to handle policy violations and security incidents. A clear classification approach also feeds data protection impact assessments.

8. Which independent audits cover the service I am buying?  Attestations such as  SOC 2 Type II  and  ISO/IEC 27001  let a vendor prove its own layer separately from the infrastructure provider’s assessment. Check that the report scope covers the application you will actually use.

9. Can you match controls to the sensitivity of each workload?  Regulated industries require finer-grain policy controls. Ask whether the vendor lets you set the level of assurance workload by workload. This approach helps your team tune controls to the sensitivity of its function and data so you have speed with control.

10. What does leaving your ecosystem look like?  Portability and interoperability are sovereignty features. Ask how the platform connects to the other tools and models you use and how you would export your projects and history.  The format of data exports is important; exports often yield datasets that are complex, poorly structured, or intentionally obfuscated, making them difficult to process without technical restructuring. A vendor confident in its product welcomes easy exports and open integrations.

Sovereignty helps organizations embrace flexibility  No vendor will give perfect answers on all ten of these questions, and requirements will continue to evolve, but the architecture you choose should be poised to absorb changes resiliently.

Teams get the most from AI when they can decide what their organization controls and how. That’s why GitLab believes customers should be able to choose which models they use and where they run. Take these ten questions into your next vendor conversation and see which vendors take sovereignty as seriously as you do.

If you’d like to see how GitLab measures up (we do!), review how we handle customer data and infrastructure in our  AI Transparency Center .

article_content:
An agent’s true cost isn’t only the tokens it burns. It’s the review that calls your code “safe to merge” after seeing the diff, but without any context on the pipeline. We call that artificial confidence, not artificial intelligence. Agents guess because code is all they can see; they can’t see the merge request that last changed it, the pipeline that ran it, the vulnerability it carries, or the people who wrote and reviewed it.

Guessing is expensive. If you’ve tried running agents in a large monorepo, one with tens of thousands of files, you know how it goes: the agent iterates, pinging the backend again and again for the information it needs to complete the task. Every round trip costs more time and more tokens. Eventually the agent gives up.

The model isn’t the constraint. Context is.

That’s the constraint that GitLab Orbit removes. Now generally available, Orbit is the context graph for your software lifecycle: a live, queryable view of all your code, merge requests, work items, pipelines, vulnerabilities, and ownership, with every relationship continuously updated as you ship. Every agent and engineer can work from one connected view of the lifecycle. In GitLab testing, agents connected to Orbit needed up to 45x fewer retries and used 4.5x fewer tokens on the same tasks with the same model.

Grounded agents get answers right the first time  An agent like Claude Code, connected to GitLab Orbit through MCP, stops crawling files and instead asks the graph. The first response comes back with real callers, recent changes, and owners, so your follow-up prompts can refine the answer rather than correct it. The difference is measurable. Compare the Market, one of the UK’s largest price comparison platforms, tested four context approaches for an internal AI code reviewer across 79 real merge requests. The GitLab Orbit-grounded reviewer matched about 70% of expected inline comments; RAG managed about 58%, worse than no added context at all.

“GitLab Orbit gave us an AI code reviewer that actually understands our codebase, not just the diff in front of it. We tested it against RAG and a few other approaches across real merge requests, and the gap was clear. Better comment placement, better summaries of what actually changed.”

— Ryan Harvey, Head of AI Engineering, Compare the Market

Fewer retries means fewer tokens  A recent analysis from a leading research and advisory firm found that the cost of an undisciplined agent session is dominated by retransmitting context that didn’t change between turns. That token cost comes from how the agent is set up, not from the model itself.

GitLab Orbit changes that engineering. The agent gets one bounded answer from the graph instead of reloading everything that might matter. In GitLab testing, agents connected to Orbit used up to 4.5x fewer tokens on the same tasks with the same model: each turn carries less context, and fewer turns go to work that never ships. Because the graph is shared, that cost doesn’t repeat per agent. Duo agents, Claude Code, Codex, and your own tools all query the same graph, so the context you build for the first agent is already there for the second.

Questions you couldn’t answer before  Since GitLab Orbit entered beta in June, we’ve worked with design partners running it against real codebases, real incidents, and real merge requests. Their first win was almost always a question they couldn’t get answered before.

Here are a few questions design partners asked Orbit that they couldn’t answer before, and what came back:

Which production services  are exposed to this vulnerability ?  A single query returns the services that include the component, the merge requests that introduced it, the environments it reached, and the teams that own each one. One design partner answered a security-coverage question across 34 million entities in seven minutes; through the API, the same question would have taken half a day. When a vulnerability lands, security has a complete remediation plan within the hour, not a partial list by the end of the day.

What breaks if I change this?  Before a push, a developer or their agent can ask which services, jobs, and environments a change touches, across every project in the group, not just the one open in the editor. Review agents bring the same answer to the merge request, so a “safe to merge” comment reflects the whole system instead of the diff. Across 79 real merge requests, Compare the Market’s reviewer flagged more real issues in the right places than their RAG-based version. Problems get caught in review, before they become outages.

Why does this CI job keep failing, and where else?  GitLab Orbit shows how often a job fails across every project that runs it, which projects have drifted from the shared CI configuration, and who owns them. What used to be a Slack thread asking three teams “has anyone seen this?” becomes one answer. A financial services company used this to trace a build-system outage to a CI job failing 50% of the time, a pattern nothing else had correlated.

What depends on the thing we’re about to migrate?  Every dependent service, job, environment, and owner comes back in one result. One design partner finished a multi-repository upgrade by asking the question directly: which projects are still on the old version? The last stragglers could be surfaced in one query with no spreadsheet or repo-by-repo audit to contend with.

Not every context graph can answer them  Context graphs are becoming a category, and most of them stop at code. GitLab connects the code change to the pipeline, the deployment, the vulnerability, and the owner, with your permissions intact. This means your team and agents can:

Start with a graph that already exists.  GitLab Orbit draws on the data you already have in GitLab, which means there is no connector to configure, no ETL pipeline to maintain, and no second system of record to keep in sync. Enable it for a group and the graph is ready. A graph assembled from the outside takes months of integration work before it answers its first question. Orbit is also built to extend to non-GitLab data sources.

Index the whole lifecycle.  GitLab is the system of record for the entire software development lifecycle, and GitLab Orbit connects it into one graph. Code indexes stop at the code. Work graphs stop at the ticket.

Keep your permissions without rebuilding them.  GitLab Orbit mirrors nested groups, roles, and security-domain access. A graph that lives outside GitLab has to rebuild all of that and keep it in sync.

Give every agent and every engineer the same graph.  Duo agents, Claude Code, Codex, custom tools, and the Data Explorer all query the same graph the same way. You invest in context once and every agent you add after that is cheaper than the last.

Bring the agents you already use  GitLab Orbit doesn’t ask you to change how your team works. The agents and tools you already run connect to one graph:

Agents on GitLab Duo Agent Platform query GitLab Orbit natively, with nothing to configure.

Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Antigravity, and any other MCP-compatible agent connect through MCP or the GitLab CLI:

glab auth login

glab orbit setup

Custom agents and internal tooling connect through REST.

Engineers query the same graph through the Data Explorer.

Every path asks the same graph the same way, and the graph keeps up. GitLab Orbit indexes every push, merge, and deploy as it happens, so agents reason from the lifecycle in its most current state; at GitLab’s scale, that’s more than 1.5 million projects and 8TB of graph data in under 2 hours. Indexing runs as its own service beside GitLab, so however hard your agents use Orbit, GitLab itself never slows down.

Pricing: One shared query pool for your whole organization  GitLab Orbit is sold as query packs that form one shared pool sized for your organization. Everyone in your GitLab org draws from it, humans and agents alike, so usage flows between occasional users, power users, and the agents working on their behalf. Nobody requests access or gets assigned a seat. A query is one request to the Orbit graph, whether it comes from an agent (such as Duo Agent Platform, Claude Code, or Cursor), an experience built into GitLab, or the API.

Each query pack is $30 in GitLab Credits per user per month and adds 1,000 queries to your organization’s shared pool; usage beyond the pool is billed at 33 queries per GitLab Credit, about $0.03 per query. Promotional pricing is available this quarter for early customers. Contact your GitLab account team to learn more and size the right number of query packs for your organization.

title: GitLab Orbit: Find vulnerability blast radius without the manual hunt
author:
Rebecca Carter
            https://about.gitlab.com/blog/authors/rebecca-carter/
description:
A critical vulnerability needs a fix and a map. The fix is usually fast. Finding where the vulnerable component lives, who owns it, and whether it's exposed to the Internet is what costs you time. Most security teams piece that answer together from scanner reports, spreadsheets, and a Slack thread asking who owns a service nobody recognizes, and you stay exposed for every hour that takes.

GitLab Orbit , now  generally available , replaces this manual work with a single query. Orbit connects cod...
article_content:
A critical vulnerability needs a fix and a map. The fix is usually fast. Finding where the vulnerable component lives, who owns it, and whether it's exposed to the Internet is what costs you time. Most security teams piece that answer together from scanner reports, spreadsheets, and a Slack thread asking who owns a service nobody recognizes, and you stay exposed for every hour that takes.

GitLab Orbit , now  generally available , replaces this manual work with a single query. Orbit connects code, merge requests, pipelines, security findings, and ownership in one graph that stays current as your teams ship. Ask which projects are affected and who owns them, and you get an answer in minutes. Agents answer from the graph instead of crawling repositories and stitching together API calls, so they need fewer retries and fewer tokens to get there.

Why scanners alone can't answer the question   PHP2Shell , the set of critical PHP flaws disclosed last week, illustrates the problem. PHP is usually installed as a system package, compiled from source, or baked into a container image, not managed as an application dependency. Vulnerable versions can sit on web servers, in container images, in old CI jobs, or in internal tools nobody remembers building. The fix was a version upgrade. Finding every affected installation took time.

Security tools provide different views of the environment. Dependency scanning identifies vulnerable application dependencies. Container scanning detects vulnerabilities in operating system packages, language dependencies, and other software components. Code search helps locate where images and configurations are referenced. But identifying a vulnerability is only part of the job. Teams still need to know which services are affected, who owns them, which pipelines build and deploy them, and where to apply the fix. That information is often spread across multiple systems.

That leaves your team to connect the dots, each holding a different piece. Your security engineer can assess the severity but may not see every affected system. Your platform engineer owns the base images and CI templates that hundreds of projects depend on, but can't see every project that uses them. Your developers get pulled off their roadmap to search repositories for a component they may not know they own. Your CISO has to tell leadership whether the company is exposed before anyone has a full list.

An attacker only needs to find one vulnerable system. You need to find all of them. Exploiting a vulnerability is now the most common way breaches begin, at 31% in  Verizon's 2026 report , and the same report found attackers  using generative AI at several stages of an attack . The map needs to exist before the advisory lands.

A first-party graph of your entire SDLC  Orbit draws on the data GitLab already runs on: your merge requests, pipelines, deployments, and vulnerabilities. A CVE in Orbit's graph connects directly to the services, pipelines, environments, and teams it touches. Because the graph is first-party, there's no second system to keep in sync and no new instrumentation to stand up.

Without Orbit, an agent or analyst can usually find the vulnerable code but not the full exposure. Someone assembles that picture by hand, tool by tool, and the gaps show up as the long tail of services nobody checked. With Orbit, one query maps the CVE to the services, pipelines, environments, and owners that depend on it, and the output is a scoped, prioritized list your security team can act on.

Agents without Orbit hit the same wall: they can't see the whole system, so they guess. In GitLab's testing on the same tasks with the same model, agents running through Orbit were up to 11 times faster, used up to 4.5 times fewer tokens, and needed up to 45 times fewer retries. During an incident, faster answers arrive while the team is still triaging, lower token use keeps queries across a large group from becoming a cost problem, and fewer retries mean your team can act on the first answer instead of re-running the question.

Watch the demo to learn how GitLab Orbit can help you understand your exposure:

One graph that connects a CVE to its owner  Blast radius is how far a vulnerability reaches: which projects contain the flawed component, how it got there, who owns those projects, and what changed recently. GitLab already holds most of those facts in separate places, and Orbit connects them. Turn it on for a top-level group, and Orbit  indexes projects, merge requests, pipelines, work items, security findings, and source code  into one graph of how they relate.

From there, you ask in plain language instead of correlating systems by hand: which projects use this library, which merge requests brought it in, and who owns each project? An agent traverses the graph and answers from indexed project data, and you can audit the  graph queries behind each answer .

Access follows the  roles you've already set , so people and agents see only what they're permitted to see. GitLab's built-in agents, including the  Security Analyst Agent ,  use Orbit directly , and external agents such as Claude Code and Codex reach the same graph over  MCP .

Contain your exposure quickly  After PHP2Shell, leadership's first question is whether you're exposed. Without a map, your answer is "we're checking." With Orbit, your answer is a list: these projects contain PHP, these teams own them, and these pipelines build them.

The first hour with Orbit looks like this:

Find every PHP project.  In  GitLab Duo Agentic Chat , ask: “Use Orbit to map the blast radius of PHP in this group. List every project that contains PHP code, grouped by subgroup, with owners.”

Confirm the base image and version.  Use  exact code search  at the top-level group with regular expression mode on. Run  lang:Dockerfile ^FROM.*php  to find container base images, and  file:composer\.json$  to find Composer projects with no Dockerfile. Compare each  FROM  tag with the fixed versions.

Find open findings.  Once scans have run, ask Agentic Chat to collect every container scanning finding for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 across the group from the  vulnerability report . This requires Ultimate and the  Security Manager role .

Check against what’s running.  Orbit and code search cover what your repositories declare on the default branch. Compare that list with your runtime inventory from configuration management or cloud tooling, starting with internet-facing services, since PHP can also run on hand-built servers outside any repository.

The  PHP2Shell remediation guide  covers fixed versions and how to check for compromise. Teams on GitLab Self-Managed or GitLab Dedicated can start with the guide's advanced search and repository languages API steps until Orbit reaches their instance.

Run the same check for any shared component  The steps above work beyond PHP. When a widely used library ships a security fix, a package you depend on is flagged as malicious, a CI template many projects inherit needs a change, or an internal SDK ships a breaking security upgrade, you start with the same question: what depends on it, and who owns it? Orbit answers from the same graph each time, so your team starts from a list instead of a search.

Map your blast radius before the next disclosure  GitLab Orbit is now generally available for Premium and Ultimate customers, starting with GitLab.com today and reaching Self-Managed and GitLab Dedicated over the coming weeks. Customers can try it free for 30 days through their GitLab account team. If you're new to GitLab,  talk to our team  about getting started with a paid plan, and we can add an Orbit trial as part of it.

Check out the  documentation  to get started. For a broader view of your security posture,  request your GitLab Security Standard assessment  to see how blast radius mapping fits into the rest of your security program. If your teams run PHP, start with the  PHP2Shell remediation guide  and upgrade now.

title: What happens when vulnerabilities are discovered faster than you can fix them?
author:
Bill Staples
            https://about.gitlab.com/blog/authors/bill-staples/
description:
We're entering a new era of application security. Frontier AI models are uncovering complex flaws that traditional tools overlooked, and attackers are using the same models to exploit them faster. Remediation isn't keeping pace: Verizon's 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report (DBIR) measures the median time to fully remediate a known-exploited vulnerability at 43 days, up from 32 in 2025.

Security teams are already stretched across growing application portfolios, third-party dependencies, and ...
article_content:
We're entering a new era of application security. Frontier AI models are uncovering complex flaws that traditional tools overlooked, and attackers are using the same models to exploit them faster. Remediation isn't keeping pace: Verizon's 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report (DBIR) measures the median time to fully remediate a known-exploited vulnerability at 43 days, up from 32 in 2025.

Security teams are already stretched across growing application portfolios, third-party dependencies, and a steady stream of new disclosures. And while agents that find vulnerabilities and write fixes are becoming more accessible, integrating them into how enterprises actually build and ship software remains difficult.

A generated patch still needs to be tested. Security policies need to be enforced. Changes need to be reviewed and approved. And eventually, the fix needs to reach production safely.

This is where I believe the next major shift in application security will happen.  We need to put autonomous agents to work inside the software factory. That's why we've brought Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5.1 into GitLab, and why we're connecting discovery, remediation, and prevention in one trusted workflow.

When critical vulnerabilities emerge, the clock starts ticking  Critical vulnerabilities like PHP2Shell send security teams scrambling to understand exposure. For a large organization, that means assessing impact across hundreds or thousands of repositories, applications, and dependencies.

Identifying exposure is only the first step. Teams then need to assess exploitability, prioritize affected applications, coordinate fixes, run tests, and get changes into production. Every handoff takes time, and speed is vital: 31% of breaches now start with vulnerability exploitation, the top initial access vector for the first time in the DBIR's 19 years.

As more critical vulnerabilities emerge, the traditional model of manually investigating findings, assigning tickets, and waiting for developers to write fixes becomes harder to sustain.

The time between vulnerability discovery and verified remediation needs to shrink dramatically.  That requires security workflows capable of operating at machine speed, while preserving the controls organizations depend on to ship reliable software.

Bring agentic remediation into the software factory  AI agents can do impressive work in vulnerability discovery and remediation. The challenge is making that work reliable and repeatable across an enterprise.

An agent can generate a patch in seconds. Whether it understood the application, whether it validated the change against the real build, and whether it followed your security policies are separate questions. They get harder to answer, and more expensive to get wrong, as you deploy agents across thousands of projects.

At GitLab, we're bringing agentic security workflows into the environment where teams develop, test, and ship software.

Everything an agent does rests on how well it understands your system, and that understanding extends beyond the repository.  GitLab Orbit , a live context graph of your software lifecycle, connects findings to the changes that introduced them, the pipelines that shipped them, and the teams who own the fix. It's also how you answer the questions that follow a disclosure like PHP2Shell: Are we exposed? Is it reachable? How far does it spread, and how do we fix it without breaking production?

GitLab Duo Agent Platform  investigates findings  in the context of your software and how it's built, filtering out likely false positives and prioritizing by exploitability and reachability.

For the findings that matter, Duo writes a fix and puts it through your pipeline to check for regressions and rerun security scans. In a single merge request, developers review the change, Duo's explanation, and the pipeline results.

Security teams move from understanding exposure to initiating remediation in one pass, and developers shift from chasing findings to reviewing fixes. Because these workflows run inside the software factory, agents operate within the same processes and controls that organizations already use to deliver software.

That's how we turn agentic security from an isolated capability into something an enterprise can trust and operate across thousands of projects, at machine speed.

Put frontier AI to work on the most critical vulnerabilities  Some of the most dangerous application vulnerabilities require a deep understanding of how software is intended to work: missing authorization checks, broken ownership logic, and business logic flaws that expose customer data or let users take actions they shouldn't.

Traditional scanners struggle with these issues because finding them requires reasoning about the application's behavior and the relationships between components.

Our new  Business Logic Security Analyzer , the first GitLab capability to support Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5.1, examines how your application enforces its rules: it reads the whole repository and incoming merge requests, infers what each endpoint should enforce, and flags the gaps that pattern-based scanners often miss.

But the real opportunity comes from connecting those discoveries to the workflows teams already use. When a critical flaw is found, teams need to understand its impact, initiate remediation, validate the proposed fix, and ship it safely. Integrating frontier AI into the software factory creates a path to run that entire process at machine speed.

The intelligence of the model is only as valuable as your ability to act on it.

Prevent risky code from reaching production  Finding vulnerabilities earlier is valuable, and keeping vulnerable code and unsafe packages out of production altogether is even better. These protections become even more important as agents gain autonomy.

Security controls need to be embedded throughout the software factory and enforced independently of the people and agents making changes, with every change clearing the same gates before it moves forward.

GitLab Ultimate brings static analysis, dependency and container scanning, secret detection, policy enforcement, and approval gates directly into the software delivery process. Those policies are set centrally and apply consistently across projects and pipelines, so the author of a change, human or agent, cannot change or waive the controls evaluating its work.

The same scrutiny needs to extend to third-party software. Modern applications rely heavily on open source dependencies, and a vulnerable or malicious package can introduce serious risk before developers write a single line of code.

GitLab's Dependency Firewall blocks policy-violating packages before they enter your build.  GitLab Secrets Manager  lets each job access only the credentials it requests and is authorized to use, so a compromised dependency can reach only the secrets of the job it runs in.

Agents need the freedom to work quickly, within boundaries they can't cross. GitLab Duo Agent Platform gives each agent a composite identity that limits it to the permissions it shares with the requesting user, a sandbox that's destroyed when the task ends, and a record of every action. These boundaries are part of the  GitLab Security Standard , under which agents earn more autonomy only as the controls at each stage are proven to hold.

The controls that make a change trustworthy need to hold at every step, even when the work happens at machine speed.

The next chapter of security will be defined by trusted execution  Frontier models will keep improving, security agents will get more capable, and vulnerabilities that were once difficult to discover will become easier to find. That progress will put enormous pressure on how organizations respond.

A security team can deploy the most advanced models available, but its ability to reduce risk will still depend on how quickly and safely it can turn findings into production-ready fixes.

This is why the software factory matters. It's where agents get the context needed to understand applications, where changes are validated against real builds and tests, where security policies are enforced, and where human oversight applies without slowing every step of the process.

At GitLab, we're bringing these capabilities together so you can automate remediation, uncover complex flaws, and prevent unsafe changes from shipping, all inside the workflows you already use.

The next security advantage will come from how quickly organizations can turn a critical discovery into a verified, trusted fix.

We invite you to run your next security sprint on us. Qualifying teams can request access to GitLab Ultimate, GitLab Duo Agent Platform, GitLab Orbit, and GitLab Secrets Manager, with free credits.  Request access to the security sprint offer .
