article_content:
The majority of U.S. venture capital nowadays goes to companies founded or led by men who are already billionaires.

This is not a difficult stat to unearth. So far this year, just seven companies raised more than half of all seed- through growth-stage investment. They’re mostly familiar names:  OpenAI ,  Anthropic ,  xAI  (now part of  SpaceX ),  Anduril Industries ,  Databricks ,  Prometheus  and  The Boring Co.

These companies raised more than $260 billion in equity funding in the first 10 months of the year. That’s just over 50% of the U.S. seed and venture investment over the same period, per Crunchbase data.

Founders and CEOs of these seven companies are also well-known — and exceptionally  well-off to boot.

The world’s wealthiest men

Two founders are particularly famous. They are the world’s wealthiest men:  Elon Musk  and  Jeff Bezos .

Musk founded xAI and The Boring Co., and also co-founded OpenAI, (though he has no known equity stake in the latter). And while outside investors funded these companies, Musk could have also afforded to do so himself.

Ditto for Bezos, who in 2025 launched the physical AI startup Prometheus, which raised $12 billion earlier this year. Bezos’ own net worth, meanwhile, is calculated at more than $350 billion.

AI’s leading names

The two highest valuation startups — OpenAI and the soon-to-be-public Anthropic — also have prominent billionaire founders and CEOs. However, they have mixed backstories to their wealth.

OpenAI co-founder and CEO  Sam Altman  primarily made his vast wealth through investments in  Y Combinator  startups, including  Stripe  and  Reddit . Altman has said he  does not have an equity stake  in OpenAI beyond a sliver from an old YC round. Co-founder  Greg Brockman , by contrast, has a larger stake in OpenAI that was reportedly valued around $30 billion earlier this year.

At Anthropic, meanwhile, all seven company co-founders have similar-sized equity stakes, and each is worth billions. This includes the AI giant’s most famous co-founder, CEO  Dario Amodei .

Databricks, Anduril and others

Databricks and Anduril, meanwhile, both have founders serving as CEOs who have amassed billion-dollar-plus net worths during their tenures.

Databricks co-founder and CEO  Ali Ghodsi  has a reported  $7.6 billion net worth , with the company he leads valued at around $190 billion following an August financing.

Anduril co-founder and CEO  Brian Schimpf , meanwhile, has an estimated $1.5 billion net worth as a result of his stake in the $61 billion valuation defense industry disruptor. Co-founder  Palmer Luckey , who sold his virtual reality startup  Oculus  to  Meta  for $2 billion in 2014 before starting Anduril, has an estimated $5.9 billion net worth.

Several other founders and CEOs of startups that raised some of this year’s largest rounds are billionaires too. This includes  Wonder  founder  Marc Lore ,  Figure  founder  Brett Adcock , and  Surge AI  founder and CEO  Edwin Chen , among others.

Billionaire categories

We can split the billionaires who founded this year’s most heavily funded startups into two broad subcategories. There are those who became billionaires through the startup that just raised capital. And there are those who were already billionaires through prior companies or investments.

Ghodsi, Amodei and Brockman fit in the first group. In the second group, of course, we can put Musk and Bezos, as well as Altman and Luckey, who became a  21-year-old billionaire  following the Oculus sale.

Historically, neither billionaire type was a particularly common recipient of venture funding rounds. The term “unicorn” as a moniker for private companies valued at $1 billion or more only entered the lexicon in 2013, when this asset class became noticeably large. In prior decades, founders and CEOs mostly only hit billionaire status after their startups went public or sold in high-priced acquisitions.

Updating the venture archetype

But times change. And in tandem, our image of what a startup funding recipient looks like should evolve as well.

True, quite a bit of capital still flows to the stereotypical venture recipients: first-time founders or serial entrepreneurs whose prior companies didn’t make them fabulously wealthy. But a majority of venture funding now does not go to these classic startup types.

Instead, it goes to companies with valuations already high enough to warrant billionaire status for their stakeholders as well as ventures founded by men who are already billionaires.

article_content:
Global venture funding in October totaled $59 billion, a 45% jump from a year earlier, per Crunchbase data, in large part due to a record-setting deal for China’s  DeepSeek . The company’s $15.9 billion funding round marked the largest-ever venture deal for a Chinese company ever, and came in the same month that two other frontier labs raised blockbuster Series A rounds totaling at or close to $1 billion.

The bulk of October’s venture funding was invested in the two leading countries for startup investment, with companies based in the U.S. and China raising $28 billion and $20.6 billion last month, respectively. The last time more than $20 billion was invested in China in a single month was June 2018, when  Ant Group  raised $14 billion in its Series C funding.

Funding concentration

Funding concentrated in seven companies that raised billion-dollar rounds, accounting for just over 40% of October’s venture funding. These large amounts were invested in frontier labs, manufacturing, energy, semiconductors, prediction markets and spend management software. Private equity led much of this funding, along with a few multistage venture firms including  Sequoia Capital ,  Index Ventures  and  Lux Capital .

DeepSeek ’s $15.9 billion raise at a valuation of $90 billion marked the largest private funding by a Chinese tech company on record. The deal places DeepSeek among the Top 10 most highly funded private companies. It also makes it the second  most highly valued Chinese company  after  ByteDance , and the third most highly valued private frontier lab after U.S. companies  Anthropic  and  OpenAI .

DeepSeek wasn’t the only Chinese frontier lab to raise big in October.  Moonshot AI , a rival open-source lab, reportedly reached a $50 billion value in October, making it the 11th most valuable private company on  The Crunchbase Unicorn Board . The startup has also reportedly confidentially filed to go public on the Hong Kong stock exchange.

Massachusetts-based manufacturing startup  Re:Build  raised the second-largest funding deal last month, a $2.1 billion round. The company partners with industrial companies and innovators from the product design phase to large-scale production and says it has 2.4 million square feet of manufacturing capacity.

Other large rounds last month went to  Axiom , which raised $2 billion for power and grid capacity build out for data centers; spend-management platform  Ramp , which raised $1.85 billion and said its ARR has reached $2 billion; open-source semiconductor company  Tenstorrent , which says it  raised a $1.5 billion Series E funding and recently moved its  headquarters to Silicon Valley from Canada; prediction market  Kalshi , which raised a $1 billion Series E; and frontier lab  Flapping Airplanes , which raised a $1 billion Series A.

AI-driven

A further eight companies raised rounds north of $500 million last month. They spanned industries ranging from frontier labs, robotics, legal and chips, to agentic AI and healthcare. Among the most notable was  TypeSafe AI , which says it raised an $870 million Series A funding on the heels of rapid developer adoption of its decision model Jev.

A total of 66% of global funding was in AI-driven companies in October, with semiconductor companies gaining market share this past month.

Exits

The U.S. IPO market was slow in anticipation of Anthropic’s November IPO. The offering could surpass even  SpaceX ’s record-setting June listing  that raised $85.7 billion .

On the M&A front, at least nine venture-backed companies were acquired for more than $1 billion last month, including  Uber ’s acquisition of 19-year-old  ezCater  for $2.3 billion.

Looking ahead

With two months remaining, 2026 has already set records for acquisitions, IPOs and funding rounds across major venture markets. October extended that momentum, but also highlighted how concentrated this cycle has become: Seven companies accounted for more than 40% of global funding, while AI-driven businesses captured two-thirds.

The question heading into year-end is how widely that momentum will spread, as Anthropic prepares to list in what could be the largest IPO of all time.

Global Venture Funding In 2026

Global Venture Funding To AI Startups In 2026

Global IPOs For Venture-Backed Companies In 2026

Global M&A In 2026 For Venture-Backed Companies

Methodology

The data contained in this report comes directly from Crunchbase, and is based on reported data. Data is as of Nov. 2, 2026.

Cohere  is targeting a $5 billion funding that was announced in October,  without reporting an initial or final close . This funding was not included in the October monthly totals.

Note that data lags are most pronounced at the earliest stages of venture activity, with seed funding amounts increasing significantly after the end of a quarter/year.

Please note that all funding values are given in U.S. dollars unless otherwise noted. Crunchbase converts foreign currencies to U.S. dollars at the prevailing spot rate from the date funding rounds, acquisitions, IPOs and other financial events are reported. Even if those events were added to Crunchbase long after the event was announced, foreign currency transactions are converted at the historic spot price.

Glossary of funding terms

Seed and angel consists of seed, pre-seed and angel rounds. Crunchbase also includes venture rounds of unknown series, equity crowdfunding and convertible notes at $3 million (USD or as-converted USD equivalent) or less.

Early-stage consists of Series A and Series B rounds, as well as other round types. Crunchbase includes venture rounds of unknown series, corporate venture and other rounds above $3 million, and those less than or equal to $15 million.

Late-stage consists of Series C, Series D, Series E and later-lettered venture rounds following the “Series [Letter]” naming convention. Also included are venture rounds of unknown series, corporate venture and other rounds above $15 million. Corporate rounds are only included if a company has raised an equity funding at seed through a venture series funding round.

Technology growth is a private-equity round raised by a company that has previously raised a “venture” round. (So basically, any round from the previously defined stages.)

When I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like  The Jetsons , even if just for an hour.

The device that arrived at my building belongs to Tau Robotics, a local startup. Its long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but the technology isn’t quite there yet. For now, humans pilot the robots remotely, watching them work through onboard cameras.

There were some unexpected challenges along the way, but also moments that felt like a glimpse of the future.

Find out how well the machine cleaned my home—and how close we are to truly autonomous domestic robots .

A visit to Samsung’s massive new semiconductor hub

Generative AI models depend on stacks of specialized memory chips. To meet soaring demand, Samsung is building a vast new semiconductor manufacturing campus in Pyeongtaek, South Korea.

I visited the sprawling campus south of Seoul, where three fabs already operate around the clock, a fourth is coming online, and thousands of workers are racing to build a fifth.

title: I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.

I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner. I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser. But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. article_content:
I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner. I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser. But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like  The Jetsons , even if just for an hour.

I was also motivated by journalistic interest. In order to ensure an authentic experience, I didn’t tell Tau Robotics, the startup behind the X post, that I was a journalist—though I did use my real name, so it’s possible someone looked me up. Tau’s long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but they’re not quite there yet: For now, the robots are piloted remotely by humans, who watch what’s going on via cameras mounted in the robots’ heads and wrists. As the robots clean, they collect data that Tau will use to train up their more independent descendants. Every counter successfully wiped and T-shirt successfully folded will help the models that power the robots learn to do better on the next go-round.

Because this data is so valuable to Tau, the company charges less for cleaning than one might expect for such a cutting-edge product. At the time I booked, Tau was offering $30 for an hourlong cleaning with a single robot; now the charge is $60 per weekly cleaning with two robots, or $100 for a one-time visit. But even at the cheaper rate of $30 per hour, Tau’s robots aren’t a great bargain. They are thorough but slow, so if you, like me, are tempted to stand around watching them for their entire visit, it would probably be a better use of your time to just take care of the cleaning yourself. 

But the robots are physically capable of cleaning, and they’re undeniably cute. Tau has armed each four-and-a-half-foot-tall robot with a 3D-printed “head” with antennae that allow it to communicate with Tau’s headquarters, as well as two 3D-printed claw “hands” (the more humanlike alternatives apparently aren’t durable enough, and claws do surprisingly well for most cleaning tasks). Mine was wearing a Tau Robotics shirt, and grippy socks so that it didn’t scratch hardwood floors.

With all the human support they need, the robots are closer to radio-controlled cars than Waymos. Many tasks, such as making the bed and folding laundry, require what’s called kinematic guidance: The human pilot performs the necessary motions, and sensors transmit those movements to the robot, which copies them. These kinematically guided tasks produce especially valuable training data. Tau’s AI models might not have solved laundry folding yet, but learning from the examples of robots that have completed the task in the real world is how they’ll get there.

But according to Tau cofounder Cornelia Weinzierl, to whom I came clean as a journalist a few weeks after the cleaning, the robot can already complete some other tasks—such as vacuuming and mopping—without any human help. If Tau succeeds in using all the data it is collecting to train truly autonomous cleaning robots, they could even become  San Francisco’s newest tech tourist attraction  as Waymos become more commonplace countrywide.

The cleaning robot that came to my building last month was already a bit of a spectacle. It arrived in a blue minivan, out of which it was helped by Weinzierl and another Tau employee. That’s when the robot encountered its first obstacle: the eight stairs leading up to the building’s front door. I’d come down to greet Weinzierl and the robot, so I had a front-row seat to its struggles with my steps. It climbed as if it were drunk. Each successful step was as likely as not to be followed by a stumbling backward stagger that erased all its progress—though, impressively, it never entirely lost its footing.

When I later discussed my experience with Weinzierl, she explained that the robot sometimes walks strangely because it is operated remotely from Tau’s headquarters, and the short signal transmission delay can affect its coordination. “The amount of work and time that we spend just optimizing, for example, timings and connectivity is crazy,” she said.

Inside, the carpeted staircase leading up to my apartment defeated the robot entirely, and Weinzierl had to lug it up the last few steps. This, it turned out, was not typical. As the robot cleaned, it repeatedly stalled out, something Weinzierl attributed to it overheating in the unseasonably hot weather—until she heard from one of her colleagues that the heat had shut down not the robot but the equipment that its human controller was using to watch its progress through my apartment. Without remote assistance, the robot couldn’t clean, and so it, and Weinzierl, departed before my booked hour was up. (Back in September, Weinzierl or another Tau representative remained with the robot throughout its visit, but she says that’s no longer necessary.)

You can’t fault Tau on customer service, though. Weinzierl quickly emailed me to apologize, comp the visit, and offer me another on the house (minus whatever price I assign to my data privacy)—and that was all before I told her I was a journalist. I scheduled the next cleaning for about a month later, after a couple of trips out of town, and it went much more smoothly—the robot got up my stairs without much assistance, though still with the drunken stagger.

In the hour it was there, it did a creditable job of cleaning my kitchen (though it didn’t brave the stove) and even saved me my most dreaded cleaning task, the toilet. That was its most impressive performance: Three times the head fell off its toilet cleaning wand, and three times it managed to reattach it by poking around with the handle until it made contact at just the right angle.

The robot is still rough around the edges, which is to be expected for a product in beta. It repeatedly left my taps dripping, it knocked over a (closed) bottle of olive oil, and it couldn’t manage to right an air purifier that it had toppled. But I easily forgave all those missteps because of how charming it was. As I watched it wipe down my countertops, I felt the same fond gratitude that I feel when a Waymo delivers me safely home after a night out.

Still, it’s not all slapstick and whimsy. If Tau Robotics or its competitors succeeds in training robots to clean autonomously and inexpensively, people could lose their livelihoods, and the United States is a long way away from implementing policies to take care of those left unemployed by AI. 

But Weinzierl maintains that someday turning over cleaning work to robots could make a lot of sense. “Cleaning is not a job that a lot of people really actively want to be doing—there’s high turnover, there’s a high risk of injury,” she said when we spoke after the cleanings. “We need people, and we don’t have them, and no one wants to do it.” She said that the company is also starting to consider someday deploying the robots for other dangerous or physically challenging jobs, such as mold remediation and home health care.

Tau Robotics still has a long way to go: The amount of data needed to train robots to do the varied and complicated tasks of apartment cleaning is probably enormous, and the company has completed only a couple hundred cleanings so far. But it’s remarkable that there are now humanoid robots able to clean your toilets and mop your floors, even if they need quite a bit of human help to do so.  The Jetsons  no longer feels quite so far away.

Texas was the new epicenter of the AI data center buildout. That might be kaput.

Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech’s largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position.

Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat, Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor, and Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. They won after making data centers a central issue on the campaign trail.

The swings could spell trouble for hyperscalers with ambitious plans in the state. They also add to growing anxiety that America’s AI buildout could stall.

Here’s how the election results could reshape AI’s future .

—James O’Donnell

What’s next for US energy policy after the midterm elections?

Democrats have taken control of both the House and the Senate, but we probably won’t see major federal climate and energy legislation while Trump remains president. The midterm elections could, however, be a big deal for energy at the state and local level.

The results could shape everything from the state grid and data center development to renewable energy and greenhouse gas emissions.

Find out what the midterms could mean for the future of US energy .

—Casey Crownhart

A new bill could change how the US builds energy infrastructure 

A sweeping bit of legislation designed to cut red tape could speed up the buildout of energy infrastructure in the US.

On November 9, the Senate is set to vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA). It’s a plan that could start an overhaul of the slow, complicated process for getting energy projects approved. But some environmental groups oppose the bill, or parts of it.

Explore the trade-offs behind America’s proposed permitting overhaul .

—Casey Crownhart

article_content:
A sweeping bit of legislation designed to cut red tape could speed up the buildout of energy infrastructure in the US.

With the dust barely settled on this week’s momentous midterms, the Senate is set to vote on the  Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act  (BAAJA) on November 9. It’s a plan that could finally start an overhaul of the slow, complicated process for getting energy projects approved, as part of something called permitting reform. People on both sides of the political aisle have been pushing for this type of change for some years.

The key question is whether this will cut greenhouse-gas emissions from the US energy sector or push them higher still.  

The federal permitting system is designed to protect the environment against industrial pollution from large projects like power plants, transmission lines, and natural-gas pipelines. Today, permitting is governed by a range of laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act. And if there’s one thing you might know about the current state of permitting in the US it’s that it’s slow and incredibly complicated.

So in its 417 pages, BAAJA attempts to tighten things up. The bill has provisions that narrow the sorts of projects that need to apply for federal permits and others that enact deadlines in hopes of speeding up a process that today can take years. (There are also specific provisions about transmission planning, mining, and the rest of the kitchen sink; this thing is  dense .)

One thing to know about this bill is that it’s largely technology neutral: It opens the doors for the buildout of projects involving both fossil fuels and renewables. So there’s a weird mishmash of legislators and outside groups supporting it.

The bill’s four sponsors in the Senate are two Republicans and two Democrats. The White House has backed this permitting reform bill, with its Council of Economic Advisors finding that it would reduce review times and have economic benefits like boosting GDP.

Clean energy groups like the American Clean Power Association have largely come out in favor of the bill too, with the group’s  analysis  finding that it could unlock 350 gigawatts of new clean energy for the grid.

Some environmental groups, however, oppose the bill, or parts of it. An  assessment  from the Natural Resources Defense Council says the parts about transmission could have substantial benefits for the grid, but the narrowing of environmental reviews could be damaging for public and private lands.

Many in the climate world have long been calling for permitting reform, arguing that renewables stand to benefit more than fossil fuels. The thinking is that solar and wind power are some of the cheapest sources available today, so if we unlock the ability to build more energy, they are likely to win out economically.

A few early analyses have tried to quantify just what BAAJA would mean for emissions in the US. One, from the think tank Rhodium Group,  found  that in the best-case scenario, the bill would cut economy-wide emissions by 4%, reduce annual energy bills by $78 per household, and add 200 gigawatts of new clean energy by 2040. In the worst case, emissions would stay about the same.

Another  report , from the nonprofit research group Resources for the Future, found that the bill could cut power-sector emissions 6% by 2041 and save more than $350 billion on system costs by midcentury.

But there are some concerns that this permitting bill’s real effect would be to open the floodgates for new natural-gas plants. As data centers have put more pressure on the grid, a wave of such plants have been announced.

“You get down to a trade-off between essentially growing the clean electricity industry on the one hand and then, as a compromise, growing the fossil-fuel industry on the other,” says Kevin Kircher, an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue.

To quantify that trade-off, Kircher also modeled the potential emissions effects of the bill and found that if BAAJA had been in place in 2025, energy sector emissions would have been higher than the actual baseline. Health and mortality risks associated with air pollution would also have increased.

This bill is scheduled for a Senate vote on November 9, well before the next Congress takes control. It’s not clear what the dramatic victories for Democrats might mean for the legislation, which was expected to pass the Senate with largely Republican support if a few Democrats got on board. Democrats could decide to wait for next year, when they’ll have control of both chambers. But any deal would ultimately need to win Trump’s signature, limiting what a future bill might be able to change. 

In a world where permitting new projects is easier, we’ll see more clean energy, but we’ll see more natural gas, too. And while prices could get lower, that could push demand for electricity higher, leading to more emissions overall.

Simplifying the permitting system and cutting red tape is a worthy goal. But when it comes to emissions, it still really matters what, exactly, you want to build.

This is today’s edition of    The Download  ,  our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

These startups hope “blended” food will cut our appetite for red meat 

In the fall of 2025, Jeff Dodge served hungry students steaming marinara sauce and meatballs. The students loved them: 92% of those who tried them wanted them on the menu. Few could guess that mushrooms had been mixed into the meat.

Dodge was testing a new product called 50/Cut from the company Joyn. The blend of seemingly simple ingredients—available as meatballs, burgers, and ground meat—could help solve one of the biggest challenges of the climate crisis: getting people to eat less meat, particularly beef.

Joyn is among a wave of startups creating “blended meat,” which combines plant proteins with the real deal. The logic: The best meat replacement is … better meat.

Get a taste of the startups betting on greener beef .

—Meghan McCarron

This implant can restore sight for patients with macular degeneration

More than 5 million people have an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) called geographic atrophy, in which retinal cells die off. Until now, no treatment could restore their vision. A system called PRIMA changes that.

It combines a retinal implant with camera-equipped eyeglasses to improve sight in patients who develop a blind spot in the middle of their vision. After training sessions, more than 80% of recipients could read, do crosswords, and use their phones.

Find out how the sight-restoring implant works .

—Linda Marsa

MIT Technology Review Narrated: The agentic web is here

In 2001, a decade after inventing the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision: an internet navigated by autonomous software agents that address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves.

At the time, the idea seemed far-fetched. But a quarter-century on, AI agents are beginning to make it a reality. They can triage your inbox, do your grocery shopping, and even access your bank accounts.

This new era is being called the agentic web, and it will inevitably transform the internet.  Whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess .

title: Securing the agentic enterprise with data lineage
author: MIT Technology Review
description: A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes. The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep. No human checks either handoff. article_content:
A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes. The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep. No human checks either handoff. When it’s discovered that the proposal includes unapproved, confidential, and sensitive information, no one can trace where the problematic data entered the workflow or how it spread across systems, files, and agents.

DOWNLOAD THE REPORT

This scenario illustrates why AI governance needs to evolve, rapidly and dynamically. As more enterprises begin to use agentic AI in daily workflows, they’re realizing that they must manage more than static files; they must manage moving and fragmented data that is continuously ingested, copied, summarized, transformed, reused, and redistributed in new forms. In short, AI security isn’t a tool problem; it’s a data visibility problem.

Consequently, traditional security approaches built solely around applications, systems, networks, or endpoints are no longer sufficient. Securing agentic AI at scale requires understanding how data moves. Teams, therefore, need to establish data lineage in order to effectively manage  governance, accountability, and trust  across human, agentic, and hybrid workflows.

article_content:
This is today’s edition of    The Download  ,  our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check

A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules.

While game theory predicts how rational actors behave under particular rules, reverse game theory designs rules to elicit the behavior we want. Think of splitting a cake: if one person cuts it and the other gets first choice, the cutter has an incentive to make the portions equal.

Researchers believe the approach could align AI more closely with our rules and instructions. But big questions remain about whether these mechanisms will work in practice.

Here’s how reverse game theory could help make AI agents behave .

—Amit Katwala

Here’s who is falling in line for Trump’s “Super Intelligence” loyalty test

At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order with just one directive: government agencies must rebrand artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.”

One month on, the rebrand is slowly appearing across government websites and documents, but it hasn’t caught on with everyone. Even some of the biggest names in tech still use “AI.”

But the bigger concern is the new term becoming a political loyalty test: Those who use it signal allegiance to the administration. Those who don’t become targets for attacks.

So one month in, who’s on board?

—James O’Donnell

title: From synthetic enterprise data evaluations to real Microsoft Copilot AI confidence
author: Microsoft Research
description:
At a glance

Evaluating Microsoft Copilot at enterprise scale requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations, yet real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances.

To resolve this tension, we built Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform: full-scale synthetic enterprise environments grounded in publicly available real-world data sources such as O*NET occupational data, online job postings, and SEC fil...
article_content:
At a glance

Evaluating Microsoft Copilot at enterprise scale requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations, yet real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances.

To resolve this tension, we built Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform: full-scale synthetic enterprise environments grounded in publicly available real-world data sources such as O*NET occupational data, online job postings, and SEC filings.

The synthetic environments mimic real business workflows, helping Microsoft find issues that generic benchmarks would miss.

Safety and privacy are built into the platform by design. Every environment is fully synthetic and automated content-safety checks keep the generated data free of harmful or personally identifiable material.

Every day, millions of knowledge workers around the world rely on Microsoft Copilot to draft documents, summarize meetings, surface relevant information, and accelerate productivity. Behind the scenes, this is powered by a network of AI systems, and ensuring they work as intended requires a thoughtful approach to evaluation. At Microsoft, we know that high performance doesn’t come from guesswork. It comes from testing, measuring, and iterating constantly.

Healthcare organizations are constantly synthesizing safety signals from across teams so that they can make faster, better decisions that directly influence patient outcomes and regulatory confidence.

They may ask Copilot to summarize a meeting and extract action items for their teams. Within seconds, Copilot delivers a structured summary citing specific discussion points from the transcript. But how do we ensure this response is accurate, complete, and properly grounded in the meeting content? This is where our evaluation system comes in.

We’ve developed a structured evaluation strategy called  Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform , which includes industry specific evaluation datasets designed to test AI systems against realistic enterprise scenarios, grounded in three core pillars:

Synthetic enterprise environments : simulated Microsoft Copilot environments with realistic users, meetings, emails, documents, and organizational structures that replicate the complexity of real organizations without using any customer data

Automated query generation pipelines  for rapid, reproducible creation of evaluation datasets

Structured quality frameworks  to ensure synthetic data meets the bar for meaningful evaluation

Figure 1: Components of Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform

Together, these pillars help us answer two fundamental questions:  Is Microsoft Copilot actually doing what our users need it to do, and can we prove it without ever touching their data ?

In this blog post, we’ll walk through our evaluation system and processes, from synthetic environment generation to automated query pipelines, and how it all comes together to establish the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot.

Synthetic enterprise environments

Evaluating enterprise AI requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations: reporting structures, project histories, communication patterns, and domain specific workflows. But real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. This is the central tension we set out to resolve.

Rather than relying on small, manually curated test fixtures, we generate  full scale synthetic environments : simulated enterprise workspaces, each with realistic organizational structures, communication histories, and work artifacts. In Microsoft terminology, each of these simulated workspaces is called a “tenant”. A tenant is an isolated organizational environment with its own users, data, and configurations. These environments are scalable baselines that teams and organizations can build off of however they want. They are designed to exhibit the same structural and behavioral properties that make enterprise AI evaluation meaningful.

Grounding in real world signals

To ensure our synthetic environments are realistic, we grounded them in publicly available real world data sources.

O*NET data  from the U.S. Department of Labor’s occupational database was used to make synthetic employee roles and responsibilities realistic, calibrate the mix and frequency of work activities assigned to different roles, and tailor industry specific workflows such as clinical trial reviews or portfolio updates.

Online job postings  provide realistic role titles, reporting hierarchies, and departmental compositions.

SEC filings  inform organizational scale, business unit structures, and financial contexts. All of these sources are publicly available and have been reviewed and approved by Microsoft’s legal and policy organization.

Figure 2: Real signals from public datasets that are used to ground the evaluation data generation

Importantly, these synthetic environments are not static snapshots. They simulate dynamic, time-evolving organizations with meeting histories, project timelines, email threads that develop over weeks, and organizational changes that unfold naturally. This temporal dimension is essential because a large class of Copilot queries are inherently time aware. Questions like “What did the team decide last Thursday?” or “What’s changed since the last quarterly review?” only produce meaningful evaluations if the underlying data has a genuine temporal structure.

Industry specific simulation

We generated three synthetic environments across multiple industries, each with distinct characteristics that mirror real world usage:

A pharmaceutical environment that includes regulatory submission workflows, clinical trial discussions, and cross functional safety review meetings

A capital markets environment featuring deal pipelines, compliance communications, and client portfolio reviews

An IT/software company that simulates sprint planning, code review discussions, and product launch coordination

Figure 3: Industries targeted for industry evaluation data generation

This industry specificity ensures that our evaluation queries test Copilot against the kinds of questions real users in those domains actually ask, rather than relying on generic test cases that may not surface domain specific failure modes.

Automated query generation

While synthetic environments provide the substrate for evaluation, they face a key limitation: we still need realistic evaluation queries. These are the questions that test whether Copilot can surface the right information, synthesize it correctly, and present it helpfully. Manually writing thousands of grounded, industry specific queries is prohibitively expensive and slow. That’s where our automated pipeline comes in.

The six-stage pipeline

Figure 4: Query customization pipeline that turns generic query templates into realistic, industry-specific queries

We built an automated pipeline that turns simple, generic query ideas into realistic, industry-specific questions for Copilot. It starts with a large library of common workplace tasks, narrows them down to what’s relevant for a given industry, and adapts them using domain-specific language and context. The system then uses AI to generate queries grounded in the synthetic environment’s data, rewrites them to sound more natural and human, and validates each one for accuracy and uniqueness. The result is a rich set of high-quality, lifelike queries that enable scalable and reliable evaluation of Copilot across real-world scenarios.

Validating synthetic quality

Of course, generating synthetic data is only part of the challenge. We also need to ensure the data is good enough to produce meaningful evaluations. We assess synthetic environment quality using our internal semantic evaluation framework which measures quality across three dimensions:

Structural fidelity : Does the organizational structure reflect realistic reporting hierarchies, team sizes, and cross functional relationships?

Contextual relevance : Are the queries and workflows representative of actual enterprise usage patterns?

Behavioral realism : Do the simulated users exhibit human-like communication patterns and collaboration dynamics?

Content safety : Is the generated content free of harmful, offensive, or personally identifiable material, and does it avoid impersonating real individuals?

End-to-end automation

While our synthetic environments and query pipelines provide the methodology, they face several practical limitations without proper automation, including:

Reproducibility : Manual processes produce subtly different results each time, making it difficult to compare evaluations across releases.

Scale : The number of industry verticals and configuration variants exceeds what any team can reasonably produce by hand.

Iteration speed : Manual creation takes days, delaying essential feedback and slowing down development cycles.

Cross-team consistency : Without standardized tooling, different teams produce evaluation datasets with incompatible formats and quality levels.

This automation reduced evaluation dataset creation from a multi-day manual process to automated runs. We estimate savings of approximately $100,000 per evaluation dataset and $300,000 in total project savings. But the more important outcome is that any team can now regenerate an evaluation dataset from the same configuration and get identical results.

PODCAST SERIES

AI Testing and Evaluation: Learnings from Science and Industry

Discover how Microsoft is learning from other domains to advance evaluation and testing as a pillar of AI governance.

Listen now

Opens in a new tab

Privacy and safety by design

Enterprise grade evaluation demands more than good methodology. It requires a privacy posture that allows teams to move fast without compromising user trust. A non-negotiable design principle of our industry evaluation datasets is that  no real customer data is used at any stage of the pipeline . Every element, from organizational structures to email content to meeting transcripts, is synthetically generated, with no customer data inputs. Because the data is both fully synthetic and safety-screened, teams can share and reuse it widely without introducing reputational, compliance, or  Responsible AI  risk.

Our safeguards include privacy preserving aggregation techniques where real-world statistical distributions are referenced, expert legal review and approval of all public data sources, and clear data provenance and lineage tracking throughout the pipeline.

This means teams across Microsoft can use these evaluation datasets freely for experimentation, benchmarking, and regression testing without privacy review overhead or data handling restrictions that would otherwise slow down iteration. The privacy design is not a constraint on the system. It is what makes broad adoption possible.

Results and impact

Since starting this project, we have observed significant improvements across multiple dimensions.

On  synthetic data quality , our internal scoring system showed significant quality gains in the structural, contextual, and statistical fidelity of the generated data. Across our composite quality metric (which measures how closely synthetic data mirrors the complexity and patterns of real enterprise environments), scores improved 39% compared to our initial generation approach. Some industry-specific environments reached quality scores above 0.9 out of 1.0, demonstrating that domain focused generation produces highly realistic evaluation environments. The improvements were obtained in part by incorporating realistic, industry signals and in part by automating quality improvements via key composite quality metrics that help improve the structural integrity, contextual coherence and statistical diversity of our synthetic industry environments.

On  scale and efficiency , each synthetic environment now contains hundreds of users with complete communication histories across three industry verticals. Evaluation dataset creation has gone from multi-day manual effort to automated pipeline runs.

On  organizational adoption , our industry evaluation data generation platforms have been published to an internal shared catalog for cross-team reuse and established as the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot. The difference wasn’t just incremental. It was a shift in how teams approach evaluation: from ad hoc, manual processes to standardized, reproducible infrastructure.

Conclusion

As we continue to expand what Microsoft Copilot can do, from single turn Q&A to agentic multi-step workflows, our commitment to evaluation remains at the heart of our approach. In enterprise AI, quality isn’t just about accuracy or speed. It’s about trust. Organizations need confidence that AI systems handle their information correctly, and that confidence can only come from thorough, repeatable evaluation. That trust rests on two commitments woven through everything we build: rigorous privacy protection and proactive content safety.

Looking ahead, Microsoft Copilot is tackling even more exciting evaluation challenges: How do we assess the quality of multi-turn agentic interactions? How do we extend synthetic environments to capture organizational dynamics evolving over months or years? How do we build evaluation frameworks for AI systems that take actions, not just generate text? These are the kinds of questions our team is working on next.

At Microsoft, we’re not just building AI. We’re building the infrastructure to ensure it works reliably for every enterprise, in every industry, at every scale .

Thanks to everyone who’s worked on Industry Evaluation Datasets !

title: Microsoft Research Focus – Edition #97
author: Microsoft Research
article_content:
What’s new in research?  

You may already be familiar with the  Research Focus newsletter  (opens in new tab)   on LinkedIn. Now, you can catch up on highlights from across the research community at Microsoft on our social channels, YouTube, and major podcast platforms, too. 

In this edition of  Microsoft Research Focus , host Sowbhagya Suresh shares some of the latest news and cutting-edge research from across Microsoft—from understanding the challenges facing coding agents to uncovering how people use AI at work and improving extended-range weather forecasting. 

Catch up on the ideas, tools, and discoveries researchers are exploring today and get a quick look at what’s coming next.

Related links:

Research Focus newsletter on LinkedIn  (opens in new tab)

ForkPilot: Self-Evolving Policy for Retrospective Search in Long-Horizon Agents

Code Understanding is a Bottleneck for Coding Agents

TeleTune: Evolving Agent Skills from Offline Telemetry

Why Copilot use looks so similar across industries, and what that misses  (opens in new tab)

Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools

New AI framework bridges a critical gap in mid-range weather forecasts

BioEmu2 in public preview  (opens in new tab)

Chapters

03:22:  Looking beyond similarities in AI use   (opens in new tab)

04:15:  Helping teachers make more time for teaching   (opens in new tab)

04:52:  Improving extended-range weather forecasting   (opens in new tab)

Transcript

[MUSIC]

SOWBHAGYA SURESH:  Hi, I’m Sowbhagya Suresh. Welcome to  Microsoft Research Focus .

You’ve probably read our newsletter. And now you can get highlights from across the research community at Microsoft here, on YouTube, and major podcast platforms. Whether you read, watch, or listen to it,  Research Focus  is your source for research news at Microsoft.

Coming up in this edition: what everyday AI use reveals about the way we work; how a new AI model could help scientists better understand proteins; a new approach to improving weather forecasts weeks in advance; and more. So here’s what’s new.

A self-improving agentic framework

More and more, AI agents are handling tasks that are complex.

[MUSIC FADES]

Tasks that require multiple steps, decisions, and interactions with external tools. But how can we count on AI agents to do the work if their ability to adjust when things go wrong may require a lot of resources with no guarantees of a better result?

A new self-improving framework called ForkPilot learns when it’s worth revisiting earlier decisions to find a different approach and adapts its strategy based on new outcomes.

Tested across six benchmarks and leading AI models, ForkPilot measures up to the best existing methods while reducing AI processing demands by up to 59%. These results suggest that AI agents can solve complex problems more reliably and efficiently, making them more practical and cost-effective to deploy at scale.

[TRANSITION MUSIC]

Understanding coding agent success and failure

Coding agents execute user queries by reasoning about, editing, and running code. Understanding why these agents fail is critical if we want to build more capable and reliable coding agents. Unfortunately, existing benchmarks often make it difficult to identify which factors contribute to success or failure.

CABRA is a framework for generating coding challenges from scratch. It lets researchers increase complexity in a controlled way and pinpoints the skills that are most difficult for agents.

Across thousands of generated challenges, the researchers found that agents often overcame coding problems by using tools. Yet the agents still struggled when they needed to understand unfamiliar codebases. The findings suggest that understanding existing code, rather than modifying it, remains one of the biggest obstacles to developing more effective coding agents.

[TRANSITION MUSIC]

Evolving agent skills with activity logs

Computer-use agents are AI systems that are designed to complete tasks that require clicking and typing. They can fill in forms, process requests, and navigate websites. To do this effectively, they need to learn the procedures that people use to get work done. User activity logs can offer a way to capture this knowledge. But activity logs typically don’t record the intent behind each action and often combine tasks.

The new framework TeleTune learns reusable skills and workflows from these logs. It also infers the task goals associated with the sequences of actions.

In evaluations across software and browser tasks, TeleTune outperformed existing approaches. By learning from existing activity, TeleTune offers a scalable way to help AI agents adapt to unfamiliar software and carry out complex, multi-step workflows

[TRANSITION MUSIC]

Looking beyond similarities in AI use  (opens in new tab)

Workers across industries may appear to be using AI in surprisingly similar ways, but a closer look reveals a different story.

Microsoft researchers analyzed aggregated Copilot Chat activity across a broad range of customer categories and found that editing documents led all classified activities, accounting for more than 20 percent.

But when researchers set aside the 20 most common activities, differences between customer categories became substantially more pronounced. The most common uses of AI may be hiding important differences in how organizations use it for more specialized work.

For business leaders, the takeaway is clear: don’t assume you have the same AI needs as others in your industry. Finding the right opportunities means looking beyond usage statistics to understand what employees actually do, how they work, and what outcomes matter most.

[TRANSITION MUSIC]

Helping teachers make more time for teaching

A new study shows how Shiksha Copilot—a human-in-the-loop AI tool—could transform teacher workflows in Global South classrooms.

The study in low-resource schools in India found the tool reduced the time teachers spent on bilingual lesson planning and bureaucracy. That gave them more time to craft more engaging classroom activities.

More than a thousand teachers participated, and many reported reduced stress levels and a positive impression of how AI can help them. These teachers actively engaged with Shiksha Copilot, using their professional expertise to adapt and repurpose materials to suit their own classrooms.

[TRANSITION MUSIC]

Improving extended-range weather forecasting  

Ten-day weather forecasts have become remarkably dependable. But what about the weeks that follow?

The two-to-six-week window remains a major challenge for forecasting models, which is a problem. That’s when a wide range of critical decisions get made related to farming, managing wildfires, and preparing for extreme weather.

A new machine-learning framework called Probabilistic Bias Correction, or  PBC , is helping close that gap. PBC learns from a weather model’s past mistakes and helps correct them.

And the early results are promising.

PBC took top honors in a global competition focused on improving extended-range forecasting. It’s also being deployed in Kenya, where it’s helping improve critical monsoon forecasts for farmers.

This development could help make weather predictions more useful across a broad range of applications.

[TRANSITION MUSIC]

BioEmu2 now available in public preview  (opens in new tab)

BioEmu2, a new foundation model for understanding biomolecular structure, dynamics, and function, is now available in public preview.

Developed by the Microsoft Research AI for Science team, BioEmu2 builds on Biomolecular Emulator, a deep-learning model designed to help scientists better understand how proteins work.

That understanding could have important implications for medicine. By learning more about how proteins function, scientists could move closer to developing more effective medications that enhance beneficial protein activity or prevent proteins from causing harm.

Go to the  BioEmu2 Microsoft Research GitHub repository  (opens in new tab)   to explore the model and learn more.

[MUSIC]

And that’s your  Research Focus .

From more capable AI agents to better weather forecasting, these are just a few of the developments researchers are exploring at Microsoft.

Want to learn more and stay connected? Explore the latest research, discover the people behind it, and keep tabs on the ideas shaping what’s next by following Microsoft Research on major social platforms.

I’m Sowbhagya Suresh. Thanks so much for tuning in. We’ll see you in the next  Microsoft Research Focus.

[MUSIC FADES]

Show more

title: Flint-interactive: A language for creating interactive data visualizations
author: Microsoft Research
description:
At a glance

Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions.

Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators.

Improves reliability and reduces development effort...
article_content:
At a glance

Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions.

Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators.

Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations.

Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another.

AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports with data visualizations. They help users examine patterns more efficiently than by reading verbose text. However, when we’re feeling exploratory, we want to go beyond static visualizations. :  We want to interact with charts to zoom in on details, compare data across charts, or even highlight related text in the document from a chart selection, and vice versa. This requires agents to be able to create interactive data visualizations that communicate information while letting readers explore beyond the author’s chosen view, ideally with the quality of interactive stories in sophisticated data journalism. This leaves us wondering: 

(As a user) Can I interact with charts directly in chat to explore the data and ask follow-up questions based on what I select?

(As a developer) Can I enable the AI agents I build for my customers to generate interactive visualizations that help them explore and understand their data?

Yes, it’s possible, but there is a significant practical gap. Even with capable frontier models, we still face:

High generation cost. Agents rarely produce a fully satisfactory interactive visualization in one turn. Repeated rounds of reasoning, coding, and debugging consume tokens and time.

Reliability. Interactive visualizations are challenging enough that expressive interactive charts introduce poor layouts or broken interactions easily, and we risk introducing new problems when trying to fix them.

These challenges help explain why consistently generating high-quality interactive visualizations remain difficult in real-world use. Meanwhile, built-in interactions in some visualization libraries are not expressive enough on their own to create bespoke interactive charts. And these challenges are results of the lack of an expressive yet high-level language to specify visual interactions.

video series

On Second Thought

A video series with Sinead Bovell built around the questions everyone’s asking about AI. With expert voices from across Microsoft, we break down the tension and promise of this rapidly changing technology, exploring what’s evolving and what’s possible.

Explore the series

Opens in a new tab

Flint-interactive

Flint-interactive  (opens in new tab)   is a language for creating interactive data visualizations on top of Flint. It allows users to create dashboards, data stories, and interactive artifacts more easily. The power of Flint-interactive comes from Flint’s compiler, which translates user interactions into semantic events that capture the meaning behind what users select. It then uses high-level operators to update visualizations in response to those events, making sophisticated interactions far easier to create and maintain. This shifts the heavy burden of resolving complex dependencies between interaction and visual logic to the compiler, so the user (or the agent) can easily describe expressive interactions with high-level specifications.

Example 1: We can enable the user to brush one visual view, and the chart highlights all groups of country selected by the user with a simple preset interaction linked-brush.

How to use

1. Use Flint in your chat

Use Flint Interactive directly in your chat or canvas environment through Flint-MCP and MCP Apps, following the MCP setup guide. With the latest release, tell your agent what to chart and which interactions you want; it can generate an interaction_spec alongside the Flint chart spec and render the interactive chart in your conversation.

Example 2: Using Flint-interactive in the chat environment, allowing the agent to produce interactive charts more reliably with simple Flint specifications. It also enables the user to select and pass context to the follow-up turns.

2. Build an interactive app with Flint

Build interactive charts in a dashboard, data story, or other application with Flint Interactive Canvas. Your app can use event handlers to process semantic events emitted by Flint Canvas, for example to filter a table, update another chart, or change application state. To let your app’s widgets control how the chart updates, send update operators to Flint Canvas.

Example 2: Flint-interactive allows developers to define interactions between charts and external elements (e.g., table, paragraph). Here, the user can click the table to highlight points in the chart and verse versa.

3. Create bespoke interactions

To create bespoke interactions beyond Flint’s presets, define a trigger and a custom handle function with the programming API that maps semantic events to custom chart update sequences. For example, a handler can highlight a clicked country and label it by name. It combines set-style and set-annotation without manipulating renderer-specific marks.

Example 4: The agent can create bespoke interactive visualizations with Flint’s programming API. In this DimpVis example, the user can drag the point along the time path to visualize how all cities’ temperature and precipitation changes.

How it works

Flint Canvas is a state machine that tracks user interactions on the canvas and manages visual rendering state. Flint makes interaction specification easy by separating visual logic, managed by the compiler, from interaction logic, specified by the user at the semantic level:

Visual logic: The compiler automatically resolves raw triggers, such as clicks, drags, and key presses, into semantic events that identify chart elements and data. It also translates update operators into rendered canvas changes, handling hit testing, and low-level visual updates.

Interaction logic: The user specifies interactions by mapping semantic interaction events to chart update operators, such as set style to highlight data, set annotation to label a point, or set viewport to pan or zoom. The user can also use those semantic events to update external tables, widgets, or application states. 

Figure 1:  Flint interactive allows the agent to describe interaction logic by mapping “what semantic event is the user interacting with” to “what updates they want for the canvas surface”. The compiler takes the heavy lifting of resolving visual updates and manages the runtime, which makes interaction authoring more reliable  c and cost effective.

This separation means users do not need to reverse-engineer rendering logic or manipulate renderer-specific marks, making interactions easier to specify and maintain. Furthermore, because event generation and visual updates are compositional, the same model also connects Flint with tables, text, other charts, and widgets to build interactive stories and dashboards.

Try it now!

Chart users:  Set up Flint in your chat  (opens in new tab)   and ask your agent to create an interactive chart. Find inspiration in the interaction gallery.

App builders: Build interactive dashboards, data stories, and connected views with the  programming API  (opens in new tab)  . Share the interaction-author skill with your coding agent to add presets to your app.

Interaction designers: Explore the  bespoke examples  (opens in new tab)  , design a new interaction, and turn it into a reusable preset. Propose a preset on GitHub and share your prototype or implementation to help expand Flint’s interaction vocabulary.

title: Solving a 31-year-old grand challenge in mathematics – the KLS conjecture
author: Microsoft Research
description:
Microsoft researcher and collaborator combine new mathematical ideas with human-directed AI to resolve a central problem in high-dimensional geometry and probability

At a glance

Fundamental scientific breakthrough:  Researchers resolved the Kannan-Lovász-Simonovits (KLS) conjecture, a 31-year-old problem widely regarded as one of the central open questions in high-dimensional geometry, with implications for statistics, optimization, algorithms, and computer science.

A universal geometric prin...
article_content:
Microsoft researcher and collaborator combine new mathematical ideas with human-directed AI to resolve a central problem in high-dimensional geometry and probability

At a glance

Fundamental scientific breakthrough:  Researchers resolved the Kannan-Lovász-Simonovits (KLS) conjecture, a 31-year-old problem widely regarded as one of the central open questions in high-dimensional geometry, with implications for statistics, optimization, algorithms, and computer science.

A universal geometric principle:  The result establishes a universal geometric principle for log-concave distributions, showing that simple flat cuts can capture their narrowest bottlenecks within a fixed factor, regardless of dimension. 

Human-AI collaboration:  The breakthrough emerged from a human-directed agentic research process in which AI systems explored mathematical possibilities while researchers evaluated, pruned, and redirected the search.

Independent confirmation:  Multiple independent researchers have validated this research, identifying its central criterion as the key breakthrough, followed by a machine-checked formal verification. 

For decades, a fundamental question about the difficulty of computing in high-dimensional spaces has resisted proof. New research resolves this question, removing a major theoretical obstacle to understanding the efficiency of randomized algorithms used across science and computing.

The Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits (KLS) conjecture was proposed in 1995. It asks whether, for a broad class of high-dimensional probability distributions, the best flat or hyperplane cut is always nearly as effective as the best cut of any shape. More precisely, KLS predicts that the two differ by no more than a universal constant, regardless of the number of dimensions. This would establish a dimension-free geometric principle with important consequences for high-dimensional geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. Because the geometry of these cuts governs how quickly random walks can explore a distribution, KLS also plays a central role in the theory of high-dimensional sampling.

Figure 1: An illustration of the KLS Conjecture (simplified) on regular tetrahedron.

Since 1995, mathematicians have accumulated evidence that the conjecture was true, but a complete proof remained elusive. Now, two researchers, including Xinzhi Zhang from the Machine Learning and Optimization group at Microsoft Research, have  proved the KLS conjecture  (opens in new tab)  . They have shown that the relationship holds with a fixed bound, regardless of how many dimensions a shape has. Before this work, the  best known result  (opens in new tab)  , established in July 2026, allowed that bound to grow slowly as the number of dimensions increased. This work establishes a fundamental geometric principle: high-dimensional spaces are better behaved than previously known, and the obstacles to navigating them do not grow without bound as dimensions increase. 

The importance of the KLS conjecture was recognized across the field long before it was resolved. In its 2017-18 Annual Report, the  Mathematical Sciences Research Institute (MSRI)  (opens in new tab)   called it “a central open problem in high-dimensional convex geometry.” The  Simons Institute  (opens in new tab)   described it as “one of the most important open problems in convex geometry.” In the proceedings of the  2022 International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM)  (opens in new tab)  , Ronen Eldan noted its broad implications for high-dimensional convex and computational geometry.  Quanta Magazine  (opens in new tab)   wrote that KLS “lies at the heart of many questions in statistics and computer science.”

Technical details

The authors began by improving the July 2026 result in order to make the mathematical bound more precise. Working with AI agents in a structured, human-directed process, they explored more than 100 candidate approaches, many involving lengthy calculations with higher-order tensors. This produced a new mathematical criterion that became the foundation of the final proof.

The authors then discovered that the new criterion could be applied recursively. Each improved bound could be fed back into the same argument to produce a still tighter one. In the October 1, 2026 version of the paper, this reduced the dependence on dimension to the iterated logarithm. This function grows extraordinarily slowly, but it still grows with the dimension and therefore did not yet fully resolve the conjecture.

The final step was to repeat the entire recursive refinement, rather than applying it only once. This idea was inspired by the authors’ earlier work on fast algorithms for linear programming. The authors proved that the small errors introduced at each stage shrink fast enough that their total remains bounded by a universal constant, independent of the dimension. This eliminated the dependence on the number of dimensions and completed the proof in the October 4, 2026 version of the paper.

The recursive method, its repeated application, and the proof that the accumulated errors remain bounded are original contributions of the researchers. AI tools helped explore candidate approaches, carry out detailed derivations, prepare the manuscript, and perform internal proof checks. The researchers determined the mathematical direction, selected the promising ideas, assembled them into the final argument, and verified the proof.

Independent confirmation

On the same day that the authors posted their complete proof, a separate group of leading experts  posted a full proof  (opens in new tab)   that they developed in parallel. Their work built upon the findings in the  first version  (opens in new tab)   of the Microsoft paper, calling it “the crucial step in the proof.” A  third proof  (opens in new tab)   which appeared separately on the same day relies on a closely related idea. In addition, a  Lean 4 formalization  (opens in new tab)   was subsequently released, combining the key criterion from the first Microsoft paper with additional research. 

Independent proofs are among mathematics’ strongest forms of validation because they demonstrate that a result does not rest on a single chain of reasoning. The subsequent appearance of alternative approaches and formal verification further strengthens confidence that the field has uncovered a genuine underlying principle rather than a fragile technical argument. The authors have also shortened their proof and verified the streamlined argument in Lean; they plan to release both after final review. Together, these developments provide complementary forms of confirmation.

Human-AI guidance

In the process of proving KLS, this research also demonstrates the power of having researchers direct AI rather than simply asking AI to solve a complex problem through a single end-to-end run of a frontier model or agent. The authors used an agentic search process with iterative, human-assisted “pruning”: As multiple agents explored variations of an idea in parallel, the researcher examined their intermediate result, eliminated unpromising directions, and passed the most promising result to the next round. Roughly one hundred research trajectories were explored before the key breakthrough emerged. 

In a separate track of the project, the authors made repeated unguided attempts to solve the same problem with several leading AI models, using roughly the same total token budget as the main process. That effort fell short of the goal. The eventual success depended on both the capabilities of the AI systems and the mathematical judgment of the researchers. 

Conclusion

Taken together, resolving KLS settles a central problem in high-dimensional geometry. A wide range of results that previously relied on the conjecture as an assumption can now be stated unconditionally. The proof therefore provides a stronger foundation for research in convex geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science.

The work also demonstrates how carefully guided human-AI collaboration can contribute to genuine scientific discovery while reinforcing, rather than replacing human insight. It highlights the continuing importance of scientific judgment in identifying promising directions, recognizing conceptual connections, and seeing when a partial insight points toward a deeper result. The authors are now simplifying the proof and extending its formal verification so that the mathematics and theoretical computer science communities can more easily examine the result and build on it.

Acknowledgements 

Thank you to our co-author Zhao Song for his contributions to this work, and  Victor Reis  (opens in new tab)   and  Ishai Menache  for helpful discussions throughout the project.

title: Proof-based general-purpose computing with Magnetar
author: Microsoft Research
description:
At a glance

A new form of computing . Zero-knowledge proofs let you run a workload and receive, alongside the result, a short proof that the program ran correctly.
